Preface 

THIS volume is the outgrowth of the authors' experience in teaching the survey course in the History of Western Civilization. We have become convinced that the presentation of cultural history must be accompanied by a strong factual treatment of political and constitutional history, for in most cases it cannot be assumed that the student is familiar with even the commonplaces of general history. 

The basic problem in a work of this kind is, of course, the selection of the material to be presented and the determination of relative emphasis. In essaying this task we should indeed be optimistic to think that the proportion of our work will meet with unqualified or universal approval. We hope, nevertheless, that the significant movements, institutions, and cultural contributions in the history of our Western civilization have been adequately and accurately discussed and that our work will provide a usable and sufficiently comprehensive manual for students in the survey course. 

In this revised edition, in addition to making some changes and corrections, we have attempted primarily to bring the history up to date by including two new chapters on World War II and its aftermath. While the treatment of these periods is more detailed than of earlier ones, we feel it is justified because of the need of the young college student to understand the complexities of the postwar world on the foundation of his own civilization's past. 

The bibliographies obviously are not intended to be exhaustive, since the purpose has been merely to present lists of books suitable for student reading. But in this revised edition new books have been added to these lists, especially for the recent periods. Three new maps have been included to illustrate World War II. 

We are particularly indebted to Professor Allan Nevins, editor of the Heath New History Series, for his encouragement and the many valuable suggestions he contributed for the improvement of the book.

C. E. S.

INTRODUCTION 

IVILIZATION may be defined as a complex way of life, a stage in man's cultural evolution. It has been customary to distinguish the stages of savagery, barbarism, and civilization in the process of cultural development. The question therefore arises: 

What are the factors that serve to differentiate civilized existence from barbarism? In the first place, civilization presupposes partial conquest of physical environment, through the invention and utilization of tools and the development of basic processes of craftsmanship and industry such as weaving, smelting, forging, and moulding, as well as the techniques of agriculture. The operations of natural laws are discovered by scientific investigation, and frequently science and invention succeed in applying or modifying them to man's advantage. 

The economic order must be sufficiently advanced on the productive side to make possible division of labor and specialization. Facilities for the distribution of the products of agriculture and industry must be available, and there must be a tenable basis for the exchange of the labor of the individual for basic wants produced by other individuals or groups.

Civilized existence is possible only after social institutions such as the family, the kindred, and the tribe have in turn been integrated into political organisms such as city-states, kingdoms, or democracies, wherein governmental devices ensure harmonious relations among individuals. Custom, tradition, and expediency are developed into law, which, however, must retain sufficient flexibility to reflect changing economic and social conditions and conform to existing political. patterns. Civilization also anticipates the maintenance of peaceful and rational relations among political entities as well as among individuals; it is in this respect that mankind has proved most backward, as is evidenced by the frequency of armed conflicts. 

One cannot visualize civilized existence without the anterior development of speech, language, and writing, which make possible

xvi 

INTRODUCTION 

the transfer of thought and, through the medium of literature, the bequest to posterity of the accumulated knowledge of past and present. Educational facilities must be available to implement the transfer of community knowledge to the young and to stimulate and enlarge the contributions which they will make to the cultural heritage upon their attainment of maturity.

In the civilized stage of cultural growth, there are abundant opportunities for the expression of man's creative impulses and the satisfaction of the need for emotional outlet. Literary works, written to give expression to exalted thoughts and ideals, frequently in forms intrinsically beautiful, afford opportunity for creative activity to their authors and, in a more passive way, give wisdom, inspiration, and pleasure to their readers. Works of art, such as statues and paintings, likewise cater to civilized man's craving for satisfactions that transcend mere utility. Architecture, on the other hand, admirably blends the aesthetic and the utilitarian; public buildings, places of worship, and other structures also express the artistry of their designers and the craftsmanship of the builders, and offer opportunity for the contemplation of beauty to those not actively associated with their construction. Music, the most subtle of the arts, joins the art of the composer with that of the performer and exercises the widest range of emotional appeal to the listener. 

No matter how far man progresses in his investigation of the material world, no matter how complete his understanding of the natural laws that govern his physical environment, he inevitably will try to apply this particular knowledge to his search for ultimate truth. 

What is the meaning and purpose of life? What are the all-embracing truths that give unity and coherence to the fragmentary knowledge derived through the particular sciences? It is the province of philosophy to offer suggested solutions to such problems, and every civilized people will have its philosophers who endeavor thus to integrate existing knowledge. The great majority of men, however, do not consider such fundamental problems through the rational processes of philosophy but utilize the emotional, subjective approach of religion. 

Belief in the supernatural, and the attendant development of dogma and ritual, have been vital components of the civilized pattern whether in Ancient Egypt or in our modern world. 

There is obviously no uniformity in the degree and rapidity of cultural evolution. Some peoples have never attained the level of civilization; some regions, such as the Tigris-Euphrates valley, which were great centers of civilization in ancient times, are far behind the

INTRODUCTION 

xvii cultural development of other regions in the modern world. Rate of progress likewise is not uniform in the various cultural phases that mark the attainment of civilization. All would probably agree that in our day technological advance, mastery of the forces of our physical environment, has far outstripped the evolution of social and governmental institutions, which should be adequately responsive to the changes wrought by science and invention. Civilization therefore must not be considered as a static and final stage in human progress. Civilized existence when once attained does not become an inalienable possession. The cultural heritage of the past must be understood and constantly augmented by the contributions of the present. When civilization ceases to be dynamic, it soon ceases to be civilization. 

History may be defined as the partial reconstruction of the past on the basis of such written records of the past as have survived. 

The written materials, however – particularly for the study of the more remote past are scanty; hence the historian must rely to a considerable degree on other sciences that are concerned with man's past existence. Of these sciences, archaeology is by far the most important, since excavations of the sites of ancient cities, burial places, or temples, for example, frequently unearth material remains such as tools, weapons, pottery, jewelry, and other articles of utility and adornment which serve to vivify the tenuous knowledge of the remote past ascertainable from written records. Epigraphy, or the study of inscriptions, and paleography, which takes as its special province the study of scripts, must also be drawn upon by the historian, since written records frequently are difficult to decipher and translate. The particular science of chronology is likewise an indispensable tool in view of the complexities of ancient reckoning of time.

It should be noted, however, that history, strictly speaking, is concerned only with that portion of man's past which is subsequent to his invention of writing. Compared with the prehistoric period, or that portion of man's past which is prior to the beginning of written records, this period is of almost negligible length. Indeed, the total length of man's sojourn on this planet is but a fleeting moment relative to the age of the earth and to the age of this one of many universes of which our planet is a component part. 

It has been estimated by biologists and anthropologists that man has lived on earth at least 500,000 years. For thousands of years, primitive man was engaged in a pitiless struggle with a hostile en-

xviii 

INTRODUCTION 

vironment. He survived because he possessed certain natural advantages that differentiated him from lower members of the animal kingdom. He had a greater brain capacity; moreover, his brain was capable not only of memory but also of the infinitely more important power to reason. His skeletal structure facilitated the permanent adoption of erect carriage, while the structure of his mouth made possible the evolution of articulate speech. The marvellously efficient human hand was another tremendous asset. 

After millennia, primitive man learned to seek the shelter of caverns and overhanging ledges. The discovery that fire could be kindled and maintained was a step of the utmost importance in his gradual emancipation from helpless subjection to his environment. Early in his existence, primitive man doubtless broke off branches and used their jagged ends to ward off the attacks of hostile beasts. Sometimes, too, he found stones that were naturally shaped for use as crude tools and weapons. Gradually, however, man learned that he could make for himself tools superior to these eoliths that had been formed by nature. By pounding on pieces of flint with a stone grasped in the hand he could shape the flint into useful tools, and with this discovery man entered upon the stage of his existence that is known as the Paleolithic or Old Stone Age. The first successful tool to be made by man was the fist-hatchet, a wedge-shaped tool about ten inches long, which was grasped in the hand and used for cutting, thrusting, or striking. Man continued to gain his livelihood from hunting and fishing, supplementing his meager diet with wild roots, berries, and grasses.

In the Middle Stone Age, tools were more finely fashioned. The implements were no longer shaped by pounding but by pressing and scraping along the edges of the piece of flint with stones or bones. 

In view of the brittleness of flint, it was possible to shape the tools and impart a fairly satisfactory cutting edge by this flaking process. 

Moreover, a greater variety of tools could be produced. Punches, awls, daggers, and hatchets were made from flint, while needles of bone were employed to stitch together the skins of animals to produce rude clothing. The invention of the bow and arrow, as well as the throwing stick which enabled him to hurl javelins greater distances with increased velocity, went far to afford primitive man protection from his animal adversaries. The famous Cave Art of prehistoric times likewise was begun during the Middle Stone Age as man decorated the walls and ceilings of caverns with pictures, especially pictures of animals. This Cave Art was more than an expression

INTRODUCTION 

xix of man's creative and artistic impulses, for it was doubtless intimately associated with his primitive religious beliefs. Hunting was a major source of food while the attacks of wild beasts constituted an everpresent danger. It is not surprising, therefore, that the earliest religious beliefs centered in animal worship. Man believed that the exorcism of pictorial representations of animals would aid him in acquiring control over them; he could better ward off their attacks, and they would more easily fall prey to his hunting prowess. The outline of the figure to be painted was first scratched or punched on the cave surface to be decorated, after which the paint, made by the mixture of mineral salts or vegetable pigments with fat or marrow, was applied. The most famous example of the Cave Art is the roof of the cavern at Altamira in Spain. 

In the Neolithic Age, implements were made of polished flint, and sharp edges were given to the tools by grinding with whetstones. 

Such tools were far superior to those of the preceding stone age; indeed, a modern craftsman, equipped only with a Neolithic hatchet, was able experimentally to construct a satisfactory house in eightyone days.

Man's greatest advance in the Neolithic Age, however, was the beginning of agriculture. Seeds of wild grasses were sown, perhaps inadvertently, and when the relation between sowing and plant growth was discovered, it was not long until primitive hoe culture was begun. Before the close of the Neolithic Age, however, the plough was invented and utilized with the resultant greater success of agricultural operations. About the same time or, according to most recent scholarly opinion, shortly after the beginning of agriculture, animals were domesticated. The dog probably was the first to be tamed, but sheep, oxen, cows, and swine were likewise pressed into the service of man prior to the opening of the historic period. 

It would be difficult to exaggerate the effects of agriculture and the domestication of animals on man's cultural evolution. Small areas now could support relatively denser populations; the evolution of community life in turn provided a tremendous impetus to the development of social and governmental institutions. Custom, tradition, and religion regulated the relations of the villagers to each other, and the emergence of the concept of private property in land and chattels hastened the hardening of custom and tradition into law. 

Relations of prehistoric communities to each other were not always peaceful, for the discovery of skeletons with embedded arrowheads or other signs of death by weapons proves the frequency of warfare.

XX 

INTRODUCTION 

Many remains of Neolithic villages have been found in Switzerland, north Italy, and Denmark. These villages were built on piles driven into the beds of lakes or ponds. A rude boat or flimsy bridge gave access to the villages of these Lake Dwellers which for defense against man and beast could be isolated from the shore. Refuse was thrown out of the openings of the crude huts built of branches and twigs. In the course of generations, shell heaps or kitchen middens accumulated, and examination of these by archaeologists has resulted in the discovery of utensils and weapons in great profusion. 

Many fragments of pottery have been found in the kitchen middens as well as in Neolithic burial grounds. The process of ceramic manufacture probably began when baskets were coated and lined with wet clay which was then dried so as to make a water-tight receptacle. Gradually the primitive craftsman learned that vessels could be moulded out of clay without a basket framework and the utensils could be baked in a fire to almost stonelike hardness. The process of baking in closed ovens and the use of the potter's wheel were unknown, with the result that Neolithic pottery is rather coarse in texture and imperfectly shaped. Decorative designs, however, were impressed into the utensils prior to firing or were painted thereon after baking.

Religion continued to develop. Man identified the natural forces that exercised such a great control over his fate with spirits which he classified as good or evil. It was particularly necessary to propitiate the evil spirits by proper sacrifice and incantation to avert calamity. 

A belief in immortality evolved even as early as the Middle Stone Age, for tools and implements have been found in the graves buried for the use of the dead in the after-world. Enormous blocks of stone, known as megaliths, were apparently erected by Neolithic man as religious or burial monuments. Sometimes these stones were set up so as to form a great circle; the most famous example of this is the enclosure at Stonehenge in England.

Toward the close of the Neolithic era, man invented crude techniques for the smelting and casting of metals. Copper was first employed, but ultimately it was learned that the admixture of zinc to form bronze made it possible to fashion harder and consequently more satisfactory implements. Bronze, in turn, came to be largely superseded by iron. It must not be supposed, however, that the introduction of metal came about everywhere at the same time or that the Neolithic Age was sharply differentiated from the Copper Age. Neolithic implements continued to be made and used for cen-

INTRODUCTION 

xxi turies after the introduction of metals; indeed, tools of polished flint have often been found in the same strata with those of iron. The widening use of metals, however, roughly synchronized with the invention of writing; and, as was previously pointed out, this invention signalizes the inauguration of the historic period.

CHAPTER Ancient Mesopotamia 

ESTERN culture had its roots in the fluvial civilizations that developed in the valleys of the Tigris-Euphrates and the Nile. Recent discoveries in Iraq seem to prove that the civilization of the Tigris-Euphrates valley arose somewhat earlier than that of Egypt. Twenty-six cultural levels have been uncovered at Tepe Gawra, and the most recent of these has been dated to 

3500 B.C.

Both the Euphrates and the Tigris rise in the Armenian mountains. The former, after flowing in a southwesterly direction for about 

1100 miles, is turned into its prevailing southeasterly course by the Arabian plateau. The Tigris, much shorter than the Euphrates, although it carries a greater volume of water, flows southeast for virtually its entire course. The rivers parallel each other in their lower courses and are but 30 miles apart at modern Bagdad. They carry much silt which they deposit into the Persian Gulf. These precipitations of silt have built up a great delta which is constantly extending farther into the Gulf, so that towns which were on the Gulf in ancient times are now more than 160 miles inland. 

The "Valley of the Two Rivers " forms the eastern horn of what Professor Breasted has termed the "Fertile Crescent." This is a narrow strip of arable land, in the shape of a crescent open to the south, with its western limit in Palestine and its eastern terminus at the head of the Persian Gulf. It is bounded on the west by the Mediterranean, on the north and east by mountains, and on the south by the Arabian desert. For centuries nomads from the fringes of the desert and mountain tribes, attracted by the fertile land of the Crescent, migrated into the region, only to have their tenure subsequently challenged. The ancient history of the Near East is largely the account of perennial struggles for possession of the Fertile Crescent. 

Prolonged summer drouths alternate with winter seasons of torrential rains. The rivers reach the flood stage early in the spring,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

overflow their banks, and inundate much of the valley. With reversion of the rivers to their normal levels, a deposit of rich alluvial soil is left on the area covered by the flood. The annual deposits of alluvium replenish the fertility of the soil, but extensive irrigation is necessary during the dry season.

The fertility of Mesopotamia, as the valley was called in ancient times, was its basic economic asset. Herodotus, the Greek historian, declared that grain crops of two to three hundredfold, with the blades of grain as wide as four fingers, were usual. The Roman geographer Strabo reproduces a statement that the date palm, which was prolific in the region, was used for more than three hundred different purposes. With two great waterways linking Akkad, the northern part of the valley, with Sumer, the delta region, development of commerce was inevitable. Commercial contact was further promoted when the highly developed craftsmanship of Sumer became dependent upon supplies of ores and other raw materials from the north.

It is possible that the earliest inhabitants of the lower valley were of the same racial stock as the so-called Painted Pottery Folk who, prior to the opening of the historic period, dwelt along the northeast shore of the Persian Gulf in the region subsequently known as Elam. 

Another racial group, which spoke a Semitic language, probably migrated into the delta from the grasslands bordering the Arabian desert. They were a dolichocephalic (long-headed) race, with dark complexions, small features, and prominent, somewhat hooked noses. 

Earliest pictorial representations depict them garbed in loin cloths wrapped about their bodies in horizontal bands, with the end thrown over a shoulder.

By far the most important racial element to come into the valley, however, were the Sumerians. There is a wide divergence of scholarly opinion as to their original habitat. Certain resemblances in seals and terra cotta work indicate that they originally may have dwelt in the Indus valley. Another plausible hypothesis holds that they came from the foothills of the Zagros mountains, although the fact that the earliest representations of their deities depict them in a sylvan and mountainous environment is also reconcilable with the Indus theory. Their clean-shaven faces were in sharp contrast to the heavy beards of the Semites, and they dressed in flounced skirts instead of loin cloths. With their arrival in Sumer, the Semites were driven farther up the valley, where they settled in Akkad. For centuries 

Sumer and Akkad stood in sharp contrast; gradually, however, the

ANCIENT MESOPOTAMIA 

3. superior culture developed by the Sumerians was assimilated by their neighbors to the north. A general leveling process was constantly under way, promoted, as we shall see, by the conquests of Sargon the Great (c. 2600 B.C.) and consummated by the work of King 

Hammurapi of Babylon (c. 1900 B.C.) 

A number of prehistoric Sumerian villages have been unearthed by recent archaeological expeditions. The villages usually were constructed on mounds, surrounded by marshy terrain. Dwellings of mats had their thatched roofs supported by arched beams and were equipped with hearths. Barley was the staple crop, and all domestic animals save the horse were kept, and probably also the camel. Finely fashioned Neolithic implements were found, together with a few of copper and bronze, indicating that the villages were built toward the end of the Neolithic Age. The temple was the center of the village, and there was an inseparable connection between religion and the ruling authority. The dead were buried in a crouched position, frequently in large pottery coffins. The presence of tools, weapons, domestic utensils, and other objects in the graves proves that primitive ideas of immortality had been evolved. Since life after death was considered a prolongation of earthly existence, it was deemed necessary to provide the dead with articles which they used while alive. 

Before the middle of the nineteenth century, knowledge of the history of Mesopotamia was based almost exclusively on the Bible, the history of Herodotus, and the account of Berossus, a Chaldean priest of the third century before Christ. Today, king lists, omen texts, inscriptions, and the products of artist and craftsman unearthed by the spade of the archaeologist have enabled historians to reconstruct the ancient past of the region with reasonable assurance, although serious chronological difficulties are still encountered. The king lists must be used with caution, since they often ascribe impossibly long reigns to rulers and often fail to distinguish between successive and concurrent reigns, but recent discoveries on the site of ancient Ur have somewhat increased confidence in the essential accuracy of the lists. Omen texts, which are records of rites of divination practiced by the priests, often contain accounts of the circumstances leading up to and following the prophecies; they are therefore valuable historical sources. 

At the beginning of the historic period, there were a number of city-kingdoms in the Valley of the Two Rivers. Each was autonomous, with its own gods and priesthoods. From time to time, however, one or another of these city-states succeeded in imposing its

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

suzerainty upon neighboring states. Such conquests, frequently connived at by the mercantile class in the subjugated cities, normally entailed little interference with local government. Recognition of suzerainty and payment of tribute to the state exercising hegemony were the only results of the establishment of the ephemeral empires. 

The first state to exercise hegemony over several of its neighbors was Kish, the ruling dynasty of which was established at some indeterminable date subsequent to 4000 B.C. Fragments of a sandstone vase are preserved in the British Museum which record the fact that King 

Utug deposited the vase at the shrine of Enlil at Nippur. Not only is the antiquity of the dynasty of Kish established by these relics; they also afford proof that the city of Nippur already enjoyed the religious preeminence it was to retain for centuries. Mesilim, another ruler of Kish, is credited in a later inscription with the adjudication of a boundary dispute between the cities of Umma and Lagash, and this is fairly conclusive evidence of the hegemony of 

Kish in Sumer.

A great flood probably was responsible for the end of the dynasty. 

This disaster, which looms large in Babylonian literature, probably was the origin of the story of the Flood as recounted in the Old Testament. The Hebrews magnified it into a world-wide catastrophe and invested it with religious significance. Following the flood, a ruling dynasty was established at Erech, but thus far little is known of this city beyond the fact of its existence. 

About 3500 or 3400 B.C. - it is as yet impossible to give any certain date - the great First Dynasty of Ur flourished. The site of this city, once the important terminus of the Euphrates trade, has recently been excavated by British and American archaeologists. The tombs of Kings Mes-anni-padda and A-anni-padda, constructed of stone at the bottom of deep shafts, were uncovered. Roofs of the structures were supported by arches; indeed, there is reason to believe that the dome also was employed by the architects. Human sacrifice was practiced; in one of the royal tombs were found the remains of sixtyfive courtiers who had accompanied their ruler in death. Exquisitely fashioned objects, such as the gold helmet of Prince Meskalam-dug, a cow's head of cast silver, the headdress of Queen

Shub-ad, and a beautiful harp, ornamented with gold, ivory, and lapis lazuli, show that the Sumerian craftsmen were unequaled in their skillful alloying, casting, and fashioning of metals. Some centuries of development must have been requisite for such a brilliant culmination, and we have here additional evidence of the great antiquity of

ANCIENT MESOPOTAMIA 

5 Sumerian culture. Moreover, since no progress in taste or technique is discernible from the art of the First Dynasty to that of the Third, approximately one thousand years later, it is evident that Sumerian culture had virtually reached its zenith as early as 3500 B.C. 

As centuries of luxury, ease, priestly dominance, and racial mixture weakened the energies of the dynasty of Ur, Lagash emerged by about 3000 B.C. as the most powerful state of Sumer. The ruins of Lagash have been found near modern Tello by De Sarzec. Ur 

Nina, who had a peaceful reign as a lawgiver and pious builder of votary temples, founded the dynasty. With the close of his reign a bitter struggle began with the neighboring city of Umma. The conflict was aggravated by the desperate need for water, which was attainable only by control of vital irrigation canals. Umma for a time was victorious, but the conquests of King Eannatum, commemorated by his famous "Stele of the Vultures," established the supremacy of 

Lagash. The stele depicts the king at the head of a phalanx, smiting his enemies, while vultures hover overhead ready to devour the slain. 

The reign of Urakagina (c. 2850-2825 B.C.), who dedicated himself to the achievement of economic and social reforms, might be said to mark a significant advance in morality. Hitherto the poor had been the helpless victims of priestly exploitation and the rapacity of the nobles. Excessive fees formerly exacted by the priests for the performance of religious functions now were forbidden, and owners of small plots of land were extended legal protection against confiscation and forced sales at ruinous prices. These reforms were one of the foundations for the development of Babylonian law that materialized in the famous code of King Hammurapi. 

Urakagina's reforms naturally provoked lively opposition from the vested interests adversely affected by the legislation. Disaffection doubtless paved the way for the conquest of Lagash by Lugal-zaggisi of Umma, who shortly before 2600 B.C. succeeded in making himself master of an empire which, as his inscriptions boast, extended from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.

While the dynasties of Sumer were flourishing, Akkad played a minor rôle. The Semites gradually absorbed the superior culture of the south, and with the rise of Sargon of Agade (c. 2600 B.C.) Akkad vaulted to predominance. According to tradition Sargon, an abandoned son of a temple concubine, was rescued and reared by a gardener in the employ of the king of Kish. Upon reaching manhood he too entered the service of the king and ultimately rose to a position of responsibility. He then led a palace revolution, overthrew

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

his royal benefactor, and established himself as an independent ruler at Agade. The empire superficially organized by Lugal-zaggisi was conquered with ease. The cities of Sumer, with their trade strangulated, hastened to acknowledge the suzerainty of the Semitic conqueror. An expedition to the west then resulted in the conquest of 

Syria as far north as Lebanon. Sargon's Syrian campaign was doubtless an instance of economic imperialism. Trade routes were opened to the Levant; ores and fine woods were brought back, together with plants for experimental cultivation in Akkad. 

Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, energetically defended the empire and probably extended its eastern frontier by the wars commemorated by his famous "Stele of Victory." Weaker successors, however, proved unable to withstand the onslaughts of Gutium to the east, which by 2500 B.C. had reduced Sumer and Akkad to vassalage. 

In the meantime Ur was slowly recovering the power and prestige enjoyed by the rulers of the First Dynasty, and under Dungi (c. 2300 

B.C.) dominion over all Sumer was established. It was during this period that the great ziggurat, or step temple, was constructed. Ur ultimately fell before the attacks of the Amorites; dynasties at Isin and 

Larsa then had brief periods of glory, only to be overshadowed by 

Babylon. 

Babylon was a sizable city as early as 4000 B.C. Inscriptions speak of it as an important center in the age of Sargon. Its population was basically Amorite; with the accession of Hammurapi to the throne (c. 1900 B.C.), its position as the ruling city of the Tigris-Euphrates valley was soon secured. The fusion of Sumer and Akkad begun by Sargon was complete. Under mediocre successors, however, the power of Babylon rapidly waned. By 1800 B.C. the Kassites, who had entered from the west, were in possession of virtually the entire valley.

THE CULTURE OF ANCIENT MESOPOTAMIA 

The city-kingdoms, the characteristic political units of ancient Mesopotamia, were ruled by priest-kings, known as patesis. There were no elements of representative institutions or popular participation in governmental affairs. Since the rulers were bound to consult the omens preparatory to exercising their judicial, religious, or military powers, the priests specifically charged with conduct of the rites of divination were in a position to wield considerable influence in the determination of royal policies.

A major contribution of Babylonia to the civilization of the an-

ANCIENT MESOPOTAMIA 

7 cient Near East was the great code of law prepared in the reign of Hammurapi. This code doubtless incorporated earlier legislation, such as the laws of Urakagina and the code of Dungi of the Third Dynasty of Ur. A text of Hammurapi's code was found at Susa, engraved on a black diorite tablet at the top of which is a relief depicting Hammurapi receiving the law from Shamash, the sun god.

Inequality of social classes was a fundamental principle of Babylonian law. The nobility, middle class, and peasantry enjoyed legal rights commensurate with their respective stations, but the law also imposed responsibilities proportional to the privileges of each class. 

Slaves were protected to a considerable degree, for they could protest their transfer to a new master, or, on the other hand, demand their sale if persistently mistreated. They were permitted to own property and conduct business enterprises; indeed, some of them even possessed slaves. The fact that most slaves were war captives, merely victims of what might well be but temporary misfortune, probably accounts for their humane treatment. 

The position of women under the law was enlightened in some respects and archaic in others. A married woman was permitted to own property and conduct commercial transactions free from the control of her husband. In the event of separation, she secured the return of her dower as well as a share of property jointly acquired during the marital union. On the other hand, a wife could be handed over to her husband's creditors to liquidate his debts and could be dismissed for sterility, infidelity, or conduct that cast discredit on her spouse. Marriage was a civil act, devoid of religious significance. 

The parents of the couple concluded the betrothal arrangements, which were recorded by scribes on clay tablets and guaranteed by the posting of forfeits. Children were under the absolute control of their parents and could be sold into slavery or even put to death, but their claims to inheritance of parental property were strongly protected by law.

A basic principle of criminal law was retaliation, and there was virtually no distinction between crimes, or offenses against the state, and torts, or injuries to private individuals. If a contractor, for example, erected a building which subsequently collapsed, resulting in the death or injury of any occupants, he or his son was put to death or mutilated in reprisal. Likewise, if a physician operated on a patient who died as a result of the operation or suffered the loss of an organ, the physician's own fingers were cut off as a penalty. 

In civil cases, plaintiff and defendant were obliged to resort to a

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mashkin, or public arbitrator, before proceeding to actual trial of the case. If the arbitrator failed to secure an amicable adjustment of the matter at issue, the parties litigated before a bench of four judges on which the mashkin sat to vote in case of a deadlock. Documentary evidence was utilized whenever possible; witnesses who were sworn in preparatory to testifying were employed only to supplement written evidence. There was no preliminary arbitration in criminal cases.

Agriculture was the economic foundation of all the city-states, save those like Ur that were exceptionally well situated for the conduct of trade. Although there were large plantations, owned by the patesis, nobles, or endowed temples, and cultivated by slave labor, small freeholds and tenant farms were common. Towns and villages frequently operated tracts in communal fashion. Wheat and barley were the most valuable crops, although beans, onions, and spelt were extensively raised. The irrigated land was thoroughly ploughed; sometimes an ingenious combination of plough and sower was used. 

In this forerunner of modern agricultural machinery, the plough was equipped with a hopper and funnel through which the seeds dropped as the plough was pushed along the furrow. Grain was threshed by drawing heavy sledges back and forth after it had been scattered on the threshing floor.

Commerce, particularly the river trade between Sumer and Akkad, was conducted on a large scale. Politics and mercantile interests were often entwined; indeed, the rise of one or another of the city-states to a position of hegemony, if not impelled by the desire to expand irrigation facilities, usually was motivated by the prospect of expanded or stabilized trade relations. Caravan routes reached both the Levant and the Black Sea. Over these caravan routes ores, cedar, walnut, and building stones were brought into the Tigris-Euphrates valley, while grain, cloth, dried fish, and finished metal wares were exported. A standard system of weights and measures was employed. 

Merchants maintained branches in important towns and frequently employed travelers on a commission basis to transact their business. 

Barter was widely utilized in the absence of coined money, but weighed amounts of metals frequently served as media of exchange. 

Precious metals could be borrowed with interest at from 20 to 33 per cent.

Small industrial establishments, where the craftsman was assisted by a few apprentices or slaves, existed side by side with larger factories operated by the rulers or the priesthoods. Metal ware, pottery,

ANCIENT MESOPOTAMIA 

9 leather, and cloth, especially linen and a fleecy woolen fabric, were staple products.

The scribes of ancient Babylonia usually wrote by impressing wedge-shaped characters on a soft, moist clay tablet by means of a blunt stylus. The tablets then were dried in the sun or in kilns and sometimes were coated with wax as a preservative. More than three hundred fifty characters, made by varying the number and position of the wedge marks, were utilized, with the result that long training, sometimes secured in schools, was requisite for the scribe's profession.

Sir Henry Rawlinson rendered by far the greatest service in the decipherment of the cuneiform script, so called from the Latin word cuneus, meaning wedge. By continuation of the method of Grotefend with proper names, he identified fourteen of the thirty-nine letters of the Persian alphabet. He then studied the famous Behistun 

Inscription, cut in a cliff more than 300 feet above the Persian Royal Road from Sardis to Susa. The inscription, written in Persian, Susian (a Persian dialect), and Babylonian, tells of the suppression of a revolt by the Persian king, Darius I (522-485 B.C.). From a precarious position on a scaffold, Rawlinson completed the arduous, indeed dangerous, task of copying the inscription and then deciphered the Persian version. The Persian text reproduced the Babylonian. · Since Persian writing was a simplified, alphabetical form of the cuneiform script, he finally succeeded in reading the Babylonian text by a process of minute comparison. Thousands of hitherto meaningless tablets, seals, and monuments thus were made available to the scholar, with the result that the history of ancient Mesopotamia was reduced to a scientific basis and is steadily being illumi nated by archaeological research.

The best-known Babylonian literary production is the Epic of Gilgamesh, which deals with the creation of the world and its destruction by a flood. Ea, an incarnate deity, prophesies the impending disaster and Utnapishtim hearkens to the warning and constructs a ship in anticipation of the flood. A torrential rain which continues for six days and nights results in the predicted flood. Utnapishtim and his family, together with specimens of every creature, survive on the ship. When the water begins to recede, the boat is beached on a hilltop, after a raven which has been released fails to return. 

Doubtless the Hebrew story of Noah's ark is at least partially based on the Gilgamesh epic. Another well-known epic tells of the search of Etanna for immortality. Virtually all Babylonian literature dealt

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

with religious themes. The poetry, in which pious phrases are repeated in ritualistic fashion, has both rhyme and meter. 

In addition to local gods who served as protectors and patrons of the city-kingdoms, there were a number of deities that were generally venerated, such as Anu, god of the heavens, and Enlil, god of wind and rain. The worship of Enlil centered in the city of Nippur, which enjoyed a position of religious preeminence in both Sumer and Akkad. With the rise of Babylon under Hammurapi, the cult of 

Marduk became comparable in scope with that of Enlil. 

Rites of divination bulked large in religious practice. A favorite means of foretelling the future was by examination of the livers of newly sacrificed animals. Clay models, showing the significant spots upon which the predictions were based, usually were made. Interpretation of dreams, the flight of birds, the diffusion of drops of oil in water, and the flight of arrows also were utilized for prophetic purposes. Astrology, or the belief that the stars and other heavenly bodies influenced human affairs, was an integral phase of religious belief. The heavens were carefully scrutinized for harbingers of earthly happenings, and incidentally some discoveries of scientific value were made. The concept of immortality was not emphasized. It was believed that proper burial of the dead was necessary in order to prevent their spirits from haunting the living. The spirits of the dead who were properly laid to rest lived in a state of suspension that was neither life nor oblivion.

The arch, the tower, and the ziggurat, or stepped temple, were the chief Babylonian gifts to architecture. Since building stone was not available unless imported, mud bricks were the standard material. 

The bricks, either square or convex, were made in moulds and dried in the sun or baked in kilns. Sun-dried bricks made up the inner core of walls, while the kiln-dried ones, which frequently were glazed, were used for exterior facing.

Reliefs are the best examples of Babylonian art. The famous “Stele of the Vultures," of which seven fragments are preserved, portrays on one side King Eannatum of Lagash at the head of a phalanx, defeating the enemies from the rival city of Umma. On the other side 

Ningirsu, patron deity of Lagash represented as an eagle, is depicted catching and dispatching enemy soldiers. Another well-known monument is the "Stele of Victory," which portrays Naram-Sin, grandson of Sargon, in a campaign against the hill tribes to the east of the Tigris. Both these famous reliefs are characterized by good composition and a well-developed dramatic sense. There are, of course,

ANCIENT MESOPOTAMIA 

I I technical crudities, especially the conventional faces and the stiff, heavy torsos which betray the anatomical ignorance of the artists. 

The best specimens of statuary in the round are the portrait statues of Gudea of Lagash. The artistry of Sumerian metal workers has already been referred to in the description of some of the objects found in the royal tombs of Ur. Another famous specimen is the silver vase of King Entemena of Lagash. It is 28 inches high and stands on a copper base. It is engraved with a lion-headed eagle (Ningirsu), which has its talons embedded in the backs of two lions which probably represent subjugated city-kingdoms. 

Babylonian science did not reach the culmination of its development until the age of the Chaldean Empire (625-539 B.C.). Interest in astrology, however, naturally led to a number of elementary astronomical discoveries. Most of the common principles of plane geometry were known, and the practice of divination by observing diffusion of oil in water led to the discovery of the principles of the reflection and refraction of light as well as the relation of refraction to the primary colors. A curious sexagesimal method of computation was employed, in which 60 was the basic unit and multiples were shown by varying the position of the figures. This system of counting, supplemented by duodecimal units when necessary, was the origin of the practice of dividing the circle into 360 degrees, the degree into 60 minutes, and the minute into 60 seconds.

CHAPTER Ancient Egypt 

ECATAEUS, the ancient Greek geographer, aptly termed Egypt the "Gift of the Nile." Rising in equatorial Africa, the river flows in a predominantly northerly direction for more than 4000 miles. During the greater part of the year the stream is narrow and sluggish, but its appearance abruptly changes in early summer, when, swollen by the torrential rains of central Africa and the melting snows of the Abyssinian mountains, it overflows its banks and inundates the surrounding countryside for an average width of 30 miles. By the middle of October the flood reaches its height, after which the waters rapidly revert to their original channel. With the recession of the flood a heavy deposit of alluvial soil is precipitated, and the fertility of the soil is thus annually replenished. 

This central geographic factor had a number of important consequences in the development of Egyptian society, economic life, and government. Since the arable land is little more than a narrow strip running through the desert, concentration of the populace, and with it the early development of a complex society, were promoted. The annual floods deposited new layers of top soil; hence, cultivation of staple crops was feasible without danger of soil exhaustion. Such conditions were ideally suited to the evolution of a plantation economy wherein the labor of the servile masses was exploited to support a small leisure class in prodigal magnificence. The patronage of the leisure class, in turn, encouraged the rapid development of architecture, art, and literature. Since there is practically no rainfall, the necessity for conserving the water that was so abundant in the season of the inundation soon was realized. Measures also had to be taken to control the floods in order to avoid disastrous consequences. 

These conditions imperatively demanded the evolution of a strong, centralized government to plan, construct, and maintain elaborate irrigation facilities.

The geographical position of Egypt was of considerable signifi-

ANCIENT EGYPT 

13 cance. On the one hand, it was sufficiently removed from other powers of the ancient world to enable it to develop a unique culture. On the other, it was joined to Asia by the Isthmus of Suez and the peninsula of Sinai. This was a vulnerable point, and Hyksos, Assyrians, and Persians ultimately came into the land by this route and subjugated it. Moreover, proximity to Asia made commercial expansion into Syria and Palestine, and consequently cultural contact with the civilization of the Fertile Crescent, inevitable. Egypt was well supplied with natural resources. The great quarries, particularly those of Syene, furnished virtually inexhaustible supplies of granite, sandstone, and limestone. The copper and turquoise resources of Sinai were exploited; indeed, the possession of Sinai was an infallible barometer of the general vigor and prosperity of the Egyptian kingdom.

The racial origins of the ancient Egyptians are conjectural. A credible hypothesis is that the inhabitants of south Egypt were racially akin to the Nubians, whereas the northern group, likewise aboriginal, were related, probably, to the Hamite Libyans and Somali. An Armenoid migration from Asia provided a great impetus to cultural development, and the ancient Egyptian represented a fusion of these three primary racial elements. 

Evidences of a highly developed prehistoric culture in Egypt were discovered through the excavations of Sir W. M. Flinders-Petrie at 

Nakada. Examination of objects found in the shallow circular or elliptical graves showed that the remains belong to the late Neolithic Age. The pottery gave proof of marvelous technical attainments; the potter's wheel had not yet been invented and the utensils were baked in an open flame, but the vessels had been exquisitely fashioned by the hands of the prehistoric craftsmen. Iron salts in many of the clays imparted a brick-red color to the articles. Sometimes the vessels were placed with their mouths in the fire. Since oxygen thus was cut off from the part immersed in the flame, the black oxide of iron was formed around the mouths of the pieces, producing the famous black-topped ware." Petrie classified the pottery and worked out the ingenious system of "sequence dating " by which he concluded that this pre-dynastic culture could be dated to about 5000 B.C. 

The ancient history of Egypt commonly is divided into five major periods. First, there was the period of the Old Kingdom, from about 3500 B.C. to 2500 B.C. This was followed by the Feudal Age (c. 2500-2200 B.C.), so called because during this era royal authority virtually disappeared and was supplanted by the usurped powers of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

nobility and priesthood. With the restoration of royal authority and centralized government the Middle Kingdom was inaugurated (2200-1800 B.C.). About 1800 B.C., Egypt was conquered by the 

Hyksos, who crossed from Asia Minor. It remained under the dominance of Hyksos rulers until the foundation of the New Kingdom by Ahmose (1580 B.C.). The period of the New Kingdom or Empire is usually considered to extend to the Assyrian conquest of 

Egypt in 671 B.C. Manetho, an Egyptian priest of the third century before Christ, prepared a list of Egyptian kings in which the rulers are grouped into thirty-one dynasties. While the reason for the grouping is not always clear, the classification, in the main, is still followed by modern Egyptologists.

With the invention of writing and the opening of the historic period, there probably were at least three petty kingdoms in Egypt.

In the north, in the Delta area, was the Hornet Kingdom, or the Kingdom of the Red Crown, named after its royal escutcheons. Farther up the Nile was the Reed Kingdom, the royal standard of which was the papyrus reed. In the south, extending probably as far as the 

First Cataract of the Nile, was the Hawk Kingdom, the patron deity of which was represented as a hawk. This kingdom conquered its neighbor to the north in the reign of Ka (the Scorpion), and the Hornet Kingdom likewise was annexed. Unification of these petty monarchies marked the foundation of the Old Kingdom. Narmer, the second ruler of the First Dynasty, completed the work of conquest. A relic of this ruler, a slate palette, is preserved in the British 

Museum. It portrays the king inspecting the bodies of slain northerners. He is shown trampling on papyrus leaves, while Horus, patron deity of the south, hovers overhead, the head of a slain northerner in his beak. Aha, who probably should be identified with the 

Menes of Manetho's list, and his successors devoted themselves primarily to organizing an administration to rule the consolidated kingdom. Egyptian culture had already reached a high level in the period of the First Dynasty, as is shown in the tombs of the kings at Abydos. 

Semti's tomb, found intact, was lined with brick and paved with granite blocks; many finely fashioned objects of gold and ivory, beautiful vases, and fragments of glass indicate the high standards of art and craftsmanship.

The period of the Second Dynasty seems to have been largely devoid of lasting and constructive achievement. The pharaohs of the

Third Dynasty are notable chiefly because they constructed a new style of royal tomb, which ultimately evolved into the pyramid.

ANCIENT EGYPT 

15 King Khasekem had a rectangular limestone tomb, or mastaba, constructed. Imhotep, royal architect of King Zoser, built the famous "step pyramid” of that monarch, in which successive rectangular steps of regularly diminishing size were superimposed. King Snefru had several of these step pyramids built at Sakharah and improved them by filling in the recesses to form true pyramids. 

The period of the Fourth Dynasty is known as the Pyramid Age. 

Construction of the colossal edifices at Gizeh demanded gigantic mobilization of man-power and materials, but the work was not necessarily a great burden on the populace. Much of the work was done during the flood season when agricultural labor was impossible, and thus constituted a form of work relief for the peasantry. The 

Great Pyramid, built in the reign of Khufu (Cheops), now 451 feet high, is the largest structure. It contains more than 2,500,000 stone blocks, and its gross weight has been estimated at 5,750,000 tons. Before the second pyramid, built in the reign of Khafre, stands the famous Sphinx, which is a portrait head of the ruler on a reclining body of a lion. The third, or Little Pyramid, built in the reign of Menkaure, is the most graceful and symmetrical of the group. 

Royal authority rapidly declined after the Pyramid Age. While partial recovery followed the establishment of the Sixth Dynasty, especially during the long reign of Pepi II, the forces of disintegration could not be permanently arrested. Nobles and priests of endowed temples, secure in the possession of enormous wealth, nullified efforts to preserve centralized administration, the functions of which they largely usurped. The period known as the Feudal Age (2500-2200 B.C.) marked the triumph of the forces of, particularism.

It was not, however, an era of cultural stagnation. Opulent nobles vied with one another in constructing lavish palaces, collecting libraries of papyri, and affording patronage to architects, artists, and craftsmen. Moreover, the rise of a middle class resulted in a wider diffusion of culture.

Restoration of centralized monarchial government in the period of the Middle Kingdom (c. 2200-1800 B.C.) began with establishment of the Eleventh Dynasty at Thebes. Intefo, founder of the dynasty, continued to extend his authority with Thebes as a nucleus. 

With the foundation of the succeeding dynasty by Amenemhet I, the task of reconstruction was virtually completed. 

Amenemhet, one of the greatest statesmen of the ancient world, married the heiress of the Memphite line in order to strengthen his position. Introduction of the practice of investing a co-regent with

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

authority discouraged usurpation, since the death of a pharaoh did not disturb the continuity of royal administration. In several of his inscriptions Amenemhet expresses pride in his efforts to ensure the well-being of his subjects. This "Dawn of Conscience," as Professor 

Breasted has termed it, indicates that the concept of the state was emerging, and enlightened rulers recognized the responsibilities incident to tenure of the throne. 

About 1800 B.C., Egypt was subjugated by the Hyksos, or “Men of the Desert," who swept across the Isthmus of Suez from Asia Minor. Their utilization of cavalry and archers gave them a great tactical advantage which enabled them to conquer the "Land of the Nile" with comparative ease. Centuries of Hyksos rule implanted in 

Egypt an inveterate hatred of Asiatics that partially explains the Egyptian campaigns in Syria and Palestine in the imperial period. 

These began as retaliatory enterprises. One constructive result of the Hyksos occupation was the introduction of the horse, hitherto virtually unknown in Egypt.

Hyksos domination finally was shattered by Ahmose, founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty (c. 1580-1321 B.C.). A standing army was established, with cavalry and companies of archers as integral divisions, effectively to defend the land against renewed attacks. It was necessary to make some compromises with the nobles and the powerful priesthood to secure support for the royal program. By the close of the reign, however, the restoration of centralized government had been accomplished, and with the foundation of the New Kingdom, Egypt entered upon the most brilliant and spectacular period of its history. By the reign of Thutmose I (1545–1514 

B.C.), recovery from the effects of the Hyksos conquest had so far progressed as to make possible an invasion of Asia Minor, undertaken primarily to avenge the disaster of 1800 B.C. The expedition resulted in the establishment of suzerainty over Syria and Palestine. 

In 1501 B.C., Queen Hatshepsut came to the throne. This capable and energetic ruler was one of the few of her sex to play a major part in the affairs of the ancient world. Female rule, however, was a great shock to conservative elements; consequently the queen took a consort, the future Thutmose III, who became the nominal ruler. An outstanding event of her reign was the famous commercial expedition to Punt (Somaliland). The complete story of the enterprise is told in the famous pictures on the walls of Hatshepsut's temple in the Valley of the Kings at Der-el-Bahri. Although the primary purpose of the venture was to procure myrrh and other aromatics, the

ANCIENT EGYPT 

17 vessels returned to Thebes laden with ivory, ebony, cinnamon, cosmetics, pelts, baboons, monkeys, dogs, and slaves. The queen erected two huge obelisks, each 974 feet high, to commemorate her reign. 

The tall, tapering shafts were hewn out of solid granite at the quarries of Syene and floated down the Nile on barges. 

In 1479 B.C., Thutmose III, who long had resented the domination of Hatshepsut, became ruler in his own right. He promptly mutilated the monuments of his late wife; jealousy even drove him to hide the inscriptions on her obelisks by a layer of masonry which, ironically enough, served to preserve them.

The news of the accession of Thutmose had been followed by a major rebellion against Egyptian suzerainty in Syria and Palestine. 

Thutmose, sometimes called the "Napoleon of Egypt," conducted fourteen brilliant campaigns which resulted in the firm establishment of an Asiatic empire that extended beyond the Euphrates. An official known as the "Governor of the North Provinces " was put in charge of the conquered territory. Egypt was the acknowledged master of the known world, while Babylonia languished under Kassite domination and Assyria was still in its infancy. Considerable work on the temple of Karnak, the most imposing monument of the Eighteenth Dynasty, the rearing of obelisks, and the organization of commercial expeditions that included one to Punt absorbed the energies of Thutmose in the intervals between the Asiatic campaigns.

The reign of Amenhotep III (1412-1376 B.C.) was a period of luxury and prodigal magnificence. The Tell-el-Amarna Letters, archives of diplomatic correspondence found near the modern village of that name, testify to the international preeminence of Egypt. The letters, written in Babylonian cuneiform, which seems to have been generally used for diplomacy, are replete with acknowledgments of suzerainty, flattering salutations, and reports of the dispatch of tribute and presents. Trade was developed to unprecedented levels. A Red 

Sea fleet was constructed to handle the increased volume of exports and imports. A marine police and a customs bureau were added indications of commercial prosperity.

Attempted religious innovations fostered by Amenhotep IV (1376-1362 B.C.) paved the way for the loss of the empire and the decline of the great Eighteenth Dynasty. This young mystic ruler was obsessed with the desire to introduce a monotheistic religion reflecting the universality of Egyptian culture that had been promoted by the Asiatic conquests. Worship of Aten, represented as a solar disk with its downward rays terminating in hands, was de-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

signed to replace the national worship of Amen and the multitude of local cults. To signalize his conversion to the new monotheism, the new ruler, whose efforts were ably seconded by his queen, Nefertiti, changed his name to Ikhnaton (“Aten is satisfied"). These innovations promptly aroused the opposition of conservatives of all classes as well as the natural resistance of the established priesthoods. 

With the energies of the kingdom thus dissipated in internal strife, Syria and Palestine successfully revolted. The succeeding rulers of the Eighteenth Dynasty were at best mediocre. Much interest has been shown in the reign of Tutenkhamen, since his tomb was recently found intact. The magnificent jewelry, splendid furniture, and other objects from this tomb now repose in the Cairo Museum. 

Temporary recovery of the power and prestige of the kingdom came in the reign of Ramses II (1300-1233 B.C.) of the Nineteenth 

Dynasty. The Hittites, who had become the most formidable power of Asia Minor, were defeated and induced to sign a treaty providing for mutual respect of territorial integrity and extradition of fugitives. 

After this brilliant epilogue, however, decline proceeded more rapidly than ever. The foreign possessions were irretrievably lost, and internecine strife produced virtual chaos. In this weakened condition, Egypt fell an easy prey to the successive domination of Assyria and Persia. Liberation from Persian rule was promptly followed by incorporation in the empire of Alexander the Great. With the division of Alexander's empire in 301 B.C., Egypt came under the rule of the Ptolemaic Dynasty, which maintained the independence of the country until the defeat of the forces of Antony and Cleopatra at the battle of Actium in 31 B.C., established Roman rule. 

THE CULTURE OF ANCIENT EGYPT 

Although in theory the Egyptian rulers, who were regarded both as divine and as high priests of their people, were invested with despotic authority, there were a number of practical limitations on their absolutism. Tradition and court routine in some measure dictated their actions, and the influence of priests and powerful courtiers likewise exercised a practical restraint. The pharaohs, or “Dwellers in the Big House," dispensed justice in person or through their subordinates, conducted diplomacy, supervised building projects, and appeared at the head of armies. Since all land nominally belonged to the kings, they controlled irrigation facilities and regulated agricultural activities. The extension of commerce was in large measure the result of royal initiative, while the demand of the court for the prod-

ANCIENT EGYPT 

19 ucts of fine craftsmanship not only led to the maintenance of royal workshops but also stimulated the activity of shops operated by endowed temples and private individuals. 

An important official was the vizier, who exercised judicial powers in the name of the king and received reports from local officials and traveling inspectors. He and the royal treasurer supervised the preparation of the elaborate census lists and were responsible for the collection of taxes, which were for the most part paid in kind. For purposes of local administration the country was divided into about twenty nomes, each under an appointed official known as the nomearch. Towns were governed by appointed mayors, while country squires exercised petty jurisdiction in rural areas. The status of the minor officials was not enviable, since they were held personally liable for deficits in the collection of assigned tax quotas as well as for the policing of their respective jurisdictions. 

Little is known about the law of ancient Egypt and its enforcement by the courts, since no legal code has been found. There was a court in the south known as the "Court of the Thirty Great Ones"; apparently six courts, presided over by the vizier, administered justice in the north. Procedure in the courts was conducted primarily on the basis of documents and written depositions. Professional expounders of the law were employed to clarify and interpret difficult legal questions.

Agriculture was, of course, the basic economic activity. Virtually all the arable land was cultivated by the servile peasantry for the king or for the proprietary priesthood and aristocracy. If the crops were sown by early November, immediately after the recession of the Nile flood, no ploughing was necessary; otherwise, at least surface scraping was requisite. Wheat, barley, and flax were the staple crops, although virtually all the common vegetables likewise were cultivated. Figs and dates were grown, as were olives and castor beans, which were valuable chiefly as sources of oil. Harvest time came in 

April; grain was cut by sickles, trampled by asses on threshing floors, and winnowed by hand by women and children. It was then stored in conical or elaborate celled granaries, many of which were maintained by the government. Cows, oxen, goats, and pigs were raised on a large scale.

Commerce flourished especially in the periods of the Twelfth and Eighteenth Dynasties. The Nile was a great arterial waterway; in some periods at least, a canal connecting the river with the Red Sea was in use. The establishment of the Asiatic empire naturally proved

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

a great stimulus to trade, and economic motives doubtless were largely responsible for the Thutmosid campaigns of conquest. Trade with Crete was a source of mutual cultural stimulation; the Cretans probably learned their basic techniques of pottery manufacture from Egypt, while Cretan refinements in turn were adopted by the Egyptians. Ores, fine woods, and articles of luxury were the chief imports; while grain, flax, pottery, and linen were the staple export commodities. No coinage was in use, although gold and silver bullion began to supplement barter by the time of the Eighteenth 

Dynasty. 

Industry was predominantly domestic, in view of the absence of machinery and the lack of mass purchasing power. The clothing, rude furniture, and elementary domestic utensils used by the common folk were produced in the household. There were, however, small-scale manufacturing establishments where the artisans, assisted perhaps by members of their families, apprentices, or a slave or two, made their wares and sold them directly to the consumer. The most skilled craftsmanship was drawn into the luxury industries that catered to the court and the leisure class. Exquisite jewelry, finely fashioned furniture, glassware, beautifully modeled and ornamented pottery, and delicate fabrics, such as have been found in the royal tombs, demonstrate the technical mastery, artistry, and creative imagination of Egyptian craftsmanship. 

Egyptian writing went through four major stages of evolution.

Pictographs, whereby thoughts were conveyed by objective depiction, were employed in the prehistoric period. In the second, or ideographic stage, the characters represented not only objects but ideas associated with the objects. Next, it became necessary to make the difficult transition to the use of phonetic signs to represent words and syllables of speech. In the final stage of development, the writing became partially alphabetical, and a small number of characters therefore could be employed to build syllables and words. 

The ancient Egyptian script did not fully attain this stage, for a large number of word signs were retained. 

The characters employed by the ancient Egyptian scribes are known as hieroglyphics. They were often written with ink and quill pen on papyrus, which resembles paper. The sheets were made by pounding, pressing, and rolling papyrus reeds, which exuded a sticky liquid that caused them to cling together. It was not until about a hundred years ago that a beginning was made in the decipherment of the multitude of inscriptions and papyri. During Na-

ANCIENT EGYPT 

21 poleon's memorable campaign in Egypt (1798), one of his soldiers discovered, near the Rosetta mouth of the Nile, a great triangular stone covered with inscriptions. The inscriptions are in three scripts; hieroglyphic, demotic (a later style of Egyptian script), and Greek. 

Champollion, a prominent French Egyptologist, undertook the work of deciphering these Rosetta Stone inscriptions. He first succeeded in deciphering the names of Antony and Cleopatra from cartouches, or royal signatures, on the base of an obelisk. He then proceeded to demonstrate that the Greek inscription on the Rosetta Stone reproduced the hieroglyphic version; and by working from the known to the unknown, he determined the Greek equivalents of the Egyptian characters. His monumental achievement opened the vast treasure of Egyptian epigraphy and inaugurated modern scientific Egyptology.

Egyptian literature was chiefly of a religious character. By far the most elaborate work was the Book of the Dead, a product of centuries of evolution. It is a vast collection of prayers, hymns, ethical precepts, and magical formulas. Other religious works are the Hymn in Praise of Pharaoh and the passion play telling of the death and restoration to life of Osiris, the god of immortality. The great national epic was the Epic of Pentaur, which commemorates the campaign of Ramses II against the Hittites and tells, in highly exaggerated fashion, of the pharaoh's prowess. There was a great deal of popular literature characterized by vivacity and light-hearted romanticism. Perhaps the best-known work of this type is the story of 

Sinuhe the navigator and his wanderings, a prototype of the Sinbad stories of the Arabian Nights. Moral precepts, particularly the Maxims of Ptahotep of the period of the Fifth Dynasty, who might be termed the "Poor Richard" of his day, were widely circulated.

The nobles, particularly in the Feudal Age, collected sizable libraries of books in the form of rolls of papyri which were kept in inscribed or labeled jars.

Egyptian religion was a medley that included concepts ranging from crude magical lore to exalted spirituality. According to generally accepted myth, Neb and Nut, rulers of the heavens, had two sons, Osiris and Seth, and a daughter, Isis, to whom Osiris was betrothed. The jealous Seth, god of death, slew Osiris and hacked him to bits which he thereupon scattered over the earth. Isis, after a patient quest, recovered the fragments of her lover, who thereupon was restored to life to become the patron deity of immortality. 

Horus, represented as a hawk, was believed to be the son and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

avenger of Osiris. Sun worship was a standard feature of religious practice. During the period of the Old Kingdom, the worship of Re was nationally observed, and with the foundation of the Theban line the cult of Amen was identified with the older worship of Re. 

Ikhnaton's Aten cult failed to secure acceptance because of its monotheism, which was in contravention to deep-seated tradition and opposed to the vested interests of the priesthoods dedicated to the older cults. Its universality was incompatible with national pride and the characteristic intolerance of the ancient Near East. In view of the vital importance of the Nile in the life of Egypt, the worship of Hapi, the river god, naturally was emphasized. Thoth, god of wisdom, was another deity generally venerated. In addition to national gods, there were many local deities and cults. 

Belief in immortality was a basic concept of Egyptian religion. It was believed that every person had a Ka or spiritual double which survived death, just as the rising sun dispelled the darkness of night.

It was further believed that the heart of the deceased would be weighed in the balance; the wicked would be condemned and the righteous saved by this last judgment. Since corporeal decay was believed to result in the commensurate wasting of the Ka, it was necessary to preserve the body of the deceased. This was the reason for the elaborate tombs and the practice of mummification. Tombs of the wealthy were hewn in solid rock and were stocked with provisions and implements for the use of the departed. The care taken in the preparation of the mummy for entombment naturally depended on the means of the family of the deceased. Ordinarily, after the vital organs were removed, the corpse was immersed in a strong brine for a period of seventy days which was observed as a time of deep mourning by relatives, friends, and servitors of the deceased. The body then was wrapped, together with packets containing the preserved organs, with layer after layer of linen sprinkled with spices and aromatics. A heavy canvas cover was put on and fastened by bands, after which the body was placed in a sarcophagus and conveyed to the tomb by a procession of priests, relatives, and hired mourners, with noisy demonstrations of grief. The tomb preferably contained both a mortuary chapel and a tomb chamber. The sarcophagus was placed in the latter, after which the officiating priests symbolically restored sensory powers to the deceased and walled up the tomb chamber.

Three primary factors influenced the development of Egyptian architecture. First, there were abundant supplies of fine building

ANCIENT EGYPT 

23 stones such as granite and sandstone. Enormous quantities of granite were cut with consummate skill in the quarries of Aswan (Syene). 

Egyptian religion, with its tenets of immortality and the necessity of corporeal preservation of the dead, led to emphasis on durability and massiveness in tomb and temple architecture. Lastly, it must be remembered that the pharaohs enjoyed the power to regiment enormous numbers of laborers and thus could gratify their predilection for imposing structures. 

Basic architectural contributions of the Egyptians were the column, the pyramid, the clerestory window, and the basilica. The column was employed as early as the period of the Fifth Dynasty and soon became an integral feature of temple architecture. The early massive rectangular forms were superseded by cylindrical columns. Capitals of the columns often were ornamented, frequently with sculptured and conventionalized representations of the lotus flower.

The pyramid developed from the step pyramids of the Third Dynasty. These, in turn, probably represented an elaboration of the earlier rectangular stone tombs or mastabas. The enormous structures of the Pyramid Age are beautiful in the majesty of their proportions and the daring of their design. Although some may consider them mere monuments to the vanity of the rulers for whom they were built, nevertheless they symbolized the conquest of death and were the visible embodiment of the durability of the kingdom, the strength of its institutions, and the magnitude of its resources both human and material.

Many Egyptian temples were of the type later known as basilicas. 

This type was employed by the Romans for public buildings, and was adopted for the edifices of the early Christian Church. In this style the roof of the central portion, or nave, was supported by columns of considerably greater height than those of the two flanking aisles. Along each side of the nave, near the ceiling, were clerestory windows which admitted a soft indirect light to the interior in a manner conducive to sustenance of the religious mood. The first major use of the clerestory was in the temple of Khafre of the Fourth Dynasty. The slits near the ceiling of this structure were the forerunner of the later tall windows that the term clerestory ordinarily suggests.

The most imposing manifestations of the Egyptian architectural genius are the famous temples of Karnak and Luxor at Thebes. A temple had been constructed on the site as early as the period of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Twelfth Dynasty, but the alterations by the rulers of the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Dynasties were so extensive as to constitute reconstruction. A colossal pylon, with the entrance flanked by two great rectangular towers, led to an open columned forehall. This, in turn, led to the awe-inspiring hypostyle hall, 170 feet in length. The nave of the hall was formed by two rows of enormous columns, each 70 feet high, with capitals sufficiently large to support more than one hundred standing men on each. The roofs of the aisles on each side of the nave were supported by a veritable forest of columns - 136 in all. Tall clerestory windows lighted the nave; the façade of nave and flanking aisles was 338 feet wide. The famous Avenue of 

Sphinxes connected the Karnak temple with the Luxor edifice, which was built in three parts on the plan of an Egyptian house. 

West of the Nile, at Der-el-Bahri, is the famous Valley of the Kings, in the rock cliffs of which were hewn the tombs of the imperial pharaohs. Before these tombs are the ruins of royal temples, the most famous and best preserved being that of Queen Hatshepsut.

Other famous structures are the temples of Ramses II at Thebes and at Abu Simbel in Nubia.

The ancient Egyptians emphasized sculpture. A life-sized diorite statue of Khafre, now in the Cairo Museum, shows that the art had been developed to a high standard as early as the period of the Fourth Dynasty. Another well-known work is a bronze statue of Pepi I and his son of the Sixth Dynasty. In the Feudal Age and the Middle 

Kingdom, while productivity was stimulated by wider patronage, there was no major technical advance. In the imperial period, colossal statuary was a favorite artistic form. The best-known examples are the two colossi of Amenhotep III, each 72 feet in height, which stand in the desert west of Thebes. A colossal statue of Thutmose III, found at the Karnak ruins, has been compared with a mummy of the same ruler and proves that the features of the pharaoh were accurately portrayed even on a gigantic scale. The finest of the colossal figures are the four statues of Ramses II, each 94 feet high, which are hewn in the cliffs at Abu-Simbel, guarding the entrance to his great temple. The colored limestone portrait head of Ikhnaton and his wife, Nefertiti, are among the finest products of Egyptian sculpture. So lifelike are the statues of these young rulers who dared defy religious conservatism, that their dreamy mysticism and introspective temperaments are mirrored in their countenances.

The obelisk was a unique contribution of Egyptian art. These lofty, exquisitely tapered shafts of granite, probably equipped with

ANCIENT EGYPT 

25 pointed burnished metal caps, were erected for commemorative purposes. From a religious standpoint, they probably symbolized the victory of the sun over darkness and the conquest of death by the immortality of Osiris. Hatshepsut erected two obelisks; her successor, Thutmose III, outdid her by setting up five. One of Thutmose's obelisks now stands in London; another was brought to 

Central Park, New York, where it is erroneously known as Cleopatra's Needle." 66 The Egyptian talent for painting was expressed primarily in murals and the ornamentation of pottery. The murals are especially valuable from the historical standpoint since they portray military and commercial expeditions, religious festivals, and a multitude of scenes from the daily lives of those of high and low degree. Technically, the work did not attain the high standards set by sculpture.
