Perspective is poor or even wholly lacking; conventionality, which was the result both of technical limitations and tradition, is another prominent feature.

A great scientific contribution of the Egyptians was their invention of a calendar. Their calendar was based on the lunar year, with twelve months of thirty days each. The difference between lunar and solar years was observed, however, and five days devoted to festivity were added to each year to compensate for the discrepancy. 

The year began when the rise of Sirius, or Sothus, the dog star, synchronized with the beginning of the rise of the Nile. Since the solar year is not 365 days but 3654, the calendar lost a quarter day each year, or a full day every four years. This meant that it was not until four times 365, or 1460, years elapsed that the synchronization of the dog star and the Nile rise again occurred. The interval of 1460 years is known by Egyptologists as a Sothic cycle. By calculating back from known dates it has been determined that the Egyptian calendar began in the year 4236 B.C., which can be termed the first known date in history.

Since the recession of the Nile flood usually made it necessary to resurvey fields and relocate boundary marks, it is not surprising that the ancient Egyptians learned the elementary principles of plane geometry. A decimal system of computation was in use. Engineering problems incident to the construction of pyramids, temples, and other structures demanded acquaintance with the inclined plane, the pulley, the screw, and other basic principles of physics. The construction and upkeep of the vast irrigation projects required a knowledge of hydrostatics. Metal workers, stone cutters, leather workers,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

potters, and other craftsmen naturally were familiar with many practical applications of scientific principles. Systematic recordings of the heights of the Nile inundations and the preparation of census lists based on such data were likewise indicative of a scientific attitude of mind.

CHAPTER The Age of the Great Oriental Empires 

HE history of the Near East in the first millennium before Christ was marked by the rise of the Assyrian, Chaldean, and Persian empires. None of these powers made significant original contributions to Western civilization, yet cumulatively they performed an indispensable function. They welded the diverse peoples of the ancient Near East into centralized empires and imposed cultural uniformity largely by means of the dynamic force of religious intolerance - though the Persians were singularly tolerant. 

Their synthetic culture, drawn primarily from Babylonian and Egyptian sources, was disseminated among the barbarous tribes absorbed by the expansion of the empires; the cultural homogeneity thus largely attained was an essential prelude to the Graeco-oriental cultural fusion inaugurated by Alexander the Great. 

ASSYRIA 

The nucleus of the Assyrian Empire was the city-state of Assur, located in the northeast corner of the Fertile Crescent, on the west bank of the Tigris. A geographic factor of enormous significance in the evolution of Assyria as a militaristic state was the fact that in its formative period it was surrounded by powerful and belligerent neighbors. To the north was the kingdom of Van; west and northwest were the Mitanni and Hittites. To the south were the Kassites, who had conquered Babylonia about 1800 B.C., while barbarous nomads in the foothills of the Zagros mountains continually menaced the eastern frontier. Stern military discipline and efficient mobilization of man-power and material resources were necessary to cope with the exigencies created by Assyria's exposed position. 

The soil of the plateau on which Assur was located was fertile and much of it could be cultivated without resort to irrigation. Building stone and mineral deposits were available, while proximity to the Hittites facilitated importation of iron to augment domestic supplies.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The Khabur river gave access to the Euphrates and was a vital link with the caravan routes to the Levant; successive periods of Assyrian expansion invariably were connected with acquisition of control of the Khabur valley. The Upper and Lower Zab likewise served as avenues of expansion to the east. 

Racial origins of the Assyrians are thus far obscure. A recently discovered king list shows that the city-state of Assur was in existence as early as the Pyramid Age. It is probable that the Assyrians came into the region from the west after they had adopted a Semitic language; the hypothesis that they were colonists from Akkad now is virtually abandoned. With their settlement in Assur, probably named after their chief deity, they entered the orbit of Sumerian cultural influence.

The history of Assyria can be reconstructed with unique fullness and accuracy. Inscriptions are of great historic value and more than 

22,000 clay tablets of the library of King Assur-bani-pal are preserved in the British Museum. The accuracy of the Assyrian calendar and the survival of many of the limu lists, or lists of officials honored by the application of their names to calendar years, have greatly facilitated the solution of chronological problems. The biblical information, especially as contained in Isaiah and Kings, is of inestimable value, especially where correlation with Assyrian inscriptions is possible.

There were three major periods of Assyrian expansion. The first, from c. 1300-1200 B.C., synchronized with the decline of Egypt and internal dissensions that vitiated the strength of the Mitanni. A second period of expansion came in the reign of Tiglath-Pileser I, c. 

1125-1100 B.C., and was facilitated by the decline of the Hittite power that followed the great struggle with Egypt in the reign of Ramses II. The armies of the Assyrian conqueror reached the Mediterranean coast where Tyre and Byblos were made tributary. The commemorative prisms of the king boast that he led twenty-seven expeditions across the Euphrates. Both these early expansion movements proved premature, based as they were on superficial military conquest without assimilation of conquered peoples and commensurate development of administrative institutions. The chief factor, however, in the loss of the conquests was the rise of Aramaic citystates, particularly Damascus. These cities sundered Assyrian caravan connections with the Levant which, after all, were the major economic foundations of Assyrian imperialism. Not until the capture of Damascus was the way opened for the last and greatest pe-

TEMPLE OF KARNAK TEMPLE AT EDFU

KING KHAFRE THUTMOSE III PORTRAIT STATUES OF RAMSES II, TEMPLE OF ABU-SIMBEL

riod of imperialism, inaugurated with the reign of Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 B.C.). 

The accession of this ruler seems to have been irregular, for many of his monuments were effaced or mutilated by his successors. His elevation may have represented a triumph of the militaristic nobility over the influential priestly class. Suzerainty over Babylon and 

Van was asserted, while aggressive policies in the Levant were resumed. Judah, oppressed by Israel, successfully besought Assyrian intervention, and this fatal step soon was to culminate in the subjugation of both Hebrew kingdoms.

Sargon II (722-705 B.C.), who succeeded to the throne after a brief period of lethargy in the reign of Shalmaneser V (727-722 B.C.), carried on the penetration of Palestine by the conquest of Samaria and the deportation of 27,000 of its people whose lands were allocated to colonists. This meant that the people of Samaria henceforth were aliens and accounts for the antipathy between Jews and Samaritans that prevailed in the time of Jesus. The outstanding problem of 

Sargon's reign was the existence of Chaldean and other anti-Assyrian groups in Babylon under the leadership of a disaffected governor.

Coalition of Babylon with the Elamites along the head of the Persian Gulf aggravated the danger. Sargon suppressed the hostile demonstrations, but his unwise attempt to employ conciliation merely served to defer definitive settlement of the problem. In order to commemorate his reign, he built a new capital at Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad); its enormous walls and magnificent palace were among the greatest architectural feats of the ancient world. 

Sennacherib (705-681 B.C.) inherited the Babylonian problem that had so greatly plagued his father. A formidable coalition, including 

Elam and Judah, organized under the leadership of Babylon, finally was crushed, and eighty-eight towns in the lower Tigris-Euphrates valley were destroyed to discourage rebellious activities in the future. Judah was soon punished for its adherence to the coalition, for in 701 B.C., Sennacherib's forces appeared before Jerusalem after devastating the surrounding countryside. While the siege was abandoned, according to the biblical account because of the outbreak of a pestilence, the campaign indubitably established more firmly the vassalage of Judah.

Assyrian control of Syria and Palestine was continually menaced by the intrigues of Egypt. The pharaohs, although forced to relinquish political control of these regions, were by no means reconciled to permanent renunciation of commercial interests in the Levant.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Consequently, it was primarily the desire to stabilize Assyrian rule along the eastern Mediterranean that led Esarhaddon (681-668 B.C.) successfully to undertake the conquest of Egypt. By 671 B.C., with the fall of Memphis, Assyrian mastery was assured. The Assyrian

Empire, now including Egypt as well as all the Fertile Crescent, had reached the zenith of its expansion. 

There were many reasons for the success of Assyrian imperialism. 

Well-disciplined armies, comprised primarily of nationals, enjoyed enormous advantage in combat with the mercenaries or hastily assembled levies of enemy powers. Chariots and heavily armed cavalry, operating in conjunction with infantry, revolutionized tactics; before the innovations were generally emulated, the Assyrian forces enjoyed overwhelming superiority. Then, too, the Assyrian soldiery employed iron weapons, and their metal helmets and iron breastplates made them virtually invulnerable to antagonists who enjoyed no such protection. Partially centralized administration, strengthened as it was by a system of military roads, facilitated the maintenance of control over conquered peoples, as did the transportation of captives and allocation of their lands to Assyrian colonists. Systematic terrorization, incredibly cruel as it was, discouraged rebellion, although the implacable hatred it fostered among the vassals was ultimately disastrous.

The empire disintegrated with great rapidity after the close of the reign of Assur-bani-pal (668-626 B.C.). Palace revolutions, strife between nobles and priests, and recurrent rebellions of vassal states paralyzed the energies of the state with the result that a coalition of Media and the newly established Chaldean kingdom overthrew it with apparent ease. Assur was captured in 614 B.C.; two years later 

Nineveh was destroyed.

Years of practically constant warfare, with the consequent cost in man power and the waste of material resources, had exacted their inescapable toll. By far too great a proportion of the populace had been diverted from agriculture and other productive enterprises, and the magnitude of the conquests exceeded the assimilative power of the state. The Hebrew prophet Nahum expressed the prevalent jubilation at the fall of the empire in the words: "Woe to the bloody city! It is full of lies and rapine. All that hear the report of thee clap their hands over thee, for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?"

THE M.-N.WORKS

CHALDEA 

The Chaldeans began their migration into Babylon and its environs soon after the close of the reign of Hammurapi. They spoke a Semitic language and originally dwelt in the grasslands along the eastern border of the Arabian desert. The establishment of Kassite rule in Babylonia for a time curbed the infiltration, but with the decline of the Kassite power and the rise of Assyria, the Chaldeans constituted an increasingly strong element in Babylon. On a number of occasions, they joined with the Elamites and other powers of the ancient Near East to constitute a serious menace to Assyrian suzerainty in the lower Tigris-Euphrates valley. With the internal weakness of the Assyrian Empire fully revealed at the close of Assur-banipal's reign, the Chaldeans, under the leadership of Nabopolassar, combined with the Medes, under Cyaxares, to destroy Assur and Nineveh and assure the independence of the allied kingdoms. 

Chaldea (which means Neo-Babylonia, and might fittingly be called by that name) soon demonstrated its intention to take over 

Assyrian interests in the Levant. In 605 B.C. Nebuchadrezzar, son of the founder of the kingdom, gained a decisive victory at Carchemish, where he frustrated the designs of Egypt to capitalize upon the collapse of Assyria. Syria and Palestine were annexed and the hopes for independence which the Hebrews had cherished were quickly dispelled. 

Nebuchadrezzar (605–561 B.C.) succeeded to the Chaldean throne soon after his brilliant exploit at Carchemish. He was doubtless one of the foremost statesmen and conquerors of the ancient Near East.

The outstanding event of his reign was the desperate effort of Judah to secure its liberation. In 599 B.C. King Jehoiakim, despite the warning of the prophet Jeremiah, refused to pay tribute and expelled Chaldean governing officials. Jerusalem was promptly captured, and the Chaldean victory was followed by the deportation of a number of Jewish artisans for the double purpose of intimidating the disaffected vassals and promoting the economic development of the conquerors. In the same year, King Zedekiah, relying on promises of Egyptian aid, renewed the hopeless struggle. As Jeremiah had foretold, the Egyptian troops soon withdrew, leaving Zedekiah to bear the full brunt of Nebuchadrezzar's wrath. When the Chaldean invaders again captured Jerusalem, the royal palace and Solomon's temple were destroyed. Zedekiah was blinded; his sons were put to death. Virtually the entire able-bodied Jewish populace now were

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

deported to Chaldea. The Babylonian Captivity had a profound effect on the religious development of the Hebrews. Prolonged exile and the consequent hardships were considered to be Jehovah's punishment for the apostasy of the "Chosen People " so bitterly berated in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Religious beliefs became inseparably entwined with the hope for repatriation. Concepts of Jehovah became broader and more spiritual; He not only guided the destinies of the Hebrews, but all peoples were governed by Him in accordance with His inscrutable purposes.

After a campaign against Egypt to discourage further interference in Syria and Palestine, Nebuchadrezzar devoted his attention to the rehabilitation of Babylon. A temple dedicated to Marduk and a magnificent palace were built; the famous "Hanging Gardens" became one of the marvels of the ancient world. 

Dissension wracked the kingdom with the death of Nebuchadrezzar. Nabonidus, his successor, made no effective efforts to arrest the encroachments of Persia, until in 539 B.C., the Chaldean army, commanded by Belshazzar, the crown prince, was overwhelmed by the forces of Cyrus of Persia (558-529 B.C.). With the capture of

Babylon, Chaldea became part of the Persian Empire. 

THE RISE OF THE PERSIAN EMPIRE 

The Medes and the Persians probably migrated into the Iranian plateau from the grasslands of Central Asia. From lingual resemblances, it has been conjectured that they were of the same race as the ancient Hindus. The Medes settled east of the Zagros mountains, from the Black Sea to the Persian Gulf. Six tribes coalesced early in the seventh century, but no expansion was possible until the way was opened by the collapse of the Assyrian Empire. We already have seen how Cyaxares, king of the Medes, in collaboration with Chaldea, played a major part in the overthrow of Assyria. 

In the meantime, the Persians pushed into Elam and organized several tribal kingdoms. One of these, Anshan, eventually succeeded in asserting its hegemony, so that when Cyrus (558-529 B.C.) became king, a compact Persian kingdom had been created, although he did not assume the title of "king of Persia " until eight years later.

Dissension among the Medes afforded Cyrus an opportunity to take the first step in the foundation of the Persian Empire. He captured Ecbatana, the Median capital, largely as a result of the mutiny of the army of King Astyages. Since Medes and Persians were of the same racial stock, and there were no geographical, economic,

or religious obstacles in the way of rapid fusion of the two peoples, the Medes lost all trace of separate identity within a generation or two.

The expansion of Persia naturally threatened Chaldea, and King Nabonidus therefore hastened to enter into an alliance with Croesus, king of Lydia, which by this time had become the most powerful state of Asia Minor. Nabonidus, however, deserted his ally and thus brought about his own ruin as well as the fall of Lydia. Sardis, the 

Lydian capital, was taken in 546 B.C., after Cyrus surprised and vanquished Croesus, who had begun to disband his army at the approach of winter. The Persian conquest of Lydia was destined to have important effects. Since Asia Minor had been extensively colonized by the Greeks, many flourishing Greek city-states now passed from Lydian to Persian rule. The entry of the victorious 

Persians into Sardis in reality had made inevitable a great struggle between Persia and Greece. 

Nabonidus paid dearly for his failure to support Croesus. In 539

B.C., the Persian forces marched against Chaldea, already weakened by internal strife. After feeble resistance, Babylon fell into the hands of Cyrus, who thus also acquired the Chaldean control of Syria and Palestine. The enlightened policies of Cyrus soon reconciled Chaldea to the acceptance of Persian rule. Babylon was honored by designation as one of the capitals of the empire; temples were repaired or rebuilt and captured idols restored to their proper shrines. The Persian conqueror also took pains to identify himself with the cult of 

Marduk, the leading Chaldean deity.

Expansion of Persia to the Mediterranean naturally incurred the hostility of Egypt, which promptly resorted to the traditional intrigues and coalitions. Since it was impossible to hold the western conquests without subjugating Egypt, Cambyses (529-522 B.C.), the successor of Cyrus, invaded the Land of the Pharaohs and annexed it to his empire by 525 B.C. His conquest, like that of Esarhaddon of 

Assyria, was primarily designed to obviate further Egyptian interference in the Levant. While preparing to crush an insurrection that had broken out in Persia, Cambyses committed suicide, probably during one of his recurrent fits of insanity. 

Darius I (522-485 B.C.), of a related branch of the Achemenid family, succeeded Cambyses. After several years of fighting, he suppressed the revolt that had begun in the reign of his predecessor. 

He then turned to the problem of organizing an administrative system for the enormous empire which now extended from Egypt to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the Indus. It was in this field that he exhibited his governing genius. 

The Greek cities of Asia Minor revolted in 499 B.C., thus precipitating the great duel between Persia and Greece. This phase of the reign will be discussed from the standpoint of Greek history. 

PALESTINE 

As we have seen, the Hebrews were drawn, with disastrous results, into the struggles of the great oriental empires for possession of the Fertile Crescent. Situated in the southwest corner of the Crescent, where it was inevitably a battle ground in any struggle between Egypt and the powerful Asiatic empires, Palestine was precluded by location as well as by dearth of natural resources from playing a decisive role in international affairs. Nevertheless, because of their great contributions to the development of religious thought, it can be said that the Hebrews have exercised a unique influence on the history of Western civilization, wholly disproportionate to their numbers and meager material endowments. CC The story of the migration of the Hebrews into Palestine is hopelessly entangled in scholarly controversy. It may be conjectured, however, that one group came into the Promised Land" from the fringes of the Arabian desert and subsequently continued into Sinai, whence they entered Egypt at some time not precisely known, probably in the period of the Eighteenth Dynasty. By the reign of 

Ramses II, however, their condition had become intolerable, burdened as they were by taxes and forced labor, and they decided to emigrate. There is nothing intrinsically improbable in the essentials of the biblical account of the exodus, although there is no corroboration in other sources. After a sojourn in Sinai, where they were reenforced by kinsmen who recently had entered the peninsula, the joint forces proceeded into Palestine.

A long, disheartening struggle with the Canaanites finally resulted in the Hebrew conquest of the "Promised Land," although the attacks of Moabites, Midianites, and other peoples east of the Jordan jeopardized their tenure. While still exhausted from the Canaanite wars, the Hebrews were conquered by the Philistines who had established a federation of towns in the south. Shiloh, the most important Hebrew stronghold, was razed and the ark, the symbol of Jehovah's covenant with the "Chosen People," was carried off as part of the spoil. Heavy tribute was exacted and garrisons were stationed among the vanquished to ensure its payment. 

The most heroic period in Hebrew history opened with the

foundation of a kingdom by Saul (c. 1025-1000 B.C.), who, with the inspiration of the venerable Samuel, began the struggle for liberation from the Philistine overlords. Although his last battle resulted in a serious defeat that drove him to suicide, Saul's accomplishments and character seem to have been somewhat unjustly disparaged in the 

Old Testament narrative. 

Complete independence was secured by the energetic campaigns of King David (c. 1000-975 B.C.). Jerusalem, ideally situated for purposes of defense, was made the capital. The reign of Solomon (c. 975-935 B.C.) was the brilliant sequel to the achievements of 

David. Visits of distinguished personages to his splendid court, such as the well-known visit of the Queen of Sheba, testified to the growing importance of the kingdom. Friendly relations with the Phoenician cities of Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos to the north led to Hebrew participation in Phoenician commercial expeditions to the western Mediterranean. The construction of Solomon's temple was considered a fitting manifestation of gratitude to Jehovah, whose guidance and aid had delivered His people from bondage, as well as a visible demonstration of the kingdom's prosperity.

The last years of Solomon's reign were marked by growing discontent in Israel, largely fomented by the ruler's partiality toward Judah in the allocation of the heavy taxation necessitated by the construction of the temple and the upkeep of the court. Although the revolt of Jeroboam, a manifestation of this discontent, was suppressed, it was a harbinger of the schism which came with Solomon's death, c. 935 B.C. Jeroboam returned from exile to become ruler of the ten tribes of Israel, whereas Rheoboam, Solomon's son, was recognized as king by the two tribes of Judah. 

Social, economic, and even religious differences accentuated the cleavage between the two kingdoms. Mutual animosity culminated in conflict, which, in turn, hastened the Assyrian conquest. As already pointed out, the fall of Assyria transferred Palestine to Chaldean control and the efforts of Judah to recover independence led to the tragic era of the Captivity. It is quite likely that Cyrus of Persia permitted some of the Hebrews to return to their native land as a reward for their support in his successful campaign against Chaldea and thus inaugurated the movement for repatriation that culminated in the reign of Ezra. The kingdom recovered some of its former glory and power in the period of the Maccabees, but with the capture of Jerusalem by Pompey in 63 B.C. it became subject to Rome. Hopes for the appearance of a conquering Messiah kept alive a spirit of national-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ism, but efforts to overthrow Roman rule ended in failure. Titus destroyed Jerusalem in A.D. 70 and the great dispersion of the Jews throughout the Roman Empire was begun. 

CULTURAL DEVELOPMENTS IN THE ANCIENT ORIENT IN THE FIRST MILLENNIUM 

The oriental empires of the first millennium were distinguished by their development of efficient, centralized administrative machinery. 

The Assyrian Empire was divided into sixty administrative units known as pakhati, each of which was governed by officials appointed by the king. A council of four viziers, one of whom was known as the turtann or chief vizier, advised and assisted the monarchs. Recent discovery of three tablets containing fragments of Assyrian law has disproved the theory that legal development in Assyria was merely an adaptation of Hammurapi's code. There was no recognized inequality of social classes in the Assyrian courts nor was arbitration utilized in civil cases as in Babylonia. Equally striking differences existed in other features of the law. 

The Persian Empire was divided into some twenty satrapies, each under an appointed satrap or governor. Civil and military authority were kept separate, for a military governor was in charge of the army in each satrapy. As an added safeguard, each satrap was assigned a secretary who reported directly to the king. Inspectors, known as the " Eyes and Ears of the King," kept a close surveillance on the conduct of officials whom they were authorized to arrest and send to Susa, the capital, if their loyalty or competence was questioned. Heads of seven designated aristocratic families served as advisers of the Persian rulers; professional expounders of the law likewise frequently were consulted by the Great Kings. 

A potent centralizing influence in the Persian Empire was the great Royal Road. It ran from Sardis to Susa, a distance of more than 1500 miles. Bridges and ferries were maintained where needed; taverns and posting stations likewise were located at convenient intervals. 

A royal post was in operation and messengers, traveling in relays with frequent changes of mounts, covered the distance from the western terminus to Susa in from three to seven days.

Although plantation economy was characteristic in Assyria and Persia, there were many small freeholds in the former empire. Tenure by military service likewise was common; indeed, the grants of land to individuals on condition that they perform stipulated military service was not unlike this aspect of medieval feudalism. Among the

crops cultivated in Assyria, alfalfa was raised on a large scale and the cultivation of cotton is spoken of in the reign of Sennacherib. 

Assyrian commerce was conducted largely by Babylonian merchants. Mercantile interests, particularly the caravan routes to the cities on the eastern Mediterranean, were a potent factor in promoting imperialism. There was a strong prejudice against participation in commercial or industrial enterprises among the Persian aristocracy, however, with the result that the great economic opportunities incident to territorial expansion were never fully exploited. 

With the conquest of Lydia, the Persians learned the use of coinage and henceforth employed both gold and silver coins, the two metals circulating in the ratio of thirteen to one.

A prominent feature of Assyrian industry was the existence of craft gilds. These organizations stabilized prices and wages and enforced regulations in regard to apprenticeship as requisite for admission to the gilds. Masters maintained shops in the quarters of the towns allotted to their crafts and retailed directly to the consumer. The Assyrian kings frequently rewarded loyal towns by the grant of charters exempting their inhabitants from certain taxes and other civic burdens. In the gilds and the relationship of the towns to the crown, we again see striking resemblances to conditions that were to prevail in Europe in the Middle Ages. 

Assyrian script was a simplification of Babylonian cuneiform that greatly reduced the number of characters employed. Persian cuneiform, however, was alphabetical; it was this fact, as we have seen, that made possible the decipherment of the Babylonian text of the Behistun Inscription. Assyrian and Chaldean literature was for the most part merely translations of Babylonian works. Assur-bani-pal collected a great library at Nineveh which contained 22,000 clay tablets, some of which were arranged in proper order as "books,' with the first tablet bearing the opening words of the work, which served as a title. The chief Persian contribution to literature was the 

Avesta, a collection of poems, hymns, and prayers which were not completely developed, however, until the Parthian period after the middle of the third century of our era. Resemblances between the 

Avesta and the Vedic literature of the ancient Hindus are one of the arguments in favor of the hypothesis that both peoples were of common racial origin. Only one of the twenty-one books of the 

Avesta has survived intact, although fragments of others are extant. 

The religion of ancient Persia was based on the teachings of the prophet Zoroaster, who, according to tradition, was a great religious

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

teacher of the Medes about 600 B.C. The chief feature of the religion was dualism — that is, belief that there were two deities, one a god of good, the other the origin and patron of evil. The beneficent deity, known as Ahura-Mazda, god of light, was in constant conflict with Ahriman, god of darkness, who was the creator of all that was evil. 

This cosmic struggle between the gods had its counterpart in the human personality which was made up of the soul, created by Ahura-Mazda, and the body, created by Ahriman. With the aid of believers who succeeded in subordinating their corporeal natures to their spiritual existence, Ahura-Mazda was destined eventually to prevail. With his victory would come the end of the world, at which time the righteous would be absorbed in the sun and the wicked would be consigned to eternal darkness. In the Parthian period, fundamental beliefs were elaborated. Mithras was conceived as a mediator between Ahura-Mazda and the world. The Magi became an hereditary priesthood and the religion was further embellished by moral precepts, taboos, and animal worship. 

By far the greatest contribution to the development of religious thought prior to the rise of Christianity was made by the Hebrews, who were the first people to evolve a truly monotheistic religion. 

Although there were temporary deviations from the exclusive worship of one god, with erection of altars to Baal, the adoration of the golden calf, and the adoption of other cults from neighboring peoples, the prophets successfully resisted these innovations and led the people back to the worship of Jehovah. 

The conception of Jahweh or Jehovah was anthropomorphic, that is, He was endowed with human physical, mental, and emotional qualities. As the religion developed, He was considered to be transcendant, so far above man as to be incapable of approach save through the medium of an hereditary priesthood. There was an inseparable connection between religion and ethics. Jehovah was identified with righteousness; His precepts were bequeathed to the "Chosen People" in the Commandments and the Law, defiance of which endangered the relations between Him and His people and frequently brought immediate divine chastisement. Avoidance of sin was stressed rather than positive virtues; conformity to the Law and careful observance of ritualistic detail constituted a moral, religious life. The sacrifice was the central feature of the ritual. The idea was that Jehovah demanded tangible expiation of sin; therefore the sacrificial animal was symbolically loaded with the guilt of the sins committed by the believers and its death averted the conse-

quences of divine wrath. There was no emphasis on the idea of immortality. It was believed that after death the soul was consigned to 

Sheol, where it led a conscious but dismal existence. Disobedience to 

Jehovah's commands brought punishment not in eternity but by immediate disaster to the sinner or even to the whole people. 

The Old Testament is doubtless one of the most precious survivals of the ancient world. As the great national expression of the Hebrew spirit it equals if it does not surpass the Greek Iliad and the Latin Aeneid. The Psalms rank with the great poetry of all time; the 

Lamentations of Jeremiah and the Book of Job are masterpieces of tragic literature. It is also a great historical work in which is embodied a teleological interpretation of history, in large measure the product of the Exile and contact with Persian philosophy. According to this interpretation, the events of world history happen in accordance with direct providential intervention and are part of the inscrutable plan of the deity. Naturally, the historical perspective is somewhat out of proportion. If one's knowledge of the ancient world were derived only from the Old Testament, he would come to the conclusion that Palestine was its center and that such peoples as the Egyptians, Assyrians, and Chaldeans were merely the instruments of Jehovah's vengeance called to punish the "Chosen People" for disobedience to His will.

Assyrian architecture, while based on Babylonian traditions, naturally was influenced by the fact that building stone was available for foundations and façades. The construction of Dur-Sharrukin was probably the greatest achievement of Assyrian builders. Its walls were constructed of unburned brick, faced with kiln-dried brick. 

Eight gates afforded entrance to the city; winged bulls, carved out of solid rock and weighing 40 tons each, were set up at the gates. 

Within the enclosure was Sargon's palace, with its ramps, terraced stairways, and famous triple arch which later served as a model for 

Roman triumphal arches.

The chief Persian improvement in architecture was the refinement of the column, which was made more slender and better proportioned than the Egyptian style. Persian columns usually rested on bell-shaped bases and frequently were ornamented by sculptured animal figures. The great colonnaded palaces of Darius I and Xerxes at Persepolis were the outstanding structures of the imperial period. 

They were erected on a limestone terrace which was entered from a great double staircase.

Babylonian influences predominated in both Assyrian and Persian

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

sculpture. The Assyrians excelled in animal statuary; their great winged bulls and reliefs depicting hunting scenes rank with the finest examples of such art. Persian portrait statuary, particularly in the treatment of drapery, began to manifest signs of Greek influence. 

Fine bas-reliefs on the palace terrace at Persepolis depict gift-bearers and soldiers, while those on the walls of the palace of Darius show the monarch seated on his throne surrounded by the court. 

The Chaldeans were the greatest scientists of the ancient Orient, Although they inherited certain basic knowledge from the Babylonians, they made many original discoveries. As a result of their study of the heavens, stimulated by belief in astrology, five of the planets were known. The difference between solar and lunar years was observed and an intercalary month was inserted in the calendar to compensate for the discrepancy. The length of the solar year was computed to within twenty-six minutes of its actual length by the Chaldean astronomers who also compiled almanacs, tables of moon phases, and lists of planetary cycles and eclipses. Use of the twelve signs of the zodiac also was begun by them. Formulas for the calculation of the area and circumference of the circle were used by Chaldean mathematicians. Our time measurements, such as the sevenday week, the twenty-four-hour day, and the sixty-minute hour, likewise were first employed by them.

Persia made an appreciable contribution to geographical knowledge as a result of the famous voyage of Scylax, who was sent by King Darius I to explore the coast line from the mouth of the Persian 

Gulf to the head of the Red Sea. The Persians performed their greatest service to science, however, by preserving Chaldean lore and transmitting it to the Greeks. It was doubtless this Chaldean heritage that gave the original impetus to the work of the Greek scientists of 

Miletus in the sixth century before Christ.

CHAPTER The Ancient Aegean World and Greece to the Age of the Tyrants 

PRE-GREEK CIVILIZATION IN THE AEGEAN REGION 

OMER and other writers preserved a tradition to the effect that a flourishing civilization had existed in the Aegean area prior to the coming of the Greeks. These accounts were regarded as legendary until the discovery of a number of pre-Greek cultural centers by comparatively recent archaeological research demonstrated their essential accuracy. The uncovering of these sites, particularly the excavation of the great Cretan royal palace at Cnossus, constituted one of the most significant and spectacular. chapters in the annals of archaeology. 

The pioneer in this research was Heinrich Schliemann, a German who had come to the United States and, during the course of a successful business career, manifested an ever increasing interest in the Homeric poems. Upon retirement from business, he determined to devote the rest of his life to an attempt to demonstrate that the Homeric literature was rooted in historic facts. Beginning in 1870, he conducted excavations at Hissarlik in Asia Minor and ultimately uncovered nine strata of ruins, the second of which he believed to be the ruins of Troy. Later research convinced Dorpfeld that the sixth rather than the second level was to be identified with the Troy of the Iliad; and still later work by Blegen showed that Level VIIa was that of Homer's Troy. In the meantime, Schliemann transferred his activities to Greece, where on the Argolic peninsula he discovered the site of ancient Mycenae and proved that a highly developed culture existed in Greece that antedated the arrival of the Hellenic tribes. 

Even more sensational discoveries were made by Sir Arthur Evans on the island of Crete. His work, begun in 1900, has been completed and crowned by the publication of his monumental volumes describ-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ing the site of Cnossus; while Italian archaeologists have dealt capably with that of Phaestus. Cretan writing has not as yet been completely deciphered. Extant tablets and inscriptions for the most part seem to be merely business archives. In view of these facts, it is impossible to reconstruct the history of Crete much beyond the stage of conjecture. There is no doubt that the island was a kingdom with 

Cnossus as its capital. Absence of fortifications for the defense of the capital indicate that the kingdom possessed a navy sufficiently powerful to make land defenses unnecessary. Foundations of the kingdom go back at least to about 3500 B.C. Contact with Egypt and Asia 

Minor exercised tremendous cultural stimulation, but the high standards of art and craftsmanship were also in large measure the product of native genius. The kingdom reached its zenith by about 1500 B.C. and then rapidly declined until in a weakened condition it fell an easy prey to the incoming Greeks. The rapidity of the decline has led some scholars to believe that a great disaster such as an earthquake may have accelerated the political collapse of the state as well as its cultural decadence.

A most important task of the archaeologists was the careful excavation of the ruins of the royal palace. This structure, built on a hill, was rebuilt several times, and a number of additions were made from time to time. These facts account for its irregular floor plan; the Greek legend of the labyrinth in which maidens were forced to wander until devoured by a monster possibly owes its origin to the intricacy of the palace arrangement. In its final form, the various parts of the structure were grouped around a central rectangular courtyard, 190 feet long and 85 feet wide. Entrance to the courtyard was afforded by gates on the northern, southern, and western sides. On the west side were located the administrative offices and the residential quarters of governmental ministers and functionaries. 

This part of the palace also contained the great throne room used by the monarchs on ceremonial occasions. The eastern side of the palace comprised the royal residence. The walls of the palace were mainly of stone, although mud brick was used to some extent. The edifice probably was five stories in height in some parts, for ruins of a great staircase with five flights are preserved. Sanitary features of the palace were surprisingly modern, particularly in the provision of bathing facilities. Much of the drainage system, which utilized clay and copper piping, is still in working order. 

Craftsmanship and artistic tastes of the ancient Cretans were especially manifested in their ceramic ware, which has never been

excelled for texture, symmetry of form, and beauty of ornamentation. The potter's wheel and the use of the closed oven for baking probably were introduced from Egypt, although the pupils soon surpassed their teachers in the mastery of techniques. Cretan pottery, known as Minoan ware, named after Minos, a legendary king, has been classified into the Early, Middle, and Late Minoan periods on the basis of style. Each of these periods in turn has been subdivided, and the classification serves as a rough chronological framework comparable with the use of sequence dating in the study of predynastic Egypt. Specimens of Early Minoan ware have the decorative designs in light colors imposed on a dark background. In the Middle Minoan style, geometric designs in dark colors stand in bold contrast to the light background, and the texture is considerably finer than in the work of the early period. The culmination of the evolution of the ceramic arts came in the Late Minoan period, particularly with the production of the exquisite Kamares ware. In this type, the conventional geometric designs were replaced by decorative themes drawn from the world of nature and painted in brilliant colors on black or bluish black vessels. 

The artistry and craftsmanship of the ancient Cretans was also brilliantly demonstrated in metal-working. They did work not much inferior to the famous Vaphio cups, found on the Greek mainland, which, finely wrought in gold, are decorated with scenes depicting the capture and training of wild bulls for the amphitheatre. Their metal work may also be illustrated by beautifully inlaid daggers, decorated with hunting scenes, found on the mainland. In sculpture, the statues and ivory figurines, especially those that portray a mother goddess who seems to have been the chief deity, are exquisitely fashioned. It is difficult to evaluate the frescoes on the palace walls from the standpoint of technique because they are badly faded. They are of great value, however, as sources of information in regard to social customs and daily life. A number of them depict the bull fights which, in addition to being the chief amusement, seem to have been invested with religious significance. 

No Cretan literature has as yet been found. The script that has been preserved may have been developed from Egyptian hieroglyphs, but the evidence in support of the theory of independent origin is equally strong. About forty characters were employed in the script, which in its final form was linear, and the letters of each word were joined together as in our script. A chest of tablets containing inscriptions has been found, but these for the most part are

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

inventories, tax registers, and tribute lists. From them we learn, however, that the Cretans utilized a decimal system of computation. 

Weights and measures also were used, while gold double-axes and oxheads were employed to a limited extent as coins. 

Cretan religion centered in the worship of a mother goddess usually represented, in the many votive statues that have been found, as a young girl bearing a dove and a serpent in her hands. She probably was venerated as the origin of life and as the patron of reproduction and growth. A young male deity also was worshipped, who apparently was believed to be the son of the mother goddess, perhaps a mediator between her and mankind. Animal worship, particularly of the bull, was another important feature of the religion. It is also of interest to note that the cross had a symbolical significance in 

Cretan ritual.

The great palace at Mycenae was built on a hill and was surrounded by enormous walls equipped with towers and bastions. 

The walls are from 16 to nearly 60 feet in thickness and are so massive that a Greek legend ascribed their construction to the work of one-eyed giants, or Cyclops; they are therefore sometimes spoken of as the Cyclopean walls. A number of gates pierced the walls. One of these is the famous Lioness Gate. A huge triangular stone which fits into the wall surmounts the top of the gateway, and on it are two finely chiseled figures of lionesses with their forepaws resting on a pillar. In contrast to Crete, which was a naval power, the well-nigh impregnable fortifications of the citadel at Mycenae indicate that it was a land power. Since remains of roads have been found leading out from the site, it seems likely that it was the capital of a kingdom of considerable size that probably embraced at least all of Argos.

Second only in importance to the palace were the graves and tombs discovered by the archaeologists. The oldest were simply vertical shaft graves covered over with huge stone blocks. In these shaft graves were found the gold hoards, with gold diadems, deathmasks, inlaid daggers, and beautiful porcelains. Toward the close of the period of the greatness of Mycenae, the peculiar beehiveshaped tombs were employed. Their introduction may mark the infusion of a new element in the populace. 

Ruins of a great palace surrounded by Cyclopean walls were also found at Tiryns. This structure contained two large halls, one for the men of the court and the other for the women. The men's chamber was built on a rectangular court and was entered by a portico and

vestibule. It had a concrete floor and was equipped with a stone hearth; the roof was supported by rows of wooden columns of which only the stone bases remain. 

While it has been impossible to give a narrative history of these pre-Greek states, it has been irrefutably established that flourishing civilizations existed in Asia Minor, on the island of Crete, and in parts of the Greek peninsula prior to the coming of the Greeks. Although this ancient Aegean culture had declined before the Greek migrations, there is no doubt that the cultural foundation it afforded to the Greek newcomers was a basic reason for the rapid evolution of the wonderful Hellenic civilization. 

THE GREEK MIGRATIONS 

Our knowledge of the racial origins and early migratory movements of the Greeks is very meager. They probably were of 

Alpine racial stock and entered the Greek peninsula from the north, perhaps from their original homeland in the Danube valley. 

Immigration into the Greek peninsula and neighboring regions was a long, gradual process, punctuated by several successive periods of accelerated, large-scale migration. The first of these major periods of influx was the invasion of the Achaeans, about 1200 B.C., who settled in north and central Greece and probably also secured Crete and a number of the Cyclades. A large group of the 

Achaean settlers in central Greece subsequently pushed southward across the Isthmus of Corinth into the Peloponnesus, or south Greece. Others took possession of the island of Lesbos and began to colonize in Asia Minor where they were enabled to gain a foothold only after the decisive defeat of Ilium (Troy). The second major invasion was that of the Ionians who, after a short sojourn in central Greece, colonized Chios and Samos. A third group, known as the Aeolians, ultimately established themselves in Asia Minor; since the Aeolians were confused with their kinsmen, the Ionians, the region subsequently became known as Ionia. The last great migration was that of the Dorians who, about 1100 B.C., conquered central and south Greece and assimilated their predecessors in those regions. 

Geographic factors were largely responsible for the fundamental pattern of the history of the Greeks after their conquest of the peninsula. The multitude of indentations of the Greek coast-line and the large number of islands in the Aegean impelled the newcomers toward maritime activities. The many mountain ranges of the peninsula were a great obstacle to unity, and geographical barriers fostered

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the particularism which was to be reflected in the city-states as the typical political organisms of ancient Greece. Natural resources were adequate. The soil was rich and the variety of climatic conditions made possible the cultivation of a wide range of crops, of which wheat, barley, grapes, olives, and flax were the most important. 

Timber and fine building stone were available in abundance. Rich copper, iron, and silver deposits were soon discovered in various parts of the peninsula and in Thrace, affording basic sources of wealth to the states fortunate enough to possess them. 

Geographically, the Greek peninsula is divided into three welldefined portions. North Greece is separated from central Greece by mountains which, however, are pierced by several passes. The leading states of the north in ancient times were Thessaly and Epirus. 

In central Greece, the most important states were Attica, with Athens as its principal city, and Boeotia, with Thebes as its chief civic center. Central Greece is connected to the Peloponnesus, or south 

Greece, by the Isthmus of Corinth upon which was located the great ancient state of Corinth. The northeast of the Peloponnesus is formed by the peninsula of Argolis, which in ancient times contained a state of the name of Argos. West of Argolis were Arcadia and Elis respectively. In the southeast of the Peloponnesus was Laconia, all of which became subject to the rule of Sparta as did the section called Messenia, to the west of Laconia. 

Our knowledge of Greece in the archaic period is derived from careful study of the Homeric poems supplemented by archaeological evidence. The question as to the authorship of the epics ascribed to 

Homer has agitated literary critics since the days of the great Alexandrian school. With the work of Wolfe, an eminent Homeric scholar of the eighteenth century, critics became more and more convinced that the works were not the product of single authorship. 

In recent years, however, students, particularly in the United States, have largely adopted the view that the Iliad and probably the Odyssey were written by Homer, a professional bard who may have come from the island of Chios. It is doubtless true that he utilized tales and legends that long had been in circulation, but he wove them together and committed them to writing.

Upon completion of their great migratory movements, the Greeks settled in villages, and with the abandonment of their nomadic existence, agriculture became their primary means of subsistence. This transition, of course, profoundly stimulated the evolution of social and political institutions. The solidarity of the family was the core of

the Greek social structure. The patriarchal authority of the father was all-embracing, for he was the absolute master of wife, children, and the spouses and progeny of his children. Families who traced. their descent from common ancestry formed a larger social group known as the kindred, or clan. All members of a kindred were jointly bound to avenge an injury done one of their number and were likewise liable for the acts of a member of their own group. 

This meant that feuds between the clans were common; indeed, many of them continued for generations. A number of kindreds in turn made up the tribe. In addition to these basic social groups, the men belonged for military and religious purposes to voluntary associations known as phratries, or brotherhoods. 

Some centuries after the settlement of the Greeks in the peninsula, many of the tribal villages began to combine to form city-states. 

Several factors served to promote this development. Considerations of defense often impelled a number of villages to unite around a center that could be adequately fortified. Indeed, the Greek word polis, or city, originally meant fortified place. Then, too, economic reasons sometimes served to bring about the consolidation. A village located on a good harbor or near mineral deposits would flourish and ultimately absorb neighboring villages. Religion sometimes played a part, for a village might be located at or near a shrine, which would occasion its growth and the annexation of the environs. 

The city-states originally were ruled by kings, for monarchy had been developed from its roots in tribal chieftainship during the period of consolidation. A Council of Elders made up of the heads of the families of the state acted in advisory and judicial capacities and probably represented a survival of the governing councils in the tribal villages. It is likely that important matters were submitted to a general assembly of free, adult males for at least their nominal approval. Later in the archaic period, the authority of the kings was sharply curtailed by the rise of the nobles. With the evolution of the institution of private property, it was natural that some who were more capable and frugal than their neighbors should acquire larger tracts of land which grew into great estates and served as the economic basis for aristocracy. The aristocrats curbed royal authority by limiting tenure of the office, by making the kingship elective rather than hereditary, and finally by depriving the office of many former powers and functions and assigning them to elected magistrates chosen from the ranks of the nobility. 

With the rise of the large estates owned by the nobles, the yeo-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

men, or small-scale landowners, were finding it increasingly difficult to meet the competition afforded by the large estates and the growing utilization of servile labor. It was frequently necessary for them to obtain loans of seed, implements, and stock by mortgaging their lands at excessive rates of interest. When they were unable to repay such loans, they lost their lands and in many instances were reduced to the status of serfs or even enslaved to their creditors. The citystates were for the most part self-sufficient, although there were some commodities, particularly articles of luxury, such as fine pottery, glass, metal ware, and woolen cloth of superior quality which were imported through various agencies.

Greek religious belief invested the deities with human qualities. 

They walked among men and exercised direct control over worldly affairs. Zeus, lord of the heavens, was regarded as the head of the pantheon. He and his wife, Hera, presided over the abode of the gods on the summit of Mount Olympus. Demeter, goddess of fertilization, and her daughter, Persephone, as well as Apollo, the sun god, likewise were generally venerated. Each of the city-states in addition had its special patron deities. Little emphasis was placed on the belief in immortality. The blessed fields of Elysium were the reward of heroes and statesmen. It was doubtless the lack of a popular cult of immortality that was largely responsible for the rise of Orphism, which will be discussed in a later connection. 

THE AGE OF COLONIZATION 

In the period c. 800-600 B.C., most of the Greek states were engaged in colonizing activities which in broad outline were a prolongation of the earlier migratory movements. Geographical factors, particularly the large number of harbors, made inevitable the maritime activities of the Greeks. Proximity of the islands of the Aegean naturally stimulated interest in the colonization of those not already occupied, while the settlements in Ionia during the age of the great migrations served to point the way for further colonizing ventures in that region. Then, too, there were obvious economic advantages to be gained from the foundation of colonies. They could serve as markets for the products of the mother states and could also in many instances furnish new sources of necessary raw materials. 

The colonization movement to a considerable degree was an expression of the economic and social discontent that prevailed in the Greek states. The evolution of large plantations owned by the aristocrats (eupatrids), coupled with rigorous enforcement of harsh debt

laws, had reduced many small-scale farmers to penury or even servitude. Governments of the city-states had come under the control of the aristocrats who had abridged the powers of the kings, with the result that efforts to alleviate the desperate plight of the yeomanry hardly could be expected from governments which represented the very interests largely responsible for their condition. Colonization promised to be an effective solution to these problems; impoverished citizens could go abroad as colonists to rehabilitate themselves by the acquisition of new homesteads free of debt. Their removal would mean the end or at least the material diminution of unrest that might well ultimately lead to revolution and the ruin of the privileged class; therefore the governing authorities were not disposed to place obstacles in the path of colonial ventures. 

Colonizing enterprises usually began on the initiative of a number of interested individuals who petitioned the government of their state for permission. If the government approved, the prospective colonists chose a founder who, with the ratification of his selection by the authorities, served as the leader of the forthcoming undertaking. An important step in the procedure was the consultation of the Delphic Oracle; if the oracle declared that the projected colony would be successful, an invitation was issued to prospective participants. When the requisite number was secured, a charter was granted by the government in which was embodied a statement of the relations that were to prevail between colony and mother state. The charter also contained stipulations as to the allocation of lands on the site of the colony.

Many colonies were established along the coast lines of the Black Sea. Miletus, leading city of Ionia, founded settlements along the southern shore of the sea even before the great period of colonizing activity. Shortly before the middle of the seventh century before 

Christ, Megara founded Byzantium and Chalcedon; these cities commanded the Bosphorus and access to the Euxine. Megara also located colonies on the south coast of the Black Sea and on the Hellespont. 

Miletus responded by the foundation of Sinope and Trapezus; by her foundation of Cyzicus on the Propontis and Abydus on the Hellespont she neutralized the dominant advantage that had been enjoyed by Megara. In the meantime, colonies were founded in 

Thrace and northeast Greece. Most of the colonies in the latter region were established by Chalcis, leading city of the island of Euboea, and the region ultimately was known as Chalcidice. 

A number of colonies were founded in Sicily and Italy. Chalcis

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and Eretria settled Cumae and Puteoli on the bay of Naples; shortly afterwards, Chalcis founded Naples. Settlers from Messenia founded 

Rhegium, while Sybaris on the western side of the Tarentine coast owed its foundation to colonists from Achaea. The only Spartan colony was Tarentum; since Sparta enjoyed abundant opportunity for expansion in the Peloponnesus it was not necessary for her to establish dependencies abroad.

The most important colony in Sicily was Syracuse, which was destined to play an important role in the later history of Greece. It was founded by colonists from Corinth who also acquired control of the island of Corcyra. As will be seen, these Greek colonies in south 

Italy and in Sicily exercised a great influence in the development of Roman culture. Because of the presence of Carthaginian trading posts in the western Mediterranean region, there was little opportunity for the Greeks to expand west of Italy, with the result that the Phocaean colony of Massilia (Marseilles) was the only important settlement in that area.

From the standpoint of general history, the most significant result of the colonization movement was the creation over an enormously wide area of scores of cities each of which was to become a center for the diffusion of Hellenic culture. Colonization could not fail to strengthen a feeling of pan-Hellenism; common language and religion, together with closely similar institutions and customs, in large measure overshadowed differences that had loomed large in the home states.

As was anticipated, the founding of colonies greatly stimulated commerce and industry. Grain, fish, and various luxury products were imported in constantly increasing quantity by the states of the 

Greek mainland, which in turn exported cloth, pottery, and metal products. The rise of a shipbuilding industry was striking evidence of the tremendous growth of the carrying trade. Industrial development was so marked that some writers have applied the term "Industrial Revolution" to the period. Miletus became a flourishing center for the manufacture of carpets and drapery; the iron industry of the island of Chios was known throughout the Hellenic world; while the cloth of Aegina and Megara, as well as the bronze products of Aegina and Chalcis, were equally well known. 

The expansion of commerce and industry was doubtless much facilitated by the introduction of coinage. The Greek coinage was based on that of Lydia; a silver piece known as the drachma was the basic unit. Both the coinage of Aegina and that of Euboea were in
