general use throughout the Greek world. Money in turn made possible the accumulation of liquid capital the possessors of which were constantly seeking opportunities for investment. Expansion of credit facilities went hand in hand with quickened commercial and industrial activities.

The colonization movement failed materially to alleviate the discontent that was prevalent in the older states. Commercial and industrial expansion to be sure presented many opportunities for profit and the acquisition of wealth, but comparatively few persons had the ability, energy, and capital required to take advantage of such opportunities. A new aristocracy therefore was coming into existence which demanded and frequently obtained political influence commensurate with its economic importance. The new-rich were just as ready to exploit the masses as the landed aristocracy had been. 

Agricultural credit became much tighter, with the increasing employment of capital in commercial and industrial ventures, with the result that high interest rates, harsh debt laws, and foreclosure of mortgages were still inciting bitter complaint. Hesiod's Works and 

Days presents a graphic picture of the hardships under which the Greek yeomen were laboring. While he extols the dignity of labor and urges his readers to work and save, it is clear from his plaintive cry for social justice that more than his salutary advice was needed. 

Thoroughgoing reforms were requisite and failure to inaugurate them was a basic cause for the rise of the tyrants, or dictators. 

SPARTA TO ABOUT 550 B.C. 

The Peloponnesus was settled by the great Dorian migration of 

1100 B.C. Argos, on the Argolic peninsula, was the first state to evolve as a major political entity, but it soon was obscured by the growing power of Sparta. The peculiar institutions of Sparta, particularly its rigorous subordination of the individual to the interests of the state, have made its history a subject of interest for centuries. In our times, with the ideals of the totalitarian state spreading over the world, we turn with renewed interest to the state which in ancient times was the classic expression of this philosophy of government. 

The population of Laconia, like that of most of the remainder of the Peloponnesus, was Dorian. The formation of the Spartan commonwealth was part of the general movement responsible for the establishment of the Greek city-states. Five villages in the valley of the Eurotas river combined to form the city-state of Sparta, and this, in turn, was the nucleus around which the remainder of Laconia

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ultimately was organized by conquest. The absorption of Laconia, however, was merely the preliminary step in Spartan expansion. The promontories of Malea and Taenarum were annexed, as was also the island of Cythera off the southern coast. The region to the west, known as Messenia, then was subjugated, and with its acquisition Sparta had annexed all the territory it could efficiently rule in view of the comparatively small number of citizens. This explains the fact that Taras in south Italy was the only colony of Spartan foundation, for the state had found adequate opportunity for expansion in the Peloponnesus.

The status of the conquered peoples was destined in large measure to condition the future history of the Spartan commonwealth and impart a peculiar nature to its institutions. The populations of about a hundred towns were classified as perioeci. They had to perform military service upon demand, and in return were given virtually monopolistic privileges for the conduct of trade and industry. Most of the conquered people, however, particularly in Messenia, were held as belots or serfs. They were assigned to plots of arable land for the use of which they paid from one-sixth to one-half of the produce therefrom to the Spartan citizens whom their labor supported. As can be seen, the structure of Spartan society provided a scheme whereby a small minority of citizens were supported by the labors of the belots and the economic activities of the perioeci. The citizens, therefore, were free to dedicate themselves unreservedly to the service of the state.

About the middle of the seventh century Sparta was confronted with one of the gravest crises in her history when Argos recovered a large measure of her former power and Messenia rebelled. The revolt of the Messenians threatened to overthrow the whole social and economic structure of the state. With characteristic resolution and heroism the citizenry reëstablished their rule in the revolting areas. 

After the belots were reduced to obedience they were subjected to annual proclamation of outlawry, and a picked group of Spartan. youths was designated each year to hunt down and slay such of the "outlaws" as were considered dangerous to the state.

The crisis through which the state had successfully passed left a profound impression on its subsequent institutional development. 

Above all, the citizenry were convinced that the social structure of the state could only be maintained if the military supremacy of the Spartan minority would be established beyond the possibility of subsequent challenge. It was therefore necessary for the individual to

subordinate himself without qualification to the state. Democratic principles of government obviously would be incompatible with such a philosophy and were ruthlessly repudiated. The solidarity of the citizenry was further strengthened by the fact that the suppression of the Messenian revolt had exercised a levelling tendency, for the heavy-armed hoplites, or infantry, had proved their supremacy to cavalry and thus removed the military basis of aristocracy. 

The fundamental philosophy of the Spartan state was fully implemented by the institution of the so-called Lycurgan Reforms which may have been the work of a single statesman, even though it cannot be proved that Lycurgus to whom the program has traditionally been ascribed was an historical personage. With the inauguration of the reforms, the state assumed control of the lives of the citizens from the cradle to the grave. Spartan boys whose physiques were sufficiently strong to save them from abandonment as infants were trained in the home until they reached their seventh year. At that time they were taken from their parents and enrolled in cadet corps. 

Here, under the supervision of the eirenes, or older youths, they were submitted to a rigorous gymnastic training designed to fit them for their subsequent military exercises. No mental training other than the memorizing of the martial poems of Tyrtaeus was included in the program. Since a prime objective of the training was to inure the youths to hardship and suffering, they were exposed to the rigors of climate and the pangs of hunger. The meager rations were expected to goad the youths into stealing to supplement their starvation fare and thus promote cunning and resourcefulness, but they were punished by cruel floggings if caught on such foraging expeditions. As a demonstration of the success of their training, the youths submitted themselves to the agony of the lash before the altar of Artemis, and it was considered a high honor to be crowned victor at these ceremonial flagellations. The training of Spartan girls, although under the supervision of the parents, was also severe, and Spartan women were renowned throughout the Greek world for their beauty and stalwart physiques.

At the age of twenty, the young men began the intensive military exercises for which their years of gymnastic training had prepared them. They led a communal existence, living in barracks and taking their meals at the common tables. Each man brought an assigned quota of food to the table to which he belonged. His contribution, of course, came from the tract of land allocated to him and cultivated by the helots settled on it. No money, other than iron pieces,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

was legally in use. At the age of thirty, full civic status was attained and marriage was permitted. Marriage did not completely terminate the communal features of Spartan life, however, for the men were still boarded at common tables. Military training was continued until the citizen reached his sixtieth year, after which he was expected to serve the state in civil capacities. 

The state nominally was ruled by two kings, elected for life by the citizens, whose choice, however, had to be confined to the two hereditary royal families. By the period of the Lycurgan Reforms, royal authority had been sharply curtailed. The kings retained their positions as religious leaders and their jurisdiction in cases involving the adoption of children or the betrothal of orphaned heiresses. Major executive and judicial functions were vested in five magistrates, known as ephors, who were annually chosen by lot, with all citizens eligible to selection. Each of the five magistrates had equal powers, and in case of division of opinion the majority prevailed. The ephors had jurisdiction over all civil cases with the exception of those still under the competence of the kings, and exercised criminal jurisdiction in all cases involving the perioeci. They were responsible for public morals and the policing of the state. In time of war, the citizens in their assembly decided which of the kings was to be entrusted with command of the army, and two ephors accompanied him in the field to ensure capable discharge of his duties. 

Twenty-eight citizens at least sixty years of age made up the Council, a surviving aristocratic element in the constitution. The members were chosen for life by acclamation of the Assembly. 

The Council, together with the two kings, served as judges in all criminal cases excepting those involving perioeci. It also prepared legislation for submission to the Assembly. The Assembly (apella), made up of all citizens, met every full moon to accept or reject laws and policies submitted to it by the Council and ephors. Its powers of independent legislation were curbed by the rule that its acts were invalid until proclaimed prior to its adjournment by the ephors and Council. The ephors or the Council thus could exercise a veto by the simple expedient of withholding proclamation. The Assembly was a democratic governmental organ. It might readily have acquired powers comparable with those ultimately exercised by the Athenian Assembly, but with the dedication of the Spartan state to militarism such development was frustrated.

ATHENS TO ABOUT 550 B.C. 

Attica was occupied by Greek settlers as early as the Mycenaean period and was little disturbed by the great waves of Greek immigration. The coalition of Attic villages into the city-state of Athens was part of the general movement going on throughout the entire peninsula.

The Athenian state was originally ruled by a king, but the rise of a class of noble landowners (eupatrids) soon curtailed royal authority. Hereditary monarchy was replaced by elective kingship, with the tenure ultimately fixed at one year. When the office thus was opened to annual election, it had become merely a position of religious dignity. An elected official known as the chief archon (archon eponymos) assumed the civil executive powers once wielded by the kings, and another aristocratic magistrate, known as the polemarch, was vested with command of military and naval forces. During the seventh century, the magistracy was enlarged in view of the growth of the city and the commensurately more complex duties to be performed. Six thesmothetae were annually chosen to perform judicial functions; after a time, they, together with the archon eponymos, polemarch, and king (basileus) were formed into a college of nine archons. Other officials were added to administer public revenues, let contracts for public works, manage the sale of property that had escheated to the state, administer religious endowments, and exercise police functions.

Members of the college of archons, upon the expiration of their year of office, entered the Council of the Areopagus. The functions of this body were advisory and judicial; its most important function was to serve as public prosecutor for all offenses against the state. 

All citizens perhaps were eligible to participate in the meetings of the ecclesia, or Assembly. The Assembly elected magistrates, but its choice was confined to the aristocrats eligible to hold the offices. 

Legislative proposals submitted by the archons were submitted for its concurrence, but this was a mere formality since its decision was not binding.

Athenian society was timocratic, that is, political privileges were graduated in accordance with wealth. The class divisions originated for military purposes. The aristocratic hippeis, the wealthy landowners who alone were eligible to hold office, included those who could afford the equipment to serve as cavalry. The zeugitae, or yeomen, with small land holdings, served as heavy-armed infantry. The

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

poorest class, the thetes, was made up of laborers and artisans who were either exempt from military service or merely liable for service as militia with nondescript equipment. A large proportion of the total population were serfs who worked on the lands of the aristocrats and paid one-sixth of their produce as rent. If their payments lapsed, they were reduced to actual slavery. 

There was much discontent in Athens because of the undue power of the nobles. The absence of a legal code was doubtless one of the most serious grievances of the plebeians. The aristocrats were regarded as the custodians of the laws which were bequeathed from generation to generation by word of mouth. Such traditions naturally were colored by considerations of self-interest; since the law was whatever the aristocrats said it was, their political dominance and economic exploitation of the masses were strongly entrenched. 

There could be no curtailment of aristocratic prerogatives until there was an organic law that could be invoked to defend the oppressed. 

Although elemental justice demanded the codification of the law, the aristocrats successfully opposed all such efforts until a crisis demonstrated the imperative need for a conciliatory policy. 

In 640 B.C. Cylon was crowned victor of the Olympic Games.

Upon return to Athens, he attempted to utilize his popularity through an effort to seize control of the government. He doubtless had secured promise of aid from his father-in-law, Theagenes, tyrant of Megara, and he hoped that the prevalence of discontent in Athens would ensure success of the bold venture. Megacles, however, hurriedly mobilized conservatives and moderates and expelled the usurper. Although the discontented elements of the Athenian populace were not as yet ready to support the establishment of tyranny (boss rule), far-sighted aristocrats were convinced that concessions were necessary if similar efforts were to be averted. 

In accordance with this sentiment, Draco, as chief archon, was given plenary authority to prepare a code, and he completed the task in 622 B.C. Although later Greek writers declared that the laws were extremely harsh, there is no evidence in surviving fragments of the legislation to support this contention. Such harsh features as may have characterized unknown portions of the law probably represented the preservation of established practices rather than reactionary innovations on the part of the lawgiver. Portions of the laws which have been preserved deal with homicide. Prior to the issue of the code there was no distinction between deliberate and accidental homicides. When a person was slain, his kindred were bound to

avenge his death and this practice led to bloody feuds that frequently continued for generations. 

The Draconian legislation established crude methods of trial to replace the blood feuds; the rule of law superseded the rule of violence. Innocent persons pursued by avenging kindreds were granted sanctuary on the Areopagus. Here, standing on the stone of implacability, they attested their innocence by oath, and if there was no supernatural evidence that they swore falsely they were acquitted. Persons guilty of involuntary manslaughter were accorded trial in the sanctuary of Pallas before a group of judges (ephetae). If the plea of the defendant was substantiated he was allowed to go into exile, to return whenever the relatives of the slain person granted their permission. A similar method of trial was instituted for the trial of homicides in which a plea of self-defense was entered. 

Draco's codification of the law was indubitably a popular victory. 

Even if certain provisions were harsh, there was now a fixed standard to which all could appeal and which set limits to aristocratic pretensions. There was still need, however, for broad economic and political concessions, and in response to the continued agitation for reform, Solon was elected archon eponymos in 594 B.C. and authorized to inaugurate a comprehensive program. Solon was ideally fitted to assume the difficult task assigned to him. He was by birth and training an aristocrat, yet his sympathetic attitude toward the poor was well known: His liberal views gave assurance of real reform, while his aristocratic connections allayed the fears of those who had hitherto resisted reform in the conviction that it would mean the ruin of the wealthy landowners. 

A major achievement of Solon's program was the partial rehabilitation of the yeomanry by the cancellation of mortgages on small freeholds on the ground that the extortionate interest exacted had liquidated the principal. Enslaved debtors were emancipated, and future servitude for debt was forbidden. Although commercial debts were not dealt with by the reformer, who realized the importance of maintaining sound business credit, the adoption of the Euboic coinage had a stimulating effect on commerce.

The timocratic organization of the state was retained, but the highest social class, the hippeis, was divided into two groups. In the first group were placed those whose annual income was 500 units or more, each unit (medimnus) being equivalent to one and one-half bushels of grain or eight and one-half gallons of oil or wine. The second group comprised those with an income of from 300 to 500 units.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Eligibility to the magistracies was confined to these two upper classes. Most of the yeomen were classified as zeugitae with incomes of from 150 to 300 units, while the rest of the citizenry made up the thetes whose numbers were augmented by the inclusion of those recently emancipated from the serfdom to which their debts had consigned them.

A major political reform, attributed to the Solonian program, was the creation of the Council of the Four Hundred (bule), with one hundred members representing each of the four Athenian tribes. 

The new council, in which all classes save the thetes were eligible to serve, had electoral, advisory, and perhaps legislative functions. 

The ecclesia continued to meet with all citizens eligible to attend, but its authority continued to be more nominal than real. 

A most significant advance toward democracy was the creation of the jury courts on which even the thetes were permitted to serve. 

The juries afforded protection against arbitrary action by the magistrates, and the inclusion of the thetes was pointing the way to their eventual attainment of greater political privileges. Other enactments credited to Solon included the authorization of females to inherit property, the enlargement of testamentary rights so as to permit the bequest of property to non-relatives, laws against defamation of the dead, and sumptuary legislation that attempted to prevent extravagance, particularly in funerary rites. Later tradition also held that citizenship was granted to resident foreigners to encourage industrial progress.

One salient weakness perhaps has been noticed in the reforms. Although the yeomanry had benefited by the abolition of mortgages and the exemption of the persons of debtors from seizure by their creditors, no redress was afforded to those who already had lost their land by foreclosure. There still were many landless farmers, but 

Solon had refused to confiscate land from the aristocrats for distribution to the impoverished. Failure to include a land redistribution scheme in his program meant the continuance of agitation and, as we shall see, ultimately promoted the establishment of tyranny, the very thing which the Solonian reforms had been designed to avert.

CHAPTER Greece in the Age of the Tyrants 

N the period from about 650 B.C. to 500 B.C., many of the Greek states came under the control of tyrants, or boss-rulers. The term tyrant must not be thought of in its modern connotation. 

A tyrant was one who abrogated normal governing authority and ruled without constitutional sanction. He was maintained in power by military force or other coercive means, but his rule was not necessarily harsh or extortionate. It was only after tyranny was repudiated as a form of government by the Greeks that the term acquired its present meaning.

The rise of tyranny was inseparably associated with the continuance of economic and social discontent in the various states. The rise of large estates tilled by slaves or serfs had virtually ruined the yeomanry. Harsh debt laws, pitilessly enforced, drove more and more of the former peasant proprietors into the ranks of the landless and servile. Colonization had not permanently relieved these conditions, for with the expansion of commerce and industry a new aristocracy had been created whose wealth rested not on ownership of land but on successful use of the opportunities presented with increased trade. 

Governments of the states were in the hands of the aristocrats who naturally, wished to perpetuate their power and frustrate economic and social reforms that threatened their prerogatives. To be sure, grudging concessions from time to time momentarily allayed discontent, but no permanent adjustment could be reached without a comprehensive program for land redistribution and debt liquidation. 

It must be remembered that the aristocrats themselves were not in unanimity despite the identity of their economic interests. The landed aristocracy and the nouveaux riches frequently were in opposition to each other; personal jealousies and family rivalries militated against the solidarity of the wealthy. It was comparatively easy, therefore, for the masses successfully to revolt against dominant aristocracies, but it was much more difficult to organize effec-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tive governmental institutions to replace those they overthrew. The common folk were politically inexperienced, and in most states there were no institutions to implement democratic principles. In view of these conditions, it is not surprising that men of vigor, ability, and daring made use of prevalent discontent to gain power when turbulence, often approaching anarchy, demonstrated the inability of the masses effectively to govern themselves. 

The first tyrannies were established in Ionia. Thrasybulus of Miletus mobilized the disgruntled elements of the populace and usurped control of the city. Much of the subsequent prosperity of the state was due to the wisdom of his economic policies. Somewhat later, Pittacus made himself master of Mitylene, the chief city of the island of Lesbos. The fact that his regime was ratified for a ten-year term by a popular referendum shows how the power of tyrants sometimes was firmly rooted in the support of the people. 

On the Greek mainland, the first successful tyranny was created in Corinth by the Cypselids. For generations, the Corinthian state had been governed by the aristocratic family of the Bacchiadae. In 

657 B.C. Cypselus, with support recruited from all social classes, organized a revolution that resulted in the expulsion of the ruling family and the distribution of their confiscated property among the impoverished citizens. The Corinthian tyranny reached its zenith under Periander, son of Cypselus. Vigorous and enlightened encouragement of commerce gave to the city an outstanding position in the commercial life of Greece that it maintained for centuries. A lavish program for the beautification of the city gave stimulus to the evolution of architectural forms. Poets, like Arion, were encouraged by the patronage of the tyrant, and prevailing interest in the arts led to significant technical improvements, particularly in the field of sculpture. The reaction against the Corinthian tyranny was in large measure the result of the commercial expansion which Periander's policies had so ably promoted. In 586 B.C. Psammetichus, Periander's successor, was overthrown, and a commercial oligarchy imposed their rule as firmly as had the Bacchiadae prior to the Cypselid revolt.

The connection between popular discontent and the rise of tyranny was also clearly shown in Megara. The state had come under the domination of wealthy families owning the important weaving industry. When their control of the state became intolerably oppressive, the discontented citizenry supported the establishment of a tyranny by the adventurer, Theagenes. Conservatives and mod-

RECONSTRUCTION OF PALACE OF SARGON II STELE OF NARAM-SIN ASSYRIAN WINGED BULL

STONE DRAINS AT CNOSSUS

erates, however, soon joined forces and overthrew the tyrant, and the old order was restored as the only feasible means of ending the disorder caused by the revolution and counter-revolution. The ruling aristocrats, however, profited by the brief experience with tyranny and alleviated discontent by granting important economic and political concessions. Debtors were reimbursed for extortionate interest charges they had paid, and usury was legally curbed. Full civic rights were extended to those who dwelt in the rural environs of the metropolis to allay the bitterness between urban and rural populaces that had created so much difficulty. Enrollment of the rural citizens was accompanied by their inclusion in the state assembly, and the broadened base of government at least partly compensated for the power again wielded by the industrial magnates. 

The short-lived Megarian tyranny was closely related with Cylon's abortive efforts to seize control of Athens, for promises of support from his father-in-law, Theagenes, doubtless led him to attempt the coup. As we have seen, Cylon was repulsed, but the aristocrats were convinced that concessions were necessary to forestall similar attacks. It was this sentiment that motivated the appointment of Draco to serve as the codifier of the law. When discontent continued despite the popular victory that followed the promulgation of the Draconian legislation, the aristocracy introduced the memorable reform program of Solon to stave off another tyrannical regime. Solon's legislation embraced major economic and political concessions to the poor and oppressed, but his refusal to initiate a program of land redistribution caused profound disappointment.

The immediate causes for the establishment of tyranny in Athens emerged from a war between Athens and Megara for the possession of the island of Salamis. The Athenian military operations were conducted in a desultory manner, and criticism of the commanders mounted. Command finally was entrusted to Pisistratus whose energy and competence brought the war to a speedy and triumphant conclusion. Upon his return to Athens, Pisistratus was the hero of the hour and the hope of those who wished to overthrow the aristocratic government and establish economic reforms. When Pisistratus claimed that an attempt had been made to assassinate him, he was authorized to employ bodyguards. The rapidity with which he increased the size of his retinue, however, made it evident that he was plotting revolution, and before his preparations were complete, he was denounced and driven into exile. Enforced exile was not a crushing blow to the ambitious adventurer, for in Thrace he gained con-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

trol of silver mines that enabled him to accumulate financial resources to expedite his return. He recruited followers and doubtless sent bribes to influential persons in Athens to ensure a favorable reception. When the news arrived that Athens again had lost possession of 

Salamis, and efforts for its recovery had proved abortive, Pisistratus hastened to Attica and, after decisively defeating the conservative forces at the battle of Pallene (c. 546 B.C.), entered Athens in triumph.

Aristocrats and conservatives who had vainly opposed the tyrant were punished by exile and confiscation of their property. Land thus sequestered was distributed among landless farmers who agreed to pay one-tenth of their annual income to their benefactor. By this arrangement, Pisistratus assured himself a fairly constant revenue, indispensable for continued political power. Of far greater significance was the fact that the land redistribution had put the copestone on the economic reforms of Solon. 

The regime of Pisistratus proved eminently beneficial to the masses, while his brilliant foreign policy that resulted in the establishment of partial Athenian control of the Hellespont was to prove vitally important for the future of the state. The dangers of absolute rule, however, were fully demonstrated when Hippias succeeded his father as tyrant (c. 528 B.C.). His harsh and oppressive rule brought on a revolution, led by Harmodius and Aristogiton, that drove him into exile and brought about the death of his brother Hipparchus who may have been associated with him in the government of the state. Hippias ultimately found asylum in the Persian Empire; in 490 B.C. he accompanied the Persian invaders of Greece in the vain hope of restoration.

Important constitutional changes accompanied the expulsion of the tyrants. About 508 B.C. Clisthenes was invested with broad powers so to revamp the political institutions of the commonwealth as to remove the chief causes of unrest. Much of the dissension resulted from the existence of the rival parties of Hill, Plain, and Shore. Then, too, the survival of the old tribal divisions promoted particularism; allegiance to tribe and party took precedence over duty to the state. 

Clisthenes accordingly began his reforms by abolishing the four traditional tribes. He then created ten trittyes from each of the three parties of Hill, Plain, and Shore. From the thirty trittyes thus established with approximately equal party representation, he organized ten new tribes, with their three component trittyes as widely separated from each other as possible. This regrouping of the citizenry

dealt a decisive blow to provincialism and partisanship. For local government, about 150 demes were created, and when the scheme was complete every male Athenian who had reached his eighteenth year was a member of a deme, trittye, and tribe. 

Since the Council of the Four Hundred was based on the old tribal division, it was necessary to organize a body that would apportion representation in accordance with the new tribal organization. The reformer accordingly founded the Council of the Five Hundred, with fifty members from each of the ten newly created tribes. 

Choice of the members of the body was made each year by casting lots, and all males of civic status were eligible to be chosen. No citizen could serve for more than two annual terms and these could not be consecutive. Obviously, choice of council members by lot was dangerous unless invested with adequate safeguards. It was accordingly provided that the members of each outgoing Council had the right to annul the choice of a new member who was notoriously unfitted for membership in the body. Executive functions of the Council were discharged by committees of fifty members of the Council known as prytanies, or presidencies, with each committee serving for one-tenth of the year. In this manner, each member of the Council served on one of the ten committees.

The institution of ostracism has also been attributed to the Clisthenean reform program. Citizens were authorized to write on ostraka, or potsherds, the names of individuals whom they considered dangerous to the state. The shards then were deposited in public receptacles. If in any year an individual was named on a sufficiently large number of ostraka, he was required to go into honorable exile for ten years. It was hoped that this rather clumsy expedient would prevent the rise of political adventurers who might attempt to overthrow constitutional government and reëstablish tyranny. 

For military purposes, each of the ten tribes was required to furnish a contingent commanded by an elected general known as a strategus. The ten strategi were to constitute the commanding authority of the state army, with the position of commander-in-chief rotated among them. This soon was recognized as impractical; a commander-in-chief, known as the chief strategus, was then elected by the whole citizenry, and his nine colleagues were elected by the tribes exclusive of the one of which the commander-in-chief was a member. Under the stress of the Persian Wars, the office of chief strategus rapidly was invested with general executive functions aside from military activities. Upon the conclusion of the wars, it had be-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

come the chief executive office, the incumbent of which was expected to exercise active leadership of the Assembly and frame state policies for its approval.

GREEK CULTURE IN THE AGE OF THE TYRANTS 

The autonomous city-state was the characteristic Greek political institution. Nevertheless, there were a number of bonds of union between the states which, if permitted to operate without hindrance, promised eventually to achieve national unity. Despite the rivalries of the states and superficial differences in culture and institutions, there was an appreciable sentiment of pan-Hellenism. All non- 

Greeks were barbari, or foreigners; later, when Greek cultural development reached its height, the term barbarian acquired its present meaning.

Religious ties also served to promote nationalism. Twelve states comprised the Delphic Amphictyony, which held two annual congresses, one at Delphi in honor of Apollo, the other at Anthela for the worship of Demeter. While delegates to the congresses were primarily occupied by religious duties, political questions frequently received consideration. Indeed, when Delphi was threatened by the encroachments of Crisa, the League collaborated with Clisthenes, tyrant of Sicyon, in a Sacred War that resulted in the successful defense of the independence of the state. A similar religious association with a membership of seven states was consecrated to the worship of Poseidon.

Another integrating factor was a common belief in the prophecies of the Delphic Oracle which, by the Age of the Tyrants, had acquired greater and more general prestige than that enjoyed by the other great oracle in the sacred grove of Dodona. A temple consecrated to Apollo was erected at Delphi and maintained by a college of priests; in it were deposited the offerings of grateful consultants of the oracle. The structure was believed to be located on or near the navel or center of the earth. Those who consulted the oracle deposited their questions in writing. A priestess (pythia) drank the waters of the sacred spring and gave answer in unintelligible mutterings which were interpreted in hexameter verse by an attendant priest or prophetes. The prophetes naturally was in a position to give ambiguous responses in his verses, yet it must be remembered that the shrine was visited by believers from all over the Greek world so that the priests were enabled to accumulate a great fund of informa-

tion which frequently made it possible for them to give really helpful answers. 

The Eleusinian Mysteries constituted another religious bond of union, for devotees of the cult were recruited from virtually all the states. The rites, originally annual, ultimately were held every five years in a great temple at Eleusis. A central feature of the ceremonies was the great procession from Athens to the shrine in which priests, devotees, and candidates for initiation participated. The cult owed its popularity and widespread membership to the rise of Orphism, or personal religion, that was largely supplementing the older, more formal state religions. This movement is known as 

Orphism because the legendary founder was Orpheus, the Thracian music master. The Eleusinian Mysteries were dedicated primarily to the worship of Demeter and Persephone. The rites, which were witnessed only by those who had been properly initiated, probably symbolized the descent of Persephone into the underworld and her resurrection. This myth, as well as others associated with Orphism, were regarded as divine promises of immortality to man and filled a real need in Greek religious thought, for the idea of immortality had not been emphasized in the older religion. The more personal, mystic features of the cult likewise afforded for the believers an emotional outlet largely lacking in the civic cults of the city-states. 

The athletic games also exercised an obvious influence in the promotion of unity. Competitors from all parts of Greece participated, and contact with athletes from other states could not fail to strengthen bonds of mutual respect and friendship. The Olympic 

Games were held every four years in honor of Zeus. The Pythian 

Games were held at Delphi in honor of Apollo also at four-year intervals. The Isthmian Games at Corinth, dedicated to Poseidon, took place biennially, as did also those at Nemea in honor of Zeus. The 

Olympic Games were begun, according to tradition, in 776 B.C., but it is not possible to fix the inaugural dates of any of the series with certainty. The four-year interval between two successive Olympic 

Games was known as an Olympiad and was later employed by the Greeks as a unit in their chronological computations. The chief event was the stadion, or two-hundred-yard dash. Boxing, wrestling, jumping, javelin and discus throwing also became integral features, while the later addition of chariot racing and the pancration, in which any kind of fighting was permitted, also became popular. Originally, the games were completed in a single day, but soon filled five. At first,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

two judges officiated, but the expansion of the program ultimately necessitated ten.

Participants in the Olympic Games were required to be Greeks of unblemished character who underwent ten months of rigorous training. The participants and their parents had to swear that they had complied with all the conditions of entry. The contests began the first full moon after the twenty-first of June. Proclamation of a truce brought cessation to any hostilities that were then in progress. 

The winner of the pentathlon, comprised of five designated events, was crowned victor of the games. While there was no prize other than a garland of leaves, rewards of a substantial nature awaited the victor upon return to his native state. In Athens, for example, the returning hero was accorded a triumphal reception. A chariot drawn by white horses conveyed him into the city through a breach in the walls expressly made for the purpose. After a round of banquets and orations, he was given a purse of gold and silver together with the privilege of receiving meals at public expense. 

The games not only promoted good will between the states but also stimulated artistic and literary endeavor. Poems and orations were read or declaimed during the course of the games, while the latest products of brush and chisel also were exhibited. Then, too, the victors were often granted the honor of having their statues executed at public expense and this meant further encouragement and patronage for the artists.

Greek literature made great progress during the Age of the Tyrants. In poetry, the chief contribution was the evolution of lyric verse. The stately hexameter of epic poetry was now supplemented by the form known as the elegiac couplet in which lines of six and five metrical feet alternated, ideally suiting the verse to musical accompaniment, although with perfection of style much verse was written for which no accompaniment was intended. The elegiac couplet was used not only in elegies but also in epigrams, epitaphs, love poems, war songs, and moral precepts.

One of the earliest elegiac poets was Callinus of Ephesus (fl. 

650 B.C.), but little of his work has survived. Probably the earliest elegiac poet in Greece proper was Tyrtaeus of Sparta whose martial verses did much to increase the patriotic ardor of the Spartan citizenry and enable them to suppress the great Messenian revolt. Solon, the great reformer, was also an accomplished poet; indeed, he used verse as a vehicle to address the citizenry on political subjects. 

Archilochus of Paros was one of the greatest of the elegiac poets,

but his chief fame lies in his mastery of the iambic verse. This type of verse, in which a short and long syllable regularly alternate in each of the six feet of each line, afforded him a splendid medium for the expression of his tempestuous emotions. His life was a stormy one. 

He was once betrothed to Neobule, daughter of the aristocrat Lycambes, who voided the engagement when he learned of the poet's lowly birth. This called forth such bitter satires from the disappointed suitor that, according to tradition, Neobule and her father were driven to suicide. Then, too, much of his life was lived under a cloud of disgrace, for he had once thrown away his shield in battle and refused to fight, and this also evoked some of his most virulent satire. Semonides of Amorgus, a contemporary of Archilochus, was also a great master of satire. Alcaeus of Lesbos, a politician and world traveler, wrote lyrics depicting the joys of sensual pleasures, describing his wanderings, and expressing his strong hatred of both democracy and tyranny as forms of government. 

Sappho, one of the greatest poetesses in the history of literature, was a friend of Alcaeus. She was born about the middle of the seventh century before Christ and lived most of her life at Mitylene. 

She was an aristocrat and was married, although virtually nothing is known of her family life beyond the fact that she had a daughter. 

For a time, she was engaged in the instruction of young girls in lyrics, dancing, and other graceful accomplishments, and much of her verse is concerned with episodes in the lives of her young charges. About 

190 fragments of her poems have survived of which the longest are the Ode of Aphrodite and the Second Ode quoted by Longinus. 

Her style is marked by simplicity, charm, and frank expression of her feelings. Her career was unique, for Greek women were expected to devote themselves exclusively to domestic duties. They ordinarily, except in Sparta, led secluded existences, and etiquette demanded that they refrain from appearance in public unless attended by a retinue.

Pindar of Thebes excelled in all types of choral lyric; his works are said to have filled seventeen volumes, but only three complete books of Odes and part of a fourth are extant. These Odes (the 

Epinician Odes) are essentially personal songs of praise, many of them in honor of Olympic victors. The poet draws upon myth and legend and frequently adds moral reflections. Pindar was a thorough aristocrat who delighted to glorify the life of his social class. He was especially fond of the pomp and ostentation that surrounded the aristocracy and loved to trace the proud lineages of the subjects of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

his odes. Baccylides of Cos was a younger contemporary of Pindar and was strongly influenced by him. Although he chose the same type of subject and general pattern, his style is simpler and more forthright than that of Pindar.

The origins of Athenian drama may be traced to the period under discussion. Festivals in honor of Dionysus had been held in Athens since the beginning of the state. Under Pisistratus, the festivals were enlarged. A prominent feature of the festivities was interpretative dances performed by men masked and dressed in goat skins. From time to time, the dances were interspersed by chorals, many of which were written by Stesichorus. During the period of the tyranny, an innovation provided that a speaker should come forward at intervals during the performance and address the chorus in interlocutory fashion. Here was the nucleus around which dialogue was developed; dialogue, in turn, evolved into actual drama. The development of music further improved the choral work. The eight-stringed lyre and the flute were introduced, and a system of musical notation was invented. Musical accompaniments for the choruses were used with pleasing effect.

Great progress was made in architecture. While houses remained unprepossessing, much attention was given to the construction of temples. The characteristic temples were plain, rectangular structures, with one chamber known as the naos. In some, however, the naos was entered from a vestibule, or pronaos. The roofs were gabled, and the triangular surfaces at each end, known as the pediments, usually were covered with reliefs. Some temples had columns only at the entrance; others had them at each end (amphiprostyle), while the practice of surrounding the structures by columns (peristyle) was becoming increasingly popular. 

Two orders, or styles, of architecture had emerged by the Age of the Tyrants - Doric and Ionic. In the Doric style, which derived its beauty from simplicity and chaste beauty of line, the columns rested directly on the top of three steps (stylobate), and the capitals were plain. The columns were slightly tapered to prevent the illusion of sagging. The entablature was decorated alternately by three vertical lines (triglyphs) and spaces left blank or adorned with reliefs (metopes). In the Ionic style, the columns were more slender than the Doric and rested on bases. They were more fluted and their capitals were decorated by sculptured representations of curled rams' horns (volutes). The entablature was decorated with a continuous frieze instead of the alternating triglyphs and metopes.

The work of the sculptors already held promise of the artistry that was to lead up to the work of Phidias and Praxiteles. The statue of the tyrannicides, Harmodius and Aristogiton, was a famous product of the formative period. In general, the torsos were heavy and stiff because of imperfect knowledge of anatomy and technical immaturity. Polygnotus enjoyed great repute as a painter, but none of his work has survived. It is quite likely, from the description of his "Painted Porch," that the artist had largely mastered the technique of perspective.

Interest in theoretical science owed its origin to Persian preservation of Chaldean science. Thales of Miletus attracted much attention by predicting the solar eclipse of 585 B.C. He evinced a true scientific attitude toward nature, holding that all natural phenomena occurred in accordance with the operation of natural laws which, moreover, could be discovered and applied by man. He was much interested in "prime matter," or the element from which all other substances were thought to be derived. In his opinion, water was the primary element. Anaximander, a pupil of Thales, held that earth, air, fire, and water were the basic elements of matter and that water was the primary element. Anaximenes, another of the "Atomist 

School," as a result of his experiments with condensation and rarefaction, came to the conclusion that air was the primary element. 

Hecataeus of Miletus prepared a map of the world and propounded an elementary theory of evolution. Pythagoras of Samos acquired a reputation both as a scientist and as a religious mystic. He left his native island and settled in south Italy where he founded a religious sect which was permeated with ascetic ideals. He taught that the earth was a sphere and at least speculated upon the possibility of a heliocentric universe. In plane geometry, his theorem is well known, while his law of strings, i.e., the pitch of a string varies inversely according to its length, was a material contribution to physics.

CHAPTER The Struggle with Persia and the Rise of the Athenian Empire 

HE Persian invasions of Greece in the fifth century before Christ were more than a crisis in the history of Hellas, for the future of Western civilization might have been significantly affected had Greece been incorporated in the Persian Empire. 

Persia was a typical oriental despotism, with a characteristically Eastern culture that had become conventionalized if not decadent. 

Prolonged Persian rule might well have arrested the development of the embryonic Athenian democracy, and the forces of cultural standardization, so evident in the empires of the ancient East, might have hampered the manifestation of the Hellenic genius in philosophy, literature, and the arts. 

A struggle between Greece and Persia was inevitable with the transfer of Ionia from Lydian to Persian rule. Persia had expanded to the Aegean; the Greeks in the period of the migrations and again in the age of colonization had established themselves on the Aegean islands and had founded many thriving cities in Asia Minor. Two great expansion movements thus had come into direct opposition, with 

Asia Minor the center of contention.

For a time, Persian rule in Asia Minor was accepted by the Greeks with complacency. Two satrapies were organized: one known as 

Lydia had its capital at Sardis; the other, Phrygia, was governed from the city of Dascylion. Darius I wisely refrained from direct political interference with the Hellenic city-states, and since the Persians were not formidable commercial competitors, the exaction of moderate tribute was virtually the only direct manifestation of Persian suzerainty. In the main, the political development of the Ionian and 

Carian cities followed the pattern of the states in the Greek peninsula. 

Aristocratic ruling minorities were overthrown, and, when experiments with democracy failed, tyrants seized control. Darius favored

the establishment of tyrannies, for it was obviously easier for him to deal with strongly entrenched bosses than with democracies subject to frequent fluctuations of policy. When the reaction against tyranny came in Asia Minor as it did across the Aegean, Persia was identified with the repudiated form of government. The Ionian revolt which precipitated the Persian Wars can be interpreted as a movement for the overthrow of tyranny coupled with the broader project of revolt against Persian suzerainty.

A chain of events precipitated the Ionian revolt. In 512 B.C., Darius led an army into Thrace, which was conquered with ease and ultimately organized as a satrapy. The motive for the Thracian campaign probably was to establish a buffer state to safeguard Persian control of the east Aegean, but the expedition naturally occasioned alarm in Greece where it was interpreted as a prelude to an invasion of the peninsula. After the successful Thracian campaign, Darius invaded the territory between the Danube and the Pruth inhabited by the Scythians to seize gold mines in Dacia. The failure of the project demonstrated to the Ionian Greeks that the Persian army was not invincible and thus undoubtedly encouraged rebellion. 

In 499 B.C. an uprising on the island of Naxos resulted in the expulsion of the governing aristocracy. The exiled nobles thereupon appeared before Aristagoras, tyrant of Miletus, to seek his aid for their restoration. The tyrant, ambitious to secure Persian favor, consulted Artaphernes, satrap of Lydia, and persuaded him that the projected enterprise was feasible. The ensuing attack on Naxos was a fiasco; the quarrels of Aristagoras and Artaphernes did much to ensure the failure that was rendered inevitable when the warring factions on the island were reconciled and presented a united resistance. Aristagoras realized that he would surely be condemned to death by Darius since he had been the instigator of the abortive expedition; therefore, upon return to Miletus he raised the standard of rebellion.

City after city followed the lead of Miletus. Aristagoras abdicated and tyrants of other cities did likewise, for the movement was as much a repudiation of tyranny as a revolt against Persian rule. In 

498 B.C. the rebels captured Sardis, capital of the Lydian satrapy. 

During the Greek occupation the city was burned, and the Greeks were blamed, probably unjustly, for its destruction. 

In the meantime, Aristagoras had appealed for aid from Greece. 

Sparta rebuffed the overtures of the emissaries, but Athens and 

Eretria, in Euboea, agreed to furnish ships. When Thrace, Caria, and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the cities on the Propontis joined the rebellion, Darius realized the gravity of the crisis and furnished Artaphernes with sufficient forces to make a vigorous counter-attack that met with steady success. 

By 494 B.C. Miletus was besieged by a Persian army and fleet. When the Greek fleet encountered the Persian vessels off Lade, the ships of Lesbos and Samos deserted and sealed the fate of the Greek squadron. 

Miletus surrendered as a result of this naval disaster and was pillaged and burned in retaliation for the alleged Greek destruction of Sardis. 

Within two years the rebellion was completely crushed, and even 

Thrace was compelled again to acknowledge Persian suzerainty.

Darius, however, refrained from an attempt to reëstablish the Ionian tyrannies. The Great King was convinced that the aid sent from 

Athens and Eretria had been largely responsible for the duration and intensity of the Ionian rebellion. If Persian rule of Asia Minor was to be stabilized, measures had to be taken to remove the danger of recurrence of such intervention. This was the basic cause for the 

Persian invasions of Greece, for it is hardly likely that Darius envisioned the definitive conquest of the peninsula. 

In 492 B.C. Mardonius, son-in-law of the Great King, was sent with an army and fleet to invade Greece by way of Macedonia. The march of the army through Macedonia was a triumphal progress, but the fleet was wrecked in a storm off the promontory of Athos. 

Since Persian strategy usually dictated that army and fleet operate in close contact, Mardonius abandoned the enterprise, although there was no necessity for such a step.

The failure of 492 impelled Darius to make more extensive preparations for another attack. It was decided to avoid the perils of shipwreck by sailing directly across the Aegean. A great armada, under the command of Artaphernes the Younger and Datis, accompanied by Hippias, exiled son of Pisistratus, crossed the sea without difficulty and laid siege to Eretria. The city, betrayed by some of its leading citizens, surrendered, only to be pillaged and burned. Athens made no effort to assist her former ally, but when the Persian vessels anchored in the Bay of Marathon to land troops for an invasion of Attica emissaries were hastily dispatched to Sparta to seek assistance. The Spartans promised aid, but declared that religious scruples prevented action until the next full moon. 

Callimachus, the polemarch, officially entrusted with the defense of Athens, was wise enough to defer to one better fitted than he. 

Miltiades, who recently had arrived in Athens from the Chersonese, had been elected as one of the ten strategi for 490 B.C. His military

experience, largely gained against Persian troops, gave unique authority to his advice when he urged that the Athenian forces march to Marathon to intercept the invaders. 

Two roads led from the plain of Marathon to Athens. The main road, over which the Persian forces naturally would advance, ran south. The other, little more than a mountain trail, ran west of the plain. The Athenian troops hastened over the latter route and took a position cutting off this road to the Persians and, at the same time, putting themselves on the Persian flank if they attempted to proceed on the main road. The weak center of the Greek line was flanked by powerful wings; when the center was driven in, the wings encircled the Persian troops and soon scattered them with heavy losses. The victors then hurriedly moved to the Bay of Phalerum where a second Persian contingent was prevented from disembarking. The Persian commanders decided to halt the campaign before the full Greek strength would be mobilized with the expected arrival of the Spartans.

Athens had met the crisis firmly and effectively. Her prestige had been tremendously enhanced, and her democratic institutions stood vindicated. Social and economic discontent had been so completely allayed that there were none to raise their voices in support of Hippias. Only the most sanguine, however, believed that the Persian menace was ended. None of the fundamental issues had been decided, and the enmity of the Great King would be more implacable than before. The constitutional changes in Athens in the period 490482 B.C. were tangible expressions of the augmented confidence in democratic institutions. The polemarch was deprived of his military duties and invested with judicial authority in civil cases. The archonships henceforth were filled by lot, and the chief strategus ultimately was chosen from the whole citizenry to serve as chief executive as well as commander-in-chief of the armed forces. His colleagues on the board of strategi, however, were still chosen by the tribes. 

Miltiades, hero of the first repulse of Persia, soon incurred popular disfavor. An expedition against Paros to punish the island state for its Persian sympathies during the war failed, and Miltiades, who had sponsored the enterprise, was held responsible. Charges of excessive ambition and avarice were brought against him; he was convicted, and a heavy fine was imposed. Shortly after this disgrace he died of a wound suffered during the campaign.

The fall of Miltiades was followed by the election of Themistocles, leader of the opposition party of the Alcmaeonidae. This political

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

overturn was destined to have important consequences. Themistocles long had advocated the construction of an Athenian navy, and the mismanagement of the desultory war with Aegina in 488 B.C. emphasized his arguments, for had Athens possessed a fleet the conflict might have been speedily won. Election to the post of chief strategus in 483 B.C. gave him the opportunity to carry out his carefully matured plans, and in the following year 200 ships were constructed which soon were to prove the salvation of the state. 

Accession of Xerxes, son of Darius, to the Persian throne in 485 B.C. soon was followed by plans for another invasion of Greece through Macedonia. Preparations were made on an enormous scale; a pontoon bridge was constructed across the Hellespont and a canal was cut across the promontory of Athos to minimize the danger of shipwreck which had caused the failure of the expedition of 492.

Supply depots were established along the projected line of march, and when all was in readiness envoys were sent to Greece to demand earth and water as symbols of submission and acquiescence in the imposition of tribute.

The energetic and coöperative response of the Greek states, in sharp contrast to their lethargy when threatened by the attacks of Darius, revealed their appreciation of the gravity of the crisis. A congress was convoked at Corinth in 481, with representatives of thirty-one states in attendance. A Hellenic League under the presidency of Sparta was created, and it was decided to defend the pass of Thermopylae, which commanded entrance into central Greece from the north, and the Isthmus of Corinth vital to the defense of the Peloponnesus. Athens, of course, assumed responsibility for the conduct of the naval phase of the forthcoming war. 

In the spring of 480 B.C. the army of Xerxes left Susa, crossed the 

Hellespont, and penetrated Thrace. By July, Macedonia was occupied and the submission of Thessaly secured. The following month, the invaders attempted to force the pass of Thermopylae, defended by 300 Spartans under the command of Leonidas and a large number of auxiliaries. The Phocian troops deserted their post, and, after a renegade Greek betrayed the fact that the defenders now could be attacked from the rear, Leonidas and his Spartans were slain, fighting to the last. Attica, the immediate objective of the invaders, now was vulnerable. Themistocles considered the capture of Athens inevitable and urged that the noncombatant populace be evacuated and the men of military age assigned to the fleet, with the exception of a small garrison stationed on the Acropolis. After much misgiving,

his counsels, reënforced by alleged oracular approval, were followed. 

The advancing Persians thereupon ravaged Attica and captured Athens, which they partly destroyed. 

The soundness of the strategy of Themistocles soon was demonstrated. In September, the Athenian fleet was blockaded by the 

Persian squadron off Salamis. When it became known that escape through the Bay of Eleusis was cut off by the Egyptian squadron of the Great King, Themistocles persuaded his colleagues to consent to force battle. The Persian vessels were badly crowded and clumsily handled; within a short time they were in hopeless confusion and were destroyed. Since the Greek victory was likely to provoke another Ionian revolt, Xerxes hurriedly led a portion of his army back to the Hellespont, across which the troops were carried by such ships as had escaped the disaster at Salamis. 

In the meantime, the great Persian army under Mardonius evacuated devastated Attica and encamped in Boeotia so as to have the friendly city of Thebes to its rear. Sparta had selfishly confined her activities to the defense of the Peloponnesus, as yet in no real danger, but when there was reason to believe that Persia might ally with Athens, she gave ear to the appeals for more energetic action. A large 

Spartan army under Pausanias was sent into Boeotia where, reenforced by Athenians and other allies, it faced the forces of Mardonius on the plain of Plataea in August of 479 B.C. Tempted by temporary confusion in the Greek ranks, the Persians attacked, but were repelled with great loss by the disciplined Spartan hoplites. A vigorous Greek counter-attack then scattered the enemy; Mardonius was slain and his retreating soldiers were hunted down and slaughtered. The victory of Plataea was decisive; a few days later when a 

Persian squadron off Mycale was destroyed by an Athenian fleet commanded by Xanthippus, the overwhelming triumph of Greece was assured. There was added cause for rejoicing since Gelon, tyrant of 

Syracuse, had decisively defeated the Carthaginians in the battle of 

Himera (480 B.C.).

THE CONFEDERACY OF DELOS 

The repulse of the Persian invaders did not end the hostile relations between the Empire and the Greek states. A number of 

Hellenic cities in Ionia and Caria still remained under the rule of the Great King. No permanent peace could be expected or even desired so long as a single Greek city was thus held. Then, too, there was reason to believe that Xerxes would attempt to avenge the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

humiliating defeats of Salamis and Plataca. Another expedition for the invasion of the Greek peninsula was by no means impossible in view of the man-power and material resources of the Empire. Both offensive and defensive motives thus led to the formation of the 

Confederacy of Delos in 478-477 B.C. 

Themistocles long had urged the establishment of a league in which Athenian preeminence would be recognized. The need for such an organization after 479 and Sparta's failure to assume leadership brought attainment of his objective. While the League of 481 still was in existence, the arrogance of Pausanias had alienated Ionia, and the policies of the Spartan government were so short-sighted as inevitably to confine her influence to the Peloponnesus. Since the offensive and defensive policies of the new Confederacy could best be advanced by maintaining a powerful navy, the larger and wealthier states like Chios, Samos, and Lesbos were enrolled as voluntary allies on condition that they furnish squadrons to be employed for the common good. Lesser states unable to supply ships undertook to pay an annual tax (phoros) to be used primarily for naval construction and operation. The apportioning of the tax was entrusted to Aristides, renowned for his integrity and justice. His conscientious and capable handling of this difficult problem was one of the most important factors in the success of the movement to found the Confederacy. The capital of the Confederacy was located on the island of Delos; the tax, although collected by a board of ten Athenians, was deposited on the island in the treasury in the temple of Apollo. Annual congresses of representatives of all eligible member states were held. Although Athens was honored with the presidency, she theoretically enjoyed no special powers in voting or the determination of policy.

Athenian leadership in the Confederacy was due to her naval primacy. Themistocles therefore considered it necessary to maintain this supremacy and to do so required wealthy citizens in proper turn to assume the major part of the expense of naval construction and upkeep. To guard against the danger that a military power could cut the communication between Athens and her port at Piraeus, Themistocles began the construction of the famous "Long Walls,' continuous fortifications which linked the metropolis with her naval base and assured access to the sea. 

The post-war policies of Themistocles caused considerable apprehension in Sparta. The Confederacy of Delos had been formed without consulting her and, from her viewpoint, in violation of the agree-

ment of 481, which had not been officially abrogated. Construction of the city walls provoked added bitterness, for it was believed in Sparta that the fortifications were intended as a menace to her. The widening rift between the two great powers of Greece, so different in their institutions and ideals, was inexorably leading to the tragedy of the Peloponnesian War.

The policies of Themistocles had not been adopted without opposition. Partisanship, family rivalries, and personal jealousies were entwined with differences in principle. The conduct of the chief strategus was sufficiently indiscreet to make charges of avarice and arrogance plausible, and the mounting tide of opposition finally culminated in the ostracism of the great statesman. Spurned by several 

Greek states, he finally entered the service of Persia, to end his career as governor of the city of Magnesia. 

THE REGIME OF CIMON 

Cimon, son of Miltiades, hero of the victory of Marathon, was elected chief strategus after the fall of Themistocles. He was a man of wealth, culture, and demonstrated ability. Under his direction, the 

Confederacy of Delos was destined to be transformed into the Athenian Empire, that is, from a league of voluntary allies to a group of Athenian dependencies.

Control of Thrace had been secured by the conquest of the Persian stronghold of Eion. This success, which gave Athens control of the mineral resources of Thrace, was indubitably in accord with fundamental reasons for the formation of the Confederacy. The subjugation of Scyros, hitherto a piratical stronghold, likewise was advantageous to the Confederacy, although Athens was the chief beneficiary since the island commanded the ship lanes to the Euxine. 

A decisive naval victory at the mouth of the Eurymedon river, supplemented by land operations, liberated Caria from Persian rule. 

This was the most significant achievement of the Confederacy that was consistent with its fundamental purposes. 

Other policies of Cimon, however, were clearly imperialistic. 

Carystus, a Euboean city that had refused to join the Confederacy, was attacked and coerced into membership. When the island state of Naxos became alarmed at the aggressions of Athens and attempted to secede, it was defeated and forced to become a tributary state. 

Colonization and the extension of Athenian influence in Thrace. alarmed the island state of Thasos, which also attempted secession. 

The state was terribly punished for its defection. It was reduced to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the status of a dependency, and all its colonies as well as its holdings in Thrace passed to the control of Athens. On one pretext or another, naval allies of the Confederacy were reduced to the position of tribute-paying subjects until only Samos, Chios, and Lesbos retained their original status. The Confederacy had become an empire; the removal of the treasury from Delos to Athens in 454 B.C. merely signalized the completion of the transition. 

Cimon's political ruin came as a result of his pro-Spartan policies. 

He had urged that conciliation toward Sparta was the best means of furthering the interests of all Greece. An opportunity soon enabled him to try out his idea. In 464 B.C. Laconia was devastated by an earthquake, and when the state was temporarily prostrated by the disaster the perioeci and helots revolted. The Spartan government thereupon appealed to Athens for assistance under the terms of the agreement of 481 B.C. After much discussion, Cimon persuaded the 

Assembly to authorize an expedition for the relief of the hard pressed state, but he clearly staked his political future on the outcome. 

The expedition was a complete failure, for the rebels took refuge in the virtually impregnable stronghold of Ithome and repelled all efforts to dislodge them despite the skill of the Athenians in siegecraft. The Spartans finally became convinced that the failure of the 

Athenian forces was deliberate and ordered them to leave. What had begun as a conciliatory gesture thus ended in mutual recrimination. On the way back from the siege of Ithome in 461 B.C., the 

Athenian forces stopped to found a Messenian colony at Naupactus. 

Since the new colony commanded entry into the Corinthian Gulf, Corinth naturally considered its foundation a threat to her commercial interests and lodged bitter complaint with Sparta. Cimon, upon return to Athens, was promptly exiled, and elements headed by Ephialtes and Pericles returned to power.

CHAPTER The Age of Pericles and the Peloponnesian 

War

HE ostracism of Cimon and the return of the old elements to power was destined to have the most important consequences on both the constitutional development of the Athenian commonwealth and the disastrous progress of imperialism. Constitutional changes that made the government completely democratic were inaugurated while the imperialistic trends that appeared during Cimon's administration culminated in the tragedy of the Peloponnesian War.

Ephialtes was assassinated soon after his accession, and was succeeded by Pericles, who had so ably aided him in the leadership of the now dominant political party. Pericles was the son of Xanthippus, hero of the Greek victory in the battle of Mycale. Agariste, his mother, was a niece of Clisthenes the great reformer. His personality, education, and experience ideally fitted him to assume the responsibilities of the chief magistracy. His aristocratic bearing and reserve, belied by his democratic political views, as well as his frugality and forensic skill ensured the devotion of the populace, at least so long as his policies apparently were meeting with success. Under him, Athens reached the pinnacle of her greatness, yet his policies ultimately plunged the state into the suicidal strife with her great rival in the Peloponnesus that paved the way for the loss of Greek independence.

Measures introduced by Ephialtes to establish complete democracy were carried to fruition. The Council of the Areopagus, the last bulwark of conservatism and aristocracy, was virtually abolished when it was deprived of the censorial powers it had presumed to exercise and its jurisdiction was limited to certain cases of homicide assigned to its competence by the Draconian legislation. In the interval between the Persian Wars, the method of selecting archons had

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

been changed from election to lot. Only the first two Solonian classes, however, were eligible for inclusion in the panel of 500 candidates elected by the demes, from which group the final choice by lot was made. Pericles, in 457 B.C., secured the passage by the Assembly of a measure that made the zeugitae eligible for the office, and this enactment subsequently was further liberalized by extending its provisions to the thetes.

Real democracy was illusory, however, as long as there was no compensation for civic service, for obviously only those in comfortable financial circumstances could afford to devote their time to public duties. Pericles therefore secured legislation that provided stipends for jurors, members of the Council of Five Hundred, and the archons. The remuneration paid on a per diem basis was sufficient to enable the humble citizen to leave his employment to serve the state. The necessary funds to implement the democratic program were provided by a portion of the tax (phoros) paid by the tributary allies. This, of course, from the standpoint of the dependent states, was an illegal diversion of common funds for the exclusive benefit of the Athenian citizenry. Even more objectionable was the employment of the funds to defray the cost of the building program begun under Pericles and to subsidize the Athenian theatre by distributing the price of admission to the poor.

The democratic legislation was offset by the curtailment of citizenship. Pericles fostered a measure that restricted civic status to those of Athenian parentage on both sides. This reactionary legislation, if enforced at an earlier time, would have debarred Clisthenes and Themistocles from citizenship and have deprived the state of their illustrious services. Then, too, precautions were taken to discourage further constitutional changes. Sponsors of constitutional innovations were to be held guilty of offense against the state if the changes they advocated were found impractical. 

All pretense in the relations between Athens and the dependent states disappeared. Diversion of common funds to exclusively Athenian purposes was followed by the removal of the treasury from Delos to Athens in 454 B.C. By 443 B.C. the Empire was divided into five areas to facilitate the collection of the tribute. The annual congresses at Delos, which had become a travesty, were discontinued, and henceforth Athens dealt separately with each state of her empire. The secession of Samos, provoked by Athenian aid to Miletus with which she was engaged in a quarrel, was punished by the seizure of her fleet and the imposition of the phoros. The establishment of

cleruchies in the dependent states also provoked bitter resentment. 

The cleruchies were groups of Athenian colonists, usually recruited from the ranks of the impoverished and unemployed, who were thus foisted upon the subject states which all too often were embarrassed by social and economic problems of their own. The situation was made all the more intolerable by the fact that the colonists retained their Athenian citizenship and had no hesitancy in asserting their social superiority over their reluctant hosts. Athens was destined to pay dearly for her cynical indifference to the interests of the subject states. When their loyalty and support were desperately needed during the course of the struggle with Sparta, Athens found that by her selfish and arbitrary actions she had forfeited their allegiance. 

Pericles and the party he led traditionally had been opposed to any efforts to secure Spartan friendship. His foreign policy, marked by imperialistic designs even more patent than those of Cimon, soon strained relations with Sparta to the breaking point. He assumed the offensive by concluding an alliance with Argos. Negotiations for peace then were carried on with Persia through the mediation of the new ally since relations between Argos and Susa were friendly. No settlement with the Great King could be reached, however, because of his insistence on a restoration of tribute from Asia Minor. 

An alliance between Athens and Megara was additional evidence of the intention of Pericles to curtail Spartan hegemony in the Peloponnesus and to establish an Athenian land empire comparable with her maritime organization. Corinth was convinced that this measure was a direct aggression against her commercial interests and bitterly complained to Sparta. Aegina hastened to the assistance of Corinth, but an Athenian fleet soon reduced her to the status of a subject. 

In 460 B.C. an Athenian squadron was sent to secure the island of 

Cyprus still under Persian rule. In the meantime, Egypt rebelled against Persia. Pericles foresaw an opportunity to deliver a decisive blow and accordingly ordered a portion of the Cyprus fleet to proceed to the Egyptian coast to join the rebels. Persia immediately resorted to the obvious expedient of concluding an alliance with Sparta under the terms of which the Great King agreed to subsidize a Spartan invasion of Attica. Nothing came of this alliance, however, for the Spartan magistrates feared that such an invasion in behalf of Persia would provoke a general uprising of the Greek states. 

While the Athenian fleet was operating off Egypt, Corinth suddenly attacked Megara, but Myronides, with a hastily levied Athenian army composed of old men and youths, repulsed the Corinthian

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

forces (459-458 B.C.). A subsequent Spartan expedition into Boeotia was a more serious threat, since an attempt was made to organize a Theban league as a counter-poise to the Athenian Empire, but the failure to launch an offensive against Athens led to the disintegration of the league after the withdrawal of the Spartan force. 

The Athenian intervention in the Egyptian rebellion had been illadvised, and the defeat of the fleet in the lower Nile in 454 B.C. forced the abandonment of the enterprise. Argos, encouraged by this blow to Athenian prestige, disavowed her alliance, and the sentiment for peace became so strong in Athens that, in 450 B.C., Cimon was recalled and empowered to begin negotiations for a general peace. He concluded a five-year armistice with Sparta, and at the same time a thirty-year truce was arranged between Sparta and Argos. Cimon then led a naval expedition against Cyprus, but during the siege of Citium he was fatally stricken with a fever, and his death led to a decision to abandon the venture. The enterprise was not wholly abortive, however, for the Athenians destroyed about a hundred 

Persian ships off Cypriote Salamis. With the death of Cimon, Pericles and the belligerent party in Athens returned to power, and with the conclusion of a tentative peace with Persia preparations were immediately made for energetic measures against Sparta and her allies. 

War was resumed in Greece despite the truce and the conciliatory gestures of Pericles who issued an invitation for a congress of states. 

Athenian control of Boeotia was lost with the battle of Coronea; 

Phocis and Locris also renounced their alliances with Athens. In the summer of 446 B.C., Euboea rebelled; Megara massacred her Athenian garrison and sent an army into Attica. At this critical moment, Pericles made renewed overtures for peace, and a treaty was concluded with Sparta nominally to remain in force for thirty years.
