Athens virtually abandoned her hope to establish a continental empire, but many fundamental issues remained unsettled by the treaty. 

The frank imperialism of Athens, so incompatible with Greek political ideals, pointed to an inevitable day of reckoning. 

THE PELOPONNESIAN WAR (431-404 B.C.) 

The fratricidal struggle that wracked Greece in the period 431404 B.C. did more than produce the disintegration of the Athenian 

Empire. The rancor, indeed the implacable hatreds, it engendered made it virtually impossible for any of the states to assert really nationalistic leadership. Continuance of internecine strife after the war

ensured the eventual subjugation of Greece by Macedonia; even the discipline of Macedonian suzerainty failed to allay the discord until finally the Greek states came under the sway of Rome. 

Hostility between Athens and Sparta was residual in the very structures of the states. Athens was a democracy with its emphasis on the rights of the individual citizen while Sparta was a totalitarian state in which the individual existed for the all-embracing state. Cultural contrasts were as striking as the divergence of political ideals. 

In Athens, the patronage of literature and the arts were integral aspects of the commonwealth's activity; in Sparta such interests had been deliberately forsworn after the organization of the state according to militaristic pattern.

Tangible grievances served to transform mutual mistrust into hostility. Sparta had resented the organization of the Confederacy of 

Delos and each step in the transition from Confederacy to Athenian Empire had accentuated the resentment. Athenian development of the Piraeus and the construction of the fortifications had called forth strong protests in Laconia. Cimon's attempt to allay the rising enmity had ended in the humiliating fiasco before Ithome. The efforts of 

Pericles to establish a continental empire, although abortive, had virtually destroyed all hope of compromise to avert the impending struggle. Sparta could hardly extend or accept conciliatory overtures without seeming to desert Corinth and other allies whose economic interests were so clearly threatened with the extension of the Athenian Empire. Sacrifice of the solidarity of the Peloponnesus was unthinkable so long as this empire was in existence. 

The immediate causes of the war were the incidents at Corcyra and Potidaea. The island of Corcyra had been colonized by Corinth. 

Corcyra, in turn, had established the colony of Epidamnus in Illyria. 

When Epidamnus was torn by internal strife, one faction appealed to Corcyra while another obtained Corinthian intervention. Corcyra, angered at the unprecedented action of Corinth in responding to such an appeal, repulsed the Corinthian squadron and then, fearing retaliation, appealed for the protection of Athens. Pericles, still eager to extend Athenian economic interests to the west, sent a fleet with instructions to interfere only if the independence of Corcyra was evidently menaced. While the Corcyran and Corinthian fleets were engaged off Sybota (433 B.C.) the Athenian squadron joined in the battle and ensured the Corcyran victory. Corinth promptly complained to Sparta, and her charges that the incident was a palpable Athenian aggression seemed well founded. Athenian policy in the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Potidaean affair was equally belligerent. Potidaea was a Corinthian colony established during the regime of Periander. With the extension of the Athenian Empire, however, the city had been enrolled as a subject state, although it still continued annually to receive magistrates from Corinth. This impossible situation was bound to cause trouble. When Potidaea became implicated in a general anti-Athenian movement in Chalcidice, Athens ordered that the fortifications of the city be dismantled and the practice of securing Corinthian officials terminated.

Pericles saw that a general war was inevitable and accordingly banned Megara from the markets of the Empire (432 B.C.). This meant ruin for the commercial and industrial interests of that state and served to precipitate hostilities. It is quite possible that Pericles wished to force a conflict, since he was facing charges of embezzlement and his relations with his mistress Aspasia had been bitterly censured. King Archidamus of Sparta attempted to postpone the conflict by submitting an ultimatum to Athens which he realized could not be accepted. Diplomacy failed to avert the conflict, and by May of 431 B.C. war was officially declared. Sparta had the aid of all the Peloponnesian states save Achaea and Argos, and in addition had Boeotia, Phocis, Locris, Ambracia, and Anactorion. Athens nominally had all her imperial dependencies, together with Thessaly, Corcyra, Acarnania, Zacynthus, and Plataea. Athens was well prepared financially, for 6000 talents had been accumulated in anticipation of military needs. The suggestion of Corinth that the treasures of Delphi and Olympia be utilized by the Peloponnesian states was voted down because of religious scruples.

There was obviously little opportunity for quick and decisive military action. The Peloponnesian powers could not hope to challenge Athenian command of the sea, and Athens, on the other hand, had too much respect for the prowess of the Spartan infantry to attempt an offensive. Enmities of long standing in Boeotia led to the opening of hostilities, for a Theban force suddenly attacked Plataea, which had been consistently friendly toward Athens, and captured the city. When the populace recovered from its surprise, however, and realized how weak the attacking force was, a counter-attack was organized and the Thebans were driven off. The anticipated Spartan offensive then began with an invasion of Attica. Pericles refrained from offering battle to the formidable Spartan army and advised that the populace of Attica should be concentrated within the Long Walls for defense, despite the fact that his decision meant the abandonment of Attica to devastation.

The policy of Pericles was partly responsible for a terrible disaster, for largely as a result of the overcrowded and unsanitary conditions in Athens a plague broke out in 430 B.C. The disease, probably an especially virulent form of typhus, carried off thousands, and the chief strategus was made the scape-goat. He was charged with the embezzlement of five talents from the treasury and sentenced to exile. 

Phidias, the famous sculptor, likewise was banished for alleged corruption, while Aspasia was attacked and Anaxagoras was sentenced to exile ostensibly for impiety. Cleon and Nicias assumed control of the Athenian government, but when they demonstrated their inability to direct the war effectively, Pericles was recalled. Shortly after his return, however, he contracted the disease and died in 429 B.C. The Assembly, with its decisions now swayed by the harangues of demagogues, assumed untrammeled control. The ensuing blundering, irresolution, and corruption demonstrated the folly of entrusting important decisions to the direct control of a popular assembly without competent leadership.

The barbarity with which the war was waged manifested the implacable hatreds that had been incited in the Greek world. For example, when in 429 B.C. Plataea was captured, all known Athenian sympathizers were executed after perfunctory trials. The following year Mitylene attempted to secede from the Athenian Empire. The insurrection was immediately quelled, and the Athenian Assembly was consulted as to the punishment to be meted out to the people of the hapless city. The Assembly decided to send a ship with orders to massacre the entire populace of the conquered city. In the session of the Assembly held on the following day, however, the enormity of the sentence was realized, and a second ship was hastily dispatched to overtake the first to rescind the barbarous order. It arrived in the harbor of Mitylene just in time to prevent a promiscuous slaughter, but a thousand of the chief men of Lesbos were put to death. 

After several years of indecisive action, an Athenian squadron took the island of Pylos off the Messenian coast and captured the island of Cythera early the following year. Possession of these islands, of course, was of great strategic advantage, for both could be used as bases, but the effect of these victories was offset by the defeat of Hippocrates at Delium (424 B.C.) and the consequent abandonment of the Boeotian campaign. Then, too, Brasidas, one of the most capable

Spartan commanders of the war period, forced the Athenian evacuation of Thrace by a series of victories. In 422 B.C. both Brasidas and 

Cleon were killed in a battle near Thracian Amphipolis. Since both sides were eager at least for a respite, a peace was negotiated by

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Nicias and King Plistonoax of Sparta in 421 B.C. By this so-called "Peace of Nicias," Athens surrendered Pylos and Cythera in exchange for restitution of her Thracian interests. Much to the indignation of Corinth, Athens was permitted to retain cities that menaced her interests in the Corinthian Gulf. Although the treaty nominally was to remain in force for fifty years, it proved even more ephemeral than the agreement of 446 B.C.

Causes for the inevitable resumption of hostilities were embodied in the treaty which, after all, was considered by both sides as a temporary expedient. Corinth and the Boeotian states felt that their interests had been disregarded in the extension of moderate terms to Athens, and unless they were mollified there was danger that Sparta would lose indispensable allies. Enforcement of some of the clauses of the treaty proved impossible, for cities which had been ceded to Athens resisted the imposition of Athenian control and Sparta claimed, apparently with justice, that her responsibilities did not extend to the application of military force to implement the treaty provisions. The mutual recriminations incident to the non-enforcement of the treaty further embittered the rival states and served to hasten renewal of the war.

Athenian policy now was directed by Alcibiades, who was elected to the chief magistracy in 420 B.C. Nephew of Pericles and intimate friend of Socrates, he enjoyed great popularity with the Athenians, for he possessed great culture and charm. Handsome in appearance, a skilled orator, adroit in formulating plans and devising expedients, he seemed to have all the qualities requisite for statesmanship. His character, however, left much to be desired. He was selfishly ambitious and virtually devoid of conscience as his later career was to demonstrate. His skepticism in regard to democracy, his impulsiveness, and his ill-disguised contempt for religious usages created many enemies, and his superficial cleverness was a poor substitute for real statesmanship in the critical period in which he guided the destinies of the Athenian commonwealth. 

It will be recalled that during the early years of the Periclean regime there had been unmistakable signs of a desire to extend Athenian imperial interests to the west. Athenian intervention in the 

Corcyran situation which did much to precipitate the Peloponnesian War probably was envisioned as the first step in such a program. In view of the prevalence of such imperialistic designs, the shift of 

Athenian activities to Sicily is understandable.

In 416 B.C. emissaries appeared at Athens from the Sicilian city of

Segesta seeking intervention to halt the aggressions of the neighboring city of Selinus. The situation was more than a local struggle, for 

Selinus actually was a close ally of Syracuse, and her belligerent policy toward Segesta was a manifestation of Syracusan imperialism that threatened to bring about complete control of the entire island. 

Such a disruption of the balance of power in Sicily would prevent the extension of Athenian interests to the west as Alcibiades and other influential statesmen doubtless realized. The representatives of 

Segesta boasted of the wealth of their city and undertook to defray the major portion of the expense of an Athenian expeditionary force. 

The Assembly, however, refused to be hurried into action and sent a mission to investigate the Sicilian situation. These emissaries, however, were deceived by the simulated wealth of Segesta, and their erroneous report in regard to the financial prospects doubtless helped persuade the Assembly to intervene. 

A great armada was made ready with a thoroughness indicating that the Athenian government contemplated a decisive blow against Syracuse. Command of the expedition, however, was unwisely divided among Alcibiades, Nicias, and Lamachus. Since these generals, in addition to being personal rivals, had each his own plan of campaign, delay and dissension were bound to impede the conduct of the venture.

Just before the departure of the fleet a great scandal disturbed the Athenian citizenry. Vandals, under cover of night, systematically mutilated the sacred statues which stood before public and private buildings in the city. This sacrilege was ascribed to Alcibiades whose irreligious views were notorious, but when the strategus demanded an immediate trial the Assembly demurred, knowing that his popularity with his troops would ensure exoneration. Proceedings were accordingly deferred until the conclusion of the Syracusan expedition, with the result that the fleet set sail with grave charges pending against one of the commanders (415 B.C.).

When the Athenian ships reached Sicilian waters the commanders of scouting vessels divulged the fact that the Athenian envoys had grossly exaggerated the wealth of the city which the expedition was to rescue. Then inevitable disputes arose in regard to the strategy to be followed. Alcibiades believed it necessary to conclude alliances with as many Sicilian cities as possible prior to an attack on Syracuse. 

His views prevailed and much time was wasted in vain efforts to enlist allies.

With the failure of the diplomacy of Alcibiades, the commanders

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

decided to attack Syracuse. As soon as the Athenian vessels took a position in the Syracusan harbor, however, Alcibiades received orders to return to Athens to stand trial on charges of sacrilege. This absurd step, attributable to the enemies of the strategus who wished to procure his condemnation in the absence of the troops, went a long way to ensure the failure of the siege, since Alcibiades, instead of returning to Athens, found refuge in Sparta where he promptly advised Sparta and Corinth to send assistance to beleaguered Syracuse.

In the meantime, the siege was energetically prosecuted by the Athenians. Efforts were made to cut the Syracusan citadel off from the rest of the city, but the construction of counter-walls by the garrison averted this blow. The arrival of Corinthian reënforcements (414 B.C.) under Gylippus, a Spartan commander, infused new life into the defenders of the city, and Nicias realized that the altered situation necessitated aid from Athens. Just before Athenian reenforcements arrived, however, Nicias was disastrously defeated in a naval battle (413 B.C.). It was subsequently decided to raise the siege, but on the very night selected for the retreat, an eclipse of the moon occurred and the soothsayers advised the credulous Nicias to postpone the projected withdrawal for twenty-seven days. With almost incredible folly he deferred to their superstitious scruples and thus gave the Syracusans time to complete their defenses. When he and Demosthenes finally tried to break through, the attack was repulsed with heavy losses followed by unconditional surrender. Those of the Athenian army that escaped the slaughter were put to work as slaves in the Syracusan quarries where most of them soon perished. 

The failure of the Syracusan expedition was a terrible blow to Athens. In large measure, the tragedy was attributable to the incompetence of Nicias, but the Athenian government itself had pursued policies which had well-nigh ensured such a result. 

The surrender of the Sicilian force was not the only blow to Athens in 413 B.C., for King Agis led a Spartan army into Attica and seized Decelea from which all efforts to expel him failed. The slaves in the Athenian silver mines revolted, and systematic Spartan raids devastated the rural areas of Attica. In this acute emergency, the normal democratic government of Athens was superseded by the authority of ten probuli, or emergency commissioners. Under their regime, the hated phoros was cancelled and in its stead a five percent duty was levied on imports and exports, and Athenian commerce at Piraeus was not exempted from the levy. This belated justice to the imperial dependencies did not avert discontent as had been antici-

pated, and the rebellion of Chios in 412 B.C. threatened to be the prelude to the complete collapse of the Empire. To add to the dangers, King Darius II of Persia promised to subsidize Spartan military and naval activities and made efforts to recover Ionia which, however, were impeded by dissension among the Persian satraps. Continuance of the crisis strengthened the trend toward oligarchy in Athens; the Assembly was abolished and an indirectly elected Council of Five Thousand assumed control.

By 410 B.C. the Athenian government was in a sufficiently precarious plight to recall Alcibiades. He recovered control of the 

Hellespont, and his successes, following the Athenian victory in the battle of Cyzicus, did much to relieve the gravity of the situation. Indeed, the recovery of Athens had proceeded so far as to induce Sparta to offer to negotiate for peace, but these overtures were spurned. In 

409 B.C. Alcibiades recovered Byzantium, and the following year he returned to Athens in triumph with his past conduct apparently forgiven. Two years later, however, when one of his subordinates disobeyed instructions and lost the battle of Notium, Alcibiades, made the scape-goat for the disaster, retired to Thrace.

When a Spartan fleet seized the islands of Chios and Lesbos, the Athenian admiral, Conon, was sent to the eastern Aegean to block Spartan offensive moves and to recover the lost islands if an opportunity was presented. His squadron was trapped in the harbor of 

Mitylene, however, by a superior Spartan naval force. The Athenian government, realizing that disaster was imminent, virtually exhausted. its financial resources to equip another fleet for the rescue of Conon. 

This fleet finally met the Spartans off the islets of Arginusae, just south of Lesbos, and gained a decisive victory. A storm, however, came up just as the battle ended and prevented the Athenian commanders from continuing their efforts to save the crews of their vessels that had been put out of action or sunk by the enemy. Grief in Athens at the news of the heavy loss of life soon gave way to indignation directed against the commanders, who were charged with negligence and callous indifference to the fate of their countrymen. 

Six of the commanders, including Pericles the Younger, son of the statesman, decided to return and face trial. In view of the passion that was raging, their condemnation to death after a perfunctory trial was inevitable.

Shortly after this tragic event, Lysander again assumed command and moved the Spartan fleet into the Hellespont. The Athenians followed and took up a dangerous position. When the crews of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Athenian squadron went ashore near Aegospotami, Lysander captured the ships virtually without striking a blow. With the sea power of Athens destroyed, King Pausanias led a Spartan force into Attica, and Lysander's ships ultimately anchored in the Saronic Gulf. Athens was forced to accept the peace terms imposed on her. 

The treaty of 404 B.C. required the dissolution of the Athenian 

Empire and the surrender of the pitiful remnant of the once great Athenian navy. The conquered state moreover agreed to raze the 

Long Walls, and by joining the Peloponnesian League she acknowledged the hegemony of Sparta.

THE LOSS OF GREEK INDEPENDENCE 

Sparta's triumph in the Peloponnesian War was more than a vic tory; it was in reality a great opportunity. Genuinely nationalistic leadership was imperatively needed in Greece, for the tragedy of the war had demonstrated the folly of particularism. Sparta's military prestige was at its height, and her success in holding the allegiance of most of her allies during the period of hostilities indicated that if she were willing to adopt a pan-Hellenic policy and avoid the mistakes that had brought ruin and humiliation to Athens constructive results might follow the establishment of her hegemony in the Greek world. 

Internal problems, however, seriously embarrassed the victorious state. Her man-power had been dangerously depleted as a result of the prolonged hostilities, and no effort was made to compensate for this by enlargement of the citizenship to include some of the perioeci. 

The Spartan state traditionally had existed on the basis of a natural economy; after the war, however, the precious metals began to come into the state despite the prohibitions of the laws, and the partial transition from a natural to a monetary economy was producing inevitable difficulties and militating against the solidarity of the Spartan citizenry.

By her treatment of the conquered states Sparta soon indicated that she would fail to grasp the opportunity for leadership which had been afforded her after Aegospotami. In large measure the policies adopted were those suggested by Lysander. Most of the vanquished states were placed under the control of decarchies, or boards of ten tyrants, maintained in power by Spartan military governors and garrisons. Athens was placed under the rule of the “Thirty,” and citizenship was limited to 3000 whose oligarchical sentiments were well known. Proscriptions of democratic leaders and confiscations of

property attended the establishment of the regime of the Thirty and destroyed any hope of reconciliation between Athens and 

Sparta. 

The situation in Athens was not so desperate as men believed after the disaster of 404 B.C. Since the state was primarily agricultural, its basic asset - the land - still remained, with its fertility unimpaired. 

Improvements in agricultural techniques, particularly the introduction of the three-field form of cultivation, increased productivity, since each portion of arable land now lay fallow one year out of three instead of every other year as formerly. The increased productivity of Athenian agriculture thus did much to offset the effects of Spartan devastation of Attica. Commerce, especially with the states of the Black Sea area, was resumed almost immediately upon the conclusion of the war. Improved banking practices expanded credit facilities just when such expansion was urgently needed and naturally played a major part in the commercial revival. It became increasingly apparent that if Sparta failed to adopt an enlightened policy in her relations with subjugated states, there was every prospect for the eventual reconstruction of the Athenian Empire. 

Lysander's ambition and lust for power, so bitterly denounced in Ionia, soon aroused the apprehension of the home government. Upon his return from Ionia, the war-hero took an active part in politics and advocated liberalization of the rules governing candidacy for the kingship, doubtless hoping for his own elevation to the throne.

When his efforts to evade the legal and traditional practices that precluded his candidacy failed, he attempted to become de facto ruler. King Agesilaus, however, showed unexpected strength of character and opposed all Lysander's efforts to exercise a control of governmental policies. Thoroughly discredited the former admiral ceased to be a factor in Spartan politics, and the restoration of modified democracy in Athens, which ended the excesses of the period of 

Spartan rule, was a happy sequel to his fall.

Diplomatic issues with Persia soon engrossed the attention of the Spartan government. Persian satraps had aided the Peloponnesians in the struggle with Athens and subsidies from Susa had been accepted with the understanding that Sparta was to acquiesce in the restoration of Persian hegemony in Ionia. If Sparta now discharged her obligations to the Great King, all Greece would be outraged. On the other hand, repudiation of her commitments would mean the enmity of Persia and the attendant possibility of a Persian coalition with 

Athens for joint attack on the Peloponnesus.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Disturbances within the Persian Empire furnished Sparta an opportunity to sunder her unnatural alliance. In 405 B.C. Cyrus the 

Younger rebelled against his brother Artaxerxes, the rightful heir to the throne, and recruited Greek mercenaries including a Spartan contingent under Clearchus. In 401 B.C. the Greek army marched into the Empire, and the forces of Cyrus gained a brilliant victory at Cunaxa, near Babylon, but the death of Cyrus made continuation of the expedition impossible. The Greeks accordingly marched up the 

Tigris valley to the Black Sea and, after many vicissitudes, arrived at Chalcedon. Xenophon, a member of the Greek contingent, immortalized the campaign in his Anabasis, a masterpiece of Greek literature comparable with Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic Wars. 

Sparta's support of the cause of Cyrus had obviated any possibility for the continuance of her alliance with Susa. 

Persia then began an attempt to recover Ionia without Spartan aid. Sparta, in response to urgent appeals, moved to protect Ionian independence, while Persia countered by overtures to Athens. In 

394 B.C. a Spartan fleet under Pisander was crushed by the Persian navy. Negotiations for peace were prolonged, but when it became apparent that Persian aggression might serve to unite the Greek states in a common cause, the Great King signified his willingness to come to terms. The provisions of the King's Peace of 386 B.C. were practically dictated by Persia. Greek cities in Asia Minor were relinquished, with the proviso that they were to enjoy autonomy under Persian suzerainty. It was a disgraceful arrangement, an ignominious surrender of the fruits of Marathon and Plataea. 

Spartan policy now was largely dictated by King Agesilaus. In general he was committed to the preservation of the status quo, above all, of course, Spartan suzerainty in Greece. By 382 B.C. a confederacy had been organized in Chalcidice with the city of Olynthus as its center, but soon a number of Chalcidicean cities, alarmed at the patent aggressions of the confederacy, appealed for Spartan protection, and a naval expedition was sent in response. Olynthus was easily reduced to submission, and the recently created Chalcidicean Confederacy passed under Spartan control. 

A few years before, while a Spartan army was marching through Boeotia on its way to Chalcidice, Phoebidas, the commander, was prevailed upon to order an assault on Thebes without any authority to do so from the Spartan government. Since the Theban garrison was surprised by the unexpected and unprovoked assault, the city was easily taken and placed under the rule of a board of polemarchs.

When the Spartan ephors were notified of the incident they expressed official approval of the flagrant aggression. The Thebans, outraged by the Spartan action and extremely discontented with the oppressive rule of the polemarchs, appealed to Athens for aid in an endeavor to recover their independence, but in view of the traditional enmity between the two cities it is not surprising that Athens ignored the plea. The attitude of the Athenian government changed, however, when a Spartan force vainly attempted to seize the Piraeus. 

At any time Athens itself might be the victim of a wanton assault, and common prudence dictated at least a modicum of coöperation with Thebes.

Thebes regained her independence primarily as a result of a conspiracy organized by the exiled patriots, Melon, Pelopidas, and Epaminondas. After the citadel was seized by an ingenious stratagem, the Spartans were expelled, and a Theban League was thereupon reorganized for defense against Spartan attack. A contingent of carefully selected troops, known as the " Sacred Band," was placed under the command of Epaminondas and served as the nucleus of the federal army. A popular assembly, with delegates from each city of the 

League, was created as the chief governmental organ. 

Sparta's general policies after Aegospotami naturally had aroused widespread opposition among the states that passed under her control. The ill-advised aggression against Thebes in large measure solidified these anti-Spartan sentiments and facilitated the reconstruction of the Athenian Empire by 377 B.C. The constitution of the revived Empire contained a number of provisions designed to ensure the member states against a recurrence of the abuses so largely responsible for the collapse of the original organization. There were to be annual congresses of representatives of the member states to govern the Empire in collaboration with the Athenian Assembly. 

Since Athens was excluded from representation in the congresses, suspicions that she wished to dominate the organization were largely allayed. Athens further promised to refrain from the practice of sending cleruchies to the member states, and guarantee against financial abuses was afforded by the proviso that each state was to fix the amount of its contribution to the common fund. 

The unsettled conditions in the Greek world were in large measure responsible for the emergence of Thessaly as a major power at this time. Jason, a capable military commander and adroit diplomat, made himself tyrant of Pherae and, with this city as a center, enlarged his authority until ultimately all Thessaly came under his

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

sway. The tyrant had the most grandiose ambitions, for he hoped to unite all Greece under his rule preliminary to embarkation on a campaign against Persia. A Persian war, he believed, would evoke a nationalistic spirit in Greece that could be applied to the stabilization of Thessalian hegemony. Since Sparta was the chief power in a position to frustrate the attainment of his objectives, he concluded an alliance with Epaminondas. A complete reorientation of policy seemed to be demanded, even in Athens, but the assassination of Jason precipitated internecine strife in Thessaly that soon led to its withdrawal from the front rank of Greek powers.

In 371 B.C. Sparta attempted to stabilize conditions in Greece by the conclusion of a general peace at the Congress of Corinth. Epaminondas claimed the right to sign the treaty in behalf of all Boeotia, but Sparta refused to recognize the validity of this claim since such recognition would have been equivalent to sanctioning the Theban League. All efforts at compromise failed, and the withdrawal of 

Epaminondas from the Congress ensured its failure. Sparta, in retaliation, refused to evacuate Boeotia and precipitated hostilities by launching an offensive against Thebes. 

The ensuing battle of Leuctra (371 B.C.) had momentous consequences, for it ended Spartan hegemony in Greece and irreparably shattered her military prestige. Time after time the Spartan armies had triumphed largely by virtue of the fact that their strength was concentrated on their left flank, making it easy for them to turn the right flank of the enemy. To frustrate these tactics, Epaminondas concentrated his best troops on his right so that when the Spartans attempted their usual maneuver they were repulsed and soon scattered in complete disorder, necessitating immediate withdrawal from Boeotia.

Epaminondas was not content with mere defense, and he soon indicated his intention to follow up his victory by invading the Peloponnesus. The way was largely prepared, for as a result of the growing reaction against Spartan rule in south Greece an Arcadian League, with Megalopolis as its capital, had been established in defiance of Sparta. When Sparta attempted to dissolve the confederacy, appeal for assistance was promptly sent to Thebes. Epaminondas grasped the opportunity to invade the Peloponnesus with the support of the League and he continued his offensive by entering Laconia itself. For generations the military might of Sparta had made her immune from invasion, but now a pitifully small force attempted to defend the state whose impotence was so dramatically revealed.

The Theban invasion was by no means the only disaster, for Messenia revolted, the helots were emancipated, and the perioeci were encouraged to disavow Spartan rule. The whole economic structure of the Spartan state thus was destroyed, and complete collapse of the power that so long had dominated the Peloponnesus seemed imminent. 

The Athenian government followed the news of these events in the Peloponnesus with mixed emotions. There was, of course, virtually no sympathy for Sparta, but expediency dictated intervention before she should be completely ruined. Emergence of Thebes as the unchallenged master of Greece would offer no reassuring prospects to Athens; she accordingly sent an army under Iphicrates to the relief of the hard-pressed Spartans and forced the Thebans to retreat. A second Theban invasion then was repulsed by Sparta with the aid of reënforcements from Syracuse. In the meantime, the Arcadian League repudiated the protection of Epaminondas, confident in its ability to preserve its independence without his aid. Efforts to secure a general peace by the convocation of a congress at Delphi failed, and a period of diplomatic sparring ensued.

Events soon provoked another Theban invasion of the Peloponnesus. In the first place, the Arcadian League wantonly attacked 

Olympia while the games were in progress and seized the sacred treasure. Then, too, Mantinea seceded from the League in 362 B.C., and her action threatened to be the prelude to the dissolution of the confederacy. While the relations between the League and Epaminondas had not been particularly happy, he believed that its preservation as a counterpoise to Sparta was essential. He thereupon attempted to coerce Mantinea into recognizing her responsibilities to the League. During the ensuing siege, the Theban statesman was slain (362 B.C.), and there was no one of comparable ability to succeed him. The continuance of his policies, however, eventually would have been disastrous not only to Thebes but to all Greece, for Thebes under his direction had been just as selfish and provincial as Athens and Sparta had been in the past. Indeed, by his attacks on 

Sparta he had removed the one really stable force in Greece and hastened the loss of independence. His failure to meet the obvious need for genuine pan-Hellenism led inexorably to the Macedonian conquest.

CHAPTER Athenian Civilization from Pericles to Philip 

HE period from the elevation of Pericles to the chief magistracy to the loss of Greek independence was one of the most creative epochs in the cultural history of mankind. 

Democratic tendencies in Athens reached fruition. The golden age of Greek philosophy had its equally glorious counterpart in architecture, sculpture, and painting. Attic drama reached its full development, while the achievements in oratory, history, and other literary forms were equally brilliant. Although it has been customary to divide the period into the Periclean and post-Periclean ages, this division has little save tradition to justify it. 

As we have seen, the Athenian government became completely democratic in the age of Pericles. The chief strategus was the leading executive officer and he was expected to conduct diplomacy, command the army and navy, and frame broad policies for submission to the Assembly in either regular or specially summoned sessions. In theory, any citizen was eligible for the chief magistracy, but in practice, of course, choice was confined to those of wealth, aristocratic lineage, and demonstrated ability, in view of the great responsibilities with which the office was invested. The chief strategus was elected by the whole citizenry, while his nine colleagues were chosen by tribal elections.

The Council of the Five Hundred, instituted by Clisthenes, played a prominent part in the operation of the Athenian government. It was made up of fifty members chosen annually by lot from each of the ten tribes. It supervised elections and scrutinized candidates for office to determine their fitness. It also exercised supervisory functions over the navy, the state cavalry, and public buildings. Treason cases were subject to its jurisdiction and it was authorized to inflict the death penalty for this offense. Other offenses against the state

lso came within its competence provided the penalties did not exceed a fine of 500 drachmae. To facilitate the operation of the 

Council, it will be recalled, it was organized into ten committees or prytanies, each of which served for one-tenth of the official year. 

Forty regular meetings of the Assembly were held each year, that is, four in each of the ten prytanies. The order of business was carefully prescribed. In the first session of each group of four, magisterial conduct was reviewed and the condition of the grain tradeinvestigated. The session concluded with an examination of the general state of the commonwealth. In the second session, suppliants and petitioners were heard, and action was taken in response to their appeals. The third and fourth sessions were more general in character, but the order of business had to include at least three subjects pertaining to religious matters, three issues involving foreign affairs, and three subjects of a miscellaneous nature classified as "secular." 

In the time of Pericles, legislation was drafted in preliminary fashion by a committee of the Assembly, after which it was put in official form for submission to the Assembly by the Council of the Five Hundred. When the legislation in final draft was submitted, the Assembly passed or rejected it by majority vote, usually without debate, although discussion was permitted if requested. Toward the close of the period under discussion, however, a more elaborate procedure was employed. In the first Assembly session of each prytany, the thesmothetae reviewed the laws of the state in formal order. 

Proposals for the repeal or modification of these laws then were entertained. At the fourth session, these proposed changes were read and referred to a committee of the Assembly, known as the nomothetae, for final disposition by majority vote.

Pericles had discouraged excessive constitutional change by making the sponsors of such changes liable for punishment if their plans were unworkable. From this, a regular procedure to test the constitutionality of measures was developed. Any proposed law could be challenged by a writ of illegality, whereupon the sponsor of the law became the defendant in a hearing before the Assembly. If constitutionality of the law was upheld, the person who had utilized the writ of illegality was fined and forbidden to employ the writ in the future. If, on the other hand, the Assembly decided that the law in question was unconstitutional, its sponsor was disenfranchised, fined, and in some cases put to death.

Most judicial cases were tried by the jury courts established by Solon primarily as courts of appeal from the judgments of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

archons. With the decline in the powers of the archons, the jury courts became courts in the first instance, but homicides were still tried in accordance with the provisions of the Draconian law. All citizens over thirty were eligible for jury service with a modest stipend. Each year, 6000 prospective jurors were chosen, and from this number one-tenth were selected as the panel for the year and put under oath. Individual juries of 501 members each then were chosen and assigned to specific cases. The large number gave assurance against bribery or other forms of corruption, for the decision was rendered by majority vote, and the odd number, of course, prevented a deadlock.

The archons prepared legal cases for trial by taking the depositions of the litigants and their witnesses, which they subsequently read to the jury. Plaintiff and defendant pleaded their own cases, but they often employed professional orators to write their speeches. Witnesses appeared only in order to acknowledge their testimony already embodied in the written depositions. There was no crossexamination, but the jurors were permitted to ask questions and the principals in a case were empowered to question each other. The speeches delivered by the litigants had the most weight with the juries, and the professional rhetoricians who frequently prepared these addresses skillfully included political and religious issues designed to enlist the sympathies of the jurymen, who also took into account the reputation of the litigants.

The chief source of state revenues was the tax collected from the imperial dependencies. Sale of concessions and royalties from the state mines, especially the silver mines of Laurium, were other major sources of income. Rents from other state properties, as well as market and port dues, judicial fees, fines, and escheated property, also afforded a fairly constant income. It must be remembered, too, that the liturgies, whereby heavy burdens of expenditure were imposed on wealthy citizens, in large measure compensated for the apparent inadequacy of state income.

A number of weaknesses in the Athenian government already have been noted as they were especially apparent in the period of the Peloponnesian War. The control of the Assembly over the formulation of state policies both civil and military was too direct, with the inevitable result that hasty action as well as violent fluctuations of policy became increasingly characteristic. Another basic weakness was the lack of revenues adequate to defray the heavy expenditures entailed by the public building program, the subsidization of the

theatre, and the payment of stipends for state service. Personal differences and family rivalries played far too large a part in government. Corruption and indifference of the citizenry were problems that have perennially confronted all democratic governments. 

Our best source for an estimate of the Athenian population at the time of the Peloponnesian War is found in Thucydides (II, 13).

From this it has been calculated that there were from 150,000 to 165,000 of civic status of which about 50,000 were adult males. 

There were, in addition, about 15,000 aliens, or metics, and perhaps as many as 80,000 slaves. The metics played a significant role in the commercial and industrial life of the state, and their settlement in the city was encouraged for economic reasons. They paid a special head tax, were debarred from land ownership, and were required to place themselves under the guardianship of Athenian citizens who represented them in legal capacities. Citizenship sometimes was bestowed in recognition of distinguished service, but a more frequent reward was exemption from the special tax and legal guardianship. 

There were two main types of slaves: those owned by private individuals and those held by the state. War captives and convicted criminals furnished most of the slaves after the abolition of servitude for debt, but many were purchased by dealers abroad, and kidnapping was not unknown. Treatment of slaves naturally was in large measure dependent upon their value. The stupid and dangerous who could be employed only at hard labor were worked in gangs and subjected to appalling cruelty, whereas the lot of skilled workers was much easier. Masters were liable to prosecution if they killed a slave, and slaves who were persistently abused could flee to a sanctuary and request their sale to a more humane owner. Some slaves who were skilled artisans were granted virtual freedom by their masters and were merely required to pay a portion of their earnings to their owners. State owned slaves were used as oarsmen on naval vessels or as policemen, executioners, and torturers. Those who were educated frequently were assigned clerical duties. of With the Solonian reforms and the land redistribution program Pisistratus, the tendency toward the plantation system of agriculture was arrested. By the age of Pericles, a farm of 65 acres was considered large. For centuries, the two-field system of cultivation had been employed, that is, the arable land was divided into two portions which were alternately sown and allowed to lie fallow. During the last years of the Peloponnesian War, the three-field system was introduced wherein one third of the arable was sown with a spring

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

crop, the second third with a fall crop, and the remaining third allowed to lie fallow. This improvement in agricultural practice considerably increased the yield of the Athenian farms, and, as already pointed out, was a major factor in the post-war recovery of the state. 

Rainfall was too scanty to enable large crops of cereals to be grown, with the result that by the age of Pericles Athens was dependent upon importations for from one-third to one-half of her food supply. 

The importation of grain from Scythia (south Russia), Egypt, Cyprus, and Sicily comprised a major part of Athenian commerce.

Although the trade was in private hands, it was carefully regulated by the government in view of its vital importance. Athens also imported large quantities of salt, fish, hides, timber, paint, dyes, and ores, while Phoenician dates and Sicilian cheeses were also staple import commodities. Carpets, drapery, and bedding from Persia, Carthage, and Miletus were to be found in the homes of wealthy citizens. The chief exports were wine, oil, vases, cloth, cutlery, armor, and furniture. Ships of about 250 tons burden were used for commercial purposes. They were operated by merchant owners who tramped" from port to port. Space in the vessels frequently was rented to merchants who had no ships of their own. 

Banking practice seems to have kept pace with commercial expansion. Money-changers accepted funds on deposit and made loans available to those engaged in commercial and industrial enterprises. 

Despite the fact that rates of interest were very high because of the many risks involved in trade, most commercial ventures were financed by borrowed capital, and the profits of successful voyages were sufficiently large to compensate for the high cost of credit. 

Although letters of credit sometimes were arranged by private individuals, accounts usually were settled by actual transfer of coins or bullion.

As in other ancient states, industry was conducted on a small scale. 

The master of the industrial establishment was assisted by members of his family, apprentices, and perhaps a few slaves. Articles were made to order, and if the craftsman accumulated a little capital he might assemble a modest stock of his wares for direct retail sale. The famous armory of Cephalus which employed 120 men seems to have been the largest industrial organization of the classical period. 

Educational facilities in Athens seem woefully inadequate when compared with modern emphasis on the maintenance of schools. 

There was little thought of mass education; such education as there was available was primarily for the children of those in comfortable

ΙΟΙ financial circumstances. Education began with home training. When a boy reached his seventh year, he would be enrolled in a school conducted by a master who often was a slave and who made his livelihood from the fees paid by the pupils. The pupil was accompanied to school by a slave known as the pedagogue, who supervised the boy's morals and cared for his school-room equipment. Gymnastic exercises occupied a prominent place in the curricula of the schools. 

The academic portion of the work (musicé), in addition to reading, writing, and simple calculations, included some study of the epic literature, chiefly for content, but in part for the sake of illustrating grammatical principles. Singing and playing the lyre often were included in a basic education. Adolescents might undertake advanced physical training, and if they evinced unusual athletic prowess might be made ready for participation in the games. Others might study rhetoric and oratory with a view to a political career; as the government of the state became more democratic there naturally was increased interest in such studies. From his eighteenth to his twentieth years, the youth was engaged in military training and garrison duty. 

During the age of Pericles, the Sophists became very popular as teachers. Their work really represented a reaction against the abstract nature of Greek thought up to their time. They held that absolute truth was beyond the grasp of mortal minds; therefore the speculations of the philosophers would inevitably be sterile. Truth was what was true for the individual. Education therefore should be directed toward practical objectives, particularly preparation for state service. These itinerant teachers who lectured and tutored for fees laid most stress on rhetoric and oratory because of their obvious political utility.

The great age of Athenian philosophy was ushered in by the career of Socrates. He was born about 470 B.C., the son of a stone cutter. 

He saw military service as a hoplite in the Peloponnesian War and was a member of the Council of the Five Hundred for the year 406 B.C. and distinguished himself by opposing the condemnation of the hapless commanders of the fleet at Arginusae. He was a passive opponent of the Thirty, refusing to carry out their orders, and only their fall saved him from the consequences of their wrath.

The philosopher was physically ugly and his habits were extremely simple. He often lounged in the market place, possibly in order to escape the hectoring of Xanthippe, his shrewish wife. Although rumor alleged that the Delphic Oracle had called him the wisest of Athenians, he disclaimed superior knowledge and asserted

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

that his wisdom was little more than willingness to admit ignorance which, after all, was the primary requisite to the attainment of wisdom. His teaching methods were devoid of formality. He merely involved acquaintances or even casual passersby in discussion, during the course of which he brought out their ideas by a series of questions, first simple, but gradually increasing in complexity, until they plumbed the depths of the subject's mind.

Since Socrates left no extant writings, our knowledge of his teachings is derived from the works of his famous disciples, Plato and Xenophon. He apparently took as a basic premise the principle that every human act is impelled by the desire to secure happiness; therefore, evil acts are essentially the product of ignorance. One's true self is good, and reflection which leads to self-knowledge inevitably impels to the good and virtuous. Self-knowledge and control bring out the inherent good in man, and religion is therefore unnecessary for the good life. Since conduct always involves a choice among divergent motives and impulses, rigid examination of the motives is necessary to make clear ultimate purposes and enable one to choose the good.

These teachings outraged conservative Athenians who charged the philosopher with impiety and corruption of youth. His alleged sympathy with oligarchy likewise stirred up considerable political resentment. He was accordingly brought to trial on these charges in 

399 B.C. before a jury of the usual 501 members. The jury condemned him to death, expecting, however, the usual plea of the defendant for commutation to exile which would probably have been granted. 

Socrates refused to avail himself of this privilege; instead, he chided the jury and proposed that he be boarded at public expense as a state benefactor. The death sentence therefore remained in force, and the philosopher drank the hemlock in the presence of a few friends whom he edified by a moving discourse on death and immortality. 

Plato, the great pupil of Socrates, was born of aristocratic parents about 428 B.C. After the death of his master, he went to Megara and thence to Syracuse to study the Pythagorean philosophy. According to tradition, he was sold into slavery by Dionysus, tyrant of Syracuse, but subsequently was ransomed. Upon return to Athens, he founded his famous Academy. The term Academus originally referred to a grove near a gymnastic ground in the vicinity of Athens. Plato purchased a garden in this neighborhood which he equipped with seats for the open air lectures and walks which he and his pupils trod while engaged in informal philosophical discussion.

Some years later he accepted an invitation from Dionysus the Younger to come to Syracuse to introduce some of his political theories. When the Syracusans tired of these experiments he returned to Athens and resumed his teaching. 

The central feature of Plato's philosophy is the concept of the objective existence of ideas. The Demi-urge, or creative force, has created from non-being a world of ideas; the ideas of truth, beauty, goodness, etc., are the real existences. The physical world is merely the reflection of the eternal ideas. He further held that the individual soul is made up of three components: the appetitive, or sensual; the spirited, or emotional; and the intellectual. Men could be assigned to one of these three classes depending upon which of the three soul elements predominated.

In the Republic, Plato applied these principles to the political life of the city-state. He mistrusted democracy and believed that only a small minority who had attained wisdom and goodness were fit to rule. He held that the populace of a state should be divided into three classes corresponding to the three soul elements. Those in whom the appetitive element predominated would be the artisans and laborers. The soldiers, both men and women, would be chosen from those who were primarily emotional, while the intellectuals would furnish the class from which the rulers or guardians of the state ultimately would be selected. Eugenics was to be employed to eliminate the physically unfit. Education was to be afforded to all in the measure to which they were fitted to absorb it; during the course of the educational process, the citizens would be allocated to the classes for which they were fitted. Selection of the intellectuals was to be made by the time they had reached the age of twenty. They then were to be given ten years of rigorous education in which the study of mathematics was emphasized. Upon reaching the age of thirty, another selection was to be made, and the chosen candidates were to receive five years' training in logic and fifteen years of practical experience in both military and civil activities. Upon reaching the age of fifty, the small group was to be considered fit to undertake the guardianship of the state. Communism of goods, wives, children, and dependents was advocated for the guardians so as to obviate the danger of dissension among them.

Aristotle, the illustrious pupil of the Platonic Academy, and one of the greatest scholars of all time, was born in 384 B.C., at Stageirus, in Chalcidice. In 343 B.C. he became the teacher of Alexander, and after his pupil became ruler of Macedonia, he went to Athens and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

established his Lyceum. His teaching methods differed widely from those of his mentor, for he insisted on the necessity for observation and experience to supplement speculation. In his Metaphysics, where he deals with ultimate verities, he avoids Plato's static system by postulating that development or change is reality. He draws a fundamental distinction between matter and form. Matter is potentiality, that is, it has the intrinsic possibility of becoming something else, whereas form is pure actuality. In the example of the acorn, he points out that the acorn is a potential oak, while the oak is a potential house. 

Thus the oak tree is form to the acorn but matter to the house. If the chain of changes is carried back far enough one arrives at pure form, or that which creates but is not created. 

Aristotle founded the science of logic and his introduction of the syllogism gave an indispensable tool to argumentative reasoning. In the syllogism, which we all frequently employ, we start with a major premise or general concept and proceed through a minor premise or particular instance to a conclusion. For example, the statement that the planets revolve around the sun would constitute a major premise; the statement that the earth is one of the planets would be the minor premise leading to the conclusion that the earth revolves around the sun.

His Physics lays down fundamental laws of matter, motion, form, and his doctrine of causation, while astronomical principles are set forth in his De Caelo (Concerning the Sky). His works on natural history and zoology were authoritative textbooks for centuries; indeed, in the late Middle Ages, the writings of Aristotle were put virtually on a parity with the Scriptures as repositories of truth. The philosopher's two treatises on ethics were followed by a work on politics, for he believed that ethics was inseparably connected with political science. His ideal state was described in the Politics as the small, autonomous, aristocratic commonwealth. Study of the constitutions of the Greek states was an important project undertaken by the Lyceum. The constitution of Athens has been preserved as a result of these labors and it is a historical source of the utmost importance. Aristotle may also be termed the founder of literary criticism. His Poetics dealt with epic poetry, comedy, and tragedy but only the section on the last subject has been preserved intact. 

His Rhetoric was used as a model for many later manuals on oratory. 

The drama and the theatre are among the greatest gifts of Greece to our Western civilization. While the origins of Athenian drama can be traced to the Homeric poems which furnished many of the

themes, its technical evolution began in the Age of the Tyrants. 

During the Pisistratan regime in Athens, the festivals in honor of Dionysus were greatly embellished. A central feature of these ceremonies was the singing and dancing of choruses of young men masquerading as satyrs and depicting certain myths about the god. 

Even after Attic drama was fully evolved, it was customary to add a satyr play to trilogies, or cycles of three plays, in accordance with established tradition. Drama began to develop from these choral performances when Thespis introduced a speaker who came forward from time to time to address the chorus and receive their responses. 

Aeschylus (c. 523-456 B.C.) is credited with the introduction of actual dialogue. He utilized two characters in his earlier works and was instrumental in the final adoption of three as the standard practice. The dialogue between the characters carried on the major portion of the narrative, and the relegation of the chorus to a secondary role was begun. Seven tragedies of the founder of Attic tragedy have been preserved. His greatest work was the trilogy made up of the Agamemnon, Libation Bearers, and the Eumenides. Most of his themes were drawn from legend and mythology. Religious or moral conflict is a recurrent motif in his plots. Inexorable curses are laid on the families of powerful personages who have committed sins; they struggle to avert retribution, but in the end the prophecy of their final atonement is fulfilled. Indeed, with the work of Aeschylus the idea of nemesis becomes a virtually standard feature of Attic tragedy. In the Persians, the dramatist tells of the destruction of the fleet of Xerxes and shows that the cause of the disaster is in reality an old doom. While the work naturally reflects the jubilation of 

Athens over the brilliant victories of Salamis and Plataea, the horror of war is graphically expressed. 

Sophocles (c. 496–406 B.C.) was born of well-to-do parents near 

Athens. His political career was brilliant and included service as strategus. Although it is said that he was victorious in twenty dramatic competitions, including a triumph over Aeschylus, only seven plays have survived. His best known work is the trilogy which includes his Oedipus Tyrannus, Antigone, and Oedipus at Colonnus.

His work is characterized by great discernment and power of character analysis. He was primarily responsible for the adoption of the practice of employing three characters and he was the first to produce trilogies in which the component plays were not necessarily connected in theme. His use of the chorus was especially adroit, for while it was not employed to carry on the narrative, it was integral

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

to the play in that it described the sympathetic auditor's reactions to the action.

Some critics consider the Oedipus Tyrannus the finest example of Greek tragedy. It tells of the unhappy fate of Oedipus, son of Laius, king of Thebes, who, according to prophecy, was destined to kill his father and marry his mother. His parents abandon him in order to preclude fulfillment of the doom, and the boy is reared by Polybus, king of Corinth. Upon reaching manhood, Oedipus leaves Corinth in order to avoid killing Polybus who he thinks is his father. On the way to Thebes, he slays four wayfarers who had attacked him as a result of a quarrel. One of these is Laius, his father, although Oedipus, of course, is ignorant of the fact that part of the prophecy now has been fulfilled. Some time after his arrival at Thebes, he marries 

Jocasta, widow of Laius, who actually is his mother, although both are ignorant of the relationship. A plague then falls on Thebes and a seer contends that it is due to the murder and incest committed by Oedipus. Proof of his charges finally is forthcoming. Jocasta commits suicide, and Oedipus blinds himself as atonement for the sins he has inadvertently committed. The Antigone, considered by some even greater than the first play of the trilogy, narrates the story of the final disasters to overtake the family of Laius. Antigone, daughter of Oedipus, angers the new king of Thebes by burying her dead brother's body in defiance of the king's express prohibition. The king condemns her to death despite the fact that she is betrothed to his son. He countermands the death sentence, but his change of heart comes too late to save Antigone and his son who has committed suicide. Upon learning of the tragedy, the queen also kills herself, and the broken king survives, the prey of ceaseless remorse. 

Euripides (480-406 B.C.) was the great realist of his age. His attitude toward religion, tradition, and law was frankly skeptical. He expressed his own views through the mouths of his dramatic characters and this he considered of far greater importance than fidelity of character portrayal. Eighteen of his plays have been preserved, of which the Alcestis was probably the earliest while the famous Bacchae was the last he produced. His chief technical innovation was the divorce of the chorus from the action of the play and its employment merely in interludes which had no vital connection with the plot. Another change was his practice of including long prologues which delineated the setting and provided the auditor with the requisite information to appreciate the action that followed. Mythology furnished many of his themes, yet his attitude toward my-

thology was one of incredulity. Sophocles had expressed some skepticism as to the workings of the gods in human affairs. Observation led him to believe that the wicked often prospered while the virtuous were laden with misfortune. Euripides went much further. Outright atheism would have meant certain condemnation; therefore the dramatist contented himself with thinly veiled attacks on established religious beliefs. Life after death he held contrary to reason, while the evident disorder and maladjustment in the world belied the doctrine of divine intervention in human affairs. 

Aristophanes (445-386 B.C.) was the outstanding writer of comedies. Eleven of his works are extant. He achieved his effects by satirizing contemporary institutions, ideals, and manners. He was equally adept with delicate insinuation or uncouth burlesque. In his Frogs, he pilloried the literary critics of his day. Contemporary intellectual movements with their emphasis on abstraction were ridiculed in the Clouds. The Athenian proclivity for litigation furnished the theme of the Wasps, while the vagaries of government afforded the target in the Birds. His Lysistrata was a plea for peace which attained its effect by making military activities ridiculous.

His work was characteristic of Athenian comedy. It was boisterous, sensual, and often obscene. Human foibles and frailties were exposed with unerring penetration, yet with a good humor that disarmed resentment.

Greek drama was performed in open-air theatres. A theatre was built on a hillside which afforded a natural pitch to the structure; the semicircular rows of seats were arranged in ascending tiers. 

Wooden seats were employed in the early theatres, with a tier or two of stone for the magistrates and other dignitaries. In later structures, all seats were of stone. The semicircle partly surrounded a flat, open, circular space known as the orchestra. Here the actors performed, and the space was sufficiently large for the chorus and dancers. In the back of the orchestra was a tent or booth, known as the skene and used by the participants as a dressing room. The skene was the origin of the stage, for the temporary structures ultimately were replaced by permanent buildings. 

Tragedies were performed in the morning, and comedies, from which women were excluded, in the afternoon. The Athenian government, as a result of an innovation of Pericles, paid the cost of admission for the poor, as a form of state subsidy for dramatic activity. 

In order to compete for the prize at dramatic festivals, contestants were required to submit trilogies. The prize was awarded by decision.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of the spectators. An Athenian drama perhaps would seem tedious to the modern playgoer. Tragedy was largely devoid of action because of the limitations of stagecraft. Most of the action was presumed to take place "off stage" and was described in long speeches by the characters or announced by heralds. All parts were played by men. Each actor might play a number of different characters during the course of the play; transformations were made simply by changing masks. 

Our two great literary sources for the history of Greece are the works of Herodotus and Thucydides. Herodotus (c. 484–425 B.C.) 

was a native of Halicarnassus. He also resided for a time in Samos prior to his settlement in Athens. His travels were unusually wide for his day and much of the information embodied in his history was acquired by personal observation. His history is divided into nine books, books VI to IX of which embrace his account of the Persian Wars. These later books are far more valuable than the early ones which are a review of the geography and government of the Persian Empire.

The material which is based on his own observations has proved reliable in many instances where a check has been possible. When he depended on the accounts of others, he naturally often was led to erroneous conclusions. He often included legends and anecdotes merely for the interest they imparted to the work, but the incorporation of this material did not indicate that the historian was credulous, as many modern critics hold. When he encountered conflicting versions in his inquiries, he often reproduced both views and left the problem of historical criticism up to the reader. He had no knowledge of military tactics, a serious deficiency for one writing about a war period. Political bias frequently distorted his evaluation of personalities and events. He was notoriously unfair to Themistocles, yet he evinced surprising tolerance for the East. Despite the limitations and technical imperfections of his work, Herodotus merits his traditional title of "father of history." 

Thucydides (c. 460–400 B.C.), a relative of Miltiades and Cimon, was an active participant in Athenian politics. He served as strategus and was banished to Thrace because of the miscarriage of political and military plans with which he was identified. His monumental history of the Peloponnesian War covered the period from 431 to 411 B.C. and was prefaced by a long introduction in which the causes of the struggle were explained in masterly fashion. He was an eyewitness of many of the occurrences he related; when forced to rely

on the testimony of others, he employed such a high degree of critical acumen as to justify his repute as the first scientific historian. 

His style was a model of succinctness and clarity. His favorite device to enhance interest was to put speeches into the mouths of historical personages. Opposing policies were brought out by imaginary debates between their proponents.

Oratory was a leading vehicle of literary expression in the period. 

Oratorical proficiency was indispensable in the Athenian commonwealth, for the political enlightenment of the populace was virtually dependent on the spoken word. Diplomacy with foreign powers was conducted through the medium of embassies, so there was obvious need for individuals who could effectively present the Athenian arguments on such occasions. As we already have seen, procedure before the jury courts emphasized the speeches of the litigants as a prime factor in the determination of the verdict, and the ability effectively to present one's side of the case naturally was a major objective of formal education. There were three types of oratory: the forensic, utilized primarily in pleading before the juries; the epideictic, characterized by great oratorical embellishment, used in funeral orations, religious festivals, and public gatherings of a commemorative nature; and the deliberative, employed in political debate. Since there was such a widespread demand for polished orations, the appearance of the professional rhetorician was an inevitable result. Many speeches after delivery were written for circulation; indeed, in many cases, the orations were composed primarily for their literary value with no intention of practical application. The orations of Lysias were characterized by consummate mastery of technique. He learned all that his mentors could teach and then developed a unique style, distinguished by simplicity, dramatic fervor, and a talent for enlisting the emotions of his audience. Isocrates (436–338 B.C.) accurately could be termed a publicist. His artistry surpassed that of Lysias in rhythm and euphony. As an outstanding advocate of Greek nationalism, he excoriated his countrymen for their petty jealousies and expressed his willingness to support Philip of Macedon if Macedonian rule would result in the eventual uni fication of Greece. 

All the arts of the orator were the pliant tools of Demosthenes (c. 384–322 B.C.). The most famous of the Athenian orators was the son of a wealthy manufacturer. Upon the death of his father, he was defrauded of his inheritance by corrupt executors. He was physically weak, churlish, and socially repugnant. Brooding over his

IIO WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

misfortunes produced a passionate desire for vengeance. When he resolved to enter politics, he proceeded with indomitable perseverance to overcome his faults of temperament and speech. Arduous study and unflagging practice finally gave him a matchless oratorical technique, which, when employed by one of his passionate nature, could not fail to exercise a profound force. He became the leader of the anti-Macedonian faction in Athens, and in Aeschines he found an oratorical adversary worthy of his skill. His famous Philippics against Philip of Macedon, in addition to their technical perfection, are characterized by a scarcely restrained frenzy that ranks them among the greatest orations of all time. 

The great program of Pericles for the beautification of Athens received its primary impetus in the desire to repair the ravages of the Persian occupation of the city. With the inauguration of the program, however, the plans for reconstruction soon were amplified to include much new building. Tribute from the imperial dependencies defrayed the major portion of the expense. The great deposits of fine marble in the hills of Attica as well as the mineral resources of the state, particularly the mines of Laurium, made it possible to carry out the lavish program with a direct expenditure of about $2,250,000. 

The first structure to be completed was the Odeum, or music hall, the ruins of which are just east of the theatre. Wooden interior columns supported a conical roof which according to tradition was built in imitation of the conical tent of Xerxes. The temple of 

Hephaestus, completed during the Periclean regime, is the best preserved of the Greek temples. It stands northwest of the Acropolis and is built in the Doric style. 

Work on the Parthenon was begun in 447 B.C. Callicrates and 

Ictinus were the architects in charge; Phidias, the sculptor, who executed or directed most of the work of ornamentation, also participated in the planning. The edifice was divided into two chambers. 

The smaller chamber was regarded as the parthenon, or storehouse of Athena, the goddess in whose honor the temple was erected. The statue of the goddess stood in the east chamber, or cella, which was regarded as her symbolical dwelling place. The structure was in the pure Doric style and was amphiprostyle, that is, there were doors at each end, opening on porches, each with six columns. It also was peristyle, since it was completely surrounded by columns, eight on each end and seventeen on each side. The Doric columns taper with matchless grace; the beauty of the structure was primarily the result of its simplicity and perfect proportion. In order to avoid the

III illusion of sagging, the stylobate was made somewhat convex. 

Scenes of combat were depicted on the metopes, and a continuous frieze ran around the structure inside the colonnade. This frieze, designed by Phidias, depicted the Panathenaic festival. In order to avoid monotony, scenes of preparation were interspersed with processional views. The east pediment (gable) portrayed the birth of 

Athena; the west, the struggle between her and Poseidon, god of the sea.

A monumental gateway, designed by Mnesicles, served as the entrance to the Acropolis. Just inside, to the right of the entrance, was the exquisite Ionic Temple of Victory. During the Peloponnesian War, the temple of the Erechtheum was built in honor of Erechtheus, a legendary king. It was remarkable that such an undertaking should have been begun under apparently unfavorable circumstances. It may have been built in order to afford employment to impoverished artisans and laborers or, more likely, to ensure divine aid in the war. The structure was in the Ionic style. Voluted columns supported the roofs of the east and north porches, and those of the north porch are generally considered the most beautiful Ionic columns in existence. On the south of the structure was added the "Porch of the Maidens," the roof of which was supported on the heads of exquisitely sculptured maidens, who stood erect and dignified, draped with classic simplicity. An important innovation of the post-Periclean period was the Corinthian order, the distinguishing feature of which was the column, with the capital ornamented by a double row of acanthus leaves and four volutes..This style became very popular in the Hellenistic period (after Alexander the 

Great) and in Roman architecture. 

The art of sculpture reached the climax of its long period of development. Anatomical details were partially mastered before the close of the archaic period. Male nudes and draped female figures were well executed, but with the weight equally supported on both feet. Abdomens were rather crudely depicted and necks even more so. The "Critian Boy" inaugurated a new departure in that the weight was not equally distributed, while the body and head were turned in a posture of relaxation.

The full glory of the classical period opened with the work of Phidias, the friend of Pericles. While he may not have executed the entire Parthenon frieze, he probably was responsible for the conception and planning of this monumental work. His best known statues were the "Athena" in the Parthenon and the "Zeus" at Olympia

II 

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

both of which were in ivory and gold ornamented with precious stones. The human figure was idealized in the work of Phidias. 

Bodies were tall, slender, and lithe; faces austere in their sheer perfection of line. As an aftermath of the disastrous plague of 430 B.C., Phidias was exiled along with Pericles. He was accused of having embezzled some of the gold allotted for the statue of Athena, while the alleged inclusion of his own portrait among the figures of the Parthenon frieze was also cited among the charges. 

In most cases we rely on written descriptions or inferior copies for our conceptions of the masterpieces of Greek sculpture. The "Hermes with Dionysus," found during the course of excavations at Olympia, however, is considered by many to be an original of the famous Praxiteles who carried the art to a standard that has never been surpassed. Like all truly great artists, Praxiteles was an innovator. His "Aphrodite at Cnidus" was a startling break with convention in that he depicted the goddess in the nude in the act of preparing for the bath. His statues were even more graceful than those of Phidias; muscular treatment was more delicate and flesh was portrayed with finer texture. Bodies often were portrayed in leaning postures in which curves were essential instead of being mere accidental deviations from the vertical as in earlier work. Heads, depicted with curly hair, usually were idealized. In some of the work of Praxiteles, however, there was a pronounced trend toward the realism that was the dominant note of the statues of Scopas, who designed the famous mausoleum for the entombment of the ruler of Caria. 

Little is known of painting in the period. The Athenian artist, Apollodorus, was credited with the mastery of perspective so essential with the growing popularity of painting on canvas. So realistic was his work and that of his pupils that Plato was impelled to bemoan what he considered reprehensible deception. It is said that 

Zeuxis painted a bunch of grapes so realistically that birds attempted to pluck them. Vase painting which had so large a place in the art of earlier periods became conventionalized and almost devoid of merit. Miniatures, however, were developed to an extent hitherto unparalleled, while reproductions and caricatures of classic statues were well executed.

Interest in theoretical science owed its origin to the Atomists and Pythagoreans of the sixth century before Christ. Methods continued to be almost exclusively speculative; the discovery of ultimate truth was the objective. Heraclitus introduced a dynamic metaphysics that

secured wide recognition. He denied the reality of being and held that becoming or change was the essence of all things.
