A ruling reason produced and controlled the endless changes in the universe, but only a few great minds, endowed with the universal omniscience, could properly conceive of this ruling principle.

The Eleatics, however, continued their assertion that being alone had objective reality, and motion and change were illusory. Empedocles attempted to reconcile these views. He held that there were four primary elements: earth, air, fire, and water. These elements constituted being and, as such, represented the static phase of his philosophy. Elements, however, by the operation of the forces of love and hate, i.e., attraction and repulsion, could combine and separate, and with this hypothesis he managed to retain the dynamic concept of Heraclitus.

Leucippus and his pupil, Democritus, held that all matter was composed of a multitude of atoms which moved in empty space or void. 

The force of gravitation impelled the atoms to cohere to form matter. The all-pervading materialism of this hypothesis made it unattractive to thinkers, especially in Athens. The doctrines of Anaxagoras were more in harmony with Greek intellectual traditions. 

He taught that the universe was ruled by an infinite intelligence, or pure actuality. Centuries later these concepts were to become integral features of religious thought. 

Not all science was abstract and speculative. Astronomers taught the sphericity of the earth, sun, and moon. Meton invented a calendar that corrected the discrepancies between lunar and solar years and was permitted to set it up on the Athenian Pnyx. Hippocrates of 

Cos founded the science of medicine by divorcing healing from religion and superstition. Drugs, surgery, and cauterization were the only expedients of the legitimate practitioner; when they failed there was no hope. Charms, incantations, even visits to the shrine of Aesculapius, god of healing, were of no avail. Disease was attributable only to natural causes; therefore natural means alone could effect a cure. Thus in science as in philosophy, literature, and the arts 

Greece contributed a cultural heritage that was to be the very basis of our Western civilization.

CHAPTER The Macedonian Empire and the 

Hellenistic Age

T the close of the Peloponnesian War, Sparta was the leading state in Greece. She failed to measure up to the opportunity for leadership which confronted her because of the ambitions of Lysander, the policy of severity toward the conquered states, the Persian complication, and, above all, the rigidity of her governmental institutions. Thebes supplanted Sparta after the battle of 

Leuctra, but, as we have seen, she too failed to evolve a nationalistic program. The time had come for Macedonia to play her spectacular role in the history of the Greek world. 

By the middle of the fifth century Macedonia gave little promise of her future greatness. The kingdom was little more than a federation of villages and small towns. The kings were in theory autocrats, but untrammeled exercise of their powers was prevented by custom and the duty to consult an assembly of the people before infliction of the death penalty. Even as late as the Periclean Age, Macedonia was virtually synonymous with barbarism, but enlightened rulers, such as Archelaus and Perdiccas, realized the need for cultural advance and accordingly encouraged the penetration of Hellenic inspiration. Construction of roads and other public improvements stimulated commerce and promoted centralization of the kingdom. Improved methods of tax collection and greater vigilance over expenditures strengthened the financial position of the state and made possible the organization of an army. The rise of a formidable Macedonian military force, in turn, minimized the menace of the incursions of the barbarous Paoenians and Illyrians.

Upon the death of Perdiccas, who had perished in the struggle with the invaders, his son, Amyntas, was recognized as king under the guardianship of his uncle, Philip. The regency was soon ended, however, for Philip deposed his nephew and secured recognition

as ruler in his own right. The accession of Philip of Macedon was destined to mark the beginning of a new and significant era in the history of Greece. He had been taken as a hostage to Thebes in 367 B.C. in line with the attempt of Epaminondas to pacify the north. While in Thebes he familiarized himself with the military tactics so successfully employed by Epaminondas. He learned to appreciate Greek culture, and with shrewd penetration he distinguished between the enduring and the ephemeral in Hellenic civilization. The dissensions and rivalries that were speeding the Greek states toward ruin made an indelible impression on the mind of the young hostage. It was apparent that an invader of Greece need fear no united resistance to frustrate the attainment of his ambitions, and opportunity soon was afforded for Philip to prove the correctness of his evaluation of the situation in Greece.

A long period of preparation was necessary, however, before 

Philip, after his seizure of the Macedonian throne, could hope to establish his suzerainty over Greece. He accordingly inaugurated a series of reforms that ultimately gave the state financial resources and military power sufficient to support an imperialistic policy. Both the infantry and cavalry branches of the army were materially strengthened. The infantry, made up of hillsmen, was organized into territorial divisions and equipped with long spears. The usual formation was the famous "phalanx" in which the soldiers fought in close order eight to sixteen ranks deep. The "companions," or heavy-armed cavalry, operated in close coöperation with the infantry. Stationed on the flanks of the infantry, the cavalry could attempt the encirclement of the enemy while the phalanx stood firm at the center. 

Archers served to prepare the way for an attack in addition to their usual defensive functions. Philip's chief contribution to the development of military tactics was to evolve a system whereby the several arms fought as an integrated whole.

It was essential for Philip to complete the early stages of his imperialistic program without inciting the hostility of Athens. His immediate need was to secure economic resources the exploitation of which would defray the heavy cost of his internal improvements and military organization. He therefore seized Amphipolis in 357 

B.C., obviously with the view of obtaining control of the gold and silver mines of Thrace. The hostility of Athens was disarmed by the promise of the cession of Macedonian Pydna in return for Amphipolis. When Philip secured control of the Thracian mines, however, he repudiated the promise he had made in regard to Pydna and in-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

stalled a strong garrison to prevent its seizure by Athens. The 

Thracian city of Crenides then was seized and named Philippi. Philip proceeded to organize a confederacy in Chalcidice which was placed under the nominal control of the city of Olynthus which, however, was merely a puppet of Macedonia. 

The Athenian authorities, of course, saw the dangers inherent in the expansion of Macedonia, but other problems engrossed their attention and precluded firm measures in Thrace. The revived 

Athenian Empire again was in danger of dissolution, for Mausolus had set himself up as king of Caria and Lysia and was endeavoring to foment disaffection among the Athenian allies. Athens had not dealt fairly with the states of her second empire, for cleruchies had again been sent out in violation of the unequivocal promise of Athens to refrain from this practice. The intrigues of Mausolus were therefore largely successful, and Chios, Rhodes, Byzantium, and Cos seceded from the Empire. Upon the death of Mausolus in 353 B.C. the danger was lessened, but the dependencies that already had revolted could not be recovered, and since the first interest of the Athenian government was the preservation of the Empire it was hardly in a position to take the risk of becoming embroiled in a struggle with Philip.

The outbreak of the First Sacred War gave Philip his opportunity to intervene in the affairs of Greece. The immediate cause of the war was the alleged sacrilege of the state of Phocis which, it was charged, had cultivated sacred lands constituting part of the endowment of the shrine at Delphi. When the Amphictyonic Council, urged on by Thebes, decided to take measures to punish Phocis, the defiant state aggravated its guilt by the seizure of the Delphic treasury. Athens and Sparta were unwilling to permit Phocis to be crushed largely at the behest of Thebes and accordingly came to her defense. Philip intervened in behalf of the Amphictyonic League, but this obviously was merely an entering wedge for the imposition of Macedonian hegemony. His first venture miscarried, however, for he was twice defeated by the Phocian general, Onomarchus, in 353 B.C., and a reverse at Thermopylae neutralized the effects of a victory he gained the following year.

Philip's intervention in Greece aroused far more alarm in Athens than had his aggressions in Thrace. Isocrates, the orator, argued that the establishment of Macedonian hegemony in Greece would be eminently constructive. Unity and pan-Hellenism were imperatively demanded, and past experience had shown the inability of the lead-

ing Greek states to attain these objectives. Unity of Greece under 

Macedonian suzerainty, according to Isocrates, was preferable to the virtual chaos that had prevailed since the Peloponnesian War. The anti-Macedonians, however, had an even more powerful spokesman, for Demosthenes, one of the greatest orators of all time, denounced the aggressions of Macedonia and urged Athens to awaken from her lethargy while there was still time to preserve independence. His 

Philippics, or orations against the Macedonian ruler, were masterpieces in which he employed his rich talents in a cause which he regarded as vital to the very existence of Athens. 

Demosthenes urged that Athens extend assistance to Olynthus, for with the repulse of his first expedition in Greece Philip had resumed his imperialistic policies in Thrace. It will be remembered that a few years before Olynthus had been allied with Macedonia and had played a significant part in the imposition of Macedonian hegemony over Chalcidice. Now that Olynthus had served his purposes, Philip did not hesitate to attack his former ally. Athens might have responded to the pleas of Demosthenes and employed her sacred fund to finance an expedition to revive her prestige in Chalcidice, but Philip created a diversion by fomenting a revolt in Euboea that pre- 

Icluded such action.

Mutual overtures for a definitive peace led to the conclusion of a treaty in 346 B.C. Phocis which had relied on the support of Athens and Sparta in her defiance of the Amphictyonic League was punished for her sacrilege by expulsion from the League, and the place thus vacated was assigned to Macedonia. The peace was broken, however, almost as soon as it was proclaimed. Athens could hardly be expected to continue her passive attitude in the face of Macedonian aggressions that menaced her vital interests. Loss of Chalcidice was a serious blow, and the extension of Macedonian power to the Hellespont jeopardized the grain supply. When Philip laid siege to Byzantium and Perinthus it was clear that his aggressions, unless promptly countered by defensive measures, would result in the loss of Greek independence. The outbreak of the Second Sacred War brought matters to a head. The Amphictyonic League asked Philip's aid in again curbing Phocis. When he marched his army into central 

Greece, Athens and Thebes united against him, only to be crushed in the decisive battle of Chaeronea in 338 B.C. The victory of Chaeronea gave Philip undisputed mastery of Greece, but two years later he was assassinated as a result of family quarrels.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION ALEXANDER THE GREAT 

Alexander succeeded to the Macedonian throne as a youth of twenty. He was admirably fitted to deal with the serious crisis that confronted him upon his accession. His unusual gifts had been developed by education and practical training of a high order. Aristotle had served as his intellectual mentor, and physical and military exercises had supplemented mental training. Practical experience in administration and military command afforded abundant opportunity for the application of theory and precept.

News of the death of Philip stirred the Greek states with the hope of liberation. Revolts flared out in Ambracia and Thebes, and the rebellion of Thessaly constituted an even greater threat to Alexander's suzerainty in view of the fact that it hitherto had furnished large cavalry contingents to the Macedonian army. Alexander therefore marched first against this state and reimposed control without serious resistance. His success moved Athens and a number of other 

Greek states to avow their loyalty, and when Alexander reached the pass of Thermopylae, he was informed that he already had been elected to his father's position as a member of the Amphictyonic League Council and commander-in-chief of the military forces of Greece. Since an invasion of Asia already was planned, Alexander naturally turned next to Thrace, for unless disaffection in that area were promptly quelled, he was threatened with the loss of mineral resources, and, of course, if he crossed the Hellespont, Thracian hostility in his rear would militate against success. While he was engaged in subjugating the rebellious Thracian towns, a rumor was circulated throughout Greece that he had been killed in the campaign. This report encouraged Thebes to expel its garrison. A 

Macedonian army promptly laid siege to the rebellious city, and the defenders were dismayed to learn that Alexander himself was in command of the army of investment. The demoralized city was taken and razed to intimidate such other Greek states as might be contemplating rebellion. 

With Greece pacified, Alexander prepared for his Asiatic expedition. Conditions in the Persian Empire seemed favorable, for conquered peoples in the immense Empire never had been completely assimilated. Dynastic quarrels and the endless intrigues of the satraps accentuated the tendency for the Empire to disintegrate into its component parts. The army was in a decadent state, with obsolete equipment and tactics; indeed, after the expedition described by 

Xenophon, the Great King had relied largely on Greek mercenaries.

In the spring of 334 B.C. Alexander led his forces across the Hellespont. His army seemed inadequate in view of the magnitude of the task he had assigned himself, for he had but 30,000 infantry and 5000 cavalry. The phalanx, the most important branch of the army, comprised six regiments, and the Greek hoplites were assigned to the front ranks as a tribute to their prowess. Darius III unwisely divided his forces, and one contingent was overwhelmingly defeated along the banks of the Granicus river. This victory opened the way into 

Lydia, and Alexander's manifesto expressing sympathy with democratic ideals and institutions did much to smooth his path, since the Greek cities of Ionia overthrew their Persian garrisons and welcomed the Macedonian as a deliverer. Lydia was overrun; Sardis and other important cities soon were secured. Miletus, the Persian garrison of which was under the command of a courageous officer, offered resistance, but the efforts of the Persian fleet to come to its assistance were frustrated by Alexander's squadron, and the city was forced to capitulate. Despite the obvious danger, Alexander thereupon decided to disband his fleet and stake the success of his expedition entirely on the army now cut off from Europe. The capture of 

Halicarnassus then delivered Caria into his hands, but by this time winter was approaching and he decided to divide his army, appointing Gordion, in Phrygia, as the rendezvous for the ensuing spring campaign.

Shortly after the reunion of the army at Gordion, where Alexander allegedly cut the famous knot to take advantage of oracular prophecy of success, the first really decisive battle was fought at 

Issus, in Cilicia. Here Alexander's disciplined infantry withstood every Persian attack, and his cavalry soon forced the Persians, including Darius, to flee in wild disorder. 

Aside from the fact that Alexander's victory at Issus was a harbinger of the eventual collapse of the Persian Empire, it had an immediate significance in that it opened Syria to invasion. Tyre, the chief 

Persian naval base, did not surrender, however, and since it was necessary to secure control of this city in view of Alexander's plans for an invasion of Egypt, it was promptly besieged. The siege, one of the most famous in the annals of ancient warfare, was largely a problem for Alexander's engineers, for the fortress was located on an island. It was therefore necessary to construct a narrow causeway from the mainland to the island, during which operation the besiegers were constantly exposed to the missiles of the garrison. The timely arrival of ships from Aradus, Byblos, and Cyprus really decided the issue, for they afforded protection to the engineers until construction

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of the causeway had proceeded far enough to make possible the use of siege engines. The beleaguered city finally surrendered, and its loss was such a blow to Persia that the Great King made fruitless offers for peace on the basis of ceding to Alexander all his territory west of the Euphrates.

After the reduction of Tyre, Alexander carried out his design to invade the Land of the Pharaohs. His invasion encountered no material resistance; when he reached the Nile delta, he founded the city of Alexandria at one of the river mouths, a city that was destined to play a brilliant part in the later economic and cultural history of the ancient world. While in Egypt, Alexander made his famous visit to the shrine in the oasis of Siwah. Upon his return, he claimed that he had been deified and henceforth he demanded reverence as a god. 

There is reason to doubt that Alexander took this claim seriously; he realized, however, that the more he could increase the awe in which he was held by his troops, the greater the chance of preserving their loyalty during the long and difficult enterprises that lay ahead. 

The Macedonian forces then returned to Mesopotamia. The Euphrates and Tigris rivers were crossed without difficulty since the engineers had prepared bridges in advance, and the army marched down along the east bank of the Tigris until it encountered the enormous Persian force at Arbela (331 B.C.). Here the Macedonian victory was even more overwhelming than at Issus. Alexander soon was master of the heart of the Persian Empire, for the capitals at Susa, Persepolis, and Pasargadae surrendered. In 330 B.C. Media was invaded and Ecbatana, the capital, occupied. 

For the next two years Alexander was engaged in the arduous task of conquering the northeastern provinces of the Empire. Bessus, satrap of Bactria, murdered Darius III and attempted to secure recognition as king, but he was ultimately hunted down by Alexander and put to death. The Macedonian forces continued their advance across the Oxus and Jaxartes rivers, and by 328 B.C. reduced both 

Bactria and Sogdiana to submission. As Alexander's march continued, he established towns along the route, each of which became a center for the dissemination of Hellenism. 

In 327 B.C. Alexander decided to attempt the conquest of India. 

He conquered most of the Punjab, but when the army reached the Hyphasis river, the soldiers, whose credulous fears had been aroused by the unparalleled length of the march, mutinied and refused to proceed. Alexander employed every resource to reduce them to

obedience, but was finally forced to abandon the Indian project. He continued his march down the valley of the Indus preparatory to turning west for the return to Babylon. He encountered considerable resistance from the barbarous Malli and was dangerously wounded in the fighting against them. Upon reaching Pattala, Alexander, by elaborate symbolism, indicated his intention to establish a great commercial emporium in the delta of the Indus comparable with Alexandria in Egypt. His admiral, Nearchus, then was ordered to lead the fleet, which recently had been constructed, on a voyage of exploration from the Indus estuary to the Persian Gulf, doubtless as a preliminary to the commercial development that Alexander had in mind. 

In the meantime, Alexander led a portion of the army westward through the Gedrozian desert (Mekran). Blazing heat and lack of water caused the death of thousands so that only a remnant survived the terrible hardships of the march. Finally, to the great joy of Alexander and the soldiery, a junction was made near the head of the Persian Gulf with the balance of the army that had marched southwest from the Punjab. From here the return to Babylon was concluded without further important incident.

During 324 B.C. Alexander tarried at Susa, Ecbatana, and Opis, busy with the many problems of administration that the conquest of the Persian Empire had created. The following year he moved to 

Babylon preparatory to organizing an Arabian expedition. There he was stricken with a fever to which he succumbed at the age of thirtythree (323 B.C.).

The size of the Empire precluded effective assimilation of conquered peoples and the development of an efficiently functioning administrative system. For the most part, the satrapies were left intact, and the unsatisfactory expedient of placing them under the rule of native governors was utilized. Obviously, the Empire could not long survive as a political entity after the death of the conqueror who had fashioned it. 

The lasting significance of Alexander the Great in the history of Western civilization is not to be found in the story of his conquests or in the political history of his empire. He had marched into Asia sincerely regarding himself as the apostle of Hellenic civilization. 

Wherever his army marched, there marched also Greek civilization. 

Scholars, writers, and artists accompanied him on the memorable expedition. Scores of towns and cities were founded during the course of the campaigns. Even though political solidarity of the Empire could not be retained, cultural homogeneity was in large meas-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ure secured and a fusion of Graeco-oriental culture attained. Greek became the universal language; Greek literature, architecture, and sculpture became the common property of the Hellenized East, and religious syncretism, or fusion of beliefs, was promoted by the influence of Greek philosophy. As we shall see, when Rome's imperialism turned to the East, she was enabled to absorb a Graecooriental culture which it became her historic mission to transmit to the West as Alexander had diffused the Greek heritage in the East. 

THE HELLENISTIC AGE 

The period from the death of Alexander the Great to the Roman conquest of the East is known as the Hellenistic Age. It was a period during which Hellenic civilization was diffused throughout the Orient as a result of Alexander's conquests. Until comparatively recently, the age was regarded as a period of decadence and intellectual sterility. Modern scholarship has shown that cultural advances of considerable significance were made, although there was some regression from the standards set by classic Greece as was inevitable in a period that was one of racial fusion and cultural assimilation. 

Disintegration of Alexander's empire was inevitable after his death because of inability to assimilate the conquered peoples and the absence of a completely developed administrative system. No satisfactory arrangements could be made for the succession, for, since Alexander was survived only by a feeble-minded brother and an infant son, his death left the leading generals in power. Antipater was in control of Macedonia and Greece. Antigonus was stationed in Phrygia, while Perdiccas, Ptolemy, and Lysimachus took charge in Babylon. One group of officers supported Perdiccas who secured recognition as sole regent only to be murdered in 321 B.C. Two years later Antipater died, and civil war began among the surviving generals and continued intermittently until 281 B.C. 

For a time Antigonus seemed destined to reunite the Empire since he had secured Asia Minor, Syria, and Mesopotamia, as well as possession of Alexander's treasury. His success, however, incited jealousy and consolidated the opposition. After the ensuing battle of 

Ipsus in 301 B.C. all hope of preserving Alexander's empire intact vanished. As a sequel to the battle, four separate monarchies were established. Cassander assumed charge of Macedonia, Ptolemy founded a dynasty in Egypt, Lysimachus secured Asia Minor, while Seleucus established himself in Syria, and in 281 B.C. annexed the kingdom of 

Lysimachus. Macedonia survived as an independent kingdom until

conquered and annexed as a Roman province. The Ptolemaic line continued to rule Egypt until the defeat of Cleopatra by Octavian in 31 B.C. The Seleucid Kingdom was also ultimately absorbed by Rome. 

During the lifetime of Alexander, Greece had remained quiescent under the regency of Antipater, for the fate of Thebes and Alexander's victory at Issus had dispelled any hope of successful resistance.

Desultory revolts followed the news of Alexander's death, however, and the states gradually secured independence. The most important political development of the period of independence was the formation of the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues. The former was a federation of Aetolian towns for defensive purposes. A central assembly legislated on matters of common interest, while an annually elected strategus served as military commander and chief executive. The 

Achaean League was composed primarily of Peloponnesian states under the leadership of Corinth. Delegates were sent to periodic synods by the members, with the number of representatives apportioned according to the size of the states. Questions of foreign policy were settled by a general assembly which all citizens of the member states were eligible to attend. Executive duties were entrusted to a strategus and a council.

Political institutions exhibited both oriental and Greek characteristics in the Hellenistic world. Towns and cities retained a large measure of autonomy, but monarchial government, with emphasis on the oriental notion of its divine sanction, prevailed in the kingdoms. 

Warfare was minimized in frequency and intensity during the period, and the advance of humanitarian ideals led to the exchange of prisoners, respect for rights of sanctuary, and the employment of arbitration for peaceful adjudication of quarrels.

Cities were surprisingly modern in some respects, since many of them had been built in accordance with carefully prepared plans. 

Streets were broad and straight, and by their ninety-degree intersections laid out the municipal areas in squares. Paved streets, sidewalks, street lights, sewerage systems, and elaborate facilities to ensure an adequate supply of pure water were common. Theatres, baths, and elaborate public edifices likewise adorned the cities, and the wealthy citizens frequently contributed funds to make possible the building of such structures.

The authority of the monarchs in the Seleucid Kingdom was practically if not theoretically limited by the power and pretensions of princes who yielded but grudging obedience to their nominal sovereigns. Many large estates were held by nobles, contingent upon

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

their performance of stipulated services for the kings. Other lands were settled by colonists whose tenure required services in the army. 

Much land was reserved as religious endowments under the stewardship of the priesthoods. Small freeholds were occasionally found, but the tendency was for these ultimately to be merged with the large estates. On the plantations serfs almost invariably furnished the necessary labor. Although slavery was still fairly common, the tendency was to replace slavery with serfdom. Towns frequently received special privileges from the Seleucid rulers, who desired to promote commercial and industrial prosperity as well as bolster royal authority by the erection of a counterpoise to the power of the nobles. Since it was the terminal of a number of caravan routes to the Far East, cosmopolitan Antioch became one of the great commercial centers of the ancient world. Seleucia, with nearly a million inhabitants, was one of the largest cities of ancient times. 

Economic and social conditions in Egypt were basically conditioned by a system of rigidly enforced royal monopolies instituted by the Ptolemies. All land in legal theory was the private property of the kings, although practical considerations naturally dictated the grant of a large portion of it to favored nobles and priestly groups. 

The plantations under direct royal management were worked by tenants who were required to pay tithes of their crops as rental. 

These tenants were organized in corporations, under the direction of elders who served as their agents in the transaction of business with royal officials. Military tenure also was utilized, especially for the reclamation of waste areas.

Industry was operated by royal monopolies. Competition was prohibited, from production to retailing; high tariffs precluded importations of competing commodities. Workers were regimented. 

Wages, hours, and other conditions were prescribed; migration and change of employment were forbidden without governmental license. Elaborate censuses and a vast bureaucracy were necessary in order to ensure observance of the monopolies and the proper return to the royal exchequer. Village supervisors were subject to nome officials, who, in turn, were responsible to the central bureaucracy at the capital. Most manufactures apparently were on this basis, but our information is scanty, except in regard to the oil and linen industries. 

Commerce was greatly expanded with the establishment of contacts with the Far East. The explorations of Nearchus laid the foundations for the development of the trade with India by way of the

THE PARTHENON THE GREEK ARCHITECTURAL ORDERS THE ERECHTHEUM DORIC 

IONIC 

CORINTHIAN

HERMES AND INFANT DIONYSUS VICTORY OF SAMOTHRACE ATHENA PARTHENOS LAOCOON AND HIS SONS

Indian Ocean, Persian Gulf, and Euphrates. Caravans then carried the products to the Levantine coast. Overland routes to India and central Asia, with their western termini at Seleucia or Antioch, were also in use. The Mediterranean trade, centering at Alexandria, likewise was expanded. The harbor of Alexandria was among the best in the world. The great lighthouse, 400 feet in height, designed by Sostratus, had a beacon visible for miles. It was located on a small island, connected with the mainland by a mile-long causeway that divided the harbor into two parts. The center of the Aegean trade shifted from Piraeus to Rhodes. Banking facilities kept pace with commercial expansion. Letters of credit and bills of exchange were in common use. Loans were made by deposit banks on a more extensive scale. In Egypt, banking was a state monopoly. 

Population doubtless declined in the Hellenistic Age. The falling birth rate and the prevalence of infanticide doubtless reflected the impoverishment of the masses. Class distinctions widened. Society was organized, particularly in Egypt and the Seleucid Kingdom, for the exploitation of the many for the enrichment of the rulers and the privileged minority of nobles and priests.

Civic pride, exemplified in the lavish construction programs of the Hellenistic municipalities, also was manifested in education. Public support of schools was by no means unusual. Where public support was not forthcoming, philanthropists often assumed the financial obligations. Teachers were well qualified and received adequate remuneration. In publicly supported institutions, they were commonly elected for one-year terms. More attention was paid to the education of girls than in the classical period. Youths of eighteen to twenty years of age (ephebi) formerly underwent two years of military training and garrison duty. In the Hellenistic Age, they had to study rhetoric and philosophy in addition to undergoing miltiary and physical training. Students of this grade lived a communal life under the supervision of officials elected from their number, and general direction of their work was entrusted to civic magistrates. The oath taken by the youths, known as the "Ephebic Oath," has come down to us and admirably summarizes the ideals and purposes of Hellenistic education. 

Philosophy and religion were inseparably connected; the attitude of the philosophers toward fundamental problems was greatly influenced by materialism as taught by Heraclitus, Democritus, and the Cynics with their emphasis on atomic concepts of the universe. 

By far the most important contribution of the age to the field of ab-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

stract thought was the evolution of the Stoic and Epicurean doctrines. 

Zeno, a native of Citium in Cyprus, began teaching in Athens about 306 B.C. He lectured from the stoa, or porch; hence his philosophy, after being clarified and systematized by his pupil Chrysippus, became known as Stoicism. Virtue was regarded by the Stoics as the aim of life; it consisted in harmony with the universe. Knowledge was a necessary preliminary to such harmony. Man's reasoning faculties were a part of the universal wisdom, but perversions and distractions usually impeded the legitimate exercise of rational powers. 

Hence, one had to free himself from the trammels of hope, fear, pleasure, and desire, in order that through reason he might live virtuously, in harmony with universal wisdom.

Another popular philosophy was introduced by Epicurus, who was primarily indebted to the atomic theories of Democritus for his basic concepts. For him, even the soul was made up of atoms of an especially fine variety, but, unlike Democritus, he postulated the existence of free will, for he held that the attraction or repulsion of atoms was amenable to volition. Happiness was regarded as the objective of life and was defined as pleasure. The early Epicureans were not hedonists. By pleasure, they meant tranquillity and intellectual pleasure, freedom from bodily pain and mental confusion. After the doctrines attained wide popularity, however, sensual pleasures replaced the intangible joys of the philosopher.

Greek became the literary language of the Hellenistic Age. Every person of education and refinement spoke it with fluency and it became the language of business and administration. The thoroughness of its adoption is shown by the fact that the Hebrews translated the Old Testament into Greek. The Septuagint was used everywhere in preference to the Hebrew version; even Philo, the celebrated Jewish scholar, accepted the innovation.

Athens lost her position as the literary center of the Greek world to Alexandria. A library of a half million manuscripts was collected at the Egyptian metropolis and placed in the custody of a succession of brilliant bibliophiles and critics. Callimachus, one of the best known of the librarians, introduced a cataloguing system similar to that in vogue at the present time.

Comparatively little Hellenistic literature has survived and much of it failed to merit survival. Comedy was a principal literary vehicle, so far as extant materials afford a basis for judgment. Menander was the leading exponent of this form and much of his work has survived in the Latin versions of Plautus and Terence. The “New Comedy

broke definitely with the traditions of Aristophanes. Satire was seldom employed; there was rather a return to the human interest themes of the tragedies of Euripides. Perennially popular comedy situations, such as love intrigues, coincidence, and mistaken identity, were effectively utilized, although with a monotony of version that sometimes must have palled on the audiences. Choral interludes were used to depict time sequences and usually had no direct connection with the plot.

Idylls of wonderful beauty were produced by Theocritus, one of the greatest nature poets of all time. His genius rose to its greatest heights in his pastorals, and these poems served as the inspiration of 

Vergil's Georgics. Epigrams were popular, especially those of Callimachus, although the pedantry and pomposity of the famous savant detracted from their value. Indifferent epics were produced on all kinds of subjects, even those of a scientific nature. The production of mimes marked a distinct contribution to literary form. 

In architecture, the Ionic and Corinthian styles were most often used, in either pure or modified forms. Bases of columns sometimes. were sculptured, and fluting the columns for but half of their lengths was a popular innovation. Widened ambulatories were secured by broadening the stylobate and omitting the inner row of columns. 

The temple of Apollo at Didyma and that of Zeus at Athens were the outstanding works of the period, although the latter was not completed until the second century of the Christian era. 

Sculpture showed, for the most part, a serious decline in tastes and standards. Realism and novelty were the dominant notes, and the sculptors frequently were guilty of vulgarity in their obtrusive realism. The "Dying Gaul," produced at Pergamum, represented the nearest approach to the restraint and chaste beauty of the Praxitelean

Age. The Altar of Zeus at Pergamum had a sculptured base with a frieze 400 feet long, depicting struggles between gods and titans. 

Other great works of the period were the "Aphrodite of Melos and the "Winged Victory of Samothrace.” The “Laocoön" group, the most famous work of Rhodian art, depicted Laocoön and his sons in mortal struggle with constricting serpents. Agony was shown with consummate realism, yet other natural emotions such as fear and horror were not portrayed. Then, too, the sons' faces were those of grown men, and other errors of detail were made that the classic sculptor would have considered unpardonable. Chares, a pupil of 

Lysippus, produced the outstanding example of colossal statuary in his "Helios," which was more than 100 feet in height. Eutychides,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

in his "Antioch," introduced a vogue for personification that materially widened the scope of artistic imagination. 

As in the classic period, interest in painting was secondary. Apelles of Cos produced the " Aphrodite Rising from the Sea.” His technique was original in that he employed only black, red, white, and yellow in his work which he subsequently coated with a sheer black glaze as a preservative. Mosaics were introduced and were destined to become one of the glories of the art of the Near East. The best known specimen of this vehicle was a portrayal of the battle of Issus. 

While Hellenistic culture represented in most fields a retrogression from the standards of the Hellenic period, ancient science reached the zenith of its development. The Alexandrian museum, in addition to serving as a center for literary production and criticism, was a great center for scientific research. Laboratories, botanical and zoological gardens, and the marvellous library afforded research facilities without parallel until the modern age. Scientists received adequate stipends from the Ptolemies as well as the civic authorities. 

They lived without charge in a splendidly appointed mansion constructed for their use. They were permitted to teach but were not required to perform any duties aside from their experimentation. 

Theophrastus was the leading botanist of his day and his knowledge of the subject went far beyond the bounds of Aristotle's Natural History. Hipparchus was an outstanding mathematician to whom the invention of trigonometry was attributed. He also engaged in astronomical measurements and was reputed to have discovered the ratio between the solar and lunar distances from the earth. A heliocentric theory of the universe was propounded by 

Aristarchus, although the promulgation of Ptolemy's treatise, which, in common with Aristotle, held to the geocentric view, discredited his work. The heliocentric theory was not revived until the work of 

Copernicus in the fifteenth century.

The approximate size of the earth was computed by the ingenious experiments of Eratosthenes. He observed that when the sun was at its zenith at Alexandria, it was 73 degrees off the vertical at the first cataract of the Nile, approximately 500 miles from the first point of observation. Five hundred miles, then, represented of the earth's circumference. From this equation, he derived approximately 25,000 miles as the circumference of the earth and was then easily able to calculate diameter and volume.

Euclid's treatise on plane geometry is studied in modified form today. Archimedes, the great Syracusan scientist, properly can be

called the founder of the sciences of mechanics and hydrostatics. 

In the former, he discovered the principle of the lever, pulley, and screw; in the latter, he propounded the laws of sinking and floating bodies.

Medical and surgical research were rooted in thorough anatomical study. Dissection and even vivisection of condemned criminals were practiced, resulting in anatomical and physiological discoveries of basic importance. Herophilus discovered the existence of the nervous system and held that it centered in the brain. He also discovered the circulatory system, but failed to see its relation with metabolism and respiration. Erasistratus carried neurological investigations further by distinguishing between motor and sensory nerves. He refused, however, to accept the teaching of Herophilus in regard to the blood and its circulation, holding instead that the blood vessels normally were air passages.

With the Roman conquest of the Hellenistic monarchies, the Graeco-oriental culture, so uniformly diffused in the East as a result of Alexander's conquests, was absorbed by Rome and transmitted to the West.

CHAPTER 10 The Rise of Rome 

GLANCE at the map of the Mediterranean area shows three great peninsulas jutting into the sea. Italy, the central one of the three, partly divides the Mediterranean into eastern and western portions. It is sufficiently close to Greece to be touched by its cultural influences, yet, with its broad plains on the western side of the Apennines, it definitely faces the West. Geographically, Italy was ideally adapted for her historic mission which was to assimilate all that was best in Graeco-oriental culture for subsequent transmission to western Europe.

The Italic peninsula is 650 miles long and has an average width of 150 miles. It is partly separated from central Europe by the Alps, yet these never constituted a barrier to expansion because of the number of passes through the mountains. The Apennine range which runs lengthwise through the peninsula like a great vertebral column is closer to the eastern side than to the western. West of the mountains are the great plains of Tuscany (Etruria), Latium, and Campania. The range did not serve as an obstacle to political unification as did the many ranges of Greece. There are few navigable rivers: the Po on the east and the Tiber, Arno, Liris, and Volturnus on the west. The coast line is singularly devoid of indentations suitable for use as harbors. Whereas Greece with its multitude of harbors was strongly impelled toward commerce, Italy remained for centuries almost exclusively agricultural. Since much of the soil was of volcanic origin (tufa), it was very fertile, and climatic factors likewise were favorable to agriculture. Timber and mineral resources were adequate for the needs of ancient times. 

Successive waves of migration from the north populated the peninsula during the prehistoric period. Paleolithic remains have been found that probably represent the aboriginal inhabitants. The earliest Neolithic strata, however, represent newcomers whose funerary customs sharply differed from those of the aborigines. About
