SICILIAN AND IONIAN SEA 

36- -44- -48- 12 16

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

2000 B.C., another group of invaders established the famous Lake 

Villages of the north. The huts were built on piles driven into the lake bottoms, and boats or a fragile bridge which could easily be destroyed afforded contact with the shore. Implements were still largely Neolithic, but bronze was used to a limited extent. 

Somewhat later, groups of the Lake Dwellers moved farther south where they located villages in the Po valley. These villages were built on land, but the construction of the huts on piles was a tradition maintained from their lake dwellings. These Terramaran villages, so called because of the practice of modern Italian peasants in employing earth from their sites to enrich the soil of their fields, were usually built in the shape of a trapezoid, surrounded by earthern ramparts and a moat.

Some centuries later another group of villages was established in Umbria and Tuscany. These villages may have been built by Terramarans who migrated farther south, or by newcomers from across the Alps. A large village, known by archaeologists as Villanova, was erected near modern Bologna, and the term Villanovan has been applied to all sites of this type. The Villanovans apparently were in contact with Cretans and Etruscans; hence their cultural advance was more rapid than that of other peoples of the peninsula. Iron was smelted and fabricated and fine pottery manufactured by the employment of techniques learned from the Cretans.

By the opening of the historic period, the Terramarans and Villanovans had split into a number of tribes, of which the most important were the Veneti in the northeast; the Latins, just south of the Tiber; the Sabines, Samnites, Volsci, and Aequi of central Italy; and the 

Umbrians along the eastern coast.

Two basic sources of cultural stimulation were the Greek colonies of Sicily and south Italy (Magna Graecia) and the settlement of the 

Etruscans in the peninsula. The Etruscans probably came by ship from Asia Minor. They introduced the arch which, as we have seen, was invented in ancient Mesopotamia, and their practices of divination likewise indicate Asiatic origin. It is likely that the Turruschu mentioned in Egyptian records were Etruscans who vainly attempted to settle in that country prior to their migration to Italy. 

From the Etruscans Italy learned, in addition to the use of the arch, that of the chariot and of advanced ceramic and metallurgical techniques. The practice of foretelling the future by examining the entrails of sacrificed animals was taken over from them; indeed, for

centuries, the priests who officiated at such rites in Rome were Etruscans.

Our knowledge of the early history of Rome is based for the most part on archaeological evidence and traditions embodied in the accounts of historians such as Livy, who wrote centuries after the period of the founding of the city. The familiar tales embodied in 

Vergil's Aeneid seem to be completely devoid of historic foundation. According to tradition, Rome was founded in 753 B.C. as a Latin village on the left bank of the Tiber. It gave no immediate indication of its future greatness, for it was merely one of more than sixty towns loosely federated in the Latin League under the presidency of Alba Longa. The League existed for both religious and military purposes, and delegates from the member towns met annually on the Alban Mount.

Rome possessed many advantages that promoted her rise to prominence in Latium. She was located on a navigable river and commanded one of the two fords by which the Tiber could be crossed. 

Just across the Tiber were the Etruscans, and it was natural that Rome should be the spearhead of the Latins in their struggles with these powerful foes. Her exposed position made rapid development of military strength necessary and promoted the cosmopolitanism so vital to institutional and cultural growth. Control of valuable salt flats near the Tiber mouth was an invaluable economic asset and assured a measure of dependence on the part of other Latin towns. 

No matter how many such tangible considerations are cited, however, it is impossible to explain the rise of Rome without emphasizing the virility, resourcefulness, and perseverance of the Roman people. 

Indeed, one is tempted to compare these early Romans with the sturdy frontiersmen of our own history.

It is likely that Rome was under the rule of kings in the early centuries of her history. Evidence in favor of this view rests on the existence of the office of King of the Sacrifices (rex sacrorum) in the early Republic. When the monarchy was abolished, there naturally was reluctance to interrupt the contact with the gods which the kings in their priestly capacity had afforded; hence the religious functions of royalty were continued. In the constitution of the 

Republic, the executive power was vested in two annually elected consuls, each of whom exercised co-equal authority so that the veto of one would halt the action of the other. The shortness of the term of office and the principle that the negative as embodied in the veto

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

should predominate over the positive power indicate an experience with absolutism and the desire to prevent its recurrence. Then, too, the term rex (king) was one of detestation for centuries, and it is hardly likely that such anti-monarchial prejudice could have arisen unless the tradition was rooted in historic fact. The discovery of the "Black Stone," bearing an inscription of a king who cannot be identified from the extant portion, has provided additional evidence. 

Since archaeological evidence has established the fact of the Etruscan occupation of the city, it seems likely that at least the later kings were Etruscans, and therefore the revolution that overthrew the monarchy was accompanied by the attainment of independence. 

Toward the end of the sixth century, traditionally in 509 B.C., the monarchy was abolished and a Republic organized. The revolution, however, was not a popular victory, for it was led by the aristocrats who were the chief beneficiaries of the change. In the regal period, the kings had used the common folk as a counterpoise to the aristocratic patricians; the expulsion of the monarchs meant that the plebeians now were subject to the unrestrained exploitation of the nobles. According to the historian Polybius, a treaty was concluded with Carthage immediately after the overthrow of the monarchy, whereby Rome recognized the commercial monopoly of the north African power. If such an agreement was made, it was indicative of the complete control of the landowning patricians, who were quite willing that the state renounce commercial activities and remain primarily agricultural.

The executive power in the newly organized Republic was entrusted to two annually elected magistrates known as consuls. Each possessed the governing power, or imperium, in its entirety. In practice, the magistrates would partition their duties, but theoretically there was no division. If, for example, the consuls decided that one should command an army in the field and the other should remain in the city, the latter at any time could join the army and enjoy joint powers of command with his colleague. All executive and judicial powers were vested in the consuls, but in view of the arduous nature of their duties, subordinates, known as duoviri, were employed for judicial duties and the quaestors assisted in the collection and management of public revenues. There was no division of authority, however, for the subordinates were merely the agents of the consuls, who continued to possess the full powers which they had delegated. 

The founders of the Republic recognized the danger inherent in a constitution that utilized two executives with concurrent powers.

Disagreement and the consequent veto might paralyze the state in a time of crisis. To guard against this eventuality, provision was made for the appointment of a dictator to deal with an emergency. The dictators, chosen upon recommendation of one or both of the consuls, were granted absolute power for the duration of the emergency but never for a period longer than six months.

Second only in importance to the magistrates was the Senate; indeed, in view of the fact that its powers were continuous, it exercised a greater influence on the determination of long-range policies. 

The body was made up of about three hundred elderly and distinguished men, most of whom were patricians, or members of the gentes (kindreds) that presumably traced their descent from the founders of the city. Soon after the founding of the Republic, however, it had been deemed advisable to admit a number of men of less distinguished ancestry in order that the complement of three hundred might be retained. Those thus added were known as the "Conscript Fathers," but eventually the term lost its special significance and was applied to the whole body.

The senators heard the proposals of the consuls and after discussion and debate returned their responses to the suggested policies of the magistrates. Diplomacy with foreign states was especially subject to senatorial supervision, with the result that the authority of the body naturally was greatly strengthened in time of war. The body also framed laws for submission to the Centuriate Assembly for enactment, and its ratification was necessary for the validity of any legislation directly enacted by the assembly.

Of the two assemblies of the early republic, the Centuriate Assembly (comitia centuriata) was by far the more important. It elected the magistrates and legislated under the presidency of the consuls, but its legislation had to be approved by the Senate. The comitia centuriata was of military origin. In the regal period, the male citizens had been divided into five classes on the basis of the military equipment they could furnish for themselves. Each of the classes in turn was made up of a number of centuries, or groups of approximately one hundred men each. There were eighty centuries of Class 

One; twenty centuries of each of Classes Two, Three, and Four; and thirty centuries of Class Five. Eighteen centuries of cavalry (equites) were placed above Class One, while five centuries of cooks, musicians, etc. were also included, making a grand total of 193 centuries. The assembly seems to have made the transition from a mere military array to an electoral and legislative assembly with the abolition of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the monarchy and the emergence of the Republic. In theory, every adult male had a vote in the Centuriate Assembly. Voting was by century rather than by head, however, and the balloting which always began with the wealthiest class ceased when a majority was reached. Now the eighteen centuries of equites and the eighty centuries of Class One controlled ninety-eight votes, a majority of 193.

Both groups were made up of wealthy aristocrats whose interests were for the most part identical. In practice, then, the ninety-eight centuries of the rich reduced the voting rights of the less fortunate citizens to a meaningless formality and this was a fundamental cause of the constitutional struggles between the patricians and the plebeians who were endeavoring to secure political equality in fact as well as in theory.

The comitia curiata, the older of the assemblies, represented the thirty tribes or curiae. Its chief function was to witness important legal transactions, particularly the adoption of children, the conveyance of land, and the emancipation of slaves. It also bestowed the imperium on newly elected consuls, but this was merely a nominal power, for it possessed no discretionary authority in such investment.

Divination was inseparably connected with public policy, for no decision of consequence was made without consultation of the omens. This meant that the priestly colleges exercised a powerful influence on the government. The College of Pontifices, presided over by the pontifex maximus, had charge of the calendar. They determined which were lucky or unlucky days and interpreted portents. The haruspices foretold the future by examination of the entrails of sacrificial animals, while the College of Augurs prophesied by observing the flight of birds. The Vestal Virgins were charged with the duty of keeping the sacred fire on the state hearth perpetually burning.

THE STRUGGLE OF THE ORDERS 

A leading theme of the history of the Republic from 509–287 B.c. was the struggle of the plebeians for political equality with the patricians. According to tradition, the Valerian Law, passed in the same year in which the Republic was founded, safeguarded the plebeians from arbitrary punishment by the proviso that death sentences imposed by the magistrates had to be ratified by a majority vote in the comitia centuriata before which the actual trial of the case was to take place. Later its provisions were amplified to include

corporal punishment of any kind. This law sometimes has been called the habeas corpus law of Rome, for it protected the citizen against punishment without due process of law. About 494 B.C., traditionally in response to the secession or threat of secession of the plebeians from the state, provision was made for plebeian magistrates known as tribunes, who were to protect their constituents in an intercessory capacity. Their veto had the effect of stopping any legislative or judicial process considered detrimental to the interests of the plebeians; it has been likened to the modern process of injunction. 

In 471 B.C.(?), the plebeians made another significant gain with the organization of a plebeian assembly known as the comitia tributa. 

Representation was apportioned according to the twenty-one wards of the city and its immediate environs. The assembly, presided over by the tribunes, was authorized to pass resolutions or expressions of opinion known as plebiscites. These plebiscites, however, were not invested with any legal validity until ratified by the Senate and the comitia centuriata. Henceforth, a major objective of the plebeians was to secure the right of independent legislation for their representative organ.

A major constitutional weakness in the early Republic was the lack of a body of organic law. The laws of the state were merely traditions handed down from generation to generation by the patricians, and obviously this opened the door to the oppression and exploitation of the plebeians under the pretense of legality. In response to persistent agitation, a committee of ten, known as the Decemvirate, was appointed in 451 B.C. and given plenary authority to codify the laws. Since the work was unfinished upon expiration of the original term of one year, the authority of the Decemvirate was prolonged for an additional year. By 449, however, it had become apparent that 

Appius Claudius who headed the Decemvirate was plotting to prevent the restoration of normal constitutional government, and a popular rising terminated the special powers which the Decemvirate had enjoyed. The Valerio-Horatian Laws then were passed, under the terms of which the laws codified by the Decemvirate became the law of the state. They were inscribed on twelve wooden tablets which were set up in the forum and were known as the "Laws of the Twelve Tables." The Valerio-Horatian legislation also permitted the tribunes to sit at the door of the Senate house to listen to the discussions, and they were empowered to interpose their veto if any measures inimical to the interests of the plebeians were under consideration.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

About the middle of the fifth century, passage of the Canuleian legislation authorized the intermarriage of patricians and plebeians. 

At approximately the same time, however, the plebeian gains that had been made up to this time were largely neutralized by the creation of the office of consular tribune. This obviously was an expedient designed to block the admission of the plebeians to the consulship by the pretense of concession. In any year consular tribunes, instead of consuls and tribunes, could be elected by the comitia centuriata to combine the functions of the two older magistracies. While the plebeians were theoretically eligible for election to the newly created posts, the fact that election was by the Centuriate Assembly assured a patrician majority, and the plebeians thus sacrificed the advantages of having magistrates specifically charged with the protection of their interests. Another reactionary measure was the institution of the office of censor, open only to patrician incumbency. The censors were charged with the duty of preparing the official lists of those eligible for senatorial membership, and since they were authorized periodically to conduct ceremonial "cleansings" of the state they exercised control of public morals.

By 362 B.C., traditionally as the result of a provision of the socalled Licinio-Sextian Rogations of 367 B.C.(?), the plebeians were admitted to the consulship; indeed, there is reason to believe that incumbency of at least one of the annual consulships by a plebeian was made mandatory. Admission to eligibility for the dictatorship followed, and after 342 B.C. it was provided that both the highest magistrates in any official year might be plebeians. About 300 B.C. the 

Ogulnian Law admitted the plebeians to the Sacred Colleges and swept away virtually the last bulwark of aristocratic control. The plebeian victory was made complete with the passage of the Hortensian Law of 287 B.C. This enactment permitted the plebiscites of the comitia tributa to become the law of the state without the sanction of either Senate or Centuriate Assembly. By endowing the tributa with the power of independent legislation, it was made a controlling organ of the state. The transition of the government of the 

Roman Republic from an aristocratic to a democratic basis was a great tribute to the political genius of the people. The final victory of the plebeians had been attained by orderly, constitutional processes which by timely concession brought liberal governmental institutions without resort to violence or extralegal measures.

THE EXPANSION OF ROME IN ITALY 

At the same time that the Roman Republic was becoming democratic, as a result of a series of constitutional reforms, the state was acquiring control of central and south Italy. Expansion was not the result of premeditated imperialism, for successive problems were dealt with as they arose, and in a number of instances Rome was clearly on the defensive. It would indeed be difficult to prove that 

Rome was conscious of any imperialistic ambitions before the period of the great duel with Carthage, although in retrospect we can see how each episode in the history of her dealings with Italian powers was fitting into an imperialistic pattern. 

The expulsion of the Etruscans incident to the abrogation of monarchy did not mean the end of the menace of Etruscan domination. 

A number of subsequent struggles in which it is well-nigh impossible to distinguish historic fact from legend apparently were necessary to assure Roman independence. It was not until the Etruscan sea power received a death blow at the hands of Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, in 477 B.C., that Etruscan aggressions against Rome diminished. 

At the same time Rome was repulsing Etruscan attacks, she assumed the position of protector of the Latins against the assaults of the powerful Aequi and Volsci. This factor was largely responsible for a growing recognition of Roman leadership in Latium which the 

Foedus Cassianum of 493 B.C., if authentic, mirrored.

In 387 B.C. (390?) Rome was captured by Gauls, who according to tradition had decided to attack the city after the Roman government intervened to protect the Italian tribes of the Po valley from Gallic marauding. The city was thoroughly sacked; the fact that the state could recover so soon after such a disaster was indicative of the soundness of its institutions. Within ten years, the Aequi and Volsci were again defeated, and Rome's position of leadership in the Latin 

League was strengthened.

Rome's control of central Italy was secured as a result of three bitter wars with the Samnites, a branch of the Sabellian group of Italic peoples who originally had inhabited the hilly western slopes of the Apennines. A group of the Samnites had migrated into the fertile plain of Campania and had become partly Hellenized after the conquest of Greek Cumae. In 343 B.C. a group of Samnites who had remained in their ancestral homes in the Apennine foothills pushed into Campania, with the result that appeals for assistance were sent to Rome. A Roman army relieved beleaguered Capua and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

turned back the tide of invasion, after which a truce was concluded to mutual advantage.

Rome's anxiety for prompt termination of hostilities was attributable to the fact that the Latin League which had begun to chafe under Roman control had seized what seemed to be a favorable time to revolt and demand representation in the Roman government. The demands were spurned, and a Roman army under Titus Manlius and Decius Mus finally quelled the uprising. The Latin League thereupon was dissolved, and Rome began her traditional policy of dealing with each Latin town separately, awarding graduated privileges according to the loyalty manifested by each community. 

War with the Samnites broke out anew in 326 B.C. when Rome established a colony at Fregellae in Samnite territory. The war proved to be a momentous test of Roman military supremacy and the endurance of the people. During the course of the struggle, an entire consular army was ambushed and compelled to surrender at the Caudian Forks, and at one time a Samnite offensive pushed within about twenty miles of Rome. The Senate refused to make peace despite these disasters, and finally a vigorous counter-offensive restored Roman prestige. By 304 B.C. both sides were exhausted and ready to conclude peace, but since hostilities had attained no decisive result the peace could be nothing more than a truce. 

The third and decisive war broke out when the Lucanians sought the aid of Rome against Samnite aggressions. Rome found herself faced with a formidable coalition comprised of Celts, Etruscans, Umbrians, and Samnites, but a victory at Sentinum in 295 B.C. caused the rapid disintegration of the alliance, and the Samnites, rather than oppose Rome alone, sued for peace. Rome gained control of all 

Campania, and the foundation of a number of colonies in Samnite territory was the harbinger of the eventual dominance of all central Italy.

Roman expansion in central Italy clearly foreshadowed the eventual conquest of Hellenized south Italy. Tarentum, a leading Greek city of that region, had recognized this fact and had extended aid to the Samnites in an endeavor to preserve the balance of power. 

Imminent hostilities with Rome as a result of this intervention were averted, however, when a treaty was signed under the terms of which Rome agreed to refrain from sending ships into the Tarentine Gulf.

The outbreak of war between Rome and Tarentum was the resultant of two incidents. In the first place, Thurii, over which Tar-

entum exercised a protectorate, was attacked by the Lucanians, and the populace of the city, instead of appealing to Tarentum, sought Roman assistance. When Rome decided to extend the requested succor, Tarentum interpreted her action as a prelude to an attempt to subjugate all south Italy. About the same time, the Roman admiral, Volurus, was driven by a storm to take refuge in the harbor of Tarentum. This, of course, was technically in violation of the recently concluded treaty, and the Tarentines captured the vessels, slaughtered some of their crews, and sold the rest into slavery. Roman envoys who arrived to demand indemnity for the outrage were treated with derision, but even in the face of this provocation Rome hesitated to declare war.

The reason for the highhanded action of Tarentum as well as the disposition of Rome to temporize was the fact that King Pyrrhus of Epirus had offered his aid to the Tarentines. Under his command and with the aid of his forces, the dissolute and enervated Tarentines. soon were moulded into a formidable military force. When Rome finally declared war, an army was sent into south Italy, but was decisively defeated at Heraclea. Pyrrhus offered terms of peace which included demands for territorial recessions to the Samnites, but Rome refused to negotiate on that basis. Another Roman force then was defeated at Ausculum; in this battle, as at Heraclea, the use of elephants by Pyrrhus did much to demoralize the Roman soldiery and scatter the ranks of the legions. In reality, however, the Tarentine cause was not helped by these "Pyrrhic" victories. His army had sustained heavy losses, there was no opportunity for the necessary reënforcements, and his supplies had been dangerously depleted. 

At this juncture, Pyrrhus crossed to Sicily to aid Syracuse in her struggles with Carthage and the Mamertines, and this diversion cost him his chance for success in Italy, for he met with military reverses and his forces continued to melt away. In 275 B.C., upon return to 

Italy, he was overwhelmingly defeated at Beneventum by the legions commanded by Curius Dentatus and forced to flee to Epirus. The victory at Beneventum gave Rome unchallenged mastery of south Italy and foreshadowed her expansion to Sicily where she was destined to encounter a sterner foe.

The rapidity of Roman expansion in Italy was in large measure attributable to her demonstrated military supremacy. The use of the manipular organization of the legions gave unusual tactical mobility and flexibility, while the utilization of the javelin as a missile weapon was also a factor of advantage in combat with the armies of her ad-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

versaries. It must be remembered, also, that hers was a citizen army, serving to protect and advance what were considered to be the interests of all, in that they were the avowed interests of the state. Valor, integrity, and skill characterized the military leadership and permeated the ranks as well. Superior governmental organization also played a material part in the success of the wars of expansion. 

In her treatment of the conquered people, Rome evinced the governing genius and the assimilative powers that were to be leading phenomena of her history. Colonies were established in conquered territory to discourage rebellion and hasten assimilation. Maritime colonies were founded in port towns to protect commercial and naval interests. Some of the old Latin towns were incorporated in the Roman state and granted the rights of trade and marriage with the Romans but they were not given the suffrage. The degree of autonomy granted to these municipia depended upon their demonstrated loyalty to Rome.

Aside from Roman territory, the most important group of dependencies were the Latin allies, each of which had prescribed rights and privileges. The remainder of the subjugated peoples of Italy were known as the Italic allies each of which was bound to Rome by a special treaty which invariably vested Rome with control of foreign policy and the right to call for military contingents. While there was, of course, no Roman nation, the diverse parts of the Italic peninsula were united to some degree by their ties of obedience and loyalty to Rome.

CHAPTER 11 The Emergence of Rome as a World Power 

THE PUNIC WARS 

ITH the close of the war with Pyrrhus, Rome had established her domination of central and south Italy, while the northern frontier had been pushed to the Po. Roman military superiority in Italy had been unquestionably demonstrated, and the relationships set up between the ruling city and the allies were destined to prove their enduring worth as manifestations of the Roman genius for government. During the period of the wars of expansion in Italy, a series of vital constitutional issues had been settled by timely concession and reform. The Roman state was now ready to inaugurate its momentous expansion outside Italy. 

With the outbreak of the First Punic War (264-241 B.C.), the

Republic entered upon a great struggle with Carthage, hitherto the undisputed master of the Mediterranean. Without a consciously formulated imperialistic program, Rome embarked on the course of empire, until by 146 B.C. she was the acknowledged ruler of the Mediterranean world and had extended her sway over the Hellenized Near East. This tremendous expansion was destined to have well-nigh incalculable effects on internal conditions. Acquisition of provinces necessitated the development of a system of administration. Romanization of these provinces was actively promoted, but evils of provincial administration soon arose to plague the state throughout the remaining course of its history. Profound economic and social readjustments followed in the wake of the wars of expansion. The old class struggle between patricians and plebeians gave way to the more bitter struggle between the rich optimates and the populares. The cleavage between these classes, basically economic in character, progressively widened as the optimates realized to the full the economic benefits accruing from the exploitation of the provinces. 

Carthage was established as a colony of the Phoenician city of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Sidon about 850 B.C., during the heyday of Phoenician commercial activities in the Mediterranean. When the Phoenician cities were conquered by the great empires that successively arose in the East, Carthage acquired its independence and appropriated the commercial interests that its erstwhile overlords had been forced to relinquish. By the opening of the third century, Carthage controlled all north Africa from Cyrene to Gibraltar, and the Mediterranean had virtually become a Carthaginian mare clausum. Trading posts were established at strategic ports, and a seemingly invincible navy jealously guarded her commercial monopoly. The Etruscan sea power had been crushed by Hiero of Syracuse in 477 B.C., and Rome had hitherto evinced no desire to challenge Carthaginian control of the Mediterranean trade; indeed, if the account of Polybius is correct, the Republic had by treaty definitely renounced interest in such commerce.

It is probable that the Carthaginian state was originally ruled by kings who were ultimately overthrown and replaced by two annually elected magistrates known as suffetes whose functions were both executive and judicial. A Council assisted the magistrates in an advisory capacity, and the legislation suggested by the suffetes was acted upon by a Senate of three hundred members. Legislation passed by the Senate was submitted to a popular assembly of the citizenry for at least nominal ratification, and in the event of controversy between Senate and magistracy the Assembly probably made the final decision. The power of the commercial aristocracy in the state was rather evenly balanced by the influence of the landed aristocracy who had acquired enormous tracts of land with the conquest of Libya and the subjugation of the native populace. In view of this situation, the Assembly probably was able to exercise more influence in the determination of governmental policies than originally contemplated with the formation of the constitution. 

War between Rome and Carthage became inevitable with the Roman conquest of south Italy. Obviously, the next natural step in 

Roman expansion would be the annexation of Sicily, but Carthage, too, long had coveted complete control of the island so valuable in view of its productive grain fields. By gradual encroachment, Carthage had absorbed virtually the whole island, and only Syracuse in the east threatened to be an obstacle in the way of realization of the desire for complete annexation. Even had the Sicilian issue been amicably settled, Rome, now in control of all Italy south of the Po, could hardly be expected to remain permanently content to play

THE EMERGENCE OF ROME AS A WORLD POWER 145 

a negligible role in the Mediterranean, even though she was slow in realizing her commercial potentialities.

As could be anticipated, the immediate cause of the First Punic War (so called because the Romans called the Carthaginians Poeni) was a series of events in Sicily. Agathocles, tyrant of Syracuse, had enrolled a large number of mercenaries who, upon his death, were disbanded. These soldiers, now free from the strong hand that hitherto had disciplined them, marched north and seized the city of Messana. Since Messana was situated on the straits that separate 

Italy from Sicily, these Mamertines, or "Sons of Mars," as they now called themselves, were able to prey upon the commerce passing through the straits. Soon they had organized a veritable state dedicated to piracy and, as their power grew, they extended the sphere of their operations until their depredations interfered intolerably with the commerce along the whole eastern and northern coasts of 

Sicily. When Hiero II became tyrant of Syracuse, he decided to crush the power of the Mamertines and promptly invested Messana with a force sufficiently strong to ensure the capture of the city if help were not immediately forthcoming. 

One faction of the Mamertines appealed to Rome for assistance; the other group sent a plea for the intervention of Carthage. Carthage welcomed the opportunity thus to advance her grasp on Sicily. The 

Roman government hesitated, but the comitia centuriata, to which the issue was referred, decided to intervene, since it was believed that Carthaginian occupation of all Sicily would endanger Roman control of south Italy, and the prospect of securing cheap grain from 

Sicily likewise was not overlooked. A Roman force accordingly was sent to Rhegium and ultimately conveyed across the straits, where it succeeded in capturing Messana, and Hiero was prevailed upon to adopt a pro-Roman policy. 

Rome could not fight an offensive war in accordance with her military traditions, for the lack of a fleet to transport the legions to north Africa. After desultory fighting in Sicily, the Senate ordered the construction of a fleet; according to Polybius, a wrecked Carthaginian trireme was used as a model for the building of 120 ships. 

The Roman ships were equipped with gangplanks on their prows which could be raised or lowered at will. This ingenious device enabled heavy-armed soldiers stationed on the decks of the Roman vessels to board the enemy ships as soon as sufficiently close contact was established for the gangplanks to be let down. In 260 B.C. the 

Roman admiral Duilius gained a decisive naval victory in the battle

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of Myle; Rome's position as a naval power strong enough to challenge Carthaginian dominance of the seas was dramatically demonstrated.

With Rome's naval superiority strengthened by another victory off Ecnomus in 256 B.C., conveyance of an army to north Africa was feasible. The consul Regulus accordingly was sent with an army that was successfully disembarked, but when the legions seemed on the point of seriously menacing Carthage itself, the Carthaginian cavalry, commanded by the brilliant Spartan general, Xanthippus, overwhelmed them, and Regulus was taken prisoner. The survivors of this disaster perished when the fleet that was attempting to take them back to Italy was destroyed. 

Naval battles and indecisive operations in Italy prolonged the war and brought both sides close to exhaustion. The appointment of 

Hamilcar Barca to command of the Carthaginian army in Sicily forced Rome to assume the defensive. Unless command of the sea again could be secured and communications cut between Hamilcar and Carthage, Rome's plight threatened to become desperate. By the use of all available financial resources another fleet accordingly was made ready, and, under the command of Lutatius Catulus, it gained an overwhelming victory off Aegusa in 242 B.C. As had been hoped, this victory forced Carthage to recall Hamilcar, and since sentiment for peace had been steadily growing in the north African metropolis negotiations were begun to terminate the war. 

The terms of the treaty of 241 B.C. seem far more harsh than 

Rome's military successes would have justified her in imposing. 

Carthage was compelled to give up Sicily and pay an indemnity of 3300 talents ($6,150,000 gold). Both sides recognized the ephemeral nature of the peace. The war had been the first episode in what had become a struggle for survival, and there could be no lasting peace until one antagonist or the other was completely crushed. 

Events between the close of the first war and the resumption of hostilities in 218 B.C. were an important phase of the struggle. Immediately after cessation of the war, Carthaginian mercenaries mutinied upon their return to north Africa primarily because their pay was in arrears, and the state allegedly was unable to grant their demands for immediate payment. The mutiny was crushed with pitiless cruelty, but while Carthage was thus involved, Rome seized the islands of Sardinia and Corsica. Carthaginian protests at this breach of the peace were answered by the imposition of another indemnity under Roman threat of renewal of war. This flagrant Roman opportunism

THE EMERGENCE OF ROME AS A WORLD POWER 147 

makes understandable the bitterness with which Carthage was soon to prosecute the second war. 

In the meantime, the Carthaginian government authorized Hamilcar to occupy Spain, where it already had extensive interests. The economic advantages of a more intensive exploitation of the resources of the Spanish peninsula would more than offset the loss of Sicily, and the strategic value of the move doubtless was realized, for Spain subsequently might be used as a base for a campaign in Italy. 

Rome was not perturbed by this new orientation of Carthaginian policy; any military danger seemed remote, and she had no interests in Spain aside from those incident to her acceptance of a protectorate over the Greek city of Massilia. Probably at the behest of Massilia, Rome entered into negotiations with Carthage that culminated in the Treaty of the Ebro in 226 B.C. Under the terms of the treaty, Carthage promised to refrain from extending her interests north of the Ebro river, while Rome, thinking primarily of the activities of Massilia, promised to regard the river as the southern limit of her sphere of influence. Rome, however, soon violated at least the letter of the treaty by asserting a protectorate over the town of Saguntum which was located south of the Ebro. Although Carthage took no retaliatory action, the situation could easily become of sufficient gravity to precipitate hostilities.

In the meantime, Rome completed the organization of Sicily as a province. The policies that had proved so successful in dealing with the Latin and Italic allies were largely superseded because of the evident desire to exploit to the full the resources of the province for the benefit of Roman interests. The Lex Hieronica, or scheme of administration that had been designed by Hiero of Syracuse, was used as a model. While large tracts were reserved as public land, many Sicilian owners retained possession of their holdings by paying about onethird of their incomes as rent. The treatment of the Sicilian towns was more in accord with traditional Roman principles, for the status of each town was fixed by separate arrangement largely determined by its conduct during the war. Since the governing official in the province would be required to exercise judicial functions and command an army, consular and praetorian powers were combined in the creation of the provincial praetorship. 

A fateful event of the period was the appointment of Hannibal to command of Carthaginian Spain in 221 B.C. The lives of few men have been so completely dominated by hatred as was that of Hannibal, most famous scion of the Barcid family. From boyhood he had

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cherished an implacable resolution to destroy Rome's power in Italy; he literally dedicated his career to vengeance for the wrongs that he believed had been inflicted on Carthage. A born leader of men, he infused enthusiasm into his soldiery whose respect he commanded by his genius as a general and whose affection he earned by his democratic bearing.

There is little doubt that from the moment of his arrival in Spain Hannibal desired to organize an expedition for the invasion of Italy. 

In view of the pacific sentiments of the home government, however, he realized that he could obtain no support from Carthage unless he could provoke Rome into a declaration of war. He therefore captured and sacked Saguntum in the hope that Rome would take belligerent action and thus provoke Carthage to prosecute an ostensibly defensive war. Rome, confronted by the attack on her protectorate, demanded reparations and, when met by refusal, declared war as 

Hannibal had anticipated.

The Roman Senate immediately prepared to take the offensive. 

An army under Tiberius Sempronius Longus set out for north Africa, while another consular force, commanded by Cornelius Scipio, marched toward Spain with the intention of forestalling any attempt of Hannibal to invade Italy. It was confidently believed that these prompt measures would lead to the recall of Hannibal for the defense of Carthage. Hannibal, however, with an army of 50,000, augmented by 9000 cavalry and 40 elephants, marched north, crossed the Pyrenees, and eluded the army of Scipio in the Rhone valley. 

Scipio thereupon returned to Italy, but he sent his army into Spain in conformity with his instructions. This action, although often ridiculed by historians, proved to be of great strategic value, for it necessitated the maintenance of Carthaginian forces in Spain and thus relieved the pressure on Italy. As soon as it had become apparent that Hannibal's march was no mere feint, the Roman expeditionary force to north Africa was recalled.

The advance of Hannibal's army was so retarded by sporadic fighting with Gallic tribes that he was forced to undertake the crossing of the Alps with winter close at hand. About half of the army made the hazardous crossing, probably by way of the Little St. Bernard

Pass. Hannibal had no intention of marching directly on Rome. He hoped that his appearance in north Italy would be the signal for the revolt of the Italic allies who would welcome him as a deliverer from the Roman yoke. He failed to realize to what degree Rome had suc-

THE EMERGENCE OF ROME AS A WORLD POWER 149 

ceeded in securing the loyalty of the allies; his plan, as seen from the vantage point of the modern historian, was foredoomed to failure. 

Two Carthaginian victories at the Ticinus river and at Lake Trebia opened the north Italic campaign. Flaminius, one of the consuls for 217 B.C., was then disastrously defeated at Lake Trasimene in 

Etruria. Hannibal refused to march on Rome despite the entreaties of his Master of Horse, on the grounds that his forces were insufficient and his cavalry would be useless in siege operations. In view of the gravity of the situation after Trasimene, Fabius was made dictator. He carefully refrained from meeting Hannibal in battle, realizing that inaction would inevitably weaken the Carthaginians. 

The policies of Fabius soon evoked bitter criticism; indeed, it was charged that the "sluggard" was deliberately sacrificing his chances for victory, and Hannibal carefully fostered these rumors by exempting the estates of Fabius from harrying to make it appear that he was a secret ally. The Senate lost all confidence in the dictator and resorted to the unprecedented expedient of appointing a second dictator as his colleague.

In view of the public and official clamor for action, Paulus and Varo, who were elected to the consulships for 216 B.C., immediately led an army against the invaders in the hope of securing a decisive victory. They were completely outgeneraled, with the result that their army was virtually annihilated at Cannae, and heroic measures were necessary to counteract the profound defeatism in Rome. Hannibal, however, again refused to attack Rome. In this he was wise, for if he had tried to storm the impregnable fortifications, he would simply have lost men and prestige. 

By 215 B.C. Rome was in a desperate condition. Capua, in response to the continued urging of Hannibal, renounced her allegiance to Rome and openly espoused the cause of the invader. Hiero II of Syracuse died and was succeeded by a tyrant whose sympathies were openly in favor of Carthage. King Philip V of Macedonia prepared an expedition for the invasion of Italy in support of Hannibal, but Rome sent forces across the Adriatic in sufficient strength to avert this new danger.

The war continued a stalemate until in 212 B.C. Roman prospects for victory brightened with the capture of Syracuse by Marcellus, despite the defensive engines that had been designed by the famous physicist Archimedes. Capua was captured and the citizenry were terribly punished for their revolt. In 207 B.C. Hasdrubal, brother of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Hannibal, finally succeeded in leading an army from Spain into Italy, but it was cut to pieces in the battle of the Metaurus river by the Roman legions under Livius Salianator before it could effect a junction with Hannibal.

By 204 B.C. Rome at last was ready to launch a major offensive. 

Scipio (Africanus) landed a force in north Africa and with the assistance of Numidian allies forced Carthage to sue for peace. The severity of the terms, however, and the arrival of Hannibal, who had been recalled, ended negotiations and the war continued. In the ensuing battle of Zama, 202 B.C., Hannibal at last met his tactical master, for by skillful employment of hidden supports and concentration of strength on his flanks Scipio gained an overwhelming victory that left Carthage no alternative to the conclusion of an imposed peace. 

The terms of the harsh treaty that the helpless Carthaginian government was forced to accept included the surrender of Spain, naval disarmament, and the payment of an indemnity of 10,000 talents. 

Moreover, Carthage was forbidden to wage war outside Africa, and even her policies in north Africa henceforth were to be subject to Roman supervision. This last clause must be emphasized for, as we shall see, the alleged evasion of its provisions by Carthage served as a pretext for the Third Punic War (149-146 B.C.). 

Scipio returned to Rome in triumph and was saluted as “Africanus" in commemoration of his achievements. Hannibal eventually served in the armies of Antiochus III of Syria, but after the defeat at Magnesia (190 B.C.), he took refuge in Crete and subsequently in 

Bithynia. His suicide in 183 B.C. terminated the career of a great man whose life work had ended in bitter failure.

ROMAN EXPANSION IN THE EAST 

Rome's intervention in eastern affairs was largely a manifestation of imperialistic ambition incited during the Punic Wars and a resultant of pro-Greek sentiment that developed with the conquest of Hellenized south Italy and Sicily. By 281 B.C. the empire of Alexander the Great had been divided into three kingdoms: Egypt, Macedonia, and the Seleucid Kingdom. Conditions in Greece were quite disturbed. Athens and Sparta maintained precarious independence; most of the Peloponnesian states were organized into the Achaean League, under the presidency of Corinth, while the Aetolian League was endeavoring to control Thessaly. Rhodes and Pergamum were thriving states, but particularly vulnerable to attack by their powerful eastern neighbors.

THE EMERGENCE OF ROME AS A WORLD POWER 151 

When Ptolemy IV, ruler of Egypt, died, leaving a mere child as his successor (203 B.C.), Philip V of Macedonia and Antiochus III, ruler of the Seleucid Kingdom, plotted to seize the Egyptian foreign possessions. With the end of the Second Punic War, Egyptian emissaries divulged the plans of the conspirators and sought Roman intervention. The Aetolian League, alarmed at the expansion of Macedonia, likewise appealed, while Rhodes also claimed to be threatened by the aggressions. The comitia tributa favored a policy of neutrality, since no Roman defensive interests were involved and the dangers of a war so soon after the termination of the duel with Carthage were obvious. On the other hand, it was argued that the aggressions of Philip eventually would threaten Italy; his alliance with Hannibal had been proof of belligerent intentions and demanded retaliatory measures. Those with pro-Greek sentiments deplored the pusillanimity that would permit the subjugation of Greece by an ambitious adventurer. The advocates of intervention finally prevailed. Roman envoys were sent to participate at a congress of Greek powers at Athens and Philip was ordered to evacuate Greece. War was declared when he ignored the ultimatum. 1 

The First Macedonian War (200-197 B.C.) was decided by the victory of a Roman army under Flamininus at Cynoscephalae in 

Thessaly. Some time after his victory, Flamininus delivered an address at Corinth while the Isthmian Games were in progress and promised that Rome would respect the independence of Greece. His unauthorized pledge, interpreted by the Greeks as an official statement of Roman policy, was received with great enthusiasm. When 

Flamininus refused to permit the Aetolian League to annex Thessaly, he was denounced as bitterly as he had hitherto been acclaimed. 

In the meantime, Antiochus, who had left his ally in the lurch, quietly appropriated towns in Asia Minor which were surrendered by Macedonia in accordance with the treaty with Rome. He also concluded a treaty with Ptolemy in order to lend some legitimacy to these actions. The agreement included an arrangement for the marriage of the pharaoh to his daughter, and the Seleucid now could flout Rome by the continuance of his aggressive policies nominally in behalf of Egypt. The Aetolian League, angered at the Roman organization of a confederacy in Thessaly, invited him to intervene. in Greece.

There was much opposition in Rome to another war, and many 

1 Philip's entry into the Second Punic War and Rome's short countercampaign are sometimes spoken of as the first war with Macedonia.

felt that the Greeks should be left to their own devices. When it was learned that Hannibal had joined the army of Antiochus, this attitude quickly changed. The exiled Carthaginian was urging Antiochus to attack Italy, and there was always a chance that his advice would be followed. War therefore was declared in 192 B.C. Since the alliance between Philip and Antiochus had been broken by the perfidy of the latter, Rome was spared the necessity of fighting a powerful coalition. Antiochus decided to fight the war in Greece despite the entreaties of Hannibal for a direct assault on Italy. A Roman army thereupon marched into Greece in the spring of 191 B.C., forced the pass of Thermopylae, and drove Antiochus to Asia Minor. Here the battle of Magnesia (190 B.C.) brought the war to a close. Antiochus, forced to acknowledge the Taurus mountains as the northern boundary of his kingdom, was deprived of almost his entire fleet. An indemnity was imposed but there was no curtailment of the sovereignty of the Seleucid Kingdom.

Philip was by no means ready to accept the verdict of Cynoscephalae, and Roman policies in Greece threatened to frustrate permanently his ambitions in that area. He accordingly made elaborate preparations for the renewal of the struggle, but died before the commencement of hostilities. His son, Perseus, usurped the throne after the murder of his brother, Demetrius, the rightful heir, and Rome, convinced of the imminence of hostilities, declared war in 171 B.C. The war was prosecuted in desultory fashion until 168 B.C. when the consul, Paullus, won a decisive victory at Pydna. Perseus was forced to accept terms which virtually marked the end of Macedonian sovereignty, for his kingdom was divided into four autonomous republics each governed in accordance with the plan Flamininus had devised for Thessaly.

A number of Greek states were compromised by the defeat of Perseus, for examination of his archives, which were transferred to Rome after the battle of Pydna, proved conclusively that they had been in secret alliance with Macedonia. The Senate, resolved to discourage further intrigues, ordered severe punishment. Epirus was overrun, and many of its populace were slain or sold into slavery; the 

Achaean League was forced to give hostages as a guarantee of its fidelity to Rome; while the Aetolian League again was required to renounce all claims on Thessaly.

While Rome's attention was engrossed by developments in the East, Carthage recovered a large measure of its former prosperity and power. When Cato visited the city in 167 B.C. he was convinced

THE EMERGENCE OF ROME AS A WORLD POWER 

153 that prompt action was requisite to prevent the state from again becoming a menace to Rome's preeminence in the Mediterranean. 

A pretext was soon found to justify, at least technically, resumption of hostilities. The treaty of 202 B.C. had required Carthage to submit her foreign policy to Roman supervision. King Masinissa of Numidia lost no opportunity to profit from this situation by harrying the Carthaginian borders with virtual impunity, and Carthage, in despair of receiving just treatment from Rome, took the fatal step of declaring war against him, in 149 B.C. This action, however justified, was, of course, a violation of the treaty, and after some hesitation the Senate declared war. Carthage was forced to sue for peace, but when negotiations failed to deter Rome from her obvious intention to destroy the city the populace continued their heroic but futile resistance. Roman forces commanded by Cornelius Scipio prosecuted the siege with unremitting energy until in 146 B.C., when the Romans were capturing it street by street, the proud city was forced to capitulate and was completely demolished. A Roman province of 

Africa was organized, while Libya was made tributary, and the agricultural lands held by Carthage were declared Roman public domain. The treaty further stipulated that if Carthage were rebuilt the new city had to be at least ten miles inland.

While the Third Punic War was being fought in north Africa, hostilities again broke out in Macedonia. In 149 B.C. a certain Andriscus, who claimed to be Demetrius, murdered brother of Perseus, managed to foment a strong revival of Macedonian nationalism. 

Rome moved with her accustomed energy, and by 147 B.C. Metellus succeeded in quelling the uprising. The Senate, convinced of the futility of halfway measures, combined the four republics that had been created after the battle of Pydna into the province of Macedonia, which was thereupon placed under direct Roman supervision. 

Events in Greece likewise convinced the Senate that the alternatives were complete control or withdrawal. In a gesture of conciliation the hostages that had been taken from the Achaean League were released. Diaeus, one of the recipients of Roman clemency, was elected to the presidency of the League upon his return and he immediately encouraged anti-Roman demonstrations. When Roman envoys appeared at Corinth to protest the aggressions of the League against Sparta in defiance of a Roman ultimatum, they were mocked and derided, whereupon the Senate declared war against the League in retaliation. Mummius marched into Greece, captured Corinth after a short siege, and burned the city in 146 B.C. The severity of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

this action has often been condemned, but it doubtless had the effect of intimidating other members of the League. Most of the Greek states were enrolled as allies, with privileges graduated in accordance with their conduct. Years later, when the danger of precipitating a united Greek effort to secure independence subsided, the states were organized into the province of Achaea. 

INTERNAL CONDITIONS DURING THE EXPANSION PERIOD 

The outstanding effect of the wars of expansion on the constitutional development of the state was the growth in the power and prestige of the Senate, which assumed virtual control of foreign policy, although the critical questions of intervention in Messana and in Greece had been submitted to the Centuriate Assembly for decision. The Senate, for the most part, wielded paramount influence in the declaration of war and the conclusion of peace. It decided military policies and assumed the power to partition duties between consuls. Imminent bankruptcy during the Second Punic War gave opportunity for the assertion of its financial control. 

Annexation of provinces created difficult administrative problems, for the government of Rome remained basically that of a citystate, a system not designed for the rule of an empire. As a result of the Punic Wars, Rome had annexed Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, Africa, and Spain, which was divided into the provinces of Hither and Farther Spain. The eastern wars resulted in the acquisition of Macedonia, Asia, and ultimately Achaea. In order to maintain communications with the Spanish provinces, the province of Gallia Narbonensis was organized. The provinces were governed, after the first experiments in Sicily, by proconsuls or propraetors named by the Senate. 

These officials, who were usually ex-consuls or praetors, were assigned provinces after the expiration of their magisterial terms. 

There was no check on a provincial governor during his term of office, but he was amenable to prosecution upon his return to Rome before special courts with juries composed of senators. 

The plight of Italian agriculture created by the prolonged wars was a serious problem. Many farms had been devastated during the 

Carthaginian occupation; others had been abandoned because of the protracted absence of their owners on military campaigns. Frequently, when the women, the aged, or other non-combatants had attempted to work the lands, enormous debts had been incurred. 

Those with the financial resources and the courage to employ them now could profit by the damage to the Italian yeomanry by acquir-

THE EMERGENCE OF ROME AS A WORLD POWER 

155 ing cheap lands. The influx of thousands of war captives brought the price of slaves to extremely low levels, and the increasing use of slave labor served as one of the chief causes for the development of the latifundia or large plantations. The rise of the plantations frequently subjected the owners of small farms to competition impossible for them to meet. Dispossessed yeomen were degraded to the status of tenants or dependents of the plantation owners, or forced to migrate to large urban centers in search of employment. 

Since slave labor was having the same effects on free industrial labor, the influx of impoverished farmers merely aggravated the problem of caring for increasingly large, indigent, urban proletariats. Since the plantation system was best suited to the cultivation of a few staple crops, and importation of grain from Sicily had curtailed the profit from the cultivation of cereals, there was a great increase in the cultivation of olives and grapes. The problems of Italic agriculture thus briefly outlined were a basic cause of the economic and social unrest that led to the political turmoils of the post-war period. 

The prolonged wars contributed powerfully to the rise of the equestrian order (knights). For centuries Rome's commercial and industrial development had lagged behind, largely because of the prejudices of the old aristocratic families against participation in any economic activity save agriculture. Men of humbler origin, however, with great initiative and ability began to profit by the post-war opportunities to acquire capital which they employed to underwrite the collection of taxes, to purchase concessions in the provinces, and to advance funds for public works. In many instances such individuals formed partnerships and stock companies. Profits were enormous, and bribes frequently secured the connivance of officials at corrupt transactions. It was natural that the newly enriched equestrian order should demand and soon secure political powers commensurate with their wealth and importance. 

No immediate expansion of Roman commerce followed the wars of expansion. Such trade as existed was largely coastal, and Puteoli rather than Rome was the leading Italian port. Industry likewise remained relatively backward, for the self-sufficiency of the average household curtailed the market for industrial products, and the urban proletariat had little purchasing power. 

Cultural development reflected prolonged contact with Hellenic inspiration. Liberals prided themselves on their acquaintance with the literary and artistic productions of classical Greece and encouraged emulation. The history of Latin literature really began with

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the work of Livius Andronicus who, brought to Rome as a prisoner after the fall of Tarentum, translated the Odyssey and wrote dramas based on Greek models. Naevius wrote plays in which he attacked personal and political enemies and dramatized contemporary events. 

He also wrote an epic poem on the Punic Wars, only a few fragments of which survive. Ennius, native of a Hellenized town in Calabria, was a prolific writer who produced satires, dramatic poems, and plays. Fragments of about twenty of his plays have survived. He is best known, however, for his Annals, of which several hundred lines are extant. The work was arranged in eighteen books and contained a history of Rome from the legendary period to his own time (c. 

270-199 B.C.).

Although there were several forms of indigenous drama in Italy, the practice of utilizing and perpetuating the established Greek form received its greatest impetus with the work of Plautus and Terence. 

Plautus (c. 254-184 B.C.) was born in Umbria, whence he migrated to Rome. Twenty-one of his comedies are extant, although 130 have been attributed to him. His plays, modeled on Greek “New 

Comedy" of the Hellenistic period, are comedies of manners, marked by liberal use of stock figures, such as the boasting soldier, the beautiful courtesan, the prodigal son, etc. Most of the plays have prologues designed to give the audience the factual background necessary to appreciate them. The plays, in Greek meters, contain spoken parts as well as parts to be sung to the accompaniment of flute-like instruments. Terence (c. 195-155 B.C.) was born in Carthage. He was sold into Roman slavery, but eventually was manumitted and educated. 

Six of his comedies have survived. They are free from the coarseness, indeed the obscenity, that characterizes those of Plautus. The characters are more refined and portrayed with greater subtlety. 

It was natural that an interest in history should develop during the period of the wars of expansion. Fabius Pictor produced a work in 

Greek based largely on family records and concerned for the most part with genealogies of leading patrician families. Polybius was brought to Rome among the hostages from the Achaean League. 

His history of the Punic Wars is a masterpiece comparable with the work of Thucydides. His unbiased evaluation of personalities and events affords a welcome balance to the prejudice and frequent distortion of Livy, whose work constitutes our second great source for the history of the war period. 

Architecture was as yet little affected by Greek traditions. The temples and public edifices were built of inferior stone of poor color
