The Romans were not equalled in daring of conception and skill of execution of such structures until the modern age. There was little interest in sculpture and painting, and such work as was produced was merely imitative.

CHAPTER 12 Transition from Republic to Triumvirate 

THE GRACCHI 

HE conclusion of the wars of expansion found the Roman state confronted by a number of vexatious problems. One that imperatively demanded solution was the disposition of the public lands. As a result of the wars of expansion in Italy, much land had been acquired which presumably was the property of all citizens. Some of it had been leased to individuals, especially in the form of timber and mineral concessions. A great part, however, had been occupied by private persons without authorization. Prolonged occupancy led many holders of public land to consider that they had full rights of ownership.

One of the provisions of the Licinio-Sextian Rogations traditionally stipulated that no individual should hold more than 500 jugera (322 acres) of the public land, but since no enforcing agency was created and no responsibility for the application of the restriction had been specifically assigned to any governmental organ, the legislation became virtually a dead letter. The public domain never had been accurately surveyed, and the absence of records in regard to its disposition made it difficult to distinguish between public land and tracts legitimately held in private possession. Many of those who had illegally occupied public land had improved it and thereby increased both the capital value and the return. Swamps had been drained, timber and brush cleared, and buildings erected. It obviously would be unjust to require the return of the land to state ownership without compensation to the occupant for the improvements made. Then, too, tracts of the public domain in many instances had changed hands several times; individuals had purchased such land frequently in ignorance of the lack of proper title, and arbitrary resumption of state ownership would penalize innocent parties. 

One of the dangerous economic effects of the wars had been the

ruin of a considerable portion of the Italian yeomanry. It was natural that those who had lost their lands would clamor for a distribution program that would ensure them their legitimate share in the public domain that had been acquired by the common effort and sacrifice of virtually all the able-bodied citizenry. Since the Senate and the magistrates usually were partial to the interests of the great landowners, many of whom had flagrantly violated the restrictions on tenure of public land, there was little effort made to institute the necessary reforms.

The agitation for solution of the public land question finally found expression with the election of Tiberius Gracchus as tribune in 133 B.C. Although an aristocrat, Tiberius had become deeply interested in the plight of the yeomanry and the generally unsound condition of Italian agriculture. The first step in his program was to procure passage by the tributa of an enactment which revived the restrictions on public land tenure originally embodied in the Licinio-Sextian provisions. The restriction was liberalized, however, by the proviso that occupants of public tracts were to be allowed 250 jugera extra for each of not more than two sons. A commission of three was appointed and authorized to hold quo warranto proceedings to determine the ownership of all tracts where there was reason to believe that the land was originally part of the public domain. If the occupant could not validate his title, the land was presumed to be public, and all in excess of the maximum acreage allotted reverted to state ownership. The land thus recovered was to be divided into small plots of from twenty to thirty acres and distributed among the impoverished yeomanry. The problem of compensation for improvements was readily solved since Attalus III, ruler of Pergamum, had just died and bequeathed his treasure to the Roman state. Tiberius proposed that this unanticipated asset be employed to implement his land program.

The reformer's program aroused immediate opposition on the part of the landed aristocracy who were profiting by the continuance of the public land abuses. The Senate, primarily representing their interests, resorted to the expedient of bribing Octavius, one of the tribunes, to veto the proposals of his colleague and thus frustrate the reforms. Tiberius countered by deposing Octavius without constitutional sanction for such a procedure. When he defied constitutional precedent again by becoming a candidate for the tribuneship for a second successive term, the Senate speciously charged him with dictatorial ambitions, and in the ensuing excitement, the reformer

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

was slain by a group of senators while attempting to address his followers. 

With the death of the tribune, his legislation was abrogated in the wave of reaction that followed. In 123 B.C., however, Gaius Gracchus was elected tribune with the avowed purpose of vindicating his brother's memory and carrying out his policies. The land program of Tiberius was revived, but the policies announced by Gaius soon went far beyond these objectives. Support of the plebeians was secured by proposals for the establishment of colonies and public works designed to alleviate unemployment. Another popular measure was the proposal for the distribution of grain to the poor at a fraction of its market price. This policy was destined to be disastrous, for political leaders from time to time would bid for popularity with the masses by advocating expansion of these relief measures. 

There could be no hope of enlisting the support of the aristocrats for any program that included a policy of redistribution of public lands. As a counter-poise to their opposition, Gaius made material concessions to the equestrian order. One law provided that henceforth trials of cases of alleged extortion and misgovernment in the provinces should take place before juries made up of members of the equestrian class. Since the equites were heavily interested in provincial exploitation and were the ones primarily responsible for the appearance of administrative abuses, the law was virtually equivalent to a promise that extortionate practices would be overlooked in the future. A new tax also was imposed on the province of Asia, and since the equites derived much of their profit from underwriting tax collections this measure likewise was an indubitable concession to them.

Gaius was elected to a second term (122-121 B.C.), for a measure recently had been enacted legalizing tenure of the tribunician office for successive terms. The Senate attempted to obstruct his reform measures by bribing a servile colleague to undermine his influence with the plebeians by promises of greater concessions. Finally, in response to promised reforms for the benefit of the Italic allies, Gaius took the fatal step of proposing their enfranchisement. This measure was bound to occasion the opposition of all classes in Rome, for it meant the abridgement of the political prerogatives hitherto exclusively enjoyed by the inhabitants of the city and its immediate environs. Rioting broke out, and the reformer forestalled assassination by ordering a faithful slave to kill him.

No lasting benefit accrued to the state from the reform efforts of

the Gracchi. The only measure that long survived the death of 

Gaius was the policy of grain distribution, which created problems more difficult than those it was designed to solve. The chief constitutional effect of the reform era was to identify the office of tribune with radicalism, and the violation of the principles upon which the office had been created by reformers and reactionaries alike made it a post to be shunned by men of ability and political ambition. 

Much more disturbing and symptomatic of basic weakness in the Roman Republic was the resort to violence. Great political and social questions apparently now would be decided not by the orderly processes of constitutional government but by resort to the sword. 

WAR WITH JUGURTHA AND THE RISE OF MARIUS 

It will be remembered that Rome acquired a protectorate over Numidia as a result of the Second Punic War. The third war that terminated with the destruction of Carthage had been begun ostensibly in response to the obligations incurred with the Numidian protectorate.

Upon the death of the Numidian ruler, Micipsa, in 118 B.C., the kingdom was ruled jointly by his two sons, Adherbal and Hiempsal. 

Jugurtha, an. illegitimate cousin of the young rulers, thereupon challenged their rights of succession and murdered Hiempsal. Adherbal, threatened with a similar fate, appealed to Rome, but the bribes of the wily Jugurtha induced the Senate to refrain from intervention. 

In response to insistent pleas, the Senate finally sent a commission to investigate the situation. The commissioners, probably corruptly influenced by Jugurtha, recognized his claims to the throne by partitioning the kingdom between him and Adherbal, although the division was partial to the latter. Jugurtha nevertheless continued his aggressions, and a Roman embassy failed to induce him to desist. 

Finally, he captured Cirta, capital of the portion of the kingdom awarded to Adherbal, who immediately fell a victim to his cruelty. 

The slaying of a number of Roman merchants during the sack of the city greatly aggravated the tension. 

In 111 B.C. Memmius, one of the tribunes, made an issue of the 

Numidian affair by charging the Senate and the officials who had been involved in the negotiations with flagrant venality. Such an uproar was incited that the Senate dared not longer delay, and Bestia accordingly was sent to north Africa with a consular army to restore order. When he returned without striking a blow, the charges of corruption in high places seemed fully proved. At the insistence

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of Memmius, Jugurtha then was invited to Rome to testify, with guarantee of immunity, but the tribunician colleagues of Memmius vetoed embarrassing questions put to the witness, and Bestia made the farce complete by procuring immunity from examination. In 

110 B.C., the consul, Albinus, led a fruitless expedition into Numidia and was replaced the following year by Metellus, who had Marius as his lieutenant.

Marius was born in 155 B.C., the son of a landowner and member of the equestrian order. He had served as tribune, praetor, and propraetor of Spain, but his lack of aristocratic connections had so far prevented his elevation to the consulship. He now turned his position as legatus in the African army to good account by suggesting to friends at Rome that Metellus was needlessly prolonging the war, and his charges seemed plausible enough in view of the scandals that had marked the conduct of the African affair up to this point. In response to public clamor, he accordingly was elected to the highest magistracy for 107 B.C. and ordered to Numidia. Oddly enough, Sulla, who soon was to be his implacable foe, accompanied him as lieutenant. Within a short time after the arrival of the new commander, the Roman forces gained a decisive victory, and Jugurtha then was captured with the assistance of King Bocchus of Mauretania. Marius was granted a triumph upon his return to Rome, and 

Jugurtha was dragged in chains in the procession as a prelude to his execution.

The Numidian affair had been a graphic illustration of the prevalence of incompetence and corruption among the ruling aristocracy. 

The speedy termination of the war by Marius stood in sharp contrast. The Senate had hoped that appointment of Marius to command of the African army would discredit him and forestall his further political advancement; instead, the Numidian campaign made him the hero of the populares and firmly entrenched him in political power.

He soon had opportunity to augment his fame. In 121 B.C., the 

Cimbri and Teutones moved into the province of Gallia Narbonensis. 

Their invasion was no mere marauding expedition, for they were accompanied by their families and enormous baggage trains, giving every indication that they intended to make their home in the province or in other Roman territory. Roman armies sent to the Rhone valley failed to arrest their movements. From Gallia Narbonensis a large body of the barbarians moved into Spain, where they were

defeated by the legions under Caepio without basic alteration of the situation. The series of failures accentuated the demand of the populares for the appointment of Marius to the command, and in 104 B.C. he was again elected to the consulship and entrusted with an army to operate in Gaul and Spain.

As a prelude to the expedition, Marius made some fundamental changes in the legionary organization. The complement of the legion was raised from 3600 to 6000 and a new division, the cohort, established. Henceforth, the legion was divided into ten cohorts, each made up of five maniples. Numidian and Thracian cavalry, as well as the famous Balearic slingers, were employed as auxiliaries. 

The provision that each soldier henceforth carry a heavy pack greatly reduced the size of the baggage train and ensured greater mobility. Marius then led the reorganized legions to the valley of the 

Rhone where the troops were hardened by employment on a number of public works projects. 

Although no direct action had been taken to curb the migratory movements of the barbarians, Marius was re-elected to the supreme magistracy for 103 B.C., and, after several indecisive victories in

Spain, was re-elected for the ensuing year. The Gallic menace became acute with the march of the Teutones through Liguria (northwest Italy), but Marius gained an overwhelming victory at Aquae 

Sextiae. The following year, he turned back the Cimbri, who had pushed into north Italy at Vercellae. When he celebrated his triumph he was greeted as the saviour of Italy and his political power was well-nigh impregnable. Turning back the invading barbarians had not only delivered Italy from immediate danger; the way had been paved for Roman expansion to the north. From a constitutional point of view, however, dangerous precedents had been set. Marius had held the highest office in the Republic for four successive terms, and, moreover, the army was bound to him by the closest ties of personal allegiance. The evolution of dictatorship was clearly foreshadowed. 

It was unfortunate both for Marius and for the Roman Republic that his active career did not end with the victory at Vercellae. His brilliant military achievements had ensured the political supremacy of the populares, and the hero, elected to his sixth consulship for the year 100, soon found himself in a position where his popularity was being used as a screen to hide the machinations of the demagogues Saturninus and Glaucia. Radical measures, such as further reduction of the price at which grain was retailed to the poor, land allotments

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

in Cisalpine Gaul, and colonial projects ensured the support of the masses, while newly enacted lèse majesté laws precluded criticism of such proposals.

Glaucia then precipitated a crisis by illegally becoming a candidate for the consulship before expiration of his term as praetor, and there was apparently conclusive evidence that he had procured the murder of his conservative opponent in the election. Virtual anarchy was created when both conservatives and radicals resorted to intimidation and violence. Marius finally realized that he had been falsely identified with the radicalism of his colleagues and he thereupon accepted command of the conservative forces which quelled the disorder by 98 B.C. His defection created a split in the ranks of the populares and necessitated his retirement from politics. His affiliation with the conservative element had forfeited the support of the radicals, while his past connection with Saturninus and Glaucia made impossible his permanent acceptance by the conservatives. He withdrew to his estate in south Italy. The return of the aristocrats to power was followed by the disgraceful prosecution of Rutilius Rufus, who, as governor of Asia, had outraged the capitalists by his efforts to protect the provincials from their rapacity. 

The ascendancy of the conservatives did not allay radical agitation. In 91 B.C. the tribune Drusus sponsored a comprehensive liberal program which, in addition to the usual proposals for colonies and further reduction in the price of the grain retailed by the state, demanded the abolition of the practice of trying cases of provincial extortion before juries made up of members of the equestrian order. 

Obviously, this measure was inspired by the case of Rutilius Rufus. 

In order to frustrate conservative opposition to the program, the tribune demanded the inclusion of three hundred new members in the Senate. Drusus then revived the suggestion of Gaius Gracchus to enfranchise the Italic allies, with the same fatal result, for he was assassinated during the uprisings in Rome that greeted the introduction of the measure.

THE SOCIAL WAR 

Concessions to the Italic allies were long overdue. Although liable for military service, they were denied a share in the spoil and were ineligible to share in the allocations of public lands secured with their aid. The widespread plight of Italic agriculture was producing great misery, and the grain distribution policy inaugurated by Gaius Gracchus had served further to depress the price of agricultural com-

modities. With no opportunity to express their grievances through political action, it is not surprising that the allies interpreted the fall of Drusus as proof that peaceful means would not secure justice. 

They therefore organized the Confederacy of Italia, with a government modelled on that of Rome, and prepared to defend their independence by arms. Since a crisis had arisen in the East with the aggressions of King Mithridates of Pontus, the Roman government was not in a position energetically to prosecute the Social War and therefore hastened to grant concessions. The Lex Julia by offering citizenship, with the right to vote, to the inhabitants of allied towns that had not as yet rebelled was designed to produce a schism in the allied ranks. When it failed to arrest the spread of the insurrection, the Lex Papiria was passed extending the franchise to all allied towns which applied for it within sixty days after passage of the law, and a supplementary enactment extended its provisions to Cisalpine Gaul. 

Eight new wards were organized to re-apportion representation in the comitia tributa.

WAR WITH MITHRIDATES AND THE SULLAN REACTION 

Rome's haste in granting concessions to the rebellious allies was in large measure dictated by the necessity of taking strong measures to arrest the expansion of the kingdom of Pontus under its able and aggressive ruler, Mithridates VI. The Pontic ruler, encouraged by the advice of his Greek ministers, had the idea of subjugating the neighboring states of Bithynia and Cappadocia and ultimately girdling the Black Sea with states annexed to or dependent on Pontus. The actual and projected expansion of Pontus directly menaced states considered under Roman protection and promised to endanger Roman control of the province of Asia (Asia Minor), the most lucrative of the provinces. In 88 B.C. Mithridates, taking advantage of the discontent in Asia, fomented an insurrection during which thousands of Roman citizens were slain in a planned pogrom. Since immediate reprisal was essential if the province was to remain under Roman rule, the Senate declared war and prepared to dispatch an army to the East.

Sulla, an aristocrat and avowed conservative, was elected to the consulship for 88-87 B.C. and entrusted with command of the eastern army. The populares, however, condemned his selection and proceeded to elect Sulpicius and Marius, who had emerged from retirement, to the consulships. The exponents of the popular party thereupon ordered Sulla to relinquish his command, but instead of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

complying, he marched on Rome and entered the city after defeating the hastily levied army of the populares. 

Sulla then took measures to assure conservative ascendancy during his absence in the East. The Senate was arbitrarily "packed" with three hundred Sullan partisans, and a law was passed invalidating plebiscites of the tributa which were not ratified by the Senate. Octavius and Cinna then were elected consuls for the ensuing term, and both were pledged to refrain from alterations of the constitution while Sulla was absent from Rome.

With proconsular authority, Sulla then set out for Greece, where Mithridates had begun the war, and soon forced the Pontic king to retire to Asia Minor. As soon as Sulla left Italy, however, the populares seized control of the government. Cinna supported the radicals, and Marius returned from Naples to serve as the popular leader and again was inducted into the consulship. A veritable reign of terror followed the seizure of the capital city by the Marians. All known partisans of Sulla were slaughtered and their property was confiscated; frequently, avarice dictated the persecution of individuals whose sole crime was their wealth. The authority of Sulla was declared abrogated, and Flaccus and Fimbria were sent to the East to replace him. Fimbria murdered his colleague on the way, and, after an unsatisfactory conference with Sulla, proceeded to negotiate a peace with Mithridates on his own authority. Mithridates relinquished his conquests, surrendered most of his fleet, and agreed to the payment of an indemnity. Sulla, who had followed Fimbria to Asia Minor, agreed to the terms. He then punished the Asiatic provincials for their complicity in the uprising of 88 B.C. by levying five years' taxes in advance and quartering his troops at their expense during the year 

85-84 B.C.

After spending the following winter in Greece, Sulla returned to Italy in the spring of 83 B.C. Aristocrats flocked to his standard; indeed, many moderates, outraged at the excesses of the Marian faction, gave him their allegiance. With his preparations completed, Sulla marched on Rome, held by Carbo and Marius the Younger, son of the old soldier who had died in 86 B.C. After the battle of the 

Colline Gate, Sulla's forces captured the capital city, and the radical leaders were hunted down and slain.

Retaliation for the Marian reign of terror was to be expected; the proscriptions of political opponents inaugurated by Sulla made the year 82 B.C. one of the most harrowing in Roman history. Each day lists of the proscribed were posted in the forum, and anyone named

on the list was an outlaw who could be slain with impunity, with a portion of his property promised to his slayer. Jealousy, spite, and cupidity had full opportunity; it is estimated that 4700 perished, including 40 senators and 1600 members of the equestrian order. After ending the proscriptions Sulla took steps to ensure the permanent dominance of the conservatives. A political maneuver resulted in the naming of an interrex by the Senate who in turn named Sulla dictator.

One of the dictator's enactments was designed to divest the office of tribune of political importance. It provided that anyone who held this office would subsequently be debarred from the higher magistracies, thus making it inevitable that the tribunes henceforth would be men of little capacity or ambition. Another law fixed the sequence in which offices were to be held and prescribed minimum ages for incumbency. The measure also stipulated that a ten-year interval should elapse before an ex-consul would again be eligible for the consulship. This, of course, was designed to prevent the rise of political figures such as Marius who, it will be recalled, held the highest magistracy for five successive terms. 

Only one of the Sullan measures allegedly devoted to the cause of reform proved of lasting significance and application; that was the creation of the quaestiones or permanent courts for the trial of criminal offenses. Hitherto, the definition of crime had been very narrow. Most offenses, now considered crimes, were regarded as torts, or injuries against the individual, who was therefore responsible for the initiation of prosecution. Only treason and certain horrible crimes, such as sodomy, incest, matricide, parricide, and uxorcide, which it was believed were invested with public interest in that they occasioned the anger and vengeance of the gods, were considered offenses against the state. A much wider classification of offenses now came under the direct cognizance of the state in tribunals presided over by praetors in which the evidence was weighed by juries. 

THE RISE OF POMPEY 

When Sulla retired, he believed that his legislation had led the Republic from the dangerous paths of radicalism. An aristocratic Senate was in control, the tribunate was devoid of power, and the laws fixing the order of succession for the magistracies promised to prevent the rise of popular leaders to power.

Events soon proved the Sullan reforms ephemeral, for the death of the dictator in 78 B.C. brought another era in the struggle between

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

optimates and populares. Economic grievances had not been allayed by the conservative reaction. The proscriptions had further embittered the enemies of the Senate; families who had suffered during the reactionary period served as focal points of disaffection. Lepidus, one of the consuls for 78, was elected by the support of the populares, and his sympathies as well as his political obligations impelled him to propose that all the constitutional innovations of Sulla be abrogated. 

Catulus, his aristocratic colleague, vetoed the measure, however, and was sustained by the Centuriate Assembly to which the issue was referred. Upon expiration of his consular term, Lepidus was sent to 

Cisalpine Gaul as proconsul. After assuming command in the province, he led his troops on Rome with the intention of forcing the adoption of his legislative program of the preceding year. Catulus suppressed the rising and forced Lepidus to flee to Sardinia, but a remnant of his army made its way to Spain and entered the service of Sertorius, a partisan of Marius who had refused to relinquish control of Spain at the demand of Sulla. The Lex Aemilia was passed in 

75 B.C. officially removing the disqualification of the tribunes for the higher offices, a concession doubtless hastened by the rebellion. 

Catulus was aided in the suppression of the Lepidan insurrection by Pompey, who was destined to be inseparably associated with the decline of the Roman Republic and the establishment of autocracy. 

Born in 106 B.C., his family was among the most aristocratic of the state. His first military experience was gained as a lieutenant of his father during the Social War. He also had served as a subordinate of Sulla in the eastern campaign, and fidelity to his chief ensured him high place and financial gain during the Sullan dictatorship. His first major assignment was a campaign against Sertorius. The career of 

Sertorius was a remarkable one, the romance of which was described by Plutarch. He had first gained renown as a lieutenant of Marius in the war against the Cimbri and Teutones, and also had served as praetor and propraetor in Spain. With the fall of the Marian party, he had refused to surrender his authority, and the Roman government realized that decisive action was requisite not only to recover Spain but to prevent possible spread of the rebellion. Pompey therefore was sent with an army to coöperate with Metellus, whose campaign had been as unsuccessful as that of his predecessor. No appreciable progress was made even by the joint forces under the command of the two best known Roman generals of the day until Perperna, a former adherent of Lepidus, murdered Sertorius, after whose death Roman control in the Spanish peninsula soon was re-

asserted. Pompey was credited with a great victory but his military reputation was not thus far justified by his exploits. 

While the Spanish campaign was drawing to a close, Italy was harried by a slave insurrection, precipitated by the revolt of the gladiators. In 73 B.C. a group of these gladiatorial slaves at Capua escaped, led by Spartacus, a former Thracian brigand. Within a year, about 

70,000 slaves had allied with the gladiators and a slave army entrenched itself at Mount Vesuvius, where two consular armies failed to dislodge them. Command of the campaign ultimately was entrusted to Crassus who, like Pompey, was destined to play a major part in the downfall of the Republic. A zealous partisan of Sulla, he laid the foundation of his enormous fortune by seizing or cheaply purchasing property confiscated from Marian sympathizers. His wealth made him a factor in politics and he was ambitious for military distinction. 

His legions soon crushed the army of Spartacus, and Pompey, returning from Spain, annihilated the band of demoralized survivors. 

The ambitions of Pompey and Crassus made them natural rivals, but, for the time being, they decided to coöperate and both were elected to the consulship for the year 70 B.C. on a platform of opposition to the Sullan constitution. The plebiscites of the tributa again were divorced from senatorial supervision, and the tribunes recovered all their former power. Juries for provincial cases henceforth were to contain members from the populares as well as from the optimates. Censorial scrutiny of the senatorial list was revived and utilized to expel senators added by Sulla's arbitrary increase of the membership.

Renewed hostilities with Mithridates were precipitated when Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, who died in 75 B.C., willed his treasure to 

Rome, hoping thus to ensure Roman intervention if his kingdom. were attacked by the ruler of Pontus. Mithridates, in the meantime, had violated the treaty concluded with Fimbria and Sulla by alliances with neighboring powers, particularly with Armenia. He was in collusion with Cretan and Cilician pirates, and his encouragement of Sertorius in Spain had given additional affront to Rome. His invasion of Bithynian territory, therefore, was followed by prompt declaration of war, and in 74 B.C., both consuls, Cotta and Lucullus, took the field, but with no material result. 

Lucullus continued in command as proconsul of Asia and after a decisive defeat of the Pontic troops forced Mithridates to take refuge in Armenia, but he failed to follow up his victory. Greed and rejuctance to surrender his command probably induced him to prolong

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the operations, and indignation at his conduct mounted in Rome. 

His policy in the treatment of Asia was constructive, however, for debts to Roman publicans and usurers were scaled down and interest charges reduced. The Roman capitalists naturally were disgruntled at this curtailment of their levies on the wealth of Asia, and their demands for the replacement of Lucullus by Pompey increased. 

Pompey's reputation as a commander was greatly advanced in the meantime by his campaign against the Mediterranean pirates. He was granted absolute authority in the Mediterranean and fifty miles inland from the coast; within forty days, the western Mediterranean was free from piratical operations and within a slightly longer period equal success crowned his efforts in the East. His destruction of the pirate fleet and strongholds was doubtless his greatest achievement.

Lucullus continued to delay in the campaign against Mithridates, and the equites were urging that Pompey be given the eastern command which he had wanted avidly ever since his retirement from the consulship. In 66 B.C. Manilius, another of his henchmen, proposed that Pompey should replace Lucullus. Opposition to the measure was largely disarmed by the approval of Cicero, and Pompey was sent to the East where Lucullus already had so decisively defeated Mithridates as to preclude serious resistance. The remnants of the Pontic army were cut to pieces at the battle of Nicopolis, and 

Mithridates fled to the Crimea, where he committed suicide. Pompey joined Pontus to neighboring Bithynia and created the province of Bithynia-Pontus. Armenia was made a vassal kingdom, after which Syria was conquered and organized as a province. Pompey then pressed on into Palestine, where, after a short siege, he captured Jerusalem and organized Judaea as a Roman vassal kingdom. Shortly after, he organized the province of Cilicia. 

Pompey's return to Rome was celebrated with a triumph of unparalleled splendor. In making his eastern arrangements, however, he had clearly exceeded the authority embodied in his appointment to the command of Lucullus, particularly in his creation of the vassal kingdoms. The Senate, suspicious that he planned to usurp dictatorial powers, refrained from confirming the oriental settlements and refused immediately to allot lands to Pompey's veterans as he had requested. The Senate was in a strategic position. If Pompey's popularity waned, he could be ruined if held to account for his unauthorized eastern policies, while refusal to allocate lands to the veterans in the vicinity of Rome whence they could be called if their commander should attempt a coup d'état gave Pompey the alterna-

tives of disbanding his forces or making an attempt to seize the government that might well prove premature. It seems likely that immediately upon his return to Rome Pompey could have challenged the Senate successfully, but he hesitated, convinced that more powerful political aid was necessary for the attainment of his ambitions. It was this conviction that led him to join with Caesar and 

Crassus in the First Triumvirate in 60 B.C.¹ 

1 C. E. Smith and P. G. Moorhead, A Short History of the Ancient World,

CHAPTER 13 From Triumvirate to Principate 

S we have seen, the First Triumvirate owed its formation primarily to the desire of Pompey to strengthen his position AⓇ and attain his immediate objectives by affiliation with other powerful political figures. Cicero, despite his admiration for Pompey, refused to be drawn into the alliance, considering it a triple dictatorship virtually devoid of constitutional sanction. Crassus joined the group because of his ambition to secure an important military command. Julius Caesar, although his reputation was not as yet comparable with that of his colleagues, desired the consulship for the year 60-59 B.C., the promise of which was his price for joining the 

Triumvirate. Born in 100 B.C., Caesar first attracted attention when his close relations with Marius and Cinna identified him with the radical cause. In the period of the conservative reaction, he was named on a proscription list, but influential friends procured his pardon despite the misgivings of Sulla.

Caesar was elected to the consulship with the assistance of his fellow triumvirs and straightway discharged his political commitments.

Lands were allocated to Pompey's veterans, and his eastern arrangements were confirmed. The equites were reimbursed for certain funds they had advanced to finance the war against Mithridates. 

Bibulus, the conservative colleague of Caesar, vainly attempted to veto these measures, but Caesar, who one day was destined to march on Rome ostensibly to defend the right of magisterial veto, overrode the attempts of Bibulus to restrain him. Perhaps the most salutary measure of Caesar's consulship was designed to curb the abuses of provincial administration. It forbade the acceptance of bribes and gifts by provincial officials and prohibited the imposition of taxation not sanctioned by the government at Rome. Each governor henceforth was required to keep an official record of his administration which was to serve as evidence in the event of prosecution for malfeasance in office.

Upon expiration of his consulship, Caesar, by pre-arrangement with his colleagues in the Triumvirate, applied for appointment to command in Cisalpine Gaul, and the Vatinian Law was passed making him proconsul in this province for a five-year term (March 5954 B.C.). The Senate added Transalpine Gaul to his jurisdiction in view of renewed migratory movements of the Gauls in that region. 

It was also believed that the proconsul might be more strictly held to account if a portion of his powers came by direct senatorial grant. 

The unrest in Gaul had begun when German forces under Ariovistus crossed the Rhine in 70 B.C. A treaty for a time stabilized relations between Rome and the German leader, but in 59 B.C. conditions in Gaul again became troubled with the preparations of the Helvetians to leave their ancestral homes in what is now Switzerland. Caesar promptly curbed the migration of the Helvetians, but in the meantime, the Germanic Suevi were making ready to cross the Rhine to join forces with Ariovistus. Caesar accordingly took the offensive against the Germans and forced them to retire across the Rhine in 

58 B.C., and, in the following year, he defeated the Belgians. In the winter of 55 B.C., other German tribes which crossed the river were virtually annihilated. Caesar then constructed his famous bridge across the Rhine and invaded German territory primarily to demonstrate the effectiveness of the Roman army and thus deter further 

German offensive moves in Gaul. From time to time, a number of the Gallic tribes rebelled, stimulated by aid from the Britons. To prevent such assistance, Caesar led two expeditions against Britain in 55 and 54 B.C., the second of which resulted in the establishment of a military outpost on the island, a harbinger of its eventual conquest and annexation as a province. The Gauls made one last effort to recover their independence when a great coalition of tribes under Vercingetorix threatened to overthrow Roman control, but the capture of the Gallic stronghold of Alesia, after a memorable siege, ended this threat.

Caesar's conquest of Gaul and the Romanization of that area were of incalculable significance in the history of Western civilization. The great expansion of Roman culture was virtually at an end, and without Caesar's campaigns, immortalized in his Commentaries,

Gaul might never have come under Roman rule. The full import of his achievement was realized when the Roman Empire fell before the onslaughts of invading Germans, and the Gallo-Romans, particularly in the towns, gave indispensable aid in the preservation of at least a modicum of the civilization of antiquity. In serving the Roman state

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and the future of Western civilization, Caesar had of course served himself. His primary purpose had been to acquire military renown comparable with that of Pompey, and the increasing jealousy of the latter gave testimony to his success.

In 56 B.C. the Triumvirate was strengthened by the Conference of 

Lucca. Caesar received a five-year prolongation of his proconsular authority and the promise of induction into the consulship immediately upon expiration of his provincial command. Crassus and Pompey, who had for the past few years been considerably embarrassed by the radicalism of his henchmen, Clodius and Milo, arranged to hold the consulships for 55 B.C., after which Crassus would command an expedition against Parthia and Pompey would assume control of operations in Spain. Crassus, after his consular term, set out for the 

East, where he soon demonstrated his incompetence as a general. 

Plagued by the mobile Parthian cavalry, he eventually was entrapped at Carrhae, in 53 B.C., where he perished after the annihilation of his army. Pompey did not fulfil the terms of the Luccan agreement, for, upon termination of his joint consulship with Crassus, he remained in Rome plotting to ruin Caesar whose exploits were dimming the luster of his own military achievements. In 52 B.C. his political chicanery culminated in his unprecedented elevation as sole consul. The 

Senate condoned this maneuver because of growing fear of Caesar and the conviction that Pompey could be thrust aside when he had served the purpose of counter-foil to Caesar.

An open conflict between Caesar and Pompey could not be long deferred. Both were ambitious; each desired unchallenged control of the Roman state that could only be secured at the expense of the other. Pompey, as the nominal ally of the Senate in defense of governmental legitimacy, therefore moved to strike down his rival before his position became impregnable. The vulnerable point in Caesar's status was the fact that his proconsular command would expire in March of 49 B.C., and normally he could not assume the duties of consul, as he expected to do in view of the Luccan agreement, until 

January 1, 48 B.C. This meant that for nine months he would be without an army and legally amenable to prosecution on such charges as the Senate might lodge against him. Then, too, he could not come to 

Rome to conduct his candidacy for the consulship with the result that a law had been passed by the tributa in 52 B.C. validating candidacy for the highest magistracy in absentia.

Pompey's course obviously was to force Caesar out of office as a prelude to the disbanding of his troops and subsequent prosecutiɔn.

As sole consul he therefore sponsored the repeal of the measure of 52 B.C. that authorized candidacy for the consulship in absentia. 

When Caesar asked for assurance that this measure was not designed to frustrate his political plans, Pompey was evasive, and Caesar's suspicions naturally were strengthened. An even more obvious threat to Caesar was the passage of a law which provided that at least five years should elapse before an ex-consul would be eligible to assume a provincial governorship. Hitherto consuls were appointed to provincial commands immediately upon expiration of their terms. The new arrangement offered a number of advantages, particularly since it promised to obviate the scrambles for provincial offices so frequent among incumbent consuls, but for Caesar the law had a sinister meaning. Under the new plan, his successor to proconsular command in Gaul would be ready to take office in March of 49 B.C., whereas under the old practice a successor would not be available until the expiration of the consular term on December 31, 49. Caesar therefore pressed Pompey to modify the law to prolong his proconsular authority until the end of 49, but, despite the mediation of Cicero and others who were trying to avert civil war, Pompey would extend his rival's term only until November which, of course, evaded the issue, since Caesar still would be out of office long enough to bring his downfall. Caesar made several compromise proposals which included an offer to surrender command of Transalpine Gaul if he would be permitted to retain the Cisalpine province and a promise to disband his army if Pompey would do likewise with the military forces at his disposal, but both these proposals were spurned. In January of 49 B.C. the Senate proclaimed Caesar a public enemy, despite the veto of a tribune friendly to him, and called upon Pompey to undertake the defense of the state which theoretically was in jeopardy. 

Caesar now was confronted with clear alternatives of submission and inevitable ruin, or resort to force. He decided to cross the Rubicon and invade Italy, ostensibly to defend constitutional government by upholding the veto of the tribune, which had been flouted. 

Caesar had a loyal, disciplined army at his command, and his rapid movements enabled him to enroll more troops during his southward march. Pompey realized his inability to defend Italy and hastened to 

Greece. Caesar seized Rome without opposition, confiscated the public treasury, and sent lieutenants to secure the submission of Sardinia and Corsica. Caesar forced his appointment as dictator and then proceeded to Spain; Massilia opposed his march, but he left the conduct of the siege to subordinates and pressed on into Spain and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

gained the decisive victory of Ilerda. The Spanish adherents of 

Pompey submitted, and, on the way back to Rome, Caesar forced 

Massilia to capitulate.

Upon his arrival in Rome, Caesar was elected consul for 48 B.C. and abdicated his dictatorship. He then proceeded to Epirus, but could take no effective action until the arrival of reënforcements under the command of Marc Antony. When Caesar's forces retired to Thessaly, Pompey followed, only to be beaten at Pharsalus (48 B.C.). He fled to Egypt, where he was put to death by order of the pharaoh.

Caesar followed to Egypt and intervened in the civil war that was raging in Alexandria. Ptolemy, who had exiled his sister-wife, was forced to recall her, but a rebellion of the Alexandrians placed Caesar in a precarious position from which he extricated himself with the aid of reënforcements from Pergamum. Ptolemy was slain, and Caesar secured recognition of Cleopatra as sole ruler of the Egyptian kingdom. Infatuated with the charms of the Egyptian beauty, he tarried in Alexandria for the winter of 47 B.C. 

Danger in a new quarter abruptly terminated this romantic interlude when Pharnaces, son of Mithridates, attempting to profit by the Roman civil war, renewed the aggressive policies of Pontus. Caesar hastened into Pontus by way of Syria, won the battle of Zela, and restored Roman control. Returning to Rome, 'where he had been proclaimed dictator for 47 B.C., he suppressed disorders resulting from opposition to the financial burdens of the war and the intrigues of the republicans. In the meantime, the Pompeians and republicans had gathered a formidable force in north Africa, which defeated Caesar's lieutenant, Curio, with the aid of King Juba of Mauretania. 

Caesar prepared to leave for the troubled region, but had first to deal with a dangerous mutiny of his troops. After this was done, the army moved to north Africa and crushed the republican forces at the battle of Thapsus.

THE DICTATORSHIP OF CAESAR 

From July of 46 B.C. to his death in March, 44, Caesar, in possession of unparalleled concentration of constitutional and quasi-constitutional powers, was virtual monarch of the Roman state. In 46 

B.C. he had been named dictator for a ten-year term and he had held the consulship since 48 B.C. either alone or with colleagues who were mere figureheads. As tribune, he possessed the veto and other intercessory powers associated with that office, as well as the presidency

of the comitia tributa. As imperator, the title normally granted to a commander entitled to a triumph prior to his relinquishment of command, he remained in continuous command of a standing army. He held the office of pontifex maximus, and his religious authority was further implemented by censorial powers exercised as Prefect of the Public Morals. He was empowered to conduct foreign policy on his own responsibility and possessed the nominal right to appoint half the state officials whereas in reality he directly or indirectly named all of them. He enjoyed the right to express his opinion first in the deliberations of the Senate, and in 45 B.C. he was invested with sole command of armed forces and made absolute custodian of the public treasury. As the "father of his country," all sorts of honorary and religious dignities enhanced the awe with which his person was surrounded. Stripped of all pretense of constitutional sanction, however, the power of Caesar rested alone on the command of his loyal and disciplined troops.

Reforms instituted during his brief tenure of absolute power indicate that he was one of the greatest statesmen of history. One reform of enduring value was the introduction of the Julian calendar. The old lunar calendar had 365 days with intercalary days in the second and fourth month of every fourth year to make up the discrepancy between solar and lunar years. The calendar year began on March 

1, whereas the official year began on January 1. With the aid of 

Sosigines, a Greek astronomer, Caesar introduced a solar calendar with 365 days to begin January 1, 45 B.C. This new calendar remained in use until further corrected during the pontificate of Gregory XIII in the sixteenth century.

Another important reform established uniform government in the municipalities of Italy. Each town was governed, according to the new scheme, by a board of four annually elected magistrates and a council in which ex-magistrates served for advisory and concurrent legislative functions. Each town also had an assembly made up of all citizens to exercise legislative and electoral functions. 

Economic legislation was equally constructive. Grain distribution was confined to those actually in need so that the number of recipients of the dole was diminished by half. Imprisonment for debt was forbidden, and legal interest rates were fixed at a maximum of twelve percent. Partial debt suspensions were introduced, together with provision for installment payments and the application of excessive interest to the liquidation of the principal. Systematic inspections of markets were inaugurated primarily for the protection of urban con-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

sumers. A five percent duty on imports, coupled with strict administrative economy and a regular census, reduced the burden of direct taxation. Reclamation projects were begun in order to stimulate the revival of agricultural prosperity as well as to afford relief for the unemployed. The manumission of slaves was encouraged in view of the economic and social problems caused by a disproportionate number of slaves in respect to the total population. Colonies were established on the sites of ruined Carthage and Corinth to afford additional relief for the indigent and unemployed. 

Political legislation naturally was largely designed to perpetuate the dictator's powers. Membership of the Senate was increased to nine hundred, with freedmen, soldiers, and even Gauls included with the intent to divest the body of what little prestige it still retained. 

The abolition of political clubs was a salutary reform. The number of quaestors was raised from twenty to forty, and of praetors from eight to sixteen. Provinces were declared subject to the Roman state and removed from the control of the Senate.¹ 

The republicans still retained an army of considerable size in Spain under the command of Varus and Labienus. As efforts of Caesar's subordinates to subdue them failed, the dictator was forced to take the field in person in December of 46 B.C. In a decisive battle fought at Munda the following March, the republican forces were well-nigh annihilated and their leaders were slain on the field or subsequently executed.

Caesar's most enthusiastic admirers could not fail to realize that he had no intention of restoring the Republic. The Senate was reduced to sycophancy, the assemblies were impotent, and all magisterial power was held by the dictator or his servile adherents. Monarchy existed in fact if not in theory, and rumors abounded that Caesar was ready to cast aside all dissimulation and demand a crown, with Cleopatra, who recently had come to Rome, as his queen. 

The rapid development of absolutism had created implacable if smouldering opposition. Senators of aristocratic lineage, with family traditions of distinguished service to the state, naturally resented the emasculation of the Senate and the obvious break with republican practices. Former friends and supporters of Pompey longed to avenge their fallen chieftain, and many of the equites were embittered by the curtailment of opportunities to exploit the provinces. 

There also were many who opposed the dictator on principle. Passionately devoted to the republican tradition, their faith in constitu- 

1 Smith and Moorhead, Short History of the Ancient World, 447–48.

tional government was still firm despite the events of recent years. If the dictator could be overthrown, they believed that republican government could be restored and the recurrence of absolutism prevented.

Zealous republicans therefore rallied under the leadership of Cassius and Marcus Brutus in a conspiracy to assassinate the dictator, who was busy with the preparation for an expedition against Parthia to avenge the disaster to the army of Crassus. On March 15, 44 B.C.,

Caesar went to the Senate House to receive the title of "King of the Provinces." The conspirators approached him on the pretext of presenting a petition. When they had him surrounded, they drew daggers from beneath their togas and stabbed him to death in the shadow of the statue of Pompey.

THE TRIUMPH OF OCTAVIAN 

The assassination of Caesar failed to secure the popular acclaim which the conspirators had anticipated. The republican leaders had not properly evaluated Caesar's popularity with the masses or realized that, after all, passionate devotion to republican institutions was confined largely to aristocrats and those who traditionally had profited by the maladministration of the provinces. Marc Antony and 

Lepidus, Caesar's master of horse, quickly and accurately gauged the situation, and the former prepared to act as Caesar's successor. Antony's eulogy of his former chief and prompt distribution of a donative allegedly in accordance with the terms of Caesar's will ensured the obedience of the veteran legions and the homage of the mob. 

Antony then altered the provincial arrangements with the view of weakening the republicans. He laid claim to the Gallic province which had been assigned to Decimus Brutus and prepared to march against Brutus, who refused to accept the changes in the provincial assignments.

Caesar's will had named his grandnephew, Octavius, as the heir to the major portion of his estate, with the proviso that he change his name to Octavianus or Octavian. He had served as a lieutenant of 

Caesar in Spain and was studying at Apollonia in the expectation of joining his great-uncle on the projected Parthian campaign. Favors extended to him as well as the responsibilities that had been entrusted to him indicated that Caesar intended that he hold high political station in addition to inheriting much of the dictator's property. The youth set out for Italy without military escort. Cicero and other republican leaders immediately planned to use his claims to procure

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the overthrow of Antony, and, after he had served this purpose, the "boy," as Cicero termed him, could be ignored. Octavian went to

Rome, where he secured popular favor by games and adroit flattery of the legions and laid claim to his inheritance. 

When Antony reached Cisalpine Gaul, Decimus Brutus refused to acknowledge his authority and stationed his troops in the town of Mutina, which Antony promptly besieged. The Senate, relying on the support of Octavian, thereupon struck a blow for alleged gov ernmental legitimacy by ordering the consuls for 43 B.C. (Hirtius and Pansa) to force Antony to raise the siege of Mutina. Octavian was granted propraetorian authority and sent to assist the consuls. In the ensuing battle, the consuls were slain, but Antony was forced to surrender Mutina and flee to Transalpine Gaul. The Senate then revealed its intentions in regard to Octavian by granting Brutus consular authority and ordering him to pursue Antony, completely ignoring the claims of Octavian to the supreme command. Octavian, however, refused to accept such brusque dismissal. He marched on 

Rome with his loyal soldiery and forced his induction into the consulship. He also organized a special tribunal to punish the murderers of Caesar, and this threat of retaliatory measures cowed the republicans in Rome into virtual inaction.

Antony, learning of the discomfiture of the republicans, joined forces with Lepidus and marched on Rome, which Octavian prepared to defend. When the armies established contact, however, Antony and Octavian met in conference, the result of which was the formation of the Second Triumvirate, composed of Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus. The Senate had no alternative but to confer consular imperium on the members of the alliance, together with the right to appoint to offices and pass legislation without senatorial concurrence. The western provinces were divided among the triumvirs. 

Antony took the Gauls, except the Narbonensis province which, together with the Spanish provinces, was assigned to Lepidus. Octavian took Sardinia and Corsica, while Italy was to be held coöperatively by the triumvirs.

Proscription was promptly utilized against the republican leaders, and Cicero was one of the first victims. Antony moved against a republican army that had been mobilized in Thrace under the command of Cassius and Marcus Brutus. A series of battles at Philippi resulted in an overwhelming defeat for the republican cause and the suicides of its leaders. The triumph at Philippi gave the triumvirs control of the eastern provinces, and it was arranged for Antony to

proceed to the East while Octavian occupied Italy and allocated lands to the troops.

Antony arrived in the East in 41 B.C. He called a conference of eastern rulers at Cilician Tarsus to implement his demand for a tenyear advance payment of tribute. He had summoned Cleopatra to chide her for her failure to coöperate against the republicans in Thrace, but on his dramatic meeting with her completely succumbed to her charms.

Fulvia, the wife of Antony, incessantly intrigued against Octavian in Italy, but the mutual distrust between the triumvirs was partly allayed at the Conference of Brundisium in 40 B.C., where the Ionian 

Sea was adopted as the line of division between the territories under their rule. Lepidus remained in charge of Africa, which had been assigned to him after Philippi, and Italy was still nominally under joint control. The reconciliation of Brundisium was apparently sealed with the marriage of Antony to Octavia, sister of his colleague, and the promise of naval aid for his forthcoming campaign against Parthia.

Antony's Parthian venture, badly mismanaged from the outset, damaged his military prestige and weakened his position in the Second Triumvirate. Relations between him and Octavian were embittered by his attempt to attribute the Parthian fiasco to lack of the promised assistance from the West rather than to his own stubbornness and incompetence. Nevertheless, the Triumvirate had been renewed for an additional five-year term in 37 ы.c. Octavian defeated Sextus Pompey and deposed Lepidus from the Triumvirate for the assistance he had extended to Pompey. 

With Antony coming more and more under the dominance of Cleopatra, his relations with Octavian neared the breaking point when he divorced Octavia and married the Egyptian queen. He then rashly planned to establish a dynasty in the East and began to assign eastern provinces to Cleopatra and the two children he had by her. Octavian promptly utilized this mad conduct to justify an attack on his rival; when he read in the forum a document which he claimed was the will of Antony in which his eastern plans were clearly set forth, he secured virtually unanimous support for a declaration of war.

Octavian gathered an army and fleet for an eastern campaign, and Antony countered by sending a fleet to Greece for an invasion of Italy. Octavian's fleet gained a decisive victory at Actium, at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, and Antony forfeited all chance of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

success in the war by following Cleopatra back to Alexandria according to a pre-arranged plan. When Octavian appeared, the Egyptian capital surrendered and Antony committed suicide. Cleopatra attempted to exercise her wiles on Octavian as she had on Caesar and Antony, but when he brusquely repelled her, she too resorted to suicide to avoid the ignominy of appearing in Octavian's triumphal procession. 

LATIN LITERATURE IN THE CICERONIAN PERIOD 

The period from the first consulship of Pompey (70 B.C.) to the death of the emperor Augustus in A.D. 14 is usually termed the 

Golden Age of Latin literature. It, in turn, is divided into the 

Ciceronian and Augustan periods. While it is true that the writers of the Golden Age were heavily indebted to their study and admiration of Greek masterpieces, they were no mere imitators. They infused so much of their personal genius, so much of the idealism and virility of the Roman state into their works that their age ranks with the most creative periods of all literary history. 

One of the greatest writers of the Ciceronian period was Lucretius (97-55 B.C.) whose famous work, De Rerum Natura, was an attrac tive literary presentation of Epicurean philosophy. Roman educa tion placed little emphasis on the abstractions of philosophy in view of the all-pervading emphasis on practical studies such as rhetoric as prerequisites for political advancement. Even Latin scholars who journeyed to the intellectual shrines of Greece to complete their training regarded philosophic studies as secondary to their more immediate interests. Lucretius therefore was mainly concerned with popularizing, "so that the people who have not delved into it and therefore are suspicious may have their attention concentrated on and learn my philosophy." The first of the six books deals with the fundamental concepts of atoms and void which, for the author, constituted the only realities. Book two is dynamic; it attempts to explain the properties of the atoms and their motion. Book three, considered the finest of the work, deals with the nature of the soul, and, while offering arguments against belief in immortality, presents the conclusion that fear of death is to be banished from the minds of men. 

The next book is chiefly psychological, presenting explanations of the senses and attempting to reduce emotions to physiological terms. 

Book five offers theories to account for the creation of the universe, the origin of man, and his cultural advance. Natural history is comprehended in book six. Despite the difficulty of offering poetic

treatment of abstract and, at times, intricately technical themes, passages of wonderful beauty abound.

An outstanding writer of lyric verse in the Ciceronian period was 

Catullus (c. 87-54 B.C.). Member of a prominent family, he owned extensive estates and occupied minor governmental posts. He was romantically devoted to Clodia, wife of Metellus Afer, and to her, under the name of Lesbia, he ascribes the inspiration for some of the loveliest of his 116 extant poems. With penetrating observation and shrewd evaluation, he surveyed the contemporary scene and left in his works a collection of vivid word portraits of a number of typical figures of Roman society. 

One of the most erudite and prolific of all Latin authors was Varro (116-27 B.C.). A wealthy aristocrat, he held several offices, and, although for a time he opposed the First Triumvirate, he was reconciled and placed in charge of the library founded by Caesar. He wrote about seventy-four works, including books of satires, miscellaneous poems, and pseudo-tragedies. His forty-one books of annals are an important source for the study of Roman history, as are his linguistic studies for students of philology. His work on agriculture ranks with Cato's famous treatise on husbandry as an authoritative picture of Roman agricultural practice. His Hebdomades in fifteen books was probably the earliest illustrated work. It contained portraits of distinguished Greek and Roman characters accompanied with brief commentaries in verse. 

The greatest name in Roman literature, however, is that of Cicero. 

He was born in 106 B.C. at Arpinum of a family prominent in political affairs. He received an exceptionally thorough education which, in addition to rhetoric and oratory, included rigorous training in philosophy and law. Probably because he feared the displeasure of 

Sulla, one of whose friends he had vanquished in litigation, he left Rome for a two-year sojourn in Athens where he studied under the famous rhetorician, Molon of Rhodes, who did much to perfect his forensic skill. Upon return to Rome, he resumed his legal career and completed the course of political offices by election to the consulship in 63 B.C. A major factor in his political and legal career was his successful prosecution of Verres on charges of corruption and cruelty as governor of Sicily. He was largely instrumental in securing passage of the Manilian Law which bestowed the eastern command on Pompey. During his consulship, he delivered his famous orations against Catiline in which he exposed the conspiracy by which Catiline and his followers hoped to seize control of Rome.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

In 58 B.C., he was exiled as a result of specious charges brought against him by the tribune, Clodius, but he was permitted to return about a year later. In the Civil War his sympathies were with Pompey, although he took no active part in the struggle, remaining abroad until Caesar permitted him to return. With the assassination of 

Caesar, he was a recognized leader of the republicans and, as already pointed out, he hoped that Octavian could be used to bring about the downfall of Antony against whom he directed the fourteen bitter invectives commonly known as his Philippics. When Octavian and 

Antony joined forces, however, Cicero found himself in a badly compromised position and he was one of the first to be put to death by the Second Triumvirate in 43 B.C. when they inaugurated their retaliatory proscriptions.

Cicero's literary works included, besides the fifty-seven complete orations, many poems, letters, and political studies, as well as rhetorical and philosophical works. Many of the letters are wellnigh indispensable historical sources. The political works are the 

De Republica, written in the form of a dialogue in which the merits of various forms of government are examined, and the De Legibus, dealing respectively with natural law, laws as applied to religion, and magistracies. The most famous of the rhetorical works is the De 

Oratore, an imaginary discussion of the subject, including sections on the knowledge necessary for effective oratory, the arrangement of the material, and style of delivery. In his religious works, particularly in the De Natura Deorum, Cicero directs his attention to the merits of Epicureanism, Stoicism, and the views of the so-called New Academy. The Tusculan Disputations are considered by many the best of the philosophical works. In an imaginary discussion, presumably held at Cicero's villa at Tusculum, the author discusses the essentials of happiness which he holds to be contempt for death, endurance of pain, control of grief, discipline of the passions, and virtue. In somewhat similar vein are the beautiful essays, On Old Age and On Friendship. On Duty is addressed to his son, who was studying in Athens at the time the work was produced. 

The only other writer of comparable importance in the Ciceronian period was Julius Caesar, whose military and political career already has been discussed. His accounts of the Gallic and Civil Wars are indispensable sources for the student of Roman history, but their literary merit must not be underestimated. The combination of literary power of the first order with military and political genius is unique and invests with exceptional interest everything he wrote.

The famous De Bello Gallico was written primarily to defend the author's administration of the Gallic provinces. In the first book, the Helvetians and Germans are discussed; the second is devoted to the Belgians, while the coast tribes of Normandy and Brittany are the main theme of the third. Book four contains the account of the memorable first expedition against Britain, while the second and successful attack is described in book five. The second crossing of the 

Rhine is described in book six which also contains most of the author's description of the institutions and customs of the primitive Germans. The heroic attempt of Vercingetorix to overthrow the 

Roman yoke is described in book seven. The eighth book, which narrates the story of Caesar's last two years in Gaul, was probably written by Hirtius, an officer in his army. 

Other writers of considerable historical importance were Cor nelius Nepos (100-25 B.C.) and Sallust (86-35 B.C.). The sole work of Nepos that has survived is his Lives of Illustrious Men, only twenty-four biographical sketches of which are extant. The complete work apparently contained biographies of both Roman and foreign statesmen and generals. The surviving works of Sallust are his accounts of the conspiracy of Catiline and the Jugurthine War. 

Both works betray the Thucydidean influence with their emphasis on dramatic effect attained by imaginary speeches and conversations of historical personages. His history of the war with Jugurtha, virtually the only source of detailed information about the period, was buttressed by research conducted while the author was proconsul of Africa. In addition to these well-known works, Sallust also wrote a history of the events of the decade following the death of Sulla, but only fragments of this work have been preserved.

CHAPTER 14 The Roman Empire under the Julio- 

Claudians

THE PRINCIPATE OF AUGUSTUS 

HERE could be no challenge to Octavian's control of the Roman world after Antony's debacle at Actium. Whatever support might have been enlisted in Antony's cause had been forfeited by his relations with Cleopatra. The Roman world was weary of strife, eager to accept leadership that promised moderation and, above all, peace. Octavian was so sure of his position that he tarried in the East, inspecting the provinces and organizing Egypt, which was henceforth held as the private estate of the emperors. 

Upon his return from the East, Octavian celebrated a triple triumph; his war against Antony was not considered a civil war since theoretically hostilities had been directed solely against Egypt. Octavian's early policies met with immediate favor. A law was passed at his insistence forbidding marriages between Roman citizens and freedmen or non-Italians. This was interpreted as a guarantee that the traditional position of Italy in the Roman world was to be retained. Nearly two hundred senators who owed their position to appointment by Caesar in his attempt to degrade the body were expelled, which action was regarded as proof of Octavian's intention to restore the Senate to its former dignity and prestige. The grateful senators thereupon invested their benefactor with the title of "Prince of the Senate," a position that gave him the presidency of the body as well as the right to speak first in debate and to cast the first vote. 

In reality, of course, Octavian's power rested on his command of a disciplined, loyal army. Some constitutional basis could be found for his position, however. As the heir of Caesar it could be held that he had inherited the powers bestowed on his great-uncle by the Senate. 

Also, he was the sole survivor of the Second Triumvirate and as such could be considered to be in possession of all the powers originally

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

187 extorted from the Senate by that coalition. He had not relinquished the consulship, and he had been saluted as imperator by his soldiers. 

Octavian was far shrewder than Caesar in his estimation of the temper of the times. He realized that the republican tradition was still a factor to be reckoned with and accordingly aimed to keep alive the fiction that the Republic was still in existence and that the powers which he held were constitutional and reconcilable with republican government. This probably explains the curious abdication of January, 27 B.C. Octavian appeared before the Senate and resigned all the powers which he held excepting those normally associated with the consulship. The Senate, on the other hand, invested him with proconsular powers for life, and thus gave constitutional sanction for the continuance of his military command, so that he had made no real sacrifice of authority. Furthermore, the Senate saluted him as Augustus, or the "revered one." To be sure, the magistracies continued to be filled through the usual methods of election, but the princeps submitted lists of approved candidates and thus virtually assured the choice of men who could be counted on to be devoted to him.

Shortly after this incident, Augustus, as we now call him, went to Spain, ostensibly to take command of the army that was checking the depredations of the Cantabrians and other barbarous tribes. In all likelihood, however, the absence of the ruler from Rome was in reality a test of senatorial reactions. Would the Senate take the opportunity presented by his absence from Rome, unexpectedly prolonged by a serious illness, to reassert its governing powers? Agrippa, the faithful general and minister of the prince, remained in Rome to keep a close watch on the situation, but as Augustus had surmised the Senate evinced no desire to challenge his authority. 

Upon return from Spain, the princeps went through a second ceremony of abdication, and the Senate on this occasion granted him tribunician powers for life. As proconsul he commanded the armies and as tribune he possessed an absolute veto power that could frustrate the action of magistrates, Senate, or assemblies should any of these dare to oppose him. It seems hardly likely therefore that 

Augustus had any intention to establish what Mommsen called a dyarchy," or joint rule of Senate and princeps. The partition of authority was more apparent than real, and the abdications were gestures to legitimacy actually devoid of practical significance. The provinces, to be sure, were divided into the classifications of imperial and senatorial, with the former under the direct rule of the 66

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

princeps and the latter governed by propraetors and proconsuls named by the Senate as in the period of the Republic. Nevertheless, the emperor kept a close control on the choice of governors for the senatorial provinces so that here too division of authority was little more than theoretical. Legates and procurators administered the imperial provinces and were directly responsible to the emperor. Tax farming was abolished along with many other abuses that had characterized provincial government under the Republic. The fact that the imperial provinces were better governed than the senatorial ones made inevitable eventual transfer of the latter to imperial administration. Gaul was divided into four provinces: Gallia Narbonensis, Gallia Lugdunensis, Aquitania, and Belgica.

Augustus laid the foundations for the development of the bureaucracy that was destined to be a chief source of strength throughout the history of the Empire. Most of the civil servants were chosen from the equestrian order, and owed their positions not to aristocratic background but to ability, training, and experience. A new scheme for the selection of senators was inaugurated to raise the personnel to a higher level of character and competence. An original panel of thirty was appointed, each of whom thereupon named five candidates for senatorial membership. From the 150 candidates thus secured, thirty were selected by lot. The thirty successful candidates, in turn, each named five candidates and another selection of thirty was made from a panel of 150. This process was repeated until the number of senators reached 600. The priestly colleges were restored, and Augustus assumed the position of supreme pontiff. 

The public treasury (aerarium) was originally distinct from the emperor's private resources (fiscus). Frequent disbursements from the fiscus were made for public purposes, however, and the greater resources of the emperor's treasury made inevitable its eventual absorption of the aerarium. Taxes in kind were collected from the entire Empire according to assessments made every fifteen years; in addition a sales tax of one percent was levied, as was also a five percent inheritance tax.

Foreign policy in the period 23-17 B.C. was largely concerned with 

Parthia. The disaster to the army of Crassus was unavenged. Marc 

Antony's Parthian campaign had been a failure, and Caesar's preparations for an eastern campaign had been terminated by his assassination. It was imperative, therefore, that steps be taken to restore 

Rome's waning prestige in the East. Augustus, by adroit diplomacy, secured virtually all the objectives that might have been attained by

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

189 military effort. Phraates, the Parthian ruler, agreed to surrender the standards captured from Crassus on condition that Rome grant his request for the extradition of a rebel leader who had taken refuge in the Empire. Augustus granted this concession and accordingly was able to march into Rome in 19 B.C. triumphantly bearing the standards that had been lost by Crassus at Carrhae.

The eastern frontier was strengthened by a chain of “buffer states " under vassal kings. Artaxes was deposed in Armenia and succeeded by the pro-Roman, Tigranes, who agreed to recognize Roman overlordship. Cappadocia was placed under the rule of 

Ariobarzanes; the Galatian throne was occupied by Amyntas, while 

Herod was installed as vassal king of Judaea. Before Parthia could attack the provinces of Asia or Bithynia-Pontus, it first would have to subjugate the kingdoms friendly to Rome.

The outstanding event of the period 17 B.C. to A.D. 14 was the campaign along the northern frontier. The fundamental objective of the northern policy of Augustus was to push the frontier from the Rhine to the Elbe. The bend of the Rhine-Danube line would be removed and the northern frontier would be a straight line from the Black to the North Sea. He had laid the groundwork for this policy in 35-34 

B.C. with the acquisition of a part of Dalmatia, and Crassus, while governor of Macedonia, had annexed Thrace.

The campaign began when the legions under the command of the emperor's stepsons, Tiberius and Drusus, crossed the Alps. Rhaetia and Noricum were conquered and organized as provinces. The victorious army then moved down the Rhine and acquired territory that was subsequently organized as the provinces of Upper and Lower Germany. In 12 B.C. Drusus crossed the Rhine, but his death three years later caused a temporary cessation of the campaign. Tiberius was recalled and he eventually went into voluntary retirement on the island of Rhodes, largely because the birth of two sons to Agrippa and Julia, the emperor's daughter, seemed to preclude his succession to the throne, and he wished to avoid the embarrassment that his presence in Rome might occasion. Domitius was placed in charge of the Rhine legions and ultimately succeeded in reaching the Elbe. 

The estrangement of Tiberius and the emperor terminated by A.D. 

6. The grandsons of Augustus had died, necessitating reversion to the original plan whereby Tiberius was to succeed to the throne. Tiberius then was sent north of the Alps to quell the revolt of Pannonia. 

His success in this region was destined to have unexpected signififor in A.D. 9 the legions under Varus were ambushed and an-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

nihilated by the Germans led by Arminius at Teutberga Wood. 

Had this German victory followed success of the revolting Pannonian tribes a coalition might well have been formed that would have constituted a major threat to Italy. Augustus, unnerved by the disaster to Varus, abandoned the territory between the Rhine and the Elbe and renounced all further offensive plans against the Germans. His policy became a tradition which succeeding emperors carefully observed.
