It is no exaggeration to say that had Augustus succeeded in pushing the frontier to the Elbe, the course of European history would have been profoundly altered, for the Germans in all probability would have been Romanized as were the peoples of Gaul. 

INTERNAL CONDITIONS IN THE AUGUSTAN AGE 

The revival of Italian agriculture which began shortly before the rise of Octavian to power was short-lived. The dispossession of 

Italian farmers by the land allotments of the triumvirs accelerated the movement toward plantation economy. Many of the evicted Italian farmers migrated to north Africa where they increased the productivity of the soil by irrigation and other improvements. Before the end of the reign of Augustus, grain importations from north Africa were exerting the same effect in Italy as had formerly those from Sicily. Only the plantation, specializing on the cultivation of olives and grapes, could survive provincial competition. 

Commerce expanded materially in the Augustan era. Rome, Puteoli, Capua, and Marseilles were thriving commercial centers in the West, while Alexandria, Antioch, Ephesus, Byblos, and Beirut were outstanding in the East. A considerable share of the commerce now was conducted by Romans, although most of the ships were built and operated by Greeks. The vessels were from 200 to 300 tons burden, and usually tramped from port to port. There were some packet ships, however, plying to and fro between important commercial centers and some of these even specialized in passenger traffic. Puteoli remained the leading port in Italy largely because of the industries of the city which afforded shipmasters abundant opportunity to pick up cargoes. Wealthy merchants owned or leased ships, while those of more modest means were content to rent space. 

Italy could not balance her imports. Her exports were relatively few; pottery, iron and bronze ware, timber, grain, and wine were the most important. Imports, although diversified, were for the most

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

191 part articles of luxury. Asia and Bithynia-Pontus sent grain, salt, fish, timber, dried fruits, tapestries, rugs, hangings, precious stones, and fine wines. Syria furnished glass and linen, while the cedars of Lebanon were prized as they had been for centuries. The state factories in Egypt, operated for the private profit of the emperor, exported cloth, glass, paper, ivory, and wild beasts for the arena. Syria was connected with Parthian caravan routes to the Far East; and Chinese silks as well as cotton, pearls, and spices from India were distributed to all parts of the Empire. Italy's adverse balance of trade was partially liquidated by tribute and provincial investments, but the drain of specie was constant despite efforts of the government to arrest it. 

Cargoes at the ports were sold directly to wholesale dealers. These, in turn, retailed their wares in markets and shops since there was no highly developed system of distribution. The excellent Roman roads greatly facilitated internal trade. A number of arterial highways radiated from Rome and connected the leading cities. They were hard surfaced, straight, and elevated above the surrounding countryside. Travel was easier than at any other time prior to the advent of the modern railroad.

Roman industry, for the most part, failed to develop mass production and the attendant factory system. Craftsmen, assisted by a few apprentices or slaves, made their wares by simple manual processes and sold directly to the consumer. The basic reasons for the lack of industrial centralization can be found in slavery and the impetus it gave to household industry. Practically everything used by the wealthy, save imported articles of luxury, was made by their slaves. The elemental wants of the laboring class were filled by their own handicraft, and their purchasing power was too low to afford any appreciable market for specialized industry.

There were a few industries, however, conducted as large-scale enterprises. The red glazed pottery of Arretrium and Puteoli was distributed throughout the whole Roman world. The industry was concentrated because of limited accessibility to deposits of the requisite clays. Glass was also made in sizable factories, for the new technique of blowing, demanding a high degree of skill, produced finely textured articles so cheaply as to minimize household competition. The copper and bronze ware of Capua was known throughout the Empire. Specimens have been found in Britain produced by the same establishments that made articles found in Pompeii. The silverware of Naples was likewise made in establishments employing a

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

considerable number of highly skilled artisans. Ironmongering was done on a small scale, however, due to the crude technique of smelting.¹

Laborers were for the most part slaves of freedmen. Free laborers found little opportunity save at wages depressed by competition with slaves to about fifteen cents a day. Artisans were organized in colleges somewhat similar to the craft gilds of the Middle Ages. The main purposes of these organizations were social. Funerary expenses of members were paid from funds obtained by common subscription. 

Augustus made the encouragement of literary and artistic activities a cardinal policy. Maecenas, his trusted minister, was placed in charge of the distribution of the emperor's patronage. Financial assistance was granted to worthy writers who could not gain a livelihood directly from their work, since there were no copyright laws and no facilities for large-scale distribution of their productions. 

The best-known writer of the Golden Age of Roman literature was Vergil. He was born in 70 B.C. near Mantua. He was reared on a farm, but his family lost their land because of their sympathies with the republican cause. After completing his elementary education in 

Latin and Greek literature, the ambitious youth studied at Cremona and Naples. His first work to attract attention was the Eclogues, in which he bewailed the plight of Italian agriculture in the manner of Hesiod. Encouraged by the patronage of the emperor, he produced his Georgics, which portrayed the joys and beauties of pastoral life somewhat in the style of Theocritus. His monumental Aeneid, influenced by the Iliad, was received as Rome's national epic. Legendary accounts of the foundation of the state were woven together with consummate artistry. Great historical personages and events were delineated in a fashion to inculcate patriotism and' pride of ancestry.

Horace too had suffered by the confiscations of the triumvirs. His satires were embittered by his experiences, but after he received a farm from Maecenas as a subsidy for his literary work, the tone of his productions mellowed. His Odes brought the art of poetic form and sheer beauty of expression to a standard never excelled. 

Another outstanding figure of the age was Ovid. His Amores and

Ars Amatoria were avidly read by cultured contemporaries. His 

Metamorphoses was an epitome of mythological lore. When Julia, the daughter of the emperor, became involved in scandal, Ovid was banished to Tomi presumably on the charge that the moral laxity 

1 Smith and Moorhead, Short History of the Ancient World, 484-86.

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

193 of his poems was responsible for the lascivious conduct of many highborn personages.

The stirring events that marked the transition from republic to empire naturally stimulated an interest in history. Of Livy's monumental work, History of Rome, only thirty-five out of a total of one hundred forty-two books have survived. The history was of such magnitude as to necessitate reliance to a large degree on the works of secondary writers, but these works were utilized with a high degree of critical insight. The books were written for the general reader; hence, disproportionate attention was sometimes devoted to the dramatic and picturesque to the comparative neglect of economic and constitutional developments. Like Thucydides, Livy often put speeches in the mouths of historical characters in order to augment interest. The work is indispensable despite its technical imperfections and occasional biased distortion. The discovery of the lost books would necessitate major revision of Roman history from the period of the Third Punic War to the end of the Republic. Another important historical work of the period was Sallust's Jugurthine War. 

His history of the Sullan period unfortunately has been lost. The loss of Pollio's history of the Civil Wars has deprived us of another source of inestimable value.

Augustus boasted in the Monumentum Ancyranum that he transformed Rome from a city of brick to one of marble. The structures built during the reign indeed invested the city with splendor befitting the mistress of the world. The massive Temple of Apollo was constructed to house the largest library in the West. The Temple of the 

Divine Julius and the Temple of Mars Ultor, the latter in the Forum of Augustus, were worthy of comparison with the wonderful structure on the Athenian Acropolis. The Theatre of Marcellus and the 

Baths of Agrippa combined utility with architectural beauty of a high order. The domed roof of the Pantheon was an important contribution to architectural technique. Over eighty older temples were refurbished as part of the program for beautification. 

The chief religious development of the period was the influx of oriental cults. The exotic rituals afforded an emotional stimulus foreign to the formal and somewhat perfunctory ceremonies of the state religion. Slaves and soldiers returning from the East initiated. eager converts into the mysteries of Mithras, Isis, and the Great Mother. All the new religions emphasized immortality and ceremonial rites of purification as prerequisites for the survival of the soul. The prominent part played by symbolical representations of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the phenomena of germination led to orgiastic practices. Augustus vainly attempted to prevent the diffusion of these cults, but was forced to be content to prohibit their ceremonies within the walls of the capital city.

For a time, Augustus resisted attempts of the Senate to deify him. but he acquiesced in the plan to deify his memory after death. He doubtless believed that the foundation of the imperial cult would serve to promote unity and would be a symbol of patriotism much as flags are today.

Moral decadence accompanied the advent of religious skepticism among the upper classes. Slaves were utilized for all household tasks; indolence became characteristic of aristocratic life; gluttony, drunkenness, and licentiousness pervaded "high society." Only the most thrilling and bizarre spectacles could amuse the dissolute voluptuaries. The great popularity of the gladiatorial combats and the wild beast fights was symptomatic of the moral degeneracy that permeated all classes. The marital and sumptuary legislation of the emperor was a feeble and impotent attempt to arrest these developments. 

THE SUCCESSORS OF AUGUSTUS 

Augustus, as we have seen, attempted to impart a semblance of constitutional legitimacy to his reign by exercising proconsular and tribunician powers bestowed upon him by the Senate. If a dyarchy actually had existed, the Senate would have retained complete freedom to designate the successor to the princeps, but Augustus obviously regarded himself as the founder of a dynasty. After his grandsons, Gaius and Lucius, died, he reverted to his original succession plan and designated his stepson, Tiberius, as his heir. The 

Senate invested Tiberius with the powers essential to the continuity of the imperial dynasty. But Augustus required Tiberius to pass over the claims of his own son to designate his nephew, Germanicus, as his prospective successor. The authority of Augustus was so stable, peace and security were so well established, that no opposition was offered to the accession of Tiberius in A.D. 14. 

Few men were as well qualified by experience as Tiberius to rule the Empire. He had proved his exceptional competence as a military commander in the campaigns he and his brother Drusus had waged against the Germans, and his brilliant victories in Pannonia had been of inestimable importance to the safety of Italy. He had exhibited the highest diplomatic ability in the intricate negotiations with Parthia, and he was a conscientious and methodical administrator, de-

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

195 voted to the best interests of the Empire. He lacked, however, the requisites for popularity. Austere and suspicious, he made no attempt to court the approval of the populace, and the fact that many considered him merely a regent for Germanicus created an active party of opposition recruited largely from the remnants of the old aristocracy.

Opposition to the new emperor based on disapproval of his policies soon arose. His abolition of the electoral functions of the comitia tributa occasioned bitter condemnation, despite the fact that elections in the assembly had become mere travesties. The approved candidates for office chosen by Caesar and Augustus frequently had bid for the favor of the assembly by games or donatives, and it is therefore not hard to understand why the transfer of the elections to the Senate caused the common folk of the capital city to become disgruntled. The Senate was dissatisfied because the emperor transferred the administration of the provinces of Achaea and Macedonia from senatorial to direct imperial supervision. To be sure, the abuses of senatorial administration in these provinces demanded reform, but the senators foresaw in the action of Tiberius the abolition of their share in provincial administration. 

At the very beginning of the reign, formidable mutinies of the legions in Pannonia and along the Rhine threatened to overthrow the emperor's authority. No policy of Tiberius was responsible for these outbreaks, for the long enlistments, low pay, heavy work, and harsh discipline which were the alleged causes were grievances of long standing. Drusus, son of the emperor, easily quelled the Pannonian mutiny, after the superstitious fears of the soldiers were aroused by an eclipse of the moon. The revolt along the Rhine was a much more serious matter. While the disorder was at its height, the rebellious soldiers offered the imperial throne to their commander, Germanicus, if he would lead them in a march on Rome. Germanicus, however, remained loyal to his uncle and eventually managed to restore discipline.

After suppressing the mutiny, Germanicus led his legions into German territory. Several successive campaigns were indecisive. 

Although some of the standards lost by Varus in the disaster of A.D. 9 were recovered, on a number of occasions the Roman forces narrowly escaped disaster, and many more campaigns would have been necessary to conquer the territory between the Rhine and the Elbe. 

Tiberius therefore decided to adhere to the defensive policy of Augustus and recalled Germanicus from his command. There is no

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

reason to believe that jealousy led the emperor to this decision, and events subsequently proved that he was right in believing that the Germans could be weakened merely by giving free play to their internal dissensions.

Upon his return to Rome in 17, Germanicus was honored by a triumph. He then was sent to the East with full powers to stabilize conditions in Armenia, where it was essential to install a pro-Roman king to maintain the chain of buffer states established by Augustus. 

The young commander was in the main successful, for he secured recognition of Zeno as Armenian ruler without precipitating a war with Parthia. Relations were bitter, however, between Germanicus and Piso, governor of Syria. There is reason to believe that the emperor had sent Piso to the East to exercise a restraining influence on his rather impulsive superior, but if such were his instructions he exceeded them by flouting the authority of Germanicus at every opportunity. Therefore when the young prince died after a protracted illness, reports were circulated that he had been poisoned at Piso's instigation. The governor, in the meantime, had left his province without the emperor's permission, thus legally forfeiting his authority, but when he learned of the death of Germanicus, he vainly attempted to regain possession of the province by military action against the de facto government set up by the friends of Germanicus. 

When Piso returned to Rome, he was charged with a number of crimes. He was acquitted of the poisoning charge, but condemnation for his invasion of Syria was a foregone conclusion, and he committed suicide. The trial did not allay the rumors; it was even suggested, although without evidence, that Tiberius himself had connived at the murder of his nephew to clear the way for the succession of his son, Drusus, to the throne. The opposition in Rome rallied around 

Agrippina, the widow of Germanicus, and her sons. Tiberius, convinced that they were plotting to overthrow him, ordered their arrest. Agrippina and two of her sons died or were killed in prison; 

Gaius, a third son, was reared by the emperor whom he succeeded in 37.

The overthrow of Agrippina was in large measure a triumph for 

Sejanus, the emperor's favorite. A member of the equestrian order, he had risen to prominence as commander of the Praetorian Guard, which he persuaded the emperor to station in a permanent camp just outside the walls of the capital. He gradually won the complete confidence of the lonely and embittered princeps who finally retired to the island of Capri, leaving the favorite in Rome. The em-

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

197 peror remained in touch with affairs in the capital, however, and became convinced that Sejanus was a cunning schemer. When the favorite appeared before the Senate expecting to receive tribunician power, a letter of the emperor was read denouncing him, and the Senators who recently had fawned upon him ordered his arrest and execution.

The last years of Tiberius were marked by the punishment of a number of persons charged with lèse majesté. There is no evidence, however, of a breakdown in the character of the emperor, nor was there anything approaching a "reign of terror." In most instances the fate of the accused seems to have been in accord with justice. The accusations of delators, or professional spies and accusers, to be sure, frequently initiated trials, but these practices were by no means innovations of the reign of Tiberius. While some delators were rewarded by a share of the confiscated property of convicted defendants, in a number of instances severe punishments were meted out to those who had lodged false accusations.

Gaius, the son of Germanicus, succeeded Tiberius on the throne of the Caesars (37-41). As a child, he had been a favorite of the soldiers who affectionately named him Caligula, or "the man in the little boots," because of the military costume he habitually wore. He made a favorable impression immediately upon his accession. He promised to rule jointly with the Senate and agreed to dismiss the delators. He gained popularity with the masses by squandering large sums as donatives. Within six months, however, it became apparent that the emperor was hopelessly insane, and the remainder of the reign was a continuous debauch. The mad emperor posed as a gladiator and regaled the populace with his personifications of mythological figures. Funds carefully accumulated by the parsimony of Tiberius were frittered away in revels and bizarre banquets. A burlesque expedition to Britain and a number of madcap public works gave further play to folly. The reign closed when the emperor fell beneath the daggers of the Praetorian Guard. The provinces were little affected by the tragic reign. The bureaucracy continued to function even with a madman on the throne - testimony to the inherent excellence of the administrative system instituted by Augustus.

With the assassination of Caligula, the Praetorian Guard were in complete control of the capital. Claudius, uncle of the murdered emperor, was pulled from his hiding-place, quaking with fear, and, as the only available member of the imperial family, forced to as-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

sume the purple to impart a measure of legitimacy to the palace revolution. Immersed in his antiquarian studies, the new emperor had seemed a harmless, ludicrous figure, who incited the ridicule rather than the anger of Caligula. Although he had apparent weaknesses of character, he was competent and conscientious in the discharge of his duties, and his reign, particularly in administrative development, was constructive.

One of the most significant events of the early history of the Empire was the conquest of Britain and its annexation as a province. 

Julius Caesar twice had invaded the island to facilitate his conquest of Gaul, but no attempt at definitive conquest had since been made, largely because of the defensive tradition inaugurated by Augustus. 

Claudius doubtless wished to strengthen his position by securing military renown. He seems to have been influenced also by the danger of another mutiny of the legions along the Rhine and the hope that action and the prospect of booty would allay the disaffection of the soldiery. Four legions landed at Dover and, after crossing the 

Thames, defeated the British forces under Togodumnus and Caratacus. Claudius arrived in camp shortly after the capture of Camulodunum (Colchester) had ensured the success of the expedition. 

Upon returning to Rome he celebrated the first legitimate triumph the city had seen since that of Germanicus in 17.

The acquisition of Britain was not a great asset to the Empire, although the legions remained in the province until 407. Roman civilization made little progress except in the towns. The recurrent need for defense against the Picts and Scots created a problem that was not solved until the construction of the great wall across north Britain by the Emperor Hadrian (117–138).

Augustus, as we have seen, created a bureaucracy drawn primarily from the equestrian order. Under Claudius the civil service was organized into departments with carefully differentiated functions. 

One department had charge of the issue of commissions, diplomatic and military correspondence, and corporations; a second controlled financial administration; a third was devoted to the consideration of petitions, and a fourth assisted the emperor in the handling of judicial business. Public works carried to completion included two great aqueducts and improvements in the harbor of Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber.

The emperor was notoriously subject to the influence of stronger personalities. For a time he was a pliant tool of his wife, Messalina, but he finally learned of her plots to dethrone him and ordered her

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

199 execution. His freedmen ministers whom he chose to head the newly organized departments of the bureaucracy enjoyed powers due more to their personal relations with the ruler than to the importance of their offices. After the death of Messalina, the emperor ordered the 

Senate to authorize his consanguineous marriage to his niece, Agrippina. Soon after the marriage, she persuaded the aging emperor to promise the throne to her son, Nero, instead of his own son, Brittanicus. With the accession of Nero assured, Agrippina probably connived at the poisoning of her husband in 54. 

Agrippina made a tragic mistake when she believed that she could control Nero after his elevation to the throne. He was indolent, sensuous, and cruel; indeed, many of his actions, making due allowance for the exaggerations of ancient historians, indicate mental derangement. For a time the emperor deferred to the counsels of the philosopher, Seneca, his former teacher, and Burrus, the prefect of the Praetorian Guard, and while they retained his confidence governmental business was efficiently conducted. Agrippina, however, sealed her fate by opposing him and threatening to have him replaced by Brittanicus. The ill-fated son of Claudius was poisoned, and in 59 Agrippina was slain by her son's order after a plot to drown her in a simulated accident miscarried. Seneca was forced to appear before the Senate to extoll the matricide. 

The same year a great rebellion flared up in Britain. The immediate cause was the mistreatment of Boadicea, queen of the Iceni, by the provincial authorities. Since the administration of the entire province had illustrated many of the evils of Roman rule, the insurrection of the warlike Iceni was soon joined by other tribes. A number of towns, including London and Colchester, were destroyed, and thousands of Romans were massacred. Suetonius Paulinus finally suppressed the rebellion in 60, and the heroic queen committed suicide. 

The attempt to overthrow Roman rule was not entirely in vain, for it brought salutary reforms in the administration of the province. 

Largely as a result of the policies of Claudius, hostilities also broke out with Parthia. The Parthian king had placed a usurper on the 

Armenian throne as a challenge to Roman eastern interests, and Corbulo was sent to help the governor of Syria in a campaign to recover control of the client kingdom. Dissension reminiscent of the quarrels between Germanicus and Piso greatly obstructed Corbulo's efforts, and he was replaced by Paetus, who was defeated in a battle at Rhandeia. Abandoning the attempt to annex Armenia as a province, Nero restored Corbulo to command. The defeat of Paetus was

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

avenged, and the Armenian king was forced to acknowledge Roman suzerainty.

Upon the death of Burrus in 62, Tigellinus who was made prefect of the Guards became the chief minister. He and Poppaea, whom the emperor had taken as a mistress, formed, with Nero, a vicious triumvirate, and Octavia, Nero's wife, fell an early victim to Poppaea's jealousy.

A disastrous fire in 64 destroyed a large part of Rome. Rumors circulated charging that the emperor himself had plotted to destroy the city in order to rebuild it on a more lavish scale, although no evidence was ever discovered to substantiate such charges. The populace, however, could easily have been incited to violence in view of the prevailing passion, and Nero accordingly was anxious to provide a scapegoat to divert suspicion from himself. Possibly on the suggestions of Poppaea or Tigellinus, he ordered the arrest of a number of Christians who under torture allegedly admitted guilt not only of arson but of other crimes as well. The mob was convinced of their guilt and many were put to death in the arena with barbarous cruelty. 

It would, of course, be a mistake to regard this so-called first persecution of the Christians as an evidence of the hostility of the Roman government toward the new religion. The emperor probably was ignorant of the existence of the sect prior to the events of 64, and he ordered the arrest and executions not in order to suppress a religious movement but for the specific purpose of placating the outraged citizenry of the capital. There is no evidence that the outbreak of feeling against the Christians spread beyond the bounds of the capital city, but the fact that the charges that Christians were responsible for the disastrous fire were regarded as plausible by the Roman populace does indicate that the devotees of the new religion already had become unpopular at least among the lower classes. Their intolerance and exclusiveness incurred suspicion, while their alleged lack of patriotism and irreverence toward the pagan gods likewise occasioned dislike. For several generations, the status of Christians was destined to remain relatively unchanged. Subjects of popular resentment, they were spasmodically persecuted, usually as a sequel to mob violence against them and almost invariably for the crimes associated with their faith in the popular mind.

In 65 Calpurnius Piso and a group of aristocrats plotted to overthrow the emperor. The conspiracy was detected, and Seneca, the poet Lucan, Corbulo, and Petronius, the emperor's former " Arbiter of Elegancies," were among those who paid with their lives. The

THE JULIO-CLAUDIANS 

201 rebellions that led to the end of the Julio-Claudian dynasty began in the provinces rather than in the capital. Onerous taxes in Judaea led to the uprising of the Zealots. About the same time, Vindex, propraetor of Gallia Lugdunensis, revolted, in collusion with Galba, governor of Hither Spain. Vespasian was sent to quell the Jewish insurrection, while Verginius Rufus was ordered from Upper Germany to suppress the rebellion in Gaul. General revolt was imminent. Nero became panic-stricken. The Senate pronounced his condemnation, but he forestalled execution by ordering a slave to kill him.

CHAPTER 15 The Flavian and Adoptive Emperors 

HE Julio-Claudian dynasty was overthrown by a series of revolts in widely separated parts of the Empire. Within a single year after these uprisings and the knowledge of his impotence to suppress them had driven Nero to suicide, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius successively wore the purple, and the soldiery learned the dangerous lesson that emperors could be made elsewhere than at Rome.

When news of the disturbances in the Empire reached the East, Mucianus, governor of Syria, offered to support the candidacy of Vespasian for the imperial throne. Vespasian was in command of an army besieging Jerusalem to suppress the insurrection of the Jewish Zealots. He accepted the offer of Mucianus, placed his son Titus in charge of the siege operations, and prepared to set out for Italy. In the meantime, Primus raised an army in Illyria and marched into north Italy in support of Vespasian's claims to the throne. Here he ultimately was joined by Mucianus and the Syrian troops. The united army then defeated the army of Vitellius at Cremona and pressed on to capture Rome. Vitellius was slain, and the Senate, having no alternative, ratified the claims of Vespasian in 70.

Vespasian, founder of the Flavian dynasty of emperors, was admirably qualified by intellect, experience, and temperament to guide the destinies of the state in a period of reconstruction so imperatively demanded after the excesses of the last years of Nero and the upheaval of 68. Son of a money lender, he was a self-made man who had risen to responsible military command as a result of demonstrated competence. Conscientious, economical to the point of parsimony, he quietly proceeded with a program of reform. 

Wasteful methods of tax collection were abolished and exemptions, total or partial, which had been granted to Achaea and several other provinces were cancelled. Extensive tracts of public land were recovered from private individuals who had illegally usurped posses-

sion. Rigid governmental economy, coupled with the measures that increased the income of the treasury, restored financial stability. Discipline was restored in the army; indeed, the legions frequently were employed on useful public works as an additional measure of economy. 

Peace was maintained in the provinces, except for the uprising in Gaul led by Civilis. That rebel leader, a Batavian noble, had raised an army ostensibly in support of Vespasian's claim to the throne, but his refusal to disband his forces after the emperor's control was impregnably established served to divulge his motives. An imperial army under Cerealis quelled the revolt; in view of the support which Civilis had enlisted, the uprising may perhaps be interpreted as a symptom of Gallic yearnings for independence such as had appeared so strongly in the days of Vercingetorix. 

Vespasian died in 79 and was succeeded by Titus (79-81), who had prosecuted the siege of Jerusalem to a victorious conclusion in the year 70. His short reign was marked by his great personal popularity, probably the result of his affability and generosity. An outstanding event of the reign was the first major recorded eruption of Vesuvius in 79. The cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried under the great clouds of ashes and streams of lava that poured from the volcano. The excavation of the ruins of these cities, with the inimitable pictures of Roman daily life that they afford, has been one of the most fascinating and instructive achievements of modern archaeology. 

With the death of Titus, his younger brother, Domitian (81-96), was elevated to the throne. Although Tacitus and Suetonius, our chief sources, are prejudiced against him, as indeed they are against all the emperors whose reigns they describe, he seems to have been indolent and cruel. The most constructive achievement of his reign doubtless was the beginning of the construction of the limes, or line of forts along the exposed salient of the northern frontier. The Empire had a natural boundary along the Rhine and the Danube, but for about ninety miles between the head-waters of these rivers there was none. These forts would complete the Empire's protection against the incursions of Germanic tribes. Watch-towers were placed at intervals along the ramparts, and garrisons were stationed along the line, and larger bodies of troops were placed in camps whence they could readily be summoned in the event of attack.

The value of the limes was largely offset, however, by the emperor's temporizing policy in his dealings with the Dacians. Settled

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

in the region now known as Roumania, the Dacians, under King Decebalus, constituted a serious menace to the lower Danubian provinces. The emperor arranged with Decebalus to furnish subsidies to the Dacians, which were ostensibly rewards for their services in protecting the imperial frontier, but in fact were hardly distinguishable from outright payments of tribute. The effect was to embolden 

Decebalus until the inevitable hostilities broke out in the reign of 

Trajan (98-117).

Discontent was increased with the treason trials at Rome and the attendant confiscations of property. A number of court dignitaries, including the emperor's nephew and his wife, were put to death for alleged sacrilege. According to the historian Cassius Dio, they had adopted Jewish customs; it is far more likely, however, that they were recent converts to Christianity, and we have here evidence that the Christian movement was beginning to spread to the higher social classes in the Empire. The emperor ultimately was assassinated, and with his death the Flavian dynasty came to an end. 

The Senate showed exceptional courage and initiative when it named Nerva (96-98), one of its members, as emperor. The promptness of senatorial action doubtless did much to forestall uprisings in Rome and the provinces such as had terminated the reign of Nero. 

Nerva was an elderly and distinguished lawyer. The outstanding accomplishment of his reign was the institution of his famous alimentary scheme for the twofold purpose of encouraging agriculture in Italy and financing certain humanitarian activities. A revolving fund was set up by the state from which farmers were permitted to make loans at low rates of interest. As they repaid the principal, the money was returned to the fund; interest payments were used primarily for the relief of indigent widows and orphans. 

Nerva selected Trajan (98–117), a Spaniard, as his successor. After securing senatorial ratification, he adopted him as his son. The disturbances of the "Year of the Four Emperors," as well as the crisis that had followed the death of Domitian, had emphasized the imperative need for an established method of determining the succession to the imperial throne. The adoptive method promised to solve the problem. An emperor could select a successor of recognized administrative ability and competence as a military commander, and the good will of the Senate could be ensured by inviting its concurrence in the choice. With the succession provided for in advance, continuity of the imperial power would be assured and could be expected to serve as a deterrent to usurpation and civil war.
