Trajan, the first provincial to be elevated to the throne of the Caesars, was unassuming, temperate, and unusually conscientious in the discharge of military and civil duties. He soon had abundant opportunity to demonstrate his military genius. Decebalus of Dacia, emboldened by the payment of subsidies by Domitian, had enticed a number of Roman engineers into his kingdom with the announced purpose of directing a program of public works. Upon their arrival, however, he forced them to aid in the construction of fortresses and military roads obviously designed with a view to hostilities with the Empire. Trajan, realizing that war could not long be deferred, refused to continue the payment of subsidies and without formal declaration of war marched an army into Dacia in the spring of 101. 

After crossing the Danube, the legions forced the pass of the Iron Gate in the Carpathians. Since Decebalus chiefly relied on this stronghold, its capture was speedily followed by the surrender of Sarmizegethusa, the Dacian capital. Terms of peace imposed by the emperor were exceptionally mild. Decebalus was forced to acknowledge the suzerainty of Rome, and, of course, the engineers, the treatment of whom had served as the immediate cause of the war, were released. 

Trajan's failure to cripple the power of Decebalus by imposing punitive terms merely encouraged him again to risk war with the Empire. New forts were built, supply depots established at strategic points, and the hospitable reception of Roman fugitives and deserters from the army was interpreted as a studied affront. Trajan declared war in 104 and the following year led the legions across the Danube over the new stone bridge that had been constructed to facilitate an offensive campaign. Again the formidable defenses of Decebalus proved unable to check the Roman advance. The Dacian capital was burned, and the kingdom was annexed as Rome's only province north of the Danube. It remained a Roman province until abandoned by the Emperor Aurelian (270-275).

The emperor commemorated his Dacian wars by erecting a monumental column. The shaft, 100 feet high, contains a spiral relief, 600 feet long. This relief, often termed the "last great work of Roman art," is our sole source of information as to the events of the wars. 

Rome's maintenance of vassal kingdoms along the eastern frontier was the basic cause for the almost perennial conflicts with Parthia. 

Armenia had been the most important of these strategic "buffer states ever since its conquest in the Second Mithridatic War by Pompey. Consequently, when King Chosroes of Parthia intervened in 

---

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Armenia to depose a ruler friendly to Rome, the cornerstone of imperial policy in the East was seriously threatened. Trajan declared war in 113 and after extensive preparations led an army into Armenia which he ultimately organized as a Roman province. His subsequent actions soon indicated an aggressive policy against Parthia. He invaded Mesopotamia and organized the provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria. Ctesiphon, the Parthian capital, then was captured, and hostilities were terminated with the accession of a son of Chosroes to the Parthian throne. Trajan then continued his march along the Tigris to the Persian Gulf. Here he received word of a serious rebellion of the Jews, and immediately set out for Judaea, but he died in Cilicia before a campaign against the rebels could be inaugurated. 

Centralization of the imperial administration was doubtless the most significant internal development of Trajan's reign. Curatores, responsible to the emperor, were placed in charge of municipalities, while Correctores, likewise under immediate imperial supervision, were installed to oversee the government of provinces still under nominal senatorial administration. The government became distinctly paternal as the emperor personally handled details of provincial and municipal administration. Voluminous correspondence with his subordinates kept him in touch with local affairs. The letters exchanged between the emperor and Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, are well known. One of Pliny's most vexatious problems arose with the extension of Christianity in his province and the manifestations of popular hostility the movement provoked. He put a number of 

Christians to the torture, although he was unable to charge them with anything more serious than insubordination, contumacy, and "extravagant superstition." He consulted the emperor as to whether he was authorized to punish Christians because of their affiliation with the new faith, without proof of criminal acts. Trajan replied that Christians could be punished if they refused to sacrifice before the imperial image, which meant that henceforth the votaries of the faith were liable to prosecution if they refused to perform what they regarded as an idolatrous rite. The emperor ordered the governor to refrain from any attempt to seek out the Christians; he was empowered to act only in the event that accusations against them came before the courts in the usual manner, and he was to pay no heed to anonymous accusations. Trajan's refusal to permit the organization of a fire brigade in Bithynia is a classic illustration of the growing governmental suspicion toward organizations. It was feared that organizations, even of an apparently innocuous nature, might become

centers of political activity that would become subversive to the government. The fact that Christianity was becoming an organized movement doubtless affected the emperor's attitude reflected in his answer to Pliny.

Hadrian (117-138), whom Trajan named as his successor, had served as an able lieutenant in the eastern campaign. His abilities, character, and temperament had little in common with Trajan. He had no interest in military affairs; his versatile tastes were directed rather toward languages, literature, philosophy, and art. The aggressive policies pursued in the East by Trajan were reversed by the new administration. Mesopotamia and Assyria were ceded to Parthia, and 

Armenia was granted independence. In accord with Hadrian's intention to revert to the defensive policy inaugurated by Augustus, the limes along the northern frontier were completed, and Britain was protected from the attacks of Picts and Scots by the construction of a massive wall between the Tyne and the Solway. Another Jewish insurrection was quelled. Jerusalem was destroyed, and dispossessed 

Jews were scattered throughout the Empire, where they usually settled in the great urban centers. 

Administrative improvements of considerable importance were made. Both senators and equites were encouraged to enter the state service, and adequate salaries, coupled with systematic training, ensured a capable, conscientious personnel. The heads of the four departments organized by Claudius now constituted an advisory council. A privy council also was organized for judicial work in Italy. A monumental achievement was the codification of the praetorian edicts. Each year the praetors, prior to assuming the duties of office, posted a list of principles that would govern their procedure. These edicts constituted a body of precedents used in the Roman courts just as modern courts utilize previous decisions. In the course of centuries, the number of these praetorian edicts assumed such proportions as to make them difficult to use; there was much duplication and inconsistency, and many edicts had become obsolete. A commission of well-known lawyers therefore was appointed to undertake the gigantic task of editing the edicts, ultimately issued as the Edic tum Perpetuum. 

Hadrian was famous as a traveler. Absent from Rome for a total of eleven years, he visited every province at least once. His favorite residence was at Athens, which received many marks of imperial favor. When he died in 138, his remains were placed in the great stone tomb which he had constructed on the banks of the Tiber.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

This edifice, known today as the Castle of Saint Angelo, is one of the most imposing monuments of the grandeur of ancient Rome. 

Antoninus Pius (138-161), the first of the Antonines, enjoyed a peaceful reign, a tranquil contrast to the age of Trajan and Hadrian. 

Antoninus was succeeded by Marcus Aurelius (161-180), the most famous of the Antonines. The new emperor was the personification of the Stoic ideal, — retiring, simple, conscientious, and philosophical. 

But tranquillity did not last. Both eastern and northern frontiers were threatened. Parthia had resumed its aggressions in Armenia during the last years of Antoninus. As Rome's defensive policy made mandatory the preservation of the system of buffer states, Marcus sent his newly chosen colleague, Lucius Verus, to the East. Verus proved disappointing as a commander, but his lieutenant, Statius 

Priscus, managed to recover Armenia. An army under Avidius Cassius then captured Ctesiphon and Seleuceia, but the campaign had a terrible sequel. Thousands of the soldiers perished of a plague, and the epidemic was carried to the West by the returning survivors. 

The disease reduced the populace in many provinces to desperation, and it was popularly believed that the disease was an affliction visited on the people of the Empire by the ancestral gods who were angered by the impiety of the Christians. Severe persecutions of the 

Christians followed, especially in Gaul, to mollify the outraged pagan deities.

The northern frontier was menaced by the migratory movements of the Marcomanni and Quadi. These tribes passed through Bohemia and reached the vicinity of Aquilia, in north Italy. A vigorous campaign begun in 166 saved Italy from serious harrying, and offensive operations during the next few years crushed the invaders. Some of the Germans ultimately were settled south of the Danube, after promising military aid to the Empire and relinquishing the captives and booty they had taken. The remainder were forced to evacuate 

Roman territory. 

Verus, whom Marcus Aurelius had taken as a colleague and designated as his successor, died in 169. Six years later, following a rumor that the emperor had died, Cassius, who had been largely responsible for the defeat of the Parthians in the eastern campaign, assumed the purple. Marcus hastened to the East to quell the revolt, but before his arrival the usurper was murdered by his troops. Marcus then selected his son, Commodus, as his colleague and successor. 

By 177, the Marcomanni and Quadi again threatened the northern frontier. Until his death in 180, the emperor waged another success-

ful campaign against them, but he did not live to carry out his plan to annex the territory occupied by the Germans. Creation of another 

Roman salient in Bohemia and Moravia, comparable to that created in Dacia, might well have proved a powerful stabilizing influence along the frontier.

Marcus Aurelius is best known for his Meditations, which has come down to us as one of the truly great literary works of all time. 

This work was not intended to be a treatise on Stoicism. It is rather the intimate, personal diary of a philosopher-emperor whose greatness of soul is evident on virtually every page. 

When Marcus selected his son as his successor, he made a tragic mistake, for the character of Commodus possessed no redeeming feature. He was cruel, cowardly, and sensual. His thirteen years of misrule and oppression finally ended with his assassination on the last day of 192. His death signalized not only the end of the adoptive plan for regulating the imperial succession, but also the beginning of a most tragic era in the history of the Empire. 

THE CULTURE OF THE SILVER AGE 

The period from the close of the reign of Augustus to the end of the age of the Antonines is known in the cultural history of Rome as the Silver Age. It was a great creative period, particularly in literature, but from several points of view there is evidence of retrogression from the supreme accomplishments of the Golden Age. Perhaps the outstanding distinction between the literature of the two ages lies in the fact that in the Silver Age there is greater emphasis on form. 

Writers who endeavor to impart rhetorical flourish to their works sometimes produce a straining after effect and corresponding superficiality. In large measure this new literature was the reflection of the emphasis on rhetorical studies in Roman education. Imitation of 

Greek works was stressed; above all, the pupil was encouraged to develop graceful turns of expression. All the traditional literary types were represented in the Silver Age, but the satire and epigram received distinct emphasis, and the picaresque novel, or rambling tales of travel and adventure, as represented in the Satyricon of Petronius, constituted an entirely new type. The provinces, particularly Spain, were strongly represented in the literary output of the period. 

Seneca the Elder (c. 54 B.C.-A.D. 39) may be considered the founder of the Spanish school of writers and rhetoricians. His work on rhetoric is a mine of information on oratorical technique, prominent orators and their works, and methods of rhetorical instruction. Colu-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mella of Gades, also a Spanish provincial, wrote twelve books on agriculture in which his style is strongly suggestive of the influence of the writers of the Augustan Age. The content of the work is as important for the study of Roman agriculture in the imperial period as the famous treatise on husbandry by Cato is for the period of the 

Republic. Seneca the Younger (4 B.C.-A.D. 65), another exponent of the Spanish school, had an illustrious political career. As has been told, he became the tutor of Nero, on whom for a time his influence was so great that he, together with Burrus, virtually constituted the government. He gradually lost the confidence of the emperor, however, and after his implication in the conspiracy of Piso he committed suicide to escape execution. He wrote short ethical treatises, letters of moral edification, and works on natural philosophy. In all his writings, the Stoic ideas predominate; even in his natural philosophy his approach is largely ethical.

An important literary type of the age was the satire. Lucan (3965), who for a time was a friend of Nero and wrote in the tone of servile flattery of the emperor, finally assumed a boldly satirical style after his relations with the ruler became strained. He wrote an historical epic dealing with the end of the Republic in which he expressed sympathy for the republican cause. He, too, finally fell a victim to the imperial reprisals that followed detection of Piso's plot. 

The greatest exponent of Roman satire was Juvenal (60-140) about whose life little is known with certainty. Sixteen of his satires, in five books, are extant. In them, the moral indignation of the writer is forcibly expressed as he excoriates the vices and foibles of his day. 

It is primarily from his work that the early Christian writers established the tradition that Rome was an abode of vice and crime comparable with Sodom and Gomorrah. The epigram, also an important type, received its classic treatment in the writings of Martial (40-104), who wrote twelve books of epigrams, many of which were of the satiric, or "biting " type.

The greatest didactic writer of the period was Quintilian (35—95), a famous professor of rhetoric. His Institutes of Oratory remained for centuries the authoritative treatise on the subject. Its twelve books deal with the collection and arrangement of material, effective styles of presentation, voice cultivation, gestures, acquisition of vocabulary, and every phase of oratorical art of interest to the serious student.

Much history of distinguished quality was written in the Silver Age. Dominating Roman literature in this field was the work of

Cornelius Tacitus (c. 55-c. 117).

His early works that have earned lasting fame were his Agricola and the De Germania. The Agricola is a beautifully written biography of his father-in-law of that name who served as governor of Britain. The Germany is an indispensable source concerning the Germans prior to the great barbarian invasions of the Empire in the fourth and fifth centuries. His major works, however, are the Histories and the Annals. The former, originally in eighteen books, only a portion of which are extant, began with the "Year of the Four Emperors" and covered the period down to his own time. The Annals, written after the Histories, deal with the earlier period in the history of the Empire. The first four books, part of the fifth, and most of the eleventh to sixteenth books are extant. 

The complete work covered the period from the close of the reign of Augustus to the beginning of the Flavian era, and with the Histories constituted a complete history of the Empire from the Augustan Age to about the end of the reign of Trajan. Suetonius, whose work is also used, although with caution, as an authority for the history of the Empire in the first century, wrote the Lives of the Twelve Caesars, a series of gossipy biographical sketches of the emperors. His Illustrious Men is a somewhat similar series of biographical portraits of famous men of letters. There were also several Greek writers of importance in the historical and biographical fields. Cassius Dio wrote a history of Rome from the founding of the city to A.D. 229. Arrian wrote the well-known Anabasis of Alexander, one of our main sources of information in regard to Alexander's memorable Asiatic campaign. Plutarch of Chaeronea wrote Parallel Lives, a collection of biographical sketches of famous Greeks and Romans arranged in pairs. Thus there are sketches of Alexander and Julius Caesar, Demosthenes and Cicero, and so forth. Fifty of the Lives have survived, with forty-six in pairs and the other four unpaired. Few literary figures are represented; the emphasis is on statesmen. 

To the Silver Age belongs Rome's outstanding writer on science. 

Pliny the Elder (23-79) was born at Novum Comum, in north Italy, and was educated at Rome. A lawyer by profession, he held a number of official positions that necessitated extensive travels in the provinces. 

Reputed to be the most learned man of his times, he wrote works on grammar, rhetoric, history, and military science, but his Natural History is his chief claim to fame. It is an encyclopaedia in thirtyseven books, and the author claims to have consulted some two thousand works in its preparation. For centuries Pliny's work was regarded as the supreme authority on matters of scientific interest.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The author's scientific curiosity was actually the immediate cause of his death, for during the great eruption of Vesuvius in the reign of 

Titus he approached the blazing crater too closely and succumbed to the poisonous gases. The famous naturalist's nephew, Pliny the

Younger, is known in the field of literature primarily for his letters; his correspondence with the Emperor Trajan has already been discussed.

The greatest building achievement of the Silver Age was the construction of the well-known Flavian amphitheatre or Colosseum. The structure was begun in the reign of Vespasian who utilized the excavation made for Nero's artificial lake as a site. The structure is elliptical in shape. The outer wall, constructed of blocks of travertine, stands on a stylobate which in turn is raised two steps above a pavement that surrounds the entire building. The exterior wall is in four storeys, three of which are rows of open arcades. All three

Greek architectural orders are represented; the columns of the first arcade are Doric, while those of the second and third are Ionic and Corinthian respectively. The capacity of the amphitheatre has been variously estimated; 45,000 spectators could be comfortably seated and there was standing room for about 5000 more.

CHAPTER 16 

The End of the Empire in the West 

THE ORDEAL OF THE THIRD CENTURY 

HE assassination of Commodus (A.D. 192) again plunged the 

Empire into civil war. Efforts of the Senate to assert political leadership failed when Pertinax, its nominee to the purple, was slain by the licentious Praetorian Guard who thereupon sold the throne at auction to Didius Julianus. In the meantime, the news of the disturbances in the capital reached the provinces. Niger was saluted as emperor in Syria, while Albinus was proclaimed in Britain. Septimius Severus, in command of the Pannonian legions, was in the most advantageous position, however, and he promptly marched on Rome, where after the assassination of Julianus he was recognized as emperor by the Senate. By 197 his campaigns in Syria and Gaul removed his two rivals.

Septimius owed his position to the support of his soldiery, and continued tenure of power depended on keeping them satisfied. His government therefore was a military despotism, with the power of the Praetorian Guard balanced by the creation of the Parthian Legion, stationed in the vicinity of the capital. The outstanding event of the reign was a campaign against King Vologeses of Parthia which resulted in the capture of Ctesiphon and the eventual overthrow of the Arsacid dynasty. The emperor died at York in 211 while engaged in a campaign against the Scots who were harrying north Britain. 

The only noteworthy event of the reign of Caracalla (211–218), son of Septimius, who had secured sole rule of the Empire by the murder of his brother, Geta, was the extension of Roman citizenship to the provincials. The edict issued in 212 granted rights of citizenship to all males over eighteen, doubtless in response to the advice of Ulpian, Paulus, and other famous lawyers of the time. 

Alexander Severus (222-235) dedicated his energies to the reforms so imperatively needed after the excesses of his predecessor, the mad

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Heliogabalus (218-222), but the problems that confronted him were too much for his ability, and pressure on the frontiers diverted his attention from internal affairs. The Parthians again invaded Roman territory, and efforts to expel them failed. In the meantime, the 

German tribes of the Alemanni and Marcomanni menaced the northern frontier. The emperor hurriedly returned from the East to protect the exposed sectors, but instead of fighting he agreed to pay subsidies to the barbarians in return for their evacuation of Roman territory. This outraged the legions, and the emperor was speedily sacrificed to their passions.

Virtual anarchy prevailed from 235 to 270. Emperors were made and unmade by the undisciplined soldiers, while Parthians and Germans buffeted the frontiers. The fortunes of the state reached their lowest ebb in the joint reign of Valerian and Gallienus when the former was captured by the Parthians and the latter was assassinated. 

An independent state in Gaul was organized by Posthumus, while Queen Zenobia of Palmyra threatened to annex the eastern provinces. 

Collapse of the Empire was arrested, however, by the Emperor 

Aurelian (270-275) when Zenobia was decisively beaten in two campaigns and imperial control was re-established in Gaul. 

RECOVERY OF THE EMPIRE UNDER DIOCLETIAN 

The Empire survived the disasters of the third century primarily because of the reforms introduced by Diocletian, the "last great man of ancient times." An Illyrian freedman who had risen to the position of prefect by virtue of his ability, his elevation to the throne by the legions ended the anarchy that had followed the assassination of Aurelian.

A grave political weakness in the imperial government, as we have seen, was the lack of an established constitutional practice to determine succession to the throne. Civil wars and the arrogance of the legions, who came to be the final arbiters of the political fortunes of the state, were the results of uncertainty in respect to the succession. To remedy this situation, Diocletian established a tetrarchy. 

He first raised Maximian to the position of imperial colleague. He next appointed Constantius Chlorus and Galerius as caesars, or junior emperors, while he and Maximian took the titles of augusti. According to the plan, the augusti would retire upon the expiration of twenty years and yield their places to the caesars. The newly elevated augusti in turn were expected to name two new caesars to succeed them when they abdicated after twenty years. It was hoped

that the prospect of appointment and promotion would deter ambitious men from resorting to force to procure their elevation. 

Through the provision of continuous imperial authority, the crises which formerly followed the death of an emperor would be avoided, and the frontiers could be more efficiently defended with the cooperation of four colleagues each of whom was stationed at a strategic point.

An important change in local administration was the grouping of the provinces into thirteen dioceses each of which was placed under the jurisdiction of a vicar. Each of the provinces, in turn, was placed under the administration of an official known as the praeses. The court of Diocletian at Nicomedia was invested with all the trappings of oriental despotism. Elaborate rules of etiquette included the requirement that all who approached the presence of the emperor should prostrate themselves before him.

Efforts to restore economic stability met with a measure of immediate success, but some of the measures were destined to speed the eventual collapse of the Empire in the West. The practice of depreciating the coinage was halted, and the income from taxes increased when the municipal aristocrats (decuriones) were made responsible for the collections in their respective cities. To facilitate tax assessments and collections and ensure greater industrial stability membership in the industrial colleges was required of artisans; indeed, membership in these organizations was ultimately made not only compulsory but hereditary as well.

In 301 Diocletian issued a Price Edict to prevent violent fluctuations in prices and wages. Staple commodities were to be retained. within designated price limits; changes within these limits were to be accompanied by commensurate changes in wages. In view of recent governmental experiments in the economic sphere, it is interesting to note that even the threat of the death penalty failed to secure compliance with the regulations.

The reign of Diocletian also was marked by a decisive struggle between the imperial government and the Christian Church. In the early years of his reign, the emperor evinced no hostility to the new religion and permitted his wife and daughter to become converts. 

Galerius, the caesar stationed at Sirmium, however, was an implacable foe of the Christian movement and continually urged his senior colleagues to take measures against it. A mutiny in the army, apparently incited by Christians, finally convinced Diocletian that the Christians actually constituted a "state within a state" as Galerius

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

contended, and he embarked on a policy designed to extirpate the new religion.

His first edict ordered the closing of all places of worship used by the Christians and the surrender of their sacred literature. A second edict made the clergy liable to arrest and punishment. The third and most severe enactment required all citizens to sacrifice before the image of the emperor and procure a certificate attesting to their compliance with the law. Since Christians could not obey the law and adhere to the dictates of their faith they were confronted with the alternatives of abjuring their faith or openly flouting the law of the Empire. Many were imprisoned or put to death, but the organization of the church enabled it to survive the blow. A number of governmental officials were indifferent or sympathetic to the Christian movement with the result that parts of the Empire, including the provinces administered by Constantius Chlorus, were virtually unaffected by the persecutions.

CONSTANTINE AND THE TRIUMPH OF CHRISTIANITY 

Although Diocletian's tetrarchy had been instituted primarily to forestall civil war, the results proved that the tetrarchy, like the adoptive scheme of the second century, could not prevent conflict over the succession. When Diocletian and Maximian abdicated in 305, Galerius and Constantine Chlorus were made augusti, while Severus and Maximin Daza, hitherto unknown men, were appointed caesars. 

Failure to name Constantine, son of Constantius, occasioned surprise and disappointment, particularly in Gaul and Britain. Constantine, who was in residence at the court of Galerius, hastily fled to Britain, fearful that Galerius would put him to death to prevent him from challenging the succession. When Constantius Chlorus died in 306, the British legions invested Constantine with the purple. 

In the meantime, Maximian, who had reluctantly agreed to abdicate along with Diocletian, again assumed the purple and seized Gaul. 

His son, Maxentius, marched on Italy, which he secured after his defeat and execution of Severus. Licinius successfully challenged the authority of Maximin Daza in the eastern provinces after the death of Galerius in 311. The plan of Diocletian therefore had served to incite rather than prevent civil war the first time it was subjected to a major test.

Constantine crossed to Gaul and eliminated Maximian as a contender for the throne. He then entered Italy to wrest it from the control of Maxentius. The opposing forces were arrayed against

each other at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. On the eve of the battle, Constantine, as a result of an alleged emotional experience, adopted the Christian cross as his insignia. He won an overwhelming victory on the following day and agreed to share the Empire with 

Licinius (312).

A sequel to the battle was the issue of the Edict of Milan (313) under the joint authority of Constantine and Licinius. By the edict, the Christians were granted official toleration. The edict expressly stated that the traditional paganism, sun-worship, which had become very popular in the days of the Severi, and Christianity were to enjoy equal privileges. The toleration of the new religion was doubtless due in part to the futility of persecution, which the failure of Diocletian to suppress the movement had demonstrated. One need seek no miraculous explanations, no flaming crosses in the sky or celestial choruses. The Christians were an ever-growing organized group. 

Constantine earned their loyalty and support by conceding them the right to continue their activities which experience had shown could not be suppressed.

Constantine showed subsequent marks of favor to the Christians. 

A number of public buildings were assigned to them as places of worship, and the clergy were granted special legal status. In 325 the emperor convoked the Council of Nicaea to settle the bitter Arian controversy. The Arians who followed the teachings of Arius, a priest of Alexandria, believed that Christ was of necessity inferior to God the Father in that as a created being He could not be coeternal with the Father. These doctrines were repudiated by the council, and the emperor sought uniformity of belief in the interest of public order; but Arianism was destined for long survival, especially since most of the German tribes were ultimately converted to Christianity by Arian missionaries.

From the decisive victory of 313, the church soon completed its triumph. The Emperor Gratian dealt a decisive blow to paganism when he ordered the removal of the Altar of Victory from the Senate House. In 381 Theodosius forbade pagan worship and virtually made Christianity the official religion of the Empire. There were a number of reasons for the victory of the Christian faith in its struggle with the Roman government. The universality of the teachings of Christ was appreciated by St. Paul, to whose organizing genius and indefatigable missionary activity the religion owed its position as an imperial movement rather than as a mere sect of Judaism. Since the Christian faith was intolerant in its attitude toward

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

rival religions, the allegiance of its converts was not divided. The fact that the movement soon became organized was an advantage of enormous significance. The Christian faith especially appealed to the masses with its emphasis on an eternal life that would offer recompense to the poor and heavy-laden of the world. Its teachers presented with unique assurance the doctrine of immortality exemplified in the Resurrection, in which they believed with a fervor that was contagious.

The triumph of Christianity was not an unmixed blessing, however. Now, without the selective influence of the persecutions, it soon proved impossible to enforce in the admission of members the high standards which could prevail when the membership included only those whose faith was sufficiently strong to induce them to run the risk of persecution. With increased governmental favor and mounting private benefaction, the church became wealthy. The administration of the business interests of the dioceses came to absorb more and more of the energies of the bishops and other clerical officials. Indeed, since the ranks of the episcopacy were being filled more and more by men of administrative talents, increasing burdens of civil administration were transferred to them by the state, especially with the creation of the office of defensor civitatis, or defender of the city, which frequently was assigned to the bishops. Compromises with paganism were necessary with the rapid increase of church membership that followed in the wake of its triumph. Above all, relief from persecution afforded an opportunity for the outbreak of doctrinal controversies, such as the Arian movement, which perhaps constituted a greater threat to the institutional integrity of the church than was offered by the persecutions. At first, it was believed that investment of the bishops with supreme control over the faith and morals of their flocks would eliminate doctrinal controversies, but when the bishops themselves failed to agree resort was taken to the convocation of general councils. The Council of Nicaea dealt with the Arian heresy; a council at Ephesus condemned the Nestorian doctrines which held that Christ was not divine prior to His baptism; and the Council of Chalcedon repudiated the Monophysite interpretation that denied the human nature of Christ. The councils and the creeds they drew up, however, failed to allay doctrinal strife permanently. The need for absolute authority was becoming progressively more evident and doubtless served as one of the chief causes for the recognition of the bishop of Rome as the supreme authority in the church of the West.

THE COLLAPSE OF THE EMPIRE IN THE WEST 

Few problems have so engrossed the attention of historians as the attempt adequately to explain the collapse of the Roman Empire in the West. While many causes, economic, social, and political, have been cited, not even Gibbon or succeeding historians of comparable stature have presented all the factors that played a part in the "severest and most prolonged convulsion to which Europe has ever been subjected."

Economic causes doubtless played a decisive role in the collapse. 

As we have seen, the main trend in Roman agriculture after the wars of expansion was toward the institution of large estates (latifundia) with the attendant depletion of the yeomanry. Periodic land redistributions, such as followed the confiscations of the triumvirs, reclamation projects, and the assignment of lands to veterans retarded but failed to arrest this tendency. The small-scale cultivators, unable successfully to compete with the plantations, migrated to the towns in search of employment and all too often merely swelled the ranks of the impoverished unemployed in the urban centers. Other peasant proprietors surrendered their lands to wealthy landlords to receive them back as praecaria; that is, they renounced ownership of their plots and received in return the right to remain on the land as tenants at will. They paid a portion of their crops as rent to the new owners of their former holdings, who now became responsible for the payment of taxes. With the dwindling supply of slaves and the consequent rise in their price, there would be little danger of arbitrary eviction of the precarial tenants if they continued to pay the stipulated rent.

Many landless farmers were settled as colons on the estates of wealthy landlords. They performed prescribed labor on the land and in return received small plots the cultivation of which afforded them their own subsistence. Then, too, owners of the latifundia, with the increasing shortage of rural slave labor, frequently granted tracts to peasant cultivators who agreed to pay a share of their produce in return.

The entrenchment of plantation economy had a number of disastrous consequences. From a social point of view, class distinction widened with the progressive curtailment of the middle class. The base of taxation in rural areas was becoming more narrow; the government, forced to deal more and more with landlords sufficiently powerful to evade payments proportionate to their wealth, was con-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

fronted with dwindling income, while the impoverishment of the yeomanry was increasing the burden of poor relief. Increasing cultivation of the vine and the olive, partly attributable to the concentration on these staples under the plantation system and the rigid control of the grain trade by the state, led to the virtual abandonment of the cultivation of cereals in Italy. Concentration on the cultivation of staple crops on the plantations frequently led to soil exhaustion. The presence of great acreage of abandoned land, particularly in Italy, was intimately associated with the economic collapse of the Empire. 

Commerce was dwindling to an alarming degree. Depreciation of currency by the government, inaugurated on a large scale by the Severi, destroyed the security and confidence necessary for the conduct of long-term commercial transactions. With the growing proportion of base metal in the coinage and the consequent decline in its purchasing power, the amount in circulation was increasingly inadequate for the conduct of commerce, with the virtual reversion to barter in many parts of the Empire. Adverse trade balances resulting from the importation of articles of luxury from the East drained large amounts of coinage from the channels of trade within the Empire. Governmental impressment of shipowners into the grain trade, where they assumed all the risks with no prospect of substantial profits, further discouraged mercantile enterprise. Furthermore, as the provinces developed their own industries and tended to become more economically self-sufficient, the basis of trade naturally was curtailed. Prolonged agricultural depression, of course, meant depleted purchasing power; indeed, the progressive concentration of wealth in the hands of a few naturally diminished the market for consumer goods.

Industry staggered under the weight of almost prohibitive taxation and bureaucratic control. Artisans were obliged to join their respective industrial colleges in order that the collection of taxes might be facilitated. Membership in the colleges even was made hereditary; in the case of the armorers, the government ordered the artisans in that trade to be branded with an identifying insignia to prevent them from escaping. Discouragement of enterprise and the almost complete absence of technological improvement were the price exacted by governmental regimentation.

The increasing burden of taxation played a major part in the economic collapse of the state. The annonae, or taxes in produce, were collected according to assessments made every fifteen years.

The tributa, or direct land tax, likewise was collected, as were the vectigalia, or excise taxes and customs. Although the imperial government had abolished the most vicious abuses of tax farming, inequalities in assessment and collection could not wholly be avoided. The wealthy frequently evaded their just share, while the poor couldn't pay. Inevitably the burden on the productive class became more onerous.

A major cause of increased taxation was the burden of poor relief. 

It would be hard to exaggerate the disastrous consequences of the Roman system of doles. Tenant farmers and peasant proprietors could not hope to earn more than a bare livelihood from their plots; the wages of artisans and laborers were pitifully small because of the competition of slave labor. Why not abandon the effort to make a living? One could become a recipient of the dole and exist about as comfortably as he could by the fruits of productive labor. The expense of relief mounted with the necessity of expanding the gifts of "bread and circuses" to the masses; increased relief expenditures necessitated heavier taxation which in turn drove additional individuals into the ranks of the recipients of the dole. 

Population trends in the Empire were toward excessive urbanization. The price spread between producer and consumer was naturally increased, leading to high living costs in the towns and cities at the same time that low prices for farm commodities were largely responsible for distress in rural areas. Shortage of labor frequently was the chief cause for the abandonment of agricultural acreage, while at the same time large numbers of unemployed on the relief rolls in the municipalities were taxing the resources of the government to the utmost.

A salient political cause of the collapse of the Empire was the prolonged failure to establish any definite method for regulating the succession to the imperial throne. Hereditary succession, nomination by the Senate, the adoptive scheme, and the tetrarchy all failed to prevent usurpation and civil war. The legions soon controlled the political destinies of the state; he whom they supported speedily became the master of the Roman world. In a state where the civil power is clearly subordinate to military dictation, order, security, and individual liberty are impossible.

The rise and spread of Christianity has been considered by a number of historians to have contributed to the downfall of the Empire. Certainly the Christians constituted an organized group within the state the members of which qualified their obedience to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the government by their consciences and religious scruples. The 

Christian view that there was a higher law than that of the emperor, duties and obligations that transcended those owed to the state, was fundamentally opposed to the absolutism of the imperial government which by its very nature demanded the undivided allegiance of its citizenry.

Plagues and epidemics took heavy toll in the Empire; for example, the outbreak of a pestilence during the reign of Marcus Aurelius ultimately affected virtually the entire Empire. Endemic diseases, particularly malaria, sapped the physical stamina of the populace. 

In the absence of knowledge as to the cause of disease and the consequent helplessness to prevent or arrest epidemics, the microbe must be reckoned as an important agent in bringing about the disintegration of the Empire.

The solicitude of the emperors frequently was aroused by the falling birth rate. Single persons, particularly in the higher classes of society, were deferring or even avoiding marriage; married persons were loath to rear large families. While some regard these trends as causes for the fall of the Empire in the West, it seems more reasonable to hold that they were rather symptoms or results of the fundamental causes of decline.

Increasing barbarian infiltration, particularly into the army, was another important factor in the collapse of the Western Empire. 

Indeed, it can be maintained that the barbarian invasions of the fourth and fifth centuries were but the culmination of this process of gradual infusion. Then, too, the widespread use of slaves, especially in the households of the rich and well-born, contributed to the development of what some have termed a " slave pyschology." 

THE GERMANIC MIGRATIONS AND THE FALL OF THE EMPIRE IN THE WEST 

With the Empire thus weakened by the many fundamental factors just reviewed despite the efforts at reconstruction made by Diocletian and several other emperors, it was a comparatively easy prey to the Teutonic invasions which overwhelmed it. Our information as to conditions among the Germans prior to their settlement in the Empire is derived primarily from Caesar's Gallic Wars and the essay De Germania of Tacitus. Caesar studied the Germans primarily from the viewpoint of the military commander; therefore his account naturally emphasizes factors of military significance in their institutions, customs, and character. He praised them for their bravery, their magnificent physiques, and inurement to hardships. War-

fare and hunting were their chief activities. Elected chieftains led their tribes in battle and exercised absolute power during the campaigns. The tribesmen lived a nomadic existence, supplementing the produce of their herds by hunting and fishing. There was no private ownership of land; instead, each year the chieftains allocated tracts to the families. According to Caesar, these annual distributions of land prevented avarice and protected the tribesmen from the enervating effects of settled habitation. 

Tacitus, writing about one hundred and fifty years later than Caesar, may have had in writing of the Germans a desire to chide the Romans of his day for their alleged degeneracy by contrasting them with the primitive Germans. By his time, the Germans had become more settled, and agriculture was their basic means of livelihood. With the partial abandonment of their former nomadic life, permanent villages were often established, and the annual allocations of land by the chiefs were superseded by private ownership or communal tenure. Some commerce was conducted with the Empire along the frontier, but in the more remote regions of Germany money was unknown. The precious metals were not prized, and trade with itinerant Roman merchants that might occasionally visit the tribes was conducted by barter. 

The military leaders of the Germans, according to the historian, were selected for their demonstrated prowess; they led by virtue of the example of bravery they set rather than by command. The tribal priests accompanied the army in the field to ensure the support of the ancestral gods, and they were empowered to sentence to death warriors guilty of treason or cowardice. The women, too, often accompanied the army, remaining with the baggage trains during the battles to exhort the warriors to deeds of valor by their shouts of encouragement. The troops relied on the sheer momentum of their impetuous charge to gain victory. They were easily discouraged by resolute resistance and were temperamentally unsuited for sustained efforts such as the investment of fortified towns. 

Young warriors usually entered the service of valorous leaders to constitute what the Romans called the comitatus. The chieftain supported the youths and furnished them with their weapons. In return, his followers were bound to proffer their unquestioned loyalty. They shared the spoil of successful military ventures, but on the other hand were expected to undergo the same fate as befell their chieftain, whom it was a disgrace to survive if he fell in battle. 

The political institutions of the Germans, thoroughly described by

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Tacitus, are of considerable interest. Every full moon, an assembly of the tribe was held at a designated spot. Males who had been admitted into tribal membership by the bestowal of weapons after they had demonstrated their valor attended the assemblies. The meetings were slow in getting under way, for the warriors, in order to show that they attended on their own volition rather than in obedience to command, were accustomed deliberately to delay their arrival. The assembly, or Folk Moot, was called to order by the priests, after which the chieftains who had been engaged in preliminary discussion with each other submitted various proposals to the assembled tribesmen. If the assembly concurred in the suggestions of the chiefs, who spoke in the order of age and distinction, they manifested their approval by clashing their weapons against their shields. If they dissented from the suggestions of the speakers they evinced their displeasure by moans and shouts.

Judicial cases also were tried before the assembly. The plaintiff made his accusation in accordance with customary procedure, and the slightest deviation in word or gesture from the formula resulted in the immediate quashing of his case. The defendant then made a direct denial of the charge, assuming that the plaintiff had made the accusation in proper form. The assembly then chose a committee (known among the Franks as the Rachiomburgs), and the committee in turn recommended what form of proof was to be employed and on which of the parties would fall the burden of proof. Usually, the defendant was assumed to be guilty until he demonstrated his innocence by the prescribed proof; the final decision on these points, however, rested with the assembly, which could accept or reject the recommendations of the committee. Ordeals usually were employed as methods of proof. In the hot water ordeal, for example, the defendant was required to plunge his hand into a kettle of boiling water to retrieve a pebble at the bottom. The resultant wound was then bound up by the attendant priests, and if it showed no signs of infection upon the expiration of three days the defendant was adjudged innocent. In addition to the ordeals, much use was made of compurgation. In this method, the defendant was required to secure a designated number of compurgators, or "oath helpers," to attest his innocence, the number varying directly in accordance with the gravity of the offense charged and inversely in proportion to the social status of the accused. Homicides were punishable by the payment of wergelds, usually payable in cattle, with the number forfeited carefully graduated in accordance with the social status of

the slain person. In the same fashion, personal injuries of all sorts were punishable by the payment of bots to the aggrieved party or his relatives. 

The Germans were Christianized prior to the establishment of the Teutonic kingdoms. The work of conversion was begun by the 

Gothic missionary, Ulfilas, who came into the Empire as a hostage during the reign of Constantine. After his conversion to Christianity, he was given the powers of an itinerant bishop and commissioned to convert his fellow Goths. Unfortunately, Ulfilas was converted during the period of the temporary ascendancy of Arianism in the reign of Constantius, son of Constantine. All the Germanic tribes, therefore, with the important exception of the Franks, were converted to a type of Christianity that had been condemned as heretical at Nicaea and was destined ultimately to be completely repudiated. 

Religious differences between Romans and their Teutonic conquerors were a great barrier to racial fusion and were therefore largely responsible for the downfall of the Teutonic kingdoms erected on the ruins of the Empire. It is more than coincidence that the Frankish kingdom, the only one affiliated with the orthodox church, was the only one to emerge from the period of partial assimilation that followed the collapse of the Empire. 

THE MIGRATIONS 

The Germanic migrations that overwhelmed the Western Empire were, as we have seen, the climax to the gradual infiltration that had continued for centuries. Efforts at forcible mass infusion were successfully repulsed, however, until the Empire was so weakened from within by the various causes of decline already described that successful defense was no longer possible.

The immediate cause of the great wave of Teutonic migration that began in the second half of the fourth century was the westward sweep of the Huns. The Roman historian Ammonius Marcellinus has given a classic description of these invaders from the steppe region of Central Asia. Small in stature, swarthy in complexion, their beady eyes gleamed ferociously from faces with extremely flat noses. 

They led a nomadic existence; trained to the saddle from childhood, they were unrivalled as mounted warriors. Their sudden retreats and equally surprising counter-attacks usually completely disconcerted their adversaries. In the course of the westward advance, they first fell upon the great Ostrogothic kingdom, north of the Black Sea, that had been established by Hermanaric and subjugated it. The

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Visigoths, or West Goths, settled between the Danube and the Pruth, were terrified by the fate of their eastern kinsmen and pressed to the bank of the Danube where they asked imperial permission to cross the river to secure asylum in Roman territory. Permission was granted by the Emperor Valens on condition that the Visigoths surrender their arms prior to entering imperial territory. It was understood that the Roman government would undertake to support the refugees until such time as lands could be assigned and they could reap their first harvests. When they crossed the Danube, however, corrupt Roman officials robbed them of their chattels, but permitted them to keep their arms. Promises of support went unfulfilled until in desperation they began to harry Thrace. Valens hastily marched an army against them, refusing to await the arrival of reënforcements sent by Gratian, his imperial colleague in the West. The legions were overwhelmingly defeated in the battle of Hadrianople (378); Valens was killed and the impotence of the Empire to resist further Teutonic attacks was dramatically revealed.

Theodosius, who was elevated to the imperial position on the death of Valens and who became sole emperor with the death of Gratian (381), was able to pacify the Visigoths by allocating lands, enrolling their young men in the legions, and granting them the title of imperial allies. When the emperor died in 395, a new era opened in the relations between the Visigoths and the Roman government. 

The Empire again was divided. Honorius, one of the sons of 

Theodosius, received the West and was placed under the tutelage of Stilicho, a Vandal who had distinguished himself in the service of Theodosius. The East was assigned to Arcadius, the other son of the late emperor, who was placed under the guardianship of Rufinus, another minister of demonstrated competence and fidelity.

About the same time, Alaric was elected king of the Visigoths. 

Since the new king headed the faction of his people that were bitterly anti-Roman and opposed to Christianity, resumption of Visigothic belligerency was inevitable. Alaric led an army into Greece and sacked Athens. Although Stilicho cornered him at Pholoe, he did not follow up his victory, and eventually the Visigoths entered Italy (401). Alaric demanded the assignment of lands in Illyria and the position of magister militum, or commander of the imperial forces, but Honorius, shut up in virtually impregnable Ravenna, refused to grant these concessions. Stilicho, the one man who possibly could have saved Italy, was assassinated in 408. When Honorius continued to refuse Alaric's demands, despite the temporary occupa-

tion of Rome by the Visigoths in 409, the capital was thoroughly sacked in the summer of the following year (410). Shortly after this memorable event, Alaric died and was succeeded by his brother-inlaw, Athaulf. The newly crowned king led his people into Gaul and eventually Honorius gave official sanction to their occupation of the province. Under King Euric (466–484), the Visigoths entered Spain, where they established a kingdom that endured until the Moorish conquest of 711. Their militant Arianism prevented effective amalgamation with the Spanish provincials. Although they were converted to orthodox Christianity in the reign of Reccared (587-603), other causes of dissension arose and precluded effective resistance to the Mohammedan invaders.

While Italy was vainly attempting to defend itself against the Visigoths in the opening decade of the fifth century, the Vandals crossed the Rhine. They tarried for a time in Gaul, but ultimately settled in Spain. Here, pressure from the Visigoths, as well as the desire to secure the great granary of north Africa, impelled them to cross the Straits of Gibraltar under the leadership of King Gaiseric in 428 (or 429). North Africa was speedily conquered, with the provincials divided by religious heresy, and a Vandal kingdom of north Africa was established by 430.

In 450 another great Hunnic invasion led to further chaos. The 

Asiatic invaders, led by Attila, were turned aside from their attempt to seize the eastern provinces, and thereupon swept westward through central Europe and ultimately reached the heart of Gaul. 

They were turned back, however, at the battle of Chalons (451) by Roman forces under Aetius, assisted by a Visigothic army. Attila decided to return to the East, but on the way he invaded Italy (452). 

Because of the outbreak of a pestilence in his army and partly in response to the dramatic appeal of Leo, bishop of Rome, he refrained from an attack on Rome. He evacuated Italy and returned to his 

Asiatic empire, and with his death the following year, the Hunnic peril to Europe was dissipated almost as suddenly as it had arisen. 

In 455 Valentinian III, last legitimate emperor in the West, was murdered by the usurper Maximus. Possibly in response to an appeal from Eudoxia, widow of Valentinian, Gaiseric led a Vandal expedition against Rome. He captured the city and so thoroughly pillaged it that the term vandal has since denoted wanton destruction. 

With the return of Gaiseric to north Africa, the Eternal City came under the rule of a succession of Teutonic leaders who called themselves Patricians. While these Patricians did not themselves assume

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the purple, they dictated the choice of a series of "puppet emperors" whose every act they controlled. Ricimer, the first of the 

Patricians, ruled until 462 when he was assassinated and succeeded by Orestes. The new Patrician elevated his son to the throne of the 

Caesars under the name of Romulus Augustulus. In 476, however, Orestes was defeated and slain by Odovacar (Odoacer) who thereupon deposed Romulus. This event, obviously of little importance, often is interpreted as the event that marked the end of the Empire in the West.

Ten years after the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, a most significant event in this series of kaleidoscopic changes occurred with the establishment of the Frankish kingdom in Gaul. The Franks, who originally lived along the lower Rhine, crossed into Gaul under the dynamic leadership of Clovis and in the battle of Soissons defeated such Roman forces as could be mustered under the selfappointed general, Syagrius. The various tribes of the Franks were united by Clovis, and ten years after his establishment of the kingdom, he and many of his subjects were converted to orthodox Christianity, largely as the result of the influence of Queen Clotilda. As an orthodox Christian, Clovis became a favorite son of the church and consequently encountered none of the difficulties which were so serious in the Germanic kingdoms of the Arian faith. Indeed, in 507 he invaded the Visigothic kingdom of Spain, ostensibly in behalf of the true faith, but his attempt to annex the Spanish peninsula was frustrated by the intervention of Theodoric, ruler of the Ostrogoths in Italy, whose advent to power we must now briefly describe. 

While the Patricians were holding sway in Italy, the Ostrogoths recovered from the disaster of their conquest by the Huns and under the leadership of Theodoric entered Thrace. Here they began to put pressure on the Eastern Roman Empire and threatened even to attack 

Constantinople. Consequently, when Theodoric asked the emperor at Constantinople for permission to lead his people into Italy to recover it for the Empire, he was more than willing to grant the request. Theodoric led his warriors who were accompanied by their families into Italy, ultimately captured Ravenna, and put to death Odovacar. When Theodoric attempted to negotiate and have his status defined, Anastasius, who had succeeded Zeno as emperor in the East, assumed a lofty tone with the result that Theodoric assumed the title of "king of the Ostrogoths."

Theodoric, probably the most enlightened of the Teutonic rulers of the age of the migrations, had two cardinal policies. In the first

place, he promoted pan-Germanism; that is, he encouraged coöperation among the Germanic kingdoms established as a result of the invasions. Secondly, he was committed to the preservation of a "balance of power" among these kingdoms whereby none of them would become disproportionately powerful in respect to the others. 

It was this policy that doubtless dictated his intervention in Spain where he prevented Clovis from profiting from his defeat of King 

Alaric II of the Visigoths. 

During the reign of the Emperor Justinian (Eastern Roman Empire), 527-565, much of the territory lost to the Empire as a result of Scots

In 534 Justinian's general, Belisarius, conquered the Vandal kingdom of north Africa by taking advantage of the disturbed conditions brought about by the usurpation of the Vandal throne by Gelimer. North Africa was annexed to the Empire, which continued to hold it until the great expansion of Mohammedanism in the latter part of the seventh century. From north Africa, Justinian turned to Italy where dissension had arisen with the death of Theodoric. A series of campaigns, marked by heroic resistance by the Ostrogoths during the reigns of Totilla and Teia, placed Italy under imperial control by 551. The triumph was short-lived, however, for in 568 the Lombards swept into Italy under the leadership of Alboin and wrested north Italy (Lombardy) from the Empire. The capital of the Lombard kingdom

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

was established at Pavia, and imperial authority in the Italian peninsula was ultimately restricted to the region known as the Exarchate of Ravenna. Energetic successors of Alboin naturally strove to unite all Italy under their rule; this constituted an ever-present threat to the bishops of Rome and is a central fact in the period to the age of Charlemagne (768-814), particularly in the formation of the alliance between the papacy and the Frankish kingdom which will be described in a later chapter. 

With the Lombard invasion of Italy the first great period of barbarian migration into Europe closed. Roman institutions were largely replaced by Teutonic usages and customs, and Graeco-Roman culture received a staggering blow. The early Middle Ages were therefore destined to be a period of assimilation. Three elements entered into the evolution of medieval culture: what was left of the Graeco- 

Roman heritage after the collapse of the Empire in the West, the Germans, and the Christian Church. New institutions were arising, however, destined to aid in the gigantic task of reconstruction and to restore, at least in the institutional sphere, the unity lost with the fall of the Empire.

CHAPTER 17 Partial Restoration of Unity 

HE fourth and fifth centuries were a period of confusion, marked by the crumbling of the Roman Empire in the West. 

Internal causes of.decline prostrated the Empire, which was torn asunder by successive waves of Germanic invasion. The political and administrative unity, the cultural universality that characterized the Empire disappeared; and Europe seemed destined to revert to barbarism. At the very time, however, that the Empire disappeared as a political entity, new institutions and forces were exercising a unifying, cohesive tendency, which went far to relieve the centrifugal stresses.

THE EASTERN ROMAN EMPIRE 

The deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 marked the end of the Roman Empire as a political entity in the West. It must not be forgotten, however, that the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire continued in existence until the capture of Constantinople by the 

Turks in 1453.

The Eastern Empire performed a service of inestimable value to western Europe in the early Middle Ages. It absorbed the shock of many of the barbarian invasions of the second great period of folk migration. Slavs, Bulgars, Avars, and Hungarians buffeted it, but the invasions of these peoples spent their major impact without seriously affecting the West. Western Europe, beginning the slow recuperation from the disastrous migrations of the Germanic peoples and warding off incursions of Scandinavian marauders, was thus partly spared from invasions from the East, which, under the circumstances, would have greatly impeded, if not prevented, recovery.

During the reign of Justinian (527-565), the Byzantine Empire made material progress in the recovery of territory that had been lost in the West by the establishment of the Germanic kingdoms. 

The Vandal kingdom, wracked by political dissension and strife be-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tween Arian and orthodox Christians, was conquered in 534 by imperial troops under the command of Belisarius. It remained under the control of the Eastern Empire until the conquest of north Africa by the Mohammedans. The Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy, virtually impotent after the death of Theodoric the Great, was conquered by a series of invasions led by Belisarius and Narses (534-550). Italy, however, was invaded by the Lombards in 568 and the last remnant of Byzantine authority passed away with the abandonment of the 

Exarchate of Ravenna. 

One of Justinian's greatest contributions to civilization was the codification of the Roman law. A committee, under the direction of 

Tribonian, one of the greatest jurists of all time, labored over ten years at the gigantic task. The first part of the work to be issued was the Code, embodying a redaction of statute law. It contained decretals of the Roman Senate and praetorian edicts of the republican period, together with the edicts and rescripts of the emperors. The next portion to be completed was known as the Institutes and was intended to serve as a manual for students of jurisprudence. Precedents and decisions were edited in the colossal work known as the Digest (Pandects). The final portion, known as the Novels, codified all legislation of the age of Justinian. Many modern legal codes, notably the 

Code Napoléon of France, are based on the work of Justinian's reign. 

THE PAPACY 

Among the most important institutions which were exercising a unifying influence was the papacy. The controversial question of the origins of the papal office is important in that the issue is a fundamental difference between Catholics and Protestants.

The Catholic interpretation holds that Christ bestowed supreme authority in His church on Peter, who subsequently went to Rome and became the first bishop of that city; his successors inherited this authority, according to the doctrine of apostolic succession. The cornerstone of this doctrine is the well-known passage in the Gospel of Matthew (XVI, 17 ff.) wherein Christ is quoted as conferring on 

Peter the keys to the kingdom of heaven and the power of "binding and loosing." Peter is connected with Rome by the passage in First 

Peter where he writes from "Babylon." It was quite common for early Christians to speak of Rome as "Babylon "; if the epistle is authentic, this evidence is of significance. Then, too, Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans, speaks of his reluctance to “build on another's foundation." This is taken to indicate Peter's prior missionary activity

in the Eternal City. Within two generations after the Crucifixion, the tradition that both Peter and Paul had been martyred during the Neronian persecution secured well-nigh universal acceptance in the West, and the strength of this tradition is reasonably presumptive of essential validity.

Protestant students of the problem, however, point to the fact that no references comparable to the "Petrine Passage" in Matthew are found in the other Gospels. Indeed, when a dispute concerning precedence arose among the disciples, Christ is reported as having rebuked them. At best, biblical evidence is inconclusive, and non-biblical documentary sources are too meager and vague to justify any but the most tentative conclusions.

While the problem of the origins of the papal office cannot be definitively solved, the reasons for the gradual recognition of the primacy of the Roman Bishop are reasonably clear. Rome was a great city, the old capital of the Empire, around which clustered all the traditions of Rome's greatness as a world power. The intimate association of the bishop with the prestige of the city was alone sufficient to make him an important figure in the church. There were no emperors at Rome after 476, and freedom from governmental interference was an indubitable advantage. Rome was the only apostolic church of the West; moreover, by generally credited tradition at least, the Roman Church was founded by the two most important apostles, Peter and Paul.

The churches of the East were wracked by doctrinal disputes which frequently engendered schism. The Arians demurred at accepting Christ as coeternal and coequal with God the Father, while the Nestorians denied His divinity prior to His baptism. The Monophysites also held Christological views at variance with orthodoxy as defined by the Council of Chalcedon (451). Rome remained aloof from most of these doctrinal controversies; consequently the Bishop of Rome was an ideal mediator. As early as the second century, Pope 

Victor adjudicated the dispute concerning the proper date for the celebration of Easter, and this precedent of appeal to Rome was followed in a number of subsequent cases without, however, any unequivocal recognition of Roman primacy by the appellants. 

The statesmanship of Leo I (440-461) and Gregory the Great 

(590-604) contributed powerfully to the acceptance of papal claims of supremacy in the Western Church. In 452 Leo was credited with inducing Attila, the Hunnic chieftain, to refrain from an attack on Rome and three years later he at least was able to persuade Gaiseric

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

to mitigate the terrors of the Vandal pillage. Papal preeminence was vigorously asserted against Hilary of Arles, and heresy was suppressed with the assistance of secular authority.

Gregory defended Rome against the aggressions of the Lombards. 

The conclusion of a treaty with them, on his own responsibility, marks the beginning of the temporal sovereignty (political rule) of the popes in Italy. The Visigothic kingdom under King Reccared. renounced Arianism, and the Lombards, largely through the efforts of Queen Theudelinda, likewise accepted the orthodox creed. A beginning was made in the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons by the famous missionary expedition of St. Augustine, sent out by Gregory in 597. The papal patrimony in Sicily received the careful supervision of the pontiff, and the augmented revenue therefrom was a factor in entrenching the authority of the Roman See. By the close of Gregory's pontificate, the primacy of Rome in the church of the West was virtually unchallenged, but, as the acrimonious dispute with John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople, indicated, no such recognition could be secured in the East.

MONASTICISM 

Another religious development that exercised an integrating influence in the early Middle Ages was monasticism. The essence of monasticism is the ascetic ideal. The world and all its works are considered intrinsically unimportant and dangerous; the desires, appetites, and physical comforts of the individual, base and lustful. One can lead a truly righteous life only to the degree to which he withdraws from secular activities and abstains from the gratification of corporeal impulses. Monasticism is simply communal asceticism, for a group dedicated to this ideal lives under a rule designed to afford a minimum of concession to human frailty and to lay preponderant emphasis on devotional exercises. 

The popularity of asceticism in the early Middle Ages was basically a manifestation of prevalent skepticism and a reaction against growing tendencies toward materialism and worldliness in the church organization. The world of the ancients was collapsing; political turbulence, social and economic discontent, artistic and literary decadence, and moral laxity were everywhere apparent. What was more natural than that many should be obsessed with a sense of futility and turn their thoughts to the eternal life?

There were reasons, indeed, for earnest Christians to be dissatisfied with the church. Ritual, ceremony, and perfunctory conformity

had replaced the simplicity, spontaneity, and fervor of apostolic Christianity. Property was being acquired in ever larger measure and its management was engrossing no inconsiderable portion of the interests and energies of the clergy. There was complaint of unseemly solicitation of legacies and endowments, while the practice of bishops and other clergy assuming secular administrative duties likewise was censured. The theological controversies, marked by bitter invective, scurrility, and often violence, hardly seemed compatible with the teachings of Christianity. In view of these developments, it is not hard to understand why many believed that the way to salvation lay outside the bounds of institutionalized Christianity. Many besides the zealous were attracted to the ascetic way of life. Those temperamentally inclined to solitude and contemplation joined with those eager to attain holiness by sacrifice and self-abnegation. Others were drawn to the movement by the desire for public attention and approval.

The ascetic ideal first was manifested in the anchoritic form, that is, individuals retired from the world as hermits to live in squalor and solitude. St. Anthony was the first of these early recluses to attract wide attention. A youth of comfortable means in Alexandria, he decided to distribute his possessions to the poor and abjure the world. His reputation for piety spread, and his desert retreat was visited by thousands who marvelled at his austerity. Many were impelled to emulate him. He doubtless was the most important founder of the ascetic movement in Egypt; a biography of him, written by 

Athanasius, the doughty adversary of Arianism, did much to spread the movement to the West.

Asceticism in the East soon crystallized in the formation of monasteries. Pachomius of Alexandria devised a strict rule for the conduct of his famous community in the Thebaid; at one time, eight establishments were operated under his general supervision. St. Basil drew up a long list of precepts and admonitions which became the organic rule for scores of eastern monasteries. During the first half of the fifth century, communities were established in the West by St. Martin and others.

Serious abuses soon arose to cast disrepute on the monastic movement. Laxity in the enforcement of the rules was a perennial subject of complaint. Many monks tired of the restrictions imposed by the ascetic life and repudiated their vows. The "lunatic fringe" indulged in senseless, even revolting, austerities. Then, too, monasticism was striking at the institutional integrity of the church. If salvation was

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

to be achieved through the medium of asceticism, rather than through the services of the ecclesiastical organization, the basic justification for the existence of the church was jeopardized. 

The widespread adoption of the Benedictine Rule corrected the salient evils. This rule was promulgated c. 523 by St. Benedict of 

Nursia (c. 480-543), who devised it primarily for use in his monastery of Monte Cassino. The inherent excellence of the rule, however, rendered inevitable its almost unanimous acceptance by the monastic houses of western Europe. Benedict wisely provided for a one-year novitiate for all prospective monks. During this probationary period, the candidate was tested by menial tasks and other burdens to determine his fitness for the ascetic life. If he did not possess the sincerity and humility requisite for a monk, he could decline to take the vows without any reflection on his character. If, on the other hand, he successfully withstood the rigors of the novitiate, he took the irrevocable vows.

The fundamental vows were stability, obedience, and conversion. 

The first vow implied, of course, unqualified, permanent assumption of the duties of a monk. Obedience meant the virtual surrender of individual will, complete subordination to spiritual superiors. The vow of conversion required poverty and chastity; the monk was to possess literally nothing he could call his own and was to remain celibate.

A monastery of the Benedictine type was governed by an official known as the abbot (father). He was elected for life by the monks on the basis of equal suffrage. The abbot was vested with absolute authority and was primarily responsible for the orderly conduct of the house and the strict observance of the vows. Bishops were to exercise the right of visitation; that is, they were authorized to inspect monasteries in their dioceses to ensure compliance with the rule. This important provision averted a danger that monasticism would develop outside the church; henceforth the "regular" clergy constituted a branch of the ecclesiastical organization. 

The rule fully attained the essential ideals of asceticism, and its moderation and eminent practicability made strict observance feasible. The monks were to have nutritious food, the aged and infirm were to have wine, and special dietary concessions were to be allowed when warranted by the climate or other factors. An adequate supply of appropriate clothing likewise was provided. Manual work was to be performed by all physically able; thus idleness, which had produced so much mischief in earlier foundations, was avoided. A fixed routine allotted each hour of the day to work, formal devo-

tional exercises, private meditation, and other activities, and provisions for relaxation and recreation were not neglected. 

By 600, scores of monasteries of the Benedictine type had been founded in western Europe. Each establishment was autonomous, yet the rule was a common bond and constituted, therefore, one of the forces that was working to preserve a modicum of cultural unity. 

ISLAM 

The rise and expansion of Mohammedanism during the seventh and eighth centuries bound together a number of former provinces of the Roman Empire by the tie of a common religion. Christian and Mohammedan came in intimate contact in Spain and Sicily, and the superior Saracen culture was an important factor in the preservation and stimulation of the civilization of Christian Europe. 

Mohammed was born in Mecca, c. 570. Orphaned at a tender age, he came under the successive guardianship of his grandfather, Abd al- Muttalib, and his uncle, Abul-Talib. His boyhood was spent in dire poverty and he enjoyed no educational advantages. As a youth he secured employment from time to time as shepherd or camel driver.

He had, however, one claim to distinction in that he belonged to the tribe of the Koreish, the most aristocratic of all Arabia. The Koreish constituted a priestly clan to whom was entrusted the care of the temples and shrines consecrated to the polytheistic and idolatrous religion of Mecca.
