Their most important duty was the custody of the Kaaba, or sacred black stone, which, it was believed, had miraculously fallen from the heavens. 

The future prophet's marriage to Kadijah, a middle-aged, wealthy widow, who had employed him as the superintendent of one of her caravans, was a turning point in his life. Leisure gave him the opportunity to indulge in meditation and introspection; indeed, he began the practice of spending one month of each year in solitude on Mount Hira. Gradually the conviction grew in his mind that he was a man with a mission, and to one of his temperament the process of objectifying the subjective was not difficult.

Upon return from one of his annual periods of self-imposed exile, he claimed that the Angel Gabriel had appeared to him and directed him to become the prophet of the one true God, Allah. He had vainly protested that his illiteracy rendered him incapable of undertaking such a mission, but his misgivings had been allayed by the promise of divine inspiration that would make clear to him the nature and meaning of the teachings he was to disseminate. 

Kadijah, together with a little band of relatives and friends, pro-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

fessed conversion to the newly designated mouthpiece of Allah, but subsequent attempts to convert an appreciable portion of the citizenry of Mecca dismally failed. The prophet's uncompromising monotheism was counter to the traditions of centuries and subversive to the strongly entrenched interests of the priesthood. The Arabian metropolis was in the heyday of its prosperity. It was a thriving, bustling, commercial center, with a citizenry avidly seeking to exploit the opportunities thus presented. Avarice, merciless competition, even chicanery were the order of the day; therefore Mohammed's preaching, with its emphasis on righteousness, humility, and the blessings of poverty, could hardly attract sympathetic consideration.

Indifference soon gave way to active hostility. Finally, opposition to the allegedly revolutionary doctrines of the prophet culminated in threats against his life, and in 622 the danger became so acute as to necessitate his flight from the city. After a number of dramatic adventures, Mohammed and his faithful disciples arrived at Medina. 

The flight of the prophet (Hegira) is such an important event in his career that Mohammedans date events from the year 622, which is the year one of their calendar.

Favorable response to Mohammed's teachings was almost immediate in Medina. This city had long been a rival of Mecca, and the fact that Mohammed was a refugee from that city ensured sympathy and a hospitable reception. Judaism had gained considerable popularity in Medina prior to Mohammed's arrival. Since monotheism was an essential feature of the Jewish religion, there was at least a partial preparation for the reception of Mohammed's doctrines concerning the nature of God. Then, too, upheavals due to economic and social discontent had occurred, and the prophet's teachings were easily identified with these demands for social justice. 

Within a short time after Mohammed's appearance at Medina, not only was the religion of Allah triumphant, but the prophet was in supreme control of the affairs of the city. Revelations came in profusion. The prophet would fall in a swoon and upon emergence from the trance proclaim that which Allah had revealed to him. Devout believers paid careful heed to these utterances; after the death of the prophet, their recollections, aided by such notes as they had preserved, formed the basis for the preparation of the Koran. 

Success affected both the character of the prophet and the nature of his teaching. Vanity, arrogance, and opportunism became more and more apparent, and revelation doubtless was made, on occasion,

to serve political expediency, or even private ambition and desire. In the early years of his ministry, Mohammed had declared that the worship of Allah was to be spread solely by persuasion, but after his triumph he held that the sword was to be employed to force acceptance. The believers were urged to war upon the infidels; those who perished in battle were assured immediate and eternal reward in paradise. In accordance with this policy, Mecca was conquered in 630. At the death of Mohammed (632), his doctrines had been accepted by all Arabia.

Mohammed's teachings, as embodied in the Koran, are based largely on a superficial knowledge of Christianity and Judaism. The prophet consistently held that Christians and Jews had received valid doctrine, but he maintained that the revelations vouchsafed to him constituted the final and definitive dispensation for which the Hebrew prophets and Christ had prepared. On the nature of God, Mohammed differed sharply from Christian beliefs. He refused to recognize the divinity of Christ and was particularly vehement in his condemnation of the Christian concept of the Trinity, which he held to be a departure from true monotheism. 

The Mohammedan faithful were assured of immortal existence in a sensuous paradise. In the words of the Koran:

For him who dreadeth the tribunal of the Lord are prepared two gardens, planted with shady trees. In each of them shall be two fountains, flowing. In each of them shall there be of every fruit two kinds. 

They shall repose on couches, the linings thereof shall be of thick silk, interwoven with gold: and the fruits of the two gardens shall be near at hand. Therein shall receive them beauteous damsels, refraining their eyes from beholding any besides their spouses.

Those damned in the last judgment, however, were warned that: 

They shall dwell amid burning winds and in scalding water under the shade of a black smoke which is no shade, neither cool nor gracious . . . and they shall surely eat of the tree of El-Zakkourn and shall fill their bellies therewith and they shall drink boiling water thereon, even as a thirsty camel drinketh. They shall have garments of fire fitted unto them, their bowels shall be dissolved thereby and also their skins and they shall be beaten with maces of iron.

Duties of Mohammedans are much simpler and more tangible than those of Christians. Every believer is directed to conform to the four primary essentials: prayers, almsgiving, fasting, and pilgrimage; obedience ensures eternal felicity. The pious Saracen prays five

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

times a day while facing Mecca. There is no organized priesthood, but the Muezzdin summons the faithful to prayer at the proper hours. Services are held in the mosques on Fridays and are devoted to prayer and reading of the Koran, but attendance is not one of the fundamental duties. The obligation of charity is discharged by perfunctory and indiscriminate largesses which are granted, not to accomplish any social service, but merely to facilitate the salvation of the donor. The duty of fasting does not impose any arduous restrictions. During the sacred month, the believer abstains from certain foods and wine so long as he is able to distinguish a white thread from a black one without the aid of artificial light; at nightfall, of course, he is free to follow his normal dietary practices. Once in his lifetime, the believer is required to make a pilgrimage to Mecca. This can be done vicariously, however; indeed, one can avail himself of the services of a professional pilgrim. While on pilgrimage, the devout 

Mohammedan maintains strict celibacy, abstains from wine and meat, and eschews certain other bodily comforts. These restrictions lapse seven days after his arrival in the holy city. 

Mohammed's death in 632 produced consternation among his disciples. Although he never claimed divinity, many of the believers considered him immortal and therefore made no provision in regard to a successor. Extensive reversion to idolatry and the rise of impostors were the penalty for this lack of foresight. With full realization of the paramount necessity for organization if the religion was to survive, a group of leading disciples met at Medina and designated Abu-Bekr, one of the first converts, as caliph, or successor to the prophet. A council of elders and a group known as the “Companions of the Prophet" were chosen to assist the caliph in an advisory capacity.

The new organization functioned smoothly; lost ground was retrieved and expeditions under Osma began the penetration of Syria. 

In the caliphate of Omar (634-644), Persia was conquered by the well-nigh invincible forces under the command of Khalid. Mesopotamia, Syria, and Palestine were annexed, despite the efforts of the Byzantine emperors to stem the tide. The earlier policy of forced conversion was abandoned, and Islam was modified so as to mean payment of tribute and political subordination rather than acceptance of the prophet's teachings. Christians and other dissenters in the subjugated areas were granted almost complete toleration. 

The election of Omar's successor produced dissension. Othman (644-656) of the Ommiad family was elected, much to the dismay

of the supporters of Ali, the nephew of the prophet. The march of conquest, however, was uninterrupted; expansion continued in north 

Africa, while Cyprus was annexed in 652. Othman was assassinated in 656, and Ali was chosen as his successor, but the partisanship and family rivalry were not allayed. The capital of the Mohammedan empire was shifted to Damascus. Factional strife culminated in the murder of Ali, who, as the husband of Mohammed's daughter, Fatima, had both hereditary and elective rights to the caliphate. Hassin and Hosein, the sons of Ali, also were slain.

The election of Muawyah brought respite from the internal quarrels, and a second great period of conquest began. Asia Minor was conquered, and in 717 Constantinople was threatened. All of north 

Africa was under Saracen control by 708, and three years later Abuel-Tarik conquered Spain. The defeat of the Mohammedans at Tours in 732, by the Frankish army under the command of Charles Martel, marked the limit of their expansion in Europe. 

By 750, the Mohammedan world had fallen into fundamental schisms. On the question of doctrine, the Sunnites, who accepted the Sunnas, or legal code, as authentic, were opposed to the conservative Shiites, who held that these so-called revelations were spurious. 

The rise of the Abbassid caliphate at Bagdad brought about the downfall of the Ommiad dynasty, but Spain refused to recognize the Abbassid dynasty and established an independent Ommiad caliphate at Cordova. By the ninth century another dynasty appeared with the establishment of the Fatimate caliphate at Cairo.

Saracen learning was considerably in advance of that of Christian Europe, especially in the fields of mathematics and science. By the tenth century, Christian scholars frequently considered it necessary to complete their education by a sojourn in Spain. The great influence of Saracen culture on the West was not to come, however, until the age of the crusades.

CHAPTER 18 The Frankish Kingdom and the Carolingian Empire 

HE trend toward the restoration of unity and cultural revival received powerful impetus with the establishment of the Frankish Empire. When Pope Leo III crowned 

Charlemagne emperor in 800, there even seemed to be a chance for the restoration of political union as it had existed under the Roman 

Empire. 

The Franks entered Gaul during the period of the barbarian migrations. Prior to their entry they had lived along the right bank of the Rhine, near its mouth. They were organized in a number of tribes, the most important of which were the Salians and Ripuarians. 

Led by Clovis, the Franks defeated an army under Syagrius, “King of the Romans," at Soissons in 486. The basis for the assumption by 

Syagrius of the position of representative of Roman rule in Gaul is unknown; he probably had taken advantage of the confusion attendant upon the Frankish invasion to usurp command. The victory of Clovis was decisive; he and several tribal kings were in possession of that part of Gaul north of the Loire. 

Clovis, a son of Childeric, was reputed to be a descendant of Meroveus, who, according to tradition, gave the name of Merovingian to the ruling dynasty of the Salians. He married Clotilda, a niece of 

King Gundebad of the Burgundians. Clotilda had been converted to orthodox Christianity prior to the marriage, and doubtless was partly responsible for her husband's eventual espousal of Christianity. 

The conversion of Clovis in 496 was an event which more than any other fixed the destiny of Gaul." The Frankish warriors complacently followed the leadership of their king in accepting the new faith. Whereas Vandals, Visigoths, and Ostrogoths were Arians, the 

Franks adopted the orthodox, trinitarian form of the Christian faith. 

There were consequently no religious barriers to the rapid fusion of 66

FRANKISH KINGDOM AND THE CAROLINGIAN EMPIRE 243 

Franks and Gallo-Romans and this factor was largely responsible for the survival of the kingdom.

Clovis rapidly extended his authority by the incorporation of the remaining independent tribal units. Duplicity, devious intrigue, and assassination were his weapons, yet his religious orthodoxy sufficed to induce Gregory of Tours to say, in his History of the Franks, "Thus in all things did God prosper Clovis because he walked with an upright heart in the sight of God." The attempt of Clovis to annex the Visigothic kingdom of Spain (507) assumed the appearance of a crusade against Arianism and was enthusiastically supported by the Frankish Church. At the battle of Vouglé, Alaric II, the Visigothic ruler, was vanquished and slain. The project for annexation was abandoned, however, due to the forceful intervention of Theodoric the Great, who wished to preserve a balance of power among the Teutonic kingdoms. 

After the death of Clovis in 511, his kingdom was divided among four sons. The kingdom was considered the personal property of the ruler and was shared equally in accordance with the Salic law. By 

558, Chlotair of Soissons reunited the kingdom, but the conception of the state had not advanced, for in 561 at the death of the king, a second fourfold division occurred. Charibert received Paris; Chilperic, Neustria; Sigibert, Austrasia; and Gontram, Burgundy. These divisions survived, with but intermittent consolidations, until 687. 

The later Merovingian period was one of civil war, turbulence, and lawlessness that bordered on anarchy. The enmity between 

Brunhilda of Austrasia and Fredegunda of Neustria was largely responsible for these chaotic conditions. Brunhilda, a Visigothic princess, had married King Sigibert of Austrasia. Favorably impressed by her beauty and personality, Chilperic of Neustria successfully negotiated for the hand of her sister, Galswintha. Fredegunda, a concubine of Chilperic who hitherto had enjoyed great influence with the Neustrian ruler, bitterly resented this humiliation and brought about the murder of her rival. Brunhilda vowed vengeance and a deadly feud ensued. The Pact of Andelot (587) which provided for the union of Burgundy and Austrasia greatly enhanced the power of that kingdom and accentuated the rivalry with Neustria. In 612, following the death of her grandson, the nominal king, Brunhilda attempted to rule Austrasia officially, and a revolt of the nobles was precipitated which culminated in her execution. The Perpetual Constitutions of 

Paris, promulgated by the nobles in 613, indicated to what degree the turbulence of these years had weakened royal authority. The

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

nobles demanded immunity from taxation and cancellation of obligations associated with grants of land they had received from the kings. The clergy claimed freedom from the jurisdiction of secular courts and asserted the right of holding elections to church offices free from royal supervision.

Amalgamation of Austrasia and Neustria under King Dagobert 

(629-639) gave some promise of permanent union and the restoration of royal authority sufficiently strong to curb the pretensions of nobles and clergy, but after his death such hopes soon were dispelled. 

The destiny of the Frankish kingdom could not be achieved under the Merovingians.

RISE OF THE CAROLINGIAN DYNASTY 

The Merovingian kings employed officials known as Mayors of the Palace, whose duties originally were to supervise the royal households and serve as stewards of crown estates. Owing to the incapacity and indolence of most of the kings, the mayors were in a position to exercise more and more influence on governmental policies. 

They granted audiences, dispensed justice, raised and commanded troops, and were responsible for capitularies nominally issued by the kings. 

Pepin of Landen, Mayor of the Palace for Austrasia after 612, was largely responsible for the extended authority of the office. His land holdings were enormous, and his power was further strengthened by the marriage of his daughter to the son of Arnulf, archbishop of Metz. Grimowald, Pepin's successor as mayor, banished the Merovingian ruler and attempted to secure the coronation of his own son. 

This attempt proved premature, for the nobles rose in support of legitimacy, but it foreshadowed the imminent deposition of the 

Merovingian dynasty. A period of anarchy followed. Ebroin, mayor of Neustria, vainly attempted to curb the excesses of the licentious nobility. The fact that St. Leger, bishop of Autun, was a leader of the most tumultuous faction is striking evidence of the prevalent disorder. 

The elevation of Pepin of Heristal to the position of Mayor of Austrasia, in 687, was a turning point in Frankish history. He defeated the Neustrians in the decisive battle of Testry, a victory which achieved the long sought union of the two kingdoms, and Pepin was king of the Franks in fact if not in name. 

Pepin was able to establish firmly the principle of hereditary succession to the office of mayor. He extended Frankish rule to Aleman-

FRANKISH KINGDOM AND THE CAROLINGIAN EMPIRE 245 

nia, Thuringia, and Bavaria. Frisia was converted to Christianity by the missionary labors of Wilfrid of York and came under Frankish influence. Failure to prevent the creation of an independent Aquitaine, however, produced much subsequent difficulty. 

Pepin bequeathed his powers to his widow, Plectrude, who was to act as regent until a minor grandson attained majority. Charles Martel, an illegitimate son, was denied a share in the administration and imprisoned to prevent any attempt at revolt. Plectrude, however, was incapable of dealing with the problems that arose. Neustria revolted under the leadership of Regenfrid, who had usurped the position of mayor for that region. Frisia, in the midst of a pagan reaction led by Ratbod, joined the movement, as did also Aquitaine. 

Early in 715, Charles Martel escaped from custody and assumed control at this crisis. Support of the nobles was secured and steady progress was made toward quelling the revolt until, at the battle of Vincy (717), the supremacy of Austrasia was vindicated. A series of campaigns along the eastern and northeastern frontiers against the Saxons were a harbinger of their eventual subjugation by Charlemagne. 

In the meantime, the Saracens had swept into southern France from Spain. Arrest of this advance was imperative, and Charles raised a powerful army, in which he relied heavily on cavalry. Support of the nobles was secured by grants of land which Charles seized from the church. The battle of Tours (732) was an overwhelming victory for the Franks; the Saracens retreated to the south, and after several minor campaigns in Aquitaine the danger of Mohammedan domination was permanently ended. Charles had performed a great service for the kingdom and for Frankish Christianity, but the church denounced him for his confiscations of ecclesiastical property. 

PEPIN THE SHORT: ALLIANCE WITH THE PAPACY 

Upon the death of Charles Martel (741), Pepin the Short (Le 

Bref) (741-768) and Carloman jointly succeeded him. Danger of strife and disunion was averted, however, by the retirement of the latter to the monastery of Monte Cassino.

Pepin pursued a vigorous expansionist policy. The revolts of Bavaria were suppressed, and Frankish control of the duchy was tightened. An offensive campaign against Chunoald of Aquitaine resulted in the acquisition of Poitou and, in some measure, neutralized the trend toward Aquitainian independence. 

A series of synods under the presidency of St. Boniface purged the Frankish Church of some notorious abuses. Crude superstitions

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of the laity were condemned and the standard of clerical morality was raised. Adoption of the Benedictine Rule by all Frankish monasteries was strongly urged and in most instances secured. 

The main interest of the period centered in the relations between the Frankish kingdom and the papacy. Pepin realized that the continued tenure of the royal dignity by the Merovingian dynasty was an anachronism, in view of the fact that all power by this time was concentrated in the hands of the Mayor of the Palace. He accordingly sent an embassy to Pope Zacharias, requesting papal approval for the deposition of the Merovingian puppet king. The desired sanction was extended, and in 751 Boniface anointed and crowned Pepin as king of the Franks. The Carolingian Revolution was thus completed. The support of the pope laid the foundations of a close understanding between the papacy and the Frankish monarchy, and Pepin soon had an opportunity to reciprocate for the service rendered him. by the Holy See.

Italy, it will be remembered, was conquered by the Lombards, under the leadership of Alboin, in 568. The Lombard kingdom began to split up into a number of duchies with the close of the reign of Cleph (575), but unity largely was restored during the reigns of 

Authari (584-590) and Agilulf (590-615). The Eastern Roman Em pire maintained precarious control of the region around Ravenna (the Exarchate of Ravenna), but was not in a position to check further aggressions by the Lombards. Gregory the Great realized the impotence of the exarch and accordingly negotiated directly with the Lombards, procuring their promise to refrain from attacks on Rome. The conversion of the invaders to orthodoxy, due largely to 

Gregory's labors, the settlement of the land question, and the progress of Romanization did much to allay friction and produce the cordial relations of the reign of Rothari (636–652).

The situation nevertheless was dangerous to the papacy. It was inevitable that aggressive Lombard rulers would attempt to unite Italy under their sway. This inevitably would mean progress toward the annexation of Rome and consequent curtailment of papal independence. When Liutprand (712-744) attempted to unite the duchies of 

Spoleto and Beneventum with the Lombard kingdom, with the incidental incorporation of lands belonging to the papacy, the full gravity of the crisis became apparent. Gregory III appealed to Charles 

Martel for aid in resisting the Lombard encroachments, but Charles was defending the Frankish kingdom against the Saracens and therefore was unable to respond.

FRANKISH KINGDOM AND THE CAROLINGIAN EMPIRE 

247 Lombard aggression continued under King Aistulf (749–756). In view of the support granted to Pepin the Short in the deposition of the Merovingians, it was natural for Pope Stephen II to appeal for Frankish aid. At the request of the pope, Pepin sent an escort to conduct him to Frankish territory for an interview. The pontiff arrived early in 754, and his meeting with Pepin was made a dramatic occasion. Barefoot, in sackcloth and ashes, he prostrated himself before the Frankish king and implored his aid. When Pepin promised his support, the pope repeated the coronation ceremony of 751 and publicly anathematized all who would venture to impugn Pepin's title to the Frankish throne.

A short campaign (755?) sufficed to coerce Aistulf into an agreement to refrain from policies objectionable to the pope. The agreement was repudiated, however, as soon as Pepin's forces were withdrawn. In response to Stephen's truculent letters, Pepin led a second expedition across the Alps in 756, and Aistulf was decisively defeated. 

In addition to reaffirming his promises of the preceding year, he was forced to relinquish possession of the Exarchate of Ravenna, which Pepin thereupon bestowed on the pope. This was the famous Donation of Pepin (756) which created the nucleus of the Papal States. 

As a result of this event, the popes were destined to be the political sovereigns of much of central Italy until 1870; indeed, Vatican City represents the last remnant of the Papal States. Legally, of course, Pepin's action was invalid in that the Byzantine Empire still was normally sovereign in Italy. It was doubtless the realization of the precarious title of the papacy that motivated the preparation of the forged Donation of Constantine sometime during the eighth century.

THE AGE OF CHARLEMAGNE 

Charlemagne (Charles the Great) takes rank with the foremost figures of all history. He was the chief architect of an empire that was worthy of comparison with that of ancient Rome. The inspiration of his many-sided genius laid the foundations for important institutions of the Middle Ages, and his efforts in education led to a revival of cultural interest that aptly has been called the Carolingian Renaissance. From the pages of Einhard, his contemporary biographer, there emerges the picture of a man of powerful physique, boundless energy, forceful personality, and incisive intellect. 

In 768, as in 741, the Frankish kingdom was threatened with disunion and internecine strife. Charlemagne began to reign jointly with his brother, Carloman. Their clashing personalities led from mutual

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

dislike to an open break, due to divergent Italian policies. Carloman's withdrawal from a joint campaign in Aquitaine engendered bitterness that doubtless would have culminated in civil war, but his death in 771 averted this calamity.

One of the major interests of the period was the conquest of the Saxons. The Saxons lived in the region of the Elbe and the Oder rivers and had not evolved beyond the tribal stage and the primitive culture described by Tacitus. Frontier clashes between Saxons and 

Franks were perennial, and the desire to arrest these forays doubtless was a motive for Charlemagne's policy. Other motives included a sincere wish to Christianize these heathens; the desire to enhance opportunities for trade; and, of course, the eagerness for aggrandizement to be expected of a ruler of Charlemagne's personality.

The campaign of 772-774 resulted in the partial conquest and superficial conversion of the Saxons. Charlemagne's departure for 

Italy, however, was the signal for a fierce reaction, during the course of which the Christian priests were driven out and their churches destroyed. Promises of Frankish concessions in return for allegiance were made at the Diet of Paderborn (777), but these efforts came to naught when Widikind, a great national leader, arose among the Saxons and stimulated them to concerted and passionate defense of their independence.

Charlemagne attempted to intimidate the recalcitrants. In his wellknown Saxon Capitulary of 782, he ordered them to accept baptism on pain of death. The capital sentence also was to be inflicted on those who refused to pay tithes or who ate meat during Lent. This harshness merely goaded the Saxons into renewed rebellion. In 783 

Charlemagne had 4,500 Saxons beheaded at Verden in a single day.

Several thousand were deported and their lands assigned to Frankish colonists, but terrorism brought no progress toward the attainment of the fundamental objectives.

Widikind's conversion and baptism in 785 proved the turning point; Saxon resistance collapsed rapidly with the defection of its outstanding leader. Doubtless more material considerations than conversion had been instrumental in bringing about Widikind's sudden profession of Christian belief.

Charlemagne had learned the futility of severity in dealing with the Saxons and considerably moderated his policy after 785. Alcuin had prophesied that if "the same pains be taken to preach the easy yoke and burder. of Christ as are taken to collect the tithes from them," the resistance would subside; his predictions were substan-

FRANKISH KINGDOM AND THE CAROLINGIAN EMPIRE 

249 tially correct. In the Second Saxon Capitulary of 797, the objectionable features of earlier legislation were repealed or modified. With the establishment of peace, assimilation rapidly proceeded. 

The invasion of Spain was directly connected with the great schism in the Mohammedan world. By 755, there was an Abbassid caliphate at Bagdad and an Ommiad dynasty at Cordova. Disaffected

Abbassids in Spain appealed to Charlemagne to overthrow the Ommiads by conquering the Emir of Cordova. Southward expansion had been an intermittent Frankish interest since the attempt of Clovis to conquer the Visigoths. The projected expedition also had the guise of a crusade of Christians against the followers of the prophet. 

Charlemagne's expedition won a series of easy victories until checked at Saragossa. Renewed outbreak of the Saxons necessitated abandonment of the siege (778), and while the retreat was in progress, the Frankish rear-guard was ambushed by Basque tribesmen at Roncesvalles. Among those who perished was Roland, around whose almost legendary figure grew up a series of chivalric tales and romances, and these Songs of Roland occupy a place in French literature comparable to the Arthurian Romances in English.

Bavaria made an effort to regain independence in 787. The duchy had been Christianized by St. Columban and other Irish missionaries and had embraced the usages of Celtic Christianity. These Celtic practices were banned by the reform synods held by St. Boniface, under the auspices of Pepin the Short, and a smouldering resentment thus was produced that hindered the fusion of Frank and Bavarian. 

The Italian policy of Charlemagne was also bitterly resented by Tassilo, the Bavarian duke. The rebellion was suppressed by a single campaign; the Diet of Ingelheim deposed and imprisoned Tassilo and took measures to ensure Frankish supremacy. 

The frontier policy of Charlemagne was marked by vigor and foresight. The Avar "Ring" was smashed by 795, and the "Mark" (frontier province) of Friuli established to prevent their rising. The "Mark" policy also was used to curb the Slavs, resulting in the formation of the Marks of Thuringia and Bohemia. The Danish 

Mark (Denmark) was organized to ward off attacks by the Norsemen.

The policy of Charlemagne toward the papacy was a logical development of the fundamentals as established by Pepin. In 770, there was acute danger that the understanding between the Frankish kingdom and the Holy See would be terminated. Charlemagne, despite the protests of the pope (Stephen III), married Desiderata, daughter

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of Desiderius, the Lombard king, while his brother Carloman was betrothed to a Lombard princess. These acts obviously constituted a complete reversal of earlier Frankish policy, but before the effects became apparent, Charlemagne sent Desiderata back to her father for unknown personal reasons and ruptured the tentative alliance with the Lombards. His action also widened the breach with Carloman and alienated Tassilo, the Bavarian duke, who was married to a sister of Desiderata.

When a break came between Pope Hadrian I and Desiderius, because of the latter's seizure of Ferrara, Comachio, and Faenza, the pope tried to restore the Frankish alliance. Charlemagne refused to go any further than to attempt to bribe the Lombard king to restore the papal territory he had seized. In 773, however, Charles was reliably informed that Desiderius was attempting to stir up civil war among the Franks by pressing the claims of the children of Carloman. This put a different face on the matter and he accordingly marched an army into Italy in 774, defeated Desiderius, and after the capture of Pavia assumed the Lombard crown.

The papal office brought power, wealth, and the disposal of enormous patronage to its incumbent. Naturally enough, partisanship and factionalism began to accompany the choice of popes. When Leo III was elected as the successor of Hadrian, he dismissed many who had been appointed to church offices by his predecessor. The resentments thus produced flared up in riots during the course of which Leo was attacked and badly beaten (799). Sheltered by supporters until sufficiently recuperated, he secretly journeyed to Charlemagne, to whom he appealed for help in securing reinstatement. Charles sent the pope back to Rome with an escort and promised to come in person to punish those guilty of the assault. In the meantime, the issue was complicated by charges preferred against the pope; the Frankish ruler promised a full hearing.

In the winter of 800, Charlemagne arrived in Rome. Leo was permitted to clear himself of the accusations against him by his unsupported oath. Paschalis and Campanus, leaders in the attack on the pope, were sentenced to death but were subsequently pardoned. 

On Christmas, 800, Charles attended services, and while he was kneeling before the altar, the pope placed a crown on his head and saluted him as emperor. Endless discussion has been precipitated by this incident. Einhard maintained that his hero was taken completely by surprise. Certainly, Charlemagne desired coronation as successor of the Caesars and was engaged in negotiation with Constantinople to secure the approval of the Byzantine authorities. The time was

FRANKISH KINGDOM AND THE CAROLINGIAN EMPIRE 

251 propitious for his coronation. Irene had blinded her son, Constantine VI, and usurped the Byzantine throne. Legally, it could be held that a vacancy existed at Constantinople, since there was no precedent for female rule, and the coronation of Charles could be technically construed as a revival of the Western Empire. The Eastern 

Church had broken with the West on the iconoclastic issue; that is, the decrees of the Byzantine emperors against the use of images were enforced in the East but repudiated by the West. The interests of the papacy obviously were best served by alliance with the Franks. 

What could be more logical than a revival of the Western Empire, with pope and emperor acting in concert? If Charlemagne did resent the action of Leo, it was not because of any reluctance to assume the imperial office, but because of unwillingness to permit the implication that the crown was within the gift of the papacy, that the church was a higher authority than the state. 

ADMINISTRATION OF CHARLEMAGNE'S EMPIRE 

Charlemagne's authority was absolute, tempered only by deference to custom and tradition. Great emphasis was placed on oaths of fidelity. There was no regular taxation. The major revenue of the king was derived directly from crown estates. Charlemagne held 

1,615 domains, ranging in size from one to seventy manors. He was precise in the management of his estates, as testified by the famous capitulary De Villis. Tolls and market dues furnished a fairly constant source of income as did also fines levied in the courts, two-thirds of which were payable to the royal treasury. Confiscations, escheats, plunder from campaigns, and gifts from nobles and clergy augmented the normal income from time to time. 

A group of administrative officials were in constant attendance upon the king. The chaplain conducted judicial hearings and issued the capitularies. The chancellor served as an assistant to the chaplain. 

Financial matters were under the supervision of the chamberlain. 

The seneschal supervised the household servants, while the butler took care of the royal cellar. Military affairs came under the jurisdiction of the constable, who led the cavalry on campaigns. A host of lesser dignitaries, such as masters of hounds, falconers, masters of the royal beavers, etc., swelled the royal retinue. The capital of the Empire was wherever Charlemagne happened to be; his favorite residence, however, was at Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle). 

Each May the army assembled at a designated point, preparatory to the beginning of the annual campaign. Charlemagne usually took this opportunity to announce capitularies for ratification by accla-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mation. These "Mayfields" were not legislative bodies, nor were their reactions to the king's legislation official or binding. In autumn, the leading nobles and clergy were summoned to meet the king to discuss such matters as he chose to submit to them. The assembly divided into two separate bodies; the clergy discussed matters that concerned religion and the church while the lay nobles deliberated upon questions of secular interest. Joint sessions were held if the issues did not belong clearly to either category. These “Autumnal 

Assemblies" were a survival of the old Folk Moots. They were without real power for their function was solely advisory. 

The basic unit of local administration was the county, ruled by a count (graf). The counts were appointed by the crown and served at the pleasure of the king, but they never ceased to labor to make their offices hereditary. The counts performed a variety of important duties. They assembled and led the military contingents for the annual levies. They were responsible for the policing of their counties and served as judges of first instance in capital cases or those which involved the penalties of mutilation, imprisonment, or confiscation of estates.

Scabini, or assessors, well grounded in the law, assisted the counts in the discharge of their judicial duties. County court was held every forty days and theoretically was attended by all free, adult males. 

The counts were responsible for the collection of royal revenues, but they were not permitted to exercise any authority over royal estates in their counties, for these were managed by stewards responsible directly to the king. The counties were divided into units known as hundreds, which were under the control of Centenarii, or Hundred Men. The hundred court met monthly for the adjudication of petty cases.

A major problem of government was to preserve centralized authority in order to curb extortion and malfeasance by the counts. To deal with this problem, Charlemagne ingeniously devised a system of supervision by traveling inspectors known as the Missi Dominici (802). The Empire was divided into circuits for purposes of regular inspection and supervision. Two missi were assigned to each circuit and were expected to travel around it four times per year. One of the missi was a layman, the other a cleric; this arrangement was a safeguard against collusion to defeat the fundamental purposes of the system.

The missi travelled from county to county, meeting the courts which the counts summoned in anticipation of their coming. From

FRANKISH KINGDOM AND THE CAROLINGIAN EMPIRE 253 

the assembled freemen of each county, the missi selected a panel of twelve who were then sworn to answer truthfully the questions put to them. The missi then questioned the panel concerning county affairs, especially in regard to the conduct of the count. The answers were recorded and sent to Charlemagne, and if the report of the count's conduct was unfavorable, he was removed. The system was one of the roots of the inquisitorial procedure later adopted by the church and it also was a forerunner of the jury. 

CHARLEMAGNE AND EDUCATION 

Charlemagne made the encouragement of learning a paramount objective of his reign. A capitulary of 780, addressed to the abbots of the kingdom, recommended greater zeal in making available instruction for those able to profit by it "so that those who desire to please 

God by living rightly should not neglect to please him by speaking correctly, for it is written either from thy words shalt thou be justified or from thy words shalt thou be condemned." Another capitulary, issued before 800, ordered the clergy "to join and associate to themselves not only children of servile condition but also sons of freemen." He further directed that "schools be established in which boys may learn to read, and may acquire knowledge of the Psalms, the signs of writing, the songs, the calendar, and the grammar.' 

About 802 he ordered "that all laymen shall learn thoroughly the 

Creed and the Lord's Prayer." 

Sons of the nobles attached to the court were educated in the famous Palace School which was directed by Alcuin, an English scholar of international repute, whom Charlemagne had induced to come to his court. Promising boys of humbler parentage were admitted also, and the king delighted to shame indolent young nobles by the example of the industry and attainments of poor boys. Interest in adult education likewise was stimulated, and the king himself set the example by becoming one of Alcuin's pupils. He acquired a reading and speaking knowledge of both Latin and Greek, but he never succeeded in mastering the intricacies of writing, despite assiduous practice. The Frankish emperor doubtless "takes a foremost place among the benefactors of mankind as a man who himself imperfectly educated knew how to value education in others. He is a ruler to whom more perhaps than to any other single individual we owe the fact that the precious literary inheritance of Greece and 

Rome has not been altogether lost to the human race.”

CHAPTER 19 Breakup of the Carolingian Empire: 

Feudalism HARLEMAGNE'S empire did not long survive the death Co of its founder in 814. In 806 Charles provided for a threefold division of territory under his rule, assigning approximately equal portions to Charles, Pepin, and Louis. Charles and Pepin died before their father, and Louis (the Pious) succeeded to the rule of the whole Empire.

Periodic marauding expeditions of the Norsemen constituted a grave problem. Many of the forays of these hardy seafarers were motivated solely by the desire for pillage, but trade expansion also was an important consideration. By the tenth century, the desire to colonize provided the impetus for a number of Viking expeditions and resulted in the settlement of Iceland and Greenland. France was particularly vulnerable to Norse attacks because of the many rivers that led from the coast deep into the interior. England and Ireland were severely harried and portions of these countries were intermittently under Scandinavian rule; England became part of the great empire of Canute (1016-1035).

The typical Viking vessel was an open boat about 150 to 175 feet long, with high prow and stern. It was propelled by rowing, but was fitted with a square, auxiliary sail which was utilized whenever the wind was favorable. About forty rowers manned the oars; the warriors crouched in the spaces between the benches and from time to time relieved the oarsmen. The warriors carried spears, axes, swords, and large round shields, with heavy bosses, which they hung along the sides of the ship while on a voyage. An oarsman in the stern steered the boat. With nothing but the stars to guide, the navigators boldly pushed out to open sea and even succeeded in crossing the 

Atlantic. Pigeons were sometimes released to determine the direction of land when the normal means of navigation could not be utilized.

FEUDALISM 

255 The rapidity of their movements made Viking raids difficult to check. They ordinarily would row up a stream as far as possible, beach the boats, and forage the surrounding countryside for horses with which, when secured, they greatly extended the sphere of their operations. Churches, monasteries, and towns were sacked and destroyed, but walled towns were seldom attacked, since the marauders lacked time and equipment to conduct a siege. Enormous quantities of booty were secured, and successful raids naturally led to more. 

Louis the Pious (814-840) and his successors were faced with the primary duty of organizing effective resistance against the Viking forays, but largely because of dynastic quarrels, the task was not adequately discharged. Resort to tribute merely stimulated the avarice of the invaders. Assignment of responsibility to individuals hastened the collapse of the Carolingian Empire and promoted the process of feudalization which had been going on since Merovingian times.

Louis the Pious was hardly fitted to rule an empire in a time of crisis. Patient and indulgent, he refrained from severe measures where severity clearly was demanded. Conscientious and capable of acting on occasion with resolution, he was, nevertheless, too amenable to personal influences and, above all, too pliable toward churchmen. Temperamentally, he was better adapted for the cloister than for the council chamber; indeed, he frequently retired to a monastery for short sojourns. The banishment of several important ministers of 

Charlemagne immediately upon his accession, while perhaps justified on moral grounds, created a nucleus of dissension that was to plague the emperor for the duration of his reign. 

The sons of Louis the Pious bickered about their prospective inheritance and importuned their father to settle the matters at issue. 

In 817 the emperor was injured when a wooden bridge from his palace to the chapel collapsed. He interpreted his narrow escape from death as a premonition and decided to set his house in order. One son, Louis the German, was placed in charge of Bavaria and was promised Austrasia; Pepin received Aquitaine with the understanding that he was to receive Neustria at the death of the emperor; while 

Lothair, the eldest son, was placed in command of Italy and admitted as an imperial colleague.

There was an unfortunate aftermath to this division of 817. Bernard of Italy, the nephew of the emperor, had been a loyal subject, and he naturally expected to share in any division of the Empire, because Italy had been assigned to his father, Pepin, by Charlemagne's

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

arrangements of 806. His resentment was fostered by disgruntled nobles until he was induced to revolt. Louis suppressed the rebellion with unwonted speed and severity. Bernard was captured and sentenced to death. At the suggestion of Ermingarde, wife of the emperor, the sentence was commuted to blinding, but the operation resulted in Bernard's death. Louis never ceased to regret this tragic event, and his contrition doubtless was a key to his subsequent policy respect to his sons. in Louis soon had added reason to repent his responsibility in Bernard's death. Ermingarde's death within a year the emperor viewed as providential punishment for his crime. So great was his remorse that he threatened to abdicate and become a monk, but the nobles dissuaded him and urged him to remarry, and he finally became sufficiently interested in Judith of Bavaria to defer to their wishes. The marriage was to prove a calamity.

Tortured by remorse for the death of Bernard, Louis publicly confessed his guilt and submitted to penitential scourging - the penance of Attigny (822). This self-abnegation merely revived the matter in the public mind and detracted from the dignity which is one of the most effective weapons of monarchy, and greatly weakened the emperor's prestige.

In 823 Charles (the Bald) was born of the union of Louis and Judith. Judith naturally demanded the admission of her son to such territorial settlements as had been made, but since the division of 817 had made no provision for a fourth son, no territory could be assigned or promised to Charles without reducing the shares of his half brothers. When Louis finally gave in to Judith and announced a new division (829), which assigned to Charles territory originally promised to Lothair, the beneficiaries of the division of 817 rose against the emperor and deposed him. Louis refused to renounce his position, however, and public sentiment veered to his support. At the Diet of 

Nimwegen he was reinstated (830) with the aid of Louis the German.

The emperor forgave his rebellious sons, but in doing so made a serious mistake. A veritable revolution occurred in 832-833. The movement began when Pepin aimed to renounce his father's authority in Aquitaine. As the emperor prepared to quell the rebellion, Louis the German likewise revolted. The emperor made tentative peace with Louis the German by cession of some territory he had assigned to Charles the Bald. Charles was compensated by the grant of 

Aquitaine, which the emperor declared Pepin had forfeited because of his rebellion. This action obviously was unjust, for Pepin had

FEUDALISM 

257 been no more guilty than Louis the German. Lothair, who hitherto had remained aloof, then joined his brothers in the rebellion. 

In the spring of 833, the emperor faced the combined forces of his sons on the upper Rhine. Pope Gregory IV, hoping that Lothair would be recognized as emperor, journeyed to the encampment, ostensibly to mediate in the interest of peace. Actually, however, he and his legates sowed dissension in the emperor's army and induced the troops to desert. Duped, forsaken, and defenseless, Louis fell into the hands of his sons. He was forced to abdicate and to perform another public penance at St. Medard (833). Another reaction resulted in his restoration to power the following year. A new partition of territory, favorable to Charles the Bald, caused Louis the German to revolt in 838, and the death of Pepin the following year reopened the whole partition issue. The last year of the unfortunate reign was spent in a campaign against Lothair and Louis the German. 

As could be expected, the death of Louis the Pious (840) set the sons against each other. Charles the Bald and Louis the German united to defeat the forces of Lothair at Fontenoy (841) in an effort to seize possession of the rich Rhinelands to which Lothair laid claim. 

Their alliance was cemented by the famous Strasburg Oath of 842. 

This oath is of great interest, especially to philologists. The supporters of Charles the Bald took the oath in a Germanic dialect in order to be intelligible to the partisans of Louis, whereas the latter's followers repeated the oath in old French. This document shows the beginnings of two modern languages, French and German, and also shows that the eastern part of Charlemagne's empire was drawing away from the western portion; Germany and France were in the process of birth.

The matters at issue with Lothair were settled by a compromise. 

A survey of the economic resources of the territory in dispute made by a commission (842) resulted in the Treaty of Verdun of 843.

Charles the Bald received the French portion of the Empire; Louis, the German territories. A long, narrow strip from the North Sea to the Alps, bounded roughly on the west by the Meuse, Saone, and Rhone rivers, and on the east by the Rhine, was joined to Italy as the share of Lothair, who was also confirmed in possession of the imperial title. The treaty did not aim to divide territory, for division of economic resources was the basic objective; hence, natural frontiers were ignored. The great struggles between France and Germany for the possession of the Rhinelands might have been avoided had the Rhine, the natural boundary, been established as the frontier in 843.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The Middle Kingdom was divided upon the death of Lothair in 

855. The northern portion, thereafter known as Lotharingia, went to Lothair II; Charles of Provence received the Rhone region; while 

Louis II received Italy and the imperial crown. Fifteen years later (870), on the death of Lothair II, Lotharingia was divided by the Treaty of Mersen into German and French Lorraine, assigned respectively to Louis the German and Charles the Bald. 

Charles the Bald was crowned emperor in 875; the following year, his attempt to seize Germany, at the death of Louis the German, was checked at the battle of Andernach. After his death (877), the 

French Carolingians proved incapable of dealing with the Norse invasions, with the result that the Capetian dynasty was established in 987 with the coronation of Hugh Capet. In Germany, Charles the Fat was deposed in favor of Arnulf (887), an illegitimate Carolingian. 

With the choice of Conrad I (911) Germany repudiated the hereditary claims of the Carolingians and established an elective principle that was to be retained, in theory, during the medieval period. 

The progress of feudalism under the later Carolingians was clearly evident. Charles the Bald, in his Edict of Pitres, ordered the nobles to destroy the castles they had built, since they were using these strongholds as bases for brigandage and defiance of the monarchy, but the law remained a dead letter. The same king, in the Edict of 

Mersen, directed every freeman to attach himself to a lord in order to facilitate defense of the realm against the Norsemen; this, of course, only gave legal sanction to conditions already in existence. 

In the Edict of Quiercy sur Oise, Charles authorized inheritance of crown offices as a temporary expedient during his sojourn in Italy (877). Here again the law merely sanctioned a custom of long standing, for the tendency to make appointive offices hereditary was irresistible and a potent force toward feudalization. 

The ninth century then was a period of most significant transition. 

The Carolingian Empire was breaking up, due to the impact of the 

Norsemen coupled with the internal strife of the period 814-877.

Centralized government broke down, and society had to evolve institutions to discharge the basic functions of government; the result was feudalism.

FEUDALISM 

Feudalism may be defined as a spontaneous organization of society, based on land tenure and personal obligations, wherein the normal functions of government are privately performed.

FEUDALISM 

259 Roots of feudalism can be found in the late Roman Empire. Smallscale landowners, unable to meet the competition of the large estates and bear the burdens of taxation, frequently surrendered their holdings to powerful landlords and thereupon received permission to continue to occupy the land upon payment of a portion of the crops or the performance of stipulated services. This form of tenure was known as praecarium, since the former owners became tenants at will who could be dispossessed by the new owner at pleasure. Private landowners, as well as the government, often settled peasants on unworked lands as colons, or serfs, on condition that they pay a portion of their produce to the landlord or to the state. The practices in the Empire strongly suggest the economic phase of feudalism. 

Many citizens in the late Empire became clients of powerful personages in order to obtain protection against banditry, the exactions of the tax gatherers, or injustices in the courts. The clients, in return for this protection, performed stipulated services for their patron. 

The institution of clientage was similar to the relationship that existed between suzerain and vassal under the feudal regime. 

Those who contend that the roots of feudalism are to be found in the tribal customs of the early Germans emphasize the Teutonic institution known as comitatus. Young warriors often undertook to serve a chieftain in return for economic support, and the parallel with feudalism is, of course, striking. Basically, however, feudalism was a natural response of society to the conditions of the time; the roots of the institution in antiquity were perhaps ancillary, but certainly not necessary, causes for its evolution.

Feudalism was, first, an implied contract between two individuals that entailed mutual privileges and responsibilities. Entrance into this personal arrangement was known as the ceremony of homage. 

The minor party to the agreement, known as the vassal, knelt before the major party, the suzerain. He placed his hands in those of the suzerain and promised to be his man. The suzerain then raised the vassal to his feet; the vassal thereupon took an oath, known as an oath of fealty, wherein he agreed to perform faithfully the services and obligations attendant upon the homage he had done.

Homage was not exclusive, for one could become the vassal of a number of suzerains if only simple homage had been rendered. Liege homage, on the other hand, could be done to only one suzerain, and took precedence over any other feudal duties. One could be the suzerain of one individual and the vassal of another; bewildering complexity characterized feudal relationships.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

In the second place, feudalism had an economic, proprietary aspect. Normally, upon the completion of the ceremony of homage, the suzerain bestowed upon the vassal an economically valuable consideration, known as a benefice. The benefice usually was a tract of land, together with all appurtenances, and was then spoken of as a fief. In feudalism, then, personal and proprietary elements were inseparably connected. A vassal could divide his fief and grant portions to vassals of his own. This practice was known as subinfeudation. 

Feudalism was also a form of government, a political institution. 

The suzerain, within his domain, represented government to his vassals. He raised and commanded military levies, dispensed justice in his feudal court, and performed the paramount service of protection. The governmental powers of suzerains seem to have grown up as a result of the practice of granting immunities. As far back as the 

Merovingian period, the kings issued these charters of immunity which rendered the recipients free from the interference of royal authorities within the area comprehended in the grant. These grants were originally contingent and limited to the recipient, but the tendency to assert the principle that immunities, like crown offices, were hereditary, proved irresistible. The practice of granting immunities to individuals and ecclesiastical foundations increased progressively in the Carolingian period, except during the reign of Charlemagne. 

Under the later Carolingians, all semblance of conditional restriction was thrown off, and many usurped the privileges of immunity without even the formality of procuring a charter of authorization. 

The king had no place in feudal society except as one, and by no means the greatest, of the feudal suzerains. His sovereignty shrank until it embraced only feudal authority over the vassals who held fiefs from the crown estates. The national histories of several European countries during the Middle Ages revolve largely around the project of gradually restoring the concept of sovereignty. 

Feudalism was a social order, an economic system, and a form of government, the basic characteristic of which was the fusion of personal, proprietary, and political elements. The mutual obligations and privileges of feudalism were sanctioned by custom. The implied contract was bilateral, for each party derived advantage by adhering to it. The suzerain's basic obligation was to grant a fief to the vassal and to allow him to hold it so long as he performed the services incident thereto. The suzerain, furthermore, was expected to afford protection to the vassal against any third party. He was required to treat

FEUDALISM 

261 the vassal with respect; a blow or an insult to the vassal's wife or family voided the agreement.

The suzerain was required to render justice to the vassal. This obligation required him to hold a court, which the vassals attended in order to assist in pronouncing judgment. The court took cognizance of disputes between the suzerain and the vassal, as well as those which involved two or more vassals. The court was the basic organ for the interpretation and enforcement of the privileges and responsibilities of the feudal regime.

A vassal's basic obligation was military service. Usually, this duty was limited to forty days per year. The vassal was required to serve at his own expense in the army of his suzerain for the stipulated time; in the event the vassal subinfeudated his fief, he often shared the military obligations with his own vassals. A fief for which the full quota of forty days' service had to be rendered was often spoken of as a "Knight's Fee." The vassal also was required to furnish advice and counsel to his suzerain upon request. As previously stated, he was obliged to attend the sessions of the suzerain's court to render judgment, since a vassal could be judged only by his fellow vassals, his peers (pares), or equals.

The suzerain enjoyed the rights known as the feudal dues. When the vassal died, his heir was allowed to succeed to the fief upon payment of a "relief," or inheritance tax, the amount of which was fixed by custom. If the vassal's heir were a minor, the suzerain had the right of wardship; that is, until the heir reached his majority the suzerain was his guardian. During the period of wardship, the fief reverted to the suzerain's control, and all revenue therefrom went to him, with the proviso, however, that nothing could be taken which would permanently lessen the value of the fief. When the heir reached the customary age (21-25 years), he paid a relief and entered in full possession. If a woman inherited the fief, the suzerain had the right of “marriage "; that is, he could require the heiress to marry someone chosen or approved by him. This provision, of course, ensured against possession of a fief by a person inimical to the interests of the suzerain. 

Originally the suzerain had the right to levy monetary contributions (tallage) from the vassals without restriction. Custom soon limited tallage to the following payments, known as the feudal "aids." When the suzerain's eldest son became a knight, he could call on his vassals for contributions to defray the cost of the cere-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mony and the festivities that followed. Likewise, when his eldest daughter was married, he enjoyed the right to collect a similar "aid." 

If the suzerain was captured and held for ransom, his vassals were required to raise the sum demanded. After the eleventh century, vassals were often expected to pay an “aid " if their suzerain went on a crusade.

CHIVALRY 

Both suzerains and vassals were nobles; there was nothing socially derogatory in vassalage, for even kings were vassals for particular fiefs. It was a common saying in the Middle Ages that God had ordained three classes of society: the nobles, to fight; the clergy, to pray; and the common people, to work.

Chivalry was a code of ideal conduct for the nobility which emphasized military gallantry for the men and romance for the ladies. 

Nobility did not admit to knighthood. Knighthood was bestowed in recognition of conspicuous valor and military prowess and could be granted only by one already invested with the honor. The prospective knight, as a boy, served in the castle as a page; his primary duty was to serve the ladies and thus acquire the courtesy and charm of manner which his future status would require. As a youth, he served a knight as a squire, caring for his horse and weapons. When his training was considered sufficient, his master or some other knight would agree to perform the ceremony. The candidate spent the night before the ceremony in a night-long vigil before the altar, standing watch over his armor and sword. On the morrow, the candidate knelt before his sponsor who gave him the accolade, or stroke on each shoulder with a sword, and thus "dubbed " the candidate a knight. Of course, many knights were dubbed on the battlefield without these elaborate preliminaries, and on occasion, commoners were admitted to knighthood in recognition of exceptional gallantry. 

The knight usually dedicated his valor to his " lady " and wore one of her intimate belongings as a talisman; his exploits were for her benefit and honor, especially during tournaments. Much of the interest of chivalry centered in the tournaments. Individuals, sometimes groups, tilted against each other under the admiring eyes of their fair patronesses; frequently the tournament was as bitterly fought as a pitched battle. Private warfare was common; a major object was to capture opponents and hold them for ransom. 

Many of the more important feudal nobles possessed castles. These structures were designed primarily as fortifications. They were surrounded by massive walls; usually a moat crossed by a drawbridge

FEUDALISM 

263 surrounded the wall. The gate was guarded by bastions, and a heavy, spiked, barred door, known as the portcullis, could be dropped in the gateway in event of attack if time did not permit closing of the gates. The main citadel was known as the donjon, or keep. A dependable well or two would be found in every castle courtyard, and magazines of food supplies were kept filled as a safeguard in the event of an unexpected siege. Romance was second only to military exploits in the interest of the feudal nobles. Songs by wandering minstrels and recitation of romantic verse enlivened many a dull evening in the castle. "Courts of Love," wherein questions of romantic interest were discussed, were a favorite amusement.

CHAPTER 20 Germany and the Holy Roman Empire to 

1056 ERMANY, in the early Middle Ages, was part of the Carolingian Empire. Its nucleus was the old kingdom of Austrasia, to which were added by the Carolingians, Bavaria, Thuringia, Alemannia, and Saxony. The old Frankish stock never fused with the Gallo-Romans of the western part of the Empire; there was a constant centrifugal pull that made inevitable the breakup of Charlemagne's empire, even had no other causes of disintegration been present. The Strasburg Oath of 842 shows to what degree the tendency to separation had proceeded, while the Treaty of Verdun destroyed any remaining hope of preserving territorial integrity.

Louis the German, at the death of Louis the Pious (840), became the ruler of the German portion of the Carolingian Empire. He was perhaps the most capable of the sons of Louis the Pious. Upon his death in 875, his kingdom was divided among three surviving sons. 

Charles the Bald, ruler of the French portion of the Empire, attempted to despoil his nephews of their inheritance, but at the battle of Andernach (876) he was repulsed and forced to recognize the independence of the German kingdom. By 885 Charles the Fat, sole surviving son of Louis the German, reunited the German kingdom. 

In view of the fact that Charles the Simple, the only available Carolingian in the West, was a mere child, the nobles and prelates invited Charles the Fat to assume the rule of France, so that for two years France and Germany were consolidated. Charles the Fat proved indolent and stupid, and his incompetence to deal with the problem of the Norse invasions led to his deposition in Germany at the Diet of Tribur (887), and similar action was taken in France. 

When the German nobles deposed Charles the Fat, they elected Arnulf (887-899), an illegitimate descendant of Charlemagne, as

king. This marks the first assertion of the elective principle in Germany; election by designated nobles and clergy became the usual method of determining succession to the throne.

The triumph of particularism was complete. Berengar was recognized as king of Italy; Rudolph secured control of Upper Burgundy, while Boso was crowned king of Lower Burgundy. Arnulf set the seal on the disintegration of the Carolingian Empire by granting 

Lorraine to his illegitimate son, Zwentibold.

The rise of the Moravian Empire under Svatopluk threatened the existence of an independent Germany. Bohemia and Poland were incorporated and serious inroads were made along the eastern frontier; but Arnulf checked Svatopluk's campaign of expansion and hastened the dissolution of the Slavic Empire. 

In 896 Arnulf led an expedition to Rome, in response to an appeal of Pope Formosus, who was hard pressed by partisan enemies. In gratitude for this assistance, the pope crowned him emperor. This event was to have momentous consequences, for it began the fatal connection between Germany and Italy that was to be disastrous to both countries. Germany failed to achieve national unity in the Middle Ages primarily because her kings were preoccupied with the affairs of Italy. Pursuit of the chimera of empire prevented proper attention to pressing domestic problems. The attempt to assert imperial authority in Italy eventually precipitated a bitter quarrel between emperors and popes and aroused the Italic towns to resistance; these struggles powerfully contributed to the political failure of Italy.

The reign of Louis the Child, son of Arnulf (899-911), was devoid of interest. His death marked the end of the Carolingian line, and the nobles elected Conrad of Franconia (911-918). The major problem that confronted the medieval kings of Germany was the existence of the powerful duchies of Saxony, Swabia, Bavaria, Thuringia, and Lorraine. These duchies were sometimes spoken of as the stemduchies, since they were survivals of old tribal divisions. Provincialism and local jealousies were rampant, and the dukes of the stemduchies were in a position virtually to defy all attempts to establish a centralized German monarchy. The historic mission of Germany was to evolve a nation; failure to do so was largely due to the complications of the imperial policy in Italy. 

Conrad devoted himself to the establishment of royal authority over the recalcitrant dukes. He relied heavily on the support of the clergy to accomplish his ends, but the prelates extorted lands and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

immunities as the price of their loyalty. The king prevented Arnulf of Bavaria from exercising sovereign rights in his duchy, but his attempt to deprive Henry of Saxony of the duchy of Thuringia, which he claimed as his wife's dowry, failed. Erchanger and Berchtold were put to death for devastating lands belonging to the Bishop of Constance, with whom they were quarreling over the possession of Swabia. The king's severity in this instance merely accentuated the opposition of the nobles, while any attempt to assert authority over the clergy alienated a class whose support was considered indispensable. On his death-bed, Conrad advised his son to renounce any desire to secure election as his successor and directed that the insignia of royalty be offered to Henry of Saxony, the most powerful of the feudal lords, and, consequently, the one most likely to succeed in establishing a centralized government. Formal election ratified the action of Conrad; messengers sent to notify Henry (the Fowler) of his election found him engaged in his favorite pastime of snaring birds.

Henry vigorously rebuffed the attempts of the clergy to assert disproportionate influence in the government, and he signalized his break with the policy of his predecessor by refusing to permit his coronation by the Archbishop of Mainz. Since Conrad had failed to secure the allegiance of the nobles by severity and intimidation, Henry utilized the method of conciliation. Arnulf of Bavaria was authorized to appoint bishops in his duchy. He was also empowered to issue charters and mint money, and the concession of virtually unrestricted sovereignty made him an ally of the king. 

Incursions of the Hungarians along the eastern frontier constituted a grave problem. The capture of a Hungarian chieftain (924) gave

Henry an opportunity to extort a nine-year truce, during which time he agreed to pay a tribute to the barbarians. This respite was used by the king to good advantage. A number of walled strongholds were established along the eastern border. Some of the soldiers were assigned to guard duty and military training, while others labored in fields and workshops to produce necessary supplies for the garrison. 

The tasks were rotated periodically, so that each man performed the requisite amount of military duty. When the Hungarians demanded augmented tribute upon the expiration of the truce, Henry defied them. Their invasions were repulsed, and as a result of the battle of 

Unstrutt (933) they were forced to make peace. The establishment of the frontier posts gave great impetus to the development of towns and was thus of permanent value.

The reign of Otto the Great (936-973) was doubtless one of the most important periods in German history. His authority was challenged almost immediately after his accession by a formidable coalition of nobles. Thankmar, an illegitimate half-brother, was a ringleader of the rising, as was also a younger brother, Henry, who claimed to be the rightful heir to the throne in that he had been born while Henry the Fowler held royal power. Eberhard of Franconia,

Gilbert of Lorraine, and the Archbishop of Mainz also joined the movement. For a time, Otto's deposition seemed inevitable, but with the defeat of Eberhard and Gilbert at Andernach by forces under the command of Conrad the Red, loyal supporter of the king, the rebellion was suppressed. 

Otto then decided to rely on his relatives to rule the duchies, in the hope that family loyalty would obviate danger of rebellion. 

Conrad the Red, who married the king's daughter, was placed in charge of Lorraine. Henry of Saxony was forgiven for his complicity in the recent uprising and put in charge of Bavaria, while Liudolf, Otto's son, was given Swabia.

In 951 Otto was invited to intervene in the complex political situation in Italy. A number of claimants were attempting to secure recognition as king. Berengar II of Ivrea, one of the leading candidates, hoped to bolster his position by forcing Adelaide, the widow of Lothar, a former rival, to marry his son. Adelaide refused for political and personal reasons and was imprisoned in a monastery in an effort to break her resolution. A faithful retainer brought word of her plight to Otto, together with a personal letter in which she besought his assistance. Otto responded in true chivalric fashion; he led an army into Italy, rescued the unfortunate Adelaide, and subsequently married her.

The first Italian expedition had repercussions in Germany. Otto's son, Liudolf, disobeyed his father's orders and led a force into Italy in advance of the main body, and only the prompt arrival of Otto's troops extricated him from the difficulties in which his stubbornness and incompetence involved him. When chided for his rashness, he returned to Germany in high dudgeon and raised the standard of revolt. Frederick of Mainz joined the movement, and even Conrad the Red wavered in his allegiance to the king. This revolt convinced 

Otto that relatives were no guarantee against insurrection and he adopted the system of putting churchmen in high administrative posts. The scheme had obvious advantages. In the first place, the prelates usually were men of education and administrative ability.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

They had no heirs and consequently were not concerned with the establishment of hereditary dynasties in the regions committed to their charge. There was also a danger in the system. The churchmen were subject to the pope, and if pope and king ever came in conflict they would be placed in a most unfortunate position. This situation did not arise in Otto's reign, but the Investiture Struggle (10751122) brought up the problem, as will be pointed out in a later chapter.

The Hungarian menace was revived with a series of attacks in 954-955. After Otto suppressed the rebellion of Liudolf, he was in a position to take the field against the invaders, whom he defeated decisively at the battle of Lechfeld (955).

Otto's second Italian expedition was necessitated by events at Rome. Pope John XII, son of Albert, a former claimant to the Italian throne, was hard pressed by Otto's old antagonist, Berengar of Ivrea. The pope promised to crown Otto emperor if he would come to his assistance. The German forces entered Rome without encountering serious resistance, and in February, 962, the pope invested Otto with the imperial title. This event marked the beginning of what was known as the Holy Roman Empire. Most of the medieval kings of Germany followed the precedent set by Otto and procured coronation, with the understanding that they thereby became the special protectors of the Holy See.

Relations between Otto and John XII soon became strained. Sundry charges of licentiousness and administrative abuses were levied against the pope. It also became known that he was in secret intrigue with Berengar for the purpose of securing his aid in driving the Germans from Italy. Otto accordingly convoked a synod, made up primarily of churchmen opposed to the pope, and pronounced his deposition. The synod, acting at the behest of Otto, then elected 

Leo VIII to be pope. A faction of Roman nobles, alarmed at the prospect of German control of the papal office, held a caucus and elected an anti-pope, but their candidate soon was forced to relinquish the position.

The main interest in the closing years of Otto's reign was his attempt to secure recognition of his imperial authority from the Byzantine emperors. This project was coupled with the desire to procure the cession of Apulia and Calabria, still nominally under the jurisdiction of the Eastern Roman Empire. An embassy headed by 

Liutprand was rebuffed by the Emperor Nicophorus, but when John succeeded to the throne at Constantinople, he reversed the policy of

his predecessor and agreed to the marriage of the Princess Theophano to the future Otto II. 

The reign of Otto II (973-983) well illustrated the dangers inherent in division of royal interest between Germany and Italy. The power of Bavaria constituted a grave menace to the monarchy. Judith, the widow of Henry the Wrangler, ruled the duchy as regent for her son, Henry the Quarrelsome. Her daughter, Hedwig, was married to Burkhard II, duke of Swabia, while the Bishop of Augsburg was her nephew. Otto naturally desired to break up such a formidable concentration of power, and the issue was raised with the death of Burkhard of Swabia. Hedwig, relying on her mother's support, demanded the right to succeed her late husband, but Otto, to challenge the power of Bavaria, bestowed Swabia on Otto the

Younger, son of Liudolf. As the king had anticipated, this precipitated a general revolt of south Germany. Boleslav of Bohemia and

Mesco of Poland threw their support on the side of the Bavarian coalition, but the power of Saxony and the steadfast support of the bishops enabled Otto to suppress the uprising. At the Diet of Ratisbon, Henry the Quarrelsome was deposed and Bavaria shorn of much of its power by the creation of the duchies of Carinthia and Verona, the allocation of the Nordgau to Berthold of Babenberger, and the assignation of the East Mark to his brother, Leopold. All these new principalities were carved out of former Bavarian territory, and their establishment accelerated the process that was to make the map of Germany a crazy quilt" by the sixteenth century. 66 King Lothair of France attempted to take advantage of the disturbed conditions in Germany by a sudden assault on Lorraine, which he temporarily annexed to the French monarchy. As soon as the Bavarian rising was suppressed, however, Otto retaliated by an invasion of France. His armies actually threatened Paris, until recession of Lorraine induced the king to order their withdrawal. 

Obviously, Otto's duty was to remain in Germany to complete the work of pacification and centralization. Nevertheless, he succumbed to the lure of Italy and, in 980, proceeded to Rome where he assumed the imperial crown.
