He then marched into Apulia with the idea of annexing that part of Italy, nominally part of the Byzantine Empire, but actually overrun by the Saracens. A great disaster befell him at the battle of Colonne, in Calabria (982). His army was cut to pieces by the Saracens, and only luck prevented his capture. by the enemy. As an aftermath of this crushing defeat, news arrived that the Slavs along the Elbe had taken advantage of the em-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

peror's absence from Germany to revolt. The Mark system, for the most part, held firm and prevented the uprising from becoming general. While preparing for another expedition into Apulia, Otto died in Rome (December, 983).

Otto III (983-1002) succeeded to the throne under the regency of Adelaide and Theophano. His tutor was Gerbert, famous scholar and former Archbishop of Rheims. When Otto assumed personal direction of affairs, he led an army into Italy, in order to allay the disorders precipitated by the Crescentian faction. Gregory V, a 

German, was elected pope, and he reciprocated by crowning Otto emperor (996). Crescentius, however, again raised the standard of revolt as soon as Otto's troops left Italy. Fearful reprisals were visited upon the leaders of the rebellion and the anti-pope whom they had named. Crescentius himself was captured and tortured to death, and his mutilated remains were hung on a gibbet. When Gregory V died (999), Otto named as his successor his preceptor, Gerbert, who took the name of Sylvester II. Grandiose ambitions ran through the mind of Otto. He and the pope, in collaboration, would restore the Roman Empire of the Caesars; church and state would represent the same universal power in different spheres of activity. Unfortunately for his dreams, the populace of Rome was not fired with similar enthusiasms. Open revolt flared up from time to time, and the emperor dragged out his reign in vain attempts to establish his authority. 

During the period of the Saxon emperors, the elective principle was practically in abeyance. The death of Otto III brought the dynasty to an end and once more afforded opportunity for nobles and clergy to assert their traditional rights of election. The election of 1002 was marked by great bitterness; Henry of Bavaria finally seized the throne and his elevation was ratified by the electors. A major problem of the reign was the expansion of Poland under Boleslav, who had forced on his backward subjects the adoption of Christianity and a modicum of Roman culture. Efficient organization of the army and the establishment of an effectual administrative organization raised the power and prestige of the duchy. Moravia, Silesia, Pomerania, and Bohemia were rapidly annexed, and the continued growth of the Polish state naturally threatened the eastern frontier of Germany. Henry's policy was ineffectual, however, largely because of his preoccupation with the Italian problem; he consequently signed the Peace of Bautzen, wherein Boleslav was recognized as king of Poland and permitted to retain his territorial acquisitions.

Otto III. Henry invaded the peninsula in 1004 and assumed the Italian crown at Pavia, but the Polish threat necessitated his return to Germany. Ten years later he marched to Rome where he was crowned emperor by Benedict VIII, and Arduin eventually made his submission. Henry desired the imperial title primarily to lend authority to his efforts to reform the church. Simony, or the sale of church offices, clerical marriage, abuse of the rights of ecclesiastical patronage, and the ignorance and immorality of the clergy were evils that demanded correction. The emperor held a number of synods to deal with the problem. The establishment of the monastery at Cluny, in 

910, on endowments provided by William of Aquitaine, had generated a great force for reform, and now a number of monasteries of the Clunaic type were founded in Germany that became a potent factor in purging the German Church of some of the more notorious abuses. 

Conrad II (1024-1039) faced the usual revolts upon his accession. 

After the restoration of order, he led an expedition to Italy, where he was crowned emperor by John XIX. A revolt, headed by the 

Archbishop of Milan, was a harbinger of the growing opposition of the cities of north Italy to German imperialism; this opposition ultimately culminated in the formation of the famous Lombard League. 

Henry III (1039-1056) ascended the throne with the German kingdom at the zenith of its power. Bavaria, Swabia, and Franconia were directly under the control of the crown; Saxony was administered by the devoted Adalbert of Bremen. France was weak, and friction with the Danes along the northern frontier had abated because of Conrad's cession of Schleswig. Bretislav of Bohemia and

Casimir of Poland ultimately became allies; while Hungary, Christianized under King Stephen (1000-1038), was relatively quiet, although German attempts to regulate the succession to the throne were rebuffed.

Henry's piety and his subservience to the church led to excessive grants of property and immunities to the clergy; dissipation of crown estates was an especially dangerous policy. The king's interest in 

Italian affairs was incident to the project of church reform. Conditions in Rome were appalling. Benedict IX, who had disgraced the papacy by his misconduct, sold the office to Gregory VI, who wished to raise it from the degradation into which it had fallen as a result of Benedict's excesses. A faction of Roman nobles named 

Sylvester III, in opposition to Gregory, and the situation became more intolerable with the re-assumption of the papal title by Bene-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

dict. Each of the three rival popes maintained a court and issued anathemas against his rivals. 

Henry convoked the Synod of Sutri (1046) immediately upon his arrival in Rome. The rival popes were deposed, and Clement II, a 

German, was named to the office. Clement then bestowed the imperial crown on Henry. From 1046 to 1059, the popes were named by the German rulers. The passage of the Electoral Decrees (1059), in the pontificate of Nicholas II, however, provided a method of election that raised the office above the factionalism and partisanship that had brought about the revolting conditions of the tenth and early eleventh centuries. These decrees created the College of Cardinals which ever since has elected the popes.

CHAPTER 21 The Crusades 

ROM a broad point of view, the crusades constituted a chapter in the struggle between oriental and occidental civilizations that began with the Persian invasions of Greece. They were also a phase of the duel between Christianity and Islam. In the seventh and eighth centuries, Islam had been on the offensive; Spain had been won and the followers of Allah had penetrated to the heart of France, only to be turned back at the battle of Tours. The crusades represented a Christian counter-offensive. The church held that the religion of Christ was the one true religion and all other cults were false and idolatrous. True Christians were bound to propagate the faith in order to bring the priceless gift of salvation to all.

Where missionary work could not avail, use of the sword was justified, in view of the magnitude and nature of the objective. Crusades constituted an ideal manifestation of the ideal of a "church militant." 

A basic cause for the crusades was the decline of the Byzantine Empire. Its endless struggles with barbarians had taken heavy toll, and no complete recovery had been made from the exhaustion produced by the great struggle with Persia. Dynastic quarrels had arisen from time to time with disastrous effects. Religious controversies militated against ecclesiastical solidarity, for imperial interference prevented the Patriarch of Constantinople from asserting authority comparable with that exercised in the West by the pope. Productive elements in society staggered under onerous taxation due largely to the enormous expense of providing defense for endangered frontiers. 

Syria had been reconquered by 969, but when the Seljuk Turks seized control of the Bagdad caliphate, they began a new and unusually vigorous offensive against the Empire. Syria was reconquered, as a result of the battle of Manzikert (1071), and this victory opened the way to the invasion of Asia Minor. In 1089 Jerusalem fell before the Turks, and a few years later Nicaea was captured and the fall of Constantinople seemed imminent.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

After the battle of Manzikert, Michael VII appealed to Pope Gregory VII for aid. The idea of a western expedition to rescue the 

Holy Land from Mohammedan control was not new; Sylvester II had considered such a project feasible. Gregory was willing to undertake the mission, but the outbreak of the Investiture Struggle with Henry IV of Germany precluded action. The policy of Vic tor III, who in 1087 heartily endorsed the expedition sent against

Tunis by the Italian city, Pisa, was added indication that the papacy was much concerned with the advance of the Turks. 

When Alexius I appealed to Pope Urban II for assistance after the capture of Nicaea, he was assured of sympathetic consideration. 

Ever since the conquest of Syria and Palestine by the Seljukian Turks, active propaganda strongly fortified by tales of atrocities had circulated in the West. Letters of eastern churchmen and accounts of travellers and pilgrims were filled with stories of defiled churches, desecrations of the Holy Sepulchre, and persecutions of Christians. 

Many of these tales doubtless were exaggerations, and a large number were pure fiction, designed to arouse the passions of Christian Europe. While the Seljukian yoke bore more heavily upon Christian minorities than had Saracen rule prior to the eleventh century, owing to the quartering of Turkish garrisons, there was no major hardship save in the regions where Turkish and Byzantine troops were fighting, and pillage and rapine in these areas were the normal accompaniment of medieval warfare. By and large, the Turks “gov-' erned their Christian subjects in a most lenient and tolerant fashion, and even the prejudiced Byzantine historians drop a few hints at the Christians, in many cases, preferring the rule of the Sultans to that of the emperors." Yet, however unfounded the propaganda may have been, it was effective in mobilizing public sentiment to a high degree of solidarity. "Psychologically, the crusades illustrate how great numbers of humanity may be simultaneously seized with aberration or mania under the pressure of intense emotional stimuli." 

Pilgrimages long had been extolled as a pious exercise and a most satisfactory form of penance; their efficacy was directly proportional to the distance travelled. The shrines of St. Martin at Tours and of 

St. James of Compostella (Spain) were popular destinations for pilgrims. Pilgrimages to Rome naturally were held in highest esteem, since they afforded opportunities to visit not only the capital of the Western Church but also the tombs of the greatest of the apostles. 

The supreme pilgrimage, however, was to Palestine. What guilt could not be expiated by such a journey? What Christian could fail

THE CRUSADES 

275 to thrill at the chance to visit Bethlehem, to weep on the hill of Calvary, to pray before the sepulchre of the Lord?

As early as the eighth century, six pilgrimages to the Holy Land were recorded. The following century, there were twelve; the next, sixteen; and in the eleventh century the number jumped to 117, including one led by the Bishop of Bamberg in which ten thousand devout believers participated. With pilgrimage to the Holy Land assuming the proportion of a major European interest, there was a commensurate improvement of facilities for the conduct of such journeys. 

Ships plied back and forth between Italy and Syria on packet schedule. Many guide books were written for the information of the inexperienced. Hospices at strategic points facilitated land stages of the journey, while the conversion of Hungary opened the convenient Danubian route to Constantinople, a favorite point of embarkation. 

Pilgrimage to the Holy Land begot tremendous interest in the status of Christianity in Palestine, and tales of Turkish atrocities naturally stirred the emotions of the West to fanatic pitch. Then, too, the disturbed conditions resulting from the conflict between the Seljuks and the Empire multiplied the difficulties of pilgrimages and this alone would have sufficed to produce resentment. 

The pope had further reason to be in sympathy with plans for western intervention. If the Eastern Empire was extricated from its peril by aid from the West, there was every prospect for the extension of papal authority to the Eastern Church and the establishment of a universal church. The Eastern Church never had accepted papal claims to primacy without vitiating reservations. A sharp wedge was driven between the Eastern and Western Churches by the Iconoclastic Schism of the seventh century, for when the Byzantine emperor, Leo IV, decreed the abolition of the veneration of images, his orders were defied by the Western Church, and the popes were in the vanguard of the opposition. The Photian Schism of the ninth cen tury widened the breach. Nicholas I, despite virulent polemic and a succession of anathemas, failed to bring about the abdication of Photius, whom he considered illicitly elevated to the patriarchate of Constantinople. The controversy greatly embittered the relations between Rome and the Byzantine capital. Smouldering controversies over doctrine and ritualistic usages culminated in the definitive split of 1054 when Michael Celularius, primate of the Byzantine Church, formally and unequivocally sundered relations with Pope Leo IX. 

From the point of view of the popes, therefore, the crusades were largely an attempt to establish Christian solidarity.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Sentiment in favor of a crusade crystallized when emissaries of Alexius, armed with letters of appeal from secular and clerical authorities, appeared before the Council of Piacenza (1094). Urban II promised thorough discussion of the appeals at the council which was to be held at Clermont, primarily to deal with the marital case of King Philip I of France.

The Council of Clermont (November, 1095) was well attended by clergy and laity in anticipation of action with respect to crusades. Urban delivered a moving exhortation to the assembled throng, painting a graphic picture of the outrages perpetrated by the infidels in the very places hallowed by the earthly ministry of the Saviour. All who volunteered to fight for the deliverance of the 

Holy Sepulchre were assured of plenary forgiveness of sins; if they died for the faith, they would rank with the martyrs. Property of crusaders would be inviolate during their absence, and pending court proceedings against them would be held in abeyance. Creditors could not distrain the goods of debtors on crusade. Easy victory for the hosts of the Lord was assured. Could the infidel withstand the onslaught of the arm of Jehovah? The sermon was a forensic masterpiece; it evoked piety and passion, self-sacrifice and cupidity, chivalry and thirst for adventure. At the conclusion of the sermon, the audience with one voice cried, "God wills it! God wills it! " Many pressed forward to take the vow and to signalize their allegiance by sewing the white cross on their garments. Leaders were directed to assemble their forces, and the rendezvous was fixed at Constantinople, where it was expected Alexius would provide means of conveyance to Asia Minor.

The crusades exercised a tremendous and manifold appeal. Feudal lords welcomed the project for a number of reasons. First, war against the infidel promised booty and land. The principle of primogeniture had been well established by the eleventh century, with the result that many nobles were landless and impoverished. Here was a chance to acquire domains in the East; tales of fabulous wealth to be garnered by easy conquest made the enterprise seem the fulfillment of fondest dreams. The Truce of God, which required cessation of fighting from Wednesday afternoon to Monday morning, had secured general observance in Europe in response to the efforts of the church. Fighting was the business of the feudal lord, and the efforts of the church were responsible for a serious curtailment of the activity. The crusade, on the other hand, offered attractive prospects of combat with the benediction of the church, with assured

THE CRUSADES 

277 rewards, eternal and mundane, for all participants. Norman expansion in the eleventh century whetted the cupidity of the nobles. 

Robert Guiscard and his retainers had carved out principalities in Sicily; William the Conqueror had subjugated a kingdom, and rich were the rewards of his followers. Might not the crusade bring far greater gain?

The preaching of the crusade among the peasantry fell on equally receptive ears. Peter the Hermit, self-styled refugee from the Holy 

Land and reputed eyewitness of Turkish barbarities, was the apostle to the masses. Countryside, hamlet, and city alike furnished crowds of avid listeners. The credulous believed that a man of God walked among them, and they even snatched hairs from the tail of his mule to preserve as relics. Severe famines had occurred in the eleventh century; the peasant, under the most propitious circumstances, could hope for nothing beyond bare subsistence. Palestine was "a land of milk and honey "; the Bible said so. Independence, wealth, and distinction awaited the impoverished downtrodden serf who ventured to "fight the good fight," and spiritual rewards alone were sufficiently attractive to sway his decision.

Great enthusiasm for the crusade was felt in the mercantile cities of Italy, especially Venice, Amalfi, and Pisa. Saracen dominance of the Mediterranean was crumbling as a result of the Norman conquest of Sicily. The crusade would complete the process and give virtually a monopoly of the Mediterranean trade to the enterprising Italians. Commerce would be greatly stimulated, for there would be much travel to and fro, to say nothing of the transportation of supplies. Conquest of Syria promised opportunities for the establishment of trading posts in the Levant; for the Italian merchant, the crusade was an eminently sound and attractive venture. 

Contributing to the popularity of the crusade were the desire for adventure, naive curiosity, and geographical ignorance. Doubtless many joined the movement with no adequate appreciation of the difficulties involved. Crusaders in France murmured at their failure to sight Jerusalem after a day or two of marching. Even those who realized how many obstacles had to be surmounted expected providential aid to ameliorate difficulties and hardships. 

Before the movement got under way, Peter the Hermit and Walter the Penniless stirred the rabble to anticipate the main body. One motley horde reached Constantinople without untoward incident, while a second group, under Peter's leadership, marched down the Danubian valley, foraging and pillaging en route. The Hungarians

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and Bulgarians, who had cordially received the first band, shut the gates of their towns to Peter's group. Mutual bitterness culminated in a series of skirmishes and petty sieges, and the animosities engendered seriously impeded the major crusading forces that followed in Peter's wake. The "Peasant Crusaders" made themselves so objectionable to Alexius that he gladly had them transported to Asia Minor, where they were soon cut to pieces by the Saracens. Peter the 

Hermit escaped, however, and returned to Constantinople, subsequently to join the authorized crusade.

In the meantime, the main groups of crusaders began to converge on Constantinople. A French army, under Godfrey of Bouillon, marched up the Rhine valley, through southern Germany, Hungary, and Bulgaria, to Adrianople, and thence to Constantinople. 

Raymond of Toulouse led an army across north Italy and down along the Dalmatian coast of the Adriatic to Durazzo, thence due east to the Byzantine capital. The armies of Robert of Flanders, Robert of Normandy, Stephen of Blois, and Hugh of Vermandois all marched down through Italy to Bari and crossed by ship to Durazzo; 

Bohemond likewise sailed directly across the Adriatic from Brindisi and crossed northern Epirus, turning to the northeast to strike the main route from Durazzo to Thessalonica. 

Relations with the emperor were soon strained. Alexius was not at all pleased at the turn of events. He had hoped for several thousand well-armed Christian knights to fight in his armies until the Turkish advance was beaten back. Instead, he was confronted with the embattled chivalry of Europe, under the control of other hands than his. He was in the position of the "shepherd who was ruined by the accomplishment of his own wishes; he had prayed for water; the Ganges was turned into his grounds and his cottage was swept away by the inundation.”

Hugh of Vermandois was imprisoned at the emperor's orders, alfegedly because of an insolent letter; in retaliation, Godfrey ordered the devastation of imperial lands. An agreement finally was reached that allayed the salient grievances. Raymond of Toulouse became embroiled in a bitter controversy because of his refusal to take an oath of fidelity to the emperor; he capitulated, however, when Alexius adroitly capitalized on his hatred for Bohemond. After much intrigue and cajolery, Alexius induced the leaders to subscribe to an oath binding them to refrain from seizing any territory within, or nominally within, the borders of the Empire. The emperor, in return, promised to aid in the project to capture Jerusalem.

THE CRUSADES 

279 There was no commander-in-chief. Bishop Adhemar of Puy served as papal legate in nominal charge. Aloof from the jealousies and petty intrigues, he often exercised a mediating influence that did much to prevent schism. The armies were poorly equipped, for reliance on beneficent Providence in all too many cases superseded prudence. The army at best was an undisciplined, querulous horde, encumbered by a host of noncombatants. There were knights in full armor and the rabble with improvised equipment, prelates in fine raiment and peasants in tatters, monks and suttlers, consecrated virgins and camp followers.

Passage to Asia Minor was provided by the emperor. The first action came with the siege of Nicaea (May, 1097). The siege operations were conducted in desultory fashion. When the garrison was on the point of surrender, the crusaders were amazed one morning to see the imperial flag flying from the battlements. Alexius had procured the capitulation of the stronghold by secret negotiation. 

The capture of Nicaea relieved the Turkish pressure on the Empire and attained his immediate objective. He accordingly withdrew and left the crusaders in the lurch. 

The march of the crusaders was resumed; in contempt of the Saracens elemental caution was disregarded. On July 4, 1097, Bohemond's army was encircled at Dorylaeum by a strong force of Saracens, and only the prompt arrival of reënforcements averted disaster. 

In October, Baldwin led his army against Edessa and when the city surrendered announced his withdrawal from further participation in the crusade.

The remaining leaders, for strategic reasons, decided to make Antioch the next objective. For months, the impregnable fortifications were besieged. Supplies of the crusaders were exhausted; many perished from hunger and disease, and there was even occasional resort to cannibalism. Bohemond, however, managed to enter into negotiations with perfidious members of the garrison, who divulged the existence of a secret way by which the walls could be scaled; an intrepid band stole within the walls and opened the gate to admit the main body. The capture of Antioch proved only the beginning of the crusaders' misfortunes. Hundreds were carried off by disease and illness resulting from over-indulgence in food and drink. A strong body of Moslems, under Kerboga, came up and invested the city. A series of sorties failed to break through the Saracen lines, and starvation again threatened the crusaders.

When the crusaders were in the depths of despair, Peter Bartholo-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mew declared that a dream had revealed to him that the Holy Lance which had pierced the side of Christ could be found beneath the floor of the Church of St. Andrew. On the third day of search, Peter claimed to have found a lance head; some venerated it as a holy relic, others scoffed. Peter then offered to demonstrate the authenticity of the relic by undergoing an ordeal. An immense bonfire was kindled. 

Peter, bearing the lance, strode through it and was surrounded by admirers who clutched at him to seize relics. Several days after the ordeal he died; skeptics considered his death a refutation of his claims, but believers in the potency of the lance claimed that injuries sustained after the ordeal had caused his death. 

Bohemond established himself as ruler of Antioch and refused to proceed farther. The other leaders, however, decided to press on to 

Jerusalem. Preceded by priests bearing the lance and chanting litanies, the armies marched out and, after a brief struggle, broke through the Saracen lines. Jerusalem at last (June 7, 1099) lay before the eyes of the crusaders, and all fell to their knees and gave thanks that Providence had permitted them to gaze on the Holy City. Several days later, the crusaders marched around the walls of 

Jerusalem in solemn procession, chanting psalms and liturgies. A great Hallelujah was then raised in the expectation that the walls. would topple as did those of Jericho, but when a miracle did not happen, they resorted to the more prosaic methods of siegecraft. 

The city was carried by assault July 15, 1099, and the victors indulged in three days of massacre and pillage. The leaders wrote to the pope in exultation: "And if you desire to know what was done with the enemy who were there, know that in Solomon's Porch and in his temple our men rode in the blood of the Saracens up to the knees of their horses."

There was virtual unanimity as to the choice of a ruler for the newly founded Kingdom of Jerusalem. Godfrey of Bouillon consistently had refused to allow selfish, ignoble motives to obscure his dedication to the cause. With characteristic modesty, he refused “to wear a crown of gold where our Savior had worn a crown of thorns," but he finally assumed the title of "Defender of the Holy Sepulchre." When he died in the summer of 1100, his brother Baldwin succeeded him and was crowned Christmas Day.

The Latin Kingdom now comprised the principalities of Edessa, Antioch, Tripolis, and Jerusalem. Damascus remained unconquered, as did a number of strongholds in the hilly country. Laws for the new kingdom were ultimately embodied in the Assizes of Jerusalem

THE CRUSADES 

281 which introduced a ready-made feudalism. Saracens and Christians were in close contact, and intimate association brought tolerance, indeed, friendship. The Knights Templars (1118) were organized to defend the kingdom, while the Knights of St. John (1113) devoted themselves to the founding of hospices to ease the travels of pilgrims who came in great number now that Jerusalem was in Christian. hands. 

THE LATER CRUSADES 

The Mohammedans recovered rapidly under the leadership of the dynamic Zangi. Dissension and factionalism which had weakened their resistance during the first crusade were allayed. Their capture of Edessa (December 25, 1144) was a warning to Europe and precipitated the Second Crusade, of which Bernard of Clairvaux, a religious figure of international repute, was the outstanding preacher. King Louis VII of France, in contrition for the sacrilegious burning of a church at Vitry, was an easy convert. Conrad III of Germany at first demurred, but when publicly upbraided by Bernard at Spires, bowed to public sentiment and took the cross. 

Both kings had more important tasks at home. France was just beginning to achieve her historic missions of the Middle Ages - centralization and the re-establishment of royal sovereignty. Fortunately, the kingdom was placed in charge of the Abbé Suger, whose able administration more than compensated for the prolonged absence of the king. Germany was on the threshold of the great struggle between Welfs and Hohenstaufens. Conrad's presence was imperatively required, with the result that his interest in the crusade was never warm.

The French contingent, reënforced by English and Normans, mustered at Metz, while the Germans started from Ratisbon. The army concentrated at Ephesus, but before a campaign could be undertaken, Conrad's forces were almost annihilated at Laodicea; the remnant joined the French and proceeded to Jerusalem. It was decided to make the capture of Damascus the key objective. The siege progressed with promise of success until the Christians changed the site of their operations to the opposite side of the city where they found conditions completely unsuitable. Their return to the original location was prevented by the enemy, and the leaders gave up the siege in disgust.

Conrad returned to Germany, while Louis tarried in Antioch, much disgruntled with his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine, for her amor-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ous affair with her uncle, Raymond of Antioch. On the way back to 

France, he visited the pope to procure an annulment of his marriage, but the pope effected a public reconciliation. The king, nevertheless, had the marriage annulled by the French clergy shortly after his return. Eleanor then married Henry II of England and brought him

Aquitaine as her dower, thus sowing the seeds of future war and controversy between France and England. 

The Second Crusade was a fiasco which caused much grief and recrimination; even St. Bernard was moved to cavil at the inscrutable ways of Providence. The only constructive result, ironically enough, was the English conquest of Lisbon, which they had seized en route to join the crusading forces.

Mohammedan resurgence continued apace under Nur-ed-din and Saladin. Saladin secured control of Egypt as the leader of the Sunnites, returned to Arabia, and eventually pressed on to Bagdad, which he won for the Sunnite cause. Dissension wracked the Kingdom of 

Jerusalem. King Baldwin V contracted leprosy, and his regal rights passed to his sister, Sybel, the wife of William of Montferrat. After the death of William, Sybel married Guy of Lusignan, who was then elected king. The nobles resented his elevation; Raymond of Tripoli was particularly hostile. War with the Saracens was precipitated by Reginald of Chatillon's wanton attack on a caravan; the aggression was all the more heinous in the estimation of Saladin in that it occurred during the Mohammedan sacred month. The Christians were hard pressed and appeals for a new crusade were sent in ever increasing number. At last the dreaded news arrived; Jerusalem was retaken October 2, 1187. Urban III allegedly died of grief; his successor, Gregory VIII, issued a call for a crusade and ordered all western Christians to do suitable penance until the Holy City was regained.

So began the Third Crusade. Richard of England, Philip II (Au gustus) of France, and Frederick I (Barbarossa) of Germany took the cross. "Saladin tithes " of one-tenth their annual incomes were levied on the clergy and laity to help defray the cost of the enterprise. Richard and Philip signed a treaty mutually agreeing to refrain from aggressions while the crusade was in progress. Frederick made thorough preparation and took measures to eliminate factors which had militated against the success of preceding ventures. He was drowned, however, while attempting to swim a swift stream in Cilicia (1190).

Philip's forces proceeded by ship to Messina in Sicily. Richard

THE CRUSADES 

283 tarried to aid Sancho of Portugal against the Saracens, after which he followed to Sicily. There events precipitated a sharp break between 

Richard and the French king. At the death of King William of Sicily, his widow, Constance, married Henry VI, son and heir of Frederick Barbarossa. The Sicilians, under the leadership of Tancred, refused to recognize Henry as their sovereign. England was allied with the 

Welf party in Germany and Richard naturally joined with the Sicilian rebels in accordance with the anti-Hohenstaufen policy, whereas Philip supported Henry VI. Richard's efforts to secure the expulsion of the Hohenstaufens failed, and he was destined to pay dearly for his interference in Sicilian politics.¹

There was another delay at Cyprus. One of Richard's ships was wrecked, and the survivors, including Queen Berengaria, fell into the hands of a band of Cypriote brigands under the command of Isaac. Richard landed his army and overthrew the quasi state which 

Isaac had founded. The island was offered to the Templars, and when they declined to pay the stipulated purchase price it was bestowed on the exiled king of Jerusalem. 

When Richard arrived at Acre, he found a siege in progress. On 

July 12, 1191, the Saracen stronghold fell, and the Christians were overjoyed at the recovery of what was believed to be the true cross. 

The feud between Richard and the Hohenstaufens flared up anew as a result of Richard's overbearing conduct toward Leopold of Austria, who had assumed command of the German forces after the death of Frederick. The Germans were so angered that they withdrew, and their secession contributed much to the failure of the crusade. 

Relations between Philip and Richard grew steadily more strained.

Richard's marriage to Berengaria, in violation of an agreement to marry the sister of the French ruler, was one point of controversy, and the Sicilian episode accentuated the bitterness. The basic reason for enmity, of course, was the Angevin dominion in France. With

Normandy, Anjou, Poitou, Maine, and Aquitaine in the hands of the English, lasting peace between England and France was precluded. 

Philip, accordingly, feigned illness and returned to France, where he began intrigues with John, Richard's brother, who was in charge of England during the absence of the king. 

With the departure of Philip, the crusade virtually came to a halt. 

Skirmishes alternated with truces, but efforts to negotiate definitive peace failed. Mutual respect characterized the relations between

Richard and Saladin, although the two never met face to face. Richard eventually was forced to be satisfied with minor concessions, since developments in England made imperative his return. The crusaders were permitted to visit the Holy City as pilgrims; the 

Saracens agreed to respect the shrines sacred to Christians and permit free access to pilgrims. 

Richard was shipwrecked on the return journey (1193) and attempted to make his way back overland. While passing through the dominions of Leopold of Austria, he was recognized, despite his disguise, and held for ransom. Henry VI, Leopold's suzerain, demanded the surrender of the captive. Philip Augustus used his influence to hinder Richard's release but the ransom finally was paid and his return to England brought an end to John's oppressive rule; the rest of his reign was spent in warring against Philip. 

The Fourth Crusade was basically a feudal enterprise, led by Theobald of Champagne, Fulk of Neuilly, Villehardouin, and other nobles. Innocent III gave it hearty approval, and arrangements were made by the Venetians to provide passage for 85,000 marks. The crusaders assembled at Venice in the spring of 1202. They squandered their money, however, before preparations for embarkation were complete and consequently were helpless before Venetian avarice. 

Enrico Dandolo, the Doge of Venice, suggested that the crusaders could be transported to Syria if they "worked their passage " by aiding in an attack on Zara, a commercial rival. Innocent was enraged at the wanton attack on a Christian city and excommunicated the Venetians and all the crusading leaders.

There was worse in store. Alexius III had deposed the Byzantine emperor, Isaac. Isaac and his son, Alexius the Younger, appealed to 

Philip of Swabia (Isaac's brother-in-law) for aid in procuring his restoration. Negotiations were also opened with the crusaders, and the Venetians were promised favorable commercial concessions in 

Constantinople in return for assistance. Philip of Swabia possibly was the chief agent in these negotiations. As the brother and successor of 

Henry VI, his adherence to traditional Hohenstaufen policies engendered a break with the papacy and he had every reason to thwart the crusade if its failure would discredit Innocent III.

When the crusaders set out, ostensibly for Egypt, the Venetians had little difficulty in diverting the expedition to an attack on Constantinople. The Byzantine capital was taken and, after a number of disputes with young Alexius, thoroughly pillaged. Baldwin of
