The foundation of the Latin Kingdom brought at least temporary union of Greek and Roman Catholicism, and there was prospect for the permanent termination of the schism. Literature profited from the scandalous crusade by the writing of Villehardouin's chronicle, the Conquête de Constantinople. It is worthy of comparison with the epics of ancient literature. 

The grief and shame engendered by the Fourth Crusade doubtless prepared public sentiment for the mad idea of a children's crusade. 

The prevalence of sin in the ranks of the crusaders was the official explanation for the abortive nature of the projects since 1147. The 

Lord had averted His countenance from the enterprises rather than to seem to condone avarice, ambition, and lust of the soldiers fighting under His standard. Where men had failed, innocent children could succeed. "Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained wisdom" was the shibboleth that ensured the acceptance of a children's crusade. One group, led by Nicholas of Cologne, assembled in Germany; another, under Stephen of Cloyes, gathered in 

France. Some of these children, including a number of mere tots, set out for Italy or Marseilles, singing hymns and chanting prayers.

Their sufferings were pitiful in the extreme, especially those who came through the Alpine passes to Genoa. Hundreds perished of starvation and exposure, and most of those who embarked at Marseilles or Genoa fell into the clutches of Mohammedan slave dealers to be sold in the marts of Egypt and Syria. Those who visited Rome to secure the blessings of Innocent III were for the most part saved when the pontiff persuaded them to return to their homes. The tragic story is an epitome of medieval credulity, for the victims of misguided piety were sacrificed to a philosophy that expected the miraculous invariably to compensate for human folly. 

The crusade of Frederick II (1228) was primarily a phase of the duel between the popes and the Hohenstaufen emperors. Frederick had been crowned king of Germany in 1213 by Innocent III, as a counterfoil to Otto IV. Frederick bound himself not to attempt to unite his German and Sicilian possessions, and in gratitude for papal aid rashly vowed to go on a crusade. Some years later, when Frederick repudiated his promises in regard to union of Germany and Sicily and devoted himself to the imperialistic policy of the Hohenstaufens (Ghibellines) in Italy, Gregory IX used his early crusading

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

vow as a political weapon.2 Frederick was forced to set out for the 

Holy Land on threat of excommunication, but he returned a few days later to refit, claiming that sickness had broken out among his men. Gregory considered this plea a trick and excommunicated him. 

The emperor refitted his vessels and again set out; the pope again excommunicated him for his sacrilege in going on a crusade while under the ban of the church. Ironically enough, Frederick, although hardly a dutiful son of the church, gained a number of important concessions from the Emir of Egypt (1229). His crusade was more successful than any since the first; it certainly failed to bring about his ruin for which the pope had hoped. 

Louis IX of France led two crusades (1248, 1270) which had for their object the acquisition of Egypt, subsequently to be used as a base of operations against Syria and Palestine. Louis was captured and ransomed during the first venture; his death in 1270 brought the great period of crusading to a close. 

RESULTS OF THE CRUSADES 

All the crusades, save the first, failed to attain their immediate objectives; the incidental results, however, were far more important. 

Politically, the crusades did much for the preservation of the Byzantine Empire, which otherwise probably would have succumbed before the Turkish advance of the eleventh century. The rise of monarchy and nationalism was aided in the West, because of the protracted absence of the feudal lords who certainly would have postponed the triumph of these forces. The growth of towns received great impetus. Some benefited directly through increased trade; others extorted favorable charters from impecunious suzerains who desired to go on a crusade.

Economic results of the crusades were of great significance. The 

Italian cities displaced the Saracens in control of the Mediterranean trade. Venice, Amalfi, Pisa, Genoa, and other cities acquired control of the trade of the Levant and the Far East, which they maintained until the commercial revolution of the age of the Renaissance. A demand for eastern products was created in western Europe. Sugar, rice, oranges, lemons, apricots, and spices were brought in increasing quantity to the West by the Italian merchants; damask, muslin, silk, rugs, and tapestries likewise were prized as a result of the prolonged contacts with the Saracens. The Italian Fondacchi in the Levant, founded during the crusades, served as the points of junction with the Arab caravans that tapped the riches of India and China. 

2 See infra, p. 312.

THE CRUSADES 

287 The intellectual horizon of Christian Europe was widened. Tolerance was engendered wherever Saracen and Christian were in prolonged contact. Arabic science became better known to western scholars, as the number of Arabic scientific terms bears witness (algebra, alkali, alcohol, zero).

From a religious point of view, the crusades were a blow to the prestige of the church. The crusades had been fostered by the church and the popes had assured participants that they were doing the work of the Lord. Yet the crusades had failed. Preachers of the crusades had belittled the infidels, had assured the faithful that easy victory would crown the efforts of the crusaders. Walled towns would topple at the shouts and trumpet blasts of Jehovah's avenging hosts; waters would part to allow the Christians to cross dry-shod. These prophecies were not fulfilled; disillusion and reality confronted the crusaders at every hand. There were sown seeds of skepticism that were to grow into major challenges to the authority of the church and reach full stature in the Protestant Revolt.

CHAPTER 22 

England and France in the Middle Ages 

ENGLAND 

HE Roman conquest of Britain left few permanent traces. 

Institutions, language, and customs remained basically Celtic, and such Romanization as endured was confined to urban centers. Christianity gained a foothold, but was confined to 

Wales after the Anglo-Saxon conquests. 

The conquest of the island by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes was a phase of the great movement of the Germanic peoples during the fourth and fifth centuries. A number of Teutonic kingdoms were established during the period of conquest and settlement, the most important of which were Kent, Northumbria, Mercia, and Wessex.

First one then another of these petty kingdoms enjoyed a degree of hegemony. Kent, under Aethelbert, was prominent by the end of the sixth century; the conversion of the king by the missionary expedition sent by Pope Gregory the Great (597) marked the beginning of Roman Catholicism in England. Northumbria, under Eadwine, then came to the fore and was Christianized as a result of missionary activity that emanated from Ireland as well as from Rome. 

A pagan reaction, led by the doughty Penda of Mercia, resulted in the defeat and death of Eadwine (633), and Oswald, his successor, likewise was slain in battle with the Mercians (642). Oswiu, however, finally liberated Northumbria from Mercian overlordship (655).

Since both Roman Catholic and Celtic Christianity had been introduced, controversy over beliefs and practices was inevitable, but at the Synod of Whitby (664), Oswiu decided to adhere to the Roman Church.

In the eighth century, Mercia again enjoyed a period of prestige under Offa (757-796), but it was not until the accession of Egbert as king of Wessex (802-839) that the movement for the unification of the petty kingdoms made appreciable progress. The Danish invasions constituted the gravest problem of the ninth century. The vic-

tories of Alfred the Great (871-901) and the establishment of the Danelaw by the Treaty of Wedmore (879) brought respite. Alfred, an outstanding figure of English history, did much by his encouragement of learning to establish English preeminence in the world of scholarship prior to the Norman Conquest. The Danish invasions were resumed, largely as a result of the folly of Ethelred the Redeless, and England was conquered and made part of the empire of Canute the Great (1016-1035). Independence was regained with the accession of Edward the Confessor (1042-1066), but the growing influence of Normans in court and church were harbingers of the conquest of 1066.

Basic English institutions were founded in the Anglo-Saxon period. 

Division into shires and hundreds, with their respective courts, survived the Norman Conquest; the Witan yielded to the feudal Great 

Council of the early Norman period, which, in turn, developed into Parliament. The principle of local responsibility for law and order, with the attendant frankpledge and tithing, survived, as did also the fyrd, or militia. Cultural developments continued, despite the Scandinavian invasions and the turbulence and anarchy they engendered. 

The Cathedral School at York, with its famed masters such as Aelbert and Alcuin, enjoyed general prestige; the Venerable Bede, in his 

Ecclesiastical History of England, produced one of the greatest scholarly works of the Middle Ages. St. Dunstan added academic laurels to his fame as statesman and reformer of the church. The 

Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, probably begun in the reign of Alfred the Great, was a literary as well as an historical contribution of the first magnitude. The poetry of Caedmon and Cynewulf was far superior to contemporary productions on the Continent. 

The Norman conquest was the culmination of a gradual extension of Norman influence during the reign of Edward the Confessor. It was basically a movement of Norman expansion comparable with the earlier conquest of Sicily by Robert Guiscard. William's claims to the English throne were at best doubtful. The promise of Edward, if made at all, could not have abrogated the electoral rights of the 

Witan, while the promises of Harold, son of Godwine of Wessex, were extorted during his enforced sojourn in Normandy. William's expedition enjoyed the blessing of Pope Alexander II because he promised to depose Stigand as archbishop of Canterbury and restore Robert of Jumièges. Contributing factors in William's success were the invasion of north England by the forces of Harold Hardrada, king of Norway, and the desertions of Eadwine of Mercia and Mor-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

kere, the Northumbrian earl. The battle of Hastings was decisive;

William's rule could not subsequently be overthrown, although several revolts had to be suppressed and the north pitilessly harried before resistance subsided.

Constitutional development was the main theme of medieval English history. William established a strong, centralized monarchy. The 

Anglo-Saxon fyrd was retained, as were also the hundred and county courts, so that neither military service nor the dispensation of justice was feudalized to the same degree as on the Continent. The Salisbury 

Oath required every male, twelve years of age or older, to take an oath of fidelity to the king. William was every man's sovereign irrespective of feudal relations. The Domesday survey, a prelude to the imposition of taxation, was added evidence of the trend toward centralization. At least four times a year William met his Great 

Council, made up of his tenants-in-chief. This body was not made up of persons chosen because of their social or political position as was the Anglo-Saxon Witan. The basis of the Great Council was economic, resting as it did on land tenure. One of William's chief contributions to the development of medieval English government was his utilization of the economic phase of feudalism as a political instrument. 

The reign of William II (1087-1100) indicated that centralization could proceed too far. Oppression of church and baronage, aggravated by the extortions suggested or practiced by Ranulf Flambard, was responsible for the reaction toward limitation of royal power that characterized the reign of Henry I (1100-1135). Henry's Coronation Charter was negative in character, for it promised abstinence from abuses of a feudal nature rather than positive constitutional concessions. The king promised to refrain from spoliation of the church and the practice of keeping ecclesiastical offices vacant in order to enjoy the revenues therefrom. The barons were promised freedom from extortionate practices in regard to reliefs, wardships, and marriages. The sending of itinerant justices to the counties was a powerful influence toward centralization. 

During the reign of Stephen (1135–1154), the baronage virtually defied royal authority. Anarchy, exploitation of the peasantry, and oppression of the church became more and more intolerable, especially after the king became involved in a civil war with the partisans of Matilda, daughter of Henry I. The chaotic period showed that royal authority could be too greatly restricted; royal control was preferable to an untrammeled baronage. 

Constitutional and judicial developments in the reign of Henry II

(1154-1189) were of great importance. The possessory assizes substituted rational civil procedure for trial by battle in cases involving possession and ownership of land. Writs of novel disseisen were issued to reinstate those forcibly evicted from their lands. The Grand 

Assize empowered sheriffs to convoke panels of neighbors to give evidence under oath as to the ownership of land. The writ of morte d'ancestor utilized a similar procedure in cases of disputed landed inheritances.

The Assize of Clarendon established the grand jury. Royal justices on circuit were to preside over the county courts convoked by the sheriffs. Panels of twelve men were selected in each county and sworn. The juries then stated what crimes had been committed since the last visit of the justices and named the persons suspected of guilt. 

Those indicted by the grand juries were then arrested, but guilt or innocence was determined by resort to ordeals. Henry showed his skepticism toward ordeals by providing that if a strongly suspected defendant were acquitted, he should be exiled as an outlaw. 

In his controversy with Thomas à Becket, Henry demonstrated his resolve to curtail the judicial privileges of the clergy. The Constitutions of Clarendon modified the principle of benefit of clergy by assigning to royal courts the apprehension and sentencing of criminals who claimed clerical immunities; the actual trial, however, was to take place in the ecclesiastical tribunals. The Assize Utrum, particularly opposed by Becket, provided that in cases where the status of land was in dispute, the question whether it was "lay fee" or "alms," that is, secular or ecclesiastical land, was to be determined by the royal courts by a procedure similar to that employed under the Writ of Right. 

Magna Charta, issued in 1215 by John in response to the demands of the baronage, was a marked constitutional advance, for it established the principle that the king was amenable to the law. It must be borne in mind, however, that the concessions embodied in the document were feudal and as such applicable only to church and baronage. Much has been made of the privileges granted to towns, but here too only holders of burgess rights could enjoy the concessions. The provision for trial by peers likewise probably applied only to the procedure of feudal courts wherein custom long had decreed that vassals could only be judged by fellow-vassals. A clear concession of popular application, however, was the promise to make royal justice available to all and to refrain from the infliction of punishments without due process of law. 

Conflict between crown and baronage was characteristic of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION reign of Henry III (1216-1272). Growing influence of Frenchmen in court circles alienated the barons, but the fundamental cause of opposition to the crown was the unwarranted extension of royal prerogative. The use of the funds of the wardrobe was evading baronial control of financial affairs through the Exchequer, while the utilization of the privy seal frustrated efforts to influence the conduct of the government through the office of chancellor. The Provisions of 

Oxford (1258) embodied an attempt to establish a baronial commission as the chief executive agency. A permanent committee of fifteen was to meet several times a year with a committee of twelve chosen to represent the whole baronage. When this attempt failed, the disaffection came to a head. The rebellious barons, under the leadership of Simon de Montfort, who had been alienated from the king by criticism of his administration of Gascony, defeated the royal supporters at Lewes (1264). The convocation of Montfort's famous parliament was an aftermath of this victory. Henry regained his ascendancy, however, and at the battle of Evesham (1265) the barons were decisively defeated and Montfort's short-lived regime was overthrown.

Parliament owed its origin to the addition of new elements of representation to the Great Council. The practice of calling knights of the shire, representatives of the lesser barons, or country gentry, goes back at least to 1254, when Henry III ordered them to report to the

Great Council concerning local sentiment in regard to the imposition of taxes to finance the Gascon campaign. It should be noted that the knights had a specific service to perform; they merely expressed local sentiment on one particular issue. In 1261, however, the knights were summoned to treat with the king and barons" concerning common affairs of the kingdom," and not merely to report local decisions. 

When Montfort convoked his parliament in 1265, he summoned both knights of the shire and representatives of the towns, thus bringing together for the first time the two new elements of representation. But Montfort's parliament represented only the party in opposition to the king, and, moreover, convoked as it was by the leader of a rebellion against the crown, it was devoid of legality. 

In the reign of Edward I, the "Model Parliament" of 1295 contained representatives of the corporate towns together with the knights of the shire, and, by insertion of the praemunientes clause in the writs addressed to the clergy, the king commanded that they ensure the attendance of representatives of the lower clergy. For the first time in a legally convoked parliament, knights and burgesses

were included. This was a factor of enormous significance, for the two groups eventually recognized the similarity of their basic interests and coalesced to form the House of Commons. In a document known as the Confirmation of the Charters, issued in 1297, Edward agreed that no new taxes were to be levied without the consent of Parliament, thus establishing the vital principle of parliamentary financial control. In the statute known as De Religiosis, Edward forbade further gifts of land to the church so as to checkmate the concentration of land in the "dead hand" of ecclesiastical tenure. The practice of subinfeudation also was checked by the statute known as 

Quia Emptores.

The reign of Edward II (1307-1327) was, from a constitutional point of view, a replica of that of Henry III. Crown and baronage were arrayed against each other on basically the same issues. The baronial efforts to control the king by the Ordinances of 1311 proved abortive; it was the support of the disgruntled baronage, however, that enabled Mortimer and Isabella to procure the deposition of the king in favor of Edward III. 

The exigencies created by the Hundred Years' War¹ brought many opportunities for the development of parliamentary powers especially during the reign of Edward III (1327-1377). Since the war was fought in France, the English people had little immediate concern; consequently Parliament established the principle that the redress of grievances must precede the grant of funds to the crown for the prosecution of the war. In 1376 Parliament asserted the power of impeachment when it removed several unpopular and corrupt ministers of the king. In 1399 this power was expanded to include the power of deposing the king (Richard II). By 1407, the principle was established that grants of money must originate in the House of 

Commons. 

FRANCE, 987-1314 A new era in French history was inaugurated with the coronation of Hugh Capet (987). Vigor replaced the apathy of the later Carolingians, and the wealth of the Capetian house was in striking contrast to the poverty of Charles the Simple and Louis d'Outre Mer. 

The first four Capetians stabilized the dynasty. Each king procured the recognition of his son as his successor and thus, in practice if not in theory, repudiated the elective principle that had prevailed since the election of Charles the Fat (884). Royal authority was confined 

1 See infra, pp. 349–54.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

to the region around Paris, the Ile de France. The royal domain was surrounded by powerful feudal principalities. On the north and west were Flanders, Normandy, Brittany, and Poitou. Southwest and south were Anjou, Aquitaine, and Toulouse; on the east were 

Burgundy and Champagne. The historic mission of the medieval kings of France was to weld these duchies and counties into a nation. 

The Ile de France was the nucleus from which the French monarchy was to extend its power. The situation at the opening of the 

Capetian period was by no means hopeless. The Ile de France comprised perhaps the wealthiest part of France. Its central location was a factor of great importance, for it bordered on each of the great feudal territories it was to absorb. Tradition supported monarchical principles, and the church was a strong supporter, despite the marital cases of Robert I and Philip I and the attendant controversies with the papacy.

The unification of France began with the reign of Louis VI (the 

Fat) (1108-1137). Louis encouraged the growth of towns by taking them under his protection or permitting the establishment of communes. Towns were an antifeudal force and anything that promoted their growth hastened the victory of centralized government over particularism. The king also asserted his appellate jurisdiction outside the royal domain when the Count of Auvergne and the Duke of Berry were both forced to acknowledge the right of the king to intervene, even in cases involving their own vassals. Louis performed another great service to the monarchy when he entrusted the guidance of his son and successor to the Abbé Suger. Suger's ministry doubtless preserved France from the worst consequences of the pro tracted absence of Louis VII on the Second Crusade. 

Superficial observation might lead to the conclusion that the reign of Louis VII (1137–1180) was a period of retrogression. No territory was annexed, there were no dramatic assertions of royal authority outside the domain, and the loss of Aquitaine to Henry II of England engendered serious difficulties. Yet the king's espousal of the popular side of great moral issues of the day greatly enhanced the prestige of the crown. The participation of the king in the abortive Second Crusade was in accord with public sentiment even though the immediate political results were negative. Annulment of the monarch's marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine was interpreted by many contemporaries as a sacrifice of political advantage for the sake of moral principle. For five years, Thomas à Becket found asylum in the Ile de France; when his martyrdom elevated him to a foremost place in the galaxy of

medieval saints, when Canterbury became one of the most renowned shrines in Europe, lustre was cast on the king who had succored him. 

When Pope Alexander III was driven from Rome by Frederick Bar barossa, he too found refuge with Louis, who naturally advanced in public favor with the triumph of the pope at the battle of Legnano (1176). 

Philip II (Augustus) was one of the greatest kings of French history (1180-1223). Immediately after his accession, he was confronted with a formidable coalition, instigated by his mother, whose four brothers, the Counts of Champagne, Sancerre, and Blois, and the Archbishop of Rheims, were powerful enough to daunt the most intrepid king. Philip shrewdly allied with the Count of Flanders, whose niece, Isabella of Hainault, became his first wife. Artois, the dowry of the young queen, was annexed to the monarchy. The help of Flanders enabled Philip to thwart his uncles, and when the coalition collapsed, he sundered the alliance with Flanders and seized Vermandois.

The existence of the Angevin Empire constituted the most serious problem. Henry II of England held Normandy, Maine, Touraine, Poitou, Anjou, and Aquitaine. Philip encouraged the rebellion of 

Henry's sons, since partition of the English territories would have facilitated their conquest by France. The death of Henry II (1189) placed his heir, Richard, in sharp opposition to Philip, although the beginning of the Third Crusade for a time postponed open manifestation of hostility. Events at Sicily sharpened the enmity, and Philip's desertion of the crusade made war with Richard inevitable in view of the French king's collusion with John. The return of Richard, in 

1194, following the payment of his ransom to Henry VI of Germany, put Philip on the defensive, and the building of Castle Gaillard on the 

Norman frontier constituted a serious menace. Richard's death at

Limoges during a romantic quest for a mythical golden table gave Philip an opportunity to deal with a less formidable adversary. 

His first policy was to urge the claims of Arthur of Brittany to the English crown, but the death of his protégé, who was probably murdered by John, necessitated more direct methods. John, with characteristic brutality and cynical disregard for consequences, abducted Isabella of Angoulême, who was betrothed to Hugh of Lusignan, a vassal of the French king. Philip summoned John to appear for trial, claiming that he was a vassal of the French crown for his English possessions. When John failed to appear, Philip declared his possessions forfeit to the crown, and conquest gradually afforded a stronger

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

claim than feudal precedent. John made his supreme bid for the recovery of the forfeited territories in 1214, when he allied himself with Philip of Flanders and Otto IV, claimant to the imperial title. 

The battle of Bouvines (1214) was decisive; all English possessions, save Poitou and Aquitaine, were irretrievably lost; the former was annexed to the French monarchy in the reign of Louis VIII (12231226).

The Albigensian Crusade paved the way for the ultimate annexation of Toulouse. The crusade was preached by Innocent III in order to arrest the spread of the Waldensian and Albigensian heresies which threatened to sweep all southern France. The Waldensians advocated a reversion to apostolic poverty and simplicity; they were dangerous to the church in that they taught that salvation could best be achieved outside the ecclesiastical organization. The Albigensians, or Cathari, taught doctrines completely at variance with orthodox Christianity. 

Efforts to check the spread of these doctrines by preaching and persuasion failed; ineffective measures also were taken to coerce Count 

Raymond of Toulouse to suppress the heresies. When Peter Castlenau, a papal legate, was murdered in 1208, Innocent called upon the baronage of Europe to undertake a crusade against the heretics. 

The avaricious nobles rallied to the cause, and were given papal permission to retain lands and other property seized from the heretics. Pillage, rapine, and massacre were the fruits of the enterprise. 

Little care was taken to distinguish the innocent from the guilty, as the sack of Carcassone well illustrated. The proud county of Toulouse was pitilessly harried and its unique culture ruthlessly destroyed. Raymond VII finally was induced to sign the Treaty of 

Meaux wherein he agreed to the marriage of his daughter to the brother (Alfonso) of King Louis IX of France, with the proviso that the county should escheat to the French crown in default of issue to the marriage. This eventuality materialized in 1270 at the death of Alfonso and the county was annexed to France. 

In the early years of the reign of Louis IX (1226-1270), the monarchy again had to meet the challenge of entrenched feudal privilege. 

A coalition of nobles, under the nominal leadership of Peter of Brittany, sought to take advantage of the minority of the king, but the shrewdness and ability of Blanche of Castile, the king's mother, was too much for them. The administration functioned so efficiently that the absence of the king on crusades from 1248 to 1254 and again in 1270 occasioned no serious rebellions of the baronage. 

Centralization of the monarchy made further progress in the reign

of Philip IV (the Fair). The Order of the Knights Templars was suppressed with pitiless severity and its wealth seized by the king. 

The claims of Boniface VIII to exclusive control of the French clergy were repudiated, and by the close of the reign the prelacy as well as the baronage was subject to the monarchy. Champagne was annexed by the crown as a result of marital arrangements. 

ADMINISTRATIVE DEVELOPMENT IN FRANCE 

Philip Augustus founded the administrative system of medieval 

France. A curia regis exercised advisory and judicial powers. The kingdom was divided into local administrative units which were placed under the control of appointed officials known as prévôts. 

Prévôtships, in turn, were grouped into larger units known as baillages, each under an official known as a baillif, or seneschal. 

In the reign of Louis IX, the curia regis was organized into three departments. The parlement served as the high court of appeal from the courts of prévôts and baillifs. Financial affairs came under the supervision of the Chamber of Accounts, while the Council of State advised the king on domestic and foreign policy. 

The Estates General was convoked for the first time by Philip IV in 1302 in order to get their support in his conflict with Pope Boniface VIII.2 The three estates, or social classes, represented were the nobles, clergy, and townsmen. There was, indeed, promise that the 

Estates General would acquire constitutional prerogatives comparable to those enjoyed by the English Parliament, but this development failed to materialize. The fact that the Estates General met as three separate bodies doubtless vitiated its powers; since no class comparable to the English country gentry existed in France, the townsmen were unsupported by any other social element. During the Hundred 

Years' War, France was on the defensive, with the result that the

Estates General was not in a position to extort constitutional concessions in return for financial support. Then, too, the practice of holding local estates whenever possible precluded meetings of the Estates General with the regularity of the English Parliament. By the close of the Middle Ages, the Estates General had become an anachronism, and the practice of calling meetings was abandoned in 1614, not to be resumed until the eve of the French Revolution. 

2 See infra, p. 312.

CHAPTER 23 The Medieval Church 

HE church was the all-embracing institution of the Middle Ages. No adequate understanding of the period is possible without an appreciation of the many-sided interests, activities, and services of the ecclesiastical organization. The church was not only a religious institution; it exercised a virtual monopoly of social and educational services and arrogated to itself many of the judicial functions of the time. Its property holdings were enormous; perhaps as much as one-third of the arable land in Europe was administered by it in the capacity of a trustee for God. Philosophers labored to give rational exposition to its teachings, while architects and artists sought to invest its services with fitting majesty and splendor.

The church in the broadest sense was the fellowship of believers in Christ. The body of believers, in turn, was divided into the two major groups, clergy and laity. The church was universal and selfperpetuating. Everyone, save Jews and Saracens, was a member.

Christian parents were required by the law of church and state to have children baptized within two weeks after birth. The laity were expected to accept the teachings of Christianity as interpreted and expounded by the clergy. Divergence from the authoritative dogmas was considered heresy, a heinous offense, punishable by the church aided by the authority of the state. Every layman paid one-tenth his annual income to his parish priest, and payment of this tithe was obligatory according to civil as well as canon law. One-third of the tithe went to the upkeep of the parish church, one-third to the bishop, and the remainder to the poor.

The clergy fell into two categories, regular and secular. Regular clergy were those living under a rule, or regula. Both monks and nuns were included in this class, the distinguishing feature of which was their adoption of the ascetic way of life. Many monastic establishments lived under the Benedictine rule, but a number of new or-

ders had come into being since the tenth century, usually during periods where there was an active interest in church reform. 

An important monastic order that owed its origin and growth to the reform influence was that of Cluny, mentioned in an earlier chapter. The order was established in 910, when Duke William of 

Aquitaine endowed it but renounced the customary, rights of patronage, after appointing Odo as the first abbot. Each Cluniac abbot chose his successor in order to maintain continuity of reforming policies. The rule was stricter than the Benedictine. Each establishment that operated under the Cluniac rule was considered a branch of the parent establishment. Once a year, delegates from each branch met under the presidency of the abbot of the original house in order to frame regulations for the order. Monastic orders governed by these annual convocations were officially termed congregational orders. 

Another famous congregational order of the Middle Ages was the Cistercian, with its parent establishment at Citeaux. It was founded in the twelfth century by Stephen Harding. The rule was extremely severe; all conversation of monks was forbidden, each meal was accompanied by scriptural readings, and the diet was Spartan-like in both quantity and quality.

During the pontificate of Innocent III, the two great mendicant orders were established. They differed from other orders in that, in theory, corporate as well as private property was renounced; the members were to subsist on alms offered without solicitation. The 

Dominicans, or Black Friars, were founded by St. Dominic of Spain. 

Alarmed at the spread of the Waldensian and Albigensian heresies,

Dominic desired to form an organization to combat the spread of heretical doctrines by popular preaching. Preaching was to clarify and interpret orthodox doctrines so as to immunize the laity to the pernicious errors of heretical preachers. A decretal of Alexander IV 

(1284) put the Dominicans in charge of the inquisitorial procedure which Gregory IX had stipulated as the official method of combating heresy.

The Franciscans owed their origin to the piety and self-sacrifice of St. Francis of Assisi, who more nearly attained the ideals of Christ than any other individual of the Middle Ages. Social service among the lowly was the major objective of the order. Friars, imbued with the zeal for self-sacrifice of their founder, brought a measure of comfort to the hovel, assuaged the sufferings of the sick, and even labored among the outcast lepers. Before the close of the thirteenth century, the Franciscans were active in higher educational

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

work and many of the chairs in the University of Paris were held by them. The group split, however, into liberal and conservative factions; the former departed from the strict ideals of poverty postulated by St. Francis, whereas the latter group endeavored to conform literally to the original rules in this and other respects. Both mendicant orders were governed by a quasi-military organization, with generals and provincial officers, although both recognized the pope as their supreme commander.

Services in the cathedral were conducted by the bishop of the diocese. The bishop's duties, however, were far too varied and arduous to permit his discharge of this function personally, save on the important feast days. Clergy, known as canons, assisted the bishop by taking charge of the cathedral services in prescribed rotation. A group of canons, attached to a cathedral, was known as the chapter, which was headed by an official known as the dean. The canons usually were supported by incomes derived from endowments, known as prebends, the revenues of which were assigned to them during incumbency of office. In the event that the canons enjoyed the right of electing the bishop, they were known as the bishop's suffragans. 

In some chapters, the canons maintained individual domiciles, while in others they lived in chapter quarters under a monastic rule. 

Those living under a rule were Canons Regular; the two leading orders of this type were the Augustinians and Praemonstratensians. The 

Canons Regular constituted an intermediate order, for they were both monks and priests. They lived according to the dictates of asceticism, but they also were ordained and authorized to say mass and administer the sacraments.

The secular clergy were those who "remained in the world" as the non-monastic group. There were seven "orders," or grades, of the secular clergy, that of bishop being the highest. Bishops were perhaps the busiest individuals on the medieval scene. They were responsible for the "cure of souls" and discipline in their dioceses. 

They alone were authorized to administer the sacraments of confirmation and ordination. Educational work in the dioceses was their special charge, although teaching usually was delegated to subordinates specially qualified for the task. Episcopal courts constituted the tribunals of first instance for the adjudication of all cases comprehended within the canon law. The bishop's judicial duties were delegated to a subordinate known as the archdeacon. Duties of visitation made it mandatory for the bishops to supervise the conduct of parish priests and monks. Management of church property was another

onerous duty. Enormous estates had to be tilled profitably; mills, markets, and ferries often comprised a portion of episcopal property. 

The fact that the bishops were acting in a fiduciary capacity hardly mitigated the difficulty of the task. They were primarily administering deodands, property bequeathed to God; and the parable of the talents left no doubt as to the liability of the trustee. 

The church was inextricably entwined with feudalism. Much property was held by feudal tenure; the bishop, as a vassal, was required to perform services for the suzerains incident to tenure of the respective fiefs. Again, the bishop often granted portions of the property under his administration as fiefs by direct or subinfeudation. As suzerain to the recipients of these fiefs, he had to be vigilant to ensure discharge of the requisite services by his vassals. Bishops often assumed duties of state administration. As a class, they were capable, energetic, and well educated. It was natural, in view of the scarcity of men of such calibre, they should be called upon by kings to perform secular duties. Their position as great feudal lords also inevitably brought them into intimate contact with the several monarchies. 

The next highest order of the secular clergy was that of priest. The priest occupied a key position. He was in intimate contact with the laity and upon his conduct largely depended the prestige of the church organization. His primary duty was to bestow the sacraments, with the exception of confirmation and ordination, which were reserved to the bishop. An enormous influence over the morality of the laity was exercised through the medium of the penitential system with its emphasis on auricular confession. Males only could be admitted to the priesthood, and the candidate could not be deformed or servile. In thousands of cases, however, dispensations, non obstante, made possible the ordination of former serfs. Candidates for ordination were expected to possess at least a rudimentary education, but in this regard concessions frequently had to be made in deference to practical exigencies.

Legislation against clerical immorality abounds in the acts of synods and councils. There is perennial complaint of gross ignorance, incompetence, and wilful negligence in the performance of duties. Virtually every important council condemned clerical preoccupation with hunting and hawking, as well as the more objectionable pleasures of gluttony, tippling, and incontinence. The repetition of these enactments is evidence of the impotence of disciplinary agencies to eradicate these practices; the episcopal registers and visitation articles likewise indicate the difficulty of the problem. It must always be

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

remembered, however, that it was the abuse, the exceptional case, that attracted attention. Thousands of priests who performed their duties ably and conscientiously have left no trace of their work on the records of the time. By and large, clerical educational attainments and morality were considerably superior to contemporary lay society.

Priests derived their economic support locally. One-third the yield of the tithes went to them, but they were responsible for the maintenance and repair of altar and apse in the parish church, while the laity ordinarily were obliged to assume responsibility for the nave. 

Land often was set aside as an endowment for the parish priest; in small, poor parishes he worked the land himself. Many churches were subject to rights of advowson; that is, the endowment had been made on condition that the donor and his heirs were authorized to name the priest who was to officiate in the establishment. This practice obviously was open to serious abuses. 

The lower orders were primarily grades preparatory to the priesthood. Deacons and subdeacons assisted the priest in the mass. Acolytes, readers, and exorcists were of no practical significance by the eighth century. Students and teachers were considered members of the secular clergy and ordinarily took at least the lower orders. Celibacy was not required below the rank of subdeacon. 

Över both branches of the clergy was the administrative hierarchy. 

Bishops of large urban centers were designated as archbishops, or metropolitans. The higher administrative offices did not constitute higher orders of the priesthood; there was no clerical order higher than that of bishop. The archbisops had jurisdiction over areas known as provinces; they called and presided over provincial synods which issued administrative regulations which the bishops were required to enforce in their respective dioceses, and their courts possessed appellate jurisdiction. The archbishops of Rome, Constantinople, Antioch,

Ephesus, Alexandria, and Jerusalem enjoyed the further dignity of the title of "Patriarch."

Actual or titular incumbents of designated church offices in Rome were known as cardinals. The College of Cardinals was created by the Electoral Decrees of Nicholas II (1059). Its primary function was to elect the popes, but as a court (curia) and advisory council it performed important functions.

The supreme head of the church was Bishop of Rome, the supreme pontiff, or pope. The popes were elected after 1059 by the 

College of Cardinals. In the thirteenth century, the practice of im-

muring the conclave was begun. Election was by a procedure known as scrutiny; that is, the cardinals wrote the name of their favored candidate on slips of parchment, repeating the process without formal nominations until a majority was obtained. The pope was represented in all Christian countries by legates, and from time to time legates a latere were sent on special missions. Papal confirmation was necessary for the elevations of bishops, and archbishops could not enter upon the duties of their office until they received the Pallium, or scarf, which was the insignia of office. The pope was the final authority in faith and morals. He defined orthodoxy as doctrinal questions arose from time to time, either by decretals (bulls) or through the legislation of councils which he convoked and guided. 

SERVICES OF THE CHURCH TO SOCIETY 

The church performed a multitude of functions in the Middle Ages. The orthodox doctrine held that the church was the exclusive and indispensable avenue to salvation; an omnipotent and transcendent deity had bequeathed to the church the custody and dispensation of the sacraments. In the Sentences of Peter Lombard, the sacramental system assumed definitive form. The sacrament of baptism admitted to the fellowship of Christian believers; ordinarily it was performed by a priest, but, when warranted by circumstances, valid baptism could be performed by anyone who invoked the Trinity in proper formula and did so with a sincere intent to baptize. The sacrament of confirmation, conferred by the bishops, admitted the recipient to church membership. The ceremony of the mass was the 

Eucharistic sacrifice. At the consecration of the host and the wine, the bread and wine were believed to be changed by the divinely granted power of the priest into the actual body and blood of Christ. 

The term transubstantiation, as applied to this doctrine, received official adoption at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215).

A very important sacrament was that of penance, around which revolved the moral control exercised by the church. Every orthodox believer periodically confessed his sins and received absolution, or forgiveness, which every ordained priest was authorized to grant. 

Absolution did not avail, however, unless confession had been made in a true spirit of contrition. The priest, after absolution, assigned a penance, the performance of which served as visible evidence of contrition. Prayers and fasts sufficed for minor derelictions; pilgrimages usually were the penances prescribed for graver sins. 

Sins due to lack of sufficient sorrow or penance in this world left

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

a scar, or blemish, which could only be removed by the cleansing fires of purgatory. Sojourn in purgatory could be curtailed, according to the teachings of the church, by procuring an indulgence whereby the good works of Christ and the saints applied vicariously to the soul of the recipient.

Extreme unction was bestowed on the dying. Marriage by sacrament was the sole legitimate form of marriage in the Middle Ages. 

The parties bestowed the sacrament on each other, "in the sight of the church," with the priest officiating as a validating witness. A marriage legally contracted was indissoluble. Annulment could be procured from proper ecclesiastical authority if it could be shown that the presence of "impediments" precluded marriage. Most annulments were secured because of the impediment of relationship within forbidden degrees; that is, parties related by blood or marriage within the fourth degree were debarred from marriage to each other. "Spiritual relationship," or joint participation in the ceremonies of baptism and confirmation, had the same effect as blood relationship. 

Coercion, insanity, heresy, "diversity of cult," and concealed servile status were additional impediments to valid marriage. The sacrament of ordination admitted the recipient to Holy Orders and could be conferred only by a bishop.

In the Middle Ages, the church was practically the exclusive agency for the performance of social services which, today, largely have been pre-empted by the state. Great stress was placed on charity from the very beginnings of the Christian movement. One-third of the sum realized from the tithes went to the poor. Almsgiving by the laity was encouraged and many wills included stipulations for distribution of largesses to the poverty-stricken. Hagiology is replete with examples of generosity to beggars and unfortunates of all types; to be sure, practice often diverged from precept, but the ideal was deeply imbedded in contemporary moral consciousness. 

The church was the only agency to operate institutions for the care of the sick. The Knights of St. John and the Teutonic Knights were active in this field after the eleventh century. The Franciscans made the alleviation of the sufferings of the sick a cardinal objective. 

Facilities were woefully inadequate; medical practice was crude and sanitation virtually unknown; but such service as was rendered was almost solely under ecclesiastical auspices. 

Education was considered auxiliary to religion. Learning clarified the Scriptures and the teachings of the Church Fathers; in so far as it attained this objective, it was commendable. Any intellectual in-

terests, any curriculum that was not intimately associated with religion, was superfluous if not subversive. In view of this attitude, it was natural for the church to assume control of educational facilities. 

The church supported schools, prescribed curricula, and licensed teachers. Both students and teachers enjoyed "benefit of clergy." 

Elementary education centered in the monastic schools. Likely youths were trained in the rudimentary branches, primarily in anticipation of their ordination. Convents sometimes afforded comparable facilities for girls. Training in the seven liberal arts centered in the cathedral schools, and some of these schools by adding work in theology, medicine, or law attained the status of universities by the thirteenth century.

An enormous volume of judicial cases, both criminal and civil, was handled by the courts of the church. The ecclesiastical courts tried cases, civil or criminal, in which the parties were clergy. Ability to read was considered presumptive evidence of clerical status; hardened criminals frequently evaded royal justice by memorizing " neck verses," which assured trial of their cases by church courts which could not inflict the capital sentence or any penalty entailing the effusion of blood. Cases of sacrilege, heresy, and reversion to Judaism or Mohammedanism were tried by church courts. 

All cases, civil or criminal, involving widows or orphans came within the competence of ecclesiastical tribunals, since such persons were under the special protection of the church. Civil suits arising from contractual obligations were tried by the church if the contracts had been validated by oaths. Wills usually contained a "pious bequest," whereby property was bequeathed to the church, and litigation arising from such wills fell within the jurisdiction of the canon law. If no "pious bequest" was incorporated, the church nevertheless claimed jurisdiction on the theory that the omission of this provision was inadvertent. The extension of ecclesiastical jurisdiction had the support of public sentiment. In the main, ecclesiastical jurisprudence was more rational and equitable than prevailing practice in secular tribunals.

CHURCH AND STATE IN THE MIDDLE AGES 

The relative positions of church and state precipitated a burning issue in the Middle Ages. The church held that it was vested by God with all earthly powers and for the exercise of these powers it was responsible only to divine authority. Such authority as was wielded by secular rulers was delegated to them by the church; misuse of this

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

power entailed its forfeiture. This political philosophy was in direct opposition to the concept of sovereignty. As medieval kings arrested further feudalization and established centralized governments, it was inevitable that they should challenge the pretensions of the church. 

Conflict between church and state was also an inescapable consequence of the formation of the Holy Roman Empire. From the point of view of the popes, the imperial throne was the gift of the Holy See; its incumbent was primarily the protector of the papacy. The emperors, on the other hand, considered themselves the heirs of the Caesars; the church was an institution to be controlled by the state. 

Benefit of clergy was another point of friction. Certain types of cases were indubitably secular and no churchman denied the right of the state to exercise judicial functions. On the other hand, certain cases reasonably were ascribed to the competence of the church. Between these clearly defined extremes, however, there was a debatable middle ground. Some issues had both secular and ecclesiastical interests and implications. Conflicting jurisdiction, with attendant controversy, was inevitable.

Charlemagne never recognized papal claims to authority over the state. No significance can be attached to his coronation at the hands. of Pope Leo III, for shortly before this event he had sat in judgment on the pontiff. In order to avoid a semblance of obeisance to the papacy, the emperor insisted that Louis the Pious, his successor, crown himself. Even in matters of faith, Charlemagne regarded his authority as supreme. He convoked a synod to condemn the Adoptionist heresy and successfully insisted upon the insertion of the filioque clause in the creed.¹ He likewise spurned the compromise settlement of the 

Council of Constantinople, in regard to the Iconoclastic controversy, without consultation with the pope. Louis the Pious, although usually pliable and vacillating, asserted firm authority over the papacy. 

He insisted that newly elected popes procure imperial confirmation and, on one occasion, he required the pope to answer charges which had been made against him.

During the pontificate of Nicholas I the papacy gained a spectacular victory in a controversy with King Lothair II of Lotharingia. 

The king had fraudulently procured from local clergy an annulment of his marriage, in order that he might marry Waldrada with whom he was infatuated. Nicholas utilized both excommunication and interdict to force the king to return to his legitimate wife; when ec- 

1 The Holy Ghost proceeds from both God the Father and the Son (filioque).

clesiastical censures failed, he threatened to depose Lothair, with the aid of his uncles, Charles the Bald and Louis the German. Lothair was forced to comply with the papal demands; he came to Rome to be publicly reconciled and died on the return journey. His death generally was regarded as a providential punishment for his sin. Nicholas gained great prestige for the papacy by his firm stand for justice and morality. The principle had been asserted that even kings were amenable to the censure of the church. Nicholas made full use of the 

Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals to bolster his claims to authority over secular rulers. These documents purported to be authentic laws and precedents which had been codified by Isidore of Seville, a famous scholar of the seventh century. They were highly favorable to papal claims, and the fact that they were spurious was undetected until the Renaissance laid the foundation of modern historical criticism. 

The Investiture Struggle of the eleventh century (1075-1122) was an outstanding chapter in the history of the relations of church and state. The basic issue was the appointment of church officers, for bishops and other clerical officials in many instances held administrative posts in the service of the respective monarchies. They held large fiefs, in many cases directly from the crown. It was natural, therefore, that kings should attempt to control the selection of these ecclesiastical officials. On the other hand, the church claimed that control over the selection of administrative personnel was vitally necessary, as indeed it was to any institution. The root of the question was the dual position of the prelates. From the point of view of the state, they were powerful feudatories and as such should be subject to royal control; from the standpoint of the church, they were religious functionaries and therefore should be exempt from royal authority. Two conflicting viewpoints, two mutually opposed political philosophies came into direct collision and compromise was difficult, if not impossible.

Gregory VII (Hildebrand), who was elevated to the papal throne in 1073, was deeply imbued with reforming ideals. As papal secretary, he had labored to procure enactment and enforcement of legislation designed to curb simony and promote clerical celibacy and probably was responsible for the promulgation of the Electoral Decrees of 1059. He apparently was content to remain in the background, but it became a matter of common knowledge that his was the hand that guided papal policy. When the cardinals met to elect a successor to Alexander II, the populace of Rome clamored for the election of Hildebrand. The electoral college deferred to popular

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

demand; indeed, it was later charged that Hildebrand's election had been secured by the intimidation of the cardinals by the mob. 

In 1075, Gregory promulgated his famous Investiture Decrees, addressed to Henry IV of Germany. Henry had not only appointed bishops in Germany but had begun to extend this practice to Italy. 

Gregory peremptorily ordered the king to desist from interfering with the choice of clerical officials. Henry had just quelled a rising of nobles and peasantry in Saxony. Jubilant at his victory, he was in no mood to condone what he regarded as papal dictation. His answer to the pope was couched in the most disrespectful language. Gregory's title to the papal office was impugned and aspersions were cast on his motives in respect to the Investiture Decrees. The truculent missive closed with the words: "Come down, from the place which thou has usurped, come down, I say and be damned for all eternity."

Gregory was not loath to accept the challenge. He promptly excommunicated Henry and declared that unless the king made his peace within a year and a day all his subjects would be absolved from their oaths of allegiance. The German nobles, who lately had been in rebellion against the king, were elated at the turn of events; with papal support they anticipated no difficulty in deposing their sovereign. They imprisoned Henry at Speyer in order to prevent him from effecting a reconciliation with the pope within the stipulated time. 

Henry escaped and despite terrible hardships crossed the Alps and made his way to Canossa. Here Gregory was spending the winter at a castle belonging to his protégé, Matilda of Tuscany, in anticipation of proceeding to Germany in the spring. The king stood barefoot in the snow, garbed in penitential sackcloth, with ashes upon his head. 

After three days of abnegation he was admitted to the pope's presence and sentence of excommunication was lifted. 

Upon return to Germany, Henry found the nobles in revolt. At the Diet of Tribur they elected Rudolph of Swabia as king and for a time Henry despaired of restoration, since the pope was abetting the supporters of Rudolph. By 1080, however, the rebellion subsided; 

Rudolph, deserted by many of his former partisans, was forced to surrender. Henry then led an army into Italy; Gregory, fearing the king's vengeance, fled the city and found asylum in the Norman. kingdom of Sicily. There he enlisted the aid of Robert Guiscard, the

Norman king. Accompanied by a Norman army, the pope returned to Rome, which Henry had already evacuated. Soon after entry into the Holy City, the Normans began to pillage; upon withdrawal of the troops, the populace vented their fury on Gregory whom they

deemed responsible for this disaster. The pope again fled to Sicily, where he died after uttering the words, "I have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile." 

The Investiture controversy dragged on through the reign of Henry V. In 1111, Paschal II suggested that as a possible solution the clergy might renounce their properties; if they did so, kings would lose interest in the incumbency of church offices. Naturally, the clergy spurned this proposal, almost with unanimity. The Concordat of Worms (1122), concluded during the pontificate of Callixtus II, provided a practical compromise that went a long way to settle the issue. Bishops and other officials were to be elected in traditional fashion by clergy and laity. There was to be no imperial interference, although the emperor was authorized to station representatives at the election to ensure regularity. After election, the designated candidate was to present himself to the emperor to receive the proprietary rights associated with the position. If the emperor disapproved of the candidate, he could refuse to confer the temporalities and thus, in effect, exercise a veto, since no one wanted the position without the property. If the candidate met with the emperor's approval and was duly invested with the property incident to the position, he then was required to secure papal confirmation of his elevation.

Papal power over secular rulers reached its zenith during the pontificate of Innocent III. When elected in 1198 to succeed Celestine 

III, he was in his thirty-fifth year. He had studied theology at the 

University of Paris and law at Bologna. He was imbued with the loftiest ideals of papal responsibility for the affairs of the world; his organizing genius, indefatigable industry, legal acumen, and unimpeachable integrity enabled him to translate them into action.

An opportunity to assert papal authority in England came with the disputed election to the archbishopric of Canterbury. In 1205 the monks of Christ Church elected a candidate for the primacy, but King John refused to recognize the validity of the election and named his own candidate. When the matter was submitted to the adjudication of Innocent, he refused to confirm either candidate and named Stephen Langton as the new incumbent of the See (1206). 

John refused to allow the pope's nominee to land in England and the English clergy were forbidden to accept him as their primate. Innocent promptly placed England under an interdict, which forbade all church services save baptism of infants and the administration of extreme unction to the dying. The recalcitrant king was excommuni-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cated and when ecclesiastical censures did not produce the desired results Innocent threatened to authorize an invasion of England by an army under the command of Philip Augustus. The English baronage was bitterly opposed to John because of his extortionate and oppressive practices. The king feared that a coalition of his enemies would procure his deposition; accordingly, in 1213, he surrendered his kingdom to the pope from whom he then received it as a fief. As a vassal of the Holy See, John promptly appealed for Innocent's protection; the pope cancelled the proposed punitive expedition of the 

French king and renounced his support of the English baronage. 

From 1213 until the English Reformation, the kings were expected to pay tribute to the popes in recognition of their status as vassals of the Holy See.

At the same time Innocent was applying coercive measures against John, he was engaged in a controversy with Philip Augustus. The 

French king had married Ingeburg, a Danish princess. The day after the wedding, he announced his separation from his bride, who thereupon was held virtually a prisoner in a convent. Philip's action apparently was impelled by a personal repugnance toward Ingeburg, but some time after his separation from her, he married Agnes of Meran. Ingeburg appealed to the pope in a series of touching letters; 

Innocent was deeply sympathetic, but was reluctant to apply severe measures in view of the fact that he needed Philip's support in his struggle with King John. The imposition of an interdict, however, sufficed to coerce Philip to agree to the annulment of his marriage to Agnes. He was technically reconciled with his legitimate queen, but never lived with her, and the pope felt it expedient to condone his action, although the injustice toward Ingeburg never ceased to rankle.

In dealing with lesser sovereigns, Innocent gained several signal victories. Alfonso IX of Leon was forced to separate from a wife related to him within the forbidden degrees of consanguinity. King 

Ottokar of Bohemia succumbed to ecclesiastical censures and was reconciled with his queen whom he had attempted to dismiss on frivolous and spurious charges.

The focal point of papal policy was in Germany. German politics since 1125 had revolved around the implacable enmity of the Welf (Saxony) and Hohenstaufen (Swabia) families. The rivalry of these two powerful families had international complications; the Hohenstaufens favored an active imperialistic policy in Italy, whereas the Welfs were more nationalistic in their outlook. In Italy, the Welfs

were known as the Guelphs and, since they favored abstinence from German intervention in Italian affairs, they enjoyed the support of the popes, who naturally feared that the establishment of imperial authority would curtail the independence of the Roman See. The 

Hohenstaufens, or Ghibellines, as they were called in Italy, were considered the enemies of the papacy, since they endeavored to make the Holy Roman Empire a real political entity. 

A bitter struggle between empire and papacy occurred in the reign of the Hohenstaufen, Frederick Barbarossa (1152-1190). For a time,

Frederick prevailed. At the Diet of Roncaglia (1158), he issued stringent laws designed to rivet his control over the north Italian towns. 

Pope Alexander III, however, shrewdly utilized the resentments kindled in the thriving commercial and industrial centers to form the 

Lombard League. At the battle of Legnano (1176), Frederick's feudal army was decisively beaten by the militia levied from the towns of the League. He was forced to sign the Treaty of Constance (1181), wherein he renounced many of the imperial powers he had claimed at Roncaglia. 

Henry VI, son of Frederick Barbarossa, married Constance, heiress of King William II of Sicily (1190). When he succeeded his father as ruler of Germany and heir to the imperial claims of the Hohenstaufens, the danger to the papacy was greatly enhanced, for if Sicily and Germany were ruled by the same king the papacy would slowly but surely be reduced to vassalage. Henry, however, was preoccupied with his grandiose plans for a crusade; at his death in 1197 the danger to the papacy seemed averted, since his heir, the future emperor, Frederick II, was a mere child.

Constance, the mother of little Frederick, placed him under the guardianship of Innocent III shortly after his elevation to the Petrine Chair (1198). Philip of Swabia, brother of Henry VI, was recognized as king by the Hohenstaufen faction in Germany, whereas the Welfs naturally supported his rival, Otto of Brunswick. Germany was harried by civil war; Innocent, in accordance with traditional papal policy, supported Otto. In 1208, Philip of Swabia was murdered as a result of a personal quarrel with Otto of Wittelsbach to whom he had refused to betroth his daughter and whose small stature he had ridiculed. Otto of Brunswick was then crowned as Otto IV, but to the consternation of the pope he began to carry out an aggressive policy in Italy that was in no wise less dangerous to the pope than the Hohenstaufen designs. 

Innocent had a trump to play. In 1212 he sent his ward, Frederick,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

to Germany, where he was promptly recognized as king by the Hohenstaufen supporters. Otto IV and his ally, King John of England, were decisively defeated by Philip Augustus and Frederick II at the battle of Bouvines; the battle left Frederick undisputed king of Germany and he also received the imperial title. In gratitude to his patron, the pope, Frederick took a vow to go on a crusade; he also promised to renounce his Sicilian possessions so as to dispel the spectre of Italian unification which was so unnerving to the pope. 

After the death of Innocent (1216), Frederick evinced no intention of adhering to the agreement in regard to Sicily. The mild and pacific Honorius III who succeeded Innocent was not disposed to challenge the emperor, but with the accession of the irascible Gregory IX, the dormant issues were aroused. When Frederick did not prove amenable to papal chidings, Gregory reminded him of his youthful promise to go on a crusade. The emperor finally yielded to papal pressure and discharged his obligations, although the bitterness of the pontiff was accentuated because Frederick had gone on his crusade while under sentence of excommunication and this action smacked of overt defiance.

The controversy continued in the pontificate of Innocent IV. 

When the pope convoked a council to discipline the emperor, Frederick seized most of the prelates and prevented their attendance. At the Council of Lyons, however, Frederick was pronounced deposed. 

Henry Raspe, William of Holland, and other anti-emperors were crowned by the pope without altering the situation. Frederick's downfall came largely at the hands of the Lombard cities, as did that of his grandfather. Although the battle of Cortenova was a reversal of the verdict at Legnano, with the death of Frederick (1250) the Hohenstaufen cause was definitively lost. 

At the close of the thirteenth century, papal power encountered the rising force of nationalism. When Philip IV (the Fair) of France imposed a tax on the clergy of his kingdom, Pope Boniface VIII forbade the payment of the levy on pain of excommunication. Philip retaliated by placing an embargo on the export of gold and silver, which cut off papal revenues from France and forced Boniface to renounce his opposition to clerical taxation. A few years later, Philip remanded the trial of a bishop to the royal court. Boniface declared this action to be a violation of benefit of clergy. In his famous bull, Unam Sanctam, he gave the classic statement of the papal theory of supremacy over the officials of the state. The French king, fortified by the support of the Estates General, which had met for the first

time to deal with the issue (1302), refused to make any concession. 

William Nogaret and several other French nobles then made their way to Anagni, the summer residence of the popes, where they committed a disgraceful assault on the helpless and aged pontiff (1303). 

This action paved the way for the beginning of the "Babylonian Captivity."

The medieval popes had hectored and disciplined; they had crushed the proud Hohenstaufens, but nationalism was a force that could not be frustrated. In the course of these struggles with emperors and kings, the popes had been forced to fight with many of the weapons used by their antagonists, and the consequent decline of papal prestige was doubtless one of the fundamental causes of the 

Protestant Revolt.

CHAPTER 24 Economic Conditions in the Middle Ages 

AGRICULTURE 

THEN a vassal did homage to a suzerain, he ordinarily received a grant or fief, in return for his assumption of the personal obligations incident to vassalage. The fief, however, was not merely land; as such, it would have had little value to the vassal, whose time largely was absorbed by the performance of his feudal duties. The fief consisted both of land and the necessary buildings, appurtenances, and implements. It included the necessary domestic animals and the servile peasantry who were engaged in its tillage. In other words, the fief was a complete, self-sufficient, economic organism; it was made up of one or more manors. 

A manor was a plantation, or estate. Large plantations (latifundia) had existed in the Roman world, worked by slaves or, in the late Empire, largely by colons or serfs. The Roman latifundium was doubtless one of the roots of the medieval manor; the communal villages of the early Germans likewise may have served to some degree as a precedent.

The land of a manor fell roughly into three categories. First, there was the arable portion actually under cultivation. Secondly, there was the meadow land, used by lord and peasant alike for pasturage of cattle. Thirdly, there was the waste, made up of woods or swamp. A portion of the arable land, known as the demesne, was reserved for the lord. The serfs were required to work a designated number of days each week on the demesne, and the produce from this portion of the manor went into the barns and granaries of the lord.

The rest of the arable land comprised what was known as the common fields. The common fields were also cultivated by the peasants, but the crops from this portion of the manor went to them and afforded the primary means of their subsistence. Cultivation was according to the "three field " system; that is, one portion of the com-

ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN THE MIDDLE AGES 

315 mon fields was sown with a spring crop, usually wheat, while a second field was planted with a crop that was harvested in the fall, usually barley, oats, or beans. The third field was ploughed, but allowed to lie fallow or sown with grass to conserve the fertility of the soil. 

The arrangement was rotated annually, so that each portion was fallow one year out of every three. This crude expedient was the only feasible method of preventing the exhaustion of the soil; rotation of crops and the use of chemical fertilizers were unknown, and natural fertilizers were reserved for use on the demesne.

The common fields were further divided into many long, narrow strips, usually 4 rods wide and 40 rods long. These strips were separated by leaving the soil unploughed for the width of one furrow and these strips of sod, known as balks, gave access to the individual plots. Each serf was assigned one or more plots in each of the three fields. The crops harvested off his holdings belonged to him. The plots held by the individual serf were scattered; this was an equitable method of division, since each received some of the best land as well as some of the poorest.

Coöperative methods of cultivation were employed. All basic operations, such as ploughing, sowing, and harvesting, were carried on by the joint efforts of all the serfs, each one contributing such equipment as was in his possession. At ploughing time, for example, one serf would contribute the use of his plough, another would lend an ox, another a yoke; all would work together until every strip had been ploughed. Little room was left for private enterprise. The group decided when to plough, what crops to plant, and when the crops should be harvested, and each serf conformed to these arrangements. 

The serfs lived in a village which often was a considerable distance from the fields. A row of one-roomed, thatched huts, without doors, windows, or chimneys, stood on one side of the road; if the village were large, a modest parish church would dominate the cluster of dwellings. Each serf had a garden and perhaps a few fruit trees, and this produce augmented the sparse food supply derived from the strips in the common fields. Each serf was allowed to pasture his cattle in the meadow, and his privileges in the meadow often were graduated in accordance with the size of his holdings in the fields. These meadow rights were highly prized, for in the marginal economy of the manor they often spelled the difference between sustenance and starvation. The "waste" was also important to the serf, as it furnished firewood and afforded mastage for pigs as well as winter pasturage for cattle.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The serf was neither slave nor free. He could not be bought or sold as a chattel. He was attached to the manor and was forbidden to leave it, but on the other hand possession of the manor could not be transferred without transferring him, nor could he be evicted from his holdings so long as he performed the customary services. 

Week work was the serf's basic duty; that is, he was required to work from three to five days per week on the lord's land under the general supervision of the lord's steward or his bailiffs. One of the serfs on each manor was usually selected as the reeve; armed with a stick, he kept the laborers to their tasks for the performance of which he was responsible to the lord's officials. At busy seasons of the agricultural year, such as ploughing or harvesting time, the serf and his family were required to work on the demesne. The lord's crop had to be garnered before the serfs were permitted to harvest the common fields. During the performance of this "boon work" the serfs received rations from the lord; on some manors, custom decreed just how much cheese, ale, and other provender was to be served on such occasions. The serfs also performed a designated number of “ carriages" each year. They would carry a stipulated number of loads of hay to the lord's barn or a fixed quantity of produce to market, or perhaps they might be fortunate enough to be sent to a market town for articles desired by the lord. 

On most manors, the serfs made payments in kind to the lord at stipulated times. On Christmas, a designated number of prime fowls might be required; on Easter, several dozens of eggs; on Michaelmas, perhaps, a cask or two of ale or beer. These payments, of course, replenished the lord's larder at holiday seasons when the presence of guests occasioned added demands on it. 

The lord had the right to exact a heriot from the family of a deceased serf; that is, he could take the best beast from the pitifully small flock of the deceased in return for allowing the family to remain on the manor. If a serf's daughter wished to marry outside the manorial community, the lord collected a compensation known as merchet; likewise, if a son wished to enter the priesthood or go to a town to learn a trade, the lord claimed a forfeit known as chevage. 

There were a host of petty exactions, such as wood penny for the privilege of gathering firewood and ward penny to help defray the cost of maintaining a watch. The lord, moreover, maintained a mill, bake-oven, wine press, and brew-house. All the serfs were required to have their grain ground at the lord's mill, and the miller retained a portion of the flour for the lord. In similar fashion, the women of
