the village had to have their bread baked in the lord's oven and give a number of the loaves for this service; wine and beer had to be made under the same conditions. Serfs usually were subject to a head tax; those who were not were known as villeins and seem to have enjoyed a generally superior status. 

The manor was virtually self-sufficient. Food was raised; clothing and necessary tools were made on the manor. Salt, pig iron, and mill stones were about the only essential commodities that had to be brought in and these but rarely. Serfs lived their lives without leaving the bounds of the manor; those privileged to visit a town twenty miles away were personages of distinction.

Life in the medieval village obviously was one of privation, grinding toil, and hardship. The miserable, smoke-filled hovels, almost devoid of furniture, often were shared with the domestic animals. Infant mortality was terribly high and disease was rampant in the absence of even the most rudimentary sanitation. A bare livelihood was all that could be expected from unremitting toil. Yet the serf had at least a modicum of security. His duties and obligations were fixed by well-nigh inflexible custom, and tenure of his holding was the unalterable recompense for his labors. 

The gulf between lord and serf was not nearly so wide as that between the rich and poor of our own day. The manor house was a rude frame dwelling, often with but one large chamber to which was attached a kitchen. The main hall served for dining, sleeping, and general purposes. Often there was only an aperture in the roof to permit the escape of smoke and window glass was unknown. The earth floor was covered with rushes; hounds and even swine grubbed about in search of table refuse. A trestle table, a few stools, a bedstead, and several chests usually made up the inventory of furniture. 

Comfort and the amenities of modern living were just as far beyond the reach of the lord as they were of the humblest serf. 

TOWNS AND TRADE 

Municipal life was sharply curtailed with the political collapse of the Roman Empire. Only the largest urban centers survived, and these with restricted areas and depleted populations. A great revival of town life began in the age of the crusades. Towns which had been flourishing urban centers in the Empire took on a new lease of life with the expansion of trade ushered in by the crusades. New centers profited by favorable geographical conditions to participate in this trade, with consequent stimulus to their development. Impecunious

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

feudal lords often sold charters to enterprising merchants, who, free from interference, were enabled to assume control of growing towns, and the beneficiaries of the charter constituted the municipal corporation. Kings encouraged municipal growth, since towns were distinctly an antifeudal force. Royal justice gave security, protection from exploitation, and often monopolistic privileges; the town corporations naturally preferred royal authority to the turbulence and extortion of the feudal baronage. 

In some cases, towns owed their rise to military considerations. A number of the garrison posts established by Henry I to defend the eastern frontier of Germany against the Hungarians developed into flourishing towns, as did the Anglo-Saxon burghs founded by Edward the Elder. Then too, some municipal corporations in France seem to have been derived from the survival of the local authority of Charlemagne's échevins. New towns sometimes developed in the immediate vicinity of older settlements. Itinerant merchants would set up their tents or booths outside a city or castle wall and eventually would receive stipulated privileges from the feudal suzerains. 

The temporary mercantile settlements in some instances became permanent and the new towns with their trading privileges and exemptions from feudal jurisdiction eventually overshadowed the old towns of which they were once mere appendages. 

Most medieval towns were walled; in some instances town growth necessitated the erection of several concentric walls. The result was crowding, with consequent absence of proper sanitation and safeguards against disastrous fires. The second stories of shops and dwellings protruded over the narrow, dirty streets. The church or cathedral was the civil center. Its spire dominated the landscape; indeed, the picture of the town clustered about the cathedral epitomizes the spirit of the Middle Ages. Industry was organized into craft gilds. 

The gild was somewhat similar to a modern trade union, for it was basically an association of craftsmen for the attainment of specific objectives. The chief objective of the gild was to secure equality of economic opportunity for its members. Prices, hours of labor, and quality of output were carefully prescribed. No member could forge ahead by price manipulation, unusual industry, or shoddy workmanship, and competition was curtailed as far as possible. 

Precedents for the gild organization of industry could be found in the Roman industrial colleges, but of course there was no direct continuity. In the earlier Middle Ages, particularly in the age of Charlemagne, gilds for religious and fraternal purposes flourished despite

ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN THE MIDDLE AGES 

319 the opposition of governing authority. Gilds, or peace associations, for the maintenance of public order, such as the Anglo-Saxon frith gilds, likewise were in existence by the eleventh century. The immediate ancestor or predecessor of the craft gild, however, was the Gild Merchant. Those engaged in buying and selling established gilds to assure equality of opportunity and to limit the right to sell to those included in their membership. Prices were controlled and any favorable purchases made by a member had to be shared with his fellows so that all could profit equally. The Gild Merchant originally exercised control over the craftsmen whose wares it bought and retailed. The Gild Merchant became virtually an international organization, with its law based on the principle of reciprocity; that is, France would grant the same privileges to English merchants which French merchants enjoyed in England. From the parent stem of the Gild Merchant, the various craft gilds eventually branched off as independent organizations.

Conditions for admission were prescribed by the gild. In most cases, the prospective member served as an apprentice, working by the side of the master in order to attain the requisite technical proficiency. The apprentice received board, lodging, and a stipulated quantity of clothing and he usually was treated as a member of his master's household. Upon expiration of the term of apprenticeship, the prospective master became a journeyman. He went from town to town and worked at his trade for wages and in this fashion familiarized himself with processes and techniques of his trade as practiced in a number of centers. The final requirement was the production of a masterpiece which indicated thorough command of the technique of the craft. If the gild adjudged the masterpiece satisfactory, the applicant was eligible for admission as a master, provided he had sufficient capital to defray the cost of setting up an establishment. 

The gildsmen sold direct to the consumer. Every workshop was also a retail establishment, with the front of the shop devoted to the display of the master's wares. Crafts usually were segregated; the shoemakers were assigned to one quarter of the town, the goldsmiths to another. Specialization and division of labor were characteristic of the system. In the clothing industry, for example, there was a gild of carders to prepare the wool for spinning, a gild of spinners to make the thread, one of weavers, one of fullers, one of dyers, and one of tailors. A cordwainer made shoes, a shoemaker repaired them; members of one gild could not do work assigned to another organization.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

66 The gild had other objectives besides the basic economic one. It afforded a center of social activities for the members. Banquets and drinkings" were gala occasions, and many gilds had their halls where such functions could be held. Every member contributed to common funds which were drawn upon to pay funerary expenses of members and allowances to those physically incapacitated. Widows of gild members were supported for two years after the death of their husbands, and during this period the gild made efforts to find them new spouses. Religion was also an integral phase of gild activity. The gild either owned a chapel or occupied reserved space in a church and attended services in a body. Usually the gilds were dedicated to patron saints and held appropriate exercises in their honor, in which the entire membership participated.

Gild industry had indubitably attractive features. Curtailment of competitive stress gave assurance of a livelihood to all members, yet none became very wealthy. Stability and security were the ideals; the absence of these is the most disturbing feature of modern industrial conditions. The worker was a craftsman. He made articles with tools wielded by his deft hands; his work was free from the drudgery, the deadly, soul-destroying monotony of the modern factory. 

There was, of course, a divergence between ideal and practice. 

Many gildsmen violated the rules and eluded the vigilance of searchers to reap an unfair advantage over competitors by sharp practices. 

Then, too, there was an intrinsic oligarchical tendency, for those in the gild wished to make entrance difficult. This exclusive trend manifested itself by the adoption of livery. Many properly qualified applicants could not afford the sumptuous raiment used by the "liveried" gilds on ceremonial occasions and consequently were debarred. The specifications of the masterpiece might be made so expensive as to preclude compliance with them by the candidate, and this expedient also was used to deny entrance to those who had completed their training. In practice, a class of workers for wages grew up, despite the theory that every qualified applicant could set up in business as a master.

MEDIEVAL COMMERCE 

Trade was greatly curtailed with the collapse of the Roman Empire. Currency virtually disappeared from circulation, necessitating reversion to barter. Feudal lords imposed tolls and customs that were well-nigh prohibitive. Saracen control of the Mediterranean precluded all but a small, coastwise trade, with centers at Arles and

ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN THE MIDDLE AGES 321 

Marseilles. The self-sufficiency of the manors left little basis for exchange, with resultant shrinkage of local trade.

The revival of commerce in the later Middle Ages was in large measure a result of the crusades and the consequent renewal of contact with the East. Saracen control of the Mediterranean was broken and their commercial interests were taken over by the flourishing Italian cities. Eastern products were introduced in western Europe, creating a demand which the Italian merchants were in a position to supply because of their trading posts in the Levant. The power of feudal lords over urban centers was relaxed as the townsmen bought, wheedled, or extorted charters of incorporation. The rise of centralized government meant great protection to merchants and enhanced opportunities for profit. The rise of the Gild Merchant and its encouragement by government meant a reasonable uniformity of standards and, above all, enabled merchants to extend their activity even into foreign countries with some assurance of protection. Manors began to produce surpluses of agricultural commodities. 

Specialization was therefore made feasible; one manor could concentrate on the raising of foodstuffs, another on the raising of sheep. 

Since each produced a surplus of its special commodity, there was a mutual basis for exchange. 

The Italian cities of Venice, Genoa, Amalfi, and Pisa enjoyed virtually a monopoly of the eastern trade. Saracen merchants brought the products of India and China to the Levant by the ancient routes. 

One popular route was across the Indian Ocean to the Persian Gulf, up the gulf and the Euphrates, thence, across by caravan, to Acre, Antioch, or Aleppo. Another route was across the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea, up the Red Sea, across by caravan to the Nile, and down the Nile to Alexandria. Oriental wares were then purchased by Italian factors in the Levantine trading posts for shipment in Italian bottoms. 

The chief function of the Italian merchants was to distribute the eastern wares to western Europe. 

Beginning in 1317, Venice sent out annual fleets of from one to six commercial galleys, laden with oriental products. These fleets were called the "Flanders Fleets," because the ultimate destination of most of the vessels was Flanders. The government of Venice, nominally democratic, was in reality a commercial oligarchy, with the Council of Ten as its chief executive organ. The government owned and operated the commercial vessels; the admirals chosen from one of the noble families received their orders from the Council and were held strictly responsible for the profitable conduct of the voyage. January to March of each year, cargo space was auctioned to the individual merchants who were eligible to participate in the allocation of profits on a pro-rata basis. When the ships were laden at the government docks with cargo which had been stored in the municipal warehouses, the fleet set out, sometimes convoyed by war galleys, or protected by companies of archers. A ship or two might dock at Naples or Genoa and would ordinarily anchor at Marseilles. The main body, however, proceeded through the Straits of Gibraltar; about half the fleet would then dock at Bristol, while the remainder proceeded to Flanders.

The ships carried the products of the East that had been held in great esteem since the days of antiquity - silk and pottery from 

China, spices from the Spice Islands, drugs, precious stones, and fine fabrics from India. Levantine tapestries, carpets, and fabrics also usually comprised part of the cargo. On the return journey, the galleys were laden with wool, woolfells, leather, and naval stores. The balance of trade normally was in favor of Venice; the Florentine banking houses of the Bardi, Peruzzi, and Frescobaldi arranged the necessary credits. Eastern products also found their way into central Europe via the caravan routes through the Alpine passes. Interference with the caravan routes by France in 1317 was the chief reason for the memorable decision to utilize an all-water passage.

The Baltic trade was conducted by the Hanseatic League. A number of cities in the Rhine valley had organized a league to free the river trade from the depredations of robber barons. These towns joined with the important Baltic cities of Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen to form a Hansa or fellowship. In 1252, Lübeck and Hamburg acquired joint trading privileges in the Flemish city of Bruges. 

Thirteen years later, a number of north German towns agreed to observe the "Law of Lübeck." By 1293, at least twenty-six towns were affiliated with the federation and by 1360 the number had grown to fifty-two. By the Treaty of Stralsund (1370), the Hansa was given extensive commercial privileges in Scandinavia. The capital of the federation was at Lübeck, where each year delegates from the member towns met in the Gild Hall in assemblies to pass legislation of general application. Reports of these sessions, known as the Hanserecessen, have been published. From 1363 to 1450, there were thirtyeight meetings; the largest recorded gathering contained representatives of thirty-nine towns. The League maintained factories in 

Scandinavia and Russia. In London, their "Steelyard," with its great steel weighing beam, was a familiar landmark just above Lon-

ECONOMIC CONDITIONS IN THE MIDDLE AGES 325 

don Bridge, with warehouses, counting houses, and dormitories for the personnel. The basis of the prosperity of the League was its virtual monopoly of the herring fishing in the Baltic. Each year the herring came to the Baltic to spawn and enormous quantities were taken and salted by the Hansa fishermen for export to a number of commercial centers. From its Russian and Scandinavian posts, particularly Saint Peter's Courtyard in Novgorod and its twenty-two yards in Bergen, the League exported pitch, amber, furs, and lumber. 

Flanders was the crossroads of medieval trade, for both Hanseatic and Venetian vessels used Flemish ports as termini; and here took place the exchange of eastern and northern commodities. Ghent, Bruges, and Antwerp were flourishing industrial centers and their woolen cloth found a market throughout virtually the entire medieval world.

Fairs were the great intermediate distributing centers. Merchants planned itineraries to enable them to visit the chief fairs held at various times throughout the year. The fairs of Champagne were world famous and those of England were also well known. A fair opened with a proclamation of the "peace of the fair." A court was set up and all offenses or violations of fair regulations were tried by this court which, in popular language, was termed the "dusty foot" court, since most of the litigants were transients. Each commodity offered for sale was assigned to a reserved section of the grounds; one section was thronged with grain merchants, another with cattle dealers; others bustled with the activities of drapers, goldsmiths, or grocers. In the Champagne fairs, definite times were set aside for each type of business; one week would be reserved for the grain trade, another for the sale of woolen cloth. Merchants who had goods to vend purchased the right to set up booths in the sections reserved for their commodities. The fair was somewhat similar to the wholesale market of today, for merchants purchased in considerable quantity subsequently to retail their purchases in municipal markets. 

Every town had a market, which usually was open for business on Tuesdays and Fridays. The right to hold a market was an indispensable feature of municipal charters; indeed, some scholars think that the grant of market privileges marked the foundations of the town. 

Merchants who enjoyed privileges of the market hired booths where they retailed commodities which they purchased at ports or fairs. 

Gild masters usually had booths in the market for the sale of the products of their craftsmanship.

CHAPTER 25 Intellectual Life of the Middle Ages 

EDIEVAL education conformed to at least one dictate of modern pedagogy in that it had an eminently clear purpose. The function of education was to expound and clarify the teachings of the church and thus facilitate the attainment of salvation. Learning was the "handmaid" of religion; philosophy merely confirmed truths already perceived by faith. Knowledge which could not be applied to religion was "profane learning," at best frivolous, if not dangerous.

God was the source of all truth; such truth as was to be revealed to man was placed in the custody of the church, its sole authorized disseminator and expositor. The Bible and the writings of the Church 

Fathers comprehended such knowledge, and interpretation could come only through the medium of the church. These fundamental premises led to the irrefutable conclusion that education was a phase of the mission of the church and pedagogical facilities were to be established and maintained by the ecclesiastical organization. 

In most parts of Europe, educational facilities were adequate to afford training to those with the industry and aptitude to avail themselves of them. Roman schools had not entirely disappeared, at least in large urban centers; elementary schools, modeled on the Roman type, survived until superseded by church schools. Charlemagne, in his memorable capitularies on education, directed that schools be established in monasteries and bishoprics, not only for prospective clerics, but also for promising youths with no desire to enter the priesthood. The Palace School, under the direction of Alcuin, inaugurated a definite rise in intellectual interests and standards. A similar revival of interest in scholarship began in Germany in the age of Otto the Great and doubtless was a late manifestation of the Carolingian Renaissance.

By the twelfth century, virtually every monastery was a center for at least a modicum of scholarly activity. Many cloisters maintained

elementary schools conducted by brethren with pedagogical ability. 

Most establishments boasted collections of texts, and skilled monks often were assigned to the work of copying and illuminating manuscripts. Bishops established schools in their dioceses; by 1100 some of these developed into the cathedral schools which were, to some degree, comparable with modern secondary schools. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 made mandatory the foundation of episcopal schools which were to be conducted by teachers selected and controlled by the bishops.

Elementary schools were largely devoted to instruction in reading, writing, and the elements of Latin grammar. The cathedral schools offered a curriculum that nominally comprehended the seven liberal arts. This curriculum was divided into a group of elementary subjects known as the Trivium and an advanced group known as the Quadrivium. The Trivium included grammar, rhetoric, and logic. 

Instruction in grammar was based on the texts of Donatus and Priscian; rhetoric continued the grammatical training, together with illustrative material consisting largely of excerpts from classical Latin authors. Logic, or dialectic, was a favorite study. The formal rules for logical reasoning were memorized and practically applied in disputation. Litigious methods were utilized in virtually all fields of study; hence, rigorous training in logic was considered fundamental, especially after the dialectical works of Aristotle were available in 

Latin translation.

Training in the branches of the Quadrivium was much more superficial. Arithmetic included simple computations, but greatest stress was placed on the calculation of the date of Easter and other movable feasts of the church; numerology, or the supposed mystical and symbolical significance of numbers, also was emphasized. Geometry was little more than the memorizing of a few of the Euclidean theorems without the proofs and the application of some of the theorems to the calculation of areas. Music was based on the text of 

Boethius whose definitions were memorized and discussed, but there was little or no application of the principles in vocal or instrumental art. Astronomy, the fourth subject of the advanced group, was largely devoted to the pseudo-lore of astrology. Heavenly bodies determined events and affected individual personalities. These superstitions were not differentiated from the smattering of scientific truth embodied in the subject as taught by the medieval masters. 

Instructional methods were well-nigh uniform. Rules and definitions, together with a formidable array of exceptions, were com-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mitted to memory. Unstinting application of the rod prodded the flagging industry of younger pupils and was considered an indispensable pedagogical adjunct. If the master possessed a text, he normally would lecture, that is, dictate the text, which thereupon was copied by the pupils. Explanatory remarks or illustrations were interpolated from time to time and written in the margins of the pupils' copies. Debate was an esteemed instructional device in that it afforded drill and application of rules. A pupil might be asked to define a noun; another would then be told to attack the definition and thus engender critical discussion. Moral interpretations accompanied every subject of study, and labored allegory or absurd symbolism supplied edification where no direct moral or religious connotation could be derived.

The apex of medieval education was the university, and the foundation of institutions of higher learning was one of the outstanding contributions of the Middle Ages to Western civilization. The term university is derived from the Latin universitas, or corporation. 

When we speak of a university today, we call to mind campus, buildings, libraries, and laboratories; in other words, the physical plant. 

In the Middle Ages, the university was a group of people, a corporation either of masters or students. In some cases, the masters were granted the charter of incorporation and thus constituted the university while in others it was the students who enjoyed corporate status.

There were many reasons for the rise of the universities. Growing interest in education, with the consequent expansion of instructional facilities, created a demand for teachers. It was necessary to provide adequate training for these teachers and to ensure maintenance of reasonably standardized qualifications for entrance into the profession. The craft gilds prescribed the conditions for entry into practice of the respective crafts and enforced proper standards of workmanship. The university was really a projection of the gild system to education for basically the same purposes as had motivated the establishment of the craft gilds. The rise of heresy, particularly as embodied in the Albigensian and Waldensian movements, demonstrated the need for trained defenders of the faith who could refute the arguments of those who challenged the authority or doctrines of the church. Development of centralized monarchies in a number of European countries created a demand for trained administrators, particularly those learned in the law, while the expansion of trade and industry offered other fields for the employment of educated men.

An educational institution had to meet the following requirements to qualify as a university. First, there had to be more than one master. 

Second, admission of students could not be confined to one nationality. Third, the institution, in addition to the basic curriculum of the seven liberal arts, had to offer at least one of the " Higher Faculties" which were theology, law, and medicine. 

The University of Paris developed from the cathedral school of Notre Dame and was incorporated as a gild of masters. The school was an important center of learning by the eleventh century. The archbishop's chancellor was vested with custody of the library and seal; his license was necessary before students were qualified to become teachers. He was not permitted to exact a fee for the license, however, nor was he authorized to refuse the license to properly qualified applicants. King Louis VII (1137-1180) authorized the masters of the school to suspend their lectures in protest against unsatisfactory conditions and laid the foundations for the emancipation of the teachers from the jurisdiction of the chancellor. The same king later permitted the masters to form a gild and draw up by-laws for its government.

A serious riot in 1200, which involved students and masters, led to the issue of a charter by Innocent III wherein the members of the school group were declared amenable only to the jurisdiction of the court of the chancellor. The emancipation of students and masters from the jurisdiction of municipal authorities was a fertile cause for ill-feeling and subsequent " town and gown " riots. A second charter, issued by Innocent in 1210, gave important concessions to the masters. They were authorized to elect a proctor to serve as their executive officer, and their corporate status was recognized by acknowledgment of their right to sue and be sued as a group. The charter further directed that the masters wear academic costume and attend funerals of deceased colleagues in a body.

The charter of 1212, issued by the same pontiff, definitely vested control of the school in the hands of the masters. They were empowered to elect officers and pass laws. They also were permitted to assess and collect fees from students, and the chancellor was ordered to give the teaching license to all candidates passed by the masters. 

The control of fees and the requirements for the license were the essential powers; henceforth, the chancellor was merely the executive agent of the faculty.

Students of the university by 1220 were divided into four nations: 

English, Gauls, Normans, and Picards. In 1228, a group of students

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

became involved in an altercation with a tavern keeper as a result of the inevitable dispute over the amount of the reckoning. Royal soldiers arrested a number of students who were spending a holiday playing games and who had taken no part in the quarrel. In protest against violation of university immunities, students and masters seceded and accepted the invitation of Henry III to come to Oxford, but the grant of a new charter finally induced many to return. 

A document of 1245 mentions for the first time an official known as the rector, who apparently headed the liberal arts group. Ten years later there is mention of the rector of the university. This official was the executive head of the institution and by 1264 he was assisted by deans in charge of each of the faculties: arts, medicine, theology, and law.

The University of Bologna owed its origin and prestige to the revival of interest in Roman law inaugurated by the work of Irnerius. 

Frederick Barbarossa authorized the incorporation of the law professors at the Diet of Roncaglia (1158), but there is no record of the granting of degrees before 1219. In the thirteenth century, the students organized themselves into the Cismontane (Italian) and Ultramontane (foreign) groups, each under the supervision of an elected rector. By boycott and secession, these student groups wrested control of the university from the faculty. Early in the fourteenth century, the two student groups coalesced, but retained the two rectors as executive officers. In 1316, the arts curriculum was added, while in 1360 theology was introduced. The students were organized into seventeen nations, each of which was represented in the university council which advised the biennially elected rectors and passed statutes for the government of the institution. There were also treasurers, notaries, advocates, and bedels.

The organized students exercised a vigorous control over the professors. The hapless teachers were fined for absence or tardiness, although they were permitted to be absent one day on the occasion of their marriage. Fines were imposed if the instructors evaded difficult points in their lectures, but a bonus was paid for each interpolation or commentary which they inserted in the text. The masters were expected to begin their lectures promptly and were fined if they continued for more than one minute after the termination of the allotted time. They likewise were subject to a fine if the number of students in attendance at a lecture was less than five. Fees had to be arranged with the students by the masters, who doubtless spent much of their time in futile dunning.

The University of Salerno was the great center of medical studies in the Middle Ages. It owed its development to the presence in Sicily of skilled Jewish and Mohammedan physicians and surgeons who acquired a reputation throughout Europe. Some of these doctors began to offer instruction in their art at the Sicilian capital; in 1231, Frederick II gave necessary official sanction by prescribing license from these masters as a necessary qualification for the practice of medicine and surgery.

Classroom space was hired by masters or students. Since the university had no buildings of its own, its mobility was an effective weapon for the extortion of privileges from recalcitrant governmental authorities. Classes began at daybreak. In many institutions, students squatted on the floor, shivering in the unheated rooms. The master lectured from his text, while the students wrote at his dictation, inserting the professor's commentaries as glosses. Since all lectures were in Latin, students were able to study at any university without linguistic difficulties.

There were no course or attendance requirements. The granting of the bachelor's degree was contingent upon a satisfactory oral examination and public defense of a thesis; candidates for the master's degree, which authorized the holder to teach, were required to give several public lectures in addition to passing a satisfactory examination. The doctorate was awarded in theology, medicine, and law. 

Candidates who successfully passed their examinations often were honored by a procession through the streets of the town, accompanied by the tolling of the cathedral bells. A not inconsiderable item of expense was the customary duty of the graduate to fete fellow students at a banquet.

Small universities had an enrollment of approximately 100 students, while large institutions boasted of 5000 or more. Boys of twelve often studied beside men of forty; the average age, however, was about seventeen. Student poverty was proverbial, necessitating rigid economies in lodging, food, candles, parchment, and other supplies. Begging was a recognized means of securing funds, and aid to needy students was considered a laudable charity. 

Discipline often was sadly lacking. Absence of organized sports indeed, scarcity of facilities for any kind of recreation - was in large measure responsible for this condition. At Oxford, for example, playing with ball and bat was forbidden as an "insolent game." While some institutions required students to "sit still as girls," lack of normal recreational activities stimulated the carousing, dancing, leap-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ing, and dicing which sometimes even disturbed chapel services, and the well-founded complaint could be made that students frequently were more familiar with the “text of the dice " than they were with the Old Logic. University statutes at Leipzig forbade throwing stones at professors and prohibited carrying weapons into classrooms. 

At one of the universities, a student was suspended for connivance in the murder of a fellow student, while in another the authorities, with unwonted severity, expelled a student who had cut the throat of a colleague. Saloons and, indeed, facilities for indulgence in more vicious divertisements were in convenient proximity to classrooms. 

Clashes with townspeople were frequent occurrences and many of these "town and gown" encounters resulted in fatalities. 

The evolution of the college system eliminated many of these abuses. Dormitory space was provided and the life of the student outside the classroom subjected to close supervision. Merton and Baliol in England and the Sorbonne at Paris were early examples of the collegiate organization.

MEDIEVAL PHILOSOPHY 

The interpretation that considered the period from the collapse of the Roman Empire in the West to the humanistic movement of the fourteenth century as culturally homogeneous has been completely discredited along with the view that medieval thought was sterile, credulous, and dominated by absurd superstition. From the decline of the Empire to the period of Charlemagne, emphasis naturally was on the preservation of at least a modicum of such Roman culture as had survived the shock of the Germanic invasions. A major objective was to summarize in encyclopaedic fashion the Roman cultural inheritance, and the Etymologies of Isidore of Seville as well as the works of Rhabanus Maurus and Vincent of Beauvais, despite their many inaccuracies, performed an indispensable service in the history of medieval education. The Carolingian Renaissance, as it sometimes is called, stimulated the demand for epitomes of learning, but, as already pointed out, its primary contribution was to expand existent educational facilities. 

With the eleventh century, however, the era of summary and epitome yielded to broader outlooks and objectives. Prolonged contact with Byzantine cultural inspiration in the period of the crusades was a fundamental cause of this progress, but of much greater importance was contact with Saracen learning in Spain, Sicily, and the Near East. As early as the tenth century, western European scholars

supplemented their training in Christian schools by study in Moorish intellectual centers. Gerbert of Aurillac, who played an important part in the foundation of the Capetian dynasty in France and subsequently served as the tutor of young Otto III, who ultimately made him pope, was recognized as the most learned man of his day, primarily because of his studies in Spain in the fields of mathematics and science.

Aside from their contribution to the development of scientific studies, the Moorish scholars made the works of Aristotle available. to the students of Christian Europe. In the early Middle Ages, the only writings of the great Greek philosopher that were known in Europe were his Categories, preserved by Porphyry, and the summary of his logical work embodied in the De Interpretatione of Boethius. Through the medium of Arabic translations which subsequently were rendered into Latin, especially as a result of the work of the Moorish scholar, Averroes, this Old Logic was supplemented by the New Logic which included the Prior and Posterior Analytics. 

Before the close of the twelfth century, the Physics and Metaphysics also were available.

The introduction of the Aristotelean works created an acute problem for the church. Were these works to be banned, ignored, or reconciled with orthodox Catholic dogma? The decision of the ecclesiastical authorities to permit the attempt to harmonize Aristotle with Christianity was epoch-making in its significance and was destined to color the intellectual life of Europe for several centuries. 

The attempt to prove some of the teachings of the church by the application of Aristotelean logic is known as scholasticism. Reason was to supplement, never weaken, faith; heretic and infidel were to be convinced of the truths of the faith by irrefutable reasoning. The scholastic philosophers, like the great Hellenic thinkers, had boundless faith in the powers of human reason and boldly delved into questions of fundamental import which modern thinkers are all too ready to relegate to the sphere of the supernatural. Logical methods were deductive; fundamental premises were accepted as axiomatic and from them corollaries or conclusions were derived. The Scriptures, the writings of the Church Fathers, and Aristotle were placed virtually on the same plane and were considered unimpeachable authorities, citation from which was incontrovertible proof. 

At first, the attempt to reconcile Aristotle with Christian dogma produced more controversy than harmony. Berengar of Tours denied the doctrine, later known as transubstantiation, to the effect that

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the bread and wine of the Eucharist became the actual body and blood of Christ. He was vigorously opposed by Lanfranc, the Norman prelate who became archbishop of Canterbury under William the Conqueror. Roscellinus, in his memorable controversy with Anselm of Bec, held that the doctrine of the Trinity was illogical and led his antagonist to propound the view that, after all, faith and reason actually were inseparable, and reason merely clarified that which already was known by faith. "I do not know in order that I may believe, but I believe in order that I may know" was the way in which Anselm summarized this principle. 

Few works were productive of as much controversy as those of 

Abelard (1079-1142). Born in Champagne, he came to Paris as a young man in order to study under the famous William of Champeaux whom he soon made a lifelong enemy by vanquishing him in disputation. His famous love affair with Heloise, daughter of canon

Fulbert of Chartres, ultimately led to his disgrace and retirement to the monastery of St. Denis, but with the publication of his work on the Trinity he aroused the ire of the indefatigable Bernard of Clairvaux who finally had him arraigned before the Council of Sens on charges of heresy. The council ordered him to refrain from writing and lecturing.

Abelard possessed one of the most powerful minds of the Middle Ages. His intervention in the controversy that was raging in academic circles concerning the objective reality of general concepts proved decisive. The realists had held that generalities such as beauty, truth, humanity, etc. actually existed; their slogan was “the general before the particular." Nominalists, on the other hand, held that the general could exist only as the aggregate of individual instances. Abelard's compromise position that the general could exist only in the particular instances went a long way to settle the controversy and established his reputation as a scholar.

His work entitled Sic et non (yes and no) was a veritable intellectual bombshell. He marshalled an array of authoritative citations in support of a number of propositions and then listed equally authoritative passages against the same propositions. In other words, the authorities upon which the theologians relied so implicitly were inconsistent and contradictory. His work was intended to stimulate the skepticism and critical approach without which scholarly activity is inevitably sterile. Understanding should precede acceptance of ideas; freedom of thought and the inductive approach likewise were requisite to intellectual progress. Peter Lombard in his Sentences

took up the problems first stated by Abelard and attempted to reconcile the apparent discrepancies in the authoritative sources. His conclusions became indispensable polemic and apologetic weapons of the theologians. 

Conflict soon gave way to triumphant harmony. Alexander of 

Hales (died c. 1245), sometimes called the founder of true scholasticism, held that the Scriptures could be defended by logic. Albertus 

Magnus, the "Universal Doctor" (1193-1280), a Dominican monk who served for a time as bishop of Regensburg, was an even more outstanding figure of medieval scholarship. He studied the writings of Aristotle thoroughly, taught at Cologne and Paris, and was unique in the critical attitude which he manifested. His commentaries on 

Aristotle aggregated twenty-one folio volumes, of which the seventh and eighth were distinguished by the greatest degree of independence of thought. He was a pioneer investigator in the fields of botany and general biology, and his classification of plants was an important contribution to scientific advance. His insistence on the need for observation and experience in the ascertainment of truth foreshadowed the emergence of experimental science. 

Thomas Aquinas, the "Angelic Doctor" (1225-1274), was the most illustrious disciple of Albertus. He was born in Sicily and studied at Monte Cassino and the University of Naples prior to becoming a pupil of Albertus. His works fill seventeen folio volumes. His 

Summary against the Gentiles was an exhaustive array of the arguments which might be brought against Christian truth by nonbelievers and complete refutations of these arguments. His Summa 

Theologica is one of the greatest scholarly monuments of all time. 

It is even today the complete, authoritative exposition of Catholic doctrine. Aquinas adhered to the earlier views of Anselm in regard to the relation of faith and reason. Faith and reason were not in fact separate; each in its own way led to the same conclusions. Reason merely afforded logical demonstration of that which already was known by faith. William of Occam, however, challenged the Thomist view. For him, faith and reason were not identical; many religious beliefs accepted by faith could not be rationally demonstrated. He went so far as to state unequivocally that some of the dogmas of the church were rationally untenable. Occam and Duns Scotus, by their attacks on the fundamental bases of Thomism, really foreshadowed the end of scholasticism.

There was comparatively little interest in science in the Christian schools of the Middle Ages. Prevalent ascetic ideas doubtless were in

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

a measure responsible for the absence of curiosity about the physical world. If the world was intrinsically evil, if earthly existence was nothing more than a period of preparation for eternity, there was no basis for a scientific approach to man's physical environment. The church was the only authorized interpreter of truth; it set bounds to the aspirations of the human mind. If all truth were embodied in the 

Scriptures, what need was there for investigation and experiment?

Instruments of precision, such as sensitive balances, micrometers, and similar devices, were wholly lacking; there was neither telescope nor microscope. Even had medieval scholars possessed a spirit of scientific inquiry, lack of indispensable equipment would largely have precluded fruitful results. The experimental method was largely foreign to scholastic thought with its deductive approach, its symbolism, and endless summarizing of existent knowledge. There were exceptions of course. As early as the time of Gerbert (died in 1003), a few scholars profited by the study of Saracen scientific lore. Albert the Great and the famous Oxford teachers, Adam Marsh and Robert Grosseteste, pioneered with the employment of the experimental method. Roger Bacon, with his emphasis on the necessity for experimentation, was greatly influenced by the work of these men, who, although they lived in the thirteenth century, intellectually belonged to the age of the Renaissance.

Medieval mathematicians were largely absorbed in the task of devising methods for the computation of the proper date for celebrating the feasts of the church. Elaborate treatises on the mystic properties of numbers were evidence of the prevalent superstition in this respect. Alchemists distilled and compounded in search of the philosopher's stone, the marvelous substance which it was believed would transmute base metals into gold. 

Medicine in the Middle Ages was a curious mixture of religious belief, magic, and a smattering of pharmacology. There were four primary elements of which all matter was composed: earth, air, fire and water. The human body was a balance of blood, water, black bile, and phlegm. In a healthy person, the elements were in proper equilibrium. From time to time, however, vapors entered the body and by disturbing bodily equilibrium produced the symptoms of disease. 

Diseases were classified in four categories: hot, cold, moist, and dry, depending on the presence or absence of fever and perspiration. The practitioner prescribed appalling compounds made up of nux vomica, powdered snails, toad skins, and other obnoxious substances, with the idea that these would drive out the pestilential vapors responsible

for illness. In most instances, nature took its course; the patient died or recovered independent of the treatment. Medieval surgeons, on the other hand, were quite adept. Ligaturing was practiced; operations which would be considered major operations in a modern hospital were successfully performed by the medieval practitioners.

CHAPTER 26 Medieval Literature, Architecture, and Art 

S O long as historians still spoke of the Middle Ages as the "Dark Ages," and dismissed scholasticism with ridicule, it was not surprising that medieval literature failed to receive serious study or understanding. The influence of Renaissance humanists, with their revival of classical Latin and Greek, contributed powerfully to the establishment of the tradition that medieval literature was uncouth, a mere corruption of the chaste beauty and impeccable form of classical writing. Modern historiography, however, has rediscovered the beauty of medieval literature and art just as it has recognized the importance of the medieval period in philosophy and institutional development. 

Much of the literature of the Middle Ages - indeed, virtually all the work of ecclesiastics - was written in medieval Latin. Language, of course, is constantly changing with the entrance of colloquialisms and words of foreign derivation. In the last analysis, it is not the scholars but the people who pass final judgment on word usage and grammatical construction. We constantly see in our own language the admission of new words and the ultimate recognition of much popular idiom in standard literature. The best Latin authors of classical time used words of Greek derivation and occasional colloquialisms. With the Germanic invasions, words of Teutonic origin naturally came into the language. The church added a considerable vocabulary and there was a constant influx of popular idiom. The end of the Empire in the West, with the consequent breakdown of communications, obviously gave a tremendous impetus to the evolution of dialects. New words and spellings, new meanings for old words, and simplified grammatical construction distinguished the Latin of the medieval scholar from that, let us say, of Cicero, but it would be erroneous to dismiss the Latin of the period as a drab corruption of the classical style. Latin remained the language of the scholar throughout the Middle Ages; it was the language of the classroom from elementary school to university.

Of far greater significance than the modification of classical Latin was the emergence of the vernaculars. French and other Romance languages, of course, developed from the parent Latin. The earliest extant text which shows clearly how French was stemming off from Latin is the famous Strasburg Oath, taken in 842, it will be recalled, by the partisans of Charles the Bald and Louis the German to confirm their alliance. Ultimately two main forms of French emerged, although there were many local variations. That north of a line running from La Rochelle through Limoges to Grenoble was known as the Langue d'oil because of the pronunciation of the word for yes" as oil and ultimately oui. That south of the line was the 

Langue d'oc. The language of the north became the official language of the court and ultimately the standard literary form as well. In large measure the victory of the Langue d'oïl can be attributed to the virtual destruction of the so-called Provençal culture of Langue d'oc by the Albigensian Crusade. In Spain, the dialect of Castile became the official language and literary vehicle. Portugal, which had split off from Spain, developed a Romance tongue somewhat different from the Spanish. From the dozens of dialects of Italy, the language of Florence ultimately became the national tongue primarily because of the influence of Renaissance writers, particularly Dante, the great transitional literary figure from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance. 

The oldest literary monument of the German tongue is the famous Gothic Bible of Ulfilas, dating from the fourth century, now preserved in the library of the University of Upsala, Sweden. In Germany, as elsewhere, the provincialism of the period of the feudal regime meant the emergence of a great number of dialects. In the north, the language was known as Low German, while in the south, High German prevailed. The dialect of Saxony became the standard literary language of Germany largely because of Luther's translation of the Scriptures into that version of the language. English, of course, is basically Anglo-Saxon; since Beowulf is primarily Scandinavian, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle can be regarded as the earliest literary survival of the Anglo-Saxon tongue. It was begun in the reign of King Alfred and nine manuscripts are extant. Throughout the Middle Ages an extensive literature was produced in Latin, but the number of works in the vernacular was constantly augmented, and with the Renaissance the national languages came into their own, largely as a result of the influence of Dante's Divine Comedy and Boccaccio's Decameron. No longer was the use of Latin the distinction between the literate and illiterate, the learned and the ignorant.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Historical writing, in Latin, comprised a goodly portion of medieval literary activity. In the early Middle Ages, Gregory of Tours's 

History of the Franks and Paul the Deacon's comparable History of the Lombards were important works, although the styles were crude and historical perspective is somewhat faulty. The Venerable Bede's 

Ecclesiastical History of England, in addition to being valuable for later historians, was an outstanding manifestation of the cultural preeminence of Northumbria in the eighth and ninth centuries. Einhard's 

Life of Charlemagne is one of the best historical biographies of the entire medieval period; an indispensable source not only for the history of Charlemagne's reign but also for the important period of the Carolingian Revolution. In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, the work of English historians had special distinction. The Chronicles of William of Malmsbury, the Deeds of the English Kings by Henry of Huntington, and the Major and Minor Chronicles of Matthew of Paris are historical works of prime importance, characterized by a breadth of view quite in contrast with earlier annalistic treatments. 

The Ecclesiastical History of Ordericus Vitalis is valuable for the history of England and France in the Angevin period; while the 

Deeds of King Philip by Rigord covers the reign of Philip Augustus in France. In Germany, the principal contribution to historiography was the Deeds of the Emperor Frederick I by Otto of Freising. In the thirteenth century, at the threshold of the Renaissance, the outstanding historical works were Joinville's biography of St. Louis and 

Villehardouin's monumental history of the Fourth Crusade, both written in vernacular French, which some critics have gone so far as to compare with the Homeric epics.

Any discussion of the Latin literature of the Middle Ages would be incomplete without mention of the development of the liturgical literature of the church, adapted by its meter to chanting in divine service. The finest examples of contributions in this field are the 

Stabat Mater of Jacob de Todi and the Dies Irae of Thomas Celano. 

Both have been set to music by a number of composers. Rossini's 

Stabat Mater is the best known musical version of the former, while the Dies Irae inspired famous compositions by Palestrina, Bach, and Mozart.

In the vernacular literature, by far the most popular type was the chanson de geste, which developed into the romance. The earliest of the chansons de geste told of the victories of Charlemagne, Roland, and other great leaders, usually over the Saracens. The hero of the great Song of Roland, dating from the end of the eleventh century,

is an alleged nephew of Charlemagne, who accompanied him on his famous expedition into Spain. Charlemagne is represented in the tale as the Christian emperor who is the chief defender of the church against the Saracens, though as a matter of fact, the actual Spanish expedition occurred some years before Charlemagne's coronation as emperor. Departing still further from historic fact, the chanson tells of a protracted war in Spain and the final decision of the emperor to retreat. On the way back to France, the rear guard, commanded by 

Roland, is ambushed as the result of perfidy. Although Roland summons Charlemagne by a blast of his magic horn, the emperor arrives too late to save him. The saddened army ultimately arrives at the emperor's palace, where Aude, the sweetheart of Roland, appears before the king to appeal to him to avenge her lover's death. Bowed down by grief, she too dies, and her fate heightens the tragic effect of the tale. Although Charlemagne does not set out on another 

Spanish expedition, the story closes with the appearance of the Angel Gabriel, who prophesies that eventually he will conquer the Mohammedans.

The Arthurian Romances in English literature are comparable with the chansons de geste which grew up around the original story of Roland. They deal with a half-legendary king of the Britons supposed to have reigned in the sixth century, the great hero of the British Celts. Whether we allow much or little historical truth to the first stories about him by Nennius and others, beyond doubt the king and his round-table of knights as they are represented in the romances are largely the imaginative creation of the pseudo-historian, Geoffrey of Monmouth, who wrote about 1136. The later chroniclers, Layamon, Wace, and others, built upon his foundation in their version of the Arthurian tales. But Wace added the figure of Launcelot and integrated the tales of Arthur's exploits with the story of the quest for the Holy Grail, or chalice, used by Christ at the Last Supper. 

Other heroes of English romance were Guy of Warwick, Sir Bevis of Hampton, and Richard the Lion-Hearted.

In Spain, the real and mythical deeds of an actual person, Rodrigo Diaz de Bivar, served as the basis for the romances of the twelfth century of which the Cid is the central figure. The Holy Grail theme. was strongly emphasized in Germany, particularly in the Parsifal of Wolfram von Eschenbach. The love theme predominates in the immortal love story of Tristan and Isolde by Gottfried of Strassburg. 

Both these romances have been used by Wagner in two of his finest operas. In the Niebelungenlied, lesser figures of German history play

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

leading roles, with the historic facts almost completely obscured by a great wealth of legend. With the growing importance of lovethemes, the Romance of Adventure came into its own, particularly in the famous story of the love of Aucassin for the Saracen slave-girl,

Nicolette. The popularity of this work is indicated by the fact that over two hundred manuscripts are extant. Another famous story was the Romance of the Rose, which was commenced by William of Lorris about 1230, and completed by Jean de Meung. There is a strong moral note in this allegorical romance, and de Meung's part is full of scientific and political significance. 

Second only in importance to the long narrative romances of an epic character were the metrical romances designed to be sung or recited with some musical accompaniment. Languedoc was the special province for this type of literature. The troubadours, or medieval poets of southern France, who flourished for about three centuries commencing in 1100, composed the romances and recited them on great occasions, whereas the jongleurs were the professional singers most responsible for the popularization of the works. The troubadours, though largely of humble or middle class origin, included not a few nobles, while the jongleurs were poor; but many of the latter became so well known that they secured elevation to the superior status of troubadour. There were a number of conventional types of metrical romances, each with its distinctive meter. They included songs of love and praise, and in sharp contrast, songs of grief and lamentation. The trysting of lovers furnished another favorite theme, while the most serious of the metrical works were of the tenson type, where the approach was somewhat argumentative; that is, moral questions might be discussed or the feasibility of opposing courses of action weighed. Other favored types were the songs of wedlock, in which the tribulations as well as the joys of married life were presented; pastorals; and crusading songs. In Germany, the

Minnesingers recited tales similar in broad outline to the French romances; the most famous of the German composers and singers was Walther von der Vogelweide. The minstrels of England, while inspired to a large degree by French example, drew many of their themes from Scandinavian sources. The troubadours did not make their appearance in Italy until the opening decades of the thirteenth century, and it has been conjectured that the earliest Italian singers may have been refugees from Provence after the Albigensian Crusade. 

Medieval drama was largely dedicated to didactic purposes, espe-

cially religious and moral edification. The Mystery Cycles, based on the gospels, the Miracle Plays, deriving their themes primarily from religious traditions, and the Morality Plays, in which virtues were personified and evil was confounded, were popular all over Europe. 

In some instances, these plays, in which pantomime was prominent, were performed by traveling troups; in general, however, production was local and carried out under the auspices of the clergy and the craft gilds.

The type of medieval literature most popular with the masses was the fable. Many fables bitterly satirized the vices of the clergy, the extortions of rapacious nobles and priests, the conventions of chivalry, and the economic phase of feudalism. They doubtless played an important part in fomenting some of the popular revolts of the later Middle Ages, such as the Jacquerie in France (1358) and the Great Rebellion in England (1381). The beast fables had their moral lessons to teach; their personages, such as Reynard the Fox, traced their origin to the work of Aesop, and have of course become part of the folklore of Western civilization. 

ARCHITECTURE AND ART 

None of the arts is closer to the life of a people than architecture. 

Temples of worship, and indeed public buildings of all sorts, are expressive of community pride and represent, more than does any other form of artistic expression, the ideals, cultural standards, intelligence, and spirit of a large element of the populace. 

Outside of Moslem Europe, few significant innovations appear in medieval architecture prior to the eleventh century. The collapse of the Roman Empire had resulted in a tremendous decline of municipal life, a sharp curtailment of trade, and the virtual disappearance of liquid capital. National monarchies were battling for their existence, only slowly asserting their powers over feudal lords. The church, confronted with the basic task of facilitating the fusion of Roman and Teutonic elements in the West, was busy with the dissemination of the faith in unconverted areas, the development of its administrative organization, and the defense of its doctrines against the infusion of heresy. Only in Spain, as in the areas of northern 

Africa and Asia Minor conquered by the Arabs, did an important new architecture appear - the rich and varied style which the Moslems based chiefly upon Byzantine and Persian models, with fine domes, round and pointed arches, stalactite vaulting, and brilliant geometrical decoration in faïence and mosaic.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The first significant medieval contribution to architecture in Christian Europe was the evolution of the Romanesque style. Although roots of this style can be found as far back as the period of the Carolingian Empire, it did not come into its own until the eleventh century. In large measure, the new interest in architecture was the product of the great monastic movement inaugurated by the Cluniac reform (910). Monastic houses, most of them of the new orders, were endowed by noble patrons, assigned shares in growing parish revenues (impropriation), and frequently enriched, particularly in the case of the Cistercians, by their own productive labors. 

Growing public interest in monastic activity, coupled with increased financial resources, naturally stimulated the construction of larger buildings than hitherto erected. The accentuated importance of saint worship likewise played a vital part. The birthplace, tomb, or other sites associated with the careers of favorite figures of medieval hagiology frequently became shrines visited by increasing numbers of pilgrims. What was more fitting than that these shrines be suitably honored by the construction of magnificent edifices, especially if local revenues were augmented by the offerings of pilgrims? 

Veneration of relics also grew ever larger in the religious picture of the Middle Ages, especially with the beginning of the crusades, as crusaders or pilgrims returned from the East with their slivers from the True Cross, their Holy Lances, and other holy objects. Frequently the desire to provide proper housing for these treasures and to accommodate worshipers who came to be edified or relieved of their afflictions through the miraculous ministrations of the relics provided the impetus for the construction of church, chapel, or cloister.

The Romanesque style, so called because it is obviously a development and refinement of classical Roman architecture, started with the Roman basilica, wherein the central hall, or nave, was flanked by two aisles of lower height than the nave, from which they were separated by rows of columns. Byzantine, Saracen, and Norman influences were at work, however, together with practical exigencies, to produce important modifications. In the first place, the structures were made broader and higher, and this demanded stone construction rather than wood, which frequently had been employed in the early Middle Ages. Since the round Roman arch was exclusively employed, increased height and width demanded massive walls to neutralize the powerful thrusts of the vaults. The keynote of the whole structure was strength. Not only were the walls very thick,

but they were reënforced by pilasters and built-in buttresses; while the aisles as well as the nave were often vaulted. 

Most Romanesque structures were cruciform in their ground plans; that is, the nave and aisles were intersected at right angles by a transept. A windowed tower frequently was raised above the intersection of nave and transept to provide additional light for the apse, or rounded end of the nave, in which was located the altar. Towers sometimes were placed also at the corners of the main façade in front to provide ornamentation and to give additional wall strength where front and side walls met. 

Naturally there were many local variations which it is impossible even to mention in a brief account. In the main, it may be said, structural limitations, most of them incident to the employment of the rounded arch which could be raised only to a height equal to onehalf its diameter, gave the edifices a dominant quality of massiveness, stability, and repose, in contrast to the dynamic character of the later Gothic. Romanesque structures were heavy, rich, and impressive.

Romanesque architecture primarily expressed the ideals of the monk and the feudal lord. The Gothic style was fundamentally a manifestation of the virility and ideology of the middle class, which rose to prominence with the revival of urban life and the commercial expansion that characterized the age of the crusades. Gothic architecture was above all expressive of community spirit coupled with rare religious fervor. The craft gilds played a significant part in the organized community effort that made the edifices possible, while the tremendous popularity of the cult of the Virgin provided another powerful impetus, as witnessed by the large number of Gothic cathedrals and chapels dedicated to Our Lady. Artisans expressed their creative spirit as well as their piety; nobles and clergy contributed funds, while peasants cheerfully dragged stones and performed other back-breaking tasks to advance, even in a small way, the completion of the work. 

The fundamental technical innovations that marked the evolution of the Gothic style were the pointed arch and the flying buttress. As we have seen, the strength of the Romanesque vaults was limited by the use of the round arch and the consequent vault crowns of unequal height. With the pointed arch, all crowns of the vault could be made of equal height. The vaults could be made higher, since raising the height of the Gothic arches with their flexible radii actually increased the strength of the vaults because the sidethrust of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the Gothic arch diminishes with increased ratio of height to radius. 

Since all vault crowns were of equal height, it was possible to link all the crowns together with a stone "spine" which, of course, gave greater protection against horizontal thrusts in any direction. 

The vaults needed support where they rested on the side walls and where the arches curved inward to bear the weight of the roof. This problem was solved by the use of the flying buttress, one of the greatest architectural inventions of all time. The buttresses were external props or supports which bore the side-thrusts of the vault arches so as to relieve the walls of virtually all pressure and weight. 

The buttresses really represented external continuations of the vault arches to carry the weight and pressure down through the buttress piers to the ground. As the architects became bolder, double, triple, and even quadruple flights of buttresses were employed, ever more slender and graceful in design.

All sorts of intricate ceiling arrangements were now possible. 

Vaults were split; spaces between vaults fitted with ribs, between which were set concave slabs of stone. Walls became relatively unimportant and this was emphasized by the lace-like character of the decorations on façades and side walls. Furthermore, the walls could be pierced by many windows in which the pointed arch was almost invariably employed. Clerestory windows likewise frequently were utilized to provide additional light for the nave. Ground plans were broader than in the Romanesque style. The cruciform plan, however, was still largely employed, although often with the transept somewhat shortened. Usually elaborate side entrances to the cathedral were situated at each end of the transept. In addition to the chapels around the semi-circular apse, the greater width of the Gothic structures made possible the erection of chapels along the outside walls of each of the aisles. The skeleton provided by buttresses, vaults, and ribs is the essence of Gothic. Above all, the impression is one of restless, never-ending thrust and counter-thrust. 

Ribs receive the pressure of the ceiling and transmit it to the vaults whence it is carried to the buttresses and so to the ultimate anchorage in the earth.

All the resources of the artist were drawn upon for the embellishment of the cathedrals. Sculptured figures were harmoniously blended with the buildings. Indeed, the tall, slender statues of saints, particularly in the rows of such figures on the façades, were so completely integrated with the structures that the insistent note of lofty, soaring height was enhanced. The large number of windows gave

abundant opportunity for the utilization of the wonderful stained glass which is one of the chief glories of such great Gothic cathedrals as Chartres, Amiens, and Canterbury. Much of the glass was produced in Italy or by migratory Italian workmen. The glass was colored by the addition of mineral salts to the molten sand; it was not merely glass that had been painted over. The patterns were outlined in the windows by stone mullions. At first, the patterns were geometric, but ultimately the most involved and delicate tracery was employed. The individual pieces of glass were set in their place by the employment of lead. The technical imperfections of the glazier's art actually were responsible for one of the greatest charms of the windows, for the unequal thickness of the pieces, the air bubbles, and the uneven coloration gave the illusion that the window actually was studded with sparkling jewels. Most of the cathedrals are equipped with wonderful rose-windows in their main façades, so called because the circular window is divided into sections resembling rose petals.

While the historical evolution of the Gothic style is somewhat obscure, it seems definitely established that the new architectural order originated in the Ile de France. While several antecedents have been found, the first virtually complete embodiment of the technical innovations is found in the famous Abbey of St. Denis built during the regime of Suger, its abbot who, it will be remembered, served as the capable minister of King Louis VII (1137–1180). Notre

Dame of Paris, built during the period 1163-1235, was another early example, with its famous twin-towered façade and frank treatment of the buttresses. The famous cathedral of Chartres was begun in 

1194 and was dedicated toward the close of the reign of St. Louis. Its outstanding feature is the façade with the twin spires generally considered the best proportioned of the entire Gothic era. Amiens, built about 1220, is probably the finest expression of all the features of the Gothic style; its nave is particularly famous. The finest sculptured façade is that of Rheims which modern craftsmanship has recently restored after the tragic demolition of much of the structure during the World War. It has been well said that the whole spirit of 

Gothic architecture can be epitomized in the "façade of Paris, the towers of Chartres, the sculpture of Rheims, and the nave of Amiens." 

From France, the Gothic spread to other countries. Westminster 

Abbey, and the cathedrals of York, Durham, Salisbury, Winchester, and Lincoln are famous English examples. In Germany, the cathedrals of Cologne and Mainz are conspicuous, as are the churches of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Leon, Burgos, and Toledo in Spain. The Gothic, however, made much less headway in Italy, though it is exemplified in such great churches as Santa Croce in Florence, and such cathedrals as Milan and Siena. As a matter of fact, the term Gothic was applied to the new style by Italian architects as a term of derision, meaning that they considered it barbarous. Renaissance architecture in Italy started fundamentally with the Romanesque style, modified by Byzantine influences and by a return to classical patterns, particularly in the revival of the dome. That is, architects like Brunelleschi and his early fifteenth century followers founded a style based on the adaptation of Roman edifices to medieval needs. 

Although sculpture remained ancillary to architecture, marked technical improvements were made in the Gothic period representing a considerable progress from the standards of the Romanesque. 

A vigorous note of realism was introduced, and themes were drawn not only from the Bible but from the whole world of nature as indicated in the pastoral scenes, the representations of the changes of the seasons, and the exquisite treatment of foliage. While the early 

Christians extensively employed frescoes to vivify the Christian message, there was a curtailment of this form of artistic expression in both Romanesque and Gothic periods. In the Romanesque period, the structures were too dark to make feasible extensive utilization of frescoes while in Gothic edifices the amount of wall space was limited. Painted windows therefore largely supplemented the frescoes in Gothic structures. Biblical themes naturally predominated in the painting of the Gothic period. On the west wall of the cathedral was usually depicted the Last Judgment, often flanked by pictures of the ascension of Christ and the coronation of the Virgin. 

The east wall, on the other hand, commonly was reserved for pictures emphasizing the glory and majesty of the Saviour. Symbolism was most important. The basic objective of both statuary and painting to teach moral and religious lessons meant an unavoidable trend toward convention and lack of interest in form. With the thirteenth century, particularly in the work of Pisano and Giotto, appear the first traces of the new departures in art which were to culminate in the Renaissance and these will therefore be discussed as a prelude to the Renaissance. Many modern students hold that the art of the 

Renaissance must not be considered solely the result of the revival of classicism; it was largely the culmination of medieval art, a culmination that probably would have been largely attained even had the humanistic movement never occurred.

CHAPTER 27 The Political Background of the Renaissance 

THE HUNDRED YEARS' WAR 

HE outstanding international event in European history in the period 1337-1453 was the struggle between England and 

France known as the Hundred Years' War. Hostilities were intermittent, for there were several periods of peace as well as a number of truces. The war is of considerable historical interest aside from the immediate events and issues. It was largely responsible for the development of nationalism in both the countries involved. The assertion of parliamentary powers in England was considerably strengthened, since the crown could only procure the necessary funds to prosecute the war by recognition of parliamentary financial control and the principle that redress of grievances should precede the voting of money. International banking and the formation of alliances played important roles in the long conflict. England's operations were largely financed in the first stage of the war by the Florentine banking houses and the wealthy towns of the Hanseatic League. 

England was allied with Flanders and the Empire, while France, in addition to her traditional alliance with Scotland, made extensive use of Venetian and Genoese mercenaries. The effective use of the long bow by the English forces in the battles of Crécy, Poitiers, and Agincourt, as well as the employment of cannon in the last period of the war, completed the overthrow of the military supremacy of the feudal lords which had been foreshadowed as early as the battle of Legnano (1176) in the struggle between Frederick Barbarossa and the Lombard League.

A fundamental cause of the war was the English possession of Aquitaine. No vigorous French government could accept a situation. wherein a considerable part of France was under English domination. Constant disputes as to the status of the English kings as nominal

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

vassals of the French crown were the outward manifestations of the inveterate enmity between the two kingdoms which the Aquitainian situation engendered. Perhaps an even more potent cause of the war was a series of events in Flanders. A number of Flemish cities, particularly Ghent, Bruges, and Antwerp, were great medieval centers for the manufacture of woolen cloth, while England was a leading producer of raw wool. The economic tie between England and Flanders was therefore a very close one. In 1302 the Count of Flanders was expelled as the result of a rising known as the Matins of Bruges. 

An attempt to restore the count with the assistance of his suzerain, King Philip IV, was repulsed at the battle of Courtrai. In 1328, however, Philip VI (Valois) won a decisive victory at the battle of Cassel and installed Louis of Nevers as count of Flanders. In reprisal for the rebellion of 1302, a number of Flemish towns suffered the loss of their commercial privileges, and England retaliated by the imposition of an embargo on the export of raw wool. Since the situation was disastrous to the entire woolen industry, England was vitally concerned with the liberation of Flanders, and the war with France certainly had this as one of its major objectives. A contributing cause of the war was the long series of conflicts between English and French sailors in the English Channel. Virtual piracy was common, and the conflicts of the seamen assumed international character with the constant appeals to their respective governments. 

Although war was declared as early as 1337, a series of defiances, challenges, and diplomatic moves delayed the opening of hostilities.

Alliances were concluded, money was raised, and armies were mobilized, while the papacy made efforts to preserve peace. In the meantime, the Flemings again revolted under the leadership of Jacques van Artevelde, a rich draper of Ghent.
