The papacy laid an interdict on Flanders on the ground that Artevelde was in rebellion against his rightful ruler. It was doubtless this factor that impelled Edward 

III, in 1340, to assert his claim to the French throne. If he were king of France, it could be held that Artevelde was not a rebel, and the ecclesiastical weapons would be deprived of their effectiveness. Edward's claim was not devoid of plausibility. While it was admitted that his mother Isabella was ineligible to succeed to the throne, the question as to the rights of females to transmit their succession rights to male children had never been decided.

A naval victory off Sluys gave the English command of the sea and made possible an invasion of France in 1346, which culminated in a decisive English victory at Crécy. A Scottish invasion of England

was turned back at the battle of Neville's Cross. The Black Death of 

1348-1350 forced cessation of hostilities, but in 1356 the Black Prince led an army into Gascony and gained an overwhelming triumph at Poitiers. King John of France, who had succeeded Philip VI in 1350, together with the flower of French knighthood was captured and held for ransom. The English victory was followed by the revolt of 

Paris under the leadership of Stephen Marcel and the promulgation of the Grand Ordinance of 1357 designed to assure the supremacy of the middle class, or Third Estate. When the movement spread to the country districts, however, it led to the uprising of the peasants known as the Jacquerie, which ultimately was suppressed with pitiless severity. In view of the military reverses and the disturbed internal conditions, France had no alternative to the prompt conclusion of peace. Charles V, who had secured recognition upon the death of 

John and the suppression of the Parisian regime of Marcel, signed the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) wherein England was given Guienne and Poitou free of all feudal obligations and France agreed to pay a heavy ransom for the release of the captives taken at Poitiers. 

France recovered rapidly under the leadership of the new king and his brilliant general, Bertrand du Guesclin. The bands of brigands, known as the “Free Companies," which had been formed with the demobilization of the armies after the peace of 1360, were broken up, and many of the erstwhile bandits were enrolled in the newly created French standing army. When the Black Prince intervened on the side of Pedro the Cruel in the civil war that was raging in Castile, France espoused the cause of his antagonist, Henry Trastamare. 

Pedro's forces were badly defeated, and the heavy taxation which the Black Prince imposed on Gascony to finance his Castilian venture led to revolt. Gascony was definitively lost by the English. With the death of Charles V in 1380, the first period of the war came to a close. 

In the period from 1380 to the resumption of the war in 1413 interest shifted from the international issue to the internal affairs of 

England and France. Richard II, son of the Black Prince, who had died in 1376, succeeded Edward III. An outstanding event of his reign was the Great Rebellion of 1381. This uprising was primarily a manifestation of economic and social discontent which could be traced to the economic dislocations produced by the great plague. The immediate cause of the upheaval, however, was the imposition of a poll tax. Two movements began simultaneously in Kent and Essex; Watt

Tyler was the leader of the Kentish uprising, while a renegade priest, John Ball, served in the same capacity in Essex. Both groups of rebels

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

converged on London. At the Mile End Conference with the king and his ministers, the rebels were promised the abolition of serfdom, fixed rents for peasants who rented their lands, minimum wages of four pence a day for laborers, and amnesty for those who participated in the insurrection. Rioting in London could not be averted despite these concessions; the royal treasurer, who was considered responsible for the unpopular tax, was murdered, as was also the Archbishop of Canterbury. When Watt Tyler was killed in an altercation. with the king and his supporters, the rebels disbanded. The concessions which they had extorted were revoked, and royal justices on circuit hunted down the leaders.

Richard's ill-advised attempt to govern without parliamentary sanction of his policies proved disastrous to him. In 1387 a number of the barons, known as the "Lords Appellant," charged several of the royal ministers with corruption, and in the following year the "Merciless Parliament" removed and banished them. Richard continued to evade parliamentary financial control, but in the seizure of the estates of his uncle, John of Gaunt, he over-reached himself. The opposition summoned Henry of Lancaster, son of John of Gaunt, from abroad, and with his arrival Richard was deposed and probably put to death. 

Henry IV (1399-1413), who succeeded Richard, was the first of the parliamentary kings; that is, he owed his position not to inheritance but to act of Parliament. Naturally, parliamentary powers were increased; control over the household expenses of the king was asserted in 1406, and in the following year the principle was established that monetary grants must originate in the House of Commons. 

The central fact in the history of France in the period 1380-1422 was the madness of King Charles VI, which made strife inevitable among the great nobles for control of the government. The faction led by the Duke of Orleans, representing only the interests of the landholding aristocracy, was anti-English. The group led by the 

Duke of Burgundy, however, was to some degree desirous of advancing commercial interests and was sufficiently pro-English to welcome another English invasion. Strife between the two factions resulted in civil war with the murder of the Duke of Orleans in 1407. 

Henry IV had no disposition to take advantage of the disturbances in France to renew the war, especially in view of the fact that he was forced to deal with a formidable rebellion of Wales led by Owen Glendower. Suppression of the Welsh uprising and the defeat of the 

Percies (Henry, Earl of Northumberland and his son), who had re-

belled because of their alleged mistreatment by the king following their successful defense of the north border against the Scots, cleared the way for Henry V (1413-1422) to assume the offensive in France. 

The English campaign of 1415 led to a victory at Agincourt that was reminiscent of the triumph at Crécy. The Burgundian faction openly allied with the victors as a result of the battle and seized virtual control of the French government. The Treaty of Troyes in 

1420 ceded all of France north of the Loire to England. Henry married Catherine, daughter of Charles VI, and was promised the French crown upon the death of Charles VI. Henry died in 1422, the same year that brought the close of the tragic reign of Charles. The Duke of Bedford was installed as regent for the infant Henry VI in France, while the Duke of Gloucester served in a similar capacity in England. The Dauphin made no effort to assert his rights, and was derisively called the "King of Bourges."

It was in this period of defeatism in France that Joan of Arc restored the shattered morale of the soldiery and brought about the coronation of the Dauphin as Charles VII (1422–1461). In response to celestial voices which she claimed to be obeying and which were very real to her, Joan brought about the deliverance of Orleans from the English forces that were besieging the city. The Dauphin, whom she had managed to infuse with some of her own enthusiasm at their dramatic meeting at Chinon, was crowned at Rheims. An ill-advised attempt to capture Paris failed, however, and Joan ultimately was taken prisoner by Burgundian troops before Compiègne and handed over to the English. Her captors accused her of magical practices, and she was brought to trial before a court made up of Dominican monks and professors of the University of Paris and presided over by the Bishop of Beauvais. For days the girl was badgered by her learned adversaries. Subtle theological questions were propounded, and logical dilemmas shrewdly posed, but she turned back all efforts to entrap her, and it was not until she became ill that her spirit broke before the grim threats of torture and she brought the travesty to an end by expressing her willingness to abjure her "errors." She was thereupon sentenced to life imprisonment, but upon allegation that she had relapsed into her evil ways she was burned at the stake. Her great sacrifice had not been fruitless, for she had engendered a great wave of nationalistic fervor in France destined to restore unity and expel the invaders from the country. 

The turning point of the struggle came with the Treaty of Arras, in 1435, that established peace between Orleanists and Burgundians.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

It had been the strife between these two factions that enabled the English to impose the Treaty of Troyes and hold a large part of 

France. Administrative reforms inaugurated by Charles VII hastened the deliverance of his kingdom. A permanent land tax (taille) was established, and some of the revenue derived from it used to raise another army. The Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges (1438) gave the crown a large measure of administrative and financial control of the church. A truce was concluded with England in 1444 as a result of which Henry VI married Margaret of Anjou, but disputes concerning control of Anjou soon led to the resumption of hostilities. English military activities began to wane, and interest in the prosecution of the war dwindled, while nationalism in France was constantly growing. France recovered territory bit by bit until, with the recapture of Bordeaux in 1453, Calais was the sole remaining English possession in France and the war came to a close by mutual consent without a definitive treaty of peace. 

THE EMPIRE IN THE AGE OF THE RENAISSANCE 

With the close of the reign of Frederick II in 1250 the Holy Roman Empire ceased to be an important factor in international affairs. After the extinction of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, the imperial crown ultimately was bestowed on Rudolf of Hapsburg (1273–1291), and the breaking up of Germany continued unchecked. The ancestral possessions of the Hapsburg house were located in southern Swabia, and the family had been important as early as the eleventh century. Frederick 

Barbarossa (1152-1190) enhanced their holdings by the grant of Alsace and Zurich. In 1278 Austria, which had been made a duchy by 

Frederick I, was bestowed on Rudolf. The attempt to impose Hapsburg rule on Switzerland, however, was repulsed, for in 1291 three Swiss cantons (Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden) formed a federation for defense and defeated the invaders at the battle of Morgarten (1315). 

In 1314, Louis of Bavaria (1314-1347) was crowned emperor.

When he attempted to revive the Italian policies formerly prosecuted by the Hohenstaufens, he became involved in a bitter controversy with Pope John XXII. It was doubtless this factor that impelled the emperor to join England in the Hundred Years' War, for the papacy at this time was located at Avignon and was in close understanding with France. The controversy was largely responsible for Marsiglio of Padua's memorable treatise on political science, known as the Defender of Peace. In this work, Marsiglio held that governing authority resides in the people, who therefore should be free to deter-

mine the form of government that should prevail. Extending the theory of popular sovereignty to the government of the church, he argued that not the pope but a general representative council should be the chief authority in the ecclesiastical organization. 

The conflict between empire and papacy, a faint echo of the great struggles between the Holy See and the Hohenstaufens, abated with the election of Charles IV (1347-1378), who secured papal support of his candidacy by renunciation of Italian ambitions. The most significant event of his reign was the promulgation of the famous Golden Bull of 1356 by the Diet of Metz. This enactment set up a permanent scheme for the choice of emperors. The electoral right was granted to the Archbishops of Trèves, Mainz, and Cologne and to the Duke of Saxony, the King of Bohemia, the Margrave of Brandenburg, and the Count Palatine of the Rhine. These seven electors were to meet at Frankfort within three months after the death of an emperor to choose his successor. The exclusion of Austria from the electoral dignity was destined to have consequences undreamed of in 1356. 

Although the emperor annexed Moravia, Silesia, and Lausitz to his Bohemian possessions, the advantage of unity was sacrificed when he partitioned some of his vast territories among his sons. Wenzel received Bohemia, Sigismund was given control of Brandenburg, while

John was invested with Lausitz. Wenzel was elected to the imperial dignity as the successor of his father, but his debauched character led to his deposition in 1400. For ten years, the imperial throne was the object of contention, until the coronation of Sigismund was secured through the help of Frederick of Hohenzollern, who received Brandenburg as his reward. This transfer of territory was the first step in the rise of the powerful Hohenzollern dynasty under which the kingdom of Prussia was destined to emerge and dominate Germany until 1918. Upon the death of Sigismund in 1437, Albert of Hapsburg was elected, and the fifty-three-year reign of his son and successor, Frederick III (1440-1493), so firmly established the tradition of Hapsburg incumbency of the imperial throne that they retained the position until the abolition of the Empire by Napoleon in 1806. 

THE FALL OF THE BYZANTINE EMPIRE 

The Byzantine Empire that had beaten off so many attacks in the Middle Ages and that had been saved from the advance of the Seljukian Turks by the crusades finally succumbed to the onslaughts of the Ottoman Turks. The Empire never had recovered from the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

66 terrific blow of the Fourth Crusade (1202-1204) which, it will be recalled, had resulted in the establishment of the Latin Kingdom of 

Constantinople. The formation of independent emirates, particularly that of Nicaea, had, to be sure, led to the eventual overthrow of the Latin Kingdom (1261), but the very creation of these emirates had introduced a new disruptive force that militated against imperial solidarity. Then, too, the foundation of Venetian trading posts and the grant of extensive commercial privileges to Venice as well as to other Italian cities, which accompanied the rise of the Latin Kingdom, had dealt an irreparable blow to Byzantine trade. The Balkan peninsula was lost with the creation of a great Serbian empire by Stephen 

Dushan (1331-1355), and the Turkish conquests in Asia Minor meant additional territorial loss, dwindling revenues, and aggravation of the already crushing burden of taxation in the provinces still under the control of Constantinople.

The Ottoman Turks were first heard of in Bithynia (southern coast of the Black Sea) where Othman, emir of the Seljukian Turks in that province, won independence from his overlords. Under the leadership of Oichan (Orchan), the internal organization of the newly created power was largely completed; mosques, colleges, and hospitals were built and a system of coinage was adopted. With the organization of the famous Janissaries, the Ottomans possessed one of the most formidable military forces the world has ever seen. The 

Janissaries were Christians who had been taken captives as young boys and subjected to rigorous military training, living an ascetic life with the barracks their home, fighting their trade, and the Koran their religion." In 1354 the Sultan Suleiman took the decisive step of leading his forces across the Hellespont, and a few years later Hadrianople was taken. An overwhelming victory at Kossovo in 1389 shattered the Serbian Empire and removed another barrier to Turkish expansion in Europe. The rise of Tamerlane's enormous Mongolian Empire, however, brought a sudden halt to the victorious sweep of the

Ottomans, and the Sultan Bayazid was captured when his army was crushed at Angora in 1402. Tamerlane then turned to the conquest of India, but his death in 1405 led to a prompt disintegration of his gigantic empire into its major components, and the Turks were free to resume their march of conquest. Half-hearted efforts to mobilize effective western European assistance for the hard-pressed Byzantine Empire came to naught, and the Turkish encirclement inexorably closed around Constantinople. Finally, in May of 1453, the city was captured by Mohammed II after a heroic defense in which can-

non and liquid fire were spectacularly employed. The Byzantine 

Empire had performed its historic mission for western Europe. It had afforded protection against waves of barbarian migration and a source of major cultural stimulation that made its full impact felt in the period of the crusades.

POLITICAL CONDITIONS IN RENAISSANCE ITALY 

Since the Renaissance in literature and art was so intimately associated with Italy, it is necessary to have some acquaintance with political conditions in the peninsula; indeed, as will be seen, the political history of the north Italian city-states exercised a profound influence on cultural developments. Southern Italy was known as the 

Kingdom of Naples, which, with the neighboring island of Sicily, comprised the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. France and Spain vied for control of this kingdom, until in 1442 Spanish rule was definitively established to continue until the nineteenth century with few interruptions. The impetus to cultural progress which had been given by the enlightened policies of Frederick II soon spent its force, and at the opening of the Renaissance the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was the most backward part of Italy. The papal states of central Italy, under the personal rule of the popes, were poor and handicapped by archaic administrative institutions. The cultural advance of the city of Rome left them virtually untouched.

Northern Italy, the most progressive part of the peninsula, was divided into a number of city-states, the most important of which were Venice, Milan, and Florence. During the Renaissance, Venice was the most powerful political and commercial state of all Italy. Her geographical location on islands in the Adriatic ensured her political independence and at the same time allowed her to extend her control over parts of the neighboring mainland. Venice was originally a republic, but by the time of the Renaissance its government was in the hands of a commercial oligarchy. The Doge was nominally the chief executive officer and was elected for life by the populace. The Grand 

Council, however, gradually had absorbed the powers of government, and in 1297 membership in this body became hereditary in a few noble families whose right to such representation was recorded in the "Golden Book.” The unwieldiness of the Grand Council led to the eventual appointment of a powerful executive committee, known as the Council of Ten, and this group, renewed by annual elections, became the actual governing organ. 

Milan, the most important manufacturing center of Italy, was in

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

theory a ducal fief of the Holy Roman Empire, but in actuality it was an independent city-state. While the state was nominally a republic, Gian Galeazzo Visconti (1378-1402) had seized control with the aid of his condottiere, Facine, and his dominance likewise was extended over Vicenza, Padua, and for a time, Florence. Although the despot was crafty and cruel, his policies usually harmonized with the interests of the populace. Filippo Maria Visconti (1412-1447) who had succeeded Giovanna Maria as duke, was engaged in a long war with Venice. During the early years of the struggle, the Milanese troops were commanded by Francesco Carmagnola, one of the most renowned of the condottieri, but he eventually deserted to the enemy and was succeeded as commander-in-chief by Francesco Sforza. 

Filippo died while the war was in progress, whereupon Sforza married his illegitimate daughter, Bianca, and seized control of the state. 

The Sforzas continued to rule until their expulsion in 1512. The coup d'état by which Francesco Sforza had vaulted to power in 1447 later served as one of the ostensible causes of the French invasions, for 

Valentina Visconti had married Louis of Orleans.

Florence, the great banking center of Europe in the later Middle Ages, likewise was theoretically a republic. Militant democracy, by surrounding governmental institutions by a multitude of restrictions, however, actually paralyzed the government and hastened the advent of dictatorship. The powers of the chief executive, known as the 

Gonfalonier of Justice, were checked by a council, or Signoria, the members of which were elected to terms of but seven months duration. Then, too, all laws had to be ratified by a two-thirds majority in each of five separate assemblies. In the latter part of the fourteenth century, the Albizzi brothers (Maso and Rinaldo) gained control of the city and solidified their power by administrative efficiency, business acumen, and liberal patronage of literature and the arts. 

The power of the Albizzi ultimately was successfully challenged by the famous Medici family. This family owed its wealth and power to a flourishing banking business founded by Giovanni de Medici in 1251, and the firm was one of the few to survive the crash that resulted when Edward III of England repudiated his debts to the bankers who had helped finance preparations for the Hundred Years'

War. Political power came when the family sided with the lesser gilds and the proletariat in their perennial struggles with the Albizzi and the vested interests they represented. Finally, Cosimo de Medici (1429-1464) drove out the Albizzi and established the unchallenged despotic rule of his family. The period of Medici rule synchronized

with the most glorious years of Florentine history. Patronage of art and literature, particularly by Lorenzo the Magnificent (1469-1492), contributed powerfully to make this period the high point of the cultural Renaissance. 

All the despotic regimes actually were based on the employment of mercenary troops, commanded by the adventuresome condottieri who introduced more skillful methods of fighting. Battles became largely mere bloodless strategical maneuvers, and, in time, political aggrandizement depended more on diplomacy and intrigue than military operations. The age of the Renaissance was a period of social merger. The old aristocracy was fusing with the mercantile class and the greater industrial gilds, while the peasantry, the lesser gilds, and the urban proletariat were likewise becoming conscious of community of interests. Class consciousness was accentuated, with the interests of capitalists being advanced at the expense of the masses. 

This condition led to frequent uprisings, and it was the task of the despot to maintain order, advance the economic interests of his state, and mollify the proletariat by timely concessions and the preservation of popular governmental institutions. 

By the close of the fifteenth century, Italy was the most prosperous as well as the most enlightened country in Europe. Despite these advantages, national unity was lacking and the peninsula, made up of discordant and aggressive states, was the prey of constant turmoil that frequently bordered on anarchy. Venice, ambitious for conquest, had extended her control over the lesser states of northeastern Italy, and the papacy had subordinated its spiritual functions to political objectives and intrigues. Two dangers menaced Italy: the rival aspirations of the kings of France and Spain and the loss of Italian commercial supremacy with the encroachments of the Ottoman Turks and the opening of new trade routes.

The year 1492 marked a turning point in the history of Italy. The discovery of America was a final blow to the commercial supremacy of Venice and hastened her political decline. The fall of Granada led to the unification of Spain, increased her prestige, and gave her a freer hand in Italian affairs. Rodrigo Borgia assumed the tiara as Pope 

Alexander VI, and the death of Lorenzo de Medici hastened the loss of Italian independence. France came under the personal rule of 

Charles VIII, and this series of disastrous circumstances culminated in the invasion of Italy by Charles in 1494. 

The motive of the French invasion was the claim of Charles, through the House of Anjou, to the throne of Naples. In order to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

protect his kingdom from invasion during his absence and to secure a free hand in Italy, he made treaties with Henry VII of England, Ferdinand of Aragon, and the Emperor Maximilian I. The French were invited to intervene in Italy by Ludovico Sforza who had usurped control of Milan, and by the Neapolitan nobles who were tired of Aragonese misrule. The enemies of Pope Alexander VI, who wished to depose him on charges of simony and immorality, also were eager for French intervention. Charles chose to march the length of the peninsula instead of going by sea. In 1494 he crossed the Alps, took Milan and Florence without any effective opposition, and marched on Rome. The pope aptly characterized the invasion by saying that the only weapon the French needed on their march was the chalk with which they marked out the lodgings of their troops. 

Revealing unforeseen inflexibility of character, Alexander refused to yield to the demands of Charles to recognize his claims to Naples. 

Eventually, the French king capitulated, acknowledged Alexander as the true pope, and dropped his efforts to depose him. On February 

22, 1495, Charles entered Naples without striking a blow. Since he had failed to secure papal sanction for this usurpation, he was forced to crown himself king. The extraordinary ease with which the conquest had been accomplished alarmed the Italians. A formidable league was formed against Charles by the pope, the emperor, Venice, Aragon, and Milan. The French king realized his predicament; he retired from Naples and fought his way back to France. Ferdinand II of Sicily, aided by Spanish troops, expelled the French garrison from Naples, and the conquests of Charles were lost as speedily as they were gained.

Charles VIII died in 1498, before he had an opportunity to regain his losses. Since he left no male heir, the crown reverted to his nearest relative, Louis of Orleans. As Louis XII, he adopted the aggressive 

Italian policy of his predecessor. In addition to the claims of Charles to Naples, Louis also claimed Milan through his grandmother, Valentina Visconti. After contracting alliances to secure the support of northwestern Italy, he invaded the peninsula in 1499. Milan was speedily captured by the French, who now planned the conquest of Naples. To ensure success, Louis made a joint agreement with 

Ferdinand of Aragon to drive out the King of Naples and divide the territory between them. The Neapolitan king was deposed, but disagreement broke out between the allies, leading to war and the expulsion of the French. Ferdinand made himself supreme in the Two 

Sicilies, which he now reunited under a single crown.

Louis, eager for revenge, speedily resumed hostilities. Two armies were sent over the Pyrenees in unsuccessful thrusts at Spain. A third army invaded Italy in an attempt to reconquer Naples, but was disastrously defeated by the Spaniards and Italians. A third Italian war was begun in 1507. This period of widespread turmoil in Italy was used advantageously by Venice to increase her territory by the annexation of several papal towns in Romagna. Upon the pope's insistence, Venice relinquished some of her newly conquered territory; in the towns she retained, she exercised not only political control but ecclesiastical jurisdiction as well. Warlike and intrepid Pope Julius II refused to acquiesce in such control and threatened to reduce Venice to a fishing village. To this threat the Venetian ambassador replied, "As for you, Holy Father, if you are not more reasonable, we shall reduce you to a village priest." In 1508 the pope organized the League of Cambrai, consisting of himself, Louis XII of France, Emperor Maximilian I, and Ferdinand of Aragon, to humble Venice and restore its recent conquests to their original owners. Venice was not powerful enough to contend against the combined forces of the League. She entered into negotiations with the papacy and retained its goodwill by surrendering disputed towns and restoring usurped ecclesiastical powers. Julius was detached from the League of Cambrai; fired with the spirit of Italian patriotism, he prepared to free the peninsula from subjection to foreign rule. Realizing the necessity of allies in his quarrel with France, he organized, in 1511, the Holy League. With the deflection of imperial support from France to the 

League and the death of the ablest French leader, Gaston de Foix, Louis XII was driven beyond the Alps.

The death of Louis XII (1515) did not end the dream of French control of Italy, for his policy was continued by Francis I (15151547). When Francis ascended the throne, he was only twenty years of age; he was frivolous, irresponsible, and desirous of military renown. In 1515 he invaded Italy and defeated the Swiss - who were in the pope's pay - in the decisive battle of Marignano. When he occupied Milan, Pope Leo X gladly came to terms. 

On the death of Emperor Maximilian I in 1519, Francis and Charles I of Spain became rival candidates for the imperial crown. Charles had succeeded to the Spanish possessions of his mother, Infanta Joanna, "the Fool," daughter and heiress of Ferdinand and Isabella. 

By skillful bribery and threats he was elected as Emperor Charles V over his rivals, Francis I and Henry VIII of England. The union of 

Spanish and imperial territory under one ruler gave Charles the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

greatest empire that had ever been ruled by a Christian monarch. 

The general political situation of the time, the territorial rivalry of the Houses of Hapsburg and Valois, and the gradual encompassment of France by Hapsburg territories, led to the outbreak of a series of four wars between Francis and Charles, primarily for the control of 

Italy (1521-1526, 1527–1529, 1536–1538, and 1542–1544).

The opening of the first war found Charles allied with the pope and Henry VIII. The imperial forces defeated the French at the battle of Pavia in 1525. After a brief captivity in Spain, Francis signed the Treaty of Madrid (1526), renouncing his claims to Burgundy, the Netherlands, and Italy. Upon his return to France, he refused to fulfill this pledge on the grounds that compulsion exercised at the time absolved him from his oath.

The ascendency of Charles endangered the balance of power of Europe and frightened his allies into the French camp. But with the resumption of hostilities, dissension and apathy of the coalition enabled the imperialists to secure control of a great part of Italy. Charles now singled out vacillating Pope Clement VII for vengeance. Although the emperor cannot be held altogether responsible for the disgraceful event, in the spring of 1527 an imperial army of Spanish and German mercenaries marched on Rome and took it by assault. 

The ensuing pillage was so terrible that superstitious Protestants regarded it as divine punishment of the papacy, while devout Catholics regarded it as a fitting end to the political intrigues and policies of the Renaissance popes. Desecration of monasteries, convents, libraries, museums, and works of art dealt a crushing blow to learning. 

Clement hastened to negotiate peace with the emperor. Francis and his allies held out for a time but made little headway. By the general 

Peace of Cambrai (1529), French retirement from Italy was reconfirmed. The House of Hapsburg was now the unquestioned master of 

Italy; in 1530 Charles received the imperial crown from the pope. 

Charles now turned to quell the Protestant Revolt and to repulse the Turks, who had overrun Hungary and laid siege to Vienna. The 

Diet of Augsburg (1530) failed to solve the religious problem, but an expedition against the Turks succeeded in ending the threat from that quarter. The Peace of Cambrai proved but a truce, for hostilities were resumed in 1536. Finally, by the efforts of Pope Paul III, another truce, this time for ten years, was concluded at Nice in 1538. This peace was broken by resumption of spasmodic warfare in 1542, terminated in 1544 by the Treaty of Crespy. The death of Francis, in 

1547, did not end the conflict between France and Spain, for his son

and successor, Henry II, continued the struggle until the conclusion. of the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559. By this treaty, the Hapsburgs retained their hold upon Italy, while France extended her northeastern frontier by occupying the bishoprics of Metz, Toul, and Verdun. In the meantime, in 1556, Charles resigned the Spanish crown to his son, Philip II. In the following year, he abdicated the imperial throne in favor of his brother, Ferdinand I, and retired to a monastery. 

This long series of wars had significant effects upon European history. Hapsburg predominance in Italy was confirmed; France expanded her frontier towards the Rhine; the balance of power was preserved; Protestantism in Germany enjoyed a comparatively free growth, assuring its success; the Turks strengthened their power in southeastern Europe.

The comparative freedom of the Italian city-states from papal, imperial, and feudal control has been pointed out as a reason for the beginning of the Renaissance in Italy. Love of city, characteristic of 

Italians during the Renaissance, engendered rivalry among the cities which was lacking in the nationalistic states of Europe. Rivalry expressed itself in such ways as in the patronage of art, literature, and science. Leaders in these fields enhanced local prestige and the cities exerted themselves to excel their neighbors in encouraging learning. In this respect no city enjoyed greater success than Florence. 

Wealthy patrons encouraged the movement; the despots were in an ideal position to assume leadership in such activity and local preeminence in learning and the arts went a long way to reconcile the populace to despotic rule. Internal political conditions contributed to the development of the Renaissance, while external events, particularly the French invasions, promoted the diffusion of the Renaissance throughout Europe. When the sack of Rome by Charles V in 1527 virtually halted the positive movement in Italy, the Renaissance was just getting well under way elsewhere in Europe.

CHAPTER 28 Economic Changes during the Renaissance 

HE word renaissance means rebirth or revival and is usually applied to the transition from medieval to modern methods of study and thought. Traditionally, the Renaissance is that period of European history from the fourteenth to the sixteenth centuries allegedly marking a distinct break with the preceding centuries, or "Dark Ages." In this older, more specific sense, the Renaissance is an intellectual movement, originating in Italy, marked by a revival of interest in Greek and Roman civilization. Such a definition disregards developments in science, growth of nationalism, geographical discovery and exploration, and economic change. This older interpretation of the Renaissance has given way to the view that there was no distinct break between medieval and modern history; that the change from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance began in the eleventh century, largely as a consequence of the contact of Western with Eastern civilization. Knowledge did not disappear during the socalled "Dark Ages," although the period was characterized by relative intellectual lethargy. The Renaissance merely accelerated certain changes in European civilization which had begun in the eleventh century, such as the emergence of nationalism, the idea of representative government, the rise of towns, and the beginning of the gild system. Intellectually, the later Middle Ages were characterized by the rise of universities, the evolution of Gothic architecture, and the development of a characteristic medieval art. 

The Renaissance may be divided into two major phases: the Progressive and the Regressive. The Progressive phase was characterized by a definite moving forward and manifested itself in economic changes and scientific advance; the Regressive phase, by looking backward to the classical civilizations of Greece and Rome, manifested itself in art and literature. 

The Progressive phase influenced every aspect of economic activity - agricultural, commercial, and industrial. In agriculture, the basic

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

365 change was the beginning of the breakdown of the manorial system, the economic basis of feudalism. This change was rapid in England, but slow in the other countries of Europe; it did not occur in Russia until the freeing of the serfs by Czar Alexander II in 1861. The three chief changes in the manorial system during the Renaissance were: (1) The disappearance of serfdom. This medieval institution collapsed because of its inefficiency and unprofitableness, and as a result of the acute scarcity of labor following the Black Death which swept over Europe during the middle of the fourteenth century. (2) The beginning of the enclosure movement, or the fencing of land, particularly common grazing land, for sheep pasturage. During the 

Middle Ages the peasant lived on a bare subsistence level. Often the difference between living and starvation was the dairy products which the peasant secured from pasturing his cows on the common grazing lands. With the advent of the enclosure system the commons were the first lands to be fenced. Now the peasant faced shorter rations, starvation, or removal to the cities in the hope of securing employment. (3) The specialization of crops and production of agricultural surpluses through improved methods of agricultural technique. The fundamental effect of these agricultural changes was to free the rural laborers from the soil. These displaced workers were forced to migrate to the urban centers, where their influx contributed to the breakdown of the gild system.

During the Renaissance, the horizon of western Europe was further widened by the Commercial Revolution which began the overseas expansion of Europe to the Americas, Asia, and Africa. Down to the fifteenth century, European life centered about the Mediterranean, and the Italians largely controlled the commerce of western 

Europe. The Commercial Revolution of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, however, shifted the commercial balance of power from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, and Portugal, Spain, England, and the Netherlands supplanted the Italian cities as the leaders of the economic life of the Continent. This new commercial movement called for more extensive voyages which led to discovery and exploration. No significant contributions had been made to geographical knowledge by Western civilization in the period from the fall of Rome to the time of the crusades. This was primarily because of the general disorganization following the barbarian invasions and the fall of the Western Roman Empire. During the Middle Ages, the total volume of long-distance trade decreased, each area tending to become self-sufficient. Thus little stimulus was given to discovery and ex-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ploration. The influence of the church had contributed to the decline of investigation and inquiry, and as a consequence scientific geography had been supplanted by "biblical geography," in which the religious influence predominated. 

It was the crusades which brought the West strongly into contact with the East, revived intercontinental trade and the latent interest in the Orient, and gave an impetus to geographical inquiry. During the thirteenth century, Europeans began to penetrate into eastern Asia. 

The rise of the great Mongol Empire, stretching from China to Russia, made it possible for westerners to go into the unknown East with some degree of ease and safety. The most famous of these travelers was Marco Polo (1254-1324), a Venetian merchant who made an adventurous journey through the heart of Asia to the court of the Mongol ruler, Kublai Khan, at Peking. From 1271 to 1295,

Marco Polo remained in the East. He became a favorite of the Grand 

Khan, entered his service, and thus possessed an excellent opportunity to secure a vast store of information about the country. After his return to Europe, the story of this journey was written under his direction as The Book of Ser Marco Polo, a work that became the most popular travel book of the Middle Ages and aroused the interest of Europeans in the Orient. Marco Polo's information about the East did much to dispel general misconceptions of that region. 

The work of other travelers and explorers accelerated the pace of geographical inquiry, culminating in a veritable golden age of discovery in the fifteenth century.

It was the needs of commerce which largely accounted for these expeditions and voyages. Since the time of the Romans, western 

Europe had depended upon the East as the source of its luxuries. 

Spices, such as pepper, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, and ginger, were needed to preserve fresh meats and to make foods more palatable in those days before the advent of refrigerating processes. All kinds of drugs (like camphor and laudanum), gums, dyes, fragrant woods, precious stones, fine fabrics, porcelains, and perfumes were imported from the Orient. In payment for these goods, Europe was forced to export precious metals, for the greater part of her products, with the exception of Italian wines and Flemish woolens, were too bulky to be transported profitably to the East.

This intercontinental trade followed three principal routes. The first, in the north, led from the highlands of Asia by caravan, river, and the Caspian and Black Seas to Constantinople. The second was a middle journey which led directly across Asia to Damascus, thence

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

367 through Persia and Syria to Antioch, Acre, and other Syrian ports. 

The third and the cheapest of these routes lay to the south along the southern shore of Asia, up to the Red Sea to the Isthmus of Suez, thence by caravan to the Nile, and down this river to Alexandria. All of these routes were long and dangerous. The danger, together with the tolls and duties levied upon the goods at various places on the journey, increased the prices of the merchandise several fold. Since the time of the crusades, this eastern trade had been monopolized by the merchants from Venice and Genoa. These Italian towns established trading stations in the East which became the outposts of a flourishing commercial life. This control was regarded with disfavor by such rising nationalistic states as Portugal, which wished to share in this profitable trade and free themselves of dependence upon Italy. 

Other factors contributed to the breaking of this monopoly. The decline of the Mongol Empire, which had given some encouragement and support to trade, made it increasingly difficult to keep open the overland trade routes. To the south, the advance of the Ottoman 

Turks into southeastern Europe placed restrictions upon the free movement of goods. As a consequence, the belief became prevalent that a shorter, all-water route to the Indies, free from Italian control, could be found. Such a route would allow the participation of other countries in the eastern trade and would cheapen the prices on those commodities, which were rapidly ceasing to be luxuries and becoming necessities of life. 

Several reasons may be seen for this great interest in geographical inquiry. Such a movement was tied up with the intellectual currents of the time; secularization is the one word that explains this. 

Under the influence of the Renaissance, the old ascetic ideal gave way before man's interest in worldly affairs, which interest found an outlet in discovery and exploration. This breakdown of intellectual barriers came as a consequence of that zealous search for truth which characterized the Renaissance. The desire for profit was probably the strongest motive which sent men out to discover, explore, and colonize distant lands. From this came the immediate profit of gold, silver, precious stones, etc., which the explorer hoped to find in new regions. But more important still was the ultimate profit which accrued from the use of colonies as sources of raw materials and as markets for manufactured goods. An integral part of this belief was the spirit of nationalism which was growing stronger in Europe. No longer was nationalism confined to the political phase; it now was extended into the economic sphere as well. Out of this grew the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

theory of mercantilism, which as an economic philosophy may be compared with the theory of absolutism in the political sphere. The object of the mercantilists was the creation of an industrial and commercial state in which private and sectional interests should be encouraged or forced to promote national self-sufficiency. This doctrine emphasized industry and foreign trade, rather than agriculture and domestic trade, as sources of national wealth. The mercantilists believed that the prosperity of a nation was in proportion to the amount of money in circulation within the country and that the balance of trade was the true index of a nation's prosperity. They urged, therefore, that trade should be so conducted as to attract the largest possible amount of precious metals and to keep a favorable balance in international trade. This could be done by encouraging exports and discouraging imports. Large and flourishing colonies were a necessity for the success of this system, since they offered good sources of raw materials and markets for manufactured goods. The mother country attempted to prevent other countries from trading with her colonies and at the same time restricted colonial manufacturers. 

Portugal and Spain took the leadership in the acquisition of colonies, to be followed later by England, France, and the Netherlands. The 

Christian missionaries were in the vanguard of this movement as the shock troops of imperialism. Missionary zeal was put to a mercenary use by the traders and merchants who capitalized upon the work of these Christian leaders in penetrating into unknown lands. The spirit of adventure was also a great motivating force. New lands were discovered, explored, and colonized by restless spirits who were tired of the humdrum life of the Old World. It has been said that the three 

G's (gold, glory, and God) constituted the basic reasons for this great interest in discovery and exploration which swept over Europe during the Renaissance period.

The Commercial Revolution was preceded or accompanied by numerous aids to exploration. It is impossible to determine whether such developments came as a consequence of the widespread interest in navigation, or vice versa. The most important invention was the mariner's compass, introduced into Europe in the twelfth century. 

The magnetic needle had been known for centuries, but the great contribution of the Renaissance was the mounting of the needle on a card as the pivot compass. This invention freed the sailors from their dependence upon the stars and landmarks, lessening the dangers of navigation when these natural guides were invisible. The astrolabe, a device to calculate latitude by observation of the height of the sun

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

369 above the horizon, was introduced into Europe probably through the Arabs. The quadrant, a simpler device, later supplanted the astrolabe. 

The invention of the barometer (Torricelli's Tube) was another aid to the mariner. The chief navigation device lacking at this time was the chronometer, or a suitable mechanical means of measuring time. 

With the increase in shipping, chart and map making became an important science. Toscanelli (1397-1482), an Italian, and Müller (1436–1476), a German, were two great geographers during the Renaissance. Toscanelli believed that the Indies could be reached by a westward voyage across the Atlantic, and even Columbus secured geographical advice from him. The most significant contribution to cartography during the Commercial Revolution was by Mercator (1512–1594), a Flemish geographer, whose projection of the sphere of the earth on a flat surface enabled navigators to steer by compass in a straight line instead of a spiral as was necessitated by the spherical projections of his time. Manuals were prepared giving information of land and water routes, tides, currents, etc., for the benefit of travelers and sailors. Often, however, the information contained in these books was based upon imagination and hearsay and not upon actual knowledge. Ships were made larger and more seaworthy to accommodate more passengers and larger cargoes. In the designing and constructing of new types of ships, Venice with her carracks, Portugal with her caravels, and Spain with her galleons, took the lead in western Europe. The vessels were made narrower and higher to increase their speed and seaworthiness. Improvements were made in the rudder, and the practice of keeping a ship's log was introduced. 

The Italian cities in the Mediterranean Basin and the Hansa towns of the North and Baltic Seas had dominated European commerce for centuries preceding the Commercial Revolution. During the fifteenth century, the Hansa towns were declining, and Venice, the leading maritime city of Italy, was struggling to retain her trade in the Near East against the rising power of the Ottoman Turks. Venice's greatest rival, however, lay to the west and not to the east. In the Iberian 

Peninsula, two rising nationalistic states, Portugal and Spain, were preparing to challenge Italian domination of the oriental trade. They lacked maritime experience and prestige and were confronted with the problem of discovering new routes to the East free from Venetian control. It is significant that Portugal, Spain, and England drew heavily upon Italian maritime knowledge during their periods of discovery and exploration. Columbus in the service of Spain, Cabot under the English flag, and Amerigo Vespucci for Portugal and Spain,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

were adventurous spirits from Italy who might have remained in the service of their states if they had taken part in this western maritime movement. But the Italian cities, because of their geographical position in the Mediterranean and their trade ties with the East, were precluded from participating in any commercial movements outside the Mediterranean area. Portugal, Spain, and England possessed no such restraining trade ties, and their geographical position faced to the 

West and not to the East.

Portugal was the first modern European state to found an overseas empire. This expansion beyond Europe was a continuation of that crusading spirit which had led to the expulsion of the Mohammedans from Portugal. The first colonial acquisition was the Moorish city of Ceuta in Morocco (1415). Portuguese enthusiasts for discovery, exploration, and conquest found ready support in the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator (1394-1460), a younger son of

King John I. Rich, unmarried, and free from the cares of state, Prince 

Henry was able to devote his time and fortune to the promotion of navigation. He drew around him a group of intelligent and highly skilled mariners, scientists, and geographers. While showing this active interest in expansion, he did not make voyages himself, but preferred to remain at home to guide and direct the navigators. The first results were unimportant. Under Prince Henry's direction the 

Portuguese rediscovered and colonized the Madeiras and the Azores and discovered the Cape Verde Islands. This was a part of the search for a better knowledge of the Western Ocean and for a seaway along the unexplored coast of Africa to the "Western Nile" (Senegal 

River), then eastward to the mythical Christian kingdom of " Prester

John " in Ethiopia, and ultimately to the Indies. The timid Portuguese mariners did not venture far from shore, but year by year they crept southward, discovering and exploring miles of the African coastline. 

The discovery of the luxuriant Cape Verde in 1445 dispelled the belief that only parched deserts and uninhabitable lands lay to the southward. Pushing onward, the explorers reached the Guinea Coast. The wealth of this region in gold, slaves, and ivory caused the cessation of further geographical discovery until this land could be exploited. 

The pope, to whom was accorded the right to dispose of newly discovered lands and their heathen inhabitants, granted to the Portuguese these regions and any further discoveries they should make. 

These pious Christians soon made enormous fortunes by selling the benighted heathen into European slavery ostensibly in order to convert them.

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

371 The death of Prince Henry in 1460 weakened, but did not check, the impulse given by him to exploration. Although the patronage of the royal house declined, intrepid sailors pushed on down the African coast until, at last, in 1486, Bartholomew Diaz rounded the Cape of Good Hope. Any further progress was prevented by a mutiny of his crew, forcing him to return home in 1487. This voyage, however, dispelled the current ideas of the impracticability of reaching the Indies by a maritime route around Africa. Active interest in this projected all-water route to the East languished until the discovery of America in 1492 spurred the Portuguese into activity. Finally, in 

1497, Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon to Calicut, making the first all-water trip from Europe to India. His return home with a rich cargo of spices caused the jubilant merchants to take immediate steps to profit from this contact with the Orient. Under the able leadership of such men as Almeida and Albuquerque, the Portuguese broke the control of the spice trade held for centuries by the Arabs in the East and the Venetians in the West. The vigorous opposition of the Arabs was effectively crushed in a series of naval encounters. Commercial treaties were made with the natives; trading posts, such as Goa and 

Diu, were established, and strategic points fortified to protect the approach to the Spice Islands. It was the islands such as the Moluccas, and not India, which constituted the chief source of spices. Lisbon now superseded Venice as the great distributing center for eastern products, and Portugal retained a virtual monopoly of this trade until it was seized by the Dutch in the seventeenth century. 

The Spaniards were slower than the Portuguese in entering upon maritime discovery. For centuries Spain had been troubled with the internal problem of the Moors - a people who differed from her inhabitants in race, language, customs, and religion. National unity was consequent upon the expulsion of the Moors; interest in discovery and exploration, upon the achievement of national unity. In 1492, however, the last remnant of the Moors were driven from the peninsula across to Africa. Spain now prepared to participate in the Commercial Revolution, but owing to Portuguese control of the sea lanes around Africa to the East - a control that was bolstered by papal sanction she was forced to look westward for a possible opening. 

After Diaz's voyage, it became apparent that a route from Portugal to India via the Cape would be unduly long, and da Gama's voyage confirmed this belief.

Erroneous ideas so beclouded the bits of geographical knowledge of the time that no comprehensive program of exploration could be

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

carried out until a clear, scientific idea of the world was evolved. 

Although geographers were gradually accepting the idea of the sphericity of the earth and the feasibility of reaching the Spice Islands by sailing westward, a misconception of the time, popularized by geographers and dramatized by the voyages of Columbus, was that the Indies lay across the Atlantic only a few thousands of miles off the western coast of Europe, a comparatively short journey away. 

Two mistaken beliefs fostered this error. First, for thirteen hundred years Europeans had accepted Ptolemy's calculation of the size of the earth, and this reckoning was too small by one-sixth (4,000 miles). 

Second, Marco Polo's estimate exaggerated the distance from Europe to China.

These ideas, correct and erroneous alike, were accepted by Christopher Columbus, a Genoese sailor and diligent student of the scientific writings of his time. Jeered and scoffed at by doubters who called him a visionary and a madman, Columbus labored tirelessly for his projected voyage to the Indies. Poverty forced him to seek the aid of some wealthy patron. No such aid was forthcoming in Italy, for the Italians were interested in their own Mediterranean trade routes and not in the possibility of a competing route to the west. He saw that aid must come from the rising maritime states of western Europe and not from the older commercial cities of the Mediterranean. King John II of Portugal, after toying with Columbus's ideas, dropped them as impractical, being content to develop the Cape of Good Hope route. Bartholomew Columbus, a brother of Christopher, made a fruitless trip to England to secure aid from Henry VII. Meanwhile, Christopher endeavored to secure aid from Spain. 

But the times were not propitious, for Queen Isabella of Castile and King Ferdinand of Aragon needed their resources to drive the Moors from the southern part of the Spanish peninsula to complete the unification of the country. This program was of greater momentary importance to these rulers than the visionary idea of a trade route to the East.

With the expulsion of the Moors from Spanish soil in 1492, Isabella, who was Queen of Castile in her own right, agreed to finance Columbus's proposed voyage. She furnished him with three small vessels and the necessary supplies, the total cost of which amounted to only about $100,000. Columbus was given the rank of grand admiral and viceroy over the lands to be discovered, with a tenth of all the gold and silver he should find and the rank of a nobleman for himself and his progeny. The expedition sailed from Palos, Spain, on

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

373 August 3, 1492, refitted in the Canaries, and sailed on the final leg of the voyage on September 6. " America" was discovered on October 

12, and the pious leader named the island on which he landed San Salvador. Its identity is unknown, but it was probably Watling's 

Island in the Bahamas. He visited several islands in the West Indies, such as Cuba and Haiti, seeking the rich cities with their teeming populations which abounded in the fabulous East. Instead, he found primitive native villages of naked savages, whom he called Indians. 

Despite his disappointment, he believed that this was only an outlying part of the Orient, and that further efforts would lead to discovery of that rich region filled with spices and precious metals spoken of by eastern travelers. He left a small colony on the island of Santo 

Domingo and returned to Spain, arriving on March 15, 1493. There can be little doubt that the Western Hemisphere to which this voyage now opened the way had previously been visited by explorers from the Old World, particularly the Norsemen. The significance of 

Columbus's voyage, however, is that it paved the way for European penetration of the Americas.

Although Columbus returned to Spain without riches from the newly discovered lands, the Spanish monarchs received him with every mark of esteem and the country echoed with his praise. This was only natural in a new nation without the commercial traditions. of the older states of Europe. The voyage did not dispel all doubt that the Indies had been reached by a comparatively short sail across the Atlantic. The king of Portugal insisted that these lands were a part of Guinea, a possession of Portugal in Africa. This dispute was submitted to Pope Alexander VI, a Spaniard, for adjudication. The pontiff accordingly issued two bulls in which the new lands were divided between the two countries by an imaginary line of demarcation drawn from pole to pole, one hundred leagues west of the 

Azores and Cape Verde Islands. All lands, discovered or undiscovered, west of this line were given to Spain, while those east of the line were assigned to Portugal. This arrangement was unsatisfactory to the latter country, for the line was drawn too close to Africa. 

Accordingly, it was modified by another papal decree in September, 1493, and by the Treaty of Tordesillas, signed by Portugal and Spain. on June 7, 1494, which drew a line 370 leagues west of the Cape

Verde Islands. This papal division was ignored by the states of Europe when they began their colonizing ventures in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

In the autumn of 1493, Columbus returned to the New World with

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

a large, well-equipped expedition - a sharp contrast to the small fleet he had led to America in the preceding year. A number of the Indies, including Puerto Rico and Jamaica, were discovered before he returned to Spain in 1496. On his third voyage (1498), he reached the mainland of South America, at the mouth of the Orinoco River, rightly surmising that he had found a continent, although he stili believed himself on the eastern coast of Asia. His exploration was checked by his arrest and return to Spain on charges of misgovernment which had been brought against him by his enemies. The monarchs disavowed the action of their envoys and released Columbus, though they did not restore the authority they had stripped from him. In his fourth voyage, 1502-1504, he explored the coast of 

Central America. His last years were full of bitterness and disappointment, for his failure to find the riches of the Indies and his incompetence as a governor made him a great number of enemies. He died in 

1506, poor, obscure, and neglected, not knowing that the land which baffled him in his quest for the East was a new world and not a part of Asia.

In 1497, John Cabot, a Venetian captain employed by Henry VII 

of England to search for a northwest passage to India, landed on the 

North American coast, probably near Cape Breton Island. Therefore, he is generally recognized as the discoverer of this continent. After exploring the coast he returned to England, where the parsimonious king rewarded him for his invaluable work with an initial grant of ten pounds. In command of a much larger expedition in 1498, Cabot skirted the North American shore from Labrador possibly as far south as Chesapeake Bay. No attempt was made to colonize or otherwise to follow up these voyages, but Cabot's discoveries later formed the basis of English claims to the eastern portion of North America. 

The New World, however, received its name not from Cabot or Columbus but from Amerigo Vespucci, a Florentine navigator, employed first by Spain and later by Portugal. In 1504 he wrote an account of four voyages which he claimed to have made to the New World. Martin Waldseemüller, a professor of geography in the 

College of St. Die in Lorraine, accepted Vespucci's claims, and in 

1507 published a pamphlet entitled Cosmographiae Introductio in which he suggested that this New World be given the name of America. This designation was originally applied to Brazil as distinguished from the insular discoveries of Columbus, but the name "America" in time came to designate the whole of the Western 

Hemisphere.

375 The Line of Demarcation restricted Portuguese expansion in the 

New World to Brazil, which had been touched by the Spanish navigator, Pinzon, in 1499 and the Portuguese, Cabral, in 1500. In the

East, however, she controlled the lucrative spice trade which was of far more value than anything that Spain in two decades had found in her new possessions. Unceasing exploration had failed to discover a passageway through or around the extensive land mass of the American continents which blocked the way to the Indies. Ferdinand 

Magellan (c. 1480–1521), a disgruntled Portuguese sea captain who had transferred his services to Spain, believed that a strait existed and he proposed to reach the Spice Islands by sailing around South

America. In 1519 he received the command of a fleet of five vessels from Charles V of Spain. Sailing westward, he explored the eastern coast of South America, rounded this continent through the strait that now bears his name, and sailed into the "Great South Sea." He named this ocean the Pacific. He struck out boldly to the northwest in order to reach the latitude of the Spice Islands and, after much suffering, reached the Ladrone Islands with but two ships. Then sailing southward, he discovered and named the Philippine Islands, where he lost his life in a skirmish with the natives (1521). The larger of his two vessels was captured by the Portuguese, but the smaller one, the Vittoria, succeeded in reaching Spain in 1522, thus completing the first circumnavigation of the globe. This marvelous voyage added greatly to geographical knowledge and proved beyond question that the earth was round.

The second stage of exploration was on land and not on sea. In this movement Spain took the leadership, and the boldest of her adventurers came to the New World not to found colonies but to search for riches. Such a one was Hernando Cortez, who, in 1519, began the conquest of Mexico. He found this region peopled with the Aztec 

Indians, possessing a higher degree of civilization and wealth than had hitherto been found in the New World. Cortez's small but effective army crushed the resistance of the Indians, the land was despoiled, and an immense quantity of treasure was sent back to Spain. 

In 1532 Francisco Pizarro performed a similar feat in Peru. For centuries, a steady stream of gold and silver flowed from these countries into the coffers of Spain. Other adventurers seeking treasure in 

America were less successful than Cortez and Pizarro. But it was while on a quest for riches that Balboa discovered the Pacific Ocean (1513); De Soto explored the southeastern part of the United States (1539-1542); and Coronado in search for the Seven Cities of Cibola

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

explored the southwest (1540-1542). Although most of these adventurers found hardships and sometimes death instead of the riches for which they were seeking, their explorations opened up a great part of the New World to future colonization. 

The Commercial Revolution had far-reaching effects upon civilization-economic, political, social, and religious. Economically, it shifted the commercial center of Europe from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic Ocean. Such old commercial centers as Venice, Genoa,

Lübeck, and Hamburg lost their trade supremacy to rising cities like 

Lisbon, Cadiz, London, Amsterdam, Antwerp, and Bordeaux. With the decline of Italian commercial supremacy, there was a corresponding decline of the peninsula as the leading banking center of Europe, and Florence was forced to relinquish her prestige as the leading banking city in Europe to the new commercial cities. One of the ultimate results of the Commercial Revolution was an increase in prices. Medieval trade had suffered from a restricted currency, too often depleted by an unfavorable balance of trade with the East. The discovery of America opened a new source of precious metals, and as a consequence, the gold supply of Europe increased several fold during the sixteenth century alone. For the first time in centuries, the Continent enjoyed a favorable balance of trade with the outside world. The immense wealth of Mexico and Peru added greatly to the power and prestige of Spain. But ultimately she profited little from this treasure, for she merely acted as a clearing house through which the gold and silver flowed to the more basically prosperous countries of Europe in payment of goods. At home the unwise policies of her rulers had undermined the national strength. Freedom of thought had been crushed by the Inquisition; the Jews and Moors, the industrial backbone of the nation, had been persecuted and driven from the country; unwise religious policy had caused the loss of the Netherlands, the commercial and industrial center of the Empire. The acquisition of colonies had not been followed by mercantilist exploitation to augment the wealth of the mother country, for Spain was far more interested in the immediate gains than in the ultimate profits which would accrue from a wise program comprehending the whole economic system.

The increased supply of gold and silver in Europe penetrated every part of the Continent. The stream of precious metals from the New 

World during the Renaissance raised commodity prices and wages, causing a general dislocation of the economic life of Europe. This upheaval, however, did not come quickly after the discovery of

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

377 America. From 1500 to 1550 there was little increase in prices, due primarily to the poor banking facilities which failed to maintain a fluid circulation of the capital as it came in from the New World. A rise in prices depended upon a large increment of gold and silver and the improvement of banking facilities to impart a velocity to money and credit. The increase in prices led to a rise in wages, but the true purchasing power of wages was actually lower than it had been before the Commercial Revolution. By the close of the sixteenth century, an unjust stabilization in wages bore heavily upon the laborers. Professional men were well paid, their wages comparing favorably with those of the present day for the same classes. The best paid workers were those officials high in the service of the state, whose salaries were often larger than these employees deserved. 

The rise of the famous Joint Stock Companies was an important concomitant to the voyages of exploration and the ensuing colonization enterprises. As early as the eleventh century, there existed in the 

Italian cities organizations known as commendas, in which investors furnished two-thirds of the capital to finance commercial voyages to Syria, while a factor, or agent who managed the enterprise, furnished the remainder and received half of the profits. Under the terms of the accomadatio, the investors furnished all the capital, and the factor was given one-fourth of the profits for his services. In Genoa, an organization of twenty-nine shareholders was formed to exploit the resources of the island of Chios, while in England, the Merchants Adventurers received a charter as early as the reign of Henry IV. 

Large sums obviously were needed to exploit the opportunities presented by the voyages of exploration. The Joint Stock Company, in which each subscriber received shares of stock and profits in proportion to the amount of capital he contributed, was an adequate solution to the problems created by widening commercial activity. 

The organization usually was not limited to a definite period of time, and its purposes were frequently broad enough to include a variety of activities in several areas. A charter was received from the king which fixed responsibility, clearly stated rights and obligations, and, above all, extended the protection of the government to the recipients. The English London and Plymouth Companies, and the English, Dutch, and French East India Companies were among the earliest and most successful of the Joint Stock organizations. 

Individual capitalists of great wealth arose. One of the earliest was 

Jacques Coeur, a native of Bourges, who made his first commercial voyage to Syria in 1427. With Montpellier as the center of his

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

activities, because that city was exempt from the papal prohibition of trade with the Saracens, he enlarged his interests in the Levant, dealing in silks, armor, spices, furs, and other commodities. He soon owned four galleys and three smaller ships, and in 1448 was able to furnish at his own expense eleven ships for French use against England. His warehouses and branches were established in a number of cities and three hundred agents were in his employ. As his capital increased, he acquired silver, copper, and lead mines in the vicinity of Lyons, and he purchased more than thirty large estates from impecunious nobles. In 1440 he was made paymaster of the Royal Household, and he was subsequently appointed Master of the Mint and member of the king's council. His loans to the court became larger and larger, and the capital furnished by him played a major part in the expulsion of the English from France in the last stages of the 

Hundred Years' War. When Agnes Sorel, the mistress of Charles VII, died, Coeur was arrested on the preposterous charge of having poisoned her. Other accusations were trumped up against him as pretexts for the confiscation of his properties, and upon his death in 

1456 he was virtually penniless.

The Fugger family of Germany became one of the most powerful banking groups of all time. Johannes Fugger, a linen weaver of Augsburg, accumulated a modest capital which his son increased as a dealer in linen so as to enable him to leave a fortune of three thousand florins to his two heirs, one of whom established the banking business. By the sixteenth century, the family controlled mines in Germany and Spain, and their banking interests were international in scope. Funds furnished by them brought about the election of Charles 

V to the imperial throne in 1519. The Fuggers frequently served as agents for the collection of papal revenues in the Empire and they underwrote the sale of indulgences in Germany which precipitated the Protestant Revolt. The Welsers, Haugs, Hochstetters, and Imhofs also were German capitalists of enormous wealth and power. Banking remained largely in private hands, but in 1656 the Bank of Sweden was founded and in 1694 the famous Bank of England was established. 

The social life of the people was fundamentally changed by the betterment of the standards of living during the Commercial Revolution. Improvements were made in housing and the comforts of homes. 

Glass came to be used in the dwellings of the common people; tiles were used for roofing; carpets, tapestries, and bed linens became common. Europe drew heavily upon the New World and the East for new commodities such as tea, introduced from the Far East;

ECONOMIC CHANGES 

379 coffee from Arabia; tobacco, potatoes, chocolate, Indian corn or maize, from America. The New World also sent to Europe large supplies of dyewoods, medicines (such as quinine), cane sugar, molasses, fish, lumber, naval stores, and furs. 

One of the major political results of the Commercial Revolution has already been pointed out: the rise of such powerful states as 

England, France, Spain, Portugal, and the Netherlands as a consequence of the shift of the economic center of Europe from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. Germany and Austria, as parts of the 

Holy Roman Empire, were embroiled in religious strife, and they lacked governmental support and a geographical position favorable to their playing a significant part in this commercial movement. 

Russia, isolated and out of the main currents of European thought, profited little from the Commercial Revolution until the reign of 

Peter the Great (1689-1725). After the capture of Constantinople in 

1453 by the Ottoman Turks, southeastern Europe, long a center of trade, influenced the economic life of western Europe very little. 

Portugal and Spain reaped the immediate economic and political benefits of the Commercial Revolution. The wealth from her colonies enabled Spain to maintain a position as the dominant Continental power until the opening of the seventeenth century. 

The Commercial Revolution had a profound influence upon religion. As has been pointed out, the missionaries were the vanguard for the economic penetration of traders and colonizers. The newly discovered lands opened a virgin field for missionary endeavor which the various orders, particularly the Jesuits, were quick to seize. Soon after its founding in the sixteenth century, the Society of Jesus had missionaries in the heathen lands from America on the west to Japan on the east. This non-Christian territory gave the Roman Catholic 

Church an opportunity to regain some of the membership, wealth, and prestige lost by the Protestant Revolt of the sixteenth century. 

Through the establishment of asylums from religious persecution, the New World became a refuge from the intolerance of the Old. 

The important changes in the agricultural and commercial life of Europe during the Renaissance have been shown. While the parallel developments in industry were not so spectacular and romantic as those in commerce, yet they constitute the precursor of the Industrial Revolution of the eighteenth century. These two revolutions, Commercial and Industrial, in their far-reaching effects, were the two greatest upheavals in history. The industrial changes of the Renaissance marked the breakdown of the gild system - a system that was

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

inadequate for the times after the Commercial Revolution. Several causes for this collapse are apparent. The gilds were too conservative and opposed to change. Oligarchical tendencies in the gilds made them too exclusive and thousands of properly trained workers were denied membership in order to preserve the standards of an outworn economic system. The developments of new industries outside the gilds, such as cotton textiles, did not lend themselves readily to restriction by these organizations. Attempts to extend the archaic gild system with its deadening effects were firmly opposed by the leaders. in the new industries. The inauguration of the "outwork system" was perhaps the most important factor. This system originated apparently in Italy, spread to Flanders, and then to England. In this latter country, it was to enjoy its greatest development, particularly in the textile industry. The outwork system came as a consequence of the restrictions of the gilds in the employment of trained men in the trades. Under this system capitalists began to purchase the necessary raw materials and machinery and place them in the households where the workers would manufacture the goods under contract. 

This short-circuited the gilds through the elimination of any participation by these organizations. The popularity and spread of this type of manufacturing led to greater production, cheaper goods, and greater employment. The chief objection to the outwork system was the absence of any control by the capitalist over his workers. Without discipline he could not regulate the production of the workers, which was often so irregular that contracts or production scales could not be fulfilled. This weakness was eliminated by placing the workers in factories for disciplinary purposes. These were not factories in the present meaning of the word, for employees continued to work on the contract or piece method, respecting certain regulations and hours of employment. The factory system as we know it was not possible until the introduction of a central motive power — the steam engine.
