Some social and economic effects of the factory system existed in the sixteenth century, but the technological effects did not come until the Industrial Revolution of the eighteenth century.

CHAPTER 29 

Scientific Advance in the Age of the

Renaissance N ancient times, scientific knowledge was limited and little attempt was made to differentiate individual sciences. A traditional distinction was made by grouping such knowledge into the two major classifications of theoretical science (natural philosophy) and practical science (science proper). The Greeks excelled in the theoretical field, producing such notable scientists as Pythagoras, Thales of Miletus, Anaximander, Euclid, and others. The Romans absorbed this intellectual activity of the Greeks into Latin utilitarianism. Ancient science developed comparatively free from restrictive customs and taboos of religion and society. While in western Europe science was in a decadent state even before the Germanic invasions, the barbarians crushed existing knowledge so effectively that only fragments survived through the Middle Ages. The medium for the transmission of ancient science to the later medieval period was the Arabs, who preserved, assimilated, and passed on to Western civilization much Greek and Hindu scientific knowledge. The Arabs not only salvaged knowledge, but they made noteworthy contributions of their own, especially in mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. Their knowledge was disseminated to western Europe by contacts in Saracen Spain and Sicily and the crusading ventures into the Near East. 

During the Middle Ages, the people of western Europe had a more meager knowledge and more restricted conception of science than that possessed by the ancient Greeks and Romans. That condition was due to the medieval attitude toward inquiry. Medieval man had no conception of natural law - all phenomena occurred only according to God's will. Natural law could not exist in an age of miracles.

The dogmatism of the church, which claimed divine origin, authority to teach infallible truth, and the exclusive right to interpret the Scrip-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tures, was a great obstacle to scientific progress. Ecclesiastics explained their restrictions on inquiry on the grounds that no unlimited freedom existed in the world; such freedom would be unjust and unreasonable, since it would lead only to license and rebellion. The 

Bible was the ultimate source and authority for all scientific teachings. If theories and findings agreed with the Gospels, well and good; if they did not, then they must be brought into conformity or altogether rejected. Such an attitude by the greatest institution of medieval society largely stifled experimentation and investigation until the Renaissance gave men a clearer conception of the universe and freed their minds from the trammels of dogmatism. A lack of interest in the world was another characteristic attitude of the Middle Ages. The true medievalist was too deeply influenced by the ascetic ideal to understand or appreciate secular interests. Asceticism emphasized dying, not living. Secular things were ephemeral; therefore, it behooved man to devote his life to the preparation of his soul for the eternal life beyond the grave. If secular truth was needed for the understanding of spiritual truth or for salvation, then God would reveal it in His own way. Scientific development was retarded by this mental state, but the lack of scientific apparatus was a contributory cause as well. Further progress was dependent upon the invention or perfection of instruments to aid man's senses. 

The Renaissance made far-reaching contributions to scientific knowledge. The period was characterized by the abandonment of the ascetic ideal, a revival of interest in the world, and the recognition of the necessity for experimentation. These new scientific trends came as a consequence of the synchronism of the cultural and economic revolutions of the Renaissance. New ideals were produced and men's minds were prepared to accept the more secular view of the universe which had been current in ancient times. At first, the tendency was to accept the authority of the ancients and substitute it for ecclesiastical dogmatism. Gradually, however, independence of thought developed and a truly critical attitude emerged. There was insistence on the application of the inductive system of reasoning; scientists believed that there were natural laws and that these laws could be ascertained by observation and experiment. 

Roger Bacon (1214-1294), an English philosopher and scientist, was a pioneer in this movement. Although he lived in the Middle 

Ages, his advanced ideas mark him as a Renaissance, rather than a medieval, character. A liberal education at Oxford and later at Paris, from which institutions he received Master of Arts degrees, probably

SCIENTIFIC ADVANCE 

383 inculcated these progressive ideas. In no sense, however, was he the first opponent of medieval scholasticism and the champion of freedom of thought and inquiry; such teachers as Adam Marsh and 

Robert Grosseteste at Oxford had held similar views and probably influenced him.

In the development and popularization of these ideas, Bacon was guided by three basic principles: the necessity of Greek, the necessity of experimentation, and the utility of mathematics. Medieval knowledge was so firmly based upon the writings of Aristotle that an understanding of the Greek language was a prerequisite for a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures, science, or philosophy. During the Middle Ages, Aristotle had been preserved only in fragmentary or imperfect form; manuscripts had been translated from 

Greek into Arabic, and then into Latin, in which form they were used in western Europe. Because of poor translation and deliberate falsification, existing Greek texts were not suitable for thorough scholars. Bacon continually attacked the faulty text of the Bible and the imperfect translations of Aristotle. The second principle of 

Bacon's scientific creed was his insistence upon the necessity of experimentation to arrive at scientific truth. Experimentation was the door to knowledge and the criterion of truth. He criticized the scientific methods of his time and condemned the bondage of custom and popular opinion which had entrenched the deductive method in the scientific world. His third principle, that of the utility of mathematics, he considered as the key to science. Mathematics applied to observation was the only means of arriving at a knowledge of nature - a practical, rather than an abstract, use of the principle. 

Bacon's scientific vision, his scientific ideas, although not entirely free from the influence of scholasticism, as is indicated by his belief in astrology and in the existence of the "philosopher's stone," stamp him as being ahead of his time. Criticism, opposition, and even persecution were inescapable consequences of such vision and progress. During his explorations of the secrets of nature, he made discoveries which were regarded by some of his contemporaries as savoring of black magic. That some of these scientific ideas were so regarded, and even held to be in opposition to the teachings of the church, was merely incidental, for he wrote his greatest works at the insistence of the pope and for the glorification of the church. The lack of orthodoxy in his doctrines, his imprudent and inaccurate views, and his harsh and often unjustifiable criticism of his contemporaries were the chief points of opposition to his works. Freedom of ex-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

pression was denied him by a general restriction of the Franciscan Order, of which he was a member and which forbade the publication of any work without special permission from superiors. Bacon's ability was recognized by such clear-sighted men as Guy de Foulques, who became Pope Clement IV in 1266. Before his elevation to the papacy he had expressed the desire to examine some of Bacon's works, but compliance with this wish was prevented by the prohibition of the Franciscans. As pope he rescinded this prohibition, in favor of Bacon, who in 1268 dispatched for papal examination his encyclopedic Opus Majus, the Opus Minus, an alchemical treatise, and possibly the Opus Tertius. Clement could not have given these ambitious works more than a cursory examination, for he died in the same year in which they were received. Bacon's works were written primarily for the glorification of the church, an attitude shown in his Opus Majus; in this work, an exhortation addressed to Pope 

Clement, he urged the consolidation of the Roman Catholic faith as the supreme agency for the civilization of mankind. Nevertheless, freedom of expression was withdrawn by the general of the Franciscan Order, with the sanction of Pope Nicholas III. His works were condemned and he was imprisoned in 1277. About 1292, he was released and permitted to return to Oxford, where he remained until his death.

Some of Bacon's theories and experiments, long regarded as original, were probably drawn from his study of the works of the Arabian scientists. Possibly his knowledge of the composition and properties of gunpowder came from this source. His greatest work, however, was in the field of optics. He observed such principles of refraction as the apparent magnitude of the sun and moon on the horizon and he discussed the application of lenses to scientific purposes. At that time, the properties of lenses were not clearly understood, but Bacon mentioned their use in reading and viewing distant objects, both terrestrial and celestial. From this it is apparent that he understood the principles of spectacles, the telescope, and possibly the microscope, and it is conceivable that he might have made such instruments. From his studies in mathematics and astronomy, he detected errors in the calendar, which he proposed to rectify. Although the magnitude and significance of Bacon's works were recognized, his findings made no marked impression on his contemporaries or immediate successors. This lack of influence probably resulted from the condemnation of his works by the church and the opposition of this

SCIENTIFIC ADVANCE 

385 institution to further scientific inquiry. The true worth of his ideas became apparent a few centuries later. 

Another ecclesiastic, Nicholas of Cusa (1401-1464), broke with the prevailing school of scholastic thought and made significant contributions in science. As a mathematician and natural philosopher he advanced the theory that the earth rotated on its axis and was not the center of the universe. He propounded the law of inertia, experimented with falling bodies, and advanced an elementary theory of evolution. He favored a reform of the calendar along the lines laid down by Pope Gregory XIII more than a hundred years later. As a critic he was a precursor of Lorenzo Valla in declaring the Donation of Constantine to be a forgery. 

Johann Müller (1436–1476) was one of the greatest Renaissance mathematicians. Impressed by the progress made in mathematics and astronomy by the ancient Greeks and Saracens, he studied their works to gain ideas and to eliminate errors in translated versions. 

Consequently, he was able to introduce a number of innovations into western science. His De Triangulis Omnimodis, a treatise on plane and spherical trigonometry, used the sine and cosine; the Tabulae 

Directionum, while essentially an astronomical work, contained valuable tables of sines and tangents. In his Algerithmus Demonstratus, he was among the first in western Europe to use symbolic algebra. With aid of a patron, he established an observatory and a printing press at Nuremberg, from which he issued tables of eclipses and works on astronomy. He supplied the basis of modern cometary astronomy by his observations of Halley's comet of 1472. In cartography, his navigation charts and tables contributed materially to the scientific knowledge which made possible the voyages of discovery and exploration. 

Perhaps the greatest genius of the Renaissance and undoubtedly one of the most versatile men in history was Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519). His ability expressed itself in several fields – painting, sculpture, architecture, engineering, and science. As a Florentine he had an admirable opportunity to acquaint himself with the knowledge of his age. His keen intellect enabled him to acquire a great store of erudition; he arrived at many of his conclusions by brilliant intuition. Much of his scientific work was ancillary to his artistic nature, since he was motivated by the desire to perfect the things of beauty and power which he created. His versatility, however, caused him to diffuse his genius, rendering it impossible for him to perfect

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

or complete many of the tasks in which he was interested. The scope of his scientific observation and experimentation included both applied and theoretical science. The greatest achievements of his scientific career were in the applied field, as a military engineer, where his services were greatly needed during the French invasions of Italy. 

His grasp of the principles of experimental science was strengthened by a wide range of experimentation and observation. As an artist, he saw the necessity of perfecting his knowledge of anatomy. He was the precursor of Harvey in the discovery of the circulation of the blood and he made a thorough study of optics to enable him accurately to paint the human eye. The idea of discovering the principles of flying and the invention of a flying machine intrigued him as it had done mankind for centuries. He spent much time observing birds to learn their methods of flight. The lack of a suitable form of motive power checked these experiments, but not before his study of the anatomy and habits of birds had made him an outstanding ornithologist. He made significant observations in meteorology; he knew that the earth revolved around the sun and understood the effect of the moon upon the tides. He discovered the nature of fossil shells and experimented with falling bodies, while his notable achievements in the science of hydraulics probably included invention of the hydrometer.

For thirteen centuries, science generally had accepted the geocentric theory advanced by Ptolemy. It was believed that the earth was the center of the universe and the sun and stars revolved around it. During the Renaissance, this theory began to totter. It was left for Copernicus (1473-1543), a Polish astronomer, in his The Revolutions of Heavenly Bodies, to refute the geocentric theory and advance his own heliocentric theory that the earth was not the center of the universe, but that it and the planets revolved around the sun. 

It was reluctantly that he agreed to the publication of this theory, for he perceived that it did not harmonize with the Scriptures nor with the Ptolemaic theory held by the church. If it was his intention to conciliate the church by dedicating this work to Pope Paul III, such a precaution was useless, for Copernicus died on the same day that the first published copy of his book reached the pope. Since 

Copernicus possessed inadequate apparatus and limited mathematical and astronomical knowledge, his heliocentric theory was not free from errors and miscalculations; it remained for such scientists as 

Galileo, Kepler, and Newton to perfect it. 

Helmont (1577-1644), a Belgian chemist, physiologist, and physi-

SCIENTIFIC ADVANCE 

387 cian, revealed scientifically the existence of gases distinct from atmospheric air, and was probably the first to introduce the term gas into science. He believed water to be the primary, if not the ultimate, constituent of matter. In support of this theory, he carried out experiments in which he showed that plants could grow although they received nothing but pure water. He did not recognize the part played in plant growth by carbon dioxide. In medicine, he observed the acid reaction of the gastric juice, thus being an early exponent of the iatrochemical school. Toscanelli (1397-1482), astronomer and geographer, and Amerigo Vespucci (1451–1512), navigator, were leaders in their respective fields whose contributions to science were pointed out in the discussion of discovery and exploration. Pacioli (c. 1440-c. 1515), Italian mathematician, in his chief work, Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et Proportionalita (1494), epitomized the mathematical knowledge of the time. Tartaglia (c. 

1506-1559), an Italian physicist and mathematician, discovered a method of solving cubic equations, and from these suggestions his contemporary, Cardan (1501-1576), probably derived the solution known as Cardan's Method. In physics, Tartaglia studied the theory of falling bodies and the range of projectiles, publishing his findings in his Nuova Scienza. He published the first Italian translation of 

Euclid and the earliest direct translation of some of the principal works of Archimedes. 

Medieval medicine, like other sciences of the time, was permeated with superstition and based primarily upon corrupt versions of the writings of the ancients. Hippocrates (c. 460-c. 370 B.C.) and Galen (c. A.D. 131-c. 200) were the chief authorities, and from the time. of Galen to the Renaissance little or no progress was made in medicine or surgery. In keeping with medieval ideas - or lack of them western Europe tacitly accepted the scientific findings of the ancients and made few attempts to verify or augment them. The chief additions to this medical knowledge came through contacts between Western and Eastern civilization. The Saracens were heirs to the medical knowledge of Greece and Rome, and, free from the ascetic philosophy of the West, were able to add materially to this heritage. 

Although western medical knowledge had lost a great part of its ancient religious significance, much of this knowledge and its application was still in the hands of the priesthood. Practically all the hospitals of the Middle Ages were controlled by the church, and these hôtels-Dieu did a noble service to humanity.

During the Middle Ages, the leading medical school in Europe

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

was at Salerno in Italy. In time, the study of medicine was added to the curriculum of the great universities, and such schools as Montpellier in France soon gained a wide reputation. Instruction was primarily theoretical, consisting of dissertations and lectures upon the works of Hippocrates and Galen. After receiving his degree of 

Bachelor of Medicine, the student secured clinical or practical experience by serving as assistant to a practitioner. Surgery was little understood; the dissection of the human body only intermittently practiced. In medieval medical science medicine was divorced from surgery, with the result that the prestige and usefulness of surgery declined in the opinion of physicians until its general practice was relegated to such menials as barbers and bath-keepers. Probably this lack of respect is traceable to Galen's dictum that "surgery is only a mode of treatment," and to the oriental aversion to touching the human body as unclean or unholy. In the early Middle Ages, instruction in anatomy was based upon the dissection of animals, since the dissection of the human body was proscribed by law and sentiment. Emperor Frederick II removed some of the legal bans against the dissection of human cadavers, but Renaissance knowledge of anatomy continued to be gained primarily from texts and lectures. 

The revival of interest in human dissection is credited to Mundinus, a professor in the University of Bologna, early in the fourteenth century. Such great Renaissance painters as Leonardo da Vinci studied anatomy to perfect their artistic work, but it was Andreas Vesalius (1514-1564), by his work at the University of Padua, who made this study a real science.

For a time there was no advancement in pathology corresponding to the increase in surgical knowledge. Physicians were too imbued with the ancient theory of the four humors, which were black and yellow bile, phlegm, and blood. A proper arrangement of these four was necessary for good health; domination of any one would lead to physical maladjustment and man would become choleric, melancholy, phlegmatic, or sanguine, according to which humor was dominant. Few scientific developments were made in pharmacology. 

In the treatment of sickness the medieval physicians often relied upon the most nauseous and repulsive concoctions which their imaginations could conceive. Toads, eels, snakes, lizards, and earthworms were popular ingredients, although vegetable and mineral medicines were commonly used.

The Renaissance was fruitful in the development of scientific medical knowledge. Medicine was affected by such characteristic Renais-

SCIENTIFIC ADVANCE 

389 sance factors as the revival of knowledge of Greek, the decline of the ascetic ideal, the invention of printing, geographical discovery and exploration, the application of observation and experimentation, and the developments in art which contributed to a greater knowledge of anatomy. One of the pioneers of scientific medicine was 

Paracelsus (c. 1490-1541), a German physician and chemist. Although he was regarded as a charlatan by his contemporaries and immediate successors, his discoveries enriched the study of medicine and chemistry. He rejected Galenism and, discarding the prevalent theory of humors, taught that disease was caused by a disharmony of normal functions and was to be combatted with such specific chemical remedies as sulphur, arsenic, iron, and mercury. Valerius Cordus (1515-1544), a gifted Prussian physician, discovered sulphuric ether in 1540, although for three centuries mankind was still to suffer before the anaesthetic properties of ether were recognized and applied.

Sanctorius (1561-1636) described a clinical thermometer of his own devising. This instrument, too, received no practical use at the time and was forgotten for nearly a hundred years.

During the Renaissance, there were brought into use several inventions most important in their results to civilization. Possibly none of these was to have a greater influence upon the future history of mankind than the invention of printing from movable type. For centuries, Orientals, particularly the Chinese, had printed from engraved wooden blocks, each block forming a whole page. This method did not supplant the laborious method of copying manuscripts by hand, for the engraving of a page block was a slow process. Printing from movable wooden type was invented in China in the decade following 1041, but no knowledge of that invention reached Europe. Further development in printing was dependent upon the substitution of movable, metallic type for the wood blocks and characters. There is no certainty as to the actual date of the European invention of movable type, or the name of the inventor. John Gutenberg (c. 13981468) of Mainz generally is regarded as the strongest claimant to the honor, although the claims of Laurens Koster (c. 1370—1440), a

Dutch printer, have been recognized by many investigators. Gutenberg brought the art to such perfection that, in 1456, a complete Vulgate Bible was printed. Cheap paper, an essential requisite, supplanted the costly parchment and lowered the prices of books, thus greatly stimulating the spread of learning.

The introduction of gunpowder from the Orient, and its first use in firearms in the fourteenth century, proved to be the final blow to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

feudalism. Firearms made the infantry an effective force and equalized combatants; since a peasant could use a gun as effectively as a knight, the knight and his armor soon became obsolete. Another invention of the Renaissance period, the pivot compass, enabled mariners to steer without the use of landmarks or the stars and made possible the voyages of discovery and exploration. Although the principles of lenses had been known to the ancient Greeks and Romans, their application to the use of science in such inventions as the telescope and microscope widened the fields of observation and stimulated scientific inquiry.

CHAPTER 30 The Literary Renaissance 

HE Regressive phase of the Renaissance was characterized by a reaction against decadent scholasticism. In a world of wider interests, man began to discard a transcendental, ascetic concept of life, to substitute humanism with its distinctly mundane and naturalistic view. Humanism, in its wider meaning, was rebellion against the discipline of the church and its restrictions on medieval thought. In its more common and specific sense, it was a revival of interest in the classical literature of Greece and Rome. Interest in or knowledge of the classics had not entirely disappeared at any time during the Middle Ages, but the predilection for theology had caused the classics to be subordinated to religion. The writings of Cicero, Vergil, Ovid, and other ancient authors were misconstrued or perverted in their interpretation to bolster the dogma of the church. 

By the appellation "profane literature," medieval scholars distinguished classical writing from the more spiritual work of churchmen. These ascetics did not comprehend or appreciate the intrinsic value of ancient civilization; such appreciation was to be left for the humanists, who studied the classics for their innate beauty and not for any religious value.

Italy was the original home of humanism. Individuals who extolled worldly pleasure, with its freer play of sensory impulses, found their prototypes in the ancient culture of Rome and the hitherto neglected culture of Greece. The new interest was personal and emotional; humanists enjoyed the beauty of the classics and were impressed by their elegant literary style. Admiration led to imitation, in an attempt to capture and reproduce something of the spirit which they so highly prized. But the civilization which had inspired these works had been largely swept away by the barbarian invasions. While this ancient culture had not been entirely effaced in Italy, its resuscitation was only partial, and in failing to capture the intangible essence of the ancients, the writings of the humanists often degenerated into

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

barren imitation. But it was neither the form nor subject of their writings which was the most characteristic and permanent; it was their humanistic spirit.

Although the Renaissance had its beginnings in Italy, outwardly it appears that France should have been expected to take the leadership of the movement. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, France was the intellectual center of Europe and held a pre-eminent position in university education. That the Renaissance did not begin in France may be attributed to the dominance of scholasticism. Scholars who might have taken the initiative in intellectual liberalism were too engrossed in logic and theology to break the bonds of medieval thought. 

In Italy, conditions were more favorable. Here the classical civilization of Rome had not entirely disappeared and on every hand the Italian people could see evidence of the ancient grandeur of Rome. 

Proximity to Constantinople contributed to a revived interest in classical Greek culture, while commerce with the East led to contacts with the highly developed Levantine civilization. Since Italy had not been feudalized to the same degree as France and other parts of Europe and was comparatively free from control by church or empire, political freedom in her cities gave opportunity for freedom of thought and inquiry and of individual expression, which was accentuated by the aesthetic and emotional characteristics of the 

Italian people.

It is customary to begin the history of the literary Renaissance with 

Dante (1265-1321), the greatest of Italian poets. Like so many other geniuses of the Renaissance, he was born in Florence. His family was of the lower nobility and, although little is known of his youth and education, it seems that he received a thorough classical training for his day. His life was colored especially by meeting in his impressionistic childhood with Beatrice, for whom he later developed an unrequited love. Neither the later marriage of Beatrice to a Florentine noble nor Dante's subsequent marriage to Gemma Donati could destroy his pure and Platonic devotion to her. This feeling was intensified after Beatrice's early death, although there is no evidence that she returned Dante's affection. Shortly after his marriage,

Dante entered Florentine politics which, because of factional strife, promised anything but a peaceful life. At this time, the Guelph party in Florence was divided into the rival factions of "Whites" and "Blacks." The Whites, or moderates, were anti-papal and leaned toward reconciliation with the Ghibellines, who had been driven from the city; the Blacks, an extreme papal party, opposed such a

reconciliation. Dante allied himself with the Whites. Since the papacy was involved, this local squabble soon took on an international aspect. 

When the Blacks came into power in 1302, Dante, with other members of the Whites, was banished from the city. Never again did he visit Florence; he spent the remainder of his life despairing of return to his beloved home. His exile made him moody and remorseful, a mental state which is reflected in his works. 

While dates and sequences of Dante's works are a matter of conjecture, his New Life (La Vita Nuova) was probably the earliest. 

This is the story of how the poet's life was transformed by his love for Beatrice a story told so feelingly that it is difficult to distinguish her real personality from the author's ideal of beauty and virtue of which she was his symbol. Dante traces the development of this love from his initial infatuation in which her physical characteristics predominated; then, assuming a broader scope, Beatrice is progressively idealized until her human qualities tend to vanish in a blaze of idealism. 

Dante's interest in medieval philosophy is shown in Il Convito (The Banquet), in which he attempts to make the philosophy of such scholastics as Thomas Aquinas and Albertus Magnus intelligible to the layman. In De Monarchia, he reveals his continued interest in politics by propounding the theory of a divinely intended international empire, resting on brotherhood and love and ruled by a universal emperor and pope, each free of the other in their respective temporal and spiritual spheres. 

Dante's greatest work, the Divine Comedy, is an epitome of medieval learning, giving the fullest play to the author's manifold talents. 

This encyclopedic work summarized the ideas of the Middle Ages and brought the period to a close. As a transitional work, its significance in the Renaissance is that it paved the way for new culture, and, above all, was written in the vernacular. In his earlier works, Dante toyed with the use of the vernacular; in the New Life he limited its use to love poetry, for which he felt the native tongue was a natural medium. Despite experimentation in the use of Italian, Dante believed it crude and unformed and hesitated to employ it on such a theme as the Divine Comedy. This masterpiece swayed the movement towards the fuller use of the vernacular; probably no work in the world, except the Bible and Shakespeare, has given rise to so large a literature. The contemporary recognition of the greatness of the work is shown by the discovery of more than five hundred contemporary manuscripts, and five commentaries or critical discussions appeared before Dante's death. About fifty years after the death of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

author, a public lectureship on the Divine Comedy was established in Florence, with Boccaccio as the first incumbent. 

The Divine Comedy is divided into three parts: Inferno, Purgatory, and Paradise. The theme of the work is allegorical. Dante dreams that he has wandered into a dusky forest, when the spirit of the pagan poet, Vergil, representing earthly wisdom, appears and offers to conduct him through Hell and Purgatory. The journey begins with a tour of the Inferno and Dante vividly describes and characterizes the tortures of the damned, who were brought to ruin because of their individual desires and passions. From Hell, Dante and Vergil ascend to Purgatory, where the scenes are similar to those of the Inferno, but the punishments are temporary. Imprisoned souls have freed themselves of human pettiness and are cheered because their salvation is inevitable. The pagan Vergil, symbolizing human reason and intellect, cannot lead Dante on the third and final stage of the journey through Paradise. Vergil can interpret such terrestrial experiences as sin and virtue, but the beauties of the celestial world must be unfolded by a purer, higher power. The Earthly Paradise, or 

Garden of Eden, at the summit of Purgatory, is the ultimate goal that men can attain through reason and virtue, unilluminated by grace. 

Here Dante has a vision of his beloved Beatrice, and, with her as his guide, ascends to the Celestial Paradise. In this region, souls have emancipated themselves from their earthly weaknesses. The poet and his guide begin a leisurely exploration of the universe, giving Dante an opportunity to disclose his encyclopedic knowledge of medieval culture. Finally, the explorers reach the empyrean where is 

God. Here dwell the souls of the blessed who have attained enduring and triumphant happiness through their possession of the supreme qualities of love.

Because he was not controlled by the ideas of the Middle Ages, Petrarch (1304-1374) is commonly called the first humanist. Although born at Arezzo, he was of Florentine parentage and spent his formative years at Avignon, where his father was employed at the papal court. Contact with the corruption of the church administration probably accounts for Petrarch's later anti-papal bias. His education was thoroughly Renaissance in character; he studied the best 

Latin authors and learned to appreciate and imitate their classical style. His father opposed this taste for literature, and, at his insistence, Petrarch began the study of the law, first at Montpellier in France and then at the great school at Bologna. Only paternal authority prevented him from abandoning this distasteful work and following his

natural inclination to become a classical scholar. The death of his father in 1326, however, removed this obstacle. Without adequate means of livelihood, he returned to Avignon and took orders to assure him freedom for study.

Petrarch's genius expressed itself naturally and easily in his native language. Although master of Italian lyric poetry, he felt that such works were ephemeral and possessed little literary value. His chief intellectual interest was absorbed in the revival of Latin and the attainment of skill in its use. In this language alone, he felt, would his monumental works enjoy immortality. In his later years, he became so enamoured of classical Latin writers that he disdained to write in any other language. The study of Latin became such an obsession that he wrote letters to Cicero and other dead classical authors, and in writing to friends he also used the purest Latin style. 

Petrarch's literary life was inspired by an idealistic love for Laura. 

Although she was married at the time of their first meeting, in 1327, he retained a Platonic devotion even after her death. It was she who inspired and is the subject of most of the imperishable sonnets in his Canzoniere. Previously, the sonnet as a form of poetical expression had not enjoyed great popularity. Petrarch improved the crude form and his success with this perfected medium contributed to its almost immediate success. His other notable work in the vernacular, the allegorical poem I Trionfi, is written in terza rima; its only remarkable passages are those referring to his love for Laura.

It was his Latin writings, however, which he and his contemporaries most highly prized. Passionate admiration for classical antiquity and fervent patriotism is shown in the Africa, an epic of the 

Second Punic War, centering in the deeds of Scipio Africanus. This work was deemed his masterpiece and contemporaries considered it the equal of Vergil's Aeneid which it faintly resembles. In recognition of the merit of the Africa, Petrarch was crowned laureate of the civilized world. Although the epic enjoyed contemporary fame, it was dominated too much by the imitative spirit of humanism and the ancient grandeur of Rome to enjoy lasting fame. Today, it is regarded merely as a literary curiosity. 

The versatility of Petrarch's humanistic genius is astonishing; it opened for Europe a new sphere of intellectual activity. The greatest master of Latin of his age, he also wished to learn Greek, but never mastered the language. He could approach the Iliad only through 

Boccaccio's crude Latin version. He was among the earliest Renaissance figures to recognize the value of manuscripts, ancient coins,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and archaeology as sources of classical knowledge. His enthusiastic quest for manuscripts probably gave the first incentive to collection and among his discoveries were such important works as Cicero's Familiar Letters. Emancipated from the medieval belief that the glorious phenomena of nature were manifestations of the Devil, he discovered a new world of emotions in the appreciations of their beauties. His difficult ascent of Mt. Ventoux, in France (1335) for the mere delight of the experience was perhaps the first example of its kind in centuries. His love of fame was his ruling passion; his learning and genius enabled him to enjoy the patronage of such men as 

Pope Clement VI, Emperor Charles IV, King Robert of Sicily, and the Visconti of Milan. His was such an exceptional position that he boasted princes had lived with him, not he with princes. 

Boccaccio (1313-1375) shares with Petrarch the honor of initiating the humanistic movement. In his youth, he gave up business and the study of law to devote himself almost entirely to literature. He became one of the small number of Italians of his time who could read the Greek authors in the original. Since his facility in the use of Latin was not the equal of that of Petrarch, he preferred to write in the vernacular. Although honored by contemporaries for his humanistic Latin works, posterity remembers him chiefly for his great vernacular work, the sensuous Decameron. The setting of this work is the terrible period of the Black Death of 1348. One hundred tales were represented to have been told to pass the time by a company of seven ladies and three young men who fled to a country villa to escape the devastations of the plague. The Decameron is a little world within itself; the author has drawn upon a multitude of sources — the French fabliaux, folklore, contemporary life, and the classics for all those fundamental situations which confront humanity in its most universal aspects. But whatever he borrowed he made his own through his mastery of style. The stories range from the highest pathos to the coarsest licentiousness. They lack a moral sense, an idealism which would have given them a more aesthetic proportion. The Renaissance spirit of this work is reflected in its break with medieval morality. Unlike the works of the Middle Ages, in the Decameron the scoundrels are not always punished, nor the virtuous rewarded; the cardinal sin is ignorance. Indecency is the greatest blot upon the Decameron, but to it the work undoubtedly owes an appreciable part of its fame. Such coarseness is not traceable to the temperament of the author, but to the corruption of the circle in which it was written. 

---

Machiavelli's (1469-1527) The Prince may be regarded as a literary characterization of the turbulent political life of Italy at the opening of the sixteenth century. Machiavelli was an exponent of a united Italy, free from foreign control; liberation, however, was consequent upon the establishment of a strong, absolute government under efficient leadership. In keeping with this idea, he wrote The 

Prince for the private perusal of the Medici family of Florence, the logical despots to put his ideas into practice. The author analyzes the methods to be employed by an ambitious man to rise to sovereign power; after obtaining his goal, "Let a prince, therefore, take the surest course he can to maintain his life and state: the means shall always be thought honorable." Such a government would be free from all idealistic elements through the subordination of religion and morality to political expediency. The wise ruler, however, would conceal his absolutism as much as possible. Not only is force a necessity in aiding the prince to retain his office, but it also serves as a tonic for the human race to preserve vitality. Idleness leads to disorder and disorder leads to anarchy; war will prevent idleness and serve as an outlet for suppressed energy. In advancing his views on the nature of principalities, the method of uniting them, and the qualities needed for a successful despot, Machiavelli did not deal with abstract principles and arguments, but drew his suggestions from historical and contemporary examples, particularly the career of Cesare 

Borgia (1476-1507). Machiavelli's drastic and inhuman theories merely reflected prevailing political conditions in Italy; as the antithesis of enlightened political science, they have become synonymous with tyranny, intrigue, and subterfuge.

During the fourteenth century, as has been noted, Latin constituted the basis of humanistic studies, although humanists believed that the real source of classic beauty was Greek literature. Knowledge of classical Greek had practically disappeared in the West, and adequate instruction during the early Renaissance period was precluded by the lack of teachers and suitable texts. Boccaccio, as the first 

Renaissance figure known to have made any progress in the study of Greek, was the precursor of the revival of this language in the West. But it was left for Manuel Chrysoloras (c. 1355-1415) to reintroduce Greek thought and learning in western Europe, and with him, the modern study of Greek may be said to have begun. A native of Constantinople, he made his earliest contact with Italy in 1393 as an envoy in the service of the Eastern Roman Emperor. About 1397, at the invitation of Poggio, Strozzi, and the Florentine magistrates,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

he accepted the newly established chair of Greek in the Studium, or University, of Florence. Students flocked to Florence to avail themselves of this opportunity. The need for a Greek grammar was supplied by his Erotemata, the earliest book of its kind. In addition to his work at Florence, Chrysoloras taught for a time at Pavia, Milan, Venice, and probably Rome. His work in Italy was continued by other Greek scholars, such as Bessarion and Trapezuntius, most of whom came between 1400 and 1453. The restoration of Greek in 

Italy was accomplished before the capture of Constantinople by the Turks in 1453, thus refuting the oft-repeated error that the revival of Greek was a result of the flight of scholars from Constantinople to Italy. The fall of the Eastern Roman Empire, however, did strengthen Hellenism in the West by augmenting the influx of teachers. A zealous search for literary remains increased the scanty store of classical works in the West and served to transplant this literature to a new and fruitful soil. In 1423, Aurispa, an Italian scholar, brought 238 volumes to Italy. By means of copying and editing, these newly discovered works became available to a wide circle of students.

Since humanism was dependent upon classicism, it was marked by a search for classical manuscripts. During the Middle Ages there was little or no incentive to seek out and copy ancient manuscripts, for the primary function of such works was to supplement religious dogma. The humanists, however, using manuscripts for their literary qualities, subjected these works to such close scrutiny that, in time, few new viewpoints and little or no inspiration could be secured from them. New authors, new manuscripts, and fresh points of view were needed if humanism was to progress. Few of the classical manuscripts found by the Italian humanists dated back to classical times; most of them were medieval copies. Since the church had preserved learning during the Middle Ages, it was natural that scholars began their quest for manuscripts in the cathedral and monastic libraries of Italy. The search soon spread beyond Italy and the fragmentary knowledge of classical civilization was slowly but surely rounded out by the discovery of manuscripts in almost every stage of preservation and mutilation.

Petrarch and Boccaccio were the earliest leaders in the search, but the greatest figure was Poggio (1380-1459). An Italian, he studied 

Latin under John of Ravenna and Greek under that great teacher, Chrysoloras. This classical background gave him an interest and his service as papal secretary gave him the opportunity to pursue his

quest for manuscripts. Secularization, not asceticism; humanism, not scholasticism, influenced Poggio. Although his work for the papacy covered the acrimonious years of the Great Schism,¹ it was devoted to the resuscitation of classical studies and not to theology. His is one of the best examples of the contrast between the humanistic and the scholastic mind; his interest was Latin manuscripts, and not popes, anti-popes, and church councils. Among his finds were the Institutes of Quintilian; seven orations of Cicero, including his Pro Caecina; the history of Ammianus Marcellinus; twelve plays of Plautus; the 

Dialogues and De Germania of Tacitus; parts of Petronius and Livy; 

the Silvae of Statius; a fragment of Suetonius, De Grammaticis et

Rhetoribus; and others. In all, he discovered at least sixty noteworthy manuscripts. 

The critical attitude of Italian humanism, as well as its secular aspects, was exemplified by Lorenzo Valla (c. 1406–1457), an Italian humanist, known as "the first critical history student." Through the use of internal criticism he exposed the Donation of Constantine as a forgery, thus attacking the claims of the papacy to temporal dominion. Using Greek texts of the Bible, he pointed out errors in the 

Vulgate and drew upon himself the censure of the church. His 

De Elegantiis Linguae Latinae, a scientific analysis of Latin grammar and style, for the first time placed the study of this language on a scientific basis. Contemporary scholars with their irregular and popular style were so provoked by the introduction of this standard style that they hurled invectives against the author; the fiercest aggressor was Poggio. Valla was a born controversialist, and so reckless were his utterances against the church that he escaped the anger of the papacy only through the intervention of his patron, King Alfonso of Naples. After the death of Valla's inveterate enemy, Pope Eugenius IV, he was welcomed to Rome by Nicholas V (1447-1455) and given a position as apostolic secretary. Valla's entrance into the papal curia has been characterized as "the triumph of humanism over orthodoxy and tradition," and indicates the growing humanistic spirit of the Renaissance popes. 

Giovanni Villani (c. 1275-1348), although a Florentine business man with interests more commercial than literary, is considered the most modern of medieval historians. His sole work, a History of 

Florence, consists of twelve books written in the vernacular, and is the cornerstone of the history of Florence during the Middle Ages. 

Like most medieval histories, this "Chronicle of the Universe" is 

1 Infra, pp. 426–28.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

encumbered with biblical and ancient history of which the author had no adequate knowledge. The material of his own times is of greater significance. Although Villani was more a chronicler than an historian, his work is differentiated from most medieval histories by inclusion of material on economic life, customs, and arts. 

During the formative years of Italian humanism, the movement was largely in the hands of scholars or literary dilettantes whose objective was that of individual appreciation or enjoyment. There was no place for a scholar by profession, but within a brief period such progress was made in popularizing learning that it came to have its practical use. The early hostility of the church to humanism closed that avenue and left the state as the only institution for its utilitarian application. Salutati (1331–1406), as the earliest example of the humanist in politics, used his office as chancellor of Florence to bring classical learning into the service of the state. The interminable, petty wars among the Italian states increased the necessity, and consequently, the prestige, of diplomacy. The greater part of the work of 

Salutati's office devolved into "literary diplomacy," the writing of innumerable notes and documents. In the preparation of these diplomatic papers, Salutati went beyond the actual political and administrative necessities and incorporated in them much brilliant classical knowledge. So effective were his diplomatic communications that contemporaries said that a letter by Salutati was worth a thousand men. After this correspondence had served its political purposes, the most interesting portions were published as literary masterpieces. In his varied humanistic activities he studied Greek under Chrysoloras, discovered several significant Latin manuscripts, and directed the copying of Petrarch's Africa.

A natural outgrowth of the spirit of humanism was the formation of " academies," or voluntary groups of littérateurs and scholars with common tastes. Such groups, formed around learned men and wealthy patrons, were dedicated to scholarly discussion and criticism, rather than to methodical study. Renaissance Italy proved to be an especially fertile field for this movement, with Florence taking the leadership. The Platonic Academy, founded in 1438 by Cosimo de' Medici, was the greatest of Florentine academies. This society enjoyed its greatest prestige under the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici (1449-1492), and in its history numbered among its members Marsillio Ficino, Pico della Mirandola, Machiavelli, and Michelangelo. As its name implies, the Platonic Academy was chiefly occupied with the study of Plato; its greatest influence, however, was not

the contributions of its individual members to humanism, but its service as a model for similar societies in Italy and elsewhere. The 

Academy of Rome, founded about 1460 by Julius Pomponius Laetus, devoted itself primarily to the study of Latin antiquities. Additional academies were to be found in Naples, Venice, and other Italian cities, and, beginning in the sixteenth century as a consequence of the French invasions, in the cities north of the Alps.

CHAPTER 31. 

The Artistic Renaissance and the Spread of the Renaissance

HE effect of humanism, which so thoroughly dominated Renaissance thought, was felt not only in literature, but in the development of art as well. Just as the art of the Greeks reflected the life and culture of the time, so that of the Middle Ages reflected contemporary thought with its narrow limitations. The church dominated medieval art, as it did almost every other aspect of society, and art became so inextricably bound with Christianity that it was essentially ecclesiastical in character and purpose. 

Through association with religion, moral teachings of art became all important. The conservatism of the church restricted free development and prevented the retention of the classical heritage of Greece and Rome. There was no interest in perfection of form; figures became stiff and lifeless; characterization and individuality were lost. 

Under the thraldom of mysticism and convention, medieval art exhibited a fixity in subject and depiction, with the efforts of previous artists regarded as sacrosanct. Existing representations of sacred figures became so conventionalized that definite types were formulated, such as the portrayal of the Virgin always dressed in blue and St. 

Peter carrying the keys. In addition to sacerdotalism, the inhibiting influence of medieval ignorance, superstition, and ascetic ideals prevented the study of anatomy. Man and nature were no longer studied, for interest in them was regarded as sinful. Lack of understanding of the principles of technique, perspective, foreshortening, and shading caused painting to degenerate into flat, lifeless portrayals. One of the greatest contributions of the Renaissance was the rediscovery of these principles by which the painter created the illusion of reality, of three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface. 

The artistic standards of the Renaissance marked an enormous advance from those of the Middle Ages. Creative power and technical

skill were revived and formalism was abandoned. Under the influence of humanism, art was emancipated from sacerdotalism and allied with secular interests. Secularization was accompanied by a renewed interest in man, nature, and life. Through the rediscovery of the Greek techniques of perspective, shading, facial expression, and emotional attitudes, significant developments were made possible in every field of the fine arts. Painting was the outstanding art of the 

Renaissance, for it is a more fluid and expressive medium than architecture and sculpture. Since painting is highly perishable, it retained fewer classical models than architecture or sculpture. For this reason, it was only slightly influenced by humanism except by some substitution of classical for religious subjects. Possessing no utilitarian restrictions and few antique traditions, Renaissance painting was permitted to reach a higher degree of perfection than any allied art. 

Another contribution of the Renaissance which immeasurably widened the field and clientele of art was the introduction of oil painting, which tradition has erroneously attributed to the two 

Flemish painters, the brothers Van Eyck (Hubert, c. 1366–1426), (Jan, c. 1385-1441). Actually, they perfected, not invented, the medium, which had long been known in Europe. The introduction of oils revolutionized painting and was a decided step in the secularization of art, for until this invention, murals provided the main field for the artist's efforts. Oil painting not only changed the artist's status, but enabled him to paint smaller and less expensive pictures and to secure private purchasers for his works.

During the Middle Ages, the great developments in architecture and sculpture had been made, not in Italy, but in northern Europe, with its magnificent Gothic cathedrals and civic buildings. During the fourteenth century, this leadership passed to Italy which offered many unique advantages of wealth and a leisure class to patronize and encourage the development of art. The municipalities and the church had been the patrons of Gothic art, which was essentially Christian in character; in the rich, populous cities of Italy, the wealthy bourgeoisie with their secular tastes became the chief patrons. There is considerable uncertainty about the beginning of the emancipation of art; it may be said to have begun with the first signs of reaction against medieval traditions. The early Renaissance in Italy was primarily an age of transition in which the older forms and traditions were gradually supplanted by classicism. 

The splendid achievements of the Renaissance in sculpture were heralded by the pioneer work of Niccola Pisano (c. 1225-C. 1278), a

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

sculptor and architect of Pisa. His first great work was a hexagonal marble pulpit in the Baptistery at Pisa, which he adorned with basreliefs representing scenes from the New Testament. In architectural design, the work is Italian Gothic; the sculptures, however, are mainly reproductions of the classic, particularly the rich carvings of the Roman sarcophagi. From the classical spirit of this work we may trace the development of the influence which was to break down medieval tradition. The most magnificent of his works is the great octagonal pulpit in the cathedral of Siena. Since Pisano's works were derivative, they had little influence upon his contemporaries other than his son, Giovanni, who developed and extended the Renaissance in sculpture into other parts of Italy.

In the works of Giotto (1276-1336), the return to nature definitely begins in Italian art. Little is known of his early life, but he was probably born near Florence. According to tradition, his precocious artistic genius attracted the attention of the famous artist, Cimabue, who gave him his earliest instruction. In an era still dominated by the stiff, symbolical representations of medieval art, he broke with the conventionalized treatment of the human figure, began to study nature, and to draw from living models. New ideals of grace and beauty characterize his works. His figures are animated and full of expression, although the faces lack individuality; the drapery is no longer stiff, but falls in natural folds, contributing to the form and expression of his subjects. Like his contemporaries, his works are marred by crudities of style, faulty composition, and a lack of knowledge of anatomy and perspective. Giotto's works are chiefly religious in character. Among the earliest that have been preserved are a series of frescoes in the church at Assisi, depicting scenes from the life of St. Francis. Giotto was an architect as well as a painter; his greatest architectural masterpiece was the bell tower of the cathedral of Florence. The English critic, John Ruskin, in his Seven Lamps of 

Architecture, said that power and beauty in architecture reached their highest standard "only in one building in the world, the Campanile of Giotto at Florence."

Fra Angelico (1387-1455), a Florentine religious painter, was another transitional artist. A Dominican friar, he led a holy and selfdenying life and so thoroughly incorporated this spirit in his works that he has been styled the "protagonist of pietistic painting." He treated nothing but sacred subjects. He attained the beauty of his effects by expressive faces, beauty of color, and arrangement; he was able to express the sacred affections upon the human countenance as could no other artist of his time. His early works are characterized

by a deficiency in technique, but in time he eliminated most of the crudities.

Lorenzo Ghiberti (1378–1455), by a direct appeal to nature, broke through the narrow conventions that hampered the free development of sculptural art. In 1401, despite his youth, he competed against the greatest artists of Italy in designing models for the north doors of the Baptistery of Florence. He was declared the winner and for twenty years labored on the doors which in perfection of form and finish, as well as beauty of ornamentation, are counted among the finest examples of Renaissance art. A skilled goldsmith, he treated each of the twenty-eight panels of the doors as a delicate picture. 

The twenty upper panels represent scenes from the life of Christ, while the lower eight are devoted to the Four Evangelists, and Four Fathers of the church. So greatly were these doors admired that the artist was commissioned, in 1424, to execute the eastern, or main portal. This second gate contains only ten panels, but on a larger scale than the first. The subjects are drawn from the Old Testament and show greater advance in style and freedom of treatment. These east portals were completed in 1452; a century later Michelangelo pronounced them so beautiful " that they might fittingly stand at the gates of Paradise." 

Another master of naturalism, Donatello (c. 1386-1466), was the most important Florentine sculptor of the early Renaissance. He, more than any other, may be considered the founder of modern sculpture, and was one of the most prolific sculptors of the Renaissance. 

At an early period he was influenced by Brunelleschi and the study of classical models. Contrary to prevailing practice, his statues were complete and independent in themselves and not adjunct to architectural ornamentation. He caught the finest spirit of the classical revival, but added to it his individual genius, touched with the expression of realism and nature. In revolt against the medieval ascetic influence, he portrayed the Saints not as old, emaciated men, but as tall, virile, muscular youths. Even in his formative period, a high degree of ability was reached in the marble statues of Saints Peter, Mark, and George for the church of Or San Michele, as well as in a number of statues for the cathedral of Florence. In collaboration with 

Michelozzo, he made several monuments, including the tomb of Pope John XXIII. His later works are permeated with classicism; the influence of antiquity is visible in the bronze “David,” the first statue of the Renaissance conceived in the round, independent of any architectural surroundings, as well as in a bronze equestrian statue of Gattamelata, the first of its kind since antiquity.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

A new medium for artistic expression, that of glazed terra cotta, was perfected and popularized by Lucca della Robbia (1400–1482), a member of a family distinguished in the annals of Florentine art. 

He was not the inventor of the process, but its application to fine sculptured work was original with him. In time, works made by his process became known as Della Robbia ware. Most of the works ascribed to Lucca are really those of other members of the family, the most famous of whom, Andrea della Robbia (1437-1528), a nephew, made much wider use of terra cotta and extended its use to architectural ornamentation. Another Florentine, Botticelli (14471510), was inspired by the literary influences of the Renaissance and drew the themes for many of his pictures from the neglected field of classical mythology. Included in this group are two of his most imaginative works, "Primavera " and "Birth of Venus."

The Italian artistic Renaissance reached its zenith in the period 

1450-1550, in the works of its three greatest masters, Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), Raphael (1483-1520), and Michelangelo 

(1475-1564). Leonardo da Vinci was the incarnate spirit of the 

Italian Renaissance. Although born at Vinci, many of his formative years were spent in the nearby city of Florence, where he served his artist's apprenticeship as a pupil of Andrea del Verrocchio, a skilled goldsmith, sculptor, and painter. Da Vinci's work was of sufficient merit to warrant the patronage of Lorenzo de' Medici, as well as that of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan. Under the joint commission of the duke and the monks of Santa Maria della Grazie, he painted on a wall of the refectory the famous “Last Supper," a masterpiece in the study of character. The Disciples, in groups of three, with Christ in their midst, are represented at one side of a table, their faces to the spectator. The scene depicts the moment when Christ has just said “One of you will betray me," and shows in the expressions of the Apostles the varied effects of the announcement. There is nothing to detract from the dramatic interest of the situation; the grouping and background are subordinated to the central figure of Christ, from whom the principal action emanates. Each group of three is harmoniously interlinked with the next, as well as to the central figure. The delineation of character is shown by a subtle mastery of pantomime and in the faces the ineffable sadness of Christ, the villainy of Judas, the wrath of Peter. The expressive hands alone might tell the story if the faces were missing. Owing to the dampness of the walls and the artist's experimentation in the method of tempera painting, the picture soon showed signs of deterioration. 

---

More permanent, but also somewhat subjected to the ravages of time, is Da Vinci's second masterpiece, the "Mona Lisa" ("La 

Gioconda"), probably the most celebrated portrait in the world.

The subject was the Neapolitan wife of a Florentine named Francesco del Giocondo. It is said that the artist worked on the portrait at intervals for four years, with music at the sittings to retain the subtle, enigmatic smile of the subject which is the greatest distinguishing feature of the picture. The mysterious expression of countenance, the wonderful hands, and the weird background cast an irresistible impression and draw forth endless critical comments. 

Although Da Vinci's artistic career was repeatedly interrupted by other interests — engineering, architecture, mathematics, and nature - he painted many famous works, including the "Battle of Anghiari," a pictorial interpretation of his trenchant characterization of war as "bestial frenzy "; the "Madonna of the Rocks"; the "Virgin and St. Anne"; and the "Adoration of the Magi." His work as a sculptor must be judged from contemporary accounts; his greatest work, a huge equestrian statue designed and modeled for the House of Sforza, was never executed in bronze and the model was destroyed during the French invasions of Italy. Da Vinci was only slightly influenced by antiquity, for his work was founded upon patient and thorough study of nature. He excelled in form and technique, was first to attain mastery of anatomy, and was the first great master of light and shade. But it was his portrayal of emotion, with his command over the subtleties of expression, that made unique the quality of his art.

Raphael, a native of Umbria, was the epitome of later Renaissance art. From his father, a painter of some merit, he received his first instruction, which he later perfected under the teachings of Perugino, a master of the Umbrian school. In 1504, Raphael removed to Florence, which was in artistic ferment over the rivalry between Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci, and offered the young artist unsurpassed opportunities for development. He was destined, however, to achieve his greatest success in Rome, becoming pre-eminently the painter of the power and prestige of the papacy in its glorious hour before the Lutheran Revolt. In 1508 he was commissioned by Pope 

Julius II to help decorate the Vatican, which became a veritable museum of his works, containing such famous paintings as the "Disputa," the "School of Athens," and the "Jurisprudence.” Leo X, successor to Julius, encouraged art and learning, and it was during his pontificate that Raphael painted the greatest of his pictures. Upon

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the death of Bramante in 1514, Leo appointed Raphael as the chief architect of St. Peter's, and afterwards made him inspector of the antiquities and monuments of Rome. Many of Raphael's pictures are obviously designed to support the claims and pretensions of the papacy; included in this group are the " Checking of Attila by Leo I," the "Donation of Constantine," and the "Coronation of Charlemagne." The works of the Roman period, when his life was drawing to a close, reveal strikingly the qualities which make him more nearly universal than any other artist since the Greeks. The greatest work in this period was the "Transfiguration." Death prevented Raphael from finishing this painting, which was completed by Giulio Romano.

Michelangelo, a Florentine, is regarded as the most prominent artist of the High Renaissance. Like his great contemporary, Da Vinci, he was a universal genius - a painter, sculptor, architect, engineer, inventor, and poet. By preference he was a sculptor, but at the imperious bidding of Pope Julius II he turned his genius to painting. For a time in his early artistic career he enjoyed, like Da Vinci, the favor of the eminent patron of art, Lorenzo de' Medici, and lived in the society of the great humanists of the age. Later, he left Florence and went to Rome. The greatest work of this Roman period is the "Madonna della Pietà," in St. Peter's Cathedral, a masterly group representing the Virgin Mary supporting the dead Christ on her knees. This work won him instant recognition as the greatest sculptor of his day. Upon return to Florence (1501), he was commissioned to carve a huge statue intended to signify the deliverance of Florence from the Medici; he hewed the naturalistic statue of a youthful, courageous “David," the last work of his early, or realistic, period.

The second period of his artistic development was characterized by unbridled imagination. With the election of Pope Julius II (1503) he was called to Rome to build a great mausoleum which the pope wished to finish within his own lifetime. Because of political upheavals and bitter quarrels with the pope, the monument was never completed. Of the forty projected statues for the tomb, only the majestic "Moses " and the "Fettered Slaves" were executed. The "Moses" is the greatest colossal statue in modern art, portraying 

Moses with wrath and indignation frozen on his face at the moment he sees the Israelites adoring the Golden Calf. At the command of the pope, the artist was forced to abandon work on the tomb to commence the stupendous task of decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. In four years (1508-1512) of resolute toil he covered the

vast vault with nine frescoes, each of which depicts an incident from the Old Testament. This work has been characterized as the most extraordinary piece of technical work ever accomplished, and it exerted a profound influence upon contemporary artistic standards. 

In an age disturbed by the invasions of Italy by Charles V, Michelangelo found time to work on the tombs of Giuliano and Lorenzo de' Medici. The Medici dukes are represented by allegorical rather than portrait statues, seated high above the sarcophagus. On the lid of the sarcophagus are two groups of colossal reclining figures, "Morning" and "Evening," and "Day" and "Night." This masterpiece illustrates Michelangelo's highest artistic principle of carefully subordinating everything to one central thought, in this case the pensive, eternal sorrow of the powers of heaven and earth lamenting the death of the Medici princes. Commissioned by Paul III to complete the decoration of the Sistine Chapel, he painted his greatest picture, the "Last Judgment." This was his last significant achievement, for in 1542 he was appointed architect of St. Peter's and for the remainder of his life devoted himself to this work. 

To Michelangelo, physical strength was the highest manifestation of beauty and perfection; his works are characterized by a predilection for taut attitudes, depicting emotional and muscular stress. In few of his works does he attain repose, as in the "Madonna and Child" for the tomb of Lorenzo the Magnificent. Although often in the employ of the church and a man of distinct religious feeling, his art was not submissive to theology. His aim was not to portray but to express. Few men did more than he to destroy the meaning of traditional Christian art and it is difficult to detect in his works the play of any distinct religious fervor.

The most complete expression of the secularization of Renaissance art is to be found in the works of the masters of the Venetian school: 

Titian, the Bellinis, Giorgione, and Tintoretto. In an age when the mainland was subjected to foreign invasion, civil war, and disorder, Venice, through her favorable geographical position and stable government, escaped most of these calamities. The merchants of Venice possessed the wealth and leisure to patronize the arts; painting came to reflect the luxurious and purely secular tastes of a bourgeois society. The technical excellence of other artists was the heritage of the Venetians; unlike the Florentines, who were chiefly interested in the scientific study of form, the Venetians expressed themselves in a liveliness and charm of color which has never been surpassed. 

Titian (1477-1576) was the greatest master and colorist of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Venetian school. His art was characterized by secularization, whether in such magnificent paintings as the "Assumption of the Virgin," or in portraits, in which he excelled. Portraits appealed to the egotism of the worldly Venetians; unlike such masters of the Florentine school as Leonardo da Vinci, Titian did not attempt to analyze or characterize, but to please and flatter. So successful was he that he numbered among his patrons the Emperor Charles V, Philip II of Spain, and the most prominent men of Venice. 

The development of art in northern Europe was stimulated by the devastating Hundred Years' War, which drove much artistic talent from France to the neighboring commercial towns of Flanders. The patronage of Spanish officials and wealthy Flemish merchants served to encourage the development of a characteristic Flemish school of art distinguished from the Italian school which had made itself felt even this far north. The artists of northern Europe were inspired, not by a mystical passion, but by a wholesome feeling for common things and the everyday world.

The free use of the commonplace is seen in the work of Rembrandt (1606–1669), who discarded classical history and mythology and the medieval legends as subjects for his paintings, preferring, instead, themes from the daily life of the Dutch people among whom he lived. Life, character, light and shade, were his inspiration. The tone of his sacred pictures is unmistakably Protestant, with stern scenes from the Old Testament. A prolific and versatile artist, his greatest works are the "Anatomical Lesson" and "Night Watch."

The spirit which the Counter Reformation brought into art is brilliantly interpreted in the works of Rubens (1577-1640), the most celebrated painter of the Flemish school. He was a master in the mechanical phases of art; his works, however, lack the grace, refinement, and profound imagination of the Italian masters. His religious paintings are fanciful and over-emphatic, as in the famous "Crucifixion" and the "Descent from the Cross.” 

Another member of the Flemish school, Van Dyck (1599–1641), through his portraits of Charles I and the royal children of England, raised portrait painting to a new height of excellence. 

The German Renaissance was comparatively poverty-stricken in artistic genius; its greatest masters, Albert Dürer (1471-1528) and

Hans Holbein (1497-1543), were inferior to the Italian masters who influenced them. Dürer is considered the greatest master of the German school; though a few of his portraits are excellent, he is chiefly known for his etchings, wood carvings, and engravings. No longer

was art a luxury to be enjoyed only by the rich, for by engraving, Europe was flooded with reproductions available to the masses. Holbein was an engraver and woodcutter of note and he enjoyed the patronage or friendship of such eminent figures as Erasmus and Luther. His greatest fame, however, was in the field of portraiture. 

Leaving the Continent during the early years of religious strife incident to the Protestant Revolt, he went to England, where he became court painter.

The influence of humanism was shown in the most formal way in architecture. Churches and public buildings had offered the medieval architect the best opportunity for exercising his talents. Gothic architecture, which was essentially an expression of Christianity, was regarded with undeserved contempt by Renaissance architects. Gothic was northern and Franco-German and never gained a strong foothold in Italy. This medieval type of architecture, with its fanciful and lofty lines, developed in the cold, bleak north, where lighting a building was an acute problem. This necessitated the evolution of the flying buttresses, ribbed vaulting, and pointed arches which became the distinguishing characteristics of Gothic. With the development of 

Renaissance architecture, emphasis was placed upon severely plain, horizontal lines, the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders of Greek architecture, and the gentler curves of the Romanesque. Gothic buildings were virtually skeletons of stone and offered little scope for interior artistic decoration other than stained or painted windows. The basilicas of the Renaissance, however, afforded ample space on their walls, which artists covered with immense frescoes. 

The revival of Greek and Roman architecture had its origin in Italy. The Roman tradition in architecture was one of formula and precedent. It is a singular fact that the magnificent ruins of ancient 

Rome had never stimulated local architects, but were regarded merely as quarries for building materials. Irreparable damage was done before humanism created a realization of the value of the ruins and initiated efforts to preserve them. In the age of classic revival, Italian architects went back to Greece and Rome for their models and inspiration, just as the humanists went back to Greek and Latin manuscripts. 

Such, then, was the impulse of the Renaissance in architecture, of which the harbinger was Filippo Brunelleschi (1377-1446). A Florentine metal worker by trade, he had failed in the competition for the bronze doors of the Baptistery of Florence, and in 1403 went to Rome with the express purpose of studying Roman antiquity. His

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Roman studies, however, did not fetter his imagination, for the famous dome with which he crowned the cathedral of his native city did not follow the Roman form. The raised dome became the most distinctive and magnificent characteristic of Renaissance architecture. 

Renaissance architecture culminated, both artistically and historically, in St. Peter's in Rome. Under the direction of Pope Julius 

II, Bramante, the chief architect, drew plans for a vast cathedral, which in size would surpass any ecclesiastical building in Christendom. Unfortunately, no continuous program of design was executed, and the plans of the church became a plaything for artistic humors. 

Michelangelo saved all that was possible of Bramante's original plan, and created out of the confusion something aesthetically satisfactory. 

Michelangelo's magnificent dome is a monumental piece of architectural genius; but St. Peter's, colossal in conception and poorly proportioned, does not compare artistically with the supreme beauty of such medieval cathedrals as Chartres, Rheims, and Notre Dame de 

Paris. 

The departure from the medieval artistic traditions is seen in the greater attention to purely secular architecture, which reached a high degree of artistic perfection and splendor in the luxurious palaces of the Florentine nobles. Such buildings offered an impressive contrast; their exteriors were built like fortresses, while the interiors were furnished with the greatest taste and luxury. An inner court provided light and air. These structures evolved naturally in an age of political turbulence and uncertainty, providing the owner not only with a home but with a refuge from attacks by mobs. The palaces were usually two or more stories in height. The first floor had strong stone walls with few doors or windows, which were heavily barred or shuttered. Since the upper floors were less subject to attack, the walls were thinner, the windows larger, and architectural ornamentations more profuse. Among the best examples of such buildings is the 

Medici-Riccardi Palace in Florence, built for Cosimo de' Medici by 

Michelozzo. 

SPREAD OF THE RENAISSANCE 

The development of humanism in Germany was influenced by, not dependent upon, Italian humanism, with its almost pagan devotion to classical learning and frank disregard of religion and morality. The
