Reformation has been characterized as the Teutonic Renaissance. But 

Germany's lack of culture and tradition provided a rather sterile soil for the seeds of the Renaissance. The universities became the seat of

413 humanism, limiting its influence chiefly to a select group of receptive scholars, instead of diffusing it through society as in Italy. While not indifferent to the classics, German scholars turned more and more to the study of early Christian writers and the origins of the church, until they were amazed at the contrast between the simplicity of the apostolic age and the ecclesiastical grandeur of their own times. Even before the beginning of the Renaissance in Germany, the idea of returning to the primitive simplicity of the church gave rise to a semimonastic order, the Brethren of the Common Life, with its houses where men might live in community without taking monastic vows. 

The underlying principle of the organization was the development of better moral and spiritual qualities. Such communities with their schools and libraries were established in the Low Countries and adjacent parts of Germany; the most famous was the community at Deventer. 

The founder of the "New Learning" in Germany was Rudolf 

Agricola (1443-1485), an eminent Dutch humanist, who, after a period of study in Italy, sought to make classicism an effective force in Germany. He is said to have founded the first chair of Greek in the north. Through his teachings at Heidelberg, he did much to diffuse a knowledge of Greek and the spirit of the Italian literary Renaissance. A fellow humanist, Johann Reuchlin (1455-1522), continued his pioneer work in Greek, but is better known for the introduction of the study of Hebrew. He had more than a mere philological interest in the study of this language. Imbued with the humanistic spirit, he used Hebrew as a key to the critical study of the Vulgate text of the Old Testament and to further his study of the Cabbala, an ancient system of Jewish theosophy, which he and other humanists, particularly Pico della Mirandola, regarded as helpful in reconciling ancient philosophy with Christian doctrine. In 1506 appeared Reuchlin's 

Hebrew grammar and lexicon, Rudimenta Hebraica, which he, with pardonable pride, declared to be the " first attempt to execute a grammar of the Hebrew tongue." in 

The greatest of the northern humanists was Erasmus (1466–1536), a native of Rotterdam. Through a long and studious life spent travel and study in the chief countries of Europe, he succeeded in suppressing every trace of nationalism and becoming a cosmopolitan figure in learned circles. After a few years as an Augustinian monk in the Netherlands, he studied at Paris, in England, and in Italy, acknowledged and honored as the greatest Latin and Greek scholar north of the Alps. Erasmus was not a great creative genius, but few

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

other men of letters have wielded so great an influence over their contemporaries. Unlike the Italian humanists, he studied the classics as an instrument of culture, not as something to worship and imitate. 

Erasmus's prestige was enhanced by his reforming and liberalizing activities in religion, in which he insinuated his opinions without seeming to attack. He desired to reform the church and put Christian teaching on a sound foundation through education and appeal to reason. In conformity with these tenets, he published his most important work, a New Testament in the original Greek, accompanied by a Latin translation, exposing many errors in the Vulgate. 

His gift for wit and pungent satire is shown in his Praise of Folly, in which he mildly rebukes the foibles of man. Folly is represented dressed with cap and bells and singing her praises, showing that to her are due the besetting evils of the age: the ambitions of kings, the corruption of the clergy, the ignorance of schoolmen, and the superstition and credulity of the masses and the lower clergy. Although written in the tone of playful banter, it was inspired by a serious purpose the necessity for ecclesiastical reform. The same spirit of seriousness clothed in banter is shown in his Adages and Colloquies, a series of dialogues on everyday topics of religion, society, and education. While favoring reform of the church, Erasmus opposed the 

Lutheran Revolt, seeing in its theological polemics a blighting influence on scholarship as great as that of medieval scholastics. 

Geographically and spiritually the connection between the Renaissance in Italy and France was very close. The French possessed the innate capacity to assimilate the spirit of humanism, which was spread throughout western Europe by their invasions of Italy. As early as 

1458 Gregory of Tifernas had taken advantage of the growing interest in the study of the classics to secure appointment as a teacher of Greek at the University of Paris. The king and the liberals encouraged humanism and it is probable that the Renaissance would have found in France even more favorable soil than in Italy if it had not been for such unfavorable events as the wars of Francis I and the outbreak of the Lutheran Revolt, which served to stifle the Renaissance in France. Italian humanism was liberal and anti-ecclesiastical; when transplanted to France, these characteristics met with the disapproval of the clergy, the reactionary aristocracy, and the faculty of the University of Paris, who could see in it only the seeds of disorder and unrest. Francis I and members of his luxurious court appreciated the value of the new learning and gave it their patronage. 

The king's sister, Marguerite, Duchess of Alençon and later Queen of

SPREAD OF THE RENAISSANCE 

415 Navarre, became the greatest patroness of learning of her day. 

Because of the unfavorable Continental political conditions, particularly the incessant wars with Charles V which necessitated the support of the papacy, the clergy, and the upper classes of France, Francis was forced to listen to their dictates and curtail his encouragement of humanism. This conservative reaction retarded, but did not suppress, the movement. French humanism merely rid itself of its anti-ecclesiastical characteristics. Gradually, however, the old ideas and methods were abandoned, and, during the reign of Louis XIV (1643-1715), French culture and learning reached such a peak that this period is called the "Golden Age" of French civilization. It set the model for the other countries of western Europe. 

In England, returning travelers from the Continent, especially from Italy, brought back ideas which influenced a small number of Renaissance spirits. Among this group was Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 13401400), the first great English poet, whose works were influenced by the Italian humanists, Petrarch and Boccaccio. Petrarch's sonnets vitally influenced the development of Chaucer's poetic style; from 

Boccaccio, he derived lessons of plot and construction which are strikingly revealed in the plan of the Canterbury Tales previously employed by Boccaccio in the Decameron. Chaucer, however, did not follow his Italian models slavishly, but rather used them in a broad, free way, adapting them to his own literary needs. 

After the close of the Hundred Years' War and the devastating 

Wars of the Roses, Henry VII (1485-1509) and the nobles were more engrossed in reconstructing the kingdom than in patronizing the new learning. The middle class and the scholars of Oxford furnished most of the zealous devotees of humanism, although a notable exception was Duke Humphrey of Gloucester (1391-1447). Not only did he aid many scholars, both English and foreign, but, in an age when books were rare, he collected a sizable library, which he later presented to Oxford University. Included in this collection were copies of the works of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio. 

Greek scholarship in England was founded through the efforts of 

William Grocyn (c. 1446-1519), Thomas Linacre (c. 1460-1524), and William Latimer (c. 1460-1545). Grocyn was educated at Oxford, but was attracted to Italy by the superior learning in the peninsula. He studied Greek under two eminent teachers, Politian and 

Chalcondyles; on his return to Oxford he gave lectures on Greek, being among the first, if not the first, publicly to teach this language at the university. Thomas Linacre also was a member of that bril-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

liant circle of Oxford scholars who popularized the new learning in England. He went to Italy to study Latin, Greek, natural philosophy, and medicine. He received the degree of doctor of medicine from the University of Padua. On his return to England, he did much to popularize the study of Greek by his lectures. Linacre, however, was more a scholar than a man of letters, and preferred to devote his time to his chosen field of medicine. He served for a time as tutor to Prince 

Arthur and later as physician to members of the royal family. His greatest contribution to medicine was the founding of the Royal College of Physicians. Since he was not a scientific investigator, he employed his classical attainments in the translation of scientific treatises, notably the medical works of Galen.

John Colet (c. 1467-1519) was the most important of the English humanists. A graduate of Oxford, he later studied Greek as well as canon and civil law in Italy. He was little interested in the subjects which engrossed Italian humanists. He preferred to devote his learning to the regeneration of religion. At Oxford, he gave several lectures on the Pauline Epistles, in which he abandoned the antiquated methods of the scholastics and their search for hidden and allegorical meanings of the Scriptures, substituting in their stead the humanistic and literary approach. His moral enthusiasm, ability, and eloquence led to his appointment to the high clerical office of Dean of St. Paul's 

Cathedral in London. Despite this position, he continued his attacks on the old order in the church and advocated many much-needed reforms. At his own expense he founded (c. 1512) St. Paul's School for 

Boys, which was modeled on the Renaissance schools of Italy, with the control vested in a lay instead of a clerical council. Unlike the curriculum of contemporary English schools, that of St. Paul's included humanistic studies; and it is considered the earliest school in 

England dedicated to the principles of the new learning. 

The first significant English contribution to Renaissance literature was Utopia, by Sir Thomas More (1478-1535). One of the greatest figures in English politics of his day, he was also a member of that small coterie of Oxford humanists. The Utopia, written in Latin in the form of a romance, is really a witty, satirical treatise on government and society, and was probably inspired by Plato's Republic. Part one of the book is a sweeping criticism of the social, political, and religious evils of the England of his day. Part two is a description of Utopia, an imaginary island supposed to have been discovered by one of the companions of Amerigo Vespucci. In this ideal commonwealth the wrongs and abuses of society were remedied; men lived together

SPREAD OF THE RENAISSANCE 

417 under ideal conditions and enjoyed the best gifts of life. All goods and property were owned and used in common; learning was provided by a national system of education; all able-bodied adults were required to work a stipulated number of hours each day; religious dissenters were tolerated; war was made "humane." In this ideal state, however, slavery and monarchy had their place, based on the central philosophy of the book under which the good of the individual was sacrificed for the common good of society.

CHAPTER 32 Fundamental Causes of the 

Protestant Revolt

HE most significant event of the sixteenth century was the Protestant Revolt. The old interpretation of this movement as a Reformation is inapplicable, for it was more a revolt than a reformation. The word reformation implies alteration of the church from within; the movement begun by Martin Luther was a schism which divided the church into two major groups, Catholic and Protestant. The actual reformation of the church was the Catholic or Counter Reformation initiated by the Council of Trent after the Protestant Revolt had pointed out the necessity for reform. 

In the general European disorder consequent upon the barbarian invasions, the Christian Church emerged as the greatest medieval contribution to civilization. Long before the opening of the sixteenth century, the work of establishing this institution throughout Europe virtually was accomplished. The medieval church must be thought of as a great international state, presided over by the pope, with its capital at Rome. This institution heeded no political boundaries, drawing its members from practically every nation of Europe. This universality is shown by the fact that it was possible for ecclesiastics to travel from one end of Christendom to the other with comparative ease and safety. Membership in the church was obligatory for everyone except a negligible number of Jews and Saracens. A person usually became a member in infancy and remained in the church until death. Conformity with the doctrines and practices of this institution was expected of all members; questioning of its authority and doctrine was punishable as heresy. While the constitution of the church remained fundamentally the same throughout the Middle Ages, the course of history shaped its evolution towards an absolute monarchy, virtually unchallenged throughout Europe.

The development of the church to its pre-eminent position rested

FUNDAMENTAL CAUSES OF  419 

upon its twofold function to civilization: it gave spiritual guidance to its members, and took an important part in their secular lives. Its social services permeated every stratum of medieval life. Many of the services performed by the state today devolved upon the church during the Middle Ages. The church preserved the spark of learning and controlled practically all means of education; it dispensed charity and poor relief; it rendered noble service in the establishment of hospitals and care of the sick; and its holy days and festivals constituted the basis of medieval social life. 

It is now apparent that the Protestant Revolt was the inevitable culmination of dissatisfaction against the church and would have come even if Martin Luther never had lived. Dissatisfaction was deeply rooted; Luther merely came at the psychological moment and supplied the articulate opposition needed for revolt. This desire for ecclesiastical reform was a protest not against the church but against the abuses of the church; not against the papacy as an institution, but against the abuse of this spiritual office; not against the clergy but against their worldliness and corruption. It was felt that ostentatious wealth and extravagance were deviations from the apostolic simplicity of the church; from time to time there was demand for a reversion to this early, simple state. 

Fundamental causes for dissatisfaction with the church were economic. Since the institution ministered to the spiritual needs of mankind, it could not directly exploit its services to raise revenue as could secular institutions. The financial support of the church had to come indirectly through such channels as gifts and tithes. The problem of finance became acute during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries as a consequence of the changing economic conditions in Europe. which were accentuated by the Commercial Revolution. An increase in the amount of specie in circulation led to a rise in prices. Since the basic revenues of the church were derived from endowments, its income was fixed and not responsive to fluctuation. Confronted with this problem of a stationary income and increased expenditures, the popes of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries recognized the imperative necessity for new sources of revenue. New papal taxes were levied, but the opposition to this increase of exactions was caused not only by the principle involved but also by the application of this principle.

There was little opposition to local payments to the church, since the people could see a direct connection between these payments and their expenditure. The most important tax in this classification was

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the tithe, or the payment of one-tenth of one's income to the church. 

The tithe was obligatory; its payment was required by the laws of the church enforced by the state. Usually this tax was apportioned equally among the local priest, the bishop of the diocese, and the poor. Another form of local payments was the fee for sacraments, always theoretically illegal but exacted in practice. Originally, people made voluntary contributions when the sacraments of baptism and marriage were performed. The next step was to make these fees practically obligatory - an evil tendency which the church could not stop.

The greatest dissatisfaction with ecclesiastical taxation was directed against the payments to the papacy exacted from the laity, or from the clergy who ultimately drew from the laity. These payments to the pope were opposed because they were sent to Rome and not locally expended. Not only did the people fail to see any relation between their money and the services rendered, but the rising spirit of nationalism engendered criticism of this steady flow of money from the homeland to a foreign country. There were a number of such taxes. Peter's Pence was an annual exaction of one penny from each household in Christendom paid to the pope. Annates, or first fruits, were the first year's revenue from an ecclesiastical benefice. 

Offerings of the devout in Jubilee years constituted a major source of papal revenue. The first significant Jubilee was proclaimed by Pope 

Boniface VIII for the year 1300; he intended that such celebrations should be observed only once in a hundred years, but by the fifteenth century the normal period was every twenty-five years. 

There was no objection to Jubilees on spiritual grounds, but during the later Renaissance period they tended to have a more mercenary than spiritual character. Christians began to perceive that the chief motive for declaring a Jubilee was the profits which accrued to the papacy through offerings by the pilgrims. The crusading tithes, generally known as Saladin Tithes, were instituted by Gregory VIII in the time of the Third Crusade and were payable by all Christians who did not actively participate in the crusade. Even after the crusading movement had passed, the papacy occasionally imposed upon the clergy a crusading tithe. Ostensibly such payments were to be used for the promotion of crusading ventures, but actually they were diverted by the pope to other purposes. A similar tendency was shown in the exactions of "tenths" from clerical convocations to defray extraordinary expenses of the papacy. Court fees were a lucrative source of income. The pope and cardinals constituted the

FUNDAMENTAL CAUSES OF  42 I 

highest court in Christendom, civil or clerical. If the litigants were wealthy, the cases were evoked to the papal court in Rome for adjudication; exorbitant court fees were charged; and during the Middle 

Ages the tendency was to summon more and more cases before this tribunal. In addition to its endowments, the papacy held as fiefs such national domains as England and Aragon, from which it collected tribute in addition to the usual papal exaction. 

Such abuses as simony, provisions, reservations, pluralism, dispensations, impropriations, evocations, and the sale of indulgences, which were partly economic and administrative in character, contributed to the mounting criticism. During the Middle Ages ecclesiastics and laymen generally recognized simony, the sale of church offices, as an administrative abuse. The evil was apparent to the spiritual authorities, but its practice was too deeply rooted to be eradicated. The practice of granting provisions, or papal appointments to vacant ecclesiastical benefices, was condemned as an interference with local administrative prerogatives; it was contrary to the growing spirit of nationalism. This abuse was particularly prevalent in England, where most of the papal appointees were Italians. The practice of such appointees remaining at home and administering their benefices through a substitute violated the right of local control over the clergy and ran counter to nationalism. Closely allied to provisions were reservations, or promises of appointments to office when vacancies should occur. A reservation fee was collected from every prospective appointee, only one of whom could hope to secure the benefice. But the ambitious person did not need to be satisfied with one office. Too often the income from a minor ecclesiastical benefice would not support the holder; consequently, the practice of holding several offices, or pluralism, developed. This abuse persisted, despite legislation against it by the church. Italians, who enjoyed the greatest favors of the papacy, often held dozens of offices which they administered through their agents. An abuse which primarily affected the upper classes, but contributed little to the prestige of the Holy See, was the system of dispensations. This practice of setting aside or relaxing the strict letter of the canon law grew out of the recognition of the universality of the church and the difficulty of the adequate observance by all its members of any single code. Consequently, dispensations from fasting, vows of continence, etc., were granted in order to reconcile, so far as possible, the interests of the individual and society with spiritual needs. The growing complexity of society during the Renaissance led to an increased demand for dispensations;

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

after the Babylonian Captivity,¹ popes were not hesitant about selling dispensations to augment their revenues. By the practice known as impropriation, a great part of the income of the church was diverted from its original use. Portions of the incomes of benefices passed from the control and use of the secular clergy to the regular clergy for the maintenance of monastic houses; sometimes, a proprietor, instead of appropriating the revenue to the church, would turn it to his own use or even sell it. It was also common for ecclesiastics to grant tithes to laymen in return for services or in recognition of their protection. 

The sale of indulgences, while one of the fundamental causes of dissatisfaction with the church, is significant because it was also the immediate cause of the Protestant Revolt and will be discussed in that connection.

The growing nationalism in Europe accentuated this disaffection. 

Little reform of such abuses could be expected when the opposition was individual and sporadic, but with the appearance of unified states, the opposition became national and persistent. During the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, England was exploited by the papacy in much the same manner as Germany at a later date. The chief grievance of the English, and the one which led to controversy with the pope, was the abuse of provisions by filling ecclesiastical benefices with foreigners, particularly Italians. Significantly enough, the first major expression of national opposition in England synchronized with the Babylonian Captivity, during which period the English conditioned their attitude towards the papacy upon their own relations with France. In 1307, during the reign of Edward I, Parliament condemned some of the practices of the church; but the question of papal prerogatives came to a head during the reign of Edward III. In 1351, Parliament passed the Statute of Provisors, which made the recipient of a papal provision liable to imprisonment and forfeiture of the benefice. Two years later, the even more important Statute of Praemunire directly attacked the appellate jurisdiction of the Roman curia and forbade the sending of papal letters or legates into the country. This act, however, had little effect in discouraging these practices. 

In France, this evil was not so great as in England. The Pragmatic 

Sanction of Bourges (1438) freed the French Church from the more objectionable features of papal supervision. Since there was an administrative and not a theological dispute involved, this measure, too, became a dead letter after the abuses against which it was directed

423 were eliminated. The decree was repealed by Francis I, but by the 

Concordat of Bologna (1516), the French government secured an even greater control over the clergy. This nationalism of the church led to governmental opposition to the Protestant Revolt and the beginning of persecutions which drove some of the French reformers into submission, and others, like John Calvin, into exile. The effect of the Concordat of Bologna was to preserve French loyalty to the papacy. In Spain, the crown, in 1482, assumed the right to nominate to bishoprics and forbade appeals from the ecclesiastical courts to Rome. Spain, like France, remained loyal to the papacy during the Protestant Revolt. In Germany, the papal ascendency over the church was confirmed by the Concordat of Vienna in 1448. The prevalence of particularism and petty jealousy prevented development of national opposition, but early in the fifteenth century, the Imperial Diet passed resolutions against the abuse of papal prerogative. These protests were quietly ignored in Rome. In the remainder of Europe there was little evidence of opposition.

The rise of commercial and industrial interests increased the opposition to the exploitation of wealthy regions by Rome. The rising towns became the centers of antipapal feeling and objected to any external control, either ecclesiastical or secular. With such control usually went financial exploitations, for, in the changing economic order of Europe, the wealthy urban centers constituted the best source of revenue. The Italian towns are a good example of this opposition. Through a series of alliances and adroit maneuvers, these cities freed themselves of papal, imperial, and feudal control, and took the leadership in the industrial and commercial life of western Europe. In addition to exploitation, the economic life of the mercantile classes was restricted by the reduction of money as a consequence of the steady drain of precious metals to Rome. Here a great part of it was withdrawn from circulation, thus restricting the already insufficient monetary supply of Europe.

Decline of papal prestige was a fundamental cause of the revolt. 

In the centuries of political chaos following the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, the papacy, as the sole stabilizing institution in Europe, was forced to add temporal duties to its spiritual functions. 

In time, the pope was considered the supreme arbiter of Christendom in both spiritual and temporal matters. In addition to the Papal States, the pope held as fiefs the two European kingdoms of England and Aragon. These kingdoms were subservient to the Holy See when it was at the zenith of its power and nationalism was lacking; with the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

decline of the papacy and the rise of nationalism, both countries disregarded the claims of Rome. Encroachment of the church upon temporal matters could only lead to a lowering of papal prestige. 

Spiritual things must of necessity be higher than those of the world; participation by the popes in temporal intrigues and controversies lowered the prestige of their office in the eyes of the devout. Lay rulers felt that the pope should content himself with administering the duties of his spiritual office. 

Among the resulting clashes between lay rulers and the papacy, no conflicts were of greater significance than those between the popes and the emperors. Connected with ecclesiastical reform was the broader plan of wholly emancipating the church from secular control. Such a program was contingent upon the abolition of the practice of lay investiture. Emperor Henry IV (1056–1106) disregarded

Pope Gregory VII's decree prohibiting lay investiture. Political necessity forced his humiliating capitulation at Canossa, but Henry immediately renewed the struggle, emerging victorious over the papal pretensions. As a consequence of this struggle, the Empire suffered a great loss of prestige, which, however, was balanced by a corresponding decline of papal prestige and power. The struggle was renewed in the reign of Frederick II (1215-1250) by his attempt to reduce the pope to a state of dependency on imperial authority, an outgrowth of the conflict between papal and imperial policies in 

Italy. Vigorous resistance by Gregory IX and Innocent IV to Fred erick's pretensions led to a long and demoralizing struggle in which, on the whole, the emperor was beaten, but the papacy suffered irreparable damage to its prestige as a universal power. 

The conflict between spiritual and temporal power was held in abeyance until the pontificate of the next strong pope, Boniface VIII (1294-1303). His ideas of papal supremacy in ecclesiastical and civil matters were fully as exalted as those of his two great predecessors, Gregory VII and Innocent III. These medieval ideas brought him into conflict with the rulers of two rising nationalistic states, Philip IV of France and Edward I of England. Both rulers were taxing the clergy to secure revenue to carry on war against each other. Boniface issued the bull Clericis Laicos, forbidding a lay authority to impose extraordinary taxes upon the clergy without the consent of the pope. Philip retaliated with a decree forbidding the exportation of gold or silver, the effect of which was to cut off French contributions to Rome. Edward declared that if the clergy would not contribute to support the state, the state could afford them no protec-

FUNDAMENTAL CAUSES OF  

425 tion. Boniface protested and explained that he never meant to forbid voluntary gifts from the clergy or contributions necessary for the defense of the kingdom. Continued oppression of the clergy and diversion of ecclesiastical revenue reopened the struggle; Philip called the first Estates-General, in 1302, to secure national support. Boniface issued the bull Unam Sanctam, proclaiming the subjection of temporal power to the spiritual. The issuance of this decree marks the zenith of papal pretensions; its impotence, the decline of papal and and the ascendency of lay authority in the temporal sphere. 

The death of Boniface VIII in 1303 was followed by the brief pontificate of Benedict XI (1303-1304). By his lenient policy Benedict restored peace with the French court, without compromising the dignity of the papacy or the memory of his predecessor. Owing to the French and Italian factions among the cardinals, it required the conclave almost a year to elect a successor, Clement V. Clement was a Frenchman by birth, but as Archbishop of Bordeaux he was actually an English subject. His pontificate marks the beginning of a new era in the history of the papacy with the decline of spiritual and the ascendency of temporal authority. This transition was accentuated by the Babylonian Captivity of the church (1305–1377). 

Clement refused to go to Rome for his coronation, preferring to be crowned at Lyons; subservient to the wishes of Philip IV, he remained in France throughout his pontificate. From 1305 to 1309 he resided at various places, but he finally took up permanent residence at Avignon, a possession of the papacy on the border of France. 

Actually, the influence of the French kings over the Avignon popes was very slight, but it was grossly exaggerated by disgruntled Italians. Few of the popes displayed compromising friendliness to the French rulers; such pontiffs as John XXII held the dignity and prestige of their office as high as any of their predecessors. 

The Babylonian Captivity scandalized Christendom and contributed to a reduction of the moral influence of the church. While the papacy at Rome had not been free from criticism, the court at Avignon was attacked on political, social, economic, and moral grounds. 

Most Christians felt that Rome was the only rightful place for the head of the church. The papacy lost, to an appreciable degree, respect and support, as a consequence of the belief that it had become merely a convenient tool for French statecraft. The Germans had bitter quar- rels with the Holy See; and England, feeling that the papacy favored 

France in the Hundred Years' War, curtailed her ecclesiastical payments. The absence of the restraining influence of the pope in

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Rome fostered lawlessness and license and the city lapsed into virtual anarchy. The turmoil was accentuated by the economic conditions incident to the loss of papal income; chaos in Italy was a contributing factor in the decision of the pope to remain in France where order prevailed. Religion suffered as immoral and worldly conditions permeated both regular and secular clergy. The dissatisfaction with the French papacy, however, was largely economic. Later popes were not content with the simple dwellings at Avignon and decided to build a pretentious capital. This building program and the establishment of an immense bureaucracy necessitated larger financial levies upon Christendom, which was in no condition to bear them. 

In this period, Europe was swept by the devastating Black Death; 

France and England were embroiled in the Hundred Years' War. 

Any increase of papal taxation in this period of economic maladjustment could only lead to resentment.

Pressure continually was brought to bear to induce the pope to return to Rome. Premature movements, such as that of Cola di Rienzi, were foredoomed to failure. Finally St. Catherine of Siena initiated passionate agitation for the return of the papacy and even went to Avignon herself to plead with Gregory XI. Influenced by her entreaties and by the restoration of order in Rome, Gregory recognized the desirability of restoring the papacy to its traditional seat. He left 

Avignon in 1376 and entered Rome early in the following year, thus ending the Babylonian Captivity. 

Gregory died in 1378, and, in the election of a successor, the cardinals, intimidated by the demands of the Roman populace for an Italian pope, chose Urban VI. This election was canonically valid, but was declared void by the French cardinals because of the disorder which had prevailed. The real reason for opposition to Urban probably was the revelation of his indomitable character. Instead of playing the role expected of him and tacitly consenting to continuation of corruption and immorality, he initiated arbitrary reforms. 

The dissatisfied cardinals, therefore, assured of the protection of the French king, Charles V, declared Urban's election invalid and elected Robert of Geneva as Pope Clement VII. The Great Schism of the church (1378-1417) had begun. Since Urban's election subsequently was held valid, only his successors, and not those of the anti-pope Clement, have been regarded as legitimate popes. Clement settled in Avignon, while Urban remained in Rome. Europe divided in its support of the two claimants, the division being more political than spiritual in character. The greater number of the Italian and

FUNDAMENTAL CAUSES OF  427 

German states, England, Flanders, and Poland supported Urban.

France, Scotland, Spain, and the lesser nations in the orbit of France supported Clement.

Devout Christians urged the termination of the schism, since its injurious effects came at a time when waning papal prestige sorely needed bolstering. Secular power was strengthened by the concessions of the rival popes; spiritual power declined as Christians asked which pontiff was the rightful heir of St. Peter. Oppressive taxation was a consequence of curtailed revenues and the cost of maintaining two papal courts. It was clear that the schism could be ended if one or both popes would resign, or the church would act through a general council. With the refusal of the popes to resign, the only solution left was that most feared by the curial party - a church council. According to the conciliar theory, supreme authority resided not in the pope but in the collective episcopate. There were many difficulties and problems to be solved before such a council could be held. Who would call the council? Who should be summoned? Where would the council be held? How could decrees of the council be enforced? Since neither pope would call a council, the cardinals representing both factions finally invited all bishops to meet at Pisa in 1409. Both popes were ordered to attend; when they refused, the council deposed them and elected Alexander V. The refusal of the popes at Rome and Avignon to recognize their depositions or the election of the new encumbent thus not only failed to heal the schism but created a triple schism in its stead. 

A second council was inevitable, and, in this crisis, Emperor Sigismund intervened. Under his direction, a larger and more representative council was convoked at Constance in 1414. The work of this body was threefold: to heal the schism, to deal with heresy, and to consider general reform. The question of heresy was disposed of by the condemnation and burning of John Huss (1415). The council refused to take the responsibility of reforming the church, preferring to leave this task to the papacy, but it drew up a list of abuses which the pope was to consider. Turning to the problem of the schism, the council deposed and imprisoned John XXIII. Gregory XII resigned voluntarily, and Benedict XIII was deposed after the Spanish withdrew their support. In November, 1417, the Great Schism was ended by the election of Martin V. In some respects the Council of Constance was a success. It healed the schism, but its attempt to abate heresy by burning Huss was tragic; its failure to reform the abuses of the church was to have important repercussions a century later.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

All through the Middle Ages serious charges of immorality were preferred against the clergy and the failure to reform this abuse was a major cause of the Protestant Revolt. The root of the problem is traceable to churchmen whose training and moral fiber did not fit them for spiritual office, but who had entered the church merely because of its prestige and the advantages it offered. Many bishops and abbots deported themselves as secular rather than spiritual leaders, and were not content to deprive themselves of luxuries and sensory pleasures enjoyed while laymen. Some of the higher clergy rode to the hunt and even to war and lived in pretentious houses amid intemperance, gluttony, gambling, and other vices. The vow of celibacy commonly was violated; although this abuse was condemned by ecclesiastics and laymen alike, its existence permeated the church from curia to parish. Even marriage of the clergy was not unknown. 

In many instances the question of such marriages was settled by public opinion, with the demand that clergymen observe the laws or forfeit their benefices. The prestige of the regular clergy, in particular, suffered greatly from this abuse. These derelictions of the clergy were condemned by devout churchmen, who encouraged lay criticism in the futile hope that public opinion would serve to secure the observance of vows. Recognition of the crying need for reform is indicated by its prominence on the program of the church councils in the centuries before the Protestant Revolt. The councils recognized their impotence in handling this problem; their confession of failure clearly indicates the prevalence of immorality and the magnitude of the task of eradicating it.

The Protestant Revolt

PRECURSORS OF  

HE credulity with which the medieval mind regarded the teachings of the church began to dissolve under the influence of Renaissance thought. The failure of the crusades struck a vital blow to medieval dogmatism; crusaders had faced dangers and hardships with the blessings of the church and the promise of divine guidance. For the most part, the crusades had failed to attain their religious objectives; time after time, the Christian armies had been defeated by the infidels. When Emperor Frederick II led a successful crusade although he was under the ban of the church at the time, skepticism began to appear and devout Christians questioned the efficacy of clerical promises and the value of crusades. Intellectually, the Italian humanists began to break with medieval ecclesiasticism and many even avowed themselves to be pagans. Germany lacked the classical heritage of Italy and developed a humanism decidedly ecclesiastical in character. After penetrating into the origins of the 

Christian Church, however, German humanists realized the contrast between the simplicity of the apostolic age and conditions in the medieval church. This fresh knowledge was destined to lead to insistence for clerical reform. 

Another sign of the intellectual activity leading to the Renaissance was the spread of heresies. The first of these was that of the 

Waldenses, a sect founded about 1170 by Peter Waldo, a rich merchant of Lyons, as a reaction against the ostentatious wealth of the church and as a protest against the worldly and immoral lives of some of the clergy. Waldo advocated the return of apostolic simplicity, and in keeping with this tenet he sold his property and founded a lay evangelical movement to reform the clergy and to preach the Gospels freely in the vernacular. His followers, originally known as the "Poor Men of Lyons," went beyond the founder's doctrines and became gravely heretical. They believed that the Bible

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

was the all-sufficient guide for religious truth and that laymen had the inherent capacity to interpret the Scriptures, to preach, and even to be priests and administer the sacraments. They held that the bestowal of the sacraments by immoral priests was invalid. These teachings struck at the very foundations of the church and the movement was condemned by the Council of Venice in 1184. The heresy spread widely from France into other parts of western Europe. Spasmodic persecution diminished the number of adherents but the movement long persisted.

The other heresy, that of the Albigenses, first came into prominence early in the twelfth century and was of a far more dangerous character than that of the Waldenses. The Albigenses took their name from the city of Albi, in southern France, a region where they were especially numerous. The genetic connection of this sect with the Neo-Manichaeans of eastern Europe has been definitely established; the doctrines probably penetrated western Europe along the trade routes. The rise and spread of these heretical doctrines in southern France were favored by such circumstances as the wealth, leisure, and imagination of the inhabitants; their criticism of the corrupt, worldly Catholic clergy; and oriental doctrinal elements from Judaism and Mohammedanism. Our knowledge of their beliefs is tenuous, for it has come to us largely through the writings of embittered antagonists. The majority of the Albigenses were not initiated into the Catharist, or more ascetic group, and were free from the more austere religious obligations and moral prohibitions. 

The Albigenses taught the dualistic doctrines of Manichaeanism, that is, the co-existence of two mutually opposing, creative principles, one good, the other evil. The spiritual world emanated from the former; the body and all material things from the latter. Life was an eternal warfare between these contending forces, struggling for the soul of man; since sex was held to be the chief weapon of the evil spirit in this struggle, the "perfect" were to refrain from eating anything sexually propagated. They denied physical resurrection and the existence of Hell and Purgatory, for nothing could be worse than worldly existence. At death, the perfect soul assumed a celestial body, while a lost soul entered the body of some animal, preferably the one the individual most resembled in life. The Albigenses not only inveighed against clerical abuses and immorality. 

They rejected the Old Testament, infant baptism, and the sacraments of matrimony and the Holy Eucharist; they also denied the dogmas of the Trinity and the Resurrection of Christ.

The grave social and moral disorders caused by this fanaticism led Pope Innocent III to decide to extirpate it, and in 1209, he ordered the Cistercians to preach a crusade against the heretics. The Albigensian Crusade, however, was more political than religious in character; under the leadership of Simon de Montfort it was carried on with relentless barbarity, until in 1229 the struggle ended and the recusant Albigenses were handed over to the proselytizing Dominicans and the 

One of the leading figures in the rise of theological skepticism was 

William of Occam (c. 1280-1349), an English Franciscan monk.

Along with such extremists as Marsiglio of Padua, his attitude towards the church was one of protest. His advocacy of return to the primitive austerity of the church, denial of the right of the papacy to exercise temporal power or to interfere with lay rulers, and denunciation of the evils of the papacy brought down upon him ecclesiastical censure. He held that the sources of religious knowledge were authority, reason, and experience." His purpose was to show that human reason could prove neither the immortality of the soul nor the existence, unity, and infinity of God. These dogmas were known by revelation alone and not as scientific truth. For him, the authority of the teachings of the church was based essentially on the Bible; he held that "A Christian is not bound to believe, as necessary to salvation, anything which is neither contained in the Bible nor to be plainly and of necessity inferred from what is contained there." Although he rejected the rational demonstration of several fundamental truths of the church, he held firmly to these truths as a matter of faith, believing that they must be accepted in toto, either explicitly or implicitly because of one's Christian beliefs. His attitude towards the church of his day won for him the name of the "First Protestant,' and his teachings were destined to exercise a profound effect upon the doctrines of John Wyclif and Martin Luther. 29 

John Wyclif (c. 1320-1384), the "morning star of the Reformation," was one of the earliest heretics in England. He was educated at Oxford and later served there as a lecturer on divinity. Although acknowledged one of the ablest teachers in the university, particularly in philosophical disputations, his world-wide reputation came from his participation in the politico-religious conflicts of the period between Edward III and the pope relative to the tribute of the English nation as a fief of the papacy. Wyclif's ability as a theologian and his theories of the subjection of ecclesiastical property to the temporal sovereign called him to the attention of the anti-clerical, oli-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

garchic party, headed by John of Gaunt, the king's son. Owing to Edward's premature senility, John was virtual ruler of England, and, under his patronage, Wyclif enjoyed freedom to express his anti-papal beliefs. At first, his censures were directed against the political elements of the papal system, not against dogma. He worked zealously in the service of John to repress the power of the papacy in England, for the pope was then at Avignon, and France and England were embroiled in the Hundred Years' War. It was probably his political connection, rather than any heretical doctrinal beliefs, which led to his citation to appear before the Bishop of London, a declared opponent of John. Wyclif attended the convocation, escorted by powerful friends; the court was immediately broken up by a brawl between John and the bishop, and Wyclif was saved for the time from formal condemnation. In 1377, Pope Gregory XI issued a series of bulls against Wyclif because of his alleged heretical opinions. The execution of these decrees was delayed, and he was thus given time to publish his answer to the accusations, in which he emphasized individual rights and the need for separating religious and temporal powers. In 1378, he was summoned to Lambeth, but the session ended in an uproar when the crowd interposed in his behalf; he was dismissed with an injunction to refrain from preaching offensive doctrines. The beginning of the Great Schism in the same year contributed to his denunciation of the papacy. 

Between 1378 and his next citation for heretical beliefs in 1381, Wyclif began the translation of the Bible into English, a work that set the standards of English prose and gave the people access to the Scriptures in the vernacular. He began to send out his " poor priests,' who stressed preaching and individual reading of the Bible. The position which made him a true herald of the Reformation was his assertion that the individual conscience needed no priestly intermediary between it and God; the sacraments of the church, however desirable, were not essential to salvation. Wyclif was proclaimed a heretic; his books were condemned to be burned and many of his followers were imprisoned or forced to recant. But no sentence was passed upon him; he was allowed to retire unmolested to his rectory at 

Lutterworth. His doctrines were condemned by the Council of Constance, and in 1429, forty-four years after his death, his remains were dug up and burned as heretical, and the ashes were cast into the river Swift. 

After about 1387, Wyclif's followers, the Lollards, spasmodically continued his teachings. They grew strong in numbers and influence

in England and Scotland and defied persecution by church and state, although some Lollards who refused to recant were burned at the stake. Persecution continued even down to the Reformation, which in England owed something to the work of this sect. 

There was a close connection between the heretical movements in England and Bohemia, since Wyclif's doctrines cropped out in the work of John Huss (c. 1373-1415). Huss was rector of the University of Prague and of the Bethlehem chapel, the latter having been erected to supply the need for preaching in the vernacular. Influenced by the philosophical and theological teachings of Wyclif, he translated his Trialogus into Czech. In his early attacks on the clergy, Huss declaimed against spurious miracles such as the statue of the "Weeping Virgin," and the ecclesiastical greed which permitted such abuses. Bohemia was already deeply permeated by evangelical and heretical tendencies; it also began to seethe with political unrest as a consequence of German political domination and ecclesiastical control. Open revolt against clerical and political abuses was held in abeyance for the lack of national leadership, which was to be supplied by Huss. 

Huss was the real spiritual heir of Wyclif and it was his advocacy of the Englishman's doctrines which led to Huss's excommunication and the request for his attendance at the Council of Constance to defend his heretical views. His book De Ecclesia, based upon the doctrines of Wyclif, furnished most of the material for the charges against him. Huss and his co-religionist, Jerome of Prague, attended the council, under Emperor Sigismund's guarantee of safe conduct. 

This of course did not include immunity from punishment for Huss if his teachings were declared heretical, in which case he would be returned to Bohemia for punishment by the local authorities. After several examinations, in which Huss and Jerome refused to recant their beliefs, they were burned at the stake (1415). 

The Hussites vehemently condemned the treachery of the emperor which had caused the execution of their leader and initiated a revolutionary movement for the defense of their principles. This movement developed into the Hussite Wars after the death of King 

Wenceslaus of Bohemia in 1419 had brought his brother, the emperor, to the throne. The Hussites under the leadership of Ziska, and later of Procopius, repeatedly checked the joint efforts of the king and the pope to suppress them and even carried the war into Germany and Hungary. Among the Hussites there was lack of harmony; the radical Taborites alienated the moderate Utraquists, who favored

434. 

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

reconciliation with the Catholic Church. At the Council of Basel (1436) agreement was reached between the Catholics and Utraquists by which the latter were given exceptional privileges. The Taborites, thus weakened, were crushed, but remnants have survived as the 

Moravians, or Union of Brothers. 

The difficulty of reforming the church from within is well illustrated by the work of the Dominican friar, Savonarola (1452-1498). 

Mystical, given to dreams and visions, he claimed to be a special messenger of God with the gift of prophecy. He denounced the corruption and iniquity of the time, prophesying that God would send a scourge which would afflict, but also purify, the church. The invasion of Italy by Charles VIII of France, in 1494, was held to be the fulfillment of this prophecy. Inspired by Savonarola's fervent exhortations, the Florentines turned on the Medici, who were believed to be the chief cause of the city's wickedness, and drove the despots from the city. The friar assumed the leadership of the movement for political and moral regeneration, brought order out of chaos, and reorganized Florence as a republic. In this work he was enthusiastically supported. 

But a proposal to reform the corrupt Roman curia and clergy and an alliance between Florence and France which endangered the designs of Pope Alexander VI for advancing the interests of his family incurred papal displeasure and Savonarola was excommunicated in 1497. In the meantime, the sensuous Florentines were tiring of his political innovations and puritanism. A Franciscan friar challenged him to test his divine pretensions by an ordeal by fire. After all the arrangements were made, neither opponent appeared; when rain quenched the fire, the authorities declared that Heaven was against the test. The people were led to believe that Savonarola had refused the ordeal, and, infuriated, they cast him into prison. After a mock trial he and fellow victims were condemned to death "on account of the enormous crimes of which they had been convicted." They were hanged and their bodies burned.

THE LUTHERAN MOVEMENT 

Martin Luther, the leader of the Protestant Revolt, was born at 

Eisleben, Saxony, on November 10, 1483. His ancestry for many generations had been hard-working peasants; his father, Hans Luther, was a rugged, stern, irascible copper miner. Amid the privations of poverty and the severity of home and school life, Luther's boyhood was far from happy. By personal sacrifices his parents sent him to school at Magdeburg, and then to Eisenach.
