university career at eighteen, when he matriculated at the University of Erfurt, with a view to studying law in deference to his father's wishes. For that purpose he studied the liberal arts course, taking his bachelor's degree in 1502, and his master's degree in 1505. In the latter year, he ranked second among seventeen master candidates.

Although the university was permeated with humanism, Luther seems to have been rather indifferent to it. 

In 1505 the course of Luther's life was suddenly altered from the study of jurisprudence to theology. While returning to the university after a visit to his home, he was overtaken by a terrible storm. 

Terrified by an alarming lightning flash and thunderclap, he made a vow to St. Anna, the patron saint of copper miners, to become a monk if his life was spared - a characteristic medieval act which he at once regretted. This inner change was later attributed by Luther to the harshness and severity of his life at home and school, which he endeavored to escape by entering a monastery. These reminiscences, however, were necessarily colored by his later experiences and feelings. Despite the opposition of his family, he entered the 

Augustinian friary at Erfurt, two weeks after taking the vow to St. 

Anna. As a novice, he took his duties so seriously that a distinguished clerical career opened before him and in 1507 he was ordained. During the winter of 1508-1509 he taught philosophy and dialectics, and continued his theological studies towards the doctorate at the new University of Wittenberg. A business trip to Rome in the winter of 1510-1511 greatly inspired him, but also the worldliness of the church greatly shocked him. In later years, Luther held that this visit to Rome was a pivotal point in his spiritual life and theological thought. In 1511, he was again called to Wittenberg as a professor of theology, a position he held for the remainder of his life. 

These external incidents failed to touch the inner problems which agitated him as a monk and later caused his revolt against the church. 

Luther had entered the monastery tortured by the belief that he was doomed to Hell; he kept asking himself, "What can I do to win a gracious God?" Dissatisfied with uncertainty in his relations to God, he strove frantically to gain salvation through good works. Although he won the reputation of a saint, he was dissatisfied with his new life, since his first consideration was to save his soul. From the writings of St. Paul and St. Augustine he developed a doctrinal conviction of the means of salvation which differed widely from the Catholic belief that the church possessed the sole means of salvation through faith and good works. In Paul's Epistle to the Romans, he

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

found the verse (I, 17) "The just shall live by faith," from which he derived the basis of his belief in "justification by faith." 

Although Luther had repudiated the value of good works, up to about 1515 he had not openly broken with the doctrines of Catholicism. After that year, however, he began to shift and become more critical. Early evidence of this change was his opposition towards the hierarchy. His next step was to attack the church because it had become institutionalized and had ceased to function for the purpose for which it was organized. This was for him a period of spiritual growth; the discrepancy between his beliefs and the teachings of the church had not yet crystallized. It was to be in the heat of conflict, involving the question of good works, that Luther was to reach his full stature.

The pontificate of Leo X (1513-1521) was characterized by lavish expenditures for luxuries and the promotion of literature, science, and art. Within two years he dissipated the wealth left by his parsimonious predecessor, Julius II. To remedy his financial embarrassment, Leo was forced to doubtful expedients which could not fail to incite the opposition of devout Catholics. Offering no national opposition, Germany became a fruitful source of extraordinary revenue for the papacy. In 1515, Leo proclaimed an indulgence, ostensibly for the reconstruction of St. Peter's Cathedral, but in reality to enable Albert, Archbishop of Mainz and Cologne, to discharge his obligations to the papacy and to indemnify himself for expense incurred in securing his archbishoprics. Papal agents, the most famous of whom was the Dominican monk, Tetzel, preached the purchase of plenary indulgences. In their zeal for sales, the monks made unauthorized claims and promises which their critics considered misleading and as exercising an unwholesome moral and spiritual influence. 

Many people were opposed to this practice, but no effectual protest was made until on October 31, 1517, Luther posted his "Ninetyfive Theses" on the church door at Wittenberg. This act was simply an academic challenge to a disputation, not an open break with the church. Such disputations were common in the Middle Ages as a means of defining and clarifying truth and of training and quickening the faculties of debaters. Although the theses were written in Latin and were not intended for wide circulation, their publication produced a tremendous reverberation, for they were quickly translated into the vernacular and spread over Germany. Their popularity was due to the anti-papal note struck by Luther, rather than to abstruse theological contentions.

It was not the theory of indulgences, but the abuse of their sale, which Luther attacked. Indulgences were widely used during the 

Middle Ages as a supplement to the sacrament of penance, in which the guilt of sin is forgiven by God provided the sinner has contrition; the absolution by the priest after the sinner has confessed his transgressions is the evidence of that forgiveness. After absolution there still remain the temporal penalties for which divine justice requires satisfaction, either by good works here on earth or by a purifying punishment in Purgatory. The repentant sinner is offered a means of discharging these penalties in this life through an indulgence, which is a remission granted by the church of the punishment which the penitent would otherwise be forced to undergo in Purgatory. 

The principle on which indulgences are based is the teaching of the church that good works are essential for salvation. Since the saints have accomplished more good works than are necessary for their salvation, the superabundance of their works constitutes an inexhaustible "Treasure of Grace" which is administered by the pope as he deems advisable for the benefit of penitents lacking in good works. 

A draft drawn upon the "Treasure of Grace" by the pope, or his representative, the priest, is the indulgence. Since contrition for sin is a prerequisite for gaining them, indulgences are not a permission to commit sin, nor a pardon for contemplated sin. Indulgences are of several kinds, and usually require the saying of certain prayers or the performance of specified good works.

The pope ordered the general of the Augustinians to make Luther recant. But instead of recanting, the presumptuous friar continued his heretical outbursts and, with the assurance of support of the temporal princes, appealed from the pope to a general council. Unable any longer to dismiss the strife in Germany as a mere squabble of monks, the pontiff was moved to summon Luther to appear at Rome to answer for his heretical doctrines (1518). Luther did not wish to risk his safety by going to Rome; upon the intervention of his sovereign, the Elector of Saxony, the pope agreed that the papal authorities would treat with him in Germany. The church sent 

Charles von Miltiz as a special nuncio to Saxony to persuade Luther to keep quiet, or to cajole the elector to suppress him. In a meeting between von Miltiz and Luther, the latter was prevailed upon to make a qualified submission.

Still wider publicity was given to Luther's religious ideas by a debate on the general question of papal supremacy held at Leipzig in July, 1519, in which Luther and his colleague Carlstadt opposed the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

eminent Catholic theologian, John Eck. This disputation was an important factor in Luther's theological evolution. Beginning with the question of indulgences, the debate turned on the power of the pope to grant them and from that to the authority of the Holy See in general. After studying church history, Luther denied the papal claims that the office was evangelically instituted, declaring instead that its supremacy was a gradual historic process of usurpation about four centuries old. Further Luther denied that churches not in communion with Rome were for that reason schismatic. Eck skillfully forced the German friar to admit that some of these views resembled the heretical teachings of Wyclif and Huss, which had been condemned by the Council of Constance. Luther asserted that the council had erred, since many of the condemned heretical principles of Huss were in reality “most Christian and evangelic." Luther had previously condemned Huss, but was now convinced "that we are all Hussites, without knowing it." He thereby virtually admitted that both the pope and a council might err and was forced to appeal to the Bible, as interpreted by his own reason, as the sole rule of conduct and belief.

Having formulated a religion of private judgment as opposed to religion of authority, separation from the church was the only course open to Luther. He continued to develop his ideas by debates and writings and soon found many supporters among other reformers. 

He enlisted the support of the humanists who opposed clerical abuses and the old Aristotelian theological beliefs. However, Erasmus, the great humanist of the time, refused to support the revolt, believing that a direct attack on the church was valueless and feeling that time and man's intelligence would cure the evils. 

In 1520, in a series of three bold pamphlets, Luther vigorously attacked the church and set forth his program of reformation. In the first, An Address to the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, he declared against any especially instituted priestly order, and proclaimed the universal priesthood of man. He appealed to the German princes in the name of public order and prosperity to reform, by force if necessary, the abuses in the church and free their country from foreign control. In this work the doctrines of the church escaped practically unscathed, but in his second pamphlet, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, he assailed the papacy and the sacramental system and reduced the number of sacraments to three: baptism, penance, and a revised conception of the Lord's Supper. In the

third pamphlet, On the Freedom of a Christian Man, he expounded his fundamental doctrine of justification by faith; by asserting man's utter dependence on divine will, he held that the church was superfluous as a mediator between man and God.

Luther's opposition to the pope and the doctrines of the church was so critical that the Holy See abandoned negotiations and issued a bull condemning as heretical many of Luther's assertions. His works were ordered burned and he and his followers were threatened with the punishment of heretics unless they recanted within sixty days. 

The appointment of Dr. Eck to publish the bull in Germany was both unwise and imprudent, serving to prevent the exercise of untrammeled impartiality by either faction. Luther answered the challenge of the pope by burning the bull of excommunication, together with the decretals of canon law, before the gate of Wittenberg, amid great popular enthusiasm. The break between the reformer and the 

Catholic Church was now complete. 

As a denounced heretic, Luther could have been arrested by the temporal authorities and held for punishment. But his reckless, impulsive acts struck a responsive chord in the German princes and they prepared to defend him against the anger of Rome. In many cases the noblemen were not completely converted to the reformer's views, but only anxious that he should receive a fair hearing before he was condemned. The prevalence of particularism and the lack of effective imperial authority, after the death of Emperor Maximilian in January, 1519, contributed materially to the spread of Luther's beliefs. With the election of Charles V as emperor, Luther found a foe who realized the need of clerical reform, but who was opposed to any change in doctrine. Charles came to Germany in 1520 to receive the crown; although only twenty years of age at the time of his election, he recognized the responsibilities of his office as ruler of the greatest Christian empire. To settle the pressing political problems of the Empire, he called an imperial diet to meet at Worms in 1521. He was faced by an impending war with France and the more remote danger of the Turks. With these major external problems, it was essential that he relieve internal religious and political turmoil to prevent civil strife during his absence. By nature and training an orthodox Catholic, Charles recognized the need for reform in the church. 

He felt that religious harmony through Catholicism would aid him in governing his heterogeneous dominions; recognition of religious independence in Germany would only breed discord throughout his

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

empire and engender insistence for political independence as well. It was better to settle the religious problem, once and for all, with the other matters before the diet. 

Charles was convinced of Luther's guilt, but since the reformer was a national hero, the emperor dared not condemn him without trial. Luther received the imperial guarantee of safe conduct to and from the council; his friends tried to dissuade him from going, reminding him of the fate of John Huss. To their admonitions, Luther is said to have replied: "I would go even if there were as many devils there as tiles on the houseroofs." He enjoyed a triumphal progress to 

Worms, where he arrived on April 16. When questioned before the diet on the following day he had no opportunity to defend his beliefs. 

He was asked simply whether he acknowledged a pile of Latin and German books, which were laid before him and read by title, and whether he retracted their contents or persisted in his views. To the first question, he acknowledged the authorship of the writings; to the second, he requested a day for consideration because of the importance of the issue involved. On April 18 he pointed out to the diet that the subjects of his books varied. He defended the works on the evils of the church and papacy as irrefutable, but admitted that his argumentative writings were radical. These latter writings might be wrong, but they could not be retracted; they might.be overdrawn, but they were based on the word of Christ. He said that if he had erred, it should be proven by the Scriptures. When asked to recant, he refused in memorable words which are traditionally, though perhaps not quite accurately, reported: "Here I stand. I can not do otherwise. So help me God. Amen."

The diet refused to recognize his argument that the Scriptures sustained him; acting under pressure from the emperor, who hoped for papal assistance in the forthcoming French wars, it reluctantly passed the Edict of Worms, declaring Luther an outlaw and putting him under the ban of the Empire. Meanwhile, in accordance with the imperial promise, Luther had left Worms. He was seized, with his own connivance, by troops of the Elector Frederick and taken for safe keeping to the castle of Wartburg. Here he remained in disguise for nearly a year, with few of his friends even knowing what had become of him. This residence at Wartburg began the constructive period of his reforming career. In his treatise On Monastic Vows he declared vows to be wrong and invalid and urged monks and nuns to leave their cloisters. He also made his famous translation of the New Testament from the Greek text. This translation exerted a profound influ-

44I ence on the formation of the German language and provided the German people with a Bible in the vernacular. In later years, he added a translation of the Old Testament. 

In 1522, despite the danger which still threatened, Luther was forced to leave his retreat and return to Wittenberg. During his absence, his colleagues, Carlstadt, Melanchthon, and the Augustinian friar, Zwilling, had carried on his reforms, but had given them a more radical character than Luther desired. His doctrines were distorted and dishonored; monasteries were broken up, images destroyed, and even the University of Wittenberg was turned into a bake-shop by Carlstadt, who held all learning to be superfluous. At heart Luther was a conservative and had been forced into the position of a rebel against the church; he recognized the need for doctrinal and administrative changes, but knew that precipitant action was inexpedient. By means of effective sermons he easily subdued the radicals and restored the reform movement to its original purpose. Throughout the remainder of his life, he retained a bitter enmity towards radicals. He and Carlstadt drew apart; in his persecutions of the Anabaptists, Luther was as severe as the Catholics and did not hesitate to side with them in attempting to extirpate the Anabaptist sect root and branch. The spirit of unrest next cropped out in an uprising of the Rhenish Knights, an impoverished group, in economic, political, and moral decay as a result of the rapidly changing conditions in Germany. 

Their greatest enemies were the powerful landlords, the so-called Large Knights." The grievances of the petty knights were economic and political, but, hoping to profit from the prevailing religious ferment in Germany, they tied their movement to Lutheranism. Since 

Franz von Sickingen and Ulrich von Hutten, the leaders of the revolt, were friends of Luther, religious reform was unjustly accused of breeding anarchy. In 1522-1523 the revolt was easily suppressed by the disciplined and well-armed troops of the lay and ecclesiastical princes.

Despite momentary setbacks, the evangelical movement continued to spread and the Edict of Worms became a dead letter. A diet called by Pope Adrian VI, the successor of Leo X, at Nuremberg (1522) refused to enforce the edict, but demanded that a council should be called with the laity represented. A second diet, called by Clement VII at Nuremberg (1524), recognized the futility of stringent enforcement of the Edict of Worms and resolved that it should be locally enforced when possible.

By 1523, the spread and clarification of the reformed doctrines

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

were abetted by a bitter pamphlet war which had broken out between Lutherans and Catholics in north Germany. While most of these broadsides were partisan, they satisfied the desire of the people for knowledge in the days before the advent of newspapers and periodicals. Luther and his doctrines were the subjects of the majority of the pamphlets; in their glorification of the reformer, pamphleteers even drew a parallel between Luther's trial before Charles V and that of Christ before Pilate. Rabid, unsparingly critical, the opposing writers thoroughly aired the religious question, serving to popularize Lutheranism and crystallize the sentiment of north and central 

Germany in its support.

The most serious menace to the new cause, and one which alienated a great number of sympathizers, was the outbreak in 1524 of a great Peasants' Revolt in southern and western Germany. Although a class war, the insurrection was not confined to the peasants, but included the support of the lower classes of townsmen. Their common enemy was the wealthier class, which was subjecting the poorer classes to economic and social readjustment which bore heavily upon them. Such outbreaks had occurred before, but they had been comparatively mild and free from widespread fanaticism. While, like the grievances of the petty knights, the fundamental cause of the insurrection of 1524-1525 was economic, this was overlooked or ignored by numerous contemporaries who gladly used the revolt as proof of the revolutionary influence of Luther's teachings. In the light of the religious controversies of the time, in which the simple peasant was held up as an ideal figure, the teachings of Luther were interpreted by the downtrodden as the beginning of a new era of social and economic justice. The rebels put forth several programs, the most famous of which, the Twelve Articles, consisted of such reasonable demands as the right of each community to choose its own pastor, restitution of appropriated common lands, abolition of serfdom and excessive rents and services. Any of these articles not in conformity with the Scriptures were to be rejected. 

Meanwhile, the revolt was becoming more radical and bloody, with that ferocity characteristic of class warfare. In the absence of the imperial troops engaged in the wars of Charles V, the princes refused to temporize with the rebels and proceeded to crush the revolt. To the peasants' surprise Luther did not go forth to lead them, although in 1523 he had protested against the heartless injustices of the nobles. Luther was determined to keep clear of extremes; it was the danger of radicalism, of connecting the Lutheran movement with

economic and social questions, which caused him to refuse the rebels his support. He gave free reign to his hot temper and furiously urged the princes to slaughter the "thievish, murderous hordes" of peasants like mad dogs. Although the princes literally followed his advice, they needed little encouragement. The undisciplined, ill-armed peasants were no match for their adversaries; the encounters were more in the nature of massacres than battles. The rebel ranks soon broke up in a wild flight for safety. Probably 100,000 lost their lives in this hideous war.

The Lutheran cause suffered an irreparable blow from the Peasants' Revolt by the alienation of thousands of peasants who believed that Luther had betrayed them. On the other hand, many lukewarm Catholic and Protestant princes felt that Luther's teachings had inspired the rebellions, and cast their lot with the more conservative Catholic Church. As for social and economic results, the bonds of feudalism were drawn tighter around the peasants; serfdom lingered longer in Germany than in any other European country except Russia. Intellectually, the sterility of German culture during the latter half of the sixteenth century is largely attributable to the stifling of the visionary hopes of the Reformation. From this moment on, Luther and his cause deteriorated, suffering a marked decline in spiritual aims. Luther became a mere theologian, while his religious movement was characterized by increasing emphasis on dogmatism.

Popular insistence for a church council could no longer be ignored. 

In the absence of the emperor from Germany, the princes called a diet to meet at Spires in 1526 to make an interim settlement, pending the return of the emperor and the convocation of a general church council. In this, the First Diet of Spires, Catholics and Lutherans were treated on equal terms. The great question before the diet was again the enforcement of the Edict of Worms. In conjunction with the moderate Catholics, the Lutheran princes won a qualified recognition of their faith by an act, known as the "Recess of Spires," providing that "each prince should so conduct himself that he could answer for his behavior to God and the Emperor." In effect, this allowed the princes to choose between the two faiths and to determine the religion of their subjects, thus anticipating the principle of the Peace of Augsburg (1555). The emperor, seeing in the Lutheran revolt a powerful weapon which might be used with effect against the papacy, acquiesced in the promulgation of the "Recess."

By 1529, however, Charles had become reconciled with the pa-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

pacy; with the affairs of his empire in fair condition, he called a diet to meet at Spires in an attempt to settle the troublesome religious question. The Lutherans found themselves a discredited minority faced by a united, confident Catholic party. The religious decision of the previous diet was reversed, the Edict of Worms ordered enforced, and ecclesiastical property and jurisdiction held inviolate. 

This peremptory decision drew from the evangelical party a protest which held that the agreement at the diet of 1526 was in the nature of a treaty not to be abrogated without the consent of both parties. 

From this ringing protest the evangelical group became known as "Protestants," a name subsequently given to all those who left the 

Roman communion.

By 1529 Luther's greatest Protestant rival was the Swiss reformer, Zwingli. Growing hostility between the two theologians was weakening the Protestant cause. Adherents of the two factions recognized the advantage of uniting Luther and Zwingli against the common adversary. In an attempt to bring the factions together and effect a comprehensive evangelical union, Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, called a conference at his castle at Marburg (1529). From the first, the colloquy" was doomed to failure - the clash of personalities and the divergent theological and political theories constituted an insurmountable barrier. Fifteen articles were drawn up, fourteen of which were subscribed to by both Luther and Zwingli, but they could not agree on the fifteenth, which dealt with the Holy Eucharist. Both 

Luther and Zwingli repudiated the medieval doctrine of transubstantiation held by the Catholic Church. Luther maintained his doctrine of consubstantiation, that Christ was with and in the bread and wine, as fire is in hot iron. Zwingli conceived the sacrament to be not the efficacious sacrifice of Christ, but simply a memorial, a commemorative service, with the bread and wine of the communion mere symbols of the body and blood of Christ. Luther was too much a mystic, too much a medievalist, to agree with the humanist Zwingli, the most intellectually modern of all the reformers. Tolerance was not 

Luther's nature; he always assumed that he had a monopoly of truth and regarded opposition as incited by the Devil. To his iron. will, concession was the evidence of indifference or weakness. In addition to this religious impasse, Zwingli's political aims, inextricably interwoven with his theological plans, were anathema to Luther. With the latter's refusal to make concessions, the best opportunity of uniting the two faiths was lost.

The decision of the Second Diet of Spires was unsatisfactory to

both the emperor and the Protestants. In this taut moment, fraught with the danger of religious war, Charles called a diet to meet at the city of Augsburg (1530). He granted the Protestants a hearing and asked them to state their position in writing. The momentous task of drawing up this document was entrusted to Melanchthon, a close friend and colleague of Luther. As an outlaw, Luther did not attend the diet, but aided his followers with advice. Melanchthon was at heart half Catholic, and his gentle and conciliatory disposition was the antithesis of Luther's impulsiveness and hot temper. The moderate tenets of the "Confession of Augsburg " so appealed to the Lutherans that those tenets became and have remained to this day the fundamental creed of the Lutheran Church. 66 The emperor and the diet were dissatisfied with the Confession "; Protestants were given until April 15, 1531, to recant and return to the Catholic fold before coercive measures would be instituted. Threatened with the force of arms, the Protestants organized the League of Schmalkalden (1531) for mutual protection. Luther's avowed policy of abstaining from the use of force in the furtherance of his cause made him a very uncertain supporter of the league. Civil war was averted by the menace of a new Turkish invasion. Faced with this external danger, the emperor agreed to the Peace of Nuremberg (1532), which was to be a truce between the contending factions until the differences could be referred to a general council. Despite future strife and negotiations, the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 marked the success of the Lutheran Revolt. This victory was ensured by the incessant wars of Charles V, his continual absence from Germany, and the open connivance or aid of the German princes in religious innovations. Until the close of the wars of Charles against his old enemy, Francis I of France, in 1544, the history of the Lutheran movement is one tedious, drawn-out story of ineffective religious colloquies which merely preserved the peace of Europe by continuing the status quo of the Peace of Nuremberg. During this period, the new church was scandalized by the bigamy of its ablest political champion, Philip, Landgrave of Hesse. In The Babylonian Captivity of the Church Luther had asserted that polygamy was preferable to divorce, on the ground that the former was not forbidden by the Scriptures as was the latter. On December 10, 1539, a dispensation was signed by Luther and Melanchthon permitting Philip to marry a second wife. Foreseeing the harmful effect this sanction would have on his cause, Luther advised Philip to keep the matter secret and if necessary to "tell a good strong lie for the sake and good of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Christian Church." Soon the secret leaked out; while it created a revulsion of feeling against the Lutherans, its effects were only temporary.

Through the tireless energy of Luther, his writings, sermons and administration, his church was greatly strengthened, contributing to its entrenchment in northern Germany and the Scandinavian countries. The closing years of his life were characterized by virulent diatribes against any individual or sect so obstinate as to hold opinions which failed to conform to his own beliefs. Nevertheless, the years from 1525 to his death in 1546 were the happiest of his life. He symbolized his break with medieval asceticism in his Vindication of 

Married Life and his marriage to Catherine von Bora (1499–1552), a

Bernardine nun, who had renounced her religious vows as a result of Luther's teachings. This step alarmed some of his followers, like 

Melanchthon, and gave his enemies an opportunity to revile him as an apostate. His domestic life was happy; in his hospitable home he cared for many poor relatives and students. His wife, children, and fervent disciples assiduously recorded his daily conversations, and this Table Talk gives us an intimate glimpse of his thoughts and works during the closing years of his life.

The first general religious war in Germany - the Schmalkaldic War - broke out a few months after Luther's death in 1546. Charles, finally at peace with France and the Turks, prepared to suppress Lutheranism, although he maintained that he was waging war because of political insubordination. The strength of the Schmalkaldic 

League, an alliance of Lutheran princes and cities, was more apparent than real. With the opening of hostilities, the Protestant army, under the incompetent leadership of Philip of Hesse and John Frederick,

Elector of Saxony, proved no match for the imperial forces. Internal dissension among the Protestants and the defection of such leaders as Maurice of Saxony, cousin of the elector, strengthened the Catholic cause. Charles ended the war by crushing the Protestant forces at the battle of Mühlberg (April, 1547).

After the collapse of the Protestant cause, Charles was in position to dictate a religious settlement. He recognized the imperative necessity of moderation in handling the question. As a temporary expedient, until the Council of Trent should reconvene, the diet passed an ecclesiastical settlement, the Interim, which made a few concessions to the Protestants, while remaining essentially Catholic in character. 

As a result of his unwise political policies, Charles incurred the hostility of all classes of Germans. who came to regard him as a Spanish

interloper. As a result of the deft intrigues of unscrupulous Maurice of Saxony, who desired to expand his holdings, a coalition of disgruntled Protestants fomented an uprising to overthrow the emperor. 

The revolt was planned so carefully that Charles was taken unawares and was forced to flee beyond the Alps. While acknowledging the insurgents' victory, Charles refused to concede their demands for full recognition of Lutheranism. He empowered his brother, Ferdinand, to sign the Peace of Passau (1552), which again transferred the troublesome religious question to the princes. This peace was merely an interim until the convocation of the Diet of Augsburg in 1555. 

By the Peace of Augsburg, each prince was free to dictate the religion of his subjects; no form of Protestantism except Lutheranism was tolerated; all church property appropriated by the Protestants before 

1552 was to remain in their hands; Lutheran subjects of ecclesiastical states were not obliged to renounce their faith, but by the principle of " ecclesiastical reservation," any ecclesiastical prince on becoming a Protestant was to give up the property of his see. 

This peace, intended to settle the religious question of the Empire, contained the seeds of future strife; by refusing toleration of Protestant sects other than Lutherans, it laid the foundation for the 

Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).

CHAPTER 34 The Spread of the Protestant Revolt 

HE Protestant Revolt was more active in Switzerland, where it was largely an independent movement, than in any other country except Germany. During the Middle Ages, Switzerland formed a part of the Holy Roman Empire; the three Forest 

Cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, however, were opposed to Hapsburg rule, and in 1291 formed a "Perpetual League" for mutual defense against tyranny. The emperors tried vainly to make the region an integral part of the Empire. The two great victories of 

Morgarten (1315) and Sempach (1386) preserved Swiss freedom and added other rebellious cantons to the original league. Even the formidable armies of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, were routed, contributing to the ultimate annexation of Burgundy by Louis XI of 

France. Gradually the ties between Switzerland and the Empire were broken, and in 1499 Emperor Maximilian virtually renounced his rights of suzerainty. Thus, on the eve of the Reformation, Switzerland consisted of thirteen cantons, divided into Forest and City Cantons. The latter were the more progressive and became the stronghold of the reform movement. 

The position of the church in Switzerland had been weakened by its affinity to the Hapsburgs and by the presence of such heretical groups as the Waldenses. After 1500 all that was needed for a reform movement was a leader, who was found in Ulrich Zwingli (14841531), mentioned in a preceding chapter, the son of an influential Swiss burgher family. He had early contact with clerical abuses, for while still a child he secured a benefice in the church. He received a liberal education at the universities of Vienna and Basel, where he became a zealous supporter of humanism. His study of the Greek classics and the Bible was the source of his later discontent with the church and questioning of its authority. Ordained a priest in 1506, he received the curacy of Glarus, but because he espoused the papal cause during the Italian wars the opposing French faction forced his

THE SPREAD OF  

449 resignation (1519). He was transferred to Einsiedeln, the center of pilgrimages from Switzerland and south Germany to the miraculous shrine of the Blessed Virgin. In his sermons he denounced such pilgrimages as superstitious, attacked the granting of plenary indulgences to pilgrims, and favored reform of the immorality of the clergy. 

In 1519, while convalescing from the plague, he studied Luther's works and was probably influenced by them more than he subsequently admitted. Zwingli's opposition to the church was based, at first, largely on political grounds and directed against the practice of hiring Swiss mercenaries for the fratricidal wars into which the pope and temporal rulers were drawing his countrymen. In 1519 he attacked the sale of indulgences and succeeded in driving out Bernard Samson, a seller of indulgences. With growing boldness, Zwingli denied papal supremacy, proclaimed the Bible as the sole source of faith, and attacked fasting and the celibacy of the clergy. The papacy and the loyal Forest Cantons unsuccessfully tried to silence him. In 

1523, the Zurich council adopted the reformed doctrines set forth in his Sixty-seven Theses and declared the independence of the canton from the Catholic Church. As a result of this upheaval, the veneration of the saints, celibacy, good works, indulgences, pilgrimages, images, etc., were denied or abolished. The reform movement swept over the City Cantons, but received determined opposition from the Forest Cantons and such heretical groups as the Anabaptists. In ecclesiastical administration, Zwingli deviated sharply from the Lutheran monarchial government under the control of the lay princes and set up a republican form of government subject to local administration. Having secured dictatorial powers over the religious and civil life of the city, he established a theocracy. 

Zwingli and Luther were good friends during the early years of their respective reform movements. Neither sect was powerful enough to withstand determined coercive measures, if applied by temporal rulers at the direction of the papacy. With such a union of the rival faiths in mind, the Landgrave Philip of Hesse called the Marburg Conference in 1529. The common basis of the two sects was theological, but in the colloquy at Marburg, as told in Chapter 33, Luther was too much of a mystic to agree with humanistic Zwingli. 

Of the articles of faith submitted by Luther, agreement was reached on all but one - the sacrament of the Eucharist, or Holy Communion. 

Both reformers believed that the only value of this sacrament was the frame of mind in which it was taken. Zwingli thought of the Eucha-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

rist as a symbol; he had discarded the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation, but at the same time refused to accept Luther's doctrine of consubstantiation. When Luther refused to make any concessions, the conference broke up and the best opportunity of the sixteenth century to unite the two faiths was lost. 

Zwingli now gave his attention to the politico-religious problems which had split the Swiss Confederacy into two opposing factions. 

The Protestant (City) Cantons had formed the Christian Civic League, and looked to Francis I of France and the Protestant Germanic states for support; the Catholic (Forest) Cantons formed the 

Christian Union, supported by the Archduke Ferdinand of Austria. 

The Forest Cantons opposed the infiltration of Protestantism and Zwingli's social reforms, which, by condemning mercenary military service, threatened to end a major source of income. On the other hand, Zwingli objected to the pre-eminence of the Forest Cantons in the Common Bailiwicks, and their suppression of Protestantism. War between Zurich and the Christian Union was narrowly averted by the First Treaty of Kappel (1529), in which the Protestants emerged victorious owing to a Catholic concession which allowed the inhabitants of the Common Lands to choose between the rival faiths. In addition, the Christian Union was forced to renounce its alliance with Austria. The Protestants pressed their victory too far and only infuriated the Catholics. In 1531, civil war broke out, with each side accusing the other of breaking the truce. Zurich was attacked by 

Catholic mountaineers; failing to receive support from jealous Protestant cantons, Zwingli's army was routed and the reformer slain. 

By the Second Treaty of Kappel (1531) each canton was free to determine its own religion, thus foreshadowing the solution of the religious problem in Germany by the Peace of Augsburg. 

The sudden death of Zwingli left the Swiss Protestants temporarily leaderless, but the appearance of John Calvin (1509–1564) in Geneva, in 1536, gave the reformers a great theologian and an implacable foe of Catholicism. A Frenchman of middle-class parentage, Calvin was born at Noyon, Picardy. The income from a benefice, secured when only twelve years of age, enabled him to receive an excellent classical education. He first studied for the priesthood at Paris, but in 1528 his father advised him to abandon theology in favor of jurisprudence. 

Calvin reluctantly began first at Orleans and then at Bourges, the study of law, to which study he probably owed the logic and precision of his thought. After the death of his father in 1531, he was free to follow his personal inclinations.

THE SPREAD OF  

451 Calvin is said to have experienced a sudden conversion to Protestantism in 1529. He was never an ardent Catholic and he probably found little difficulty in going over to the reformed group in which his family were taking their stand. On his return to Paris, he was forced to flee when in 1534 Francis I began the persecution of heretics. He sought asylum in the Swiss city of Basel, which had already accepted Zwinglianism, and here, in 1536, he published his Institutes of the Christian Religion. This work was an exposition of the Protestant position, as contrasted with the Catholic, and was dedicated to Francis I with the purpose of influencing him to favor Protestantism. The Institutes became the basis of the Calvinistic creed. Calvin made God's omnipotent will the central fact of his new faith, reducing man to total insignificance. So sinful, helpless a creature could do nothing towards his salvation, either by the faith and good works of the Catholic Church, or the faith of the Lutherans. 

God alone could save through His merciful will; since He is allpowerful, He must know and have willed even before birth the souls that shall be saved or lost. This doctrine of election by grace, or predestination, was not original to Calvin, but became the greatest bulwark of his faith. Unlike Luther, who was ready to accept everything in the church which was not prohibited by the Scriptures, Calvin insisted that nothing should remain which was not expressly authorized by the Bible.

In 1536, while passing through Geneva, Calvin yielded to the exhortations of Guillaume Farel, a local French Protestant preacher, and established himself in that city. Geneva was in the throes of a political and religious revolution, in which the temporal authority of the Duke of Savoy was overthrown and the spiritual powers of the local Catholic bishop transferred into the hands of the civic council. Calvin was appointed chief pastor; since the inhabitants had renounced 

Catholicism largely because of political expediency and not spiritual conversion, his work of reform was a difficult one. Assisted by Farel he introduced a Protestant confession of faith, binding upon all citizens, and instituted a program of moral discipline. In 1538, after the first flush of enthusiasm had passed, Calvin's arbitrary rule aroused strong opposition and the reformers were expelled. Under the rule of the Libertine party, license and disorder increased so alarmingly that Calvin was recalled; he lived in Geneva for the remainder of his life. 

Now, at last, he had the opportunity to establish his plan of church government, a theocracy in which he was both religious and political dictator. A constitution was drawn up which recognized the Con-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

gregation as a governing body, but the supreme power was vested in the magistrate, who was Calvin. He aimed to direct all the affairs of the city and regulate the social and individual lives of the citizens. 

An executive organ, the Consistory, composed of six ministers and twelve elders, was empowered to arrest and bring to trial any person who failed to comply with local standards of conduct. As its jurisdiction was spiritual and not civil, the punishment was imposed by secular authorities. In conformity with Calvin's belief that conversion should lead to a more austere life, divorced from worldly pleasures, the government repressed all forms of amusement and regulated the morals and private lives of citizens by severe punishments for any deviations from the puritanical code. These measures quickly changed frivolous Geneva into a sober commonwealth. 

Calvin, the first Puritan, tolerated no contradiction of his views or regulations. He took full advantage of his emancipation from the papacy to formulate his beliefs but denied this freedom to his followers. Beliefs inimical to Calvinism were extirpated by fire. The most memorable of such cases, and the greatest blot upon Calvin's career, was the burning of the celebrated Spanish reformer, Michael Servetus, for assailing the doctrine of the Trinity. Servetus had fled to Geneva to escape Catholic persecution as a heretic at home; the 

Geneva theocracy seized, tried, and burned him as a heretic for opinions expressed not in Geneva but in Spain. With the burning of heretics and the expulsion of the defiant Libertine faction, Calvin's theocracy was firmly established. 

The popularity of Calvinistic doctrines and the establishment of schools in which the new theology was taught brought to Geneva many followers who on going forth diffused Calvinism throughout Protestant Europe. On the Continent, Calvinism was known as the 

Reformed Faith; in France, its followers were called Huguenots; in 

England, it became Puritanism; and in Scotland, it was styled Presbyterianism.

Scotland had been subjected to the abuses of the church during the Middle Ages, but the beginnings of the Scottish Reformation are to be traced to political rather than religious causes. Scotland was constantly torn by the rivalry of the powerful noble families, a condition. intensified by the death of James V in 1542. The crown passed to his infant daughter Mary, and for several years during which the country knew no powerful central authority, feudal lords strengthened their powers at the expense of the government. In general, the Catholic

THE SPREAD OF  

453 clergy, favoring law and order, supported the crown; the Protestants, hoping to strengthen their position, favored the nobles. 

In the beginning, the Scottish Reformation was Lutheran in form, and, by 1525, was so far advanced as to call for royal interference. 

Despite the energetic persecution initiated by Cardinal Beaton, head of the Catholic Church in Scotland, and the martyrdom of Patrick Hamilton, George Wishart, and other Protestant reformers, heretical doctrines continued to gain new adherents. The great leader of the 

Protestant movement in Scotland was John Knox (c. 1513-1572). 

His espousal of Protestant doctrines forced him to seek safety in England. There he held a chaplaincy under Edward VI and influenced the course of the Anglican Reformation in the liberal changes in the service and Prayer Book. The accession of Mary 

Tudor to the English throne in 1553 drove him and other Protestants to the Continent. While in Geneva, he made the acquaintance of 

Calvin, but Knox's theological views were moulded and confirmed rather than formulated by the teachings of the French reformer. 

Knox returned to Scotland in 1559 and, with the support of the reforming nobles, the "Lords of the Congregation," assumed the leadership of the Protestant movement. The death of the Queen 

Regent, Mary of Guise, in 1560, was advantageous to the Protestants. 

Aided by the Lords of the Congregation and the troops of Queen Elizabeth, Knox effected a political and religious revolution. A 

Parliament, composed of his friends, met in Edinburgh to settle the religious problem. It adopted the Calvinistic Confession of Faith, drawn up by Knox and his associates, which marked the consummation of the Scottish Reformation, and remained for two centuries the authorized Scottish creed. Papal supremacy and jurisdiction in 

Scotland were abolished, mass was forbidden, and the Protestant religion officially established. In the latter part of 1560, Knox's First 

Book of Discipline was adopted, embodying an essentially Presbyterian conception of the ministry, modeled upon Calvin's theory of church organization as nearly as the differences between a small citystate and an extensive kingdom permitted. For the most part, the 

Scottish reformers took the Calvinistic views regarding the relations between civil and ecclesiastical powers.

The return of Mary Queen of Scots from France (1561) was regarded with mistrust and open hostility by the Protestants, and brought vituperative attacks from Knox. Mary tacitly recognized the Protestant reforms, merely reserving for herself the right of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

private Catholic worship. For four years Scotland enjoyed a period of tranquility broken only by the rabid harangues of Knox and other ultra-Protestants. Mary soon discredited herself, however, by illadvised marriages. In 1565, she married her second cousin, Lord

Darnley; she came to despise him and formed an attachment with the 

Earl of Bothwell. In 1567, Darnley was murdered, probably by Bothwell at the instigation of the queen. Mary's subsequent marriage with the Earl alienated her subjects, who now drove her from the kingdom as a murderess. She was forced to seek safety at the court of Queen Elizabeth. After Mary's deposition, the Scots crowned her infant son as James VI, and the government was placed under the rule of a regency, headed by Mary's Protestant half-brother, the Earl of Moray. The regency was disturbed by religious agitation, but it placed Protestantism on a secure basis and decided the ecclesiastical future of Scotland.

Although England had largely escaped the religious strife characteristic of the Continent from the beginning of the Reformation, a growing number of Englishmen, orthodox and heretic alike, attacked the immorality and wealth of the clergy, useless monastic orders, and superstition. The ground was prepared by such precursors of the Anglican revolt as John Wyclif and his Lollards. Although criticism was common and widespread, the remedy for existing abuses favored by high ecclesiastics was that of the humanistic Oxford Reformers, John Colet and Sir Thomas More, who desired reform from within the church instead of revolution from without. Unlike those in Germany and Switzerland, the English revolt was gradual and conservative, the act of the monarch rather than of the people, the motives personal and political rather than religious. 

Although infiltration of Lutheranism was opposed by both the English Church and the state, the heretical doctrines gained adherents. Henry VIII (1509-1547), proud of his theological attainments, hastened to champion Catholicism in his Defense of the Seven Sacraments (1521), which won from the pope the title of "Defender of the Faith." This appellation has been retained by English sovereigns to this day, but applies to the Anglican and not the Catholic faith. 

It is doubtful that Henry would have broken with the papacy and initiated the English Reformation if it had not been for his desire for annulment of his marriage with Catherine of Aragon. He had married 

Catherine, the widow of his deceased brother Arthur, in 1509, after

Pope Julius II had granted a dispensation on the grounds that the marriage had never been consummated. Catherine bore Henry

THE SPREAD OF  

455 six children, all of whom had died except a delicate daughter, Mary. 

Wishing to leave a male heir, he decided, in 1527, to secure an annulment and marry Anne Boleyn, lady-in-waiting to the queen. Accordingly, he instructed his Lord Chancellor, Thomas Wolsey, to secure the annulment from Pope Clement VII on the grounds that the original dispensation was defective. In the meantime, the pope and his French ally, Francis I, had suffered reverses in their wars against Charles V, and Clement was virtually the prisoner of the emperor. 

The pope hesitated to weaken papal prestige by reversing the decision of a predecessor, or to incur the enmity of Charles, nephew of the English queen and cousin of the heiress Mary. Clement temporized, and delayed, and referred the matter to a legatine court of Cardinals Wolsey and Campeggio. When they failed to settle the case, it was revoked to the papal court. 

Incensed by this delay, Henry dismissed Wolsey for his failure and took matters into his own hands. The king now embarked upon a policy of clerical tyranny and intimidation and called the subservient Reform Parliament (1529-1536) to aid him. In 1531, he frightened the English clergy into paying a fine of £118,000 as a penalty for acknowledging Wolsey's legatine authority — a violation of the Statute of Praemunire- despite the fact that Henry had approved the appointment at the time. He wrung from the Convocation acknowledgment of his supremacy in the English Church, “so far as the law of Christ will allow." By the Act of Annates, Parliament empowered Henry to suspend payment of Peter's Pence and annates whenever he saw fit. In 1533, he married Anne Boleyn and appointed Thomas Cranmer as Archbishop of Canterbury, who now declared Henry's marriage with Catherine null and void and his mar riage with Anne legal. The Act of Appeals forbade appeal to Rome. 

The Act of Supremacy (1534) marked the formal breach between England and Rome by abolishing the pope's and establishing the king's supremacy in the Church of England. His arbitrary acts encountered some opposition; it was overcome with a ruthlessness in which such Catholics as Sir Thomas More and John Fisher were beheaded. Mainly on economic grounds, in the period 1536-1539,

Henry suppressed the monasteries and confiscated their property. In this he was supported by the nobility, who shared in the monastic spoils. The suppression of the monasteries and other unwise legislation were the immediate causes of the rebellion in northern England known as the "Pilgrimage of Grace," in 1536. But the fundamental cause was economic. It is significant that the rebels' banner bore a

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

plow alongside the religious symbols. The revolt was checked and its leaders executed, but conditions were not ameliorated. 

So far there had been no attack on the doctrines of the church, and 

Henry did not wish to go beyond political changes. He willingly adhered to the Catholic doctrine and refused to accept the teachings of the Protestant reformers, Luther, Zwingli, or Calvin. At this time, Englishmen were divided into three major religious groups: Catholics, who still recognized the pope as the supreme head of the church; the king's party, who rejected the authority of the pope but retained the Catholic faith; and the Protestants, who rejected papal authority and Catholic doctrine. Henry's chief advisers, particularly 

Archbishop Cranmer, had strong Protestant leanings. They secured some concessions, such as the authorization of the "Great Bible," founded upon the translations of Tyndale and Coverdale, which was placed in every parish church for the use of the laity. To supply doctrinal needs, the Ten Articles of Faith (1536) were published, recognizing the Bible and the three creeds as the sole authority of faith. 

Three of the sacraments were accepted, but indulgences and Purgatory were denied. Antipapal sentiment among the laity caused them to accept these changes without any great opposition, and even the clergy made no effectual protest to the break with Rome. The Ten 

Articles failed to fulfill the doctrinal needs; in 1539, they were superseded by the Six Articles, which were eminently Catholic. They upheld transubstantiation, communion in one kind, sacerdotal celibacy, inviolability of the vow of chastity, private mass, and auricular confession. Severe penalties were provided for denial of any part of this "bloody act," and Henry proceeded to behead "traitors" who recognized papal supremacy and to burn heretics who denied Catholic doctrine.

At the death of Henry in 1547 England was not Protestant. 

Henry had died in full theological belief of the Catholic doctrines; he had broken with the papacy only because it stood in his way of absolutism. The Church of England really did not become Protestant until the reign of Henry's son and successor, Edward VI (15471553). As Edward was only nine years of age at his accession, the kingdom was ruled by a council of regency, headed by the king's maternal uncle, the Duke of Somerset. Since Somerset, Archbishop

Cranmer, and a majority of the council leaned towards the reforming party, an era of Protestant innovation was inaugurated. The Six 

Articles were repealed, English was gradually substituted for Latin in the services, priests were allowed to marry, all images were re-

THE SPREAD OF  

457 moved from the churches, and the use of holy water was discontinued. In 1549 Cranmer's First Book of Common Prayer, the authoritative statement of the doctrinal beliefs of the Anglican Church, was adopted. After Somerset's deposition in 1549 his reforming policies were continued by his successors, but became more radical in character. By the Second Act of Uniformity (1552) an attempt was made to create a uniform Anglican Church. Transubstantiation was denied; the Second Book of Common Prayer, which was more Protestant in character, superseded the First Book of Common Prayer; and the 

Forty-two Articles of Faith presented a doctrine based on the Lutheran confession.

At the death of Edward in 1553 an unsuccessful attempt was made to continue the Protestant regime by crowning Lady Jane Grey, a cousin of Edward's, rather than the king's Catholic half-sister, Mary. 

Under Mary, there was a temporary reversion to Catholicism which at first met with favor. Parliament rescinded all ecclesiastical legislation of Edward's reign, thus restoring the Anglican Church to its status in Henry's reign, except as to monastic lands. The Catholic party was strengthened by Mary's marriage with the Spanish prince, Philip II, son of Charles V. The majority of Englishmen were still 

Catholics at heart, but many were alienated on nationalistic grounds by Mary's marriage. In addition to her religious views, Mary had personal as well as religious reasons for her antipathy to Protestantism. As the daughter of Catherine of Aragon, she would have regarded acceptance of the reformed faith as recognition of the validity of the annulment of her mother's marriage. The statutes against heresy were enforced, and her uncompromising suppression of 

Protestantism won for her the unenviable title of "Bloody Mary."

The number of Protestants executed during her reign amounted to about three hundred, an unusually large number for England. Among the martyrs were Archbishop Cranmer and Bishops Ridley and Latimer. 

The permanent establishment of Anglicanism came during the reign of Elizabeth (1558-1603). Free of the Protestant radicalism of

Edward and the Catholic radicalism of Mary, Elizabeth also opposed Calvinism as introduced by returning Marian exiles and attempted to stamp out ultra-Protestantism by persecution. She preferred to steer a middle course by returning to the system of her father but this proved impossible. The Catholics considered her illegitimate, and denied her claim to the throne in favor of Mary Queen of Scots. 

The Act of Supremacy of 1559 asserted independence of Rome and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

declared the sovereign supreme in civil and religious matters. The final act of Elizabeth's religious settlement was the adoption of the Thirty-nine Articles of Faith, which were distinctly Protestant, but were made studiously ambiguous to allow for future changes in interpretation. In the Established Church, the episcopal organization and ritual of Catholicism were retained, and the Act of Uniformity required that worship be in conformity with the new Book of 

Common Prayer. 

Scandinavia was the one considerable conquest made by Lutheranism outside Germany. As in England, the cause of the Protestant 

Revolt there was political and not religious. In 1397 the three Scandinavian countries, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, had been united by the Union of Kalmar under Queen Margaret of Denmark. Local administration was retained by the three countries, but since foreign affairs were in the control of the ruler of Denmark, Sweden and Norway became virtual dependencies of Denmark, a condition which caused considerable discontent. In 1521, a movement for political and economic independence resulted in the withdrawal of

Sweden from the Union; and the leader of the movement, Gustavus 

Vasa, was crowned king of Sweden in 1523.

With his kingdom ridden with debt and lacking adequate revenues, Gustavus sought a remedy in a program of clerical spoliation. 

His diversion of ecclesiastical revenues to secular use met with no appreciable lay disapproval, for the opulence and splendor of the Catholic Church had excited envy and hatred in the impoverished north. Gustavus encouraged the preaching of Protestant doctrines by such reformers as Olaus and Laurentius Petri, and Scandinavian students from the University of Wittenberg. In 1527, the Diet of 

Västerås sanctioned the assumption of supreme ecclesiastical powers by the king, and favored Lutheranism and disendowment. Gradually, Catholicism was displaced by the reformed faith, and, in 1593, at the Synod of Upsala, the Swedish Reformation was established by the adoption of the Confession of Augsburg, the acceptance of the Bible as the supreme authority of faith, and adoption of Luther's catechism as the foundation of religious teaching. 

In the same year that Sweden won her independence, Christian II was deposed as king of Denmark and succeeded by his uncle, Frederick I. The time was auspicious for a Protestant Revolt. Christian.

II, an opportunist, had favored Lutheranism as a means of increasing his power and weakening the nobility and clergy; in 1519 he imported a preacher of the reformed faith from Germany. Frederick I,

THE SPREAD OF  

459 although a secret believer in Protestantism, at his coronation in 1523, swore to uphold Catholicism. But wishing to make the church subservient to the state, he continued the policy of Christian in spreading Protestantism and encouraged the migration of Lutheran teachers from Germany. The desire to share in monastic spoils gained for him the support of the powerful nobles. Protestant propaganda was so effective that in 1527, at the Diet of Odense, toleration was granted to Lutherans, the clergy were permitted to marry, and the right of confirmation of all episcopal appointments was reserved to the king. 

Upon Frederick's death in 1533, an attempt by the Catholics to restore the exclusive domination of their faith and to prevent the accession of Christian III, an avowed Lutheran, was defeated. His accession sealed the fate of Catholicism in Norway and Sweden; he forced the bishops to forfeit their temporal and spiritual authority, and their property was transferred to the crown. In 1537 Lutheranism became the state religion.

CHAPTER 35 The Catholic Reformation 

AROM the outbreak of the Lutheran Revolt in 1521 until about 1550, the Catholic Church was on the defensive. After 1550, however, certain institutions began to arrest the progress of the Protestant movement, enabling Catholicism to survive and to regain some of its losses. The work of these institutions and the results, taken in the aggregate, constitute the Catholic or Counter Reformation. Of the many reasons for the partial recovery of the 

Catholic Church, the most significant were the intrinsic worth of the church and its institutions, the abolition of abuses by the Council of Trent, the organization of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits), the Inquisition, the Index of Prohibited Books, and improvements in papal administration.

The most continuous, if less spectacular, of these reasons was the intrinsic value of the ecclesiastical organization. Criticism of the corruption of the church had been common throughout the Middle Ages, but even the most vociferous and caustic critic of the church could not fail to recognize that such corruption was attributable to a small minority. In a limited medieval society, restricted by feudalism and the gild system, the church offered the only democratic opportunity for the advancement of gifted men, as shown by the careers of Hildebrand, Nicholas Brakspere, and others of lowly birth who attained the papacy or other high offices in the church. Contrary to the decentralizing, particularistic tendencies of the time, the medieval church evolved an excellent, efficient organization which enabled it to survive in an age of kaleidoscopic changes. In addition to its task of religious instruction, the church took an important part in secular affairs and assumed many functions which, in time, have devolved upon or have been assumed by temporal agencies. During the 

Middle Ages, clergymen were almost the only persons of education; consequently, they controlled education from the lowest to the highest stages, a function which was not assumed by civil authorities

until comparatively recent times. The church was distinguished for its charitable activities and the maintenance of such agencies for social service as hospitals, orphanages, and asylums.

The Catholic Reformation culminated in the Council of Trent, probably the greatest ecumenical council in the history of the church. For centuries advocates of reform had favored appeal to a general council as the natural remedy for abuses. Martin Luther had repeatedly asked for such a convocation, and the success of the Protestant Revolt made a council not only desirable but imperative. 

Emperor Charles V was soon won over to this idea of effecting a "reformation in head and members" in the hope of conciliating Protestants and restoring religious peace in the Empire. The pope recognized the need for reform, but regarded the convocation of a council with undisguised aversion. Proponents hoped that it would find some means of healing the rapidly widening breach between Catholics and Protestants and restoring the latter to the Catholic fold. 

In addition to the hostility between these two groups, there were bitter national rivalries, such as that between the Germans and Italians, and warfare between the two greatest Catholic sovereigns, Francis I of France and Emperor Charles V. The greatest obstacle, however, was the conciliar theory. At the councils of Constance and 

Basel, in the fifteenth century, the papacy had won a hard-fought battle over the theory that a council was superior to the Holy See. 

The issue was not definitely settled and the papacy preferred not to reopen it by calling a council and risk being forced to sanction unacceptable reforms and pretensions. A council would be influenced by the emperor, who had become almost omnipotent in European politics and who the pope feared might dictate the subjects of debate and usurp powers of the Holy See. In this eventuality the dormant conflict between church and state in the Catholic world would be reopened. By 1537, Pope Paul III recognized that a council was inevitable and that the church could be saved in no other way. 

As a result of the suspicion between pope and emperor and the national rivalry between Germans and Italians, a bitter struggle ensued over the choice of site for the projected council. German prelates, fearing that the council would be unduly influenced by the Italians, insisted on meeting in Germany. The pope favored an 

Italian city for the convocation. When the emperor supported the 

German contentions the pontiff finally consented to meet at Trent, in northeastern Italy, barely within the borders of the Empire but on the Italian side of the Alps.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The first attempt to open the council was made in 1542, but since there were not enough delegates present to make it representative, the pope seized the opportunity to prorogue it. The first general session opened in 1545 and lasted until 1547; other sessions were held in 

1551-1552 and 1562-1563. The tasks were threefold: first, the reform of ecclesiastical abuses - the basic task; second, healing of the Protestant schism by doctrinal decisions; and third, the discussion of a crusade against the Turks. Though the pope had made concessions as to a place of meeting, it was apparent that he was determined to keep the action of the council under his control. He was represented by three legates, who served as presidents of the body with complete control of the initiation of subjects for discussion. The vote was given only to bishops of the secular clergy and abbots of the regular clergy. The pope packed the membership with Italians; voting by head instead of by nationalities ensured perpetuation of Italian control. Protestants refused to attend, for they no longer regarded themselves as Catholics and felt that they could not get a fair hearing. 

Immediately after the opening of the council, the emperor and the pope came to cross purposes on the precedence of questions for discussion. The pope desired that matters of doctrine be considered first, while the emperor demanded that the council should begin with practical administrative reforms. Finally, a compromise was reached by which it was agreed that doctrine and discipline should be considered simultaneously in every session.

The council was divided into conservative and liberal factions; the conservatives prevailed in matters of doctrine, while the liberals triumphed in administrative reform. On the question of dogma, the 

Catholics offered no compromise with Protestantism. No attempt was made to restate all the Catholic doctrines; for the most part only vital principles attacked by Protestants were defended. This position frustrated the emperor's last hopes for reconciliation with the Protestants. Ultimately the Catholic Church gained from its uncompromising position, for it is probable that unless Catholic doctrines had been stated unequivocally, the church would have followed the Protestant example and broken up into divergent sects. The canons of the council declared that both the Bible and tradition - the mass of customs, papal decisions, and conciliar decrees - were the final source of authority and that the interpretation of the Scriptures belonged only to the church. The Protestant doctrines of grace and justification by faith were condemned; the Catholic doctrine of salvation by faith and good works was maintained. The seven sacra-

ments and their efficacy for salvation were affirmed, as well as the miraculous and sacrificial character of the Holy Eucharist. Beliefs in 

Purgatory, indulgences, the veneration of images and relics, and the invocation of saints were upheld. Issue of indulgences and the bestowal of the sacraments for money were prohibited to prevent the recurrence of those pernicious practices which had been largely responsible for the Protestant Revolt. The reform of the canon law purged the church of many salient abuses. Simony and pluralism were condemned; episcopal residence was enforced. Seminaries were ordered established for the proper education and training of priests, and a catechism was composed for the instruction of the laity. In the mass, Latin was retained as the official liturgical language, but the use of the vernacular was permitted on certain occasions. Communion in one kind and masses for the dead were retained. 

By many contemporary individuals the Council of Trent was regarded as a failure, but time has shown that, although it did not placate the Protestants and heal the schism, it was the most beneficial of all the church councils. By its eradication of clerical abuses it proved a real reformation from within. Its canons and decrees are still the authoritative standards of the church and mark a transition from medieval to modern Catholicism. Surprisingly enough, the papacy emerged with increased power and prestige. The council practically surrendered the old conciliar theory of supremacy and affirmed the powers of the pope in government and faith. 

An important factor in the Catholic revival was the formation of several new religious orders which sought not only to save souls and bulwark the position of the church but to ameliorate social conditions as well. They included the Theatines, Capuchins, Barnabites, Somascians, and Ursulines. The most celebrated, however, was the 

Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius Loyola.

Loyola was a Spanish nobleman who was forced to abandon his career of a professional soldier when permanently lamed during the defense of the fortress of Pampeluna (1521) in the wars between

Charles V and Francis I. His convalescence was slow, and to relieve the tedium he read lives of Christ and the saints. These created a spiritual enthusiasm, and the achievements of St. Francis and St. 

Dominic came to replace deeds of chivalrous knights in his imagination. After passing through a period of religious purification, he renounced worldliness and the pursuit of arms and came forth a crusader against the enemies of the church. 

Thus began Loyola's career of indomitable religious fervor. He

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

visited the Holy Land, but the authorities at Jerusalem feared that his imprudent attempt to propagate the Gospels among the infidels would cause an outbreak of the fanatical Turks and sent him back home. Upon return to Spain in 1524, he realized that his inadequate education constituted a barrier to religious teaching or advancement within the church, and, at the age of thirty-three, he began the study of Latin grammar. After two years, with a modicum of learning in the classics and arts, he entered the University of Alcala and later Salamanca. For some unauthorized attempts at religious teaching he incurred the censure of the authorities and was forced to leave Spain and enter the University of Paris to complete his education. By a coincidence, Loyola and his later Protestant antipode, John Calvin, were fellow students at Paris. Loyola's student days were characterized by poverty and hardship; his religious zeal caused him to be publicly whipped by the college officials as a dangerous fanatic. 

Although he acquired no great erudition, he gained several loyal adherents and many practical advantages which were to prove of incalculable service in his later work. 

With followers of unusual ability, he formed a pious fraternity, out of which he later developed the Society of Jesus. In 1534, this little company of seven consecrated their union by taking vows to live in poverty and chastity and to make a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. 

Their original purpose was to evangelize Palestine, but war between Christians and Mohammedans closed the way to the Holy Land. 

After some delay, Loyola and his followers went to Rome and offered their services to the pope. Although his little band had prospered remarkably without superior, rule, or tradition, Loyola saw the necessity of union and of means of training postulants to preserve the organization. In 1539, he submitted to Pope Paul III the rule of the proposed order, the great aim of which was expressed in the motto Ad Majorem Dei Gloriam (to the Greater Glory of God). In spite of opposition to the erection of another religious order within the church, the Society of Jesus was approved by the pope in 1540. The original title suggested by Loyola was the "Company of Jesus," which indicated its true leader and its militant spirit; in the papal bull of foundation, however, it was called the "Society of Jesus."

The objects of the Society of Jesus were missionary activity, preaching, guidance of the conscience, and education. Under the direction of the Holy See, the Jesuits prepared to combat heresy by education, becoming the most persistent missionaries of the six-

teenth century. Through their efforts the defection of Poland to 

Lutheranism was checked; Catholics in England and Ireland were aided during the Anglican Revolt; and Catholicism was preserved in the southern Netherlands (Belgium) and Bavaria. In the conversion of the heathen, the Jesuits outstripped the older orders of the church. 

Their work was one of civilization as well as of religion, and much of our knowledge of early America came from the accounts of Jesuit missionaries who boldly penetrated into regions hitherto unknown to Europeans. Their work in the Far East, however, was not marked by the same success as their endeavors in the New World. 

The greatest of the eastern missionaries was Francis Xavier, one of Loyola's original band, who carried his work into India, Cochin- China, the Moluccas, and Japan. But like most Jesuit missionary activity in the Orient, this work was superficial and had little lasting effect.

Loyola recognized the importance of education as a means of advancing religion, and he had, after much privation, secured sufficient education to enable him to hold his own in the company of more learned men. But the advancement of the order, and, of more importance still, the extirpation of heresy, were dependent upon education. Consequently, the Jesuits were the first to make education the special ministry of a religious order. Loyola felt that ultimately more could be accomplished by moulding the impressionable minds of youth than by endeavoring to win the mature minds of adults. Members were subjected to a period of rigorous and thorough education, and became the equal of any teachers in Europe. In all the stages of education they strove to develop the best methods of instruction and did not hesitate to adopt some methods of the Protestants. In carrying out their extensive and unified plan of education, they established schools wherever they went - whether among cultivated Europeans or naked savages. Jesuit colleges acquired high reputation for efficiency and thoroughness, which they have retained to this day. Often, Jesuits managed to become the confessors of the Catholic sovereigns of Europe and so gained their confidence and wielded a powerful political influence.

The organization of the Jesuits, their discipline, and gradations of authority showed the influence of Loyola's military training. After acceptance, the novice began a period of severe training to learn. obedience and complete subordination to authority. There were four grades of members: novices; scholastics; coadjutors, spiritual and temporal; and professed of the four vows. During the two years of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

probationary training, the novice took no vows, devoting himself to prayer, meditation, ascetic reading and practices, and the study of Loyola's Spiritual Exercises. After this disciplinary training, in which every trace of individual will was suppressed, the successful candidate took the threefold obligations, common to all Catholic religious orders, of chastity, poverty, and obedience, and became a scholastic. 

A long period of study was devoted to liberal arts, and on graduation the scholastic was sent to teach. A select group of gifted scholastics were admitted to Holy Orders and elevated to the rank of spiritual coadjutor to assist the professed fathers in preaching, teaching, and the guidance of souls. Members unsuited to serve as either priests or teachers were classified as temporal coadjutors, or lay brothers, to whom minor offices were assigned. After an extended preparation, the spiritual coadjutors took a fourth vow, that of special and unalterable obedience to the pope, and were elevated to the fourth and highest grade, that of the professed of the four vows.
