Although a small minority of the total membership, the professed composed the society in the strict sense of the word, for it was this group which directed the organization and from which the chief officials were chosen.

The government of the Society of Jesus was planned to produce a military type of efficiency and, though often spoken of as autocratic, was a striking example of a limited constitutional authority. 

At the head of the society was the general, elected for life by a general congregation of the professed. The general had supreme power, subject only to the pope, the constitutions of the society, and the general assemblies or congregations. For effective government and administration, the Jesuits created Assistancies, or provinces, formed mainly according to the principal European languages. The members of the order enjoyed some exemptions from the more austere practices of other religious orders; they were not required to live in monasteries, and had no distinctive dress, thus permitting freer activity in the world.

Jesuits conceived themselves as "Soldiers of the Pope," gave unquestioned obedience, and gladly assumed arduous duties for the glory of the church. The Society was made up of enthusiasts some of whom felt that the end justified the means, although the Society did not countenance this view. Jesuits occupied high positions at European courts, where frequently they incurred the hostility of clerics and laymen alike. They were banned successively by the governments of Europe and finally suppressed by Clement XIV, in 1773, for

66 the peace of the church." However, rehabilitation was soon under way, and the order was finally re-established by Pius VII in 1814. 

The Catholic Church did not rely solely upon persuasion to check the growth of heresy, but through the revitalized Inquisition used coercion as well. Heresy and rigorous attempts to suppress it were known from the early years of the Christian Church. By the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the activities of such sects as the Waldenses and Albigenses aroused the church to the necessity of some method of combating heresy which would prove more effective in securing evidence and convictions than the local tribunals of the bishops. A major step in the evolution of the Inquisition came during the pontificate of Innocent III (1198–1216), when the inquisitorial procedure was evolved to surmount the difficulty of securing evidence in cases of heresy. The efforts of the inquisitorial courts were still haphazard and spasmodic; the organization of the system into a regular, efficient tribunal was the work of Gregory IX (1227–1241), who may, therefore, be considered the founder of the Inquisition. He withdrew the suppression of heresy from the courts of the bishops and appointed Dominicans and Franciscans, who by their superior theological training, zealous service, and loyalty to the papacy seemed more eminently fitted to perform the task of inquisitors. In the pontificate of Alexander IV, the Dominicans were assigned control of the organization. 

The procedure of the Inquisition varied in some degree from age to age and from place to place. Since its primary purpose was to save souls, the inquisitors proclaimed a "period of grace," during which the self-confessed could clear themselves by a light penance. 

After this period, the court proceeded to summon suspects. Every effort was made to secure a full and free confession, for this alone was valid before the judges. If an admission was not forthcoming - and in instances it was not many measures were taken to extract such acknowledgment by fear of death at the stake; by close confinement, often years at a time with short rations; by visits of tried heretics, who attempted to secure confession by persuasion; and, finally, as a last resort, by the application of torture. Torture was not regarded as a mode of punishment — for the innocence or exact guilt had not been determined - but was purely a means of eliciting truth from those who prevaricated or proved obstinate. A confession secured under such conditions was not acceptable in court; the accused was allowed to retract anything he had said while under torture. A limit was placed on torture, for it was not to cause the 

---

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

letting of blood, the loss of limb, or to imperil life. These limitations, as well as the rule that torture was to be applied only once, were often disregarded. At the trial, conducted in secret, the defendant was not told the nature of his crime nor the names of his accusers. He was permitted to name his known enemies, and if his accusers were in this number the charge of heresy often was quashed. 

The defendant had difficulty in securing witnesses and legal counsel, for they, too, might be charged with the same crime. As early as the pontificate of Innocent III, lawyers were forbidden to defend a heretic; in time, however, the severity of this rule was relaxed. The accused enjoyed a number of safeguards, including the right of appeal to Rome. Heresy was not the only crime which came under the cognizance of the Inquisition, for bigamy, blasphemy, sorcery, witchcraft, and some forms of vice were also included. For this reason, the nature of punishment varied greatly. Acquittal was almost unknown. Punishment took the form of pilgrimages, fasts, prayers, flagellations, crosses sewn to one's apparel, fines, and imprisonments. Repentant first offenders were dismissed with light punishment and the admonition to refrain from future heretical practices. Capital punishment by fire was pronounced on relapsed heretics; convicted heretics who could not be apprehended were burned in effigy. Since the church could not carry out a sentence involving loss of life or shedding of blood, the inquisitors " relaxed the condemned to the secular authorities for punishment. Because of the lack of complete records, no authoritative estimate can be given of the victims of the Inquisition. “An actual count up to the year 

1540, that is, before Protestantism became a serious factor, shows that 20,226 were burned in person and 10,913 in effigy, and these figures are incomplete. . . . Roughly, for one person sentenced to death, ten suffered milder penalties."

Central and western Europe were the chief centers of the Inquisition. Scandinavia was exempt, while in England it was directed by the archbishops and their suffragans without responsibility to any inquisitor-general. The Spanish and Roman branches were the most active, with the Spanish the more dreaded and odious. Although it had been introduced into Spain in the thirteenth century, the Spanish Inquisition proper began in 1478, in the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella. Under the fiendish direction of the first Grand Inquisitor, Torquemada, the Spanish tribunal soon became a synonym for cruelty and barbarity. Its excesses were largely attributable to the fact that it became a state tribunal controlled by the royal power,

and in its administration, civil purposes overshadowed the ecclesiastical. It became so powerful that it could ignore with impunity the commands of the pope. This dread institution was at first directed against Jews and Moors who had embraced Christianity but had relapsed into their former religion. Both races were practically exterminated or driven from Spain; since they constituted the financial and industrial backbone of the nation, Spain soon drifted into a state of economic eclipse, where she has remained to this day. Few 

Protestants were subjected to the horrors of the Spanish Inquisition, for the simple reason that there were never many in the country. 

But the tribunal was a major factor in checking the spread of Protestantism in Spain.

The success of the Spanish Inquisition and the continued infiltration of heresy into Catholic lands prompted Paul III in 1542 to establish the Roman Inquisition. A central board of six cardinals, sitting in Rome, was made the final court of appeals for trials concerning faith and the court of first instance for cases reserved to the pope. It was the ambition of Paul III and his immediate successors to give the Roman Inquisition a jurisdiction as wide as that of the Catholic Church itself. The institution, however, never exercised any notable activity outside Italy, because in other European countries civil authorities regarded its existence as an infringement of national jurisdiction and notified Rome that they intended to do their own heresy-hunting. In Italy it was very effective in stamping out not only heresy but also the remnants of Renaissance humanism. 

As a natural consequence of the claim of the church to guardianship over its members, various popes and also Catholic universities had issued lists of books believed to be injurious to faith or morality and which the orthodox should eschew. The multiplication of such books after the invention of printing made it evident that a more stringent, as well as a more systematic, procedure had to be initiated to keep heterodox writings out of the hands of the faithful. A list issued by Paul IV, in 1559, was the first that bore the title Index, and was the first Roman list meant for the whole world. The Council of Trent regarded these earlier attempts as unsatisfactory and appointed a committee to carry out a comprehensive and authoritative enumeration of books deemed unsuitable for orthodox Catholics. 

This Tridentine Index was issued by Pius IV in 1564; further additions have been made from time to time. Prohibited writings were divided into three categories: the first prohibits the writings of heresiarchs, or corrupt individuals, whose works are condemned in

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

toto, no matter what may be the subjects; under the second head are named individual dangerous works; the third indicates forbidden passages in books otherwise sound. As an additional step, the Council of Trent provided that books which received the approval of the church should be given a license called the imprimatur. 

The reform of the Roman curia had been begun by Adrian VI (1522–1523), but the pontificate of that dour, phlegmatic Dutchman had been too short and unpopular for him to carry out the measures desired. His successor, Clement VII (1523-1534), was a 

Medici, and was characterized by the corruption for which his family was notorious. The pontificate of Paul III (1534–1549) marks the turning point in the Catholic reaction and the beginning of thoroughgoing reformation of the Roman curia. Realizing that the exigencies of the situation made reform imperative, he broke sharply with the traditional policy of the papacy and initiated a program which, while primarily limited to the upper offices, permeated the church from top to bottom. The dissolute cardinals, who had elected 

Paul only because he was in ill health and not expected long to survive, were surprised when he set up a commission to make a comprehensive report on reform. Spiritual rather than political interests dominated the papacy; efficient administration was insisted upon and officials were selected for ability, not by favor. Nepotism was abolished. Instead of weakly acquiescing in the Protestant Revolt and allowing it to go its way unchallenged, he organized a definite offensive, and it was during his pontificate that the Council of Trent was opened, new religious orders were formed, and the Inquisition was placed on a more efficient footing. Although Paul's successors lacked his reforming zeal and nobility of purpose, the trend in the Catholic Church continued slowly but surely upward.

CHAPTER 36 The Age of the Religious Wars 

HE wars of the period c. 1550-1650 were the inescapable aftermath of the Protestant Revolt and the vigorous counter offensive launched by the Catholic Church. Catholic and 

Protestant states stood in sharp opposition, and bigotry and militancy precluded a lasting compromise. Religion became the badge of political faction as well as the instrument of dynastic ambition. 

Problems created by the sequestration of Catholic property, in states that had embraced Protestantism, alone would have assured strife. 

In the Netherlands, the religious issue was an integral phase of the struggle for independence. As a result of the marriage of Mary of 

Burgundy, the Netherlands, including Belgium, had been annexed to the great Hapsburg Empire. Hapsburg rule occasioned a revolt of the towns, led by Ghent, but the statesmanship of Charles V (1519-1556) ultimately conciliated the disaffected elements. 

Upon the abdication of Charles, Spain and the Netherlands passed to his son, Philip II, while the Austrian and German possessions went to his brother, Ferdinand. Philip was austere and remorseless, imbued with the conviction that he was the designated agent of Providence to extirpate Protestantism. Unrest flared up in the Netherlands almost immediately upon his accession. The Spanish Inquisition was introduced, and its efforts to crush Calvinism were actively promoted by the unpopular Cardinal Granville. Onerous taxation curtailed the prosperity of urban centers like Ghent, Antwerp, and Bruges, which had been flourishing industrial centers in the Middle Ages. Mercenaries were quartered on the citizenry, with Protestants forced to assume the major share of the burden. Remonstrances to the Regent, Margaret of Parma, were futile. She was arrogant and frivolous, incapable of understanding the degree to which Spanish policies were producing resentment.

In 1566 a group of Dutch nobles rebelled. The authorities refused to heed the protests of these "beggars," as they derisively termed

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

them. The rebels adopted the epithet as their party name. A number of the leaders of the uprising, including the popular Count Egmont, were sent to the scaffold. They were regarded as martyrs, and their deaths did much to unite all elements in opposition to the hated Spaniards.

Philip decided to suppress the uprising by a campaign of terrorization, and in the Duke of Alva he found an ideal agent for such a mission. Indeed few more fiendishly cruel characters have ever stained the pages of history. An orgy of massacre, pillage, and rapine began with the arrival of Alva and his army. The "Council of Blood" hurried thousands to their deaths with trials that mocked the most elementary considerations of justice. 

When William of Orange, in 1568, consented to lead the rebel armies, the Spanish were forced back upon the defensive. All the north provinces adhered to the patriot cause, and most of the southern states were won away by economic inducements. After a series of reverses, Alva was recalled (1573), but the new commander, Alexander of Parma, did nothing to mitigate the cruelties of his licentious soldiery. By 1579 the southern states, which were predominantly Catholic, were again under Spanish control, but Alexander's efforts to reconquer the north failed. William of Orange had continually urged the creation of a federation; the Union of 

Utrecht (1579) was formed in accordance with this policy. The 

Protestant northern states were organized into a league of independent republics, but dreary years of war were necessary before the independence of the states received international recognition in the Peace of Westphalia (1648).

Queen Elizabeth of England (1558-1603) dallied with projects for intervention in behalf of Dutch independence, but confined her efforts to occasional subsidies. The threat of English intervention, however, strained relations with Spain and contributed to Philip's decision to attack England in 1588. The execution of Mary Queen of Scots furnished an immediate cause for dispatching the Great Armada. 

Mary, daughter of James V of Scotland, widow of King Francis II of France, had, it will be recalled, married Lord Darnley. She became infatuated with the Earl of Bothwell and connived at his murder of her husband. This act completed the breach with the dominant 

Protestant faction and necessitated her flight to England. Here she served as a nucleus for Catholic malcontents. Her intrigues with 

Philip brought about her execution (1587).

Philip had dreamed of the re-establishment of papal supremacy in

England since his marriage to Mary, Elizabeth's predecessor on the throne. The depredations of Drake and others had made serious inroads on Spanish commerce with the colonies; scores of galleons, laden with treasure, had fallen prey to the buccaneers. A successful invasion of England, therefore, promised the re-establishment of Catholicism, revenge for Elizabeth's meddling in the Netherlands, and the elimination of a serious obstacle to Spanish commerce. The defeat of the Spanish fleet by the indomitable English vessels under 

Lord Howard, Francis Drake, Hawkins, and other leaders was followed by the destruction of the Armada by a great storm. Only a pitiful remnant of the once formidable force returned to Cadiz. 

France, too, was torn by religious conflict. Francis I (1515-1547) forbade Protestantism and initiated spasmodic persecutions, primarily to secure the support of the established church, so badly needed in view of his Italian ambitions and the consequent struggle with Charles V. Henry II (1547-1559) added fanaticism to expediency by organizing the "Chambers of Fire" to extirpate heresy by the methods of the Inquisition.

The religious issue became critical in the reign of Charles IX, who ruled under the regency of his mother, Catherine de' Medici. Two factions of nobles vied for influence and power, one under the Catholic Duke of Guise, the other led by the Protestant Admiral Coligny. 

For a time Catherine inclined to a policy of toleration, and Huguenots were officially authorized to hold services in designated towns. Conflict began, nevertheless, when the Duke of Guise dispersed a group of Huguenots who were holding a service in conformity with the Edict of Toleration (1562). A truce, in 1570, assigned a number of towns to the Huguenots, a harbinger of the policy later to be adopted by Henry IV. On St. Bartholomew's Day, 1572, however, some 2,000

Huguenots, including Coligny, were massacred in Paris; and about 

8,000 more were killed in the provinces, as a result of a well organized plot apparently instigated by Guise and Catherine. A Te Deum was sung at Rome at the receipt of news of the tragedy, and Philip of 

Spain was reported to have greatly rejoiced.

With the death of Charles IX (1574) the religious question became a phase of the War of the Three Henries. Henry III, Henry of Guise, and the Huguenot, Henry of Navarre, contended for the throne. By 

1589, Henry of Navarre was the sole candidate and gradually won recognition, except in Paris where his Protestantism was the basic obstacle. Since "Paris was well worth a mass," he embraced the 

Catholic faith in 1593. By the Edict of Nantes (1598), the Hugue-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

nots were assigned 200 towns which they were permitted to fortify. 

They were also granted freedom of conscience in all parts of France and freedom of worship in all places where it had been allowed in 1596 and 1597, in two towns of every bailiwick, except Paris, and in the castles of the Huguenot nobles. This act, however commendable as a step toward the establishment of tolerance, was subversive to the policy of centralization which the king and his able minister Sully had inaugurated. The autonomy granted to the Huguenot towns weakened the monarchy, and these political privileges were wisely curtailed by Richelieu. The religious provisions remained in force until the revocation of the edict by Louis XIV. 

Recurrence of conflict in Germany was made inevitable by the failure of the Treaty of Augsburg (1555) to settle basic issues. Calvinism did not receive toleration by the treaty, and there was no provision to check further attempts to spread Protestantism. The clauses of the treaty which forbade further confiscations of Catholic Church property were evaded. An attack on a procession of monks at Donauwörth was a prelude to the Thirty Years' War. 

Maximilian of Bavaria took prompt action to avenge the outrage. 

Protestant states formed a league, under the leadership of Frederick, Elector of the Palatinate of the Rhine, and Maximilian countered with the formation of a Catholic League.

The first phase of the war was identified with the cause of Bohemian nationalism. Aspirations for independence were coupled with failure of the Bohemian Protestants to secure concessions which the emperor had promised. A revolt at Prague, during which imperial envoys were tossed from a window of the council chamber, was the signal for a declaration of independence. Frederick, the Elector 

Palatine, accepted the offer of the crown. His selection was due to the fact that he was the son-in-law of James I of England, from whom assistance was anticipated. But aid from England did not materialize, and the emperor, Ferdinand II, aided by Maximilian of Bavaria, easily quelled the uprising. The "Winter King" was deposed and punished by the forfeiture of about half his palatinate. 

The second phase of the Thirty Years' War was marked by the intervention of Denmark. Christian IV sought to acquire the ports on the north German Baltic coast. This motive was far more important than any desire to aid the Protestant cause. For a time, his armies were victorious, but a series of blows, delivered by the brilliant Wallenstein, compelled the Danes to withdraw. The Edict of 

Restitution (1629), issued at the end of this phase of the conflict,

provided that all property confiscated by Protestants since 1552 was to be restored and that Lutherans were to be the only Protestant group to enjoy toleration.

At this critical juncture the Protestants were rescued by Sweden's entry into the war. Gustavus Adolphus, although a passionate advocate of Lutheranism, had the same territorial and economic objectives as Christian of Denmark. While the Hapsburg forces remained under the command of Tilly, the Swedish armies won several victories, but with the recall of Wallenstein, who had been dismissed for alleged corruption, the tide began to turn. The army of Gustavus won a brilliant victory at Lützen, but the king was slain and his death curtailed Sweden's active participation in the war. 

French policy in the last years of the war aptly illustrates the point that religion was often a minor factor in the struggle. France, a 

Catholic nation guided by Cardinal Richelieu, allied herself with the Protestant states. The doctrine of "natural frontiers" was a basic feature of Richelieu's policies, and upheaval in Germany offered prospect of pushing the eastern boundary of France to the Rhine, with the acquisition of Alsace, Lorraine, and Roussillon. The brilliant generals, Condé and Turenne, gained several decisive victories, and at the close of the war Alsace and Lorraine were under French control. 

The Treaty of Westphalia (1648) was the first of a series of great European settlements. It modified the Augsburg settlement by according to Calvinists the toleration hitherto confined to Lutherans. The rulers of each of the German states were to choose which religion was to prevail in the territories under their control. 

Protestants were to hold all lands acquired before 1624. Pomerania was ceded to Sweden with the proviso that it was to remain nominally a part of the Empire. Alsace, Metz, Toul, and Verdun were ceded to France. The independence of Switzerland and the Netherlands was officially recognized.

CONSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENT IN ENGLAND IN THE AGE OF THE RELIGIOUS WARS 

By 1400, the English Parliament had acquired the powers essential to constitutional government. Financial control had been successfully asserted; the powers of impeachment, and even deposition of the king, had been exercised. Nevertheless, the development of constitutional monarchy proved premature, for the Tudors (14851603) inaugurated a vigorous royalist reaction. Tudor absolutism,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

in large measure, was a natural effect of the Wars of the Roses (1455-1485). The turbulence incident to the struggle of the Yorkist and Lancastrian factions had borne heavily on the general populace, who felt no immediate interest in the outcome. The Tudors were popular, above all, because they offered stability and order. 

With memories of the recent excesses of the barons so vivid, it is not surprising that the English people condoned a virtual restoration of absolutism. Moreover, commerce and industry were expanding, and the Tudor rulers by their wise policies further improved economic interests. Finally, England was constantly threatened with dangers from abroad. It was therefore expedient to support a government that offered vigorous defense.

Absolutism, however, again came in conflict with parliamentary principles in the reign of James I (1603-1625). The founder of the 

Stuart line cherished the most exalted conceptions of royal prerogative and the divine right of kings. A number of factors accentuated the friction with Parliament. James's foreign policy was considered pusillanimous when he failed to intervene in the Thirty Years' War. 

Negotiations for a Spanish marriage for Prince Charles likewise engendered much dissatisfaction. Dissenters and Catholics were disgruntled over the failure of the king to extend religious concessions. 

Some of the Separatists found an asylum in Holland, subsequently to emigrate to America. The civil disabilities of Catholics were increased as a result of the abortive Gunpowder Plot (1605).

The fundamental issue, however, was the royal claim that the privileges and immunities of Parliament were granted by him on his own volition, whereas Parliament asserted these privileges as inalienable rights. Impositions of customs without parliamentary consent were bitterly opposed, as were also the king's attempts to curtail the powers of the courts.

The controversy attained full virulence in the reign of Charles I (1625-1649). The new king, although possessing undeniable gifts of intellect and manner, was stubborn and oblivious to the temper of the times. His first Parliament was summarily dismissed when the 

Commons impugned the conduct of Buckingham and other royal ministers. Forced by financial needs in 1628 to convoke another 

Parliament, the king found the opposition strengthened by the scandals of the Cadiz expedition. When the impeachment of Buckingham was demanded as a sine qua non of monetary grants, Charles again dismissed Parliament, but his failure to secure funds compelled him to resort to arbitrary expedients that greatly increased the oppo-

sition. In 1628, Parliament had been able, however, to draw up the 

Petition of Right. This document asserted the principle that loans, gifts, or taxes could not legally be imposed without consent of Parliament. Imprisonment without due process of law was condemned as an aftermath of the "Five Knights Case," wherein five knights had been imprisoned for refusal to contribute to a levy imposed by the king. Quartering of troops and establishment of martial law in time of peace were likewise declared unlawful. 

Charles claimed that the failure of Parliament to vote subsidies automatically authorized him to collect tonnage and poundage as a royal prerogative; distraints and imprisonments were necessary to enforce collections. The religious issue again came to the fore, with a "Declaration" by the king that allocated religious questions to the jurisdiction of Convocation, made up largely of his appointees. When the Parliament of 1629 passed the Eliot Resolutions, which denied the royal right to impose tonnage and poundage, it was forcibly dissolved, not to be reassembled until 1640. 

In the period of personal government (1629-1640), practically every phase of royal policy aroused widespread condemnation. 

Archbishop Laud's attempt to establish conformity to Anglican usages angered the Puritans and other dissenting groups. It was widely believed that High Church doctrines were the prelude to a re-establishment of Catholicism. The crown used a number of unpopular expedients to raise funds. Grants of monopoly were sold, and widespread complaints were engendered by the resultant price increases. Fines in distraint of knighthood, coat and conduct money, forest fines, and other exactions were imposed. When John Hampden, a leading resident of an inland town, refused to pay a tax of ship money, the case was taken to court where the judges upheld this tax on the ground that it was levied as an emergency measure, ostensibly for the defense of the realm.

The attempts of Charles and Laud to establish ecclesiastical uniformity in Scotland paved the way for the Puritan Revolution. The 

Scotch countered by drawing up the "National Covenant" (1638) wherein they pledged themselves to uphold the crown and the Presbyterian religion. Futile negotiations led to the rather ridiculous 

First Bishops' War (1639). Upon the advice of the Earl of Strafford, Charles convoked Parliament in April of 1640 to procure funds for renewal of the war with the Scots. John Pym led the opposition. In a brilliant speech he arraigned the king for his interference with parliamentary privilege, violations of property rights, and attempts to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

introduce new religious practices. When the king saw that no monetary grants would be made without concessions which he was unwilling to extend, he dissolved the "Short Parliament." Renewal of the Scottish War brought matters to a crisis. Parliament again was summoned, and the "Long Parliament " began its session in November, 1640. Laud and Strafford were impeached, and the unpopular courts of High Commission and Star Chamber were abolished. A

Triennial Act made mandatory convocations of Parliament at least every three years, and the principle of financial control was reaffirmed. Rebellion in Ireland (1641) strengthened reform demands, and the Grand Remonstrance, which epitomized the struggles of recent years, was presented to the king. Encouraged by evidences of personal popularity and the split in parliamentary ranks, caused by the religious provisions of the Remonstrance, Charles attempted to arrest five parliamentary leaders. Foiled by their flight, he withdrew from London amid great excitement and shortly began the war at 

Nottingham (1642). 

The royalists were decisively defeated at Marston Moor (1644), and the reorganized Puritan army crushed them again at Naseby (1645). Charles profited by the dissensions of the parliamentarians to intrigue for Irish and Scottish assistance. “Pride's Purge" of 1648, however, left Cromwell and the Puritans in undisputed control of Parliament. A High Court was constituted, and by act of the "Rump Parliament " Charles was condemned for treason and executed (January 30, 1649). 

In March, 1649, the "Rump" abolished the House of Lords and declared kingship a superfluous instrument of government. A Council of State was created to administer the newly established Commonwealth. The new government was in reality a religious and military oligarchy. Cromwell led an army to Ireland, where royalist opposition was crushed by the infamous Drogheda massacre and the

Settlement of 1652 which outlawed Catholicism. In 1651 a Scottish uprising was quelled at Worcester and Charles II fled to France. 

Dissension in the "Rump" continued, and in 1653 Cromwell dissolved the body and convoked the "Barebones Parliament," made up of his carefully selected partisans. An "Instrument of Government" was enacted, the only written constitution England ever had. 

Cromwell was named Lord Protector (1653-1658) and subsequently enjoyed virtually unlimited powers. He enacted a church settlement sufficiently elastic to include all save Catholics and Episcopalians. The Dutch Wars were ended successfully, and a power-

ful blow was struck against Spanish commercial interests in the New World. However, the project for a union of Protestant states did not materialize.

After two years of vacillation and dissension under Richard Cromwell and military leaders (1658–1660) England was more than ready for a Stuart Restoration. Charles II returned, under the terms of the 

Declaration of Breda, which a subsequent Convention carried into effect. From 1660 to 1667, royal policies were largely framed by the 

Earl of Clarendon, who sponsored a series of reactionary laws. Dissenters were barred from public office, while the Corporation Act imposed similar restrictions on the tenure of municipal offices. An 

Act of Uniformity required all clergymen to use the revised Book of Common Prayer or resign their benefices. The Conventicle Act prohibited religious services by five or more dissenters, and the Five Mile Act forbade nonconformist clergy or teachers to come within five miles of a corporate town unless they took an oath not to bear arms or attempt forcible overthrow of the government.

After Clarendon's fall, Charles showed an increasing tendency toward absolutism, which was abetted by a small group of intimate admirers, known as the Cabal. In 1670 he concluded the secret Treaty of Dover with Louis XIV, conniving at the French invasion of the 

Netherlands and promising to make efforts to restore Catholicism.

When a "Declaration of Indulgence" was issued, extending a large measure of toleration to Catholics, Parliamentary opposition was aroused. It resulted in the prompt passage of the Test Act (1673), which again tightened the restrictions; and when the rascally Titus 

Oates charged that Catholic plotters were preparing a coup, anti- Catholic legislation increased in severity. An improved Habeas Corpus Act in 1679, however, gave England one constructive measure amid the succession of reactionary laws. 

James II, brother of Charles (1685-1688), pushed reaction too far.

After the Duke of Monmouth's rebellion was crushed, Kirke's “Lambs" and Jeffrey's "Bloody Assize" took a terrible toll. But it was the king's attempts to revive Catholicism and his intrigues for foreign assistance in this project that precipitated the "Glorious 

Revolution" of 1688. Mary and her husband, William of Orange, were called to the throne by Parliament. The Declaration of Rights (1689) embodied the basic principles of constitutional monarchy. No money was to be raised without parliamentary consent. The crown was forbidden to suspend the laws. No armies were to be levied without parliamentary approval. Arbitrary arrests and interference with

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

freedom of speech, debate, and elections were likewise forbidden. An 

Act of Settlement (1701) regulating the succession to the throne was another striking evidence of recognized parliamentary supremacy. 

By 1689, England was irrevocably committed to constitutional government.

DEVELOPMENT OF ABSOLUTISM IN FRANCE 

Development of parliamentary institutions in France, in the later Middle Ages, promised to keep pace with similar movements in England. The Estates-General ultimately failed, however, to secure powers comparable to those exercised by the English Parliament; it met only once after 1614. In the meantime, the authority of the monarchy was growing, until it reached its culmination in the reign. 

of Louis XIV (1643–1715). 

The monarchy began to recuperate from the disastrous effects of the Hundred Years' War in the reign of Charles VII (1422–1461). 

A standing army was organized and taxation put on a systematic basis with the levy of the taille (land tax), gabelle (tax on salt) and a number of excises. Ecclesiastical influence was curbed by the 

Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges (1438), which, in effect, established a national church and greatly reduced the authority of the pope in France. The nobles were reduced to a semblance of obedience. The rejuvenated government energetically resumed the struggle with 

England in 1447, and at the close of the Hundred Years' War (1453),

Calais was the only English possession on French soil. 

Centralization continued in the reign of Louis XI (1461-1483). 

A faction of nobles, known as the "Princes of Lilies," was reduced to impotence by adroit negotiations, intrigues, and conquests. The king's great struggle with Charles the Bold of Burgundy engendered a fervent nationalism in spite of the disloyalty of some nobles. When 

Charles was killed at the siege of Nancy, the western half of Burgundy was annexed to France. Arrangements were made for the marriage of Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII; and when the agreement was carried out in 1491, Brittany was annexed by the monarchy and territorial unification was virtually complete. 

Unhappily, the constructive gains made by these rulers were largely dissipated by the Italian policy of Charles VIII and his successors. Francis I was drawn into a disastrous struggle with the 

Emperor Charles V, fundamentally because of Italian ambitions which centered around claims to the Kingdom of Naples and Milan. 

Religious turmoil hastened the prostration of the monarchy, and the

War of the Three Henries, fought largely between Catholic and 

Protestant factions, led to veritable chaos.

Recovery began with the accession of Henry IV (1589-1610), who, as we have seen, renounced his Protestantism and embraced Catholicism in the interest of the nation. The Edict of Nantes, granting limited rights to Protestants, allayed religious conflict, while tangible inducements procured the coöperation of many of the nobles. The king's able minister, Sully, restored financial stability. Agriculture was aided by subsidies, and the construction of roads and canals was begun to enlarge market facilities. Protective tariffs and other aids stimulated the manufacture of silk, china, glass, and other articles of luxury. Increased prosperity augmented governmental revenues, while wasteful expenditures were eliminated by 

Sully's vigilance. With the assassination of Henry by a madman (1610), the throne passed to the young Louis XIII (1610–1643), under the regency of Marie de' Medici. Marie's incompetence and weakness gave opportunity for the nobles again to assert their independence from royal control, but disruptive tendencies were definitely curbed when Cardinal Richelieu became the chief minister to the king (1624). The cardinal's devotion to the advancement of the monarchy was paramount. He consecrated remarkable energies and talents to the attainment of objectives which would serve the cause of monarchy. He inspired the same unshakable resolution in his subordinates. Offices were filled with men in whom the cardinal reposed confidence, until a bureaucracy was created, held together by common loyalty. Another Protestant revolt was completely subdued at 

La Rochelle and Montauban, and by the Edict of Alais (1629) Richelieu required the Huguenots to dismantle their fortresses and surrender many of their political privileges, although he did not curtail freedom of worship. So firmly was royal authority established that the nobles were forbidden to engage in duels. They also were forced to dismantle their castles, unless these were situated so near the frontiers as to be in a position of possible service to the nation. A number of prominent nobles were executed for defiance of these laws. Local administrative functions were entrusted to appointed intendants (1637), chosen almost invariably from the commoners of the Third Estate, thus depriving the nobles of much of their former authority.

Richelieu and the king, who had consistently upheld his acts, died in the same year (1642); and Anne of Austria became regent for the young Louis XIV. She selected Mazarin as her chief minis-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ter, and when he attempted to continue the strong policies of Richelieu, the bourgeoisie collaborated with the nobles in an abortive uprising, termed in derision the Fronde. Mazarin pushed French policy in the Thirty Years' War to success, and the Treaty of Westphalia awarded France the territories on the eastern frontier which Richelieu had hoped to secure when he intervened in the war. In 1659, the 

Peace of the Pyrenees was signed with Spain. 

The work of Henry IV, Richelieu, and Mazarin prepared the way for the culmination of autocracy under Louis XIV, whose theories of government might be summed up in the famous aphorism (not actually uttered by him), "I am the State." He had all powers executive, legislative, and judicial — concentrated in his person, and required the presence of nobles to enhance the brilliance of his court at Versailles. Titled folk with centuries of aristocratic traditions vied for the right to perform menial services. By this painless method 

Louis XIV contributed further to the weakening of the nobility. 

Molière, Racine, and other members of the Academy, established by Richelieu, enhanced the intellectual brilliance of the reign. The 

Gobelins contributed their beautiful tapestries, and the best artists of the day their paintings, to the embellishment of the splendid palace which Louis XIV raised at Versailles.

The Royal Council, made up of his appointees, advised and assisted in affairs of state. For efficiency, it was divided into small groups, to each of which were assigned specific duties. The Council of State, presided over by the king in person, discussed foreign policy and major domestic issues; the Council of Dispatches regulated provincial matters; while questions of finance were assigned to another council. Judicial business came under the jurisdiction of the Privy 

Council. All acts had to be legalized by the imposition of the Great 

Seal, in the custody of the chancellor. Laws, after validation, were inscribed in the registers of the Parlement of Paris, which also served as a High Court of Appeal.

Economic policies were largely framed by Colbert, a firm believer in the mercantilist doctrines. Industrial gilds were regulated, primarily to eliminate waste and enhance the output of those commodities which France was best able to produce and market. Exploration and colonizing in North America were promoted. Commerce was stimulated by the abolition of many internal customs and tolls. 

Systematic accounting curbed waste and corruption in all financial activities of the government.

Unfortunately, religious persecution was revived with the revo-

cation of the Edict of Nantes (1685). Huguenots were subjected to political and social discriminations. Contingents of troops (Dragonnades) were quartered in Protestant households and committed many deeds of violence. Under the pressure of this persecution thousands of Huguenots emigrated. They were drawn, for the most part, from the ranks of the industrious, capable artisans, and their departure was a distinct economic loss to France.

The foreign policy of Louis XIV, with its aim of taking the west bank of the Rhine, was costly to France. French aggressions so strengthened the adherence of other nations to the principle of "balance of power" that every hostile move of France was promptly countered by the formation of a coalition that frustrated the designs of the Grand Monarch. In 1667, Louis laid claim to the Spanish 

Netherlands on the ground that they had "devolved" to him through the rights of his wife. A Triple Alliance of Holland, Sweden, and England opposed him and caused him to sue for peace. In the 

Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1668), he had to renounce his claim to the Spanish Netherlands; but after another war of aggression against the Dutch, the Peace of Nimwegen (1678) brought him Franche Comté, the eastern half of Burgundy, and some frontier towns. Attempts to seize territory in the Rhinelands by the pseudo-legal proceedings of the Chambers of Reunion precipitated a war with the Empire, which was ended by the Treaty of Ryswick. Again, French aggression achieved nothing in return for heavy expenditures of blood and treasure.

In 1700, at the death of Charles II of Spain, Louis claimed the Spanish throne for his grandson, Philip of Anjou. Since this plan threatened to destroy the balance of power, England, Holland, Sweden, and the Empire formed the Grand Alliance against France. 

After a bitter struggle in Europe and America, the Treaty of 

Utrecht (1713) was signed, permitting Philip to assume the Spanish throne on condition that the crowns of Spain and France would not be united. France was deprived of Nova Scotia and her Hudson Bay holdings; Spain ceded Gibraltar to England. Two years later, Louis's reign of seventy-two years came to a close. France had been irreparably weakened by the disastrous series of wars and had begun to tread the road that was to lead to revolution.

CHAPTER 37 The Expansion of Europe 

MOTIVES FOR COLONIZATION 

HE activities of the Portuguese and Spanish in exploration and discovery have been treated in an earlier chapter. The 

Portuguese navigators, Diaz, Vasco da Gama, Cabral, and

Albuquerque, had traced routes and developed their country's supremacy in the regions of the African coasts, Brazil, India, and the East Indies. The Spanish efforts by Columbus, Balboa, Ponce de 

Leon, De Soto, Cortez, Pizarro, Magellan, and others had created for Spain a sphere for trade and colonization in North, South, and 

Central America, the West Indies, and the Philippine Islands. The period of exploration merged imperceptibly into the age of colonization. Not only did the two earlier exploring countries, Portugal and Spain, turn to the development of more permanent settlements in the sixteenth century, but other European countries, such as Holland, Sweden, France, and England, began to become interested in transoceanic trade and colonization, particularly in the seventeenth century. As Portugal and Spain declined, these other nations began to challenge their commercial and colonial supremacy. 

Many motives inspired the colonizing movement. The chief was economic the desire for trade and profit. The Spanish were eager for gold and silver as well as for trade expansion, while the French and Dutch were primarily interested in furs. The English desired to acquire new sources of timber, naval stores, and fish; sought new lands for the settlement of thousands of unemployed yeomen, dispossessed by the enclosures; and in time looked upon future colonial settlements as so many markets for manufactures. 

Economic self-sufficiency was closely allied with political motives springing from national rivalries. Spain and Portugal were bent on defending the partition of the non-European world between themselves. When Spain absorbed the Portuguese colonies in 1580, Holland was already at war with Philip II and dreamed of detach-

ing some of his possessions. England and France, spurred by national pride, were loath to let the Spanish or the Dutch monopolize the wealth and trade of the Indies, East or West. 

Allied with national antipathies were the religious differences of the European states. Spain, exalted by her successful crusade against the Moors, sent out Franciscans, Dominicans, and Jesuits with the colonizers to convert the benighted natives. Jesuits likewise joined the French colonizing enterprises in Canada, the region of the Great Lakes and the Mississippi valley. On the other hand, the Protestant 

English, unwilling to see the new continents turned over to the Roman Church, were glad to support colonial ventures which would send out Protestant settlers and missionaries. 

After the Protestant Revolt, and particularly during the seventeenth century, colonies were also founded as a refuge for victims of persecution. The eastern seaboard of North America in particular became the haven of religious refugees, desirous of freedom of worship for themselves but sometimes as intolerant of dissenting religious beliefs as had been their persecutors in Europe. The Separatists (Pilgrims) settled Plymouth; the Puritans, Massachusetts Bay and Connecticut; the Baptists, Rhode Island. The Catholics, under 

Lord Baltimore, colonized Maryland; the Huguenots, driven from

France by the revocation of the Edict of Nantes by Louis XIV 

(1685), settled along the Atlantic seaboard, particularly in the Carolinas; the Quakers led by William Penn founded Pennsylvania; and the Moravians also settled in Pennsylvania. 

A large number of the persecuted religious minorities of Europe were tradesmen. It is hence not surprising that their early colonizing activities should have taken the form of chartered companies. Furthermore, with the shifting of trade routes and the consequent decline of the Hansa and Italian commercial cities, national trade superseded municipal commerce. The government of a national state did not itself engage in trade, but merely chartered companies for that purpose. Towards the end of the sixteenth and throughout the seventeenth century, the most popular method for the development of colonial trade was the joint-stock company. A charter, secured from the government, granted a monopoly of trade in a stipulated area in return for a share of the proceeds. In the territory comprised in the grant, the company was virtually a sovereign state. 

For example, the English East India Company (1600) conducted the conquest and government of India until relieved of its administrative powers by the English crown in 1858. Under the charters,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the home government protected the favored joint-stock companies from domestic competition and from the aggression of foreign powers. England, the Netherlands, France, Scotland, and other north European countries chartered "East India Companies," and the profitable West India trade was tapped by similar organizations. 

The English possessions on the Atlantic seaboard were shared by the London and Plymouth Companies, chartered in 1606. The former company colonized Virginia and founded Jamestown (1607), the first permanent English settlement in America. Conflicting commercial areas were a fertile cause of eighteenth-century wars. Spain was repeatedly forced to fight as a consequence of her extensive colonial possessions and her policy of restricting or prohibiting competitive trade. The long series of struggles between France and England, from the War of the Spanish Succession to the American Revolution inclusive, were fundamentally caused by colonial and commercial rivalry.

PORTUGUESE COLONIES 

Spurred by the successful voyage of Da Gama, the Portuguese redoubled their efforts to wrest the monopoly of the eastern trade from the Arabs. Under one after another of her great leaders — 

Da Gama, Pacheco, Almeida, and Albuquerque - Portugal won the control of the eastern seas and a monopoly of the spice trade. Between 1500 and 1525 she conquered and established trading settlements along the whole western coast of India including Diu, Goa, the Malabar coast, and Ceylon; in the East Indies at Malacca, on 

Sumatra, Java, and Celebes, in the Spice Islands, and even as far as

Macao in China; in the region of Persia at Ormuz and Muscat; in 

Africa all along the west coast, at the Cape, and then on up the east coast at Mozambique, Mombasa, and even to Abyssinia. Brazil, discovered by Cabral in 1500, was not settled until 1530. 

The Portuguese combined the character and activities of merchants and missionaries in their treatment of the natives. Interested primarily in trade, they came in relatively small numbers, settling in fortified posts along the coasts, allying and trading with chiefs and rulers in the interior, and marrying among the Negroes, Hindus, Malays, and American Indians with scarcely any racial inhibitions. 

Their colonial government was as loose as their holdings were scattered. In Lisbon the king tried to control the political administration of the colonies, while the chartered Casa da India supervised the trade and the Casa da Mina took charge of gold mining in Africa.

Beyond the Cape, over the vast Estado da India, was placed a viceroy with seven governorships and a supreme court under his authority. In Brazil a governor-general, with the aid of subordinate captains, administered the government in the name of the king.

The scattered nature of the Portuguese holdings and a weak and dishonest administration were only two of many reasons for the decline of Portugal's empire. The home resources in money.and men were quite insufficient to sustain so extended and so vulnerable a line of trading settlements. Failure to devise and adapt new methods and policies resulted in a breakdown of the machinery of government and trade. Finally, in 1580, Spain took over Portugal and her empire, restricted European trade with Lisbon, and added her own inherent weaknesses to those of Portugal. The Dutch traders refused to see their commerce decline, and being at war with Spain, sent ships to the Indies to secure the spices denied them at Lisbon. Having only feeble protection from the mother country, Portuguese traders proved to be no match for the enterprising Dutch, who soon broke the Portuguese monopoly, and such Dutch cities as Bruges, Antwerp, and Amsterdam came to supersede Lisbon as the center of eastern trade. When Portugal regained her independence in 1640 she had lost to the Dutch not only her commerce but most of her eastern colonies as well. By 1822 even Brazil had won its independence from the homeland. Today, such scattered outposts as Goa, Diu, Macao, and Timor in the Far East and the backward regions of Angola and Mozambique in Africa are the sole remnants of her former flourishing empire.

SPANISH COLONIES 

The voyages of Columbus laid the foundations of the Spanish colonial empire in America. No other colonizing nation in the New 

World accomplished so much in so short a time, for within fifty years after Columbus's first voyage, Spain had explored and established numerous settlements in one of the greatest colonial empires of all times. The first stage of exploration was characterized by the exploration of the coasts and the colonization of the principal islands of the West Indies; in the second stage, efforts were directed to the interior of the mainland and proved to be more profitable.

The restless spirit of the Spanish explorers is well exemplified in the career of Balboa, a bankrupt Santo Domingo planter, who fled the island to escape a debtor's prison. He became a stowaway on a

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

vessel carrying an expedition to the neighborhood of Panama. The leader of the expedition, a Spanish lawyer, proved to be incompetent and was sent home, carrying a letter from Balboa to the king of Spain requesting that no more lawyers be allowed to come to the West Indies, for none had ever come there "who was not a devil and who led the life of a devil." Balboa soon became the leader of the expedition and, while seeking for gold, heard of another sea not far away. Pushing through the trackless jungle of the Isthmus of Panama, he finally saw from the mountain heights the waters of the Pacific (1513). He named the body the "South Sea " and, recognizing the significance of his discovery, claimed possession in the name of his sovereign, the king of Spain. The crowning event of the age of discovery was the circumnavigation of the globe by Magellan. 

In 1513, Ponce de Leon, a Spanish adventurer, discovered and named Florida while searching for gold and a rumored fountain of perpetual youth. Although he failed to find the things for which he came, his explorations of the peninsula added greatly to the geographical knowledge of the time. His fruitless adventure did not prevent another Spaniard, Narvaez, from leading an expedition into Florida. The expedition was lured from Tampa Bay into the interior by false reports of a large Indian town and immense wealth. 

Disappointed, and faced with attacks of hostile natives, the starving Spaniards were forced back to the coast, where they built boats, killed their horses for food, made sails from horsehides and clothing, and sailed to join their supply fleet. Unable to find these vessels, the ill-fated expedition beat westward along the Gulf Coast, until the last survivors were wrecked on the coast of Texas. After several years of captivity among the Indians, Cabeza de Vaca, historian of the expedition, and four companions escaped and reached Mexico, bringing with them the usual rumors of immense treasure. 

De Vaca's glowing accounts seemed to confirm the reported existence of the "Seven Cities of Cibola " with their fabulous wealth.

Fra Marcos, a Franciscan friar, was sent to investigate and returned with such colorful stories of riches that in 1540 Francisco de Coronado set out to conquer the regions. He found that the cities were nothing but poor Indian pueblos. The expedition pushed across the plains as far eastward as the present state of Kansas, but failing to find treasure, returned to Mexico (1542).

Another victim of exaggerated reports of riches in the interior was Hernando de Soto, who had served under Pizarro in Peru. 

Anxious to gain fame and fortune in Florida, he set out in 1539,

at the head of an expedition which he personally financed. From 

Tampa Bay he marched through hostile Indian country. For two years, he wandered through the southeastern part of the United States, probably going as far northward as North Carolina and then turning southward through Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi. He discovered the Mississippi river in 1541, and, after unsuccessful exploration in the region of Arkansas, returned broken-hearted to the Mississippi, where he died in the same year. 

The Spanish dream of El Dorado seemed to have come true as persistent rumors reached Cuba of the great wealth of the Aztecs in Mexico. The Aztecs may be considered the most civilized of 

North American aborigines since they cultivated the soil, lived in pueblos, or towns, and had developed great skill in the working of gold and silver. It was this vast store of precious metal which inspired Hernando Cortez in 1519 to lead an expedition to Mexico. 

The warlike Aztecs, who were feared by their weaker Indian neighbors, proved to be no match for the small but well-armed Spanish force. After more than two years of fighting, Cortez was master of 

Mexico and proceeded to exploit its immense wealth. Scarcely had this object been accomplished, than another Spaniard, Pizarro, led an expedition to Peru (1531) and conquered the Incas, an Indian nation even more civilized but less warlike than the Aztecs. The 

Spaniards employed heartless cruelty in subjecting the natives, whose emperor was burned at the stake on the preposterous charges of heresy and of treason to Charles V. From Peru, Pizarro poured into the coffers of Spain one of the greatest treasures in all history. 

DUTCH ACTIVITIES 

The Dutch were the first to challenge the commercial monopoly of Spain and Portugal. Within a few years after Philip II closed 

Lisbon to the Dutch, the aggressive Netherlanders drove the Portuguese from nearly all of their East Indian possessions and secured 

Sumatra, Ceylon, Malacca, Java, Celebes, and the Spice Islands (Moluccas). A halfway station was established by the Dutch at 

Cape Town, which was regarded as the “frontier fortress of India.” 

This little colony expanded into the interior of the continent until, in time, it came to embrace a great part of southern Africa. Cape 

Colony was lost to the English at the close of the Napoleonic Wars, and the disgruntled Dutch farmers (Boers) trekked northward and founded states, all of which had come under British rule by the opening years of the twentieth century. Incident to the spice trade,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

such Dutch navigators as Abel Tasman made voyages of discovery in the waters of Australia and New Zealand, in the first half of the seventeenth century; but since no effort was made to retain this land, it was eventually settled and annexed by the British. 

Dutch colonization in North America dated from the discovery of the Hudson river in 1609 by Henry Hudson, an Englishman in the service of the Dutch East India Company, who sought a northwest passage to the Indies. The Hudson valley was rich in furs, and within a few years a considerable trade was built up with the Indians. A fort built on Manhattan Island was the nucleus of the flourishing port of New Amsterdam. Until the chartering of the

Dutch West India Company in 1621, New Netherland was a colony of traders, but under the direction of the company a system of colonization was inaugurated.

New Netherland was limited on the north by New France, on the east by New England, and on the south by New Sweden. The latter colony, on Delaware Bay, was on land claimed by the Dutch. 

After the end of the Thirty Years' War, in which Sweden, the Netherlands, and England had been allies, the Dutch proceeded against New Sweden and in 1655 brought it under their rule. In turn, the English laid claims to the region of New Netherland on the basis of the voyages of John Cabot. England wished to seize the 

Dutch colony because New Netherland constituted a wedge between her seaboard possessions and she coveted the lucrative fur trade. The Dutch aided English colonies to evade the unpopular 

Navigation Acts, and were most dangerous maritime rivals. By the middle of the seventeenth century Holland was the greatest commercial nation in the world and had gained control of the carrying trade, not only of Europe, but between European nations and their colonies. This enterprise was, however, contrary to the principles of mercantilism. In order to end it, the British Parliament, under the direction of Oliver Cromwell, passed the Navigation Act of 1651 which permitted only English vessels to bring goods to England, unless the goods came in vessels belonging to the country which had produced them. This and succeeding acts struck a serious blow at 

Dutch navigation and led to a commercial war between England and Holland the first of the commercial struggles which were to supersede the religious wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. At the close of hostilities, the advantage remained with the English. War broke out again during the reign of Charles II (1660-1685), who desired to increase English commerce and found new colonies. The

disputed territory around the Hudson was granted by the king to his brother James, Duke of York; a fleet was dispatched to America, and New Amsterdam surrendered when the populace, much to the disgust of the Dutch governor, Peter Stuyvesant, refused to fight (1664). The colony of New Netherland and the city of New Amsterdam were renamed New York in honor of the Duke of York.

While the conquest of New York meant the end of Dutch colonization on the mainland of North America, the Dutch acquired several rich sugar islands in the West Indies and established a colony in Guiana in South America. During the seventeenth century Holland gained a foothold in Brazil, but was finally driven out by the Portuguese.

FRENCH COLONIZATION 

The foundations of the French colonial empire in America were laid early in the sixteenth century. In 1524 Giovanni da Verrazano, an Italian in the employ of France, explored the eastern coast of North America and claimed possession in the name of the king of France. Jacques Cartier came to America in 1534, seeking a northwest passage to the Indies, but did little more than explore parts of the coast of Canada before returning to Europe. In the following year he explored the St. Lawrence valley, stopping at the present sites of 

Quebec and Montreal. An attempted settlement in 1541 proved unsuccessful. In the second half of the century colonization was resumed under the auspices of Gaspar de Coligny, a great Protestant leader, who wished to found a colony in America as a refuge for his co-religionists. Port Royal, in present South Carolina, founded by

Ribault in 1562, proved to be unsuccessful; and Fort Carolina, near present St. Augustine, Florida, founded by Laudonnière (1564), was destroyed by the Spaniards four years later.

Despite failure of their attempts at settlement, the French developed a profitable trade, particularly in Canada. Interest in colonization was revived after the close of the religious wars in France; through the efforts of Henry IV's minister, Sully, the development of colonization and commerce was stimulated and the forming of mercantile companies marked the beginnings of successful colonization. Port Royal (Annapolis), Nova Scotia, was founded in 

1604, and in 1608 Champlain founded Quebec as the key to the St.

Lawrence Basin and its fur trade. At first French colonization in 

America was limited to this region known as New France. Unfortunately for French colonial enterprise, Champlain incurred the hos-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tility of the powerful Iroquois Confederation, which checked expansion into the region along the eastern and southern shores of Lakes Ontario and Erie. New France grew slowly, consisting only of a series of trading posts, in contrast with the compact settlements of the English. Through the pioneer efforts of the Jesuits, the wilderness was penetrated, missions were established, and the way was opened for the trader and trapper. The reports of Jesuit activities, known as the Relations, stimulated interest in Canada and have provided historians with an invaluable source of knowledge of the time. 

French explorers pressed westward in the hope of reaching the Pacific, which was believed to be not far beyond the Great Lakes. 

Rumors of a great river to the west aroused French interest as a possible outlet to the Pacific. In 1673 Marquette, a Jesuit missionary, and Joliet, a trader, explored the upper Mississippi and after drifting down the river to the Arkansas, returned to New France, convinced that the Mississippi flowed into the Gulf of Mexico and not into the Pacific. Their work was completed in 1682 by La Salle, the most intrepid of French explorers, who followed the Mississippi to its mouth and claimed its basin for the king of France. After an unsuccessful attempt to establish a colony on the coast, further exploration and colonization of this region, known as Louisiana, became the work of Iberville and his brother, Bienville. Settlements were made at 

Biloxi (1699), Mobile (1702), New Orleans (1718), and strategic points in the interior.

In the meantime the French had penetrated into Guiana in South America, and the West Indies, including such islands as St. Christopher, Guadeloupe, and Martinique. Through the efforts of Colbert, the home government employed every means at its disposal to further the advancement of the West Indian colonies. Under the mercantilistic theory, such islands were the best of colonies, for their staple crops of sugar and coffee supplied commodities which otherwise would have to be imported from a rival country. Furthermore, these agricultural colonies provided a ready market for the manufactured goods of the mother country. Thus, at the close of the Seven Years' 

War, the tiny sugar island of Guadeloupe was considered a prize equal in value to Canada; it was only after some hesitation that the 

English decided to take the latter as spoils of war.

ENGLISH COLONIZATION 

Although the voyages of the Cabots were the basis of later English colonial claims in America, no attempt to strengthen these claims

by actual settlement was made until the second half of the sixteenth century. During the Tudor period, England was too engrossed in domestic problems and Continental affairs to give much attention to colonization. She as yet was neither an industrial nor a commercial power; she lacked fluid capital, and, as an international power, was inferior to Spain and France. Under Elizabeth, however, England experienced fundamental internal changes and secured enhanced international prestige.

For a hundred years after Cabot's voyage, the chief activities of the English in America were the search for a northwest passage to the Indies and the plundering of Spanish commerce. While hunting for the northwest passage, Frobisher (1576-1578), Davis (15851587), Hudson (1610-1611), and Baffin (1616) explored the Arctic regions and helped to establish claims to northern Canada. With legal trade with the Spanish colonies closed to them, such hardy English "sea dogs" as Francis Drake and John Hawkins received tacit permission of Elizabeth to prey upon Spanish commerce and treasure ships in time of peace. Thus an irregular English navy was developed with which the Armada was defeated in 1588, and England supplanted Spain as the world's foremost naval power. With the consent of Elizabeth, in 1577, Drake raided the Spanish Main. To escape a hostile Spanish squadron which would have prevented his return across the Atlantic, he sailed around Cape Horn into the Pacific and captured Spanish treasure ships on the way from Peru to Panama. 

He explored the western coast of North America, which he named New Albion and claimed for England. He returned home in 1580 via the East Indies and the Cape of Good Hope.

Even before Hispanic power was checked by the defeat of the Armada, England embarked upon a program of colonization outside the territory claimed by Spain. An attempt to found a colony on 

Newfoundland by Sir Humphrey Gilbert proved to be unsuccessful; a settlement on Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina, met a similar fate. Under the auspices of Sir Walter Raleigh another expedition was sent out in 1587 with Richard Lane as leader. 

Hostilities with Spain prevented the dispatch of supplies and aid to the settlement until 1590, when a relief expedition found the colony abandoned; no trace has ever been found of the settlers. 

Despite inauspicious beginnings, English enterprise did not lag.

In 1607, the London Company founded Jamestown. The next colonies were founded in New England: Plymouth (1620), Massachusetts (1630), and Connecticut (1635). Maryland was colonized in

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

1634 by Lord Baltimore, primarily as a refuge for English Roman

Catholics; Puritan religious intolerance led to the founding of Rhode 

Island (1636) by Roger Williams. English settlement in America was now interrupted by the struggle between king and Parliament. 

With the accession of Charles II, in 1660, English colonization was resumed with the chartering of Carolina (1663), which later was divided into the colonies of North and South Carolina. The gap between New England and the southern colonies was closed by the acquisition or settlement of the middle colonies: New York and New 

Jersey in 1664, Delaware and Pennsylvania in 1681. New Hampshire was given a separate government in 1679, and Plymouth was annexed to Massachusetts in 1691. The English colonies along the Atlantic seaboard were rounded out by Oglethorpe's founding of 

Georgia (1733), the last of the thirteen original colonies.

THE STRUGGLE FOR INDIA 

The early history of India is wrapped in legend, for the native mind lacked an historical sense. Material for its history is furnished by traditions and folklore drawn ultimately from primitive theology. 

Such records are so interwoven with myth and fancy that they provide little valid information. The epic Mahabharata, the Rig-Veda and other collections of hymns and folk-songs, and the commentaries on the Vedic hymns (Upanishads), constitute the holy scriptures of the Hindus and our chief source of knowledge of ancient India. 

These voluminous religious works trace the invasion and subsequent history of the Aryans as they moved down from the north into India. 

The date of this invasion is indefinite, but was probably around 2000 B.C. These northern invaders were the ancestors of the modern 

Hindus. Gradually forcing their way east and south, the Aryans subdued or expelled the dark-skinned aborigines, the Dravidians. 

Early Aryan civilization was simple and pastoral. In time, the social, economic, and political institutions became more complex; centuries before the Christian era, it is possible to perceive the nuclei of trends and developments which have kept India divided and subjugated. 

India was divided into numerous independent states, monarchies, and tribal republics which made the country a prey to invaders. 

While most of the early inhabitants were of the Hindu faith, another great religion was developed during this period by Gautama, the Buddha (the "Enlightened "), of whom very little is known; even the reputed date of his death (483 B.C.) is uncertain. A steady evolution of the social structure of the Hindus eventually brought the caste

system. While the early Aryan civilization seems to have been free from caste, its roots are discernible for centuries before Christ. The number of castes and subcastes has increased until today there are hundreds, derived from the four basic castes of the Brahmans, the highest or priestly caste; the Kshatriyas, the nobles; the Vaishyas, the cultivators of the soil; and the Shudras, the serfs, who are the remnants of the aboriginal tribes. 

The Aryans developed a Hindu culture which became more or less common throughout India and reached its golden age about A.D. 500. 

A diverse population prevented political centralization and engendered petty civil wars which contributed to the downfall of Hindu and the inception of Mohammedan rule (C. A.D. 1000). After the beginning of Mohammedan infiltration, India suffered successive invasions of Turks, Persians, Afghans, and Mongols, culminating, in 1526, with the establishment of the Mogul dynasty by Baber, a descendant of the Tatar leader, Tamerlane. The real founder of the 

Mogul empire in India was Akbar the Great, whose reign (15561605) synchronizes with that of Queen Elizabeth of England. He greatly extended the original bounds of his empire and promoted religious harmony among the rival religious groups, particularly the Hindus and Mohammedans. The reign of his son and successor, Jahangir (1605-1627), saw the beginnings of the power of the English East India Company. Under Shah Jehan, the Mogul empire attained its greatest magnificence. It was he who founded the city of 

Delhi, erected the famous "peacock throne," and built the Taj

Mahal, which is considered the most splendid monument of oriental architecture. The long reign of Aurungzeb (1658-1707) represents the culmination of Mogul power and the greatest territorial extent of the Mogul empire as well as the beginning of its disintegration. After his death, feeble rulers were unable to check the growing strength of the native Mahrattas and the English East India Company. The last of the Great Moguls was deposed after the Sepoy Mutiny (1857) and the government passed into the hands of the British Crown. 

The Portuguese began the European penetration in 1500 and were dominant through the sixteenth century, after which Holland began actively to break the Portuguese monopoly, creating a bitter rivalry which culminated in the victory of the English and the practical expulsion of the French. Neither nation began by annexations, but, according to the custom of the time, gave trade monopolies to companies, the English East India (1600) and the French East India (1664) Companies. The French East India Company was subjected to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the paternalism of the home government and, unlike its English rival, was practically a department of state. As a result the beginnings of the company were marked by severe economic losses, but trading stations, or "factories," were established at Surat (1668) and Masulipatam (1669), together with the more important posts of Chandernagore (1672) and Pondicherry (1674).

Although the French had entered India tardily, they were the first of the Europeans to attempt the task of empire building. The greatest of the French governors-general was Dupleix (1697-1763), who came in 1720 as a member of the Superior Council of Pondicherry, became superintendent at Chandernagore in 1731, and because of his successful administration was appointed governor-general in 1741. 

When he assumed his new position, the relations of the French with the natives were probably stronger than those of the English. Dupleix lacked military leadership, but being adept in diplomacy and intrigue, he took advantage of the impotence of the native rulers and the dissolution of the Mogul empire to strengthen French interests. 

In carrying out this program, he received scant support from Paris or the French East India Company, for Louis XV and the court party had no aspirations for an empire in India. 

By their business ingenuity and enterprise the English secured exceptionally favorable locations for their posts; before the end of the seventeenth century the foundations for their control were securely laid. The first stations were opened at Masulipatam (1611) and at Surat (1612), the latter long remaining the English headquarters on the west coast. The English company proceeded to encroach upon the rights of the Dutch in the Indian archipelago, but the latter were not prepared to lose their hard-won trading and colonial rights in the east without a struggle. Dutch wrath culminated in a massacre at Amboina (1623), in which the Dutch governor tortured and put to death twelve English residents on the charge of conspiring to seize the Dutch fort. In England, the charge was regarded as flimsy and the barbarous proceedings aroused popular indignation. Since England was not ready for war, reparations were not secured for the heirs of the victims until 1654. 

The significance of the Amboina Massacre was the tacit admission by the English East India Company of Dutch claims of a trade monopoly in the Spice Islands and the diversion of its attention to the mainland. The first acquisition of territory on the mainland was 

Madras, where Sir Francis Day built Fort St. George (1640). In 1661 the island of Bombay was ceded to the British Crown. Six years

later, the Crown turned Bombay over to the East India Company for the annual sum of £10. Although only a fishing village, the insular position of Bombay protected it from native raids and its importance increased, until by 1687 the presidency of the west coast was transferred there from Surat. Calcutta, in the rich province of 

Bengal, became an English trading station in 1686, when an older factory was removed to this site.

By 1740, Anglo-French rivalry in India was so bitter that the outbreak of the War of the Austrian Succession, in which France and England were opponents, meant a clash of the rivals in India, although in the past they and the Dutch traders had adopted agreements of neutrality during Continental wars. Dupleix had drawn into the orbit of France several of the native states, and, to supply the deficiency of white troops, had formed an army of native soldiers. ("Sepoys") who were drilled by French officers. In 1746 the French easily captured the English post at Madras, but in the Treaty of Aixla-Chapelle (1748), they restored it to England. The war in India proved to be indecisive since Dupleix had merely profited by the lack of able English leadership.

The interval between the close of the War of the Austrian Succession and the outbreak of the Seven Years' War was marked in India by the War of the Carnatic. This conflict had its origin in 

Indian politics, and came while England and France were at peace. 

Hostilities were not outwardly between the two countries. In a factional dispute over the succession to the throne as Nawab, in the province of the Carnatic, Dupleix supported a pretender whom he could dominate more easily than he could the rightful claimant favored by the English.
