Dupleix succeeded in placing his puppet on the throne, but in the ensuing war was no match for the English and their native allies, who, under the leadership of the youthful Robert Clive, captured and later successfully defended the capital of the 

Carnatic, Arcot (1751). This battle, even more than the battle of

Plassey six years later, strengthened British prestige in India. 

Robert Clive (1725-1774), the founder of the British empire in

India, was sent to Madras as a clerk in the service of the English East India Company. Moody and shiftless, he became so despondent as to attempt suicide. He had arrived at Madras in 1744, at the outbreak of hostilities between the French and English, and saw service around Madras until the war was over, when he returned to civil duties. Clive's early military reputation was established during the 

War of the Carnatic. Contrary to popular belief, it was this war,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and not the later Seven Years' War, in which he bested Dupleix and foiled his plans. Since England and France were at peace (1751), the rival East India companies began to curb their officials in India, for warfare was very expensive and might provide the spark for a Continental war. Dupleix, in particular, was considered by the French company as a turbulent and dangerous spirit. He expended great sums of money and returned meager profits to France, until, in 1754, his policies were reversed by the home officials and he was recalled. 

With the only able French leader out of the way, English success in 

India was assured.

Clive's next work was in Bengal, where British expansion around Calcutta had aroused the suspicion of the local Nawab. In 1756, the 

Nawab seized the English fort there and locked 146 Europeans in a tiny, ill-ventilated, military jail where they passed the sultry June night. Next morning only twenty-three came out alive from this terrible "Black Hole" of Calcutta. Clive led a relief expedition which regained Calcutta with little difficulty. Peace might have been restored if he had not also captured the French settlement of Chandernagore. The Nawab had held aloof from the broils of European war, but enraged by Clive's breach of peace, he allied with the French. Clive, anticipating this step, entered into negotiations with the discontented subjects and bribed a native military commander to turn traitor. In the decisive engagement at Plassey (1757), Clive's little army defeated the Nawab and his superior forces. 

The battle of Plassey made the English dominant in Bengal and laid the foundations of the British empire in India. Elsewhere in 

India, British arms triumphed over the French, who, unable to secure reinforcements from home, were forced to rely upon Sepoys. By the 

Treaty of Paris (1763), closing the Seven Years' War, France recovered her territorial possessions, but was not allowed to maintain troops in Bengal or to build forts. The French were allowed some trading privileges, but their dream of empire was dispelled.

CHAPTER 38 

Europe in the Eighteenth Century

ENGLAND 

"N accordance with the Act of Settlement (1701), Anne became queen of England in 1702. She was the daughter of James II, from whom she had been almost completely estranged because of her espousal of Protestantism, and was the wife of Prince George of Denmark, a nonentity. Modern historians have in large measure modified the traditional conception of her as being weak and dull although she was doubtless easily swayed by personal influences, especially those of the Duke of Marlborough and his wife, the Earl of Godolphin, and Harley. Passionately devoted to the Established 

Church and the preservation of royal authority, she was inclined to dislike the Whigs, who advocated toleration for dissenters and limitation of the royal prerogative. Since two major political parties pursued reasonably consistent policies and maintained fairly stable followings during the reign, party lines were sharply drawn. The 

Tories opposed religious toleration and the growing power of commercial interests. The Whigs urged governmental encouragement of trade in accordance with the mercantilist doctrines. In the main they favored progress and an emphasis on national welfare rather than class interest. The party battle opened with the introduction of the 

Occasional Conformity Bill designed to provide stricter enforcement of the civil disabilities of dissenters. The bill was defeated despite the attempt of the Tories to "tack" it to a money bill, and the Whigs were further strengthened by the elections of 1705.

The War of the Spanish Succession which had begun in the reign of William III was energetically prosecuted on the Continent. Marlborough controlled not only diplomacy but military activities as well, and his victory at Blenheim in 1704 was one of the most decisive of the war. The fundamental mistake of his diplomacy was to push 

Louis XIV too far, thus prolonging the conflict in the face of rising popular complaint.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

In 1707 the Act of Union established the Kingdom of Great Britain, with one parliament for both England and Scotland. The act provided for forty-five Scottish members in the House of Commons and for the selection of sixteen peers from the Scottish baronage for each session, and established free trade between England and Scotland. Traditional enmities, religious differences, and rival economic interests long had impeded the union of the two kingdoms despite the personal union brought about by the coronation of James of Scotland as king of England. The fact that Anne was a Stuart smoothed the path of the negotiations, conducted by the commissioners with great skill and patience. The union dealt a major blow to France, the traditional ally of Scotland, strengthened Anne's position in respect to the Jacobites, who were intriguing against her, and ultimately brought economic benefits to both countries. 

The impeachment of Dr. Henry Sacheverell in 1710 for “sedi tious" sermons produced much excitement. In a sermon at St. Paul's he had inveighed against toleration and the Whigs who sponsored it. 

When tried on charges brought by the Whig ministry and convicted, he received a light sentence which enabled him to pose as a martyr. In the attendant surge of anti-Whig sentiment, Anne dismissed her Whig ministers, replaced them by Tories, and broke off her relations with "Mrs. Freeman," as she called the Duchess of 

Marlborough. The Duke of Marlborough clung to power, but soon was engulfed by popular opposition to the war. He was dismissed from command for misappropriation of funds, which he probably had used for secret service activities. New peers created after his fall gave the Tories complete control of the House of Lords. 

The death of Anne thwarted the Tory pro-Stuart intrigues of Bolingbroke to prevent the Hanoverian succession to the crown, and 

George I (1714-1727), elector of Hanover, was called to the throne in accordance with the succession settlement. The new ruler was stolid, petulant, and disdainful toward English customs and practices, but his justice, dependability, and frugality were acceptable characteristics. Although his chief interests lay in Hanover, they coincided in the main with those of England. "The king governed Hanover and the Whigs governed England." His ignorance of the English language and the usages of parliamentary government forced him to rely on his ministers and hastened the evolution of the cabinet system of government.

Bolingbroke, who had been forced to flee to France as a result of the premature disclosure of his earlier plot to bring in the Stuart

Pretender, now sought to use a threatened uprising in the north, to bring about the restoration of the old dynasty. This uprising of 1715, however, was quelled before it seriously endangered the Hanoverian government.

Townshend, who had been George's chief adviser since his accession, was dismissed in 1716 largely because of his attitude towards the treaty with France, concluded in that year. Stanhope, his successor, was interested primarily in financial reform, and his creation of a sinking fund was a constructive measure; but a project to refund the public debt by having the holders of governmental annuities exchange them for shares in the South Sea Company ended in disaster. To forestall competition, especially from the Bank of England, the company paid a bonus to the government and also distributed shares gratuitously to important personages. The shares soared on a wave of frenzied speculation. Companies were formed for every type of mad project - to raise hulks off the coast of Ireland, to extract oil from sun-flower seeds, to make perpetual motion machines, and even to finance "an undertaking in due time to be revealed." The collapse of the "Mississippi Bubble" in France precipitated the debacle of the South Sea venture. Stanhope was forced to resign and was replaced by Robert Walpole. The defunct company's affairs were terminated on as equitable a basis as possible but many political figures were ruined as a result of the scandalous revelations that accompanied the intricate work of liquidation. 

Robert Walpole, who now became chiefly responsible for the formulation of governmental policy until his fall in 1742, had followed his father as a member of Parliament from one of the two "pocket boroughs" controlled by the family. He was appointed to the council of Prince George of Denmark, husband of Queen Anne, and in 1707 became Secretary of War. As one of the managers of the impeachment of Dr. Sacheverell, he resigned with the party overturn of 1710. With the accession of George I he was made Paymaster of the Royal Forces but within a year he was elevated to the positions of First Commissioner of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer. Energetic, likable despite frequent boorishness of manner, and punctual almost to a fault, he possessed keen judgment and a thorough grasp of problems of finance, while his accurate appraisal of men and adroit use of patronage enabled him to strengthen his dominance in the ministry and retain his control of the Commons.

Since George II (1727-1760) did not attend cabinet sessions, Wal-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

22 pole presided over the meetings and became "the first prime minister in fact if not in theory. The basic principles of cabinet government had been evolved by the absence of the sovereign from its sessions, the chief minister's choice of his colleagues, and ministerial responsibility to Parliament. 

Few brilliant accomplishments distinguished Walpole's ministry, yet his devotion to peace, encouragement of trade, and financial reforms were constructive policies of the first magnitude. Many export duties were removed and the Navigation Acts were modified for the benefit of colonial rice and sugar planters; even a number of import duties were removed or lowered. His excise bill, however, stirred up so much popular opposition that it was withdrawn. The measure provided that tobacco and wine should be stored in warehouses and taxed upon withdrawal unless re-exported. When tension arose between England and Spain as a result of the "Jenkins' Ear" incident, soon to be described, Walpole strove to avert war. 

He ultimately bowed to public sentiment, but too late, for his opposition to the war was the fundamental cause of the fall of his ministry in 1742. 

Active participation in Continental affairs followed the retirement of Walpole. The War of Jenkins' Ear was soon eclipsed by a larger struggle the War of the Austrian Succession. With English troops on the Continent, the Stuart banner was again unfurled in the north in 1745. "Bonnie Prince Charlie" decided on an invasion of England. His enterprise precipitated a run on the Bank of England, but the battle of Culloden Moor (1746), the last major battle on English soil, and the reprisals of "Butcher" Cumberland crushed the 

Stuart cause. The inconclusive Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) 

brought the Continental war to a close with Frederick the Great of Prussia as virtually the sole beneficiary. The brief interlude of the 

Pelham ministry was devoted primarily to financial reform, but the outbreak of the Seven Years' War in 1756 again directed the attention of the English government to foreign affairs with William 

Pitt as the guiding spirit.

As a result of realignments known as the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756, England was allied with Prussia in sole opposition to the coalition of France, Austria, and Spain. The loss of Minorca to the 

French in 1756 was a great blow and Admiral Byng was executed as a sacrifice to the national hysteria excited by the fear of French dominance in the Mediterranean. But French expansion in India, under the able leadership of Dupleix, was more than matched by the

genius of Robert Clive, whose victory in the battle of Plassey (1757) was the beginning of the expulsion of the French from their holdings. The main theatre of the war, however, was in North America. 

Louisburg and Duquesne were captured by English and colonial forces and the victory was sealed by Wolfe's capture of Quebec.

The accession of George III (1760-1820) inaugurated an important era in English history. The new ruler "uncultivated by study and overgrown by prejudice " was stubbornly resolved to be a king in fact as well as in name although his limited administrative talents and the entrenchment of the cabinet system foredoomed efforts to revive personal rule. A "King's Party" was created; as patronage was shifted to these new Tories, the Whigs, including Pitt and Newcastle, retired, and George Grenville became Prime Minister. 

Disaffection mounted during the Grenville ministry. John Wilkes was prosecuted for his attacks on the government, involving issues of prime constitutional significance, such as freedom of the press and the right to criticize the government. Much more formidable, however, was the rising tide of resentment engendered in the American Colonies by the imposition of taxes designed to compensate, in a measure, for the cost of the wars with France. The Sugar Act (1764) lowered considerably the tax on molasses from the non- English West Indies but provided for strict enforcement, and an extension of the Mutiny Act made the Colonies liable for the quartering of troops. Great opposition was incited by the Stamp Act of 

1765 which, as an internal levy, was an unprecedented extension of the taxing power of the mother country. A "Stamp Act Congress " stated the determined opposition of the Colonies to the imposition of internal taxation without representation in Parliament. 

Tension eased with the repeal of the Stamp Act by the Rockingham ministry in 1766, but the retirement of Chatham (Pitt) from the Chatham-Grafton ministry depressed hopes for a definitive and amicable settlement of the colonial issues.

Lord Townshend's revenue measures imposing duties on tea, lead, glass, and paints reopened the controversy with the Colonies, despite the fact that the right of Parliament to levy customs duties had not been challenged, and colonial resentment reached a critical stage in the North ministry. The "Boston Massacre" led to a wave of denunciatory pamphlets, and the attempt of the government to aid the East India Company to dispose of a large surplus of tea by permitting it to be sent to the Colonies subject only to a tax of three pence

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

per pound collectible at American ports led to the famous "Boston Tea Party." As a reprisal the British government passed the " Intolerable Acts" of 1774 which in large measure were responsible for the meeting of the first Continental Congress in 1774. The battles of 

Lexington and Concord and the appointment of Washington as commander-in-chief of the armed forces raised by Congress destroyed the last chance of conciliation. On July 4, 1776, the Colonies proclaimed their independence in a Declaration that attributed sundry oppressive acts to the King rather than to Parliament. It was a shrewd combination of an appeal to the Whig's hostility to George 

III and of the colonies' denial of Parliament's authority over them.

In the first phase of the war the struggle was localized, but with the entrance of France on the side of the colonists, following Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga, European ramifications overshadowed the military activities in America. French aid was a factor of paramount significance in the American victory. The surrender of Cornwallis at Yorktown was forced by the timely coöperation of the French fleet with Washington's army. Minorca was again lost in 1782 and a number of English possessions in the West Indies likewise were seized by the French. Military and naval reverses accentuated domestic discord in Britain. Proposals to remove Catholic disabilities precipitated the serious Gordon riots in London. Demands for governmental reform crystallized in the formation of committees of correspondence, the preparation of petitions, and the mounting strength of the Whigs. The disaffection culminated in the fall of the North ministry in March of 1782 and the inauguration of a series of reforms under the auspices of Rockingham's Whig cabinet. It was not until September of 1783, however, that peace was concluded by the coalition government of Fox and North, a successful defense of Gibraltar and Rodney's victory in the West

Indies having placed Britain in a more favorable bargaining position. 

The treaty acknowledged the independence of the Thirteen Colonies, with the northern boundary at the Great Lakes and the western at the Mississippi, navigation of which was to be open to both countries. France received negligible colonial concessions, while Spain received Minorca and East Florida. The British Empire had received a terrific blow, and discouragement and skepticism marked the end of the old colonial system. Yet it soon became evident that the great development of the Empire was still to come.

FRANCE 

When the seventy-two year reign of Louis XIV closed with his death in 1715, the throne passed to his great-grandson, Louis XV (1715-1774) who was then but five and one half years of age. The late king had arranged for the Duke of Orleans to be regent, but the supervision of the young king was entrusted to the Duke of Maine. By revocation of the decrees of 1667 and 1673 which had abridged the powers of the Parlement of Paris, Orleans secured the support of that body in bringing about the exile of the Duke of Maine. Fleury, bishop of Frejus, became the tutor of young Louis and thus laid the foundations of a personal influence over him that subsequently was to give him enormous power and pave the way to his attainment of the cardinal's hat.

The financial stringency created by the disastrous wars of the preceding reign was in no wise abated by the feeble efforts of the Orleans regime. The public debt stood at about 90,000,000 livres, and, after proposals to repudiate most of the debt were discarded, the government lent a ready ear to the plans of John Law that led to ultimate disaster. Law, the son of an Edinburgh goldsmith and banker, had gained considerable experience in banking in Scotland, Holland, and Italy, although his career had been quite disreputable prior to his arrival in France. In common with many later advocates of fiscal heresy, he believed that the prosperity of a country was directly proportional to the amount of currency in circulation and in 1715 he explained his schemes to the French ministers. In accordance with his advice, a bank was established in the spring of the ensuing year which issued paper money ostensibly redeemable in coin upon demand. Branches of the bank were founded in the provinces, and in 1718 the central bank became known as the Royal Bank. Law was made Master of Revenues and upon his espousal of the Catholic faith he was promoted to the position of Controller- 

General of Finance. 

In the meantime the Mississippi Stock Company was founded whose shares were issued to raise capital for the exploitation of the resources of the Mississippi valley as well as for other more nebulous purposes. The bank backed the shares, and adroit manipulation, buoyed up by a wave of speculation, caused the price of the shares to soar despite the fact that the amount of paper redeemable in coin was eighty times the amount of available specie. The inevitable reaction came when demands for redemption began to exceed

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the new subscriptions to stock, and the company soon proved completely unable to carry the burden of its obligations. The government tried to avert disaster by granting new monopolies to the company; and when the Parlement of Paris refused to register these new laws, lettres de cachet were issued against the members who were thereupon exiled to Pontois. These measures naturally failed, and the bursting of the "Mississippi Bubble " in the summer of 1720 was a financial catastrophe to the French government that drove it another long step along the road to insolvency. 

Religious strife was revived with the attempts to enforce the bull Unigenitus, issued by Pope Clement XI in 1713 against the Jansenists. This sect had been formed by Cornelius Jansen (1585-1638), who based his principles on the doctrine of predestination as taught by St. Augustine. Spirituality was emphasized as a reaction against abstruse theology and perfunctory conformity, but the leaders of the movement always insisted that they had no intention of leaving the Catholic Church. Remnants of the Fronde affiliated with the sect, while the adherence of powerful intellectuals such as Pascal, Arnauld, and Racine gave new vigor to the movement. The Lateran 

Council of 1728 failed to establish peace. While the "Acceptants' recognized the Lateran decision, the “ Appellants" continued to adhere to the Jansenist principles. Fleury gave fresh vigor to the controversy by his condemnation of the Bishop of Senez, and when Deacon Paris died and was buried at St. Médard, thousands believed that miracles of healing were worked at the tomb of this Jansenist sympathizer. 99 The Jesuits naturally urged persecution of the sect, and the Abbé Dubois, who had guided the foreign policy of France in the successful resistance to Spanish claims in Italy, likewise advocated their suppression as a step toward the cardinalate, which he attained in 1722, a year before his death. The Parlement of Paris made Jansenism a political weapon, for anti-clericalism in large measure reflected anti-monarchial sentiments. Indeed, as modern historians have pointed out, the popular reception of the Jansenist teachings was a symptom of the profound discontent in France that was to culminate in revolution.

Shortly after the death of the Duke of Orleans in 1723, the Duke of Bourbon became the chief minister of the king, who assumed personal direction of the government the same year. Negotiations for the marriage of the monarch occupied the attentions of the new minister, since the original plan for the king to marry the Spanish

Infanta had been abandoned. It is said that ninety-nine prospective brides were considered before Marie, daughter of Stanislaus, an exiled claimant to the Polish throne, was chosen. The decision was not very popular in view of the poverty and relative obscurity of the bride's family. Voltaire remarked that a tax would probably be levied on the French people to provide a trousseau for the bride. The marriage led to a greater French interest in the affairs of Poland, but the efforts of Louis XV in behalf of his father-in-law in the War of the Polish Succession (1733-1738) were little more than a gesture. 

The queen did not long hold the affections of her husband, who soon came under the influences of a succession of mistresses such as 

Madame de Pompadour and Madame du Barry.

Relations between the monarchy and the Parlement of Paris remained uneasy throughout the reign and led to several grave crises. 

Ever since the Middle Ages the Parlement had claimed the right to annul royal decrees by refusal to register them. To curb these annulments, Louis employed a procedure known as a "Bed of Justice." 

By this procedure the king was solemnly brought before the Parlement to order the body to register the laws in question. As we have seen, the members of the Parlement had been exiled because of their refusal to register the grants of monopoly to the Mississippi Company. When the last rites of the church were denied to a cleric of 

Jansenist sympathies, the Parlement vigorously protested and in 1753 drew up the "Grand Remonstrances" in which the clergy were severely censured and the king was reminded that even he owed obedience to law. The Parlement, which already had begun to speak of the necessity for the convocation of an Estates-General, was exiled. But the king's joy at the birth of the future Louis XVI helped to allay the discord, and the exiled members were quietly permitted to return to Paris. Again, when a controversy broke out between the king and the Parlement over the deposition of the Duke d'Aiguillon as governor of Brittany, the king issued edicts declaring that he was responsible to God alone for the exercise of his authority and that the Parlement could not impose any limits to royal powers. The 

Parlement registered the edicts under protest, but refused to continue its sessions and was again exiled. This constitutional struggle, like the 

Jansenist movement, was a harbinger of the Revolution. Popular discontent was accentuated by continued high prices, the increasingly heavy burden of taxation, resentment against the power of Madame de Pompadour, and the reverses suffered by France in the 

Seven Years' War (1756-1763) until in 1757 an attempt was even

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

made to assassinate the king. However, despite the evidence of mounting disaffection Louis "opened his mouth, said little, and thought not at all," while "the fate of France began to be decided in boudoirs, the centers of intrigue and ambition." 

RUSSIA 

An outstanding development of the eighteenth century was the westernization of Russia and its emergence as a great power. The beginnings of Russia go back to the establishment of trading posts in the Dnieper valley by the Swedes, or Varangians. Kiev and 

Novgorod became thriving commercial centers. The Slavic natives called the newcomers "Rous," or men of the oar, and the word Russia is derived from this root. Trade connections with the Byzantine Empire were close, for Constantinople was the terminus for much of the trade from the Dnieper valley. Commercial contacts facilitated diffusion of Byzantine cultural influences, with the result that Vladimir the Great (980-1015), ruler of Kiev, and with him the country, was converted to the Byzantine or Greek Orthodox form of Christianity. 

The Russian principalities were invaded and conquered by the 

Asiatic Tatars in the thirteenth century. The leaders of the "Golden

Horde " levied heavy tribute and imposed military service, but did not greatly alter the political organization. Withdrawal of the Tatars was facilitated by the disintegration of the great Mongolian Empire that followed the death of Tamerlane in 1405 and the resumption of the expansion of the Ottoman Turks. Moscow became the center of the wars of liberation, but the expulsion of the Tatars was not completed until the second half of the fifteenth century. Ivan the 

Great (1462-1505) established the authority of Moscow over about eighty principalities. Great Novgorod was annexed, and the boyars, or nobles, were held to a greater degree of loyalty to the ruler by the abolition of the right of "transmigration," or transfer of their allegiance to other lords. Ivan the Terrible (1533-1584), one of the most brutal rulers in history, virtually completed the annexation of the Tatar khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan and assumed the title of "czar." After 1577, in which year a disastrous fire destroyed a large part of Moscow, he introduced some reforms in the laws and their administration and among the clergy, and the czar relied increasingly on ministers of humble birth in order to curtail the power of the boyars. After threatening to abdicate, Ivan created the oprichina, that is, he and about 1000 nobles and lesser dignitaries retired to

LOUIS XIV CATHERINE THE GREAT ADAM SMITH FREDERICK THE GREAT

THE EAST INDIA HOUSE, LONDON THE SIGNING OF THE DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE

estates set aside for the purpose, and in large measure excluded themselves from contact with the rest of the country. In 1553 the English explorer, Richard Chancellor, visited the court of Ivan, and two years later a treaty was concluded extending commercial rights to England. The colonization of Siberia was begun during the reign, but Ivan's attempt to secure a foothold on the Baltic was frustrated by the energy of King Stephen Báthory of Poland. 

After the death of Ivan the Terrible, Boris Goudonov, a noble of vast wealth and power, served as regent for Theodore I, upon whose death in 1598, he was crowned as czar. Moscow became a patriarchate of the Orthodox Church during his reign with the formal permission of the Patriarch of Constantinople. Young nobles were sent to study abroad, and there was a considerable influx of foreigners. The serfs were bound to the soil by an ukase, or decree, of 1597, but efforts were made to ameliorate the harshness of their treatment by the landlords. Virtual anarchy followed the death of Boris in 

1605, but order was restored with the coronation of Michael Romanov in 1613, which marked the foundation of the dynasty destined to rule Russia until the revolution of 1917. 

Major progress in the modernization of Russia began with the reign of Peter the Great (1689-1725). The czar was coarse, sensuous to the point of bestiality, and almost incredibly cruel. Yet he was passionately devoted to the attainment of objectives which he considered of paramount importance to the prosperity and prestige of the empire. In 1695 he failed in an attempt to capture Azov from the 

Turks, but with indomitable energy he supervised the construction of a small navy which proved to be the decisive factor in his subsequent capture of the city.

Largely as a result of the influence of a Swiss minister, Lefort, who had gained the confidence of the czar, Peter promoted the influx of western institutions and ideas. In 1697 a great embassy of young nobles, headed by Peter himself, visited Holland, Prussia, and Austria. As Peter visited the more enlightened countries of 

Europe, he attended sessions of legislative bodies, inspected factories and shipyards, and even donned workman's attire to labor at various trades in order to familiarize himself with western industrial techniques which he hoped to introduce in his native land. 

Upon return to Russia he forced the adoption of western ideas on his subjects. Customs hallowed by centuries of tradition were ruthlessly abolished. The men were ordered to shave and to shorten their coats, and barbers and tailors were stationed at strategic points

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

to enforce these regulations. Women were exempted from the harem-like restrictions of the tirim and forced to conform to new usages in dress. Industries were modernized, the immigration of foreign craftsmen was encouraged, and industrial establishments, especially iron works, were founded. Paper money was introduced, and a number of mints were established to provide a currency more adequate for the conduct of trade. A School of Navigation and 

Mathematics was founded in 1702 and in the following year another school was created to offer instruction in geography, ethics, philosophy, and Latin. Young nobles were required to secure an education prior to marriage. The first Russian newspaper was founded in 1703 with royal approval and encouragement. Efforts were made to safeguard towns and cities against fires. The introduction of the principle of primogeniture prevented the disintegration of the landed estates of the nobility, while a law forbade the transfer of serfs unless family groups were kept together. 

The administrative bureaucracy, hitherto a model of ineptitude and corruption, was thoroughly revamped. Graft was largely eliminated and inefficiency gave way to the methods of more progressive countries. A budget was introduced in 1710, and attempts were made to secure greater uniformity in taxation. A central fiscal board and local tax offices were created to facilitate the collection of revenues which were increased by a government monopoly on the sale of spirituous liquors. The empire was divided into eight "governments," or administrative areas, which in turn were organized into districts governed by presidents and councils elected by the gentry.

There was much resentment against the policies of the czar, who was often called "Anti-Christ" by the enemies of reform. Menshikov, a former pie-seller who had become the czar's most trusted minister, also was bitterly hated. The disaffection culminated in a revolt of the imperial bodyguard (Streltsi) which was pitilessly suppressed. Peter personally decapitated many of the soldiers implicated in the uprising after they had been submitted to prolonged and horrible tortures.

Economic development of the country was hindered by the dearth of harbors. Archangel, on the White Sea, was frozen during the greater part of the year, and the Siberian ports, prior to the era of railways, were too remote to be of much service. Peter accordingly resolved to secure a "window" on the Baltic. His purpose was realized with the cession by Sweden of a strip of coast on the Baltic

as a result of the Great Northern War. Here he founded St. Petersburg, which in the face of discouraging obstacles was built to become the capital and leading port. At Peter's death, Russia was a major European power, destined to play an important role in international affairs especially in the reigns of Elizabeth (1741-1762) and 

Catherine the Great (1762-1796). Under Catherine, the Crimea was annexed, Russia was enlarged by the partition of Poland, and the internal reforms carried out, or at least instituted, justify, as we shall see, the inclusion of Catherine among the "Benevolent Despots" of the eighteenth century.

PRUSSIA 

The emergence of Prussia as a major European power was another striking phenomenon of the eighteenth century. The nucleus of this state was the Margravate of Brandenburg, which had been established along the lower Elbe by Henry I of Germany (919–936) to defend the northeastern frontier of his kingdom against incursions of Wends and Poles. In 1133 Lothair bestowed the Mark on Albert the Bear in line with his policy of strengthening the frontier against attacks of the Slavs. Albert extended the boundaries of the Mark eastward to the Oder. In 1415 the Emperor Sigismund granted the Margravate, which had been elevated to the dignity of an electorate by the Golden Bull of Charles IV (1356), to Frederick of Hohenzollern, and under this dynasty its destiny was to be achieved. Prussia, the population of which was basically Slavic, was conquered and christianized as a result of the efforts of the Teutonic Knights, a crusading order founded in 1190. Under the leadership of Herman Salza, grand-master of the order, the knights directed their military efforts against Prussia in 1226. In 1255 the advance of conquest was marked by the founding of Königsberg, and fifty-six years later Danzig was established. Poland checked the further expansion of the power of the knights, but the founding of monasteries, bishoprics, and towns had consistently accompanied their conquests up to this point and ensured the permanence of their work. 

In 1619 Brandenburg and Prussia were joined under the rule of 

George William (1619-1640). The elector proved incompetent to profit from conditions brought about in north Germany by the Thirty Years' War. His dominions were overrun by the contending armies, and the outlook was discouraging until the accession of 

Frederick William, the Great Elector (1640-1688), opened a new era in the history of Brandenburg-Prussia.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

As a result of the genius of the Great Elector, the impoverished, disorganized electorate was transformed into a strong, centralized state, the military power of which was beginning to attract the attention of the major European countries. Natural resources were developed, settlement of frugal, capable, Dutch farmers was encouraged, and the immigration of French Huguenots, refugees from religious persecution, gave impetus to the development of industries. 

Berlin was largely rebuilt, and the construction of a canal between the Oder and Spree gave the city access to the Baltic and overcame a great obstacle in the way of economic progress. An efficient administration was set up, with a Council of State as its central organ and appointed stadtholders as local officials. The landtagen, or local diets, were virtually discontinued, and refractory nobles were bent to the will of the elector so that centralized government became a reality. A standing army of 30,000 trained men replaced the crude, undisciplined levies which hitherto had constituted the only available military force.

The foreign policy of the elector, while not so successful as his domestic measures, contributed to the growing power of the state. 

He did not gain Pomerania by the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, but the recognition of Calvinism was in some measure a victory for the Great Elector, who was a devout Calvinist, although he made no effort to disturb the freedom of worship enjoyed by the Lutherans. 

His marriage to Louisa Henrietta of Orange ensured the friendship of a powerful Protestant house and enhanced the prestige of the Hohenzollerns. As a result of adroit diplomacy during the war between Poland and Sweden, the Treaty of Oliva, 1660, gave East 

Prussia to the Elector, and the nominal suzerainty of Poland in Prussia ultimately was terminated. In 1701, Frederick, son of the Great 

Elector, was crowned as "King in Prussia." Preoccupied with the trappings of royalty, he did little to advance the prosperity or prestige of the kingdom. His reign was not without importance, however, for in 1696 a Royal Academy of Arts was founded, followed four years later by an Academy of Sciences. The University of 

Halle, destined to become a leading intellectual center of continental Europe, was established in 1694. 

Under Frederick William I (1713-1740), Prussia became a veritable armed camp. Irascible and parsimonious, the king considered no expenditure too large if it enhanced the strength of his beloved army. 

Conscription and recruiting that even extended into foreign countries assembled tall, robust soldiers. Harsh discipline and constant

practice kept the efficiency of the "blue children" at a high level. 

By 1740 Prussia, twelfth among the European countries in population, had an army that ranked fourth a force of about 90,000, the maintenance of which absorbed about five-sevenths of the income of the government.

The populace was impelled to industry by the forceful policies of the ruler. The tall figure of the king, clad in an old army overcoat, was a familiar sight on the streets of Berlin. Idlers were accosted and, if not employed, soundly belabored with the king's cudgel and marched off to work. Even the apple-women were required to busy themselves with knitting while awaiting customers. A code issued in 

1723 reorganized the administrative system of the kingdom and made it a model of efficiency. Prussia made great progress under Frederick 

William, but it was in his reign, also, that "all the most unlovely and forbidding qualities of Prussianism were scourged into the kingdom." 

Frederick William's son was a disappointment to him. The future 

Frederick the Great preferred French verses to martial exercises, and practice on the flute to the deliberations of the council chamber. 

Parental discipline, which went to the length of corporal punishment in the sight of the soldiery, was unavailing. Finally, Frederick and his only intimate friend fled to Paris. The fugitives were apprehended, and upon their return to Prussia Frederick was forced to witness the execution of his beloved companion. His spirit at last was crushed; he served his apprenticeship in army and bureaucracy, but he did not abandon his friendship with Voltaire or his cultural interests. 

When Frederick (1740-1786) came to the throne, his unhappy youth was reflected in cynicism, ruthlessness, and duplicity. Austria was shorn of Silesia in the War of the Austrian Succession; West 

Prussia was acquired as a result of the First Partition of Poland for which Frederick was largely responsible. As will be seen, Prussia, aided by subsidies from England in accordance with the Westminster agreement of 1756, was the outstanding power during the Seven 

Years' War.

The internal reforms of the king are far more creditable than his foreign policies. Religious toleration promoted immigration of 

Huguenots and other refugees from religious persecution whose entry into the country was an economic asset. Serfdom was abolished on crown estates and material progress was made toward general emancipation. Reclamation projects and technical innovations in-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

creased the productivity of agriculture. Factories were established in many cases by royal subsidies for the manufacture of linen, woolen cloth, silk, glass, and porcelain. As the "First Servant of the 

State," as he liked to call himself, Frederick was greatly interested in efforts to raise the efficiency of the administration to an even higher level. Aided by Cocceji, a famous jurist, he introduced a number of salutary changes in the organization and procedure of the courts.

INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS IN THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY 

The Treaty of Utrecht, which terminated the War of the Spanish Succession, opened a new era in European diplomacy. England secured Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Hudson Bay from France and the dissolution of the great French colonial empire had begun. 

Spain ceded Gibraltar and Minorca to England and the Spanish Netherlands to Austria; the asiento permitted a modicum of English trade with Spanish America and gave the English a monopoly of the slave trade to the Spanish dependencies. Milan and Parma passed to the control of Austria.

By the Treaty of Rastadt (1714), France completed her renunciation of Italian interests by the cession of Sardinia and Naples to Austria. Sicily was assigned to the Duke of Savoy. In return for these concessions, France received a clear title to Alsace and Lorraine, for the Hapsburgs confirmed the provisions of the Treaty of Westphalia in respect to these territories.

The period 1714-1720 was characterized by the rivalry of Austria and Spain for Italian territory. Elizabeth of Parma, the Spanish queen, was ambitious to secure a crown for her son, Don Carlos, and concentrated her desire on the acquisition of Sardinia and Sicily. 

A Quadruple Alliance, comprised of England, France, Holland, and the Empire, was formed in 1720 to frustrate Spanish policy. By a compromise Sicily was transferred to the Empire and Don Carlos was promised the succession to Parma and Tuscany. 

Various claims and interests in Italy were projected into the War of the Polish Succession (1733-1738). The immediate cause of the war was a disputed election to the Polish throne. Louis XV of France backed the candidacy of his father-in-law, Stanislaus Leszczynski;

Russia, aided by Austria, supported Augustus of Saxony. The Third 

Treaty of Vienna (1738) brought the struggle to a close. Stanislaus renounced his claims to Poland and received Lorraine and the Duchy of Bar as compensation. Francis, duke of Lorraine, received Tus-

cany, in return for his cession of Lorraine, and married Maria Theresa, heiress to the Hapsburg possessions. Don Carlos of Spain renounced his claims to Parma and Milan, but was crowned king of the Two Sicilies (Naples and Sicily). The treaty stabilized Italian issues until the Napoleonic era. A Spanish dynasty ruled the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies; Austria controlled north Italy, while central Italy remained under the rule of the papacy. 

The chief objective of the diplomacy of the Emperor Charles VI had been secured with ratification of the Pragmatic Sanction, which ostensibly assured the succession of his daughter, Maria Theresa. 

When Charles died, however, Frederick the Great of Prussia repudiated the Pragmatic Sanction by the seizure of Silesia, and precipitated the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748). France, in conformity to her traditional enmity towards the Hapsburgs, allied with Prussia; war with Sweden kept Russia out of the struggle. 

Frederick gained several smashing victories, and, after his annexation of Silesia was confirmed by the Treaty of Berlin (1742), withdrew from the war. France, left in the lurch, now bore the brunt of Austrian wrath. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) ended the war practically on the basis of the status quo ante. 

When the War of the Austrian Succession began on the Continent, England and Spain were engaged in the "War of Jenkins' Ear." England had greatly exceeded the commercial privileges granted her by the asiento, and the Spanish authorities endeavored to stop the illicit trade. Captain Jenkins, charged with smuggling, suffered the amputation of an ear by a Spanish officer as punishment. 

Some years later upon return to England Jenkins complained of the treatment he had received and even Parliament took cognizance of it. Public indignation, aroused by this and other alleged atrocities, pushed England into war despite the opposition of the Walpole ministry. 

In 1756 a shift in traditional alliances occurred of such significance as to justify the term "Diplomatic Revolution." Count Kaunitz, the

Austrian foreign minister, proposed an alliance with France. After all, few valid reasons for Bourbon-Hapsburg hostility remained after the liquidation of the Italian issues. France, to be sure, coveted the 

Austrian Netherlands, but it was clear that her real enemy was 

Prussia. Common enmity towards Prussia, therefore, drew France and Austria together, and an alliance was made inevitable by the conclusion of the Convention of Westminster in January of 1756 between Frederick the Great and England, according to which Great

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Britain agreed to furnish subsidies to Frederick in return for his protection of the Electorate of Hanover. 66 The new alignments immediately were tested by the Seven Years' War (1756-1763). An English army under General Braddock had been sent to arrest French expansion in the Ohio valley. Braddock and his colonial allies were ambushed by a force of French and Indians and well-nigh annihilated. In the ensuing general war, England won America on the continent of Europe." Heavy subsidies financed Frederick's brilliant Continental campaigns that won the victories of Rossback and Leuthen. American colonial armies, aided by British forces, prosecuted the war in North America; General 

Wolfe defeated the French under Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham and captured Quebec. By 1759, however, Frederick was hard pressed on the Continent as the "three furies," as he called Maria 

Theresa, Madame de Pompadour, and Empress Elizabeth of Russia, strove to bring about his ruin. In 1761, Bute, who had succeeded Pitt, stopped the payment of subsidies, and Frederick's plight became desperate. The death of Elizabeth of Russia saved him, for Peter III, the new czar, hastened to make peace. The Treaty of Paris (1763) brought hostilities between England and France to a close. France surrendered Canada and agreed to evacuate her troops from India, retaining some trading concessions. Louisiana was ceded to Spain, while Florida passed to England. Only remnants survived the crash of the French colonial empire. Enormous financial outlays occasioned by the wars, and the loss of colonies so reduced the potential sources of revenue that by 1763 the French government was on the verge of bankruptcy. The ensuing Treaty of Hubertusburg between 

Prussia and Austria again confirmed the former's possession of Silesia.

French intervention in the American Revolution was a decisive factor in the attainment of American independence. France gained nothing in return but a measure of prestige and revenge for her losses in 1713 and 1763. England's loss of the Thirteen Colonies produced, in Europe, a skepticism in regard to colonization and a lull in imperialistic interests until the effects of the Industrial Revolution became manifest. 

The several partitions of Poland are among the most tragic episodes of history. With frontiers touched by those of Europe's most powerful nations, Austria, Russia, and Prussia, Poland's energies were sapped by internal dissension. The throne of the kingdom was elective, which made foreign interference inevitable. Economic

prosperity was curtailed by the necessity of supporting a disproportionately large, parasitic nobility. The Diet, made up of nobles and clergy, was impotent. The Liberum veto, in effect, required unanimity for any action, while, by a procedure known as “Exploding the Diet,” a single member could force adjournment of the body. 

In 1772, the three bordering nations each appropriated sections of Polish territory. In 1793, with French intervention precluded by the 

Revolution, Prussia and Russia carried through a second partition. 

With a third partition in 1795 by Prussia, Austria, and Russia, Poland disappeared from the map of Europe. Polish sovereignty was not restored until the Versailles Treaty of 1919, only to be lost again in 1939. 

During all the wars and diplomatic conflicts of the eighteenth century, the idea of "balance of power" was paramount. The acquisition of colonies complicated the issue. Concentration of colonial interests was just as disruptive of European equilibrium as more immediate dynastic interests on the Continent. The wars and the treaties they entailed flouted the doctrine of "natural frontiers" to which much lip service was rendered. Rights of minorities were disregarded, and dynastic ambitions took precedence over national interests. Since the governments of the Continental nations were despotic, there could be no popular check on policies that often were motivated by the desire of rulers for aggrandizement, even at the expense of the prosperity of their own subjects. Secret diplomacy and the tortuous intrigues of court personages with ill-defined responsibility accentuated general insecurity.

CHAPTER 39 The Age of Enlightenment 

HE seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were characterized by the advance of rationalism and the consequent weakening of dogmatism and superstition. In large measure, the intellectual currents were a prolongation of the movements initiated during the Renaissance. New ideas, as always, had to make headway against the innate conservatism of man that makes him impatient of doubt and loath to entertain ideas that disturb his mental complacency. Ecclesiastical authority, both Catholic and Protestant, clung tenaciously to revealed truth which it professed to expound. 

Ideas that were repugnant to ecclesiastical dogmatism were suppressed, in many instances with the connivance of secular authority. 

The works of Francis Bacon (1561-1626) were a powerful factor in producing a more critical intellectual attitude. In his Advancement of Learning, he held that the primary sources of error in human reasoning were reverence for antiquity, blind acceptance of popular ideas, failure to employ critical observation and experiment, and intellectual impatience, which promotes hasty acceptance of tenuous conclusions. In the Organum, he dealt with the sources of fallacious reasoning in allegorical fashion. Inherent weaknesses of human reason he described as idols of the tribe. Observation, memory, and concentration unavoidably lag; every individual is constantly beset by the tendency to subordinate reason to emotion. 

Prejudices, or idols of the cave, the products of past training and experience, can be modified but not wholly eradicated. The necessity of framing ideas into words begets the idols of the market place. 

Men tend to substitute verbiage for reason, to cherish shibboleths, to render emotional obeisance to slogans. Uncritical adherence to philosophical schools Bacon termed idols of the theatre. Reverence for great names, another prolific source of error, he described as the idol of the forum.

René Descartes (1596-1650) was another major contributor to

the triumph of reason. The scion of a noble family, his early education was entrusted to Jesuits. Left an orphan at an early age, he followed a military career and broadened his outlook by extensive travel. Soon after he devoted himself to mathematics and philosophy, he found it expedient to reside in Holland, which, because of the relative liberalism of its government, had become a veritable asylum for thinkers. As a mathematician, he was one of the founders of analytic geometry. Methods utilized successfully in the solution of mathematical problems were applied to the broader problems of philosophy. He began by a process of rigid introspection; he divested himself of all ideas and preconceptions the truth of which he had not personally ascertained. He even questioned his own existence. A categorical denial of his existence at least involved the thought of such denial. He therefore found in his reasoning power the proof of his existence; “I think, therefore I am" was the famous aphorism in which he phrased this conclusion. Having rid his mind of all ideas which his own reason had not demonstrated to be true, he held that certain self-evident truths irresistibly impinged on his consciousness; these he called intuitions. From these intuitions he deduced corollaries, which, in turn, became intuitions to serve as the basis for continued deduction. In his failure to postulate any connection between mind and body, the philosopher, of course, was at variance with the tenets of modern psychology. Spinoza, a Portuguese Jew who also fled to Holland, was his most illustrious intellectual disciple. His great contribution was to apply the Cartesian method to problems of ethics.

John Locke (1632-1704) followed the empiricism of Hobbes in his Essays Concerning the Human Understanding. He held that truth was the product of the working of experience, of sensation, on a virtually passive mind. David Hume (1711-1776) attacked the thorny problem of causation. He concluded that no necessary connection could be shown to exist among phenomena. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibnitz (1646-1716) postulated the existence of innate, intuitive truths held in every mind. Ultimate substance he held to be self-sufficient, atomic entities which he called monads. Immanuel 

Kant (1724-1804), in his monumental Critique of Pure Reason, closed the period of skepticism and empiricism and inaugurated a new era of philosophy. As a professor in the University of Königsberg, he became dissatisfied with the dogmatism of Wolff and the devastating skepticism of Hume and resolved to strike out along untried paths. He arrived at the conclusion that there are two types

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of knowledge. A priori knowledge is original, transcendant, and independent of experience. All sensations, he held, are submitted to space and time criteria; concepts of space and time are within every mind and consequently are intuitive. Knowledge a posteriori, on the other hand, is gathered by experience. There are three approaches to truth: sense, understanding, and reason. Understanding, by submitting sense impulse to time and space concepts, transforms intuitions into conceptions such as unity, plurality, diversity. Reason, in turn, acting upon conceptions, evolves ideas. His doctrine of a priori knowledge is transmitted to his ethical system. Concepts of good and evil are innate; we all possess the "categorical imperative which enables us to recognize some impulses as good, others as evil. 

The impulse to scientific investigation inaugurated by the Renaissance brought rich harvest in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Sir Isaac Newton (1642-1727) formulated his law of gravitation which was the culmination of the astronomical and physical researches of Galileo and Kepler. He shared with Leibnitz the honor of inventing calculus, a branch of mathematics of inestimable service to pure and applied science. Leonhard Euler (1707-1783) enriched virtually every branch of mathematics with his prolific researches. 

Marked progress was made in the discovery of the laws of electrodynamics. Charles du Fay discovered the existence of positive and negative electricity; Franklin demonstrated the identity of electricity and lightning. Charles Coulomb (1736-1806) showed that the law of inverse squares, which Newton had shown in connection with gravitation, applied to electrical attraction and repulsion. Volta invented the storage battery and conducted significant experiments in the measurement of electromotive forces.

Equally significant were the contributions to chemistry. Robert 

Boyle showed that the volume of gases varied inversely with the pressure imposed on them. Joseph Priestley (1733-1804) discovered and prepared oxygen; his experiments with combustion refuted the prevalent view that combustion was caused by union with "phlogiston." William Scheele (1742-1786) prepared hydrogen and was a pioneer in the employment of chlorine as a bleaching agent. Antoine

Lavoisier (1743-1794), a brilliant French scientist who fell a victim to the Terror, shared with Priestley the discovery that combustion was in reality a combination of a substance with oxygen. He evolved a system of chemical nomenclature that became standard for the science. He, as well as Henry Cavendish, demonstrated that water was composed of oxygen and hydrogen.

Discoveries of great significance were made in the biological sci-

ences. Antony van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723) completed the work of Harvey by showing that the blood coursed from arteries to veins by passing through capillaries. He also discovered the red corpuscles. 

Rudolf Camerarius (1665-1721) discovered the sexuality of plants.

Widened scientific and philosophical interests were reflected in the formation of academies and learned societies. The British Royal 

Society was established in 1645, followed three years later by the organization of the Dublin Philosophical Society. The French Academy was established in 1635, under the patronage of Cardinal Richelieu, and the Paris Observatory was founded in 1667. The famous 

Greenwich Observatory was established eight years later. 

Rationalism, with its widening conception of natural laws, was projected into the religious sphere. Deism was an important development, of which Lord Herbert in his De Veritate (1624) was the most important founder. He held that there was one supreme God who was to be worshipped. Piety and virtue were essential, as was repentance for sins since there were rewards and punishments in eternity. These were the fundamental religious tenets - other doctrinal and dogmatic teachings were extraneous. In fully developed 

Deism, God was considered a unifying, controlling force, working in the universe through natural laws. Men, endowed with free will and reason, were considered, by nature, good. Right living, then, was living in harmony with natural law. Deism had important humanitarian implications. Poverty, injustice, and other social ills were in contravention to natural law and accordingly were to be ameliorated or, if possible, eliminated.

A striking evidence of enlightenment was a number of attacks against belief in witchcraft and the barbarous persecutions engendered by this superstition. The basic idea involved in witchcraft was that individuals could enter into compacts with the devil. Satan abetted them in their nefarious activities and in return claimed their souls upon the expiration of twenty-one years. It was believed that the contracts between men and the "Evil One" were written in blood. Failure of crops, death of cattle, illness, almost any disaster in the daily life of the masses, was considered the result of the malevolence of witches. Thousands of persons, mostly old women, were tortured into admission of guilt and burned at the stake. The church had officially recognized witchcraft and prescribed the same penalties as it inflicted on heretics. Those who inveighed against these superstitions made no progress against the credulity of the masses; indeed they were greeted with contumely and vituperation by many in positions of authority in church and state.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Suppression of ideas by the imposition of censorship also came under fire during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The issue has continued to be a subject of controversy to our day. Those who justify censorship hold that writings and speeches often are subversive to government. Since any government is primarily concerned with self-preservation, it naturally will obstruct the expression of ideas which tend to undermine it. Diffusion of certain ideas may incite discontent and precipitate disorder. Since a primary duty of government is to maintain law and order, it is claimed that inflammatory ideas are to be suppressed at their source. Complete freedom of expression may encourage attacks on religion; organized religious groups naturally oppose circulation of heterodox or agnostic ideas. Also, the question of public morals is involved. While there is no common agreement as to what constitutes obscenity, it is doubtless true that books, periodicals, and pornographic pictures are issued to pander to the lascivious. On the other hand those who condemn censorship hold that any new idea is bound to incur opposition. Innate conservatism, prejudice, and selfish interest will be against any significant innovation. Censorship can be imposed so rigorously as to impede, or even prevent, the dissemination of information or ideas of great benefit to all mankind. Many governments have done lip service to the ideal of free speech; few have hesitated to abridge it on political, religious, or moral grounds. 

Prior to the seventeenth century, the right of church and state to restrict freedom of expression had not been seriously challenged.

John Milton (1608-1674) was one of the first to insist on the right to express ideas, even though they were repugnant to the overwhelming majority of his contemporaries. He separated from his wife and attempted to defend his action by a book in which he held that marriage was a human institution, free from religious implications. His ideas were bitterly attacked; the basest motives were scurrilously imputed to him. Stung to retort, he published the 

Areopagitica in which he dealt with the broader question of freedom of expression. Later writers took up the subject; Locke in his 

Letter on Toleration and Anthony Collins (1676-1729) in his Dis course on Free Thinking advanced basic arguments against censorship, as did Pierre Bayle, French exponent of liberalism.

THE POLITICAL PHILOSOPHERS 

The intellectual liberals of eighteenth century France have often been called the precursors of the Revolution. Whether or not this is

true depends, to a degree, on how much credit can be given to ideas for the accomplishment of the great changes the Revolution effected. 

A materially minded school of thinkers assigns to economic and social conditions the important role in the commencement of the revolutionary conflict. The middle-of-the-road point of view must give credit to both ideas and conditions. It seems fairly well established that the eighteenth century philosophers who were calling for reform of conditions as they existed would not have been especially happy in the way the changes they demanded were brought about.

During this century a major epidemic of philosophical discussion broke out in France. Volume after volume, pamphlet after pamphlet, expounded new views and theories concerning social, political, economic, and religious change. Out of the hundreds of writers and thinkers whose names might be mentioned, four are outstanding for the effect they had on the thought of their own time, as well as for their contributions to the sum of human knowledge - Voltaire, Montesquieu, Diderot, and Rousseau. These philosophes owed much to two Englishmen of the preceding century, Isaac Newton and John Locke, who together had admonished them to follow both experience and reason in their search for the truths of this life. 

Given these tools for research, the French thinkers applied themselves to problems of their own and, by so doing, created the foundations for a new order in which the importance of popular sovereignty, the natural rights, and the ultimate perfectibility of man found full flower.

François Arouet, known to us as Voltaire, was perhaps the most influential of the group during his own lifetime (1694-1778). He was a native of Paris, the son of a notary. He received his early training from Jesuit priests. His father insisted that he enter the legal profession, rather than follow his own inclinations in the field of literary endeavor, but ultimately the son's wishes prevailed. 

He wrote plays, poetry, history, essays, and treatises on any and all subjects, some of them so libelous in nature that he was incarcerated in the Bastille and forced from time to time into exile. A number of his plays were financially successful and from their proceeds he began a lifelong habit of speculation, most of which was highly profitable.

When in 1725 he was insulted by the Chevalier de Rohan, and replied as was his nature, he was given a sound thrashing by the nobleman's servants. A challenge from Voltaire followed, but he was

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

hurried off into English exile before a duel could take place. Life in 

England changed the content of his writings by materially modifying his intellectual outlook. The years which he spent among the 

English gentry resulted in the composition of literary works which made him one of the outstanding writers in Europe. The chief contribution of this English sojourn to his point of view came from his appreciation of the Englishman's manners and his tolerance where freedom of conscience and action was concerned. This wholehearted admiration for the British way of life was a constant inspiration to Voltaire in his endeavor to alter the course of French life, thought, and culture.

Voltaire's contact with Deism in England had a special significance in that on his return to France, he became the chief exponent of a more radical belief than prevailed in Britain. Deism was more than a belief in the existence of a God; it included a dislike of theological disputation as indulged in by the various religious sects. With this as a beginning, Voltaire undertook a lifelong attack on the church as an institution, not merely the Catholic Church, but churches in general. Perhaps one of the reasons why the Deistic movement found less opposition in England than it did in France was the fact that in the latter country the Catholic Church was an aggressive opponent of such views. Voltaire's attack was concentrated on three main issues: intolerance, superstition, and the pretensions of the church to control over the functions of the state. 

His weapon was the most satirical and caustic pen in Europe. With it he attempted to ridicule revealed religion out of existence and priests out of power. While his fight for tolerance was undoubtedly the major effort of his long life, he was himself singularly lacking in it.

Voltaire's other point of attack was the composition of the state as he found it. To his flaying of the government must be assigned whatever credit is due him for bringing on the Revolution, for with caustic insinuation, in hyperbolic style, he exposed and ridiculed judicial abuses and the evils of royal absolutism, class privilege, warfare, and the military class. He gained no decisive victories in his attacks on church and state. Much of his life was spent in hiding, to avoid persecution by the authorities. He was ever the subject of counter-attack, as he is to this day. Late in life, he spent a few unsatisfactory years at Sans Souci, with Frederick the Great of Prussia. He died an old and wealthy man, but to the last, a friend of the downtrodden and oppressed. He has been considered the most versa-

tile man of his age, but in spite of the diversity of his interests, much of his writing was based on superficial study and hasty observation. 

His work was mainly of a destructive nature; nevertheless, much had to be destroyed before constructive work could begin. 

A more constructive mind was that of Montesquieu (1689–1755). 

Born a noble, he was trained in jurisprudence. On a scientific study of government he based the theories which were published, in 1748, in his Spirit of the Laws. His conclusion was that the government of any particular country should be patterned according to the actual needs of the nation. From this, we may gather that he was the exponent of no particular type of government, except that which was best suited to the nation in question. He admired the 

English constitutional system, in spite of the faults which he pointed out as inherent in it. He became the leading advocate of the separation and balance of powers theory of government in which the executive, legislative, and judicial branches were of equal power and provided with constitutional checks and balances against the usurpation of any other branch. By some he is classed as the father of modern political science. Perhaps the best characterization of his point of view was that he believed in moderation; certainly, he would never have condoned revolution as a means to the end he desired. 

Intellectually as brilliant as Voltaire, and possessed of similar versatility, was the less renowned atheist, Diderot (1713-1784). His chief contribution was in compiling the new learning of the age in a great work known as the Encyclopedia. In this enormous editorial task, he brought together a group of contributors of varying degrees of liberal thought and created a work in thirty-five volumes which was more than a synthesis of the knowledge of the day; it constituted a liberal manifesto the publication of which, in the face of governmental restriction, was a stupendous task. The Encyclopedists used their great work as a medium for the dissemination of Deistic views, the teaching of rationalism, and the destruction of prejudice and bigotry. It attacked intolerance of church and state, governmental tyranny and incompetence, the outworn penal system, and the continued existence of slavery in the colonial possessions of the mercantilist nations. This work had a wide circulation throughout Europe and had an incalculable effect in the education of disciples of a new and better order.

The individual in this rationalistic age whose ideas had the greatest ultimate influence was undoubtedly Jean Jacques Rousseau (1712-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

1778). His literary efforts led him into the role not only of a social reformer, but also that of an extreme exponent of the revolutionary movement. He can be understood only in the light of his early life, during the first forty years of which he was unknown. Left to drift for himself at an early age, the Geneva-born philosopher and romanticist entered on a life of wandering which led him into a dozen different occupations and through as many countries. His mind became so perverted as to make the first half of his life appear an unwholesome failure. When mature, he turned to the expression of his pent-up emotions and displayed a heart and mind in which beauty, love, and generosity formed no small part. In his writings, he broke away from the spirit of his times in which rationalism had come to be a dominant principle and introduced a philosophy in which the spiritual nature of man played a greater role. His experience with the sordid and the mean in life gave him a fund of material upon which to draw, and we find him advocating a return to the contentment of primitive mankind, since, as he saw it, learning, wealth, and urbanization had brought only unhappiness in their wake. He held that man was by nature good; civilization had merely served to entrench greed, dishonesty, and wretchedness. He saw society as a condition in which the few profited at the expense of the masses. These were facts with which, he held, it was impossible for a philosophy of rationalism to deal. The works which followed one another from his prolific pen again forced him into a life of vagabondage and exile to which only death brought relief from persecution and periodic spells of insanity.

Rousseau's best known work was The Social Contract. He pointed out that the introduction of property rights into a world of free and equal men had made the strong dominant over the weak, had brought profit to the few at the expense of the many. Since this was wrong, he advocated a return to that natural state in which the people were again sovereign. Then, men might delegate their powers anew for the purpose of providing essential government. The right to delegate the sovereign power implied the right to revoke it, when and if the delegated ruler used it to the detriment of the people. The title of his work was based on this concept of obligations. From such ideas came the revolutionary concept of popular sovereignty and delegated sovereignty of a government by consent of the people. 

Just how revolutionary these views were will be understood when it is recalled that in the Bourbon concept of government, the king's will was absolute by grace of God. Whether or not The Social 

Contract set the pace for revolutionary thought in the decades

which followed its publication is still debatable. Certainly it started "back to nature" fads. The work was widely read and later liberals adopted a philosophy not widely at variance with that of Rousseau. 

The work which was directly responsible for sending into hiding one of the best intellects the age had produced was his Emile. In it he outlined, on the basis of his "back to nature" thesis, a system of education. Let the child, he declared, follow his natural inclination, rather than force on him the mannerisms and habits of an evil civilization. Teach him that which is practical, something that he may use to good purpose when he must make his own way in the world, rather than the dead languages which he learns only to forget. The influence of these teachings has not yet passed, for the principles underlying his views find a major place in the educational philosophy of our own day.

A further development in the intellectual life of the eighteenth century was in the field of political economy. The men most interested in the development of new concepts in this field of thought called themselves Physiocrats. They organized about a physician in the court of Louis XV, Doctor Quesnay, when he denounced as erroneous the mercantilistic philosophy underlying the governmental economic policies of the day. Important in the group were 

Rivière, Dupont de Nemours, Gournay, and Turgot. Their interest centered more in the material than the intellectual progress of France. In their writings they emphasized the economic rather than the political management of the state. With such aims, the group was brought to consider such subjects as agrarian economy, production of wealth and its distribution, taxation, governmental expenditure, and kindred subjects. According to one authority, the two chief contributions of the Physiocrats were the idea of the single tax on real property and the proposal to eliminate internal taxes. which the French government had placed on the grain trade. In keeping with the other philosophers of the day, they attempted to prove that these two policies were based on natural law, and, as such, were the epitome of justice. In the logical evolution of such proof they arrived ultimately at the doctrine of laissez faire as the best possible way for a government to promote the industrial and commercial welfare of the state.

In contrast, the mercantilists believed that if the citizens of a state were prosperous, the nation itself would prosper. The state was therefore bound to assist and aid its citizenry in every possible way to attain a competence. Such governmental paternalism took the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

form of state regulation of manufacturing and commerce to the minutest detail, the chief purpose of which was to preserve and enhance the nation's total gold supply. The various mercantilist nations of Europe had entered a period of colonization with a view to sending manufactured articles to their colonies in return for raw products which they expected would more than pay the costs of manufacture and transportation, thus creating a balance of trade and the desired surplus of gold. Such policies required strict regulation of imports and exports, the subsidization of industry and the carrying trade, and the creation of a large naval force for the protection of the colonies and their trade. The mercantilistic policies adopted by Colbert carried the system to extremes. In brief, the mercantilist called for colonies which could produce raw materials unavailable in the mother country. He wanted the colonies to possess no industries which could compete with those at home or enhance the prosperity of any other nation. He expected the colonies to pay a portion of the costs of the home government. The apparent injustices of such a system gave the Physiocrats sufficient cause for demanding reform.

The penetration of physiocratic principles into Great Britain resulted in the popularization of the doctrine of laissez faire through the writings of the Scotchman, Adam Smith. His Wealth of Nations was published in 1776. In it he held that the manner in which a capitalist used his resources was no concern of the government. He enunciated in clear form the concept of the economic freedom of the individual from governmental regulation and interference. Freedom of trade, of labor, and of the use of one's abilities and personal possessions were the natural rights of mankind; it was not the function of the government to interfere. The doctrine had been previously evolved and named by the Physiocrats. It was to serve as the foundation stone of governmental economic policies for well over a century.

The laissez faire doctrine has been seriously questioned during the past two decades, and in some nations has already been discarded. 

The evils of which the Physiocrats complained, unequal distribution of wealth, unfair taxation, exploitation of the weak, were not eliminated through the adoption of the philosophy popularized by Adam Smith. Much that was great was accomplished while its principles were followed, but reformers of the present generation have pointed out that it carried much evil in its wake. Even England has been forced to abandon her free trade policy. Italy, Germany, and

Russia have returned to strict governmental regulation of trade and commerce. In the United States, some regulation has been carried out within the limits of the Constitution. 

The investigative procedure and punishments permitted under the harsh European criminal legal systems served to arouse almost all of the social reformers of the time. Torture was still a fixed part of the investigative procedure except in England.
