It was the means, in many instances, whereby a confession was obtained whether the defendant was guilty as charged or not. Secret trials were the order of the day. The accused was often without benefit of counsel; penalties were, by custom, summarily inflicted. Not only was the judicial procedure unfair and horrible in its application, but it did not effectually check crime. The very harshness of the system served to harden the criminal classes rather than start them back on the road to a better life. Hanging was common even for minor offenses, while major offenders suffered torture and death on the bone-breaking cartwheel. The loathsome condition of the prisons roused humanitarians of the day. Lacking in light and cleanliness, prisons generally were cesspools of filth and charnel houses for the unfortunate inmates.

An early and influential exponent of penal reform was the Italian nobleman and jurist, Cesare Beccaria (1738-1794). In his short study,

Crimes and Punishments (1764), he called for substantial revision of the criminal law and procedure as practiced in Europe. He believed that a law was best which best served the greatest number. He advocated the idea that only reasonable and fair law or punishment was essential to the preservation of society. There could be no rational excuses for laws which were more severe than conditions demanded. 

His practical recommendations were as sound as his theory. He proposed the compilation of short and understandable codes of criminal law for the reasonable safety of the state as well as the individual. 

He advocated the abolition of torture in investigation, trial, and punishment, the equality of all men before the law, public trials, and the abolition of capital punishment. He insisted that the interests of society could be better served with a mild code of criminal law which was quick and positive in its conviction of criminals. The ideals of Beccaria were of widespread interest throughout Europe, but their immediate effect was slight. His service was to sow the seed of judicial and penal reform; more than a generation later, the English reformers were to take up the task he had so capably begun.

CHAPTER 40 

Conditions in Europe on the Eve of the French Revolution 

ANY medieval institutions persisted in France to the outbreak of the Revolution. In some respects, the Revolution may be considered as a transition from feudalism and absolutism to democratic governmental forms. The manorial system, with its many faults and abuses, still prevailed; serfdom was rather common. The gilds, too, constituted a powerful reactionary force in the fields of commerce and industry. An important medieval survival was the influence of the church in the affairs of state; especially was this true in the control which it exercised over education. French society was divided into three major classes or estates: the Clergy or 

First Estate, the Nobility or Second Estate, and the Third Estate. 

The stratification of society was considerably more complex than this simple statement would seem to indicate, and was rendered obnoxious by virtue of the rights, privileges, and opportunities which were the prerogatives of the favored classes. While the privileges and exemptions were enjoyed by the two upper estates, governmental and private exactions fell heaviest upon the Third Estate, which was a decided majority of the whole population. 

With the exceptions of Switzerland, Holland, and Great Britain, the typical government in Europe was that. of royal absolutism, brought to the peak of development in France under Louis XIV (1643-1715). During the fifty years preceding the French Revolution, however, a number of European rulers were, to a degree, cognizant of the need for reform in the governmental and social institutions of their respective countries. While they continued their advocacy of the doctrine of the divine right of kings, they sought to bring about some measure of reform through their personal efforts. 

Hence they have been termed the "Benevolent" or "Enlightened 

Despots." Chief among them was Frederick II (1740–1786) of Prus-

EVE OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION 

531 sia, a despot to the core, yet a man who did much to advance reforms. 

He granted religious freedom, founded towns, drained lowlands, aided and encouraged industrial progress, and did much that was frankly liberal in a world that was ostensibly more devoted to absolutism. Catherine the Great (1762-1796) of Russia, was another enlightened ruler of the period. A German princess, she married

Czar Peter III whom she succeeded when a palace revolution deposed him. While her actual reforms were of little moment, her intentions probably entitle her to the distinction of "Benevolent." A third ruler in this group was Joseph II (1780-1790) of Austria. In his ten-year reign, wholehearted attempts to bring about a better order were defeated, but he had at least made a sincere effort.

The government of France, under the later Bourbons, was marked by tyranny, corruption, and ineptitude. The root of these conditions lay in the fact that the king claimed the right to rule by grace of God, rather than by the consent of the people. Hand in hand with the doctrine of divine right was the absolute nature of the king's power. France possessed no active parliamentary institutions like those found in England. The Parlement de Paris might refuse to register a law, but it had no power to propose or pass one. Even the power to refuse registration of a law had been nullified during the reign of Louis XIV. By the ceremony known as a lit de justice (Bed of Justice), the king could force the Parlement to register a law or become subject to summary dismissal. The Parlement de Paris was, therefore, a judicial rather than a legislative institution. 

Centralization of the government in the hands of the king was not necessarily a fault. Unless the king happened to be incompetent to discharge his multitudinous duties, centralized, though not unified, government functioned in satisfactory fashion. Under Louis XVI the national administration was continued in four divisions of which the chancellory was perhaps the most important for the initiation of legislation and judicial control. The Chancellor was peculiarly secure in his tenure of office as compared with other officials in the upper brackets of the administration. There were four Secretaries of State respectively assigned jurisdiction over the king's domestic establishment, foreign relations, naval affairs, and war. They were charged with territorial administration as well. The Controller- 

General possessed wide financial jurisdiction and powers. His position was especially trying during the decades before 1789 because of the financial plight of the government. The last of the administra tive departments, the Royal Council, was itself divided into four

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

different councils of varying size and importance. These were: the 

Privy Council, the Council of State, a financial council, and a Council of Dispatches. Centralized as the administration may have been in theory, it will be seen that the very complexity of its machinery ultimately led to wasted effort, discord, and confusion. That the monarchy was able to postpone internal strife so long seems to have been attributable to the long tenure of the bureaucracy which attended to routine affairs in the capital, and to the competent, well established local officials throughout France.

Another factor in the promotion of governmental abuses was the influence which "favorites" had with the monarch, his queen, or someone else within the royal household. The high point of this development came during the later years of the reign of Louis XV, when, with the rise to power of Madame de Pompadour, control of the kingdom seemed to have fallen into inept and selfish hands. 

During the reign of Louis XVI, court favorites received nearly one hundred million dollars in one form or another. Advancement, position, and wealth were gained not by merit but by the proper word, at an opportune moment, to some reigning royal favorite.

Wasteful expenditure in ostentatious display at Versailles, though possibly in keeping with the powers of the monarch, was in sharp contrast to the plight of the Third Estate. Masquerades and lavish balls, salon life, dramatic presentations, pageants, and other diversions, made up a continuous round of pleasure for about two thousand courtiers. The number of servants domiciled at Versailles approximated eight or nine times that number; the cost of this establishment to the nation obviously was enormous. To maintenance of the court must also be added the ever-increasing cost of pensions, sinecures, and gifts to those in favor at the moment.

Taxes were wastefully collected and inequitably levied. Though there were numerous taxes, four of them warrant special consideration. The taille was a land tax, assessed twice annually by the Royal 

Council on real property in one section of France, and as a personal tax in other portions of the country. The tax fell most heavily upon the peasantry who, whether they owned the land or not, paid the levy out of the returns from their labor. Most infamous of the taxes during the Ancien Régime was the gabelle, or salt tax, which was notorious for the inequality with which it was levied. Unequal tax impositions on so essential a commodity were an inducement to smuggling and thousands were severely punished each year for infractions of the law. The octroi were taxes or internal tariffs on

EVE OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION 

533 country foodstuffs, assessed when such goods were brought into a city. It is hardly necessary to point out that a tax of this nature handicapped local trade and fell most heavily on the consumer and small farmer. A last tax was the corvée, or forced labor, exacted from the peasantry for the upkeep of roads and the transportation of troops. 

Collection of indirect taxes was not in the hands of government officials. The administration, in a time of financial stringency, had begun the practice of anticipating its income from future taxes by borrowing in advance of collections. To obtain better terms, the practice was begun of farming out the tax collection concession every six years to a group of contractors. These financiers and speculators, numbering between forty and sixty, were known as the "Farmers General." The system was one which usually yielded a great profit to the "Farmers General," and resulted in a consequent curtailment of income to the government. That such methods would lead to abuses was inevitable, and again hardships fell most heavily upon the Third Estate. The clergy were of course largely exempt from taxation, while the exemption of the nobility from many of the more onerous duties was an intolerable abuse.

Another governmental evil during the Ancien Régime was the maladministration of justice. Under Bourbon absolutism, the king was the source of all justice. Royal courts numbered into the hundreds and operated throughout the kingdom. The diffusion and multiplicity of these courts seem to have been due, in part, to the practice of selling judicial positions to the highest bidder. Once the post was acquired, it was considered family property which could be abolished only through repurchase by the government, a means seldom invoked by a government in perpetual need of funds. The thirteen parlements were courts of final jurisdiction in their particular districts. Lower courts included rural, urban, and district chambers. While their jurisdiction was of a general nature, there were further special tribunals for the adjudication of cases involving commercial, maritime, and financial law. The judicial system was cumbersome, unjust, and often venal in operation. The application of different laws in north and south France further hindered the attainment of justice. Other major legal and judicial faults were inequality before the law and the practice of arbitrarily imprisoning individuals by means of lettres de cachet, royal writs providing for arbitrary arrest and indefinite imprisonment without trial. These writs were considered essential for the proper policing of the country, but they were also often used by the upper classes for the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

control of family matters. Another judicial abuse was the practice of torture. France had not yet accepted the teachings of Beccaria. 

Consequently, torture was still frequently applied as part of the procedure in the examination of the accused. Capital punishment was cruelly administered, often for minor offenses. 

The inefficiency of the bureaucracy was another important factor. 

Without farsighted leadership in the determination of fundamental policies, the administrative system was disintegrating; that it lasted as long as it did, was attributable to the stabilizing force of routine and precedent. Higher offices were reserved to the nobility; opportunities for the non-noble in the government service were sharply limited. There were also numbers of useless offices, granted generally to favorites as sinecures, a practice which not only cost enormous sums, but, at times, stood in the way of necessary fiscal reforms. "Red tape" and needless routine further hampered efficient administration of governmental functions. In the army, the commoner virtually was barred from advancement, for the higher ranks were reserved to the nobility. Under such a military organization, reform and improvement were well-nigh precluded; tactics were out of date and equipment was obsolete. 

Although it was by no means impossible for the commoner to attain noble rank during this period, the breach between Second and Third Estate was wide. Nominally, the noble lived on the income of his estates. Earlier attempts on the part of the monarchs or their ministers to curb the powers of the nobles had led to their concentration at Versailles. The luxury and magnificence of court life hardly encouraged desire to return to the dullness of the provinces. Absenteeism resulted, and demands for increased income to defray expenses of court social activity on the part of the lord led to more onerous exactions upon the peasants. More oppressive collection of rents, the requirement of all the customary services permitted under the old manorial system, and the maintenance of hunting rights for the nobles are among the evidences of an appreciable feudal reaction during the decades immediately preceding the Revolution. 

The nobility thus largely achieved its parasitic character through the development of absenteeism, fostered by the national policy of centralization. One could become a noble by inheritance, by purchase, by filling particular governmental posts, or by meritorious military service. Even the nobility was divided into classes. There were first the Princes of the Blood, of the royal family, and the Nobles of the Sword whose titles could be traced back to the Middle

EVE OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION 

535 Ages. Next in rank were the Nobles of the Robe who were drawn largely from the middle class and whose dignity for the most part was connected with the offices they held. Although many of them resided on their country estates for a good part of the year, most of them retained judicial or administrative offices, like intendants and judges in the parlements. Those of the lowest rank were known as the hobereaux, or "Sparrow Hawks," poor country nobles, often without any landed possessions. In all, there must have been about a quarter of a million persons of noble status. The number was so great primarily because each child of a French nobleman was noble.

A further factor in the development of the vain, frivolous, and parasitic character of the noble class was the fact that while they could sell the products of their estates, they were forbidden, on pain of losing caste, to enter any trading or commercial pursuits. As a consequence, the son of a noble had to enter the army, the church, or the legal or administrative service of the government. An illustration of the tenacity with which the nobility monopolized the higher offices in the realm is that, of the thirty-six ministers in the fifteen years preceding 1789, only Necker was a commoner. 

The First Estate was composed of the clergy; although this class constituted less than one per cent of the population, the church corporation was the most powerful in France. The clerical class resolved itself into three major divisions, the highest and least numerous of which was the upper clergy or prelacy. This wealthy group was so inclined to idleness and ostentation that it materially reduced the effectiveness of the more sincere laborers in the service of the church. A second group, and five or six times larger, were the lower clergy who were grossly underpaid and inadequately financed for the work they were performing. It is not strange, therefore, that representatives of this class sided with the Third Estate in the early days of the Revolution. The third clerical division, equal in numbers to the second, was the regular clergy, made up of monks and nuns in the various orders. This last group was the most affluent. The various orders possessed enormous landholdings, which were tax free since the church was considered civilly dead. However, at approximately five-year intervals the church met in general assembly to vote freewill gifts to the government. It is pertinent to note that most of the more than one hundred and thirty bishops during this period came from the noble ranks; high office, in church, as well as in army or government, was reserved for members of the Second Estate. 

The fountain head of French economic philosophy was the mer-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cantilistic system, and the nation's policy was decidedly paternalistic. 

The government salt and tobacco monopolies, though productive of considerable revenue, were restrictions on trade. Wheat and bread prices were regulated by the administration. France was divided into three major customs districts. The twelve provinces about Paris were called the "Five Great Farms "; inside this area, trade was little hampered by tariffs. In a second district, goods moved from one province to the next only on the payment of a tax, and from one customs district to another, only on the payment of duty. Certain other areas acquired after 1664 received the same tariff treatment as foreign nations. These restrictions on trade and commerce were extremely harmful to business interests in general. While some attempts were made in the years immediately preceding the Revolution to abolish restrictive features of the gild system, they came too late to be entirely effective. The heavy tax burdens on the mercantile and industrial classes have already been noted. The bourgeoisie were not given an opportunity, in return, to voice their views concerning the conduct of the government. Here was just cause for complaint and one reason why the French Revolution was an essentially middle class uprising.

It is not easy to measure the effect of the writings of Voltaire, Montesquieu, Diderot, Rousseau, the Encyclopedists, and the Physiocrats. These precursors of the Revolution do seem to have prepared the French people for reforms greater than they had originally intended. To what extent the American Revolution influenced French revolutionary opinion is a debatable question. Thinking Frenchmen declared that France was not America, that conditions and problems were different. Of course they were, yet some spark of democratic hope seems to have been transferred to French shores from the New World. This much is not speculative however. French participation in the American Revolution did hasten national bankruptcy in France. This resulted in the calling of the Estates-General for May, 1789, which in turn ushered in the French Revolution.

CHAPTER 41 

The French Revolution until the

End of 1790 HE prodigious amount of research and literary endeavor which has been expended upon the Revolutionary period. (1789-1815) is well illustrated by the bibliographical compilation of Frederick M. Kircheisen, whose list includes some 100,000 titles dealing exclusively with the Napoleonic era. The principal significance of the Revolution to France lay in its eventual transformation of an absolute monarchy, encumbered with numerous medieval institutions, into a constitutional democracy, in which feudal institutions were eliminated and those of a modern bourgeois republic established. The militant and apostolic nature of Revolutionary ideals resulted in their spread throughout much of Europe; the task of completing their dissemination was accomplished by Napoleon Bonaparte. Wars, which were a natural consequence of this attempt to extend Revolutionary concepts to the absolute monarchies, embroiled virtually all Europe in a struggle from 1792 till 1815. So wide was the scope of this conflict that, ultimately, the 

United States was involved.

Although opportunity was afforded, Louis XV did not become a member of that group of benevolent despots who on their own volition attempted to achieve reforms. With his passing in 1774, he left to his grandson and successor a record of administrative incompetence, progressive financial prodigality, and discouraging military reverses. The handicap was much too great for Louis XVI. Had he possessed superlative administrative abilities, had he even possessed power of sustained mental effort, it is conceivable that something of a constructive nature might have been accomplished by peaceful means. With each year of royal ineptitude, however, it became clearer that force was the only practical solution of an intolerable situation.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The old thesis that the Revolution was cataclysmic has been discarded. It was at all times a bourgeois movement; it did not emanate from or come under the control of the masses. The period from 1789 till 1795 may be divided into two major phases: that preceding and that following the attempted flight of the king to Varennes. During the first phase, the Revolution, based on conservative principles, was led by such moderates as Mirabeau and Lafayette, who were exponents of constitutional monarchy. The Revolution was not precipitated when conditions in France were at their worst. There is abundant reason to believe that economic conditions were improving during the decade before 1789, but the rate of improvement was not sufficiently rapid. On the other hand, there is evidence to indicate the existence of what might be termed a “feudal reaction" against liberal reforms during this same period, the effect of which was to hasten the revolutionary outbreak. The abortive attempt of the royal family to flee from France initiated a second and more radical phase of the Revolution. During this period, republican and democratic ideals predominated, and it was in this stage of the Revolution that excesses occurred.

Imminent bankruptcy of the national government was the immediate cause of the Revolution. The situation had been provoked by a century of governmental prodigality and fiscal mismanagement. 

There had been an attempt during the Regency of Louis XV (17151723) to liquidate the public debt by a plan born in the fertile brain of the Scotch adventurer and banker, John Law. His private bank, which became the National Bank in 1718, issued enormous quantities of bank notes which, for the time being, found ready acceptance. 

Law's plan had other ramifications of a private nature which, enmeshed with the governmental bank, brought on a financial collapse in 1720, known as the "Mississippi Bubble." The wars of the eighteenth century, in which France was greatly involved, resulted in both military victories and defeats; in either event, the public debt was materially increased. Loss of the major part of her colonial domain in 1763 cut off France's supply of raw materials, vitally affected her mercantilistic economy, and was most humiliating to national prestige. The loss of the colonies had wider implications, however, for it made possible the supremacy of Great Britain upon the sea, a deciding factor in the long struggle between Napoleon and England. The extravagances of the court at Versailles have already been described, as has the wasteful system utilized in the collection of inequitably levied taxes. Exemptions of the clergy and nobility from

the major portion of the tax burden limited the sources of income for the retirement of the public debt. Archaic restrictions upon commerce and industry further crippled the economic development of the nation. Paradoxically, the middle class was advancing in a material way despite such restrictions; their complaint was chiefly that progress was being retarded. Finally, the character of the ruling family contributed materially to the imminent bankruptcy of the nation. Louis XVI had an unenviable heritage from his predecessor, and his incompetence to deal realistically with the exigencies of the situation ultimately led him to the guillotine. He was a well-meaning, kind-hearted, trusting individual, whose indolence and distaste for administrative problems allowed conditions to grow from bad to worse. His queen, Marie Antoinette, was known to the French people as "The Austrian." She possessed many of those mental powers which the king lacked, but, in her private as well as in her public life, she was almost devoid of discretion and a comprehension of the realities of her position.

That the abuses were great is unquestionable; however, numerous attempts were made to reform the French fiscal system. To fill the office of controller-general of finance, Louis XVI chose Turgot (1774-1776), an administrator who had made an enviable record as intendant of Limoges. But soon afterward the king, seeking popular approval, disregarded his wishes and reëstablished the thirteen parlements abolished by Louis XV. This measure made the parlements rallying points for reactionary elements in the French nation. Turgot's financial policy was characterized by strict retrenchment; his slogan was "no bankruptcies, no new taxes, and no loans." While his achievements on this score were gratifying, the king failed to coöperate by reduction of expenditures for pensions, gifts, or court maintenance. The minister's first reform edict, issued in the fall of 

1774, abolished governmental regulation of the grain trade, allowing free inter-provincial commerce in that commodity. The scheme failed because of a crop shortage and the opposition of speculators who forced prices to such a level that fear of famine necessitated a change of policy. Turgot also established a Bank of Discount, and, in 1776, two other reforms were carried out, which proved to be the last which he was permitted to inaugurate. They were the abolition of the hated corvée, the burdensome labor tax for road construction and maintenance, and the disbanding of the gilds. With such measures, Turgot earned the hostility of the privileged classes and angered the queen. His plans for the creation of local elective

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

assemblies and a national assembly the king himself opposed, and finally the queen was able to procure the dismissal of the minister. 

In the reaction which followed, most of the reforms were nullified. 

The king then summoned Necker, the best known banker of the period, a Genevan and a Protestant, as director-general of finance.

He was a strange person who, in spite of his idiosyncrasies, possessed remarkable financial acumen. The fiscal crisis forced immediate adoption of a loan policy and curtailment of governmental expenditures. His task was complicated by the entry of France into the struggle of the American colonies against Great Britain. Although the war was a success in its military outcome, it served to aggravate the financial difficulties. The director-general then turned to reform of the machinery of government in order to effect economy in administration. By centralized collection of taxes, improvement of the system of national accounts, lotteries, and flotation of numerous new loans, he was able temporarily to improve governmental credit and enhance his own fame. His fiscal policies were far from sound, however, for they ultimately served to increase the pace at which the nation was traveling towards disaster. Serfdom was abolished on the royal lands, and the use of torture was restricted in some forms of judicial procedure to attest his humanitarian interests. He further proposed the extension of representative forms to certain of the provinces and established several provincial assemblies. Opponents of his reforms impelled him to print and distribute, in his own defense, the Compte rendu au roi. This was an extraordinary financial statement which credited the director-general with a balance in the treasury; moreover, it showed clearly how tremendous was the cost of the royal court to the nation. Publicity of this nature was so distasteful to recipients of royal favor that they attacked Necker with redoubled vehemence. Denial of his request for full ministerial rank as controller-general served as an excuse for his resignation (1781) with the nation's financial affairs still in a precarious condition.

For two years (1781-1783), several ministers vainly attempted solutions of the problem. Calonne was called to this difficult task in the late fall of 1783. He was well aware of the fact that the wealthy had lost their confidence in the ability of the government to weather the financial storm. He knew that the future income of the nation was already pledged and that resources and credit were near exhaustion. Despite this discouraging outlook, he inaugurated a program by which it was hoped to restore faith in the eventual success-

THE BASTILLE VOLTAIRE LOUIS XVI ROBESPIERRE

THE CONGRESS OF VIENNA 

NAPOLEON

ful solution of the fiscal problems confronting the kingdom. To accomplish this end, he further taxed credit by floating heavy loans. 

With some of the money thus acquired he silenced opposition, concealed the real status of the treasury, liquidated a portion of the public debt, and began the construction of a vast number of public works. The period of inflation generated by this policy lasted until 

1786 when the inevitable reaction began. In some respects, Calonne's plan was to spend the nation out of impending bankruptcy. After exhausting numerous superficial expedients, he presented a comprehensive reform program which the king reluctantly agreed to submit to an Assembly of Notables.

This body came together during February, 1787; its membership consisted of 144 delegates from the First and Second Estates. Privi leged representatives of the upper classes were not inclined to accept diminution of their rights under the old order as suggested by the controller-general. Calonne's plan proposed the establishment of provincial assemblies, the elimination of internal customs, the abolition of the corvée, the revision of the taille and the gabelle, the establishment of a state bank, and the levy of a land tax which would fall upon all three estates. Refusal of the Assembly of Notables to adhere to such a comprehensive program of reform brought about Calonne's dismissal. The chief importance of the Assembly was the publicity which its deliberations gave to the faults in the French fiscal system.

Calonne's successor, Brienne, soon became an advocate of the same reforms his predecessor had proposed. His suggestions, too, met with the opposition of the Assembly of Notables, so, in May, 1787, the king dissolved that body. Brienne had clear alternatives; he might obtain the support of the parlements for his reform measures or he could ask the king to summon a meeting of the Estates-General, which had last met in 1614. The king refused to adopt the latter suggestion, and, when Brienne approached the parlements, they took the position that no body except the Estates-General could give the consent necessary for new taxes. This amounted to a declaration that there could be no taxation without representation, and this principle was to become a rallying point for those opposed to absolutism and the old order. Continued opposition to the government eventually forced the king to yield. He issued edicts during July and 

August, 1788, calling the Estates-General to meet on May 1, 1789. 

When, in August, 1788, Brienne suspended treasury payments, he was forced to resign. Necker was recalled as director-general and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

given the rank of minister of state. Popular confidence in his ability to cope with the financial crisis served to support the government until the spring of 1789.

The Estates-General had been formed in the early fourteenth century by the introduction of certain urban representative elements into the Curia Regis, thus laying a foundation for the division of the whole into the three estates. There were hardly more than a score of meetings in which all the estates were represented. After 

1614, Richelieu permitted the institution to lapse into desuetude, and it was not called thereafter until the meeting ordered for May, 1789. 

Some mention has already been made of the Philosophes. If nothing more, they were gifted publicists who had created an effective sounding board. In an attempt to influence opinion, men in all walks of life deluged Paris with a storm of pamphlets during the years 1787-1789. 

This provocative literature dealt especially with the problems of representation, a written constitution, judicial reform, and feudal survivals. The authors were usually anonymous because of the strict censorship. Out of this prodigious mass of literature, three lines are well known today. These are the queries and answers of Abbé Sieyès: "What is the Third Estate? Everything. 

What has it been hitherto in the political order? Nothing. 

What does it ask? To become something."

Early in 1789 the king invited all Frenchmen to elect representatives to the Estates-General and to send with them detailed instructions as to what they wished accomplished at Versailles. The Estates-General was called upon to do more than legislate; it was to determine and establish certain principles and institutions of government. The three orders held separate elections in each of the many districts of France. The First and Second Estates elected their dele gates in the primary assemblies, while the Third Estate chose its delegates indirectly by two or three successive assemblies. At the primary district electoral meetings, petitions and remonstrances were compiled to determine popular desires and to outline instructions to the delegates. These remonstrances were known as the Cahiers. 

The Cahiers of the First Estate were often colored by the views of the lower clergy who formed a majority in the electoral meetings. 

The Cahiers of the Second Estate came almost directly from the persons concerned. Those of the Third Estate passed through the intermediate electoral assemblies and cannot be classed as primary Cahiers.

They varied greatly in content, for the grievances of the rural districts usually related to feudal exactions, while those of the urban districts dealt with political and social reforms. In the main, the 

Cahiers agreed on several propositions and demonstrated the conservatism still prevalent in France. They generally held that France should remain monarchial in its government, that only the Estates- General could legally vote taxes, and that legislative power should be vested jointly in the king and the Estates-General. What this really meant was that the people desired a constitutional monarchy, with some degree of popular representation. While the Cahiers generally agreed that property was inviolable, they demanded that special privileges be abolished. When, however, privilege was a form of property, there was bound to be dissension. 

The most difficult problem awaiting solution was that relating to representation within the Estates-General. It had been conceded that the Third Estate should have double representation, that is, as many delegates as the other two estates put together. The inability of the king to determine whether the three estates should vote by head in one body, or separately by estates, was the blunder which brought on the actual revolutionary outbreak. The Third Estate insisted that all the delegates meet as one body and vote par tête (by head), but the king and the other two estates declined to accede to this viewpoint. 

By May 1, 1789, most of the 1700 delegates and alternates had been elected and were in Versailles. The king received them formally on the following day; the Estates-General officially was opened on May 

4, with the saying of mass. The first session was held on May 5, when, after a tardy entry, the king delivered a brief address in which he announced that he would permit voting by head on financial matters. On political questions, however, the deputies were ordered to vote by estates, that is, in three separate bodies. Necker read an exceedingly long speech which straddled most issues. At its close, his secretary called on the delegates separately to verify their credentials. The Third Estate refused, since such action would have forestalled voting by head and thereby frustrated constitutional reform. 

For nearly five weeks affairs were deadlocked, since the Third Estate refused to verify their credentials, except in a single group with the other two estates. During the interim, Mirabeau, a constitutional monarchist, suggested that the lower clergy be urged to join the 

Third Estate. On June 12, on the initiative of the Abbé Sieyes and in direct defiance of Louis XVI, the members of the Third Estate began to verify their credentials, not as deputies of that estate, but

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

as deputies of the nation. In the days which followed, members of the lower clergy joined them. When, on June 17, they adopted the name, National Assembly, the body began to function as the nation's legislative organ. This action may be considered as marking the beginning of the French Revolution. It must be kept in mind that the 

Third Estate, which had formed the National Assembly, represented about nineteen-twentieths of the French population and that the name was, therefore, appropriate. Two days later (June 19) the clergy as a group voted to join the National Assembly. 

In an attempt to frustrate trends which appeared to be divesting him of much of his authority, the king announced that a "Royal Session" would be held on June 22, in which he promised to outline his policy of reform. On June 20, the members of the National 

Assembly found their hall closed, ostensibly in preparation for the Royal Session." They retired to an indoor tennis court close by, where, on the suggestion of Mounier, they swore not to disband until a constitution had been drawn up and put into effect. The taking of the oath, while a dramatic incident, was of no great historical significance, for the initial step in the revolutionary movement had been taken when the rebellious Third Estate announced the formation of the National Assembly. 

The "Royal Session" was postponed until June 23. A “Royal

Session" may be compared in parliamentary procedure with the lit de justice in judicial procedure. The king planned to come before the deputies to announce what he expected them to do; under the absolutist theory of government the representatives then would be bound to defer to his wishes. The court party, led by the queen and the king's brother, the Count of Artois, urged the sovereign to take strong measures to control the situation. Necker, however, proposed a conciliatory plan. The king compromised by threats of force if his suggestions were not accepted. In his speech to the deputies, in the "Royal Session" of June 23, the king ignored what had already taken place by stating that he wished the three estates to remain separate and distinct. He conceded that certain items might well be discussed in joint session, but he absolutely forbade consideration of questions of a constitutional nature in any except separate meetings. The king's program of reforms advocated: (1) the granting of numerous financial powers to the Estates-General, (2) the elimination of the worst financial and feudal abuses, (3) equitable taxation of all classes, (4) respect for all property rights, (5) establishment of provincial legislatures, and (6) guarantee of per-

sonal liberties. This was certainly not reactionary when compared with the old order. Louis closed his speech, however, with a threat to disband the fractious deputies and carry out the plan himself if it was not accepted. His offer of reform came too late. The majority of the nobles and the clergy followed the king when he left the hall, but the commoners remained. When they were ordered to disband by the master of ceremonies, Mirabeau is credited with replying that they had been sent by the will of the people and could be prorogued only by force. The king chose to condone such strong language; for several days he appeared to have accepted the Revolution as an accomplished fact. This seems to be demonstrated by the fact that, on June 27, he ordered the remaining deputies of the two upper estates to join the National Assembly.

One significant event after another crowded the following months; the revolutionary fervor was approaching the high pitch it was to attain during the days of the Terror. On July 9, 1789, the 

National Assembly adopted a new name and was henceforth known as the National Constituent Assembly, to indicate that it was both a legislative and a constitutional body. There was a great deal of constructive reform which the people of France could expect from the labors of the Assembly, especially if it was sustained by Louis. 

The king, however, ordered 20,000 mercenaries to Versailles, ostensibly to protect the Assembly from the Parisian populace but actually to force its dissolution. Troop concentration began in early 

July, and as a consequence the maintenance of order became too great a problem for the municipal authorities of Paris. Mirabeau proposed that the Assembly send a deputation to the king to protest the concentration of troops and to ask instead the formation of a bourgeois guard. The king facetiously suggested removal of the 

Assembly to some more distant place if its members feared the troops then in Versailles.

This reply gave the liberals in the Assembly an inkling of the king's intentions. When he dismissed Necker and replaced his ministry with a conservative group, the action was accepted as a challenge (July 11). Popular excitement was fanned to a high pitch when news of Necker's dismissal reached Paris. Camille Desmoulins called the crowds in the Palais Royal to arms. All day and through the night of July 12, the mob marched through the city. By the following day, the former electors, chiefly propertied and business men, had organized a bourgeois guard for the maintenance of order. When a rumor circulated that arms were available in the Hôtel des Invalides,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

it was sacked; another mob moved on the Bastille. This old fortress had been used as a state prison and was symbolic of all that was despotic. By accident, the mob succeeded in taking the stronghold. 

The import of the fall of the Bastille on July 14 lay chiefly in the fact that this action of the Paris mob checked the king in his scheme for eliminating the Assembly. The king ordered the troops from the vicinity of Paris (July 15) and recognized the militia organization, so hastily established during the days of rioting, as a National Guard. 

He reappointed Necker on July 16 and the next day donned the tri-colored cockade to indicate his acceptance of the new order. 

Members of the court party, led by the Count of Artois, looked on the king's acquiescence in the new order as little short of cowardice and for their own safety began what was to be a long series of emigrations. 

While a Paris mob was attacking the Bastille, the provinces were not quiescent. Famine and fear of what might or might not be done at Versailles gave rise to what had been called the "Great Fear."

During the late summer of 1789, peasants in the country districts. rose up against their lords, burning châteaux to destroy manorial records and indulging in other acts of brigandage. Local officials had not the means to cope with this rampant terrorism. The towns and cities, too, had their attacks on local bastilles; and their municipal governments were reconstructed, local National Guard units were formed, and eventually order was restored. The towns then used the guard to subdue the rioting peasantry. The Revolution had become more than a demand for constitutional government; it was rapidly degenerating into class conflict.

News of such violent insurrections came as a shock to the deputies deliberating at Versailles. Some proposed that the peasants be chastised, but on August 4 the chief cause for peasant revolt was removed when the nobles rose in the Assembly to renounce their privileges. 

They were followed by the clergy and the rich bourgeoisie. This episode marks the end of the Ancien Régime. The decrees incorporating these concessions became law a week later. Actually, the "August Decrees" were more a program of reform than reform itself, for it was the function of the Assembly to implement the decrees.

The National Constituent Assembly voted to accept the Decla ration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen on August 27, 1789. This was, in most respects, a bourgeois document which announced that certain rights belonged to men, because they were men and not be-

cause any government had granted those rights. Many of the ideas included were the common aspirations of liberals in England, France, and America. It contained few original ideas, but a synthesis involving numerous compromises. The Declaration appealed to the 

French masses, but when its principles were translated into action in the constitution the commoners were destined to disappointment. 

The Declaration has had a wide influence on liberal thought in Europe. It states that all men possess equal rights, that the purpose of government is to preserve the natural rights of liberty, security, property, and freedom from oppression. A government should receive its power from the people, whose general will should be expressed, through representative machinery, in the law of the land. 

Men should be free from arbitrary arrest and imprisonment and be presumed innocent until proved guilty. Men must be free to express opinions on any subject, including religion, within the bounds of a legally established public order. Taxes to support a governmental power to enforce such laws should be assessed equally on all citizens according to their respective means, and public officials should-be held accountable for their actions.

The Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen did not receive the full support of the king. On September 14, 1789, he called the Flanders Regiment to Versailles. Again, his nominal aim was to protect the Assembly from the menacing Parisian populace. A banquet, given by the royal bodyguard in honor of the Flanders Regiment, was held at Versailles on October 1. At this affair, no toasts were drunk to the nation, and, what seemed more serious, the national cockade was trampled upon. News of this outrage reached 

Paris on October 3 and provoked the violence of the famous “October Days." On October 5, a mob sacked the Hôtel de Ville and eventually marched to Versailles to demand guarantees from the king that Paris would have bread. News of the approaching mob reached the Assembly, and it decided to send a deputation to the king. That evening they obtained his sanction of the constitutional decrees. Lafayette arrived in the meantime and posted a guard about the palace. Early the next morning, the mob found an unguarded entrance and began milling about inside the palace. When detected, they were fired on, and in the panic which followed, the queen barely escaped with her life. To quiet the crowd, the king brought the royal family to the balcony and received considerable applause. 

When the mob began to shout, "On to Paris! " the king had to acquiesce. That night, he, Marie Antoinette, and the Dauphin reached

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the Louvre. Parisians referred to them as "the baker, the baker's wife, and the baker's son," whose presence in the city, they hoped, would be a guarantee against famine. On October 16, the Assembly followed the king to Paris.

The outstanding leader in the National Constituent Assembly during this period was Mirabeau. He had spent the greater part of his adult life in the custody of jailers. Almost a dozen lettres de cachet had been issued to punish him for sundry escapades or to prevent him from further disgracing his family. These many years of confinement had afforded him the opportunity to read, to think, and to write about those subjects which were eventually to place him in the role of a moderate politician and statesman. Before the calling of the 

Estates-General, he had expressed himself as a proponent of: (1) the abolition of feudalism, (2) religious toleration, (3) civil equality, (4) sound governmental finances, (5) nationalized secular education, (6) a limited monarchy with representative institutions, and (7) freedom of manufactures and trade. Though a powerful orator, his reputation robbed him of supporters. His role had to be that of a prompter, never that of a party leader. His tireless labors for limited monarchy helped to cause his death in April, 1791. He had attempted an alliance with Lafayette, but the general distrusted him and nothing worthwhile came of the effort. Mirabeau also had allied with the king, receiving pay for advice which was more honored in the breach than in the observance. With the death of Mirabeau, the last restraint upon the king was gone, and, a few weeks later, the royal family attempted to escape from France, thus bringing on the second and harsher phase of the Revolution. If any one man could have warded off the excesses which resulted, it would undoubtedly have been Mirabeau.

The Assembly had begun work on a constitution in July, 1789. 

This first written constitution of the nation has been variously called that of 1789, 1790, or 1791. The last date seems the most proper. Although the Declaration was adopted in 1789 and numerous edicts were promulgated in each of the years mentioned, the whole was perfected, codified, and placed in a single document which the king accepted on September 3, 1791. The Assembly made short shrift of all suggestions that a republic be formed. Moderate views prevailed, so that the document established a constitutional monarchy in which the chief principle was that power resides in the people, who delegate it to representatives and to the king. The constitution provided for a Legislative Assembly whose members were to be chosen in-

directly by qualified citizens. Frenchmen were to be either active or passive citizens; the former were designated as twenty-five-year-old males, paying an annual direct tax equal to three days' wages or more. 

The ratio of active to passive citizens was as four to three. Thus, three-sevenths of the male citizens of twenty-five years or more were denied the franchise. Every one hundred active citizens were permitted to choose an elector from those among them paying an annual direct tax of about the equivalent of 150 days' wages. The electors then chose the deputies who were to sit in the Legislative Assembly and the judges. While there was no property qualification for the deputies, it was expected that the well-to-do electors would choose men who thought as they did.¹ It will be seen that this constitution was a decidedly bourgeois document. Such restrictions on the franchise seem hardly in keeping with the profession of equality and the Declaration of Rights which formed the introductory part of the constitution itself. While the constitution took from the king his power to make laws, it gave him a suspensive veto, empowering him to delay enactment of a law. A further constitutional reform provided for formation of eighty-three departments from the thirty-two provinces of France. This, in form, meant almost excessive decentralization of the administrative system. The departments were divided into arrondissements, which were in turn subdivided into cantons, communes, and municipalités. France still adheres to these governmental subdivisions. The legislative committees governed local affairs as minutely as ever had been the case under the Ancien Régime. Such practices were continued, not under the constitution, but in spite of it, and this must be assigned as a major cause for the short-lived existence of that document. 

The financial condition of the government became steadily worse during the summer of 1789. The taxes of the old order had been abolished and three new ones levied in their place. These were a land tax, a personal property tax, and a tax on the revenues from trade and manufacturing. Taxpayers were lax in making payments and the government's income was exceedingly meager. Necker again was forced to resort to his old methods of bank loans and unsuccessful public bond issues. In October, Talleyrand, who had become the Bishop of Autun, proposed confiscation of the property of the church for the reduction of the public debt. It was argued that the church was a corporate organization, holding lands in trust for the performance of certain services; if the state assumed the tasks 

1 For a time, tax payment of one silver mark was requisite.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of educating the young, caring for the poor, and providing the means of public worship, it could, with justification, expropriate the church lands. The Assembly voted on November 2, 1789, to confiscate church property; in mid-December, some of it was indirectly offered for sale by the issue of assignats, really treasury bonds, redeemable in church lands rather than in currency. The experiment was not successful and, as further guarantee that the state would back up its assignats, they were practically made legal tender (April 17, 1790). Two days later, the nation assumed actual control of the church property. From time to time, laws limiting the total issue of assignats were passed, but the tendency was to expand the volume to unheard of amounts. Continued inflation of the currency led to a decline in the value of the assignats until by 

1796 they became virtually worthless.

Then, to compensate the church for the loss of its lands, the Assembly passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which granted the clergy state salaries but also required that they be elected by the people or their representatives. Since the pope forbade ecclesiastics to take the required oath, the clergy became divided into juring and non-juring groups. 

2 See infra, pp. 573-574, for Concordat of 1802.

CHAPTER 42 The Revolution: 1791-1795 

T was believed in 1791 that the adoption of the constitution and the establishment of constitutional monarchy marked the end of the Revolution. But the Revolution had merely begun, for, aside from the dissatisfaction of the lower classes with the constitution, economic distress had not been alleviated. The constitution did not provide for the abolition of all feudal dues, but stipulated that the peasants should liquidate their obligations. The manner in which this was to be done caused much hardship and led to considerable active insurrection. The ambition of many a poor peasant to acquire through the distribution of the church lands a tract on which he might sustain his family was not realized. Since the 

National Constituent Assembly had been sorely in need of funds, the church lands were in most instances sold to persons with a cash surplus for investment in such property. Out of this developed an agrarian unemployment problem which accentuated unrest. During the early months of 1791, a perceptible commercial revival followed the removal of restrictions on internal trade, the abolition of the gilds, and the desire to exchange assignats for commodities. 

Nevertheless, increased unemployment, both rural and urban, eventual decline in the value of the assignats, and demands of laborers for wage increases rather than the reductions they had been forced to accept, brought on an economic crisis. Food prices soared; of all causes for unrest, this was most potent.

So great was the king's personal opposition to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, that he was impelled to act on his own initiative. 

While the noble émigrés had been leaving the country, the queen had considered various ways of escaping from France. The restraining influence of Mirabeau was no longer present to hinder such schemes. 

Flight would likewise encourage Austria and Prussia to intervene. 

In keeping with the spirit of international custom at the time there were numerous projects for foreign intervention. Emigrés, located

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

in the small German states on the French frontier, appealed openly to the monarchs of Europe to intervene. Such requests were, however, generally more for the advantage of the émigrés than for the benefit of Louis XVI; that the king understood these motives is illustrated by the fact that he disavowed the activities of his two brothers, Condé and Artois. Louis hoped for a different type of foreign intervention, a mere show of force on the French border. In the meantime, the queen was in regular correspondence with her brother, Leopold II of Austria. Her urgent appeals for aid were put aside, because other problems at that moment precluded such an enterprise. By the summer of 1790, friction between Austria and Prussia was allayed, but a Polish crisis arose. Catherine the Great of Russia was planning a second partition of Poland. She consequently urged Leopold to intervene in France to enable her to carry out her Polish schemes. Leopold, aware of her plans, declined to do so. Frederick William II of Prussia would willingly have intervened in France had Austria joined with him, but since Leopold opposed the scheme nothing was done. 

Louis eventually decided that his last recourse lay in flight. Although preparations were made in secrecy, information concerning the plans leaked out. An attempt of the royal family to spend the 

Easter holidays of 1791 at Saint-Cloud was frustrated when a Parisian crowd and the National Guard turned the royal carriages back to the Tuileries. This flight has been variously interpreted; some hold that the king really tried to flee; others, that he wished to have the services of a non-juring priest. There is also reason to believe that the king merely wished to demonstrate to France and to the world that he was virtually being held prisoner in his own palace. During the following month, at a secret meeting in Mantua, Austria, Spain, Prussia, and a few lesser German states agreed to come to the aid of the 

French dynasty.

More elaborate flight plans were now devised and completed by June 20. One of the royal generals had agreed to furnish a cavalry escort for the royal carriage to the Luxemburg border, but the suspicions this cavalry troop aroused forced it to take to a side road where it failed to meet the king. The royal coach moved slowly, and, although its occupants were recognized by a number of people, only one dared to give the alarm. This resulted in the detention of the whole party at Varennes, where, on the morning of June 22, orders arrived for the king's arrest. 

The coach with its royal occupants returned to Paris through truculent mobs. With the king and his family again within the Tui-

leries, the situation of the Bourbons became precarious. The king, presuming that his plans would be successfully consummated, had left, as a communication to the nation, a declaration of his reasons for opposition to the constitution, an attack on coercive measures, and an expression of chagrin at the insults he and the queen had endured. 

The National Constituent Assembly suspended the king on June 

25, but in mid-July, as a face-saving measure, absolved him of all responsibility for the flight. The Assembly provided that he would be restored as the constitutional king as soon as he accepted the revised constitution. This he did on September 14, 1791. Meanwhile, the Cordelier Club, led by Danton, demanded that the king be brought to trial and suggested the establishment of a republic. On 

July 17, two supposed spies were lynched by a mob assembled at the Champ-de-Mars. This act caused the Assembly to take direct action by ordering Lafayette to establish martial law. When the soldiers were stoned and General Lafayette was fired upon, the troops fired into the mob. This massacre of the Champ-de-Mars resulted in the temporary exile of Danton and marked the commencement of renewed bloodshed.

Bourbon efforts to obtain foreign intervention eventually were partly successful. On August 27, 1791, Leopold of Austria and Frederick William of Prussia jointly issued the famous Declaration of 

Pilnitz, which announced that the restoration of the Bourbon dynasty in France was of common interest to all nations of Europe and suggested coöperation for the attainment of that objective. Prussia and Austria had already agreed to an offensive and defensive alliance a month before; the Declaration was an announcement that Austria and Prussia would not intervene in France unless supported by the rest of Europe.

Mention has been made of the Cordelier Club. There were numerous organizations of this nature, most important of which was the Jacobin Club, known originally as the Society of Friends of the Constitution. Its more popular name resulted from the fact that the meeting place was in a former Jacobin convent. In its original form, only leftist, or radical, deputies were members. Affiliated clubs were organized in the provinces until they numbered nearly 500. Jacobin meetings became a clearing house for petitions, demands, proposed laws, and schemes of all sorts. When the society voted to support a measure, its members in the Assembly sponsored it. Until 1791, the club was moderate in its policy; its chief service was to maintain a watchful eye on the activities of the Assembly. The Cordeliers, too,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

were so named because their meeting place was in a former convent of that order. Their fees were lower than those of the Jacobins and their consideration of measures and men was less deliberate. Perhaps the most colorful of its members were Jean Marat, Camille Desmoulins, and Danton. There were numerous other revolutionary clubs, but these two were the most influential and powerful. 

Of the revolutionary journals, Jean Marat's Ami du peuple was outstanding. The editor was a disgruntled physician with a remarkable sense of the dramatic and the ability to sway the masses by his pen. As the self-chosen "Friend of the People," Marat kept a suspicious watch on the nation's leaders. His journal was not a newspaper as we think of one today; it was a medium for the expression of his views on current events rather than for the reporting of news. 

A capably edited conservative organ was the Moniteur, advocating the views of the constitutionalists. Almost every leader of consequence had his journal for selective reporting of events and the dis semination of propaganda. 

The last meeting of the National Constituent Assembly took place on September 30; on the following day, the deputies of the new 

Legislative Assembly took their seats. A serious error had been committed by the National Constituent Assembly when, by the "Selfdenying Ordinance," it decreed that none of its members were eligible for election to the new Legislative Assembly. The new deputies were therefore inexperienced. 

The Legislative Assembly had no unified policy. It was divided into three major parties. The conservatives, numbering about 260, sat on the right of the assembly chamber and belonged for the most part to the Feuillant Club, organized by conservative Jacobins after the massacre of the Champ-de-Mars. Its leaders were such men as the 

Abbé Sieyes and General Lafayette. The left, or radical deputies, numbering about 130, held membership in either the Jacobin or Cordelier clubs. Most of the Jacobin members followed Maximilien 

Robespierre and were subsequently known as Montagnards, or the "Mountain," because of the high tier of seats they occupied in the assembly hall. Some followed Brissot and were known at first as 

Brissotins, but later as Girondins. They were generally young men, idealistically minded, coming chiefly from the department of the Gironde. Perhaps the chief factor integrating this leftist group was the conviction that any treasonable activity on the king's part must result in his downfall. In the center sat the moderates, the largest group in point of numbers, who voted with right or left as they saw

fit. A major fault of the new governmental organization was the lack of intimate contact between the king's ministers and the Assembly. 

This constitutional weakness had been pointed out at various times, but the separation of powers theory had been so indelibly impressed that it had curbed attempts to create a responsible ministry. 

Since the attempted flight of the king to Varennes, events moved rapidly towards the establishment of a republic. One of the steps leading to this change was the declaration of war against Austria in April, 1792. The Girondins, the chief exponents of this war, saw in it an opportunity to increase their own popularity and importance. Hostilities would force the king into an open declaration of his purpose and thus deprive him of the powers he still possessed. 

Lafayette, on the other hand, favored war as a means of increasing the powers of the monarch. Louis appealed anew for intervention accompanied with a display of force great enough to halt radical trends in Paris. Robespierre was almost alone in his opposition to the war and he used to the utmost his reputation as "The Incorruptible" to frustrate belligerent policies. He pointed out that if France was successful in a war of this nature, the only type of government which could follow victory would be one possessing a strong executive. 

Until that time, he pointed out, one of the major aims of the Revolution had been to eliminate the strong, centralized government of the monarchy. 

On March 1, 1792, Leopold II of Austria died, and his son and successor, Francis II, showed himself more ready to intervene in French affairs. During the same month, the French ministry fell and was replaced by one including a number of Girondins, with Dumouriez as the leading figure. He wanted a short and successful war; from that time on, there could be no doubt as to the coming conflict, which the king and the Assembly voted on April 20, 1792.

The war was destined to continue with only brief interruptions until 1815.

Dumouriez planned an invasion of Belgium, but he reckoned without full knowledge of the disorganized condition of the French forces. The army, weakened by the emigration of many of its officers and by the desertion of hundreds of troops of the line, turned in disorderly flight at the Belgian frontier. To add to the troubles, Prussia entered the conflict as an ally of Austria (May 1, 1792). These powers, however, were unable to profit by the disorganized condition of the French army because of the Polish situation. 

Το prepare the nation for war, the Assembly passed a series of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

decrees, the most drastic of which made it possible to deport priests who declined to accept the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Other measures provided that an army be raised for the defense of Paris against internal as well as foreign foes. The king disapproved both of these measures and vetoed them. When Roland, the Girondist 

Minister of the Interior, rebuked the king in public print for these vetoes, the Girondin ministry was dismissed. Dumouriez, thus relieved of his duties in the ministry, left Paris to take command of the northern army.

The reaction of the Parisian populace to this turn of affairs was demonstrated when a mob attempted to force the king to rescind his vetoes. Resentment towards the monarchy rapidly increased as troops continued to pour into Paris in preparation for its defense. 

The spark to set off this revolutionary tinder was provided when, in reply to a request of Louis XVI, the allies published, in the Moniteur of August 3, the famous Brunswick Manifesto. This pronouncement did as much as any other single incident to increase the revolutionary activity of the Jacobins and to unite the French nation against the invaders. The error made in the Manifesto was that it was aimed at all Frenchmen, rather than merely against the Parisian radicals. The document stated that, while the powers of Europe had no desire to intervene in French internal affairs, they demanded that Louis XVI be restored to his full powers. If, under any circumstances, he was harmed, the allies threatened to devastate Paris. Louis disavowed the 

Manifesto, but during the week following its publication, preparations were made for a march on the Tuileries. On the morning of 

August 10, the royal household fled for safety to the meeting place of the Assembly. Nearly 1,000 Swiss mercenaries and menials guarding the palace lost their lives in the onslaught of the mob. 

In the disorder which accompanied these events of August 10, a revolutionary government, known as the commune, was established for the control of Paris. It did not dissolve the Assembly, since that body still had the support of the provinces which were yet predominantly Girondist in their sympathies. The commune made clear, however, that it intended to call a new convention for revision of the constitution and for the trial of Louis. While the Assembly agreed to the convocation of a constitutional convention, it refused to do more than suspend the king until its meeting. With the king suspended, some substitute was essential for the administration of the executive affairs of the realm. To the extra-legal commune and the Legislative Assembly was added, therefore, a third body which

might well be considered an executive council. It was composed of six ministers, chief of whom was Danton, the Minister of Justice who had been credited with organizing the insurrection of August 10. 

In the following weeks, the Prussians were victorious and entered French territory on August 19. Danton attempted to raise sufficient man power to turn back the invader and to crush opposition to the Revolutionary government within France. When news reached Paris of the imminent fall of Verdun, volunteers in the capital determined to rid themselves of all possible danger from the enemies they would be leaving in their rear when they marched to halt the invaders. They hearkened to the cry of Marat for “heads," and began the "September Massacres

September Massacres" which extended into the districts. In Paris alone, 1,000 were slain. The Assembly was too frightened to interfere, and the commune was not disposed to halt the massacres. Even if he had tried, it is questionable whether Danton could have done much to stop the carnage. 

The elections for the National Convention took place during the height of these anti-royalist demonstrations. Military affairs took a turn for the better when, on September 20, at the "Cannonade of 

Valmy," the Prussians, under Brunswick, were halted. On the following day (September 21, 1792), the National Convention, with little delay, unanimously decreed the abolition of the monarchy, merely legalizing what had been a fact since August 10. On the following day, the Convention voted to date future public papers from the Year One of the French Republic. 

As in every past legislative body, factions developed within the National Convention. The Montagnards, or the Mountain, were composed of Jacobins like Marat, Danton, and Robespierre. Then there was the larger group known as the Center, and a third group, the Girondins. The chief point of difference among them, late in 

1792, was the disposition to be made of Louis XVI. The Montagnards, especially St. Just, demanded the trial and execution of the deposed monarch; the Girondins attempted to delay trial. 

The Convention arraigned the king in early December, and his trial lasted for about a month. During this period, an iron box, made by the king and containing his correspondence with Mirabeau, was found. The disclosure served to silence the opponents of the king's execution and the deputies unanimously convicted him of conspiracy against the nation. They decided against submitting the question of punishment to a referendum and voted 387 to 334 for the death

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

penalty. On January 21, 1793, Louis died on the guillotine, preserving his admirable fortitude to the last.

The trial and execution of the king shocked the rest of Europe and caused the Convention, on February 1, 1793, to declare war on 

Great Britain and the United Provinces (Holland). On March 7, war was declared against Bourbon Spain. Before the year was out, most of Europe was at war with France. This combination, fostered by Great Britain, is known as the First Coalition. Republican France was surrounded on all sides by the armed forces of Austria, Prussia, the United Provinces, Spain, and Russia. The German states of the 

Holy Roman Empire entered the coalition the following year. 

With the foreign threat came defeats for the forces under General Dumouriez, who ultimately deserted to the enemy. Disaster struck also at General Custine in the region of the Rhine; open rebellion against the national government broke out in the Vendée, and, when famine threatened portions of the country, the situation became grave. The necessity for a unified governing power to cope with the national emergency was realized; during the spring of 1793 a series of reform decrees were passed, one of which created the 

Committee of Public Safety. On the first committee of this name,

Danton was the most influential personage. The powers of the Committee extended to the control of the ministry and it had a large expense fund at its disposal. While created for only a month, its tenure was prolonged to July, 1793. Among the other decrees passed was one giving virtually unlimited powers to deputies sent as “Representatives on Mission" to the various armies and departments. 

Within the Convention, factional quarrels became vitriolic with the defection of Dumouriez. Danton was attacked for his friendliness with the traitor. Marat allied with the Mountain in a counterattack on the Girondins. They, in turn, attempted to impeach Marat, but failed. The controversy led eventually to the expulsion of the 

Girondins from the Convention (June 2, 1793), at the instance of a new commune which controlled the Convention and which, in turn, was dominated by the Jacobin element. Paris had come to control the course of the Revolution, and the departments could do little but revolt against the usurpation of power. To suppress these revolts, to make the national government supreme, extreme measures were demanded if the impending foreign invasion was to be turned back. 

The Convention had been called to frame a new constitution and, during the period from June 10 to 24, it adopted one which never went into effect. This was a relatively liberal document, providing

for universal manhood suffrage and eliminating most property qualifications. While this constitution was being framed, the Committee of Public Safety was attempting to organize a national government, but it was seriously embarrassed by military defeats and the disaffection of the departments which were demanding a federal type of government. The pressure on the Committee became so great that by July 10, 1793, it was dissolved and a new one created which excluded Danton. This new Committee was rather unified in purpose, but almost at the time of its creation, Marat, the outstanding Montagnard deputy, was assassinated by Charlotte Corday (July 13, 1793).

Thus, with Danton out of power and Marat dead, the way was open for the ascendancy of Robespierre. He became a member of the 

Committee on July 27. In this same month, the federalist revolts in the departments were suppressed and the organization of national resources for the conflict with the foreign enemy was begun on a large scale.

Such preparations did not yet warrant the promulgation of the new constitution. Internal and external affairs were still in such condition that it was deemed inexpedient to attempt the election and installation of a new government; the Committee of Public Safety consequently continued in control. When, in September, food supplies ran low because of bad crops, profiteering, and the failure of the government to regulate prices, and news reached the capital of the surrender of Toulon to the English, demand arose for terroristic methods to extirpate opposition to the government. In harmony with this demand, the Committee retained its power by a policy of terrorism until the death of Robespierre (July 28, 1794). The 

Jacobin clubs throughout France were ordered to denounce persons suspected of opposition to the policies of the Committee. Local administration was loosely but arbitrarily regulated by the Committee of Public Safety through the "Representatives on Mission." By early December, 1793, the Terror government was a unified organization.

The government was headed by the Committee of Public Safety, whose most important members were Robespierre and Carnot. This group appointed the members of the Committee of General Security, charged with the policing of the country. A third division was the Revolutionary Tribunal, created to try persons accused of anti- Revolutionary sentiments or activities. The Tribunal began its work by condemning Marie Antoinette to death on October 16, 1793. It then condemned some score of the Girondins previously expelled

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

from the legislature. Before its work was done, this court and local judicial bodies put to death some 20,000 men, women, and children of all classes. Under the stress of revolution and foreign invasion, some bloodshed was inevitable; violence was inherent in the very nature of the situation; but such excesses were heartrending to Danton, who became active again by lending support to the moderates. 

His opposition made him, with the radical Hébertists, fit fodder for the hungry guillotine; on April 5, 1794, his head fell into the basket.

Robespierre was now in full control, and the "Incorruptible proceeded to establish his idealistic "Republic of Virtue.” Aside from moral implications, he aimed at the further centralization of power in the hands of the Committee; so effectively was this accomplished that the period from June 10 to July 27 has been designated the "Great Terror." During these weeks some 1,300 persons were sent to the guillotine by the Revolutionary Tribunal. Such excesses, the harsh laws of the government, and a growing realization that the nation was no longer in imminent danger of invasion, led to the reaction of Thermidor (July 27, 1794). This was an attack aimed at 

Robespierre rather than at the Committee as a whole; it succeeded because he failed properly to gauge the strength of his opponents.
