By July 27, his enemies had gained control of the Convention, and on the following day the "Incorruptible" and a number of his henchmen were victims of the blade they had prepared for so many others. 

The blot left by the Terror on the pages of history has hidden the constructive accomplishments of that government. Perhaps the cardinal point in the revolutionary program of the Committee was centralization of power in order that its war machine might become a national force for ridding France of the foreign foe. It also improved commercial conditions by removing numerous restrictions on trade.

The Thermidorians, the middle class group which overthrew Robespierre and the Jacobins, began a policy of governmental decentralization. Their problems were numerous, but perhaps the most serious was the suppression of the Jacobin revolt which broke out against them. They concluded a series of treaties which effectively ended the First Coalition. The best known of these treaties were those of Basel with Prussia (April 5, 1795) and with Spain, although two others were concluded between March and July of that year. Only Austria and England remained at war with France. 

The Thermidorians next turned to the problem of providing a rea-

sonably sound constitution, instead of revising the dormant Constitution of the Year I.

The weakness which the Convention itself had displayed was avoided under this constitution by the creation of a bicameral legislature, known as the Corps Législatif. This corps consisted of two houses, the Council of Elders with 250 members and the Council of Five Hundred. The latter could initiate and discuss legislation; the former could pass or reject measures presented by the lower house. At certain times and for certain reasons, the two houses might hold joint sessions. The Constitution of the Year III provided for manhood suffrage with a slight property qualification. The executive, distinct and separate in powers from the legislative branch of the government, consisted of five directors, chosen by the Elders from a list of former deputies, at least forty years of age, nominated by the Council of Five Hundred. One director was to retire every year, and each was to serve for three months, in rotation, as president of this executive board. The local administrative system was not materially changed. The constitution establishing the government of the "Directory" so well provided for the separation of the powers that when inevitable disputes arose, resort to force was the alternative to inaction.

One last important act of the Convention was a decree requiring that 500 of its members be chosen to membership in the new legislative councils. So unpopular was this "Two-thirds Ordinance" that it, with sundry other causes for complaint, served to provoke the insurrection of 13th Vendémiaire (October 5, 1795). Some 20,000 men marched on the Tuileries in which the Convention was meeting; hardly one-fifth that number of troops were available for defense. 

But those soldiers had been placed under the command of a young Corsican artilleryman, Napoleon Bonaparte, who so effectively placed his men and cannon that it took but a “whiff of grapeshot' to break up the assault. On October 26, 1795, the Convention ended, and the government of the Directory was inaugurated. 99

CHAPTER 43 The Career of Napoleon to the Coup d'État of 1799

WITH the outbreak of the Revolution, such an effective beginning was made in the decentralization of the French government that only by terroristic methods could the Committee of Public Safety maintain a central administration strong enough to repel the First Coalition. Robespierre had prophesied, when opposing the belligerent policy of the Girondins, that a successful war would inevitably lead to dictatorship. With dissension and disorder prevalent throughout France, the necessity of maintaining autonomy against external foes, as well as against treason and reaction, clearly foreshadowed the rise of dictatorship. 

The question of whether personalities influence the course of history, or events and conditions shape the careers of historic personages, is a most interesting one. The mass of Napoleonic literature gives ample evidence to argue either side of this question. In general, the biographer inclines to the personality thesis; the historian rejects it. There are, for example, so many "ifs" in the early life of Napoleon Bonaparte that one could reasonably accept the view that his career was shaped by events; during the height of his regime, there seems little reason to doubt that he materially guided the trend of history.

There has been considerable dispute over the exact date of Napoleon's birth, since he himself used several as expediency dictated. We may, however, accept August 15, 1769, as correct. Since Corsica came under the control of France in July of that year, Napoleon just barely acquired French citizenship by birth. His father, Charles 

Bonaparte, was of the lesser Corsican nobility. His title was registered in Paris shortly before his death. The support of the eight children fell on the shoulders of the proud, frugal, and accomplished mother, Laetitia. Napoleon entered the military school at Brienne

when about ten years of age, with the aid of a royal pension. Because of his poverty, his uncouth French, his small stature, and his Corsican pride, he became the butt of many a schoolboy joke. A sickly boy, he was morose and sullen; he found some relief from his unhappiness by concentrating on historical works and the study of mathematics. After five years at Brienne, he spent a year in the Paris 

Cadets' School, where he took post-graduate work in artillery warfare and continued his extensive reading. When little more than fifteen years of age, he was commissioned a sub-lieutenant and ordered to report to his regiment at Valence. 

It was natural for him to adopt as his youthful ambition the liberation of Corsica. During his early years of army service he spent much of his time on furloughs on his native island, and his stays were on several occasions prolonged without permission. In Corsica, he occupied himself with writing and revolutionary activity; eventually, military superiors lost patience and he was cashiered. His insurrectionary activities on the island brought him into conflict with domestic authorities; when his arrest was ordered he hastened to 

Paris, where he became an intimate of Robespierre. While in Paris he observed the sack of the Tuileries. Instead of being brought to trial for desertion, he was advanced to the rank of captain by the new government. Again he returned to Corsica instead of reporting to his regiment, and his intrigues resulted in the destruction of the Bonaparte home and the subsequent flight of the family to France. 

From this time Napoleon's Corsican patriotism waned, and he began thinking and acting as a Frenchman.

The incompetent generals charged with reducing the English stronghold at Toulon found in Napoleon a competent artillery strategist. Successful termination of the siege attracted favorable attention and gained for him the rank of brigadier-general. Following the execution of Robespierre, the young officer was imprisoned because of his friendship with the "Incorruptible." Appeal to the Convention eventually procured his liberation on the grounds that he could be of service to the army. The reaction of Thermidor eventually resulted in the assignment of Napoleon to the infantry, a detail which seemed to him an unbearable demotion. He again failed to report for service, but this time he remained in Paris. By the presentation of a brilliant plan for the conduct of an Italian campaign, he won a place in the Operations Department, only to lose it for insubordination. 

Two weeks after this incident he was requested to accept actual command of the small force charged with the defense of the Con-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

vention during the uprising of 13th Vendémiaire against the Twothirds Ordinance. His successful disposition of the cannon which 

Murat had obtained made possible dispersal of the mob. The thanks of the Convention were accompanied with an assignment to the com mand of the Army of the Interior. 

Barras, nominally in charge of the military defense of the Convention, in November, 1795, became one of the five directors under the Constitution of the Year III. Barras had considerable faith in the rising star of his subordinate. When the general in charge of the 

Army of Italy belittled Napoleon's plan, he was recalled, and Napoleon was selected by Barras to replace him. During 1796, France was still at war with Great Britain, Austria, Piedmont-Sardinia, and Spain. The Italian assignment was the most difficult facing the 

French military command, but Napoleon accepted it with alacrity. 

Prior to his starting for the south, he married Josephine de Beauharnais, a native of Martinique and the widow of a nobleman executed during the Terror. She was the mother of two children, Eugene and Hortense, both of whom eventually proved more loyal to their stepfather than his own brothers and sisters. 

There are numerous accounts of Napoleon's first meeting with his troops. The veterans scorned this small, sallow-faced, sickly commander and wondered what the Directory could be thinking of to send such a general. However, he soon demonstrated that he knew what he was about, that he possessed courage and efficiency, and that he could give succinct orders which he expected to be obeyed; in a remarkably short time he won the admiration of his men. It now appears that the speech, so often quoted, that Napoleon presumably delivered to his troops before embarking on the first Italian campaign, was one written while he was drafting his memoirs at Saint Helena. But in this campaign, Napoleon exhibited most of the characteristics prominent in the remainder of his military career. His most effective weapons were the mobility of his troops and his adroit use of artillery. His strategy was generally to feint with a small force to divide his enemy, whereupon he would throw his full strength on the divisions of the enemy and defeat each in turn. 

The French military campaigns mapped out for the year 1796 included two in the Rhine valley under the commands of Generals Jourdan and Moreau, and the one in Italy under Bonaparte. The 

Italian troops were good soldiers, numbering some 40,000 men, but they had been poorly paid. Many were in want of food, clothing, arms, and ammunition. Napoleon took command in early April, and

in a series of brilliant marches separated the Sardinians from the Austrians and then forced both to retreat. An armistice and peace were soon arranged with Sardinia. Napoleon realized that his real foe in Italy was the Austrian army, with which he soon fought the bloody battle of Lodi, after which he marched into Milan. He laid siege to Mantua in early June. The Austrians sent one army after another to the relief of the besieged garrison, but the wily Napoleon defeated each expedition by meeting its separate divisions with the full force at his command. Most famous of these battles were those of Arcola (November 15-17, 1796) and Rivoli (January 14, 1797). Rivoli was the decisive encounter in the campaign, and within a few days Mantua was opened to the victorious invaders. During the spring of 1797, the French generals in the Rhine region were advancing rapidly. When Napoleon came within one hundred miles of Vienna, he offered an armistice to the Austrians rather than permit the honor of victory to pass to other French commanders.

The preliminary Peace of Leoben was signed on April 18, 1797, contrary to the expressed wishes of the Directory. France gained preliminary title to Lombardy and the Austrian Netherlands, regions already hers by conquest. During the next few months, Napoleon busied himself with diplomatic affairs in Italy. On July 9, the Cisalpine Republic was proclaimed, based on Lombardy. Then the 

Ligurian Republic was created out of Genoa. In the meantime, royalist opposition to the government of the Directory resulted in an attempt to overthrow the established order. When the scheme was ascertained by the more radical directors, they called on Napoleon to suppress the movement. This he did by the coup of 18th 

Fructidor (September 4, 1797), and established a Directory which relied on force to maintain itself. The question was how long the generals, especially Napoleon, would permit it to govern. 

After Leoben, negotiations were continued to bring about definitive peace with Austria. This was accomplished by the Treaty of 

Campo Formio, signed October 17, 1797. By its clauses, many of which were secret, Austria recognized French annexation of the Austrian Netherlands and ceded to France almost two-thirds of the territory of the Holy Roman Empire west of the Rhine. There was an understanding to the effect that the dispossessed German princes would receive lands elsewhere in the Empire. In exchange for Lombardy, Austria received Istria, Venice, and Dalmatia. There were numerous reasons why France should not have signed this treaty, for it amounted to a declaration of war rather than peace, but the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

terms were so popular that the Directory could do nothing but acquiesce.

Napoleon had acted independent of and often in opposition to the instructions of the Directory in the development of his Italian system. His excuse was that he was on the field and could better understand the circumstances. Then, too, was he not sending wagon train after wagon train filled with loot and tribute, exacted from the rich Italian cities, to the bankrupt Directory? The directors began to fear his strength and popularity, but, since they owed their offices to his intervention during Fructidor, and since open opposition to his policies would incur popular disfavor, they refrained from action. Napoleon had firm faith in his own good fortune; he sincerely believed that his "star" would rise to unheard-of heights. 

His problem, as he saw it, was merely to await the proper moment. 

The conqueror of Italy returned to Paris in December, 1797, where he conducted himself modestly despite the ovation tendered him. 

His presence in Paris made the government itself seem unimportant and the directors became as eager to have him out of Paris as he himself was to get away from the life of the capital. 

It will have been noted that all the members of the First Coalition, except England, had been humbled by France. The Directory now suggested to Napoleon that he attempt an invasion of the British Isles. While he prepared for the expedition, he came into contact with the astute schemer, Talleyrand, one-time Bishop of Autun, now recently returned from exile to become foreign minister under the Directory. Both Talleyrand and Napoleon were interested in an eastern expedition, and they soon entered into intrigues which convinced the directors of its feasibility. 

The Egyptian campaign was the first of three major Napoleonic attempts to humble Great Britain. He saw in a French conquest of 

Egypt the opportunity to cut the English “life line" to India, to revive the French empire in India, and to strike at the source of England's commercial prosperity. He failed to take into account the fact that Britain was passing through the Industrial Revolution and that her prosperity was basically the result of the mechanization of her industries. The Egyptian expedition was of great significance to scholarship. What appeared to many as an exotic adventure, gained respectability when Napoleon gathered about him a number of competent scientists who made extensive plans for a survey of the resources of the Land of the Pharaohs. Their work laid the founda-

tion for modern Egyptology; a most valuable result was the discovery of the tri-lingual Rosetta Stone. 

The expedition left the French coast in May, 1798, and, after eluding the British fleet under the command of Admiral Nelson, captured the island fortress of Malta. This incident brought Russia into the coalition against France. By July 1, 50,000 French troops arrived at Aboukir Bay in Egypt. Alexandria was taken, and, on 

July 21, Napoleon defeated the army of the Mamelukes in the battle of the Pyramids. Thus far, the expedition had been successful, but eventually Nelson located the French fleet anchored in Aboukir Bay. 

On August 1, in the battle of the Nile, he almost totally destroyed the enemy squadron; Napoleon and his army were now without a line of communication to France. In September, Turkey joined 

Russia and England, thus giving Napoleon an opportunity to march into Syria, where he laid siege to Acre. When he received information that the British fleet was transporting a Turkish army to Egypt, he abandoned the siege and returned to Egypt in time to inflict a decisive defeat on the Turks in the battle of Aboukir. This victory was his last one of consequence in Egypt, for, without a regular line of communication with France, he could no longer hope to conquer the Turkish Empire. His inability to take the port of Acre and 

Wellesley's defeat of the forces of insurrection in India made it clear that his first attack on the supremacy of England had failed. 

In the meantime, numerous changes had taken place within the Directory until by mid-June, 1799, the two councils had effectively changed the make-up of the executive branch of the government. 

One of the new directors was the Abbé Sieyès, whose aim was to provide a better charter for the Republic. His plan was to provide a democratic government sufficiently centralized to afford effective administration. To accomplish his ends, he sought a capable military leader to protect the Republic without dominating it. Napoleon at 

Acre received word of the change in French internal affairs and soon determined that he could advance faster in France than in Egypt. 

He abandoned his troops and with a small party made his way back to France, which he reached early in October; the Egyptian expeditionary forces finally surrendered in 1801. The falsified or exaggerated reports sent to France by Napoleon telling of his victories in the East guaranteed him a flattering reception. In Paris, Talleyrand, Sieyès, and Bonaparte came together for a discussion of the situation. The scheme they evolved was a rather simple one and,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

since it had momentous results, there is reason for giving it in some detail. The conspirators set 18th Brumaire for the coup. Under their plan, Sieyes and Lucien Bonaparte were to persuade the Council of Elders to remove the two legislative bodies to Saint-Cloud, near Paris, but far enough away to be free from intimidation by the Parisian populace. Napoleon would then take charge of the troops in 

Paris and use them to prorogue the councils and coerce certain directors to resign. Finally, an executive council, composed of three consuls, was to be established to draw up a permanent constitution. 

The coup was accomplished on 18th-19th Brumaire (November 

9-10, 1799). Everything was carried out according to the plans, except that on the latter date Napoleon fainted at a critical moment, but, when the whole stake seemed lost, Lucien Bonaparte rescued him. That night, Napoleon, Sieyès, and Ducos were declared provisional consuls. The Republic continued to exist legally; in reality, a decade of revolutionary activity had brought into power a military dictatorship. The nation was indifferent to the events of 

Brumaire, feeling that if force was requisite to restore peace and order, to maintain civil advantages won by the Revolution, military dictatorship was justified. The turbulence of the past ten years had left in its wake a surfeit of problems to test the ability and good sense of any form of government. Napoleon entered on a program of reconstruction which began by consolidating the accomplishments of the Revolution.

Sieyes, with two committees, began work on the task of revising the constitution. His scheme placed Napoleon in the position of a well-paid, but powerless, super-king. For this reason, and because the progress of the committees was slow, Napoleon brought the revision process to an abrupt end by incorporating some of his own ideas with those of Sieyes and the document was ready by December 15, 1799. The overwhelming ratification of this constitution, 3,000,000 for, to 1,500 against, was hardly a ratifying vote since the constitution was already in effect before the referendum. 

The Constitution of the Year VIII went into effect before Christmas, 1799, when the Provisional Consulate established on 19th Brumaire was succeeded by the Ten Year Consulate. The executive power under this constitution was vested in three consuls, elected for ten years and eligible to re-election. In reality, Napoleon, the 

First Consul, possessed dictatorial powers; the other consuls were figure-heads. The constitution restored universal suffrage for twenty-one-year-old males, but the franchise gave little power to

the rank and file, for the manner of electing officials was complex and indirect. The legal voters in a district chose one-tenth of their number to a communal list. Those elected to the communal list elected one-tenth of their number to the departmental list, and then the elected members of the departmental list chose one-tenth of their number. The members of this last selective group were eligible to serve in national public offices, and appointments had to be made from this list. So complicated a system, even if strictly followed, made popular government out of the question. 

Four legislative bodies were provided by the Constitution of the Year VIII; so intricate was the system of checks and balances placed over them that little effective action could be expected. A Council of State, whose membership eventually numbered forty-five, was nominated by the First Consul, and had the right to introduce legislation. When it did so, it was generally on orders from the First 

Consul. The Tribunate had a hundred members; it debated the merits of the laws presented to it by the Council of State. A third house, the Legislative Body, composed of three hundred deputies, passed or rejected a law without discussion. A fourth house, known as the Conservative Senate, had functions somewhat like a supreme court in that it could invalidate a law, the constitutionality of which was questioned. Of these four bodies, the Council of State did the most work and was, by far, the most important. 

While the Constitution of the Year VIII retained most of the attributes of a republican form of government, it failed to provide a bill of rights and, actually, it hid within it the constitutional machinery requisite to the development of the sole dictatorial power of Napoleon Bonaparte. It was not strange that after ten years of revolutionary strife, the French people condoned the usurpation.

CHAPTER 44 The Napoleonic Empire and Its Fall 

N APOLEON'S program for the restoration of peace and order within France was well under way when he found himself faced with another war. He made peace proposals to both 

Great Britain and Austria, knowing they would not be accepted, yet hoping thereby to throw the blame for renewed hostilities on his enemies. Again he had to strike at a foe who could be reached without a navy. Moreau's army crossed the Rhine and forced the Austrians to retreat as far as Ulm. Massena in north Italy retained an 

Austrian army in that region to watch him. Napoleon, using troops released by cessation of civil strife in the Vendée, marched over the 

Great Saint Bernard Pass into the Po valley (May, 1800). When the

Austrians discovered Napoleon's position, they began a concentration of troops against his armies in north Italy during early June. 

The Austrian general, Melas, struck at Marengo. At first the fighting was decidedly in favor of the Austrians, but the arrival of reënforcements gave ultimate victory to the French. An armistice was arranged between the two commanders, under which the French occupied Lombardy to the Mincio river. 

Marengo was more than a great military victory for Napoleon; it entrenched him in power. Besides eliminating the possibility of his overthrow by enemies in Paris, the battle again gave him access to the rich cities of northern Italy, upon which he levied heavy tribute. Since no definitive peace was arranged during the period of the armistice, war was resumed during the winter of 1800. The major operations took place in the north where, at Hohenlinden, Moreau's troops decisively defeated the Austrians and pressed on until within a few days' march of Vienna, where Moreau finally granted an armistice. During the truce, the Austrians capitulated by signing the 

Treaty of Lunéville (February 9, 1801).

The chief clauses of the treaty reaffirmed the distribution of territory made by the Treaty of Campo Formio (1797) regarding the

Austrian Netherlands, the left bank of the Rhine, and northern 

Italy. Emperor Francis II agreed to recognize the Kingdom of 

Etruria (Tuscany), created by Napoleon to satisfy a portion of his agreement with Spain concerning the transfer of Louisiana to France. 

The emperor also agreed to recognize the formation of the Batavian (Holland), the Helvetic (Switzerland), and the Ligurian republics. 

The only Italian possession left to Austria was Venetia. The treaty gave France supervisory rights over the assignment of land within the Holy Roman Empire to those princes who were deprived of their possessions on the left bank of the Rhine. 

Again, France was at war with Great Britain alone. Both nations desired peace, England for the opportunity to develop her trade, France to solve her internal problems. After the English conquest of 

Malta, the capitulation of the French troops in Egypt, and the defeat of the Danish fleet by Nelson at Copenhagen, the British government felt that peace could be arranged without dishonor. Pitt's government had been replaced by that of Addington and, on October 1, 1801, preliminary articles of peace were signed at London. 

The definitive treaty was signed at Amiens, March 25, 1802. The 

Treaty of Amiens was a decided victory for Napoleon since by its terms England recognized his supremacy on the Continent and left him free to carry on his plans and policies. The treaty was significant because of what it failed to treat. Napoleon refused to negotiate concerning matters covered by the Treaty of Lunéville, and the treaty likewise failed to include a commercial arrangement greatly desired by Britain's business interests.

Under the Treaty of Amiens, England recognized French conquests, including Napoleonic control of Holland, Belgium, and the left bank of the Rhine. The colonies of Spain, France, and Holland which had been captured by the English navy were returned to their former owners, with two important exceptions. Dutch Ceylon and 

Spanish Trinidad were retained by Great Britain, although the Cape of Good Hope was restored to the Dutch. Malta was given back to the Knights of Saint John. This was satisfactory to Great Britain and especially pleasing to the czar, who deemed himself the protector of that order. It did not place a sufficiently strong government in control of the island to deter Napoleon should he wish to continue his eastern schemes. Egypt was restored to the Turks, the French agreed to evacuate Naples, and the English consented to leave Elba. The failure of the treaty to deal with issues which had kept England in the conflict and the fact that so many things were left undone or

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

superficially done made the Treaty of Amiens a truce rather than a peace.

Notice has been taken of the fact that the second Italian campaign interrupted the reorganization of France under Napoleon's guidance. The campaign provided him with a source of revenue from the north Italian cities to continue his reconstruction program. The distinguishing feature of his reforms was centralization. His law of 

February 17, 1800, is still the basis of local administration in France. 

Under that law, he accepted numerous innovations of the Revolution but incorporated reforms of his own. Departments were placed under administrative officials called prefects, districts were put under sub-prefects, and the cities and towns were governed by mayors. Each of these administrative officers was supplied with an advisory council, and all officials, administrative and advisory, were appointed by the First Consul. A law of March 18, 1800, revised the judiciary system, centralizing it in contrast to the decentralization of the Ancien Régime. All judges were appointed by the First Consul. 

One interesting innovation was the addition to each court of a national officer, charged with seeing that justice was done, that the procedure was correct, and that nothing inimical to the national government took place within the court room. It was the duty of all these judicial and administrative officials, under the direct control of the national government, to maintain internal quiet and order, a task they performed with remarkable success. 

One of the major reforms of the Consulate was in the field of taxation. We have already referred to the income obtained from regions conquered by the Napoleonic armies. The First Consul also set about centralizing the internal taxation of France. He cut the operating budget of the nation to a minimum and placed the collection of direct taxes under the minister of finance. A rate of assessment was established and rigorously maintained, a real estate census was taken, and collections were promptly begun. A major source of income was afforded by the sale of church lands. Coöperation between the local officials and the central office in Paris was such that almost from the beginning of the reform movement collections were efficiently made.

Napoleon's financial policy was not absolutely fair to all concerned, but it had the merit of restoring faith in the government and bringing about a feeling of financial security. The value of government bonds increased rapidly after the Coup d'Etat because of the creation of a sinking fund and the levy of a heavy war tax. Sufficient

funds for the operation of the Provisional Consulate had been advanced by bankers on the basis of these reforms, and the establishment of the Bank of France (1800) made possible eventual elimination of depreciated currency. The bank issued notes, liquidated government obligations in specie, and made possible early restoration of confidence. Three years later, the bank, which had been given a monopoly of note issue for the city of Paris, earned enormous profits for its shareholders, one of whom was Napoleon. 

The religious question found Napoleon an impartial arbiter. He was well aware that the French people were predominantly of the Roman Catholic faith. He realized, too, that a settlement of the church issue would facilitate restoration of concord throughout the nation. A further argument in favor of coming to terms with the Holy See was the fact that until the church recognized as legal the government's disposition of its expropriated lands, titles of purchasers would be precarious. Early in 1801, Pope Pius VII and 

Napoleon began negotiations which lasted until July, when the Concordat was accepted by the French government. The preamble to the Concordat shows to what extent compromise was carried; it was significant in declaring that the Roman Catholic faith was recognized by the French government as the religion of most of the French people. The papal desire to have the Catholic religion declared the state religion was thus thwarted. Under the agreement, the First 

Consul could appoint all French bishops and the pope could pass on the appointments, although the church retained the right of installation. The bishops, in turn, were to appoint lesser church officials, The government agreed to pay the salaries of churchmen and to provide them with places of worship, on condition that they took an oath to support the state. The pope, in exchange, recognized the confiscation and sale of church property. The Concordat thus preserved the civil gains made by the Revolution, while it restored a working relationship between the French government and the papacy of undoubted benefit to both.

A clause in the Concordat had given Napoleon police and regulatory powers over public worship. In the Organic Articles, he provided a series of regulations by which the administration could control Protestant as well as Catholic churches of France. These Articles were joined with the Concordat without the consent of the pope; the two were printed and issued as if they were a single document. 

This was an act of bad grace on the part of the First Consul, and he was eventually to rue the day when he had over-emphasized the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cause of Gallicanism. The peace with the church was celebrated, nevertheless, at Notre Dame, on April 18, 1802. 

Napoleon made it clear that anyone willing to support his government need not remain in exile for past activities. He granted amnesty to the émigrés, their relatives, the non-juring priests, rebels, reactionaries, royalists, and suspects of all sorts, on condition that they maintain peace. To indicate his lack of animus against any group, as well as his political acumen, he placed about himself ministers and public officials of every degree of political faith. These ranged from 

Talleyrand, the noble who became minister of foreign affairs, to Fouché, the radical Jacobin who became minister of police. Because of this lenient policy, many émigrés returned to France and again took some part in her political, economic, and social life. 

While First Consul, Napoleon began the reorganization of the French legal system. He was not an innovator in this field. Previous attempts at revision had been made, but during the period of revolutionary strife various attempts to correlate the new laws with the old had failed. The work of bringing together a Civil Code was begun in 1800 and completed four years later. This code, known as the Code Napoléon, was a compilation of the civil accomplishments of the Revolution, corrected and made to conform with much that was fundamental in the law of pre-Revolutionary France. Its basis was centuries of French practice and the Code of Justinian. It was relatively brief and clear and took a position midway between the legal system of the Ancien Régime and the radical hodge-podge of the Revolutionary period. The Napoleonic Code has an importance greater than mere adoption in France could have given it, for it followed the Napoleonic armies into Switzerland, Germany, Italy, and Belgium, and eventually extended the Revolutionary ideals and principles to such far-flung areas as Louisiana, Egypt, Japan, Canada, and portions of South and Central America. A number of other codes also became law during the period of the Empire. Among them should be mentioned the Code of Civil Procedure (1806), the 

Commercial Code (1807), the Code of Criminal Procedure (1808), and the Penal Code (1810). 

The period from the Coup d'État until the coronation of Napoleon as Emperor of the French in December, 1804, was one of a progressive centralization of the powers of government. The Provisional Consulate of 1799 was soon succeeded by the Ten Year Consulate. By 

1802, Napoleon believed his position secure enough to consolidate his power, and the Life Consulate resulted. It was his boast that he

held power by the consent of the people he governed. In this instance, to keep up the fiction, he gave Frenchmen an opportunity to vote whether he should hold the Consulate for life. The vote was 

3,500,000 for the proposal and about 8,000 against it. This new arrangement necessitated some revision of the constitution; the socalled Constitution of the Year X was adopted on August 4, 1802, although it merely amended that of the Year VIII, which continued in operation. The amendments created a Privy Council; reduced the future size of the Tribunate; created electoral colleges in place of the district, departmental, and national lists of citizens eligible to office; and further limited the meager powers of the legislative houses. 1 The two years which followed were a period of further consolidation and concentration of power in the hands of the Life Consul. 

When, during 1804, he announced the discovery of a royalist plot to overthrow the established regime, he was able to carry out the last step in his governmental ambitions. With a view to the future of Europe, which he envisioned under a single ruler, he now proposed the establishment of the Empire. The plan was embodied in the Constitution of the Year XII (May 18, 1804). The document declared the title hereditary and practically destroyed the powers of the legislative bodies created in 1799. Napoleon referred to the voters of France not the question of whether an empire should be established, but how the crown should be inherited. The Empire was an established fact before the plebiscite. 

Napoleon invited the pope to attend the coronation in Notre 

Dame in Paris. On December 2, 1804, he received the crown from the pontiff, placed it on his own head, and then crowned Josephine. 

In return for the service Pius VII had performed, Napoleon agreed to supplant the Revolutionary calendar by the Gregorian. The manner in which Napoleon conducted his coronation did little to better relations with the church, although papal recognition assisted in gaining recognition elsewhere. The republics he had created, with 

Austria and Prussia, soon recognized his title; but England, Russia, Sweden, and Turkey refused to acknowledge its validity. 

Meanwhile, Napoleon had broken the Peace of Amiens by what was obviously an attempt to expand the boundaries of France and to restore the former French colonial empire. Hostilities were resumed in May, 1803. To break down Britain's commercial supremacy, Napoleon aimed at the domination of all Europe to sever his island foe from Continental markets. Causes and incidents which

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

provoked this new outbreak were numerous. Napoleon had interfered in Holland and in Switzerland; he had espoused a plan for the revival of a French empire in the Mississippi valley; and he had refused to negotiate a commercial treaty with Great Britain. His influence over Holland gave him control of the Cape of Good Hope; and this, with his renewed interest in Egypt and the dismemberment of Turkey, served to bring the British back into a conflict which was to last over a decade.

During the autumn of 1803, Napoleon began concentrating troops at Boulogne preparatory to invading England. His early plan contemplated the transportation of these troops by means of flatboats, but when this was found too difficult, the scheme was altered. 

Numerous interpretations of Napoleon's real intentions at this stage of his career have been ventured. It would seem safe to say, however, that he really intended to invade Britain, and it was evident that English statesmen like Pitt were convinced of it at the time. 

Early in 1804, the plan of invasion was changed so that the flatboats would be convoyed by the French navy. The scheme required that a portion of the fleet start for the West Indies with the view of drawing off the English fleet. Then the French fleet was to hurry home and assist in convoying the transports before the British ships could return. Unfortunately for the plan, when Admiral Villeneuve tried to lose Nelson in the West Indies he failed. At this moment news of Austrian mobilization caused Napoleon to march his Grand Army from Boulogne against the old foe. On September 3, Austria declared war. Not until Napoleon reached Vienna did he receive word of the disastrous end to his scheme for the invasion of England. The battle of Trafalgar (October 21, 1805) resulted in the decisive defeat of the combined French and Spanish navies by 

Lord Nelson. Like the Elizabethan victory over the Spanish Armada, it ensured England's mastery of the sea.

The royalist plot of 1804 against Napoleon which facilitated his assumption of the imperial title had implications of another nature. 

It implicated a Bourbon prince whom the French authorities took to be the young Prince of Enghien, living in Baden. On orders from 

Napoleon, he was kidnapped, given a mock trial, and executed, despite the fact that Napoleon knew of his innocence. Bonaparte considered this murder essential as a warning to the Bourbons, but it was also a major factor in forcing Russia into an alliance with Great Britain against France and had its part in arousing the Austrian court against the Napoleonic government. The Anglo-Russian

agreement served as the basis of another anti-French coalition including Austria and Prussia.

We left Napoleon marching his Boulogne Army against Austria in the fall of 1805. This was a brief and decisive campaign. Russian aid was on the way, but before it could reach the Austrians, Napoleon surrounded General Mack's force at Ulm and brought about its surrender. With little hindrance, the French troops marched into 

Vienna, where Napoleon awaited the concentration of the Russians under Czar Alexander, and the arrival of the Austrian army from Italy. Before the latter's arrival, the Russian command decided to attack. The brilliance of Bonaparte's counterplan made the battle of 

Austerlitz (December 2, 1805) the most masterly stroke of his military career. This disaster to the Russians destroyed the coalition; the Allied losses were three times as great as the French. 

During this campaign Napoleon had received aid from several German states, and in the Peace of Pressburg, accepted by Austria on December 26, 1805, they received their compensation in emancipation from Austria and the Holy Roman Empire. By the treaty, Francis II recognized Württemberg and Bavaria as kingdoms, while Austria gave up Venice and all her possessions in south Germany and Italy. The treaty provided for the creation of a German Confederation, under French tutelage, to take the place of the defunct Holy Roman Empire. To the creation of the Confederation, Talleyrand devoted six months. He made separate arrangements with each of the German states involved and on July 13, 1806, proclaimed the establishment of the Confederation of the Rhine. It contained fifteen states, a number which more than doubled within the next few years, and constituted what might well be termed a third Germany if Austria and Prussia be counted as the first two. By the creation of this Confederation, many smaller German states were merged into the larger ones, and Napoleon was therefore responsible for a major step toward the ultimate unification of Germany. He agreed to serve as protector of the Confederation, in return for which it was to furnish him with troops and supplies in any future war he might wage. The official end of the Holy Roman Empire came on August 

6, 1806, when Francis II changed his title to "Hereditary Emperor of Austria."

Napoleon's concept of a great European empire was brought nearer fruition by the victory of Austerlitz and the Treaty of Pressburg. In Italy, the queen of Naples, a sister of Marie Antoinette, had openly opposed the Napoleonic regime, and the emperor de-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cided to make an example of her by ordering her deposition. His brother, Joseph, was made king of Naples in March, 1806; and during June of the same year, another brother, Louis Bonaparte, was crowned king of Holland.

No peace had been arranged with Great Britain or Russia. Napoleon's duplicity with regard to Hanover estranged the Prussian ruler, Frederick William, who in July made a secret alliance with the czar. Russian and Prussian troops were called to the colors in 

August, 1806; and when late that month a Nuremberg bookseller was executed for distribution of an inflammatory pamphlet, a major nationalistic movement was launched in Germany. Prussia, however, was unprepared for entry into a war with the trained forces under Napoleon. In the two decisive battles of Jena and Auerstadt, the 

Prussians were routed. Less than a fortnight later, the French forces were in Berlin and the king had fled. This short campaign gave 

Napoleon control of north Germany as Austerlitz had given him south Germany. He was now able to turn his attention to Russia. 

The czar had declined peace terms after Austerlitz, but following the dismemberment of Prussia, he was again face to face with the Napoleonic armies. The czar was an interesting personage. His reign dated from the murder of the Czar Paul, and at the time gave every indication of becoming noted for liberalism. But with each passing year he became a bit more of a mystic, a bit less the reformer, more the autocrat and less the benevolent despot.

The Grand Army fought a bloody battle with the Russians at Eylau in February, 1807, but the French troops were too exhausted to pursue their opponents and make the victory a decisive one. With the coming of spring, after prodigious work and adroit planning on the emperor's part, the superior French forces defeated the Russians again in the battle of Friedland (June, 1807). Following the battle an armistice was arranged, during which the two rulers, Napoleon and Alexander, held conferences aboard a raft in the Niemen river.

Frederick William was an interested but seldom-consulted participant. Their agreements were included in two secret and two open treaties, one each between France and Russia, and one each between France and Prussia. These were known as the Treaties of 

Tilsit, after a neighboring town, and were accepted July 7-9, 1807. 

Since Frederick William was the pawn in the emperors' game, Prussia was practically forced to meet the costs of the campaign which had just been concluded.

By the Peace of Tilsit, Alexander allied himself with Napoleon

against England, agreed to certain territorial changes already made by Napoleon, accepted the French emperor's demand that half of Prussia's population be taken from her, recognized the creation of the Kingdom of Westphalia, which was placed under the rule of Jerome Bonaparte, and the formation of the Grand Duchy of Warsaw, under the nominal control of the king of Saxony. For all these concessions, Alexander was given the promise of a free hand in affairs of the East. Napoleon had, however, overreached himself in the Peace of Tilsit, for his future acts, where Russia was interested, were not in keeping with its terms. This led eventually to the defection of the czar and the disastrous Russian campaign of 1812. 

The development of the "Continental System" was one of three major Napoleonic attempts to destroy the commercial prosperity of England, and through this her political supremacy in Europe. His other chief assaults on British prosperity and prestige had been the Egyptian expedition and the proposed expedition of the Boulogne Army. To be correctly understood, the Continental System must be considered not only as an economic weapon against England, but as a means of creating a united Europe under Napoleonic domination. 

Under the mercantilistic economic philosophy of the time, governmental regulation of trade had been common. During the latter part of the eighteenth century, laissez faire doctrines began to permeate the economic policies of the trading nations. Especially was this true of England, where the Industrial Revolution was taking place. The background for the diplomatic disputes arising out of the 

Continental System is to be found in the Rule of 1756, which declared that trade closed in time of peace could not be opened in time of war. The Continental System was not begun by Napoleon, but by the National Convention, which, in a decree of May 9, 1793, authorized French vessels to seize enemy or neutral goods bound for an enemy port. American shipping was exempted under this decree. 

British Orders in Council were passed in retaliation for the French decree. On July 2, 1796, the Directory decreed that French vessels might seize vessels, cargoes, and men just as English vessels were doing. 

In May, 1806, a British Order in Council announced that the French coast was blockaded from the Elbe to Brest. In retaliation for this order, Napoleon issued his famous Berlin Decree, which declared the British Isles blockaded; since he had no effective navy, it was but a paper blockade. To enforce his blockade, the nations with which Napoleon negotiated treaties, like Prussia and Russia, and the regions

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

which he had conquered, annexed, or controlled, were forced to prohibit the entry of English ships or goods. Order in Council followed decree from 1806 until 1810, affecting not only combatants, but important neutral nations like the United States. Thus it was that in selfprotection and retaliation, the United States passed an Embargo Act in 1807, a Non-Intercourse Act, and the Macon Bill No. 2. In 1812 

America entered into a war against Great Britain for the second time. 

In her commercial warfare, England aimed not at starving France, but at increasing her own trade in manufactured goods with the countries of Europe. Thus England had become the greatest industrial center of Europe. Because of her large trade she was able to furnish huge subsidies, in both money and goods, to Napoleon's enemies on the Continent. Since England could not be reached by Napoleon's armies because of her isolated position and her control of the seas, Napoleon aimed at bankrupting her. He intended also to obtain for French manufacturers the markets which English goods had been serving. To enforce his land blockade of the British Isles, it was necessary for him to attempt the conquest of Portugal. This led him to interfere in 

Spain, where he wasted so many troops and such sums of money that he was to meet ultimate defeat. The necessity of an honest and capable bureaucracy to maintain such an extensive blockade, the prevalence of smuggling, and the eventual licensing of trade with England doomed Napoleon's plans to failure. One of the by-products of this 

European attempt at self-sufficiency was the sugar beet. When, late in 1810, Napoleon tried to force the czar to end smuggling of British commodities to Russia, Alexander defied him, and the Continental 

System collapsed.

By 1810 Napoleon had reached the zenith of his power; he was in control of central Europe, his Continental System was hurting England, and his armies were having fair success in the Iberian peninsula. 

In 1804, he had entered on a comprehensive and extended program of internal improvements, canals, roads, bridges, drainage of lowlands, as well as the beautification of the capital. Enormous sums were spent, and the results were of permanent value and often of lasting beauty. 

His educational reforms were begun in 1802 and completed by 1808, with the creation of the University, which was not a single institution of higher learning, but the whole French educational system. The chief function of Napoleonic education was to provide uniform instruction in the ways of obedient citizenship, rather than freedom to search out the truth. The Napoleonic formula demanded guidance of the young through conservative and Catholic precepts. The emperor

aimed at stabilizing social conditions and at preserving the Napoleonic regime. The system was not successful, although it did establish certain principles which served as precedents in later educational reform, such as state-supported education, schools open to all, and nonclerical teachers.

One new social group was introduced during the period of the Empire. This was the new nobility. Mention has already been made of an upper or court nobility, but a Legion of Honor was created to honor civil as well as military servitors of the state, regardless of birth. 

Napoleon insisted that talent should have its reward even if it be a mere title, a "bauble" as he called it. The creation of a noble class was a reactionary measure, but it was intended to help reconcile the rest of Europe to Napoleonic rule in France and, to a degree, it tended to accomplish this.

Napoleon had sent his veterans into Spain during 1807, but a rising Austrian nationalism, fostered by younger leaders like the Archduke Charles and the Empress of Austria, caused him again to turn attention to his inveterate enemy. Austria fought her war for liberation alone, although Russia favored her and England furnished subsidies. 

Although the French army contained thousands of untried recruits, Napoleon, with characteristic acumen, led them into Bavaria, forced out the Archduke Charles, and, within a month, was again in Vienna. 

Two indecisive battles (Essling and Aspern) caused terrific losses for both combatants; the battle of Wagram resulted in the defeat of the archduke. The Austrian emperor obtained an armistice after this engagement and, on October 14, 1809, the Treaty of Vienna, or Schönbrunn, established a definitive peace. By the treaty, Austria lost 

Trieste, Galicia, Salzburg, and other regions. She was forced to break her English alliance and to adhere to the Continental System. The consolidation of Polish Galicia with the Grand Duchy of Warsaw appeared to Czar Alexander as but a step in the re-creation of an independent Poland and therefore served to estrange Russia before Napoleon was prepared for the loss of his nominal ally. 

Establishment of the Empire had created one problem for which Napoleon had found no solution. He believed that sovereignty ought to descend from father to son, but as yet he had no direct heirs. He determined to divorce his creole wife Josephine and negotiate a dynastic marriage with one of the oldest ruling families in Europe. He first made a diplomatic request for the hand of the czar's young sister and then hurriedly arranged terms with the Austrian emperor for betrothal to his daughter, Marie Louise. Thus was a princess sacri-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

ficed to afford Austria a brief breathing spell. The divorce was hurriedly arranged, Josephine was sent to Malmaison, and the marriage to Marie Louise took place on April 1, 1810. The marriage added prestige to Napoleon's rule and resulted in the birth of a son during the spring of 1811. At last the Corsican could feel secure in the permanence of his civil and military conquests. 

The multifarious ramifications of the Continental System had forced Napoleon to intervene in the affairs of the Iberian peninsula. 

As early as 1807, in the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau, he had made arrangements with Spain for the conquest and partition of England's traditional ally, Portugal. A French army, under Junot, attempted the conquest of that country, but the royal family succeeded in escaping to Brazil. Affairs in Spain now gave Napoleon an excuse to intervene. 

The government of Spain was in the hands of the incompetent Charles IV, his immoral queen, and her unscrupulous paramour, Godoy. A family quarrel involving these three and Crown Prince Ferdinand gave Napoleon the opportunity he desired, for he induced them, one by one, to abdicate after a display of force and characteristic diplomatic skill. In June, 1808, Joseph Bonaparte was made king of Spain; 

Napoleon's brother-in-law, Murat, replaced him as king of Naples. 

Spain, however, rose in a nationalistic revolt before Joseph was comfortably seated on his new throne, and this rebellion against foreign rule lasted until the end of the Bonapartist regime. Wasteful expenditure of thousands of tried French veterans against the guerilla attacks of the Spanish patriots proved Napoleon's undoing, for these troops were badly needed elsewhere. An important factor in the eventual defeat of the French in Spain was the leadership of Sir 

Arthur Wellesley, later Duke of Wellington. French liberalism and revolutionary ideals took shallow root in Spain. Napoleon's decrees of 1808 abolishing the inquisition, the feudal system, the internal customs, together with limitation of the number of monasteries and convents, were intended as the basis of other general reforms, but these the French were unable to enforce. The Spaniards themselves promulgated a liberal document, known as the Constitution of 1812, which served the rebels as a charter of government until Ferdinand VII was placed on the throne in 1814. This Constitution of 1812 was to serve as the basis of still other revolutionary struggles. 

The estrangement between the czar and Napoleon had become marked by 1810. Differences with regard to Poland, Turkey, and the 

Far East, as well as Russia's role in the enforcement of the Continental System, so aggravated the quarrel between the two rulers that mili-

tary and diplomatic preparations were made for inevitable conflict. 

Prussia was unwillingly forced into an alliance with Napoleon, and Austria, too, agreed to support him. Sweden, under Bernadotte's control, and England allied themselves with Russia. In the summer of 

1812, Napoleon, with the largest force ever under his command, began his invasion of Russia. All told, effectives and reserves numbered over 500,000, of a score of nationalities. The emperor planned to march straight from Königsberg toward Moscow, going into winter quarters at Smolensk, about two-thirds of the way. The Russians continued to retreat before the moving French columns and declined to engage in the pitched battle Napoleon so much desired. Since he had not met the enemy in sufficient numbers to inflict a decisive defeat, he continued the march instead of wintering at Smolensk. A bloody but indecisive battle was fought at Borodino; it opened the way into 

Moscow, which Napoleon found deserted and in flames. The czar still refused to negotiate and Napoleon finally gave the order to retreat. The disastrous flight, one of the most terrible in the annals of warfare, was made in the dead of a Russian winter. The survivors numbered less than 100,000 emaciated men. 

Napoleon had left his army, in early December, for a hurried return by sledge to Paris. Official censorship and falsified reports minimized the extent of the disaster. Prussia and Austria, however, had an opportunity to observe the veterans returning to France and came to an early appreciation of the fact that the great Napoleon was no longer invulnerable. With full knowledge of the disadvantage the 

Russian debacle entailed, the emperor began preparations for renewing the conflict in the spring. Prussia, meanwhile, had been making extensive preparations against this day.

The basis for a German uprising had been laid by Fichte, who in 1807 began preaching German nationalism, based on her historic past. 

The work of arousing national consciousness was eagerly undertaken and ably expounded by the professors in the German universities, especially in the newly founded University of Berlin. Idealistic reformers like Fichte, Niebuhr, Humboldt, and Savigny were ably seconded by more practical men. Outstanding in this group was the 

Baron Stein, whose reforms served to put virility into the Prussian government. Military reforms were accomplished through the intelligent efforts of Scharnhorst so that a national army, made up of huge inactive reserves, was created within a short time, despite the Napoleonic restriction on the size of the active Prussian force. 

These preparations culminated in the Prussian declaration of war

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

against France (March 17, 1813). This was to prove the German war of liberation. In its inception, it was marked by a patriotic appeal to the people by Frederick William and an aroused public resentment against foreign domination. Metternich meanwhile broke the Franco- 

Austrian Alliance of 1810 and announced that henceforth Austria would act as an armed neutral, ready to mediate with force, if need arose. The fighting began in Saxony where Napoleon defeated the 

Prussians and Russians at Lützen, and again at Bautzen. An armistice was arranged following this engagement. During the lull, news arrived of a French defeat in Spain. Austria, after having dallied with her policy of armed mediation, then entered the war. The concentrated forces of the two opposing armies totaled nearly 1,000,000 men. Napoleon's plans were well laid, but he and his subordinates erred in executing them. After his last victory at Dresden, his “star rapidly fell. Finally, in the decisive battle of Leipzig, known generally as the Battle of the Nations (October 16-19), Napoleon met irretrievable disaster. Thus was Germany liberated, the Confederation of the Rhine left without a "protector."

Eventually the major allied forces invaded Holland and reached the Rhine; southern France was penetrated by Wellington; and northern Italy was reconquered. Metternich offered peace on terms of the "natural boundaries of France," but when Napoleon hedged, he appealed to the French nation to accept a reasonable peace which their ruler had declined. Thus was Bonaparte's support further undermined at home. Early in 1814, three allied armies entered France. 

With a small and mobile force, Napoleon fought the most brilliant defensive campaign of his career. Near the end of this campaign, Castlereagh of England obtained the signatures of the allies to a treaty in which they agreed to make no separate peace. Late in March, Paris fell and Napoleon's day was over. On April 11 he abdicated and, in accordance with the Treaty of Fontainebleau of the same date, was exiled, with the title of emperor, to the isle of Elba. From this island Napoleon watched the diplomatic squabble going on at the Congress of Vienna and, through old friends, felt the pulse of a France again under the rule of a Bourbon (Louis XVIII). He took a long chance when, on March 1, 1815, he arrived in France and began a march toward Paris. Soldiers sent to arrest him joined their old commander, and within three weeks Louis XVIII thought it expedient to leave the capital. The Congress of Vienna outlawed the returned emperor, and the allied armies girded themselves for a last and decisive conflict with the great opportunist. The engagement took place south

of Brussels, near Waterloo, on June 18, 1815. While Wellington received reinforcements from Blücher, Napoleon failed to receive any from Grouchy and therefore suffered a severe defeat. Again forced to abdicate and unable to escape, he surrendered to the captain of an English vessel, the Bellerophon. Soon afterward his captors transported him to Saint Helena, where he died in lonely exile, May 5, 1821. He took revenge on his enemies, however, by occupying himself in the dictation of his memoirs which became the source of the Napoleonic Legend," a legend so strong that in its name another 

Bonaparte was one day to rule France. 66

CHAPTER 45 The Conservative Reaction 

QUARTER century of warfare and twenty years of military dictatorship had bred in the hearts and minds of European peoples a longing for lasting peace and for economic, political, and social security. This desire achieved form in the "Conservative Reaction." The French Revolution had enunciated a new political faith, and Napoleonic imperialism had widely disseminated its doctrines of "liberty, equality, and fraternity." The post-Napoleonic period was but a continuation of the struggle between liberals and conservatives, between revolutionaries and reactionaries, except that during this era conservative and reactionary principles were in the ascendency. High priest of the reaction was the Austrian minister,

Prince Metternich, after whom this generation has often been named. 

The problems facing Continental rulers, after the Napoleonic abdication in 1814, were multiple and of extreme gravity for the preservation of the peace of Europe. Business man and peasant were even more anxious than politician and statesman to establish permanent peace. 

In this manner alone could the farmer and the laborer, the storekeeper and the professional man hope to achieve prosperity and social security. In France, especially, there was opposition to conscription of man power and a pronounced unwillingness to sacrifice further the lives and resources of the nation. Support for the continuance of 

Napoleon's schemes of an imperialistic nature had become extremely meager. Twenty-two years of warfare, with the constant shifting of international alliances, had created so much distrust, dissension, and jealousy, even among allies, that acceptable terms of peace were arranged with extreme difficulty. The problem was not merely one of settling accounts with France, but of satisfying, as well, the many issues in dispute among the allies. The re-establishment of a new balance of power became a major aim of the diplomats of the period. 

Beginning with his first Italian campaign, Napoleon had entered on a diplomatic policy, the chief function of which was the rearrange-

ment of European boundaries with the view to ultimate unification of all the nations of the Continent under one hierarchical ruler. He had two major fields of endeavor in this regard, Italy and Germany. 

By depriving Austria, the papacy, and a number of independent princes of their possessions in Italy, he brought the peninsula under French control, thus wiping out numerous boundary lines. In Germany he had consolidated south Germany into the Confederation of the Rhine and united a portion of it in the Grand Duchy of Warsaw. 

Thus, he eliminated numerous free cities, minor principalities, and duchies, and created in their stead larger and more integrated states. 

The diffusion of the Revolutionary ideals into the various conquered regions had altered their old institutions and had introduced new ones into their political structure. This was done in a manner which created the question of whether they should be retained wholly, or in part, or be abolished. The Napoleonic arrangements with the papacy had created further problems, as had his educational system. 

The abrogation of the feudal system left open the question of its possible revival.

Allied diplomats weighed several possible solutions of the French problem. Some saw no objection to the restoration of Napoleon, if proper safeguards were placed on his powers. Metternich favored the recognition of the King of Rome, Napoleon's infant son, as Napoleon II, under a regency. Still others proposed that Marie Louise be permitted to continue as Empress of France. Some hoped that constitutional government would be established: whether it be limited monarchy or republic depended on the particular exponent of the policy. The solution finally arrived at, however, was the restoration of the Bourbons, in the person of Louis XVI's brother, the Count of Provence, who became Louis XVIII. Credit for the restoration, if credit can be given, is due Talleyrand, who organized demonstrations in favor of the Bourbon claimant and did his utmost, as head of the provisional government, to promote the cause of the legitimists. The 

English diplomat, Castlereagh, favored the policy, and Metternich acceded to this solution of the problem in order to thwart the czar who, at the time, favored placing Bernadotte, Crown Prince of Sweden, on the French throne. It was a matter of accepting the least unsatisfactory solution of a difficult problem. There was little or no popular enthusiasm for the restoration of the Bourbon dynasty. 

In the establishment of peace, two major treaty arrangements must be considered. The first of these was the Treaty of Paris (May 30, 1814), and the second, the Final Act of the Congress of Vienna (June

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

9, 1815). By the Treaty of Paris the victorious allies, with commendable moderation, forced France to resume her boundaries as of January 1, 1792, except for a part of Savoy and some territory in northeast France. The Revolutionary and Napoleonic conquests of some thirty millions of people were relinquished. Holland was returned to the House of Orange. Austria, by giving up her claims to the former Austrian Netherlands, gained title to Lombardy and Venetia in north Italy. A loose German Confederation or Bund, to take the place of the Confederation of the Rhine, was sponsored by Metternich and recognized under the treaty. Genoa was ceded to 

Sardinia. The treaty recognized that these arrangements did not comprise a full settlement and provided for the convocation of a congress of the powers to draw up a definitive peace. Thus was the Congress of Vienna brought into being.

The.Congress of Vienna began in October, 1814, and lasted until the Final Act on June 9, 1815. Its primary function was to divide the spoils and to announce the division of territory to the rest of Europe. The term "congress" gives an erroneous impression of this meeting, for there was no joint opening session in which all the delegates were assembled and no plenary session. It consisted, rather, of a series of meetings between the representatives of the various powers either in called meetings or at social affairs. On such occasions the particular question in dispute was argued and settled by the diplomats of the countries concerned. Each agreement, then, was a separate arrangement. The summary of all these various treaties was called the Final Act. The Treaty of Paris had obliged France, by a secret clause, to accede to all decisions handed down by the four great powers, England, Prussia, Russia, and Austria. The representatives of these nations were known as the "Big Four ": Castlereagh for 

Great Britain, Metternich for Austria, Hardenberg for Prussia, and 

Nesselrode for Russia. The presence of the colorful Czar Alexander served to minimize the importance of his young minister so that he is the least known of the group. By previous agreement, the Polish, Italian, and German settlements were to be arranged in the councils of the "Big Four." The Congress was a brilliant gathering in which the princes and ex-princes of all Europe found alternate hope and fear. Some aimed merely to retain their positions, some to regain what they had lost, but, through it all, they maintained a social life which led to the phrase, "Congress dances." A policy of settling affairs on the basis of legitimacy was announced; that is, whatever had been established by Napoleon was illegitimate. That which had been

in existence before the Revolution was legitimate. It is hardly necessary to say that there was very little adherence to this oft professed rule of "legitimacy."

Certain questions gave rise to acrimonious disputes. Russia and 

Prussia came to an agreement concerning the disposition of Poland, outside the councils of the Congress. The arrangement was that the 

Russian demand for all Poland would be recognized by Prussia in return for Russian support in gaining Saxony for Prussia. England and 

Austria were unalterably opposed to this disposition of Polish territory. When it appeared that Prussia and Russia were prepared to go to war with the other two nations of the "Big Four," Talleyrand, the representative of France, stepped into the diplomatic breach and forced his way into the councils of the allies in so adroit a manner that he gained for France a negotiated, rather than an imposed, peace. 

This diplomatic coup, accomplished by the wily French minister, proved a major blessing to France.

In the final settlement, Poland was joined in a personal union with Russia, under which the czar became king of Poland. Of her former 

Polish possessions, Prussia retained only Posen. Cracow was made a free city. Prussia received indemnification for giving up her Polish claims by receiving about two-fifths of the territory of Saxony. This action was condoned on the ground that the king of Saxony had been overpartial to Napoleon and deserved some punishment. It will be seen that the Prussian-Russian agreement was substantially fulfilled in spite of English and Austrian opposition. The disposal of a portion of Saxony is an interesting illustration of the failure of the Congress to adhere to the principle of legitimacy. The Kingdom of Saxony remained, although depleted in territory and population, and was able to retain both Dresden and Leipzig. Sweden gave up Pomerania to 

Prussia and was given compensation in another part of Europe. 

A Rhineland barrier was created to protect Germany against further French aggression by the erection of three contiguous buffer regions. The Kingdom of the Netherlands was established by the unification of Holland and the former Austrian Netherlands. Farther up the Rhine, territory was turned over to Prussia, while still farther up, a neutralized and expanded Switzerland was created. The addition of Belgium to the Dutch possessions of the House of Orange was partial indemnification for the loss of the Cape of Good Hope to England. Austrian relinquishment of the Netherlands was compensated by the reacquisition of the Tyrol and the addition of Lombardy, Venetia, and Dalmatia to her territory in north Italy.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Austrian control of Lombardy-Venetia, added to the fact that Parma, Modena, and Tuscany were placed under rulers willing to accept Austrian domination in the Italian peninsula, gave Austria complete supremacy in north Italy. The arrangement satisfied England, since French control of the Mediterranean need no longer be feared. The Papal States were restored to the church. England gained no Continental territory but got the Island of Malta, the Cape of 

Good Hope, Ceylon, Saint Lucia, Tobago, and Trinidad, and was made protector of the Ionian Islands. These English acquisitions served to extend and to reinforce her trade routes, especially the "life line" to India. Russia was assured of control over Finland in return for the loss of which Sweden received Norway. The Braganzas, in 

Brazilian exile, were restored to the Portuguese throne. The Bourbons, Louis XVIII and Ferdinand VII, were restored in France and Spain. In both instances, the returning monarchs agreed to some form of constitutional government, but Ferdinand VII repudiated the promise in Spain. About the sole liberal pronouncement of the Congress of Vienna was a general condemnation of the slave trade. 

Metternich has been mentioned as the outstanding exponent of the conservative movement with which the Congress of Vienna stamped the following century. His was no blind conservatism, however, for he realized that if nationalism, republicanism, and liberal thought were permitted to thrive in an empire like Austria, its diverse racial and cultural groups would soon make it a political nonentity in the councils of Europe. As a consequence, he was the strongest proponent of a loosely confederated Germany under Austrian domination as opposed to the nationalistic aspirations for a strongly united Germany voiced by the capable Baron Stein. Throughout the Congress the role of Castlereagh was that of a mediator. He, of all the diplomats, was the most interested in the creation of a balance of power between the nations of Europe. To gain support for his aims, he obtained the admission of Talleyrand to the councils of the "Big Four." 

His whole aim, however, was not that of an enlightened statesman, but of a preserver of England's commercial and naval supremacy. 

Like Metternich, he succeeded. Hardenberg had been exposed to liberal influences through his connections with Stein, but when face to face with the problems of the Congress, he worked for Prussian aggrandizement rather than for the creation of a united Germany. The most liberal spirit at the Congress was Czar Alexander, but he, too, kept his own nation's aspirations closer to his heart than those of the world in general. His insistence on Russian acquisition of all Poland

When news reached the notables at Vienna that Napoleon had escaped and was back in France, he was outlawed (March 13, 1815), and the "Big Four" agreed to keep their armies in operation against him until he was no longer capable of creating a disturbance. With the final abdication of Napoleon, the Prussians and Austrians demanded that France be reduced to the role of a minor European power, but the good sense and calmer counsels of Castlereagh and the czar prevailed. The Second Treaty of Paris reduced French territory to the boundaries of 1790 and imposed an indemnity of 700,- 000,000 francs, to be paid within five years. It also established an army of occupation in northeastern France. It would appear that France escaped with her European position practically intact and received a most moderate punishment.

The Congress of Vienna had created a new map of Europe much as Napoleon had done. The factors most potent in accomplishing this result had been fear of further French aggression, the desire of the victors for territorial additions, and the hope of the allies to restore affairs in Europe to a condition approaching that which existed prior to the outbreak of the French Revolution and the disturbing years of Napoleon's supremacy. The decisions which the Congress forced upon a war-weary Europe provided the basis for a century of dispute between liberal and conservative factions. Considering the longrange consequences of its work, the Congress failed to achieve its aspirations. This was due to several outstanding blunders, among them, the failure of the plenipotentiaries to take into account the nationalistic spirit of the peoples about whom they drew boundary lines. The German nationalists, the Poles, the Italians, the Norwegians, the Belgians, and the Finns were all dissatisfied with the disposition of their countries. Especially was this the case in Germany. 

When Napoleon destroyed the Holy Roman Empire and reduced some three hundred states to less than forty in order to create the Confederation of the Rhine, he took a major step towards ultimate unification of Germany. Metternich's sponsorship of the loosely confederated Bund had defeated the next logical step in the evolution of a unified German people.

The adoption of conservative policies was accomplished by religious reaction. The best example of the force of this spiritual movement is to be found in the pronouncement of the czar that he would henceforth rule Russia in keeping with the teachings of Christianity.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Some of the powers adhered to a treaty to this effect; some merely acceded to the principles the czar had outlined. More practical statesmen than the mystical czar looked on this Holy Alliance as a mere statement of well-intentioned ideals having no force whatsoever. The 

Holy Alliance is of importance in that it was, and still is, confused in the minds of many with the effective political and military alliance binding England, Russia, Austria, and Prussia which was but a continuation of the allies' anti-Napoleonic military coöperation. This is properly called the Quadruple Alliance. Three years later (1818) 

France was admitted to the group, which then became the Quintuple Alliance. The purpose behind this arrangement was the preservation of the status quo as of 1815. The agreement included the stipulation that periodic congresses be held. The chief sponsor of these meetings was to be Metternich. It was intended that this league of reactionary governments should curb future French aggressions and resist all attempts to foment popular uprisings. Thus was machinery of intervention and repression created which needed but the slightest excuse to go into action. Metternich made himself the watchdog of Europe, ever prepared to strike down rebellion, liberalism, and attempts to establish constitutional governments.
