The Austrian minister's influence over Frederick William III of

Prussia gave him an opportunity to exert restraint over the liberal and nationalistic movements in Germany. Considerable disappointment was felt because of the failure of the diplomats at Vienna to provide for a unified Germany. When Napoleon returned from Elba, the Prussian king had further aggravated the situation by promising constitutional reforms in return for additional military forces and then failing to keep his promise. During the early period of the German nationalistic movement, secret societies like the Tugendbund had been formed to increase the patriotic fervor of the people. Mention has already been made of the part men like Fichte, Scharnhorst, and Stein played in this movement, as well as university professors like 

Niebuhr, Humboldt, Savigny, and others. Students who had fought in the "War of Liberation" for idealistic and patriotic motives found by 1815 that their efforts had been in vain, despite allied successes. 

Thus it was that a group of serious-minded former soldiers, in attendance at the University of Jena, founded a patriotic society which they called the Burschenschaft. It was a secret order, favoring a united 

Germany, with the slogan, "honor, liberty, fatherland." The movement spread to other universities and in 1817 the various chapters held a congress at Wartburg. The place and date had a significance, for it

was the three hundredth anniversary of the posting of Luther's famous ninety-five theses as well as the anniversary of the battle of Leipzig. The congress was intrinsically a rather inconsequential affair. 

Some speakers pointed out that the German "War of Liberation" had failed to gain its purpose, but the temper of the speakers was on the whole moderate. A few of the less responsible spirits held an impromptu bonfire in which they burned several books, among them a history of Germany written by Kotzebue, who was looked upon as a Russian spy. The importance of the so-called Wartburg Festival lies not so much in what was done as in the effect which falsified and exaggerated reports of the affair had on powerful conservatives like Metternich.

A belief persisted that a widespread conspiracy against the established regime existed which was no longer confined to student societies. At Metternich's insistence a harsh policy of repression was begun. This was a deciding factor in making the Burschenschaft a dangerous organization. One unbalanced member took it into his head to assassinate the publicist, Kotzebue, with the result that such methods of direct action were generally regarded in conservative circles as typical of the motives of the order. The Carlsbad Decrees established a strict surveillance over student activities, over professors in the lecture room as well as in their writings. At Metternich's dictation, it was made a crime even to express the desire for a constitution in Germany. These repressive measures dissolved the Burschenschaft, set up an inquisitorial commission to ferret out revolutionary societies and activities, and established censorship of the press and of individual expression. The dissolution of the society caused the foundation of dozens more like it, though of a more radical and less responsible nature.

Metternich's policy of repression and intervention came to grips with a serious situation when, some five years after the Congress of Vienna, revolution raised its head around the borders of the Mediterranean. Since the days of Napoleonic intervention in Spain, there had been distress in the peninsula. Ferdinand VII had been restored by the Congress, but his promise to maintain the liberal constitution of 1812 had been broken almost as soon as he assumed power. Instead, he had begun a major war of persecution against all liberals. When an expedition was ordered to America to subdue revolting colonists, the soldiers, ordered to service so far from home, rebelled. Their companions in arms throughout Spain took up the banner of revolt and the king was forced again to subscribe to the constitution. Revolu-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tion soon became epidemic, for when Spain's neighbors saw how successful the revolt had been, they attempted to emulate the Iberian patriots. Revolt broke out in Portugal, in Naples, and eventually in Greece.

The proximity of the Neapolitan revolt to Austrian territory gave Metternich the necessary excuse for calling a congress of the Quintuple Alliance. A first congress met at Troppau in 1820, another at 

Laibach in the following year, and a third at Verona in 1822. Over the protests of Great Britain, who opposed intervention in the internal affairs of other countries, Austria was authorized to intervene for the suppression of revolts in Naples and Piedmont, tasks which were easily accomplished in 1821. A French army was commissioned to restore Ferdinand to absolute power in Spain (1823). It is to be noted that the royal armies of France were much more successful in forcing conservatism on Spain than the liberalizing Napoleonic forces in the preceding decades. When the Spanish king asked similar aid in regaining his revolted colonies in the New World, the new English minister, Canning, opposed the plan on the ground that it would be detrimental to Great Britain's commercial interests. His opposition was seconded by the United States who proclaimed the now famous Monroe Doctrine (1823). This document announced the opposition of the United 

States to European intervention in the Americas and, with several important additions and reinterpretations, especially at the Chapultepec and Rio conferences of 1945 and 1947, remains one of the fundamental principles of American foreign policy. 

The many restrictions which the Congress of Vienna and the reactionary policies of the Age of Metternich saddled on the liberties of the people of Europe served to breed discontent. Harsh and repressive measures increased the development and dissemination of republican and democratic idealism. Further revolutionary activity was inevitable, for those ideals to which the French Revolution had given birth had taken deep root. Coupled with this factor was the growing nationalism in those countries and regions which had been parcelled out at the Congress of Vienna without thought of racial, linguistic, or geographical boundaries. The policy of conservatism and reaction with which Metternich sowed a war-weary Europe was to yield a harvest of revolution.

CHAPTER 46 The Industrial Revolution 

ISTORY is the record of change. Although change is constant, its velocity varies. In some periods change is gradual, almost imperceptible; in others it is so rapid and thorough as to constitute a veritable revolution. The Renaissance and Reformation engendered changes of great magnitude, yet these movements produced few alterations in the living conditions of the masses. Society remained primarily agricultural, and even the decline of feudalism and serfdom brought no commensurate change in agricultural techniques. Industry still operated under either the gild or the outwork (domestic) system, utilizing methods that in some cases were employed in prehistoric times. The masses were still ignorant and superstitious, and archaic means of communication inevitably fostered provincialism. The Industrial Revolution, on the other hand, brought changes that profoundly affected all strata of society in every civilized country of the world and was doubtless one of the most significant movements in history. 

The economic changes of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries included agricultural improvements, improvements in communications, the entrenchment of capitalism, and the emergence of the modern factory. The essence of the Industrial Revolution, however, was technological advance. A series of inventions, in large measure the fruit of discoveries in theoretical science, made possible large-scale production and the concentration of industry in factories. Expanded production by machinery lowered prices, increased consumption, and eventually raised the standard of living of the masses. The factory meant regimentation and often untrammeled exploitation of workers, thus creating social problems of the utmost significance. 

Factories developed in an age wherein economic thinking was inclining to the doctrine of laissez faire. Free competition was the shibboleth, and governments were to abstain from the regulatory activities that characterized the age of mercantilism. According to

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

this doctrine the relations of employer and employee were no concern of government. Labor acquired a commodity status and, as such, was subject to the operations of presumably immutable economic laws. Employment was an agreement mutually entered into by worker and industrialist. The former accepted conditions of employment theoretically on his own volition, and wages, hours, and other essential features were consequently not within the province of governmental regulation. Workers lost all semblance of independence. 

Recurrent unemployment, precipitated by factors they could neither understand nor control, brought dire want. Industrial accidents exacted a terrible toll, and chronic illness, engendered by barbarous working conditions, was an even greater peril. Unscrupulous employers, secure in an atmosphere of governmental indifference, exploited women and children in mine and factory. Towns and cities grew rapidly without plan or regulation, and slum areas, with their squalor and degradation, were the inevitable result.

Class distinctions widened. Those with the capital to purchase machines reaped huge fortunes, while the workers received a niggardly share of the profits. Rich and poor, employer and worker, stood in sharp, often ominous, contrast. Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, and others saw in this conflict of interest the basic interpretation of history. Class conflict, they held, would increase in virulence until solidarity of the workers would be sufficiently achieved to make feasible the establishment of the proletarian state. 

The Industrial Revolution was basically the result of the augmented demand for articles of manufacture created by the commercial expansion and the advance in theoretical science which began in the age of the Renaissance. Although empiricism produced inventions such as the cotton gin and spinning jenny, in many instances practical application was the culmination of research in pure science. The experiments of Boyle, Black, and Joule laid the foundation for the steam engine, and chemical research was a prelude to revolutionary changes in the steel industry.

England took the lead in the mechanization of industry. She had forged ahead in the commercial expansion of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with the result that capital had accumulated. 

The gilds, with their conservatism and inflexible restrictions, had yielded to the domestic, or outwork, system. There were many swift streams to furnish power prior to the invention of the steam engine. 

Adequate supplies of coal and iron in convenient proximity were an enormous advantage, especially after the introduction of steam power.

English industry produced staple commodities such as textiles, and this type of industry was much better adapted for mechanization than the "luxury" industries of France. England escaped the ravages of the Napoleonic Wars; indeed, the wars accentuated the demand for manufactured products. Its government was more liberal than those of Continental powers. The upper middle class was represented in 

Parliament and consequently could secure the adoption of policies conducive to the advancement of its interests. Property rights and contractual obligations had adequate legal foundations; extortionate taxation and arbitrary restrictions on trade were precluded by the nature of the government. Patent laws developed sufficiently to afford protection to inventors, yet inventors of epoch-making machines sometimes were defrauded of their just reward. The eighteenth century was marked by great popular interest in mechanical devices. 

There were societies for the promotion of invention, institutes for the study of practical science, and periodicals for the dissemination of scientific knowledge.

By the middle of the eighteenth century, the textile industry had so expanded that the number of properly qualified weavers and other artisans was inadequate to raise production to the level of demand. 

There was, however, plenty of unskilled labor, largely because of the agricultural changes of the eighteenth century. Jethro Tull (16741741) invented a seed drill to plant crops in rows far enough apart to allow weeding and cultivating, which greatly increased the yield. 

Lord ("Turnip ") Townshend obtained even more profitable results by combining Tull's methods with crop rotation and the greater use of clovers and turnips. Robert Bakewell's experiments in stock breeding led to a rapid expansion of cattle raising and an improvement in the quality and quantity of meat and wool. The adoption of scientific farming for crops and livestock gave impetus to a movement for the enclosure of lands into large estates. The greater efficiency of these enclosed estates reduced employment and tenantry and therefore contributed to the decline of the yeomanry. 

The textile industry was the first to be mechanized. England had been the leading source of wool in the Middle Ages, and, with the immigration of Flemish weavers, she soon attained equal importance in the manufacture of woolen cloth. Cotton fabrics became popular by the eighteenth century, and the acquisition of most of India afforded an adequate supply of the fibre. Those interested in the woolen industry for a time obstructed the manufacture of cotton fabrics through parliamentary restrictions. Importation of cotton fabrics

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

was forbidden, but since the demand for them did not abate, the prohibition served to encourage domestic manufacture. In 1736 an act of Parliament legalized the weaving of cotton cloth, provided a flax warp was used in conjunction with a cotton weft. All restrictions on the industry were removed, however, by an act of 1774. The invention of Whitney's cotton gin (1793) greatly increased the quantity of cotton available.

The introduction of the stocking frame of the Lombe brothers in 1589 heralded the coming revolution in the textile industry, but mechanization made no marked progress until the invention of the flying shuttle in 1733. Prior to this invention, the weaver pushed the shuttle carrying the weft back and forth across the warp. Where the warp was more than three-quarters of a yard wide, a weaver on each side of the loom was requisite. Thomas Kay devised an ingenious appliance which employed a spring-propelled hammer to knock the shuttle back across the warp. When the weaver threw the shuttle across the warp, it was automatically returned. The invention precipitated a serious dislocation of the textile industry. Weavers could produce cloth much faster than thread could be supplied. A spinning machine was demanded that could restore equilibrium. 

Wyatt and Paul experimented with machines to replace the ageold spinning wheel. Although they were unsuccessful, some of their ideas were incorporated in later devices. The first successful machine was the spinning jenny, invented by James Hargreaves in 1765. It used a wheel and belt to drive eight spindles simultaneously, but successive improvements greatly increased its efficiency. The problem of thread production, however, was not yet solved, for the jenny spun only coarse, loose thread which had to be made more durable by the admixture of flax. The water frame (1769), introduced by Richard

Arkwright, who derived the basic ideas from others, remedied these difficulties. The skeins were run through two sets of rollers, the second of which rotated faster than the first. The yarn was thus drawn out preparatory to spinning and a much finer and tougher thread was produced. Since the machine was too cumbersome to be turned by hand, the application of water power gave it the name "water frame." Arkwright installed several of these machines and employed a number of hands to operate them, thus probably establishing the first true factory.

Crompton's “mule,” invented about 1779, was a still greater advance. In this machine the strands were pulled and twisted preparatory to spinning. All these operations were performed in a continuous

process. Then great interest was aroused in efforts to invent a power loom. Prizes and other inducements were offered, but it was not until 

1785 that Edmund Cartwright, a clergyman of Kent, perfected a loom that could be operated by water power. It did not displace the hand looms to a great extent. Not until the improved Harrock's loom was made and sold by Sharp and Roberts in 1822 did the hand loom yield to the machine, bringing distress among the artisans whose services hitherto had been in great demand. 

The invention of a method of printing by rollers enormously cheapened calicoes, which could not be made on a large scale as long as block printing was necessary. Improved methods of dyeing and the discovery of the bleaching properties of chlorine were other factors that gave great impetus to the cotton industry. By 1835 England was producing 63 per cent of the world's output. 

The utilization of water power limited the expansion of the textile industry. The location of the factories was prescribed by the necessity of relying on rapid streams, and available power could not be increased. There was imperative need for a mechanical prime mover that would free industry from these restrictions. 

The steam engine inaugurated a new epoch in industrial progress. 

Engines which utilized the condensation of steam to create a partial vacuum were used to pump water out of mines as early as the seventeenth century. The Savery and Newcomen engines also applied the condensation principle. James Watt, an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, devised an engine wherein the expansive force of steam was applied directly to the piston head. He took out his first patent in 1769. In the first engine, the piston was driven in one direction by steam pressure and returned by its own momentum. In later models Watt used the reciprocation principle; that is, both forward and backward movements of the piston were steam propelled. The inventor also discovered the principle that the efficiency of the engine was dependent upon the difference of the temperature before and after condensation of the steam. In the first engines, valves were opened and closed by hand. This method was, of course, too cumbersome, and Watt added a camshaft to open and close intake and exhaust valves in proper rhythm. Since the inventor did not have the capital to build engines commercially, he entered into a partnership with Matthew Boulton in 1773. A shop was established near Birmingham, and engines were built to order. 

Increase in the size and power of steam engines was made possible by improvements in the iron and steel industries. For centuries iron

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

had been smelted with charcoal, but by the period of the Industrial Revolution shortage of wood constituted a serious problem. Dudley experimented in smelting with coal as early as 1619 without success, but by 1710 Darby successfully employed coke. Furnaces which used rotary fans instead of bellows were in use by 1760. The puddling process invented by Onions and Cort in 1783 was a great advance, since it produced wrought iron, less brittle and of greater tensile strength than cast iron, and needed in the construction of engines and other machinery.

Large-scale production of steel began with the invention of the Bessemer converter (c. 1855), in which a blast of hot air blown into molten iron produced steel. In 1866 Karl Siemens invented the open hearth process wherein the furnace was charged with pig iron, scrap, coke, and nickel or manganese to control hardness. These substances were reduced to a molten state by a blast of hot air, the impurities were drawn off as slag or gas, and the molten steel then was tapped from the bottom.

Industrial expansion was facilitated by the revolutionary changes in transportation that made possible economical marketing of the products of the new industry. Seventeenth century roads were often quagmires, not infrequently infested with highwaymen. The English 

Turnpike Acts of 1663 authorized the private construction of roads and the collection of tolls for their use, but there was little improvement. In the latter half of the eighteenth century, however, Metcalf, McAdam, and Telford introduced grading and hard-surfacing, innovations which gradually became general. By the close of the century large urban centers were linked by fairly satisfactory roads. The same period was marked by the construction of canals, in which development the Duke of Bridgewater was a pioneer. The engineering skill of James Brindley solved many of the problems incident to canal building. The invention of the steam locomotive by George Stephenson began an era of railroad construction. The Stockton and Darlington line was opened in 1825, and by 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester was completed.

Experiments with steam-propelled boats were conducted by Papin in 1690 and Hulls in 1736. John Fitch demonstrated by 1790 a satisfactory vessel which utilized a crude screw propeller instead of the usual paddle wheel. Surprisingly little interest in the steamboat was shown until the successful runs of Robert Fulton's Clermont in 1807. 

In 1819 the Savannah, a sailing vessel equipped with an auxiliary engine, crossed the Atlantic largely on steam power. Nineteen years

later the Sirius and the Great Western made the crossing entirely on steam power in eighteen and fifteen days respectively. The following year the Cunard steamship line was established. 

EFFECTS OF THE REVOLUTION 

The mechanization of industry and the developments in transport made possible the cheap production of goods with commensurate reduction in price. Production soon threatened to outstrip consumption, since few industrialists recognized the need for high wages if domestic purchasing power was to keep pace with the expanded output of the factories. Demand for new markets was largely responsible for the revival of imperialism during the nineteenth century. 

Population increased rapidly, leading Malthus to utter his prophecy of the ultimate inability of the world to afford economic support. 

Ricardo noted a tendency of workers' families to increase rapidly in periods of general prosperity and held that this would inexorably depress wages to a subsistence level. With the concentration of industry in factories there was a great shift in population to large urban centers. Manchester, Birmingham, and other industrial towns grew with great rapidity. The population shifts dislocated the apportionment of parliamentary representation until the notorious injustices were corrected by the Reform Bill of 1832. Increase of population that outstripped the construction of suitable housing for the workers resulted in overcrowding and squalor in the industrial centers, and low wages and high rents prevented workers from obtaining more suitable dwellings.

Workers lost their independence as industry was centralized in factories. Machines were expensive and usually performed only one operation of the manufacturing process and, consequently, only persons with considerable capital could set up a factory. Lowered prices resulting from machine production made competition impossible for artisans who employed manual methods. Efficient operation of factories required discipline. Strict rules and rigid supervision by foremen replaced the informality and personal relationships of the gild or domestic (outwork) systems. Workers themselves became virtual automatons as they performed the same humdrum mechanical tasks day after day.

Sixteen- to eighteen-hour days were not unusual, and wages were pitifully low. Wages for mature men ranged from $2.50 to $5.00 per week. Since the operation of the machines required neither great strength nor technical skill, children and women were preferred, and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

actually comprised about three-fourths of the number of industrial employees. Wages for these victims of the factory system ranged from $1.00 to $2.25 per week. Many children were farmed out by almshouses to employers as "pauper apprentices." Children eight years of age were worked until they literally fainted from exhaustion, only to be revived by applications of the overseer's strap. The most elementary hygienic safeguards were ignored. Workers were often killed or maimed by the whirring machines which were not fitted with protective devices. Employers were not required to indemnify the victims unless their personal negligence could clearly be proven. 

Women were employed to drag carts where mine passages were too cramped to permit the use of mules. Children in the mines sat fourteen hours a day in utter darkness to open and close the "traps," and some became mentally deranged from prolonged exposure to such barbarous conditions.

In 1833 a father testified before factory commissioners as follows: 

My two sons (one ten, the other thirteen) work at Milnes factory at Lenton. They go at half past five in the morning; don't stop at breakfast or tea time. They stop at dinner half an hour. Come home at quarter before ten. They used to work till ten, sometimes eleven, sometimes twelve. They earn between them 6s. 2d. per week. One of them, the eldest, worked at Wilson's for two years at 2s. 3d. per week. He left because his overlooker beat him and loosened a tooth for him. I complained and they turned him away for it. They have been gone to work sixteen hours now; they will be very tired when they come home at half past nine. I have been obliged to beat 'em with a strap in their shirts, and to pinch 'em, in order to get them well awake. It made me cry to be obliged to do it. 

Collective action by the workers to procure amelioration of such conditions was illegal until the formation of trade unions was authorized in 1824. As public attention gradually was attracted to these evils, remedial legislation, in the form of successive factory acts, eventually was secured. The reform movements of nineteenth century England eliminated the worst abuses, with the result that the teachings of the socialists did not secure extensive acceptance. 

SPREAD OF INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION AND RISE OF SOCIALISM 

By 1850 the Industrial Revolution had become a world movement. 

England for a time attempted to preserve her industrial supremacy by prohibiting the export of machinery, but the futility of these efforts was realized by 1825. In general, mechanization of industry

proceeded rapidly in other countries. The gradual development such as had occurred in England was not necessary, since the new techniques were introduced in integrated form. The modernization of 

French industry came with the triumph of the middle class in the Revolution and the abolition of the gilds, although progress was not comparable with that of England. Necessary natural resources were meager, and political upheavals frequently disruptive. The country remained primarily agricultural, and industry largely was devoted to the manufacture of articles of luxury requiring craftsmanship of a high order.

Germany, on the other hand, became a great workshop after 1871. The Franco-Prussian War consolidated the states and made. feasible a national industrial program. The acquisition of Alsace and 

Lorraine furnished new supplies of iron and coal, and the indemnity paid by France had a stimulating effect. Intelligent government patronage and unusually capable promotion of foreign trade also were important factors.

The industrial growth of Russia came after 1890. Wise government policies, fostered by Count Witte, led to the construction of railways, usually considered the basic factor in the modernization of Russian industry. The emancipation of the serfs and relaxation of the corporate liabilities of the mirs (rural villages) created a fluid supply of labor. Italy, Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Scandinavia likewise were materially affected by the Industrial Revolution. By 1900 the United States, which had closely followed England in the mechanization of industry, had become a powerful competitor in the markets of the world. Western penetration of the Far East brought modernized industry to Japan, which today is one of the most highly industrialized nations.

The industrial changes produced social problems common to all these countries. Adherence to the theories of classic economists, like 

Smith, Ricardo, Mill, and Bentham, would have meant the perpetuation of the evils of the factory system or the naive expectation of remedial action motivated by enlightened self-interest. Voices soon were raised against eighteenth century economic “liberalism.”

Saint-Simon, Louis Blanc, and Robert Owen with their various schemes of social reform were called the "Utopian" socialists. Karl 

Marx, however, developed a philosophy and program for socialism based on the inevitability of working-class victory in its coming conflict with capitalism. These socialist reformers declared that goods should be produced for consumption rather than for the ac-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cumulation of private fortunes which really depended on the preservation of scarcity.¹

The acceptance of the Marxist views has been retarded by factors not adequately evaluated by the philosopher. The tenacious middle class still confounded the prophecies of the progressive widening of class distinctions. The peasantry of the European countries have become in large measure proprietor cultivators. Trade unionism has progressed in the attainment of satisfactory working conditions, especially in England. Above all, state socialism, with its adoption of many of the practical reforms first advocated by the socialists, has allayed unrest from time to time. Its continued success is prob lematical. 

1 See Chapter 49 for a discussion of socialism and communism.

CHAPTER 47 Liberalism in the Nineteenth Century 

ENGLISH REFORM MOVEMENTS TO 1914 

HERE was imperative need for reform in eighteenth century England. The slave trade with all its horrors was strongly entrenched, and slavery was the foundation of the economy of the British West Indies. Punishments for criminals were barbarous, and the capital sentence was imposed for over two hundred offenses. The Test Act and other discriminations curtailed religious and civil liberty. The indigent were cared for by the Speenhamland system of "outdoor relief," whereby monetary contributions by the parish augmented wages which were below the subsistence level. Migration of laborers in search of employment was forbidden, while the administration of the poor laws discouraged thrift and industry, depressed wages, and imposed exorbitant taxation. Many social problems grew out of the Industrial Revolution. 

The exploitation of women and children, starvation wages, overlong hours, unsafe and unhealthful factories, and overcrowded, disease-breeding slums attracted public attention and caused increasingly insistent demand for reform. 

One of the most successful of the early reform movements culminated in the abolition of the slave trade. England had been active in this nefarious business since the days of Drake and Hawkins. Indeed, the asiento clause of the Treaty of Utrecht gave her a monopoly of the trade to Spanish America. William Clarkson, an Oxford student, studied the details of the trade and published a book that embodied shocking revelations. He joined with William

Wilberforce, whose persuasive eloquence and organizing ability admirably supplemented his own industry. From their combined efforts grew a society dedicated to the abolition of the traffic (1787). 

The society issued pamphlets and sent petitions to Parliament. William Pitt, whose ministry already had been distinguished by important administrative and financial reforms, finally appointed

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

parliamentary committee to hold an investigation of the trade. An appalling story was told, but vested interests were sufficiently strong to forestall the remedial legislation introduced by the prime minister (1788). Similar efforts in 1789 and 1792 likewise were defeated. The society continued to agitate, encouraged by the Mansfield judicial decision (1772), which stipulated that Negro slaves could not be held in England. Success came with the passage in 1807 of a bill abolishing the trade. England was largely instrumental in procuring an international condemnation of the trade at the Congress of Vienna. The methods used to achieve the reform were characteristic of subsequent movements. Interested individuals at first began the agitation on a small scale. Later a society was formed and papers were published until the matter reached the attention of Parliament. 

Parliamentary investigation greatly enhanced public interest, and, after a period of obstruction, remedial legislation was passed. 

Another early reform movement that attained partial success was inaugurated by John Howard. A wealthy dissenter, he became high sheriff of Bedfordshire in 1773. His office brought glaring evils in penology to his attention. Jails were loathsome, and the prevalent fee system for the payment of wardens was responsible for grave abuses in management and the treatment of inmates. In some instances, persons who had been acquitted were held in prison because of fees they had incurred while awaiting trial. Investigation proved that frightful conditions, such as the prevalence of jail fever, were general. The interest aroused by Howard's revelations resulted in the passage of two bills in 1774. Salaries were provided for jailers to replace the fee system, and regulations were issued to ensure proper sanitation. Evasion and indifference offset the gains, but the reformer continued his agitation. A series of monographs on the 

State of Prisons did much to prepare public sentiment for the reforms of the nineteenth century.

The French Revolution brought a cessation of reforming activity. 

Indeed, when England entered the struggle against the Revolutionary government in 1793, legislation assumed a reactionary tendency. 

The Habeas Corpus Act was suspended in 1795, and newspapers virtually were taxed out of existence. The Treasonable Practices 

Act enlarged the definition of treason to include mere speaking or writing against the king or the government. The Seditious Meetings Bill forbade political gatherings without previous notice by a responsible person and authorized justices of the peace to disperse even legally convoked assemblies, although these laws were

not rigorously enforced. Liberalism was identified with upheaval and violence, and conservatives saw in the Reign of Terror and the rise of Napoleon the vindication of the fears expressed by Edmund 

Burke in his Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

Reactionary policies prevailed even after the collapse of the Napoleonic Empire. Risings in 1816-1817, caused by the misery incident to post-war deflation and technological unemployment, were suppressed with severity. More restrictions were imposed on freedom of expression and assembly, and the Habeas Corpus Act again was suspended. In 1819 bad harvests and renewed industrial depression again stimulated unrest. Demands for parliamentary reform centered in unrepresented industrial cities. In Manchester a mass meeting was held in St. Peter's Fields without magisterial authorization. When the crowd refused to disperse, the magistrates attempted to arrest the speaker and ordered mounted soldiers to charge. Five were killed and about fifty injured. The "Peterloo Massacre," as it was called, caused great excitement, but the government continued to pass repressive legislation which included further restrictions on public meetings and the press. Improvement in economic conditions, however, reduced the discontent and removed the necessity for enforcing the reactionary laws.

Resumption of reform began with the entrance of liberal Tories in Lord Liverpool's cabinet (1822). Robert Peel became home secretary, while George Canning succeeded Castlereagh, who had committed suicide, as foreign secretary. William Huskisson, appointed president of the Board of Trade, began an assault on entrenched privilege by modifying the Navigation Acts on a basis of reciprocity. 

His policy was the prelude to the repeal of the acts in 1849. Tariffs were lowered, obsolete taxes were repealed, and progress was made towards a more equitable distribution of taxation. In 1825, trade unions were legalized, with safeguards against the employment of threats or intimidation by either side in labor disputes. When death terminated Lord Liverpool's long ministry, Canning, after considerable royal opposition, succeeded him. A measure to modify the 

Corn Laws of 1815 was blocked by the House of Lords. It was the only major measure sponsored by Canning, who died in August, 1827. He was succeeded by the Duke of Wellington, the personification of conservatism.

The first major issue of the Wellington ministry was the Catholic question. Catholics were excluded from both houses of Parliament, barred from civil offices, and deprived of the franchise. In Ireland,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the injustice was aggravated by tithes and quit rents. Daniel O'Connell, a Catholic barrister, became the leader in the movement for emancipation and founded the Catholic Association in 1823. In 1828, the Test and Corporation Acts were repealed, removing the disabilities of dissenters. The following year, the Catholic Emancipation Act removed the major survivals of the age of religious persecution. By 1830, demands for parliamentary reform were too insistent to be ignored. Commercial and industrial interests were not adequately represented, nor were the shifts of wealth and population resulting from the Industrial Revolution reflected in rights of suffrage or the apportionment of parliamentary seats. Lancashire, with its thriving, populous cities, had nineteen seats, while Cornwall, with one-quarter the population, had forty-four. Dunwich, a deserted fishing hamlet partially submerged by the sea, had representation, as did Malmesbury with a total population of thirteen, all illiterates. Yet cities which had grown tremendously with the rise of factories were inadequately represented or in some cases not represented at all. Representatives of "pocket boroughs were appointed in accordance with rights of patronage that dated to the later Middle Ages, while in "rotten boroughs" the seats were openly sold or the small number of qualified electors bribed. 

Laws restricting the suffrage were obsolete and often absurd. In the shires, the vote was restricted to owners of 40s. freeholds, in accordance with a law of the reign of Henry VI (1430). In four centuries, of course, the rise of prices and the consequent depreciation of the purchasing value of money meant that owners of even the smallest parcels of land could vote while tenants on large farms or leaseholders were ineligible. A bewildering variety of practices characterized the franchise laws in respect to the boroughs. In some cases the vote was restricted to those who had inherited or purchased rights of burgage; in others, only resident householders were eligible. “Scot and lot " boroughs granted the franchise to those who paid certain taxes which had survived from medieval times, while in the "Potwalloper" towns, only those who occupied dwellings with kitchens were permitted to vote. "Close boroughs" confined the vote to the incumbents of designated municipal offices. 

With the accession of William IV, a ministry was formed under Earl Grey. A bill for parliamentary reform, introduced in the Commons by Lord John Russell, received so many restrictive amendments that Grey dissolved Parliament and appealed to the country

on the issue. In the campaign which ensued a general demand appeared for "The Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill." The 

Whigs triumphed and the bill passed the Commons with a majority of 109 votes, but the House of Lords rejected it. Riots throughout the country followed the failure of the bill, and the working people even threatened to withdraw their money from the banks in protest. 

The ministry resigned, but after Wellington vainly attempted to form a cabinet Grey was recalled. The reform bill again was passed by Commons with a large majority, but it still encountered obstruction by the Lords. Grey was authorized by the king to threaten the creation of new peers to force passage. Thereupon Wellington and a group of ultra-conservative lords absented themselves and the bill became law.

Parliamentary representation was now apportioned more equitably. Fifty-six boroughs with populations under two thousand lost their seats, while thirty with less than four thousand inhabitants were deprived of one representative each. One double borough lost two of its four. The 144 seats were allocated to forty-three boroughs, primarily the industrial centers hitherto inadequately represented. 

There was also a modest extension of the franchise. In the counties the vote was granted to £10 freeholders, copyholders, and longterm leaseholders. A £50 qualification was fixed for holders of leases for less than sixty years and tenants at will. In the boroughs, householders who paid rents of at least £10 per year were made eligible. 

The bill shifted political power from the landed aristocracy to the middle class and increased the electorate from 450,000 to 650,000. 

The vast army of workers were still deprived of the franchise. Further liberalization would therefore be necessary in order to give to the working classes sufficient political power to assure adequate economic and social reform.

A number of reforms were carried through by the impetus towards liberalism created by the First Reform Bill. In response to continual agitation for the abolition of slavery in the British dependencies, a bill was passed in 1833 providing for gradual emancipation. All slave children below the age of six were freed and children subsequently born to slaves were to be free. As this plan proved unworkable, four years later emancipation was granted to all and £20,000,000 was appropriated to indemnify the owners. The Factory Act of 1833, sponsored by Lord Ashley, brought some improvement of conditions in the factories. A preliminary act of 1802 had regulated the labor of pauper apprentices, but the act of 1833 was of general

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

application in the textile industry. Labor of children under nine years was prohibited, while children from nine to thirteen could not be employed for more than eight hours a day. Thirteen hours a week were to be spent in school. "Young persons" from thirteen to eighteen were restricted to twelve hours a day. A provision for paid inspectors made this the first factory act to be effectively enforced. 

Nine years later, Ashley secured the appointment of a parliamentary committee to investigate mines and factories, despite the opposition of industrialists and proponents of laissez faire. The report revealed that women were forced to crawl through cramped mine passages, drawing carts by chains which were fastened to girdles.

The testimony was so revolting that the labor. of women in mines was entirely forbidden. In 1844, Ashley, assisted by Peel who had recently been converted to the cause, secured passage of another factory act, under the terms of which women could not work more than twelve hours a day, and children under thirteen were restricted to half time, either a six-hour day or alternative days of twelve hours. 

The Poor Law of 1834 corrected many of the abuses which the 

Speenhamland system of "outdoor relief" had created. Restrictions on the migration of paupers in search of employment were removed, and payment of doles was forbidden. Workhouses were established to care for the indigent who could not secure employment; parishes were grouped so that the burden of maintaining these institutions could be more equitably shared; and a board of three was appointed to administer local relief in accordance with the act. 

The operation of the Corn Laws of 1815 imposed great hardship on the poor. No grain could be imported without almost prohibitive duties unless the domestic price exceeded 10s. a bushel. This act, of course, had been passed in the interests of the landowners by a parliament that represented primarily that element of English society. 

Attempts were made from time to time to lower the duties. During the brief ministry of Canning (1827) a measure to install a sliding scale of duties was blocked by the Lords. Manufacturers joined the movement for abolition of the laws, since high food prices meant continued agitation of workers for higher wages. Richard Cobden and John Bright took the lead in the establishment of the Anti-Corn Law League in 1839. Lectures and pamphlets, financed primarily by the Manchester manufacturers, brought the issue before the masses. 

Peel was partially converted to a free trade policy in 1842 when he lowered tariffs on a number of commodities and noted evidences

of industrial stimulation. In 1843 he abolished duties on wool and again results were favorable. In 1845 export duties were abolished and import duties on a number of commodities lowered. It was, however, the failure of the Irish potato crop in the fall of 1845 that brought the question of the Corn Laws to a crisis. Since potatoes had supplanted bread as the staple food of the poor, the blight caused actual famine. Peel's Tory government, of course, was traditionally representative of the landowners' interests, and the prime minister was personally committed to a policy of protection. The Whigs, under the leadership of Russell, boldly espoused free trade. When

Peel's cabinet refused to support him in repeal legislation, he resigned, but resumed office after Russell failed to form a ministry. A bitter parliamentary battle ensued, but on May 15, 1846, the repeal measure was passed.

One of the effects of the repeal of the Corn Laws was to allay the agitation of the Chartists. In 1836, a Workmen's Association had been founded in London which soon adopted the attainment of political rights as its paramount objective. The depression of 1838 and the attendant misery of the workers gained strength for the movement. William Lovett, one of the leaders of the organization, drew up the People's Charter, based on the conviction that political rights were prerequisite to redress of economic grievances. The charter's six points demanded manhood suffrage, vote by secret ballot, annual parliamentary elections, equal electoral districts, the abolition of property qualifications for parliamentary membership, and payment of members of the House of Commons, who up to this time had served without salary.

Mass meetings were held throughout the country; it was said that 

300,000 assembled at Manchester. At a convention held in 1839 a petition was drawn up and presented to Parliament. Rejection of the petition precipitated riots. "Physical force" Chartists marched on London, but the arrests of the leaders broke up the demonstration. Excitement subsided with a return of better conditions in business, but in 1843 the "Great Turnout," somewhat similar to the general strikes of our times, gave evidence that the leaders were still active. The following year, with the formation of Friendly Societies and renewed interest in trade unionism, much of the force of the Chartist movement was diverted. The abolition of the Corn Laws, and the consequent alleviation of misery, increased the defection from its ranks. Revolutions on the Continent in 1848, however, stimulated a brief revival. About 20,000 workers, led by Fergus

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

O'Connor, marched on London, which was heavily policed in preparation for their coming. The demonstrators brought a monster petition, alleged to contain 5,000,000 names. The document, weighing 584 pounds, was carried in three cabs. This final demonstration proved to be an impotent gesture, however, because special constables, recruited for the emergency, overawed the petitioners, and Parliament discovered only 2,000,000 names were attached, many of which were fraudulent.

The Second Reform Bill of 1867 ushered in another period of social and economic advances. As early as 1859 the Conservatives under Disraeli proposed a wider suffrage in rural regions. The Liberals defeated it because it did nothing for the artisans of the towns. 

Their more generous bill of 1866 was likewise defeated, and the Conservatives again came into power. The next year Disraeli proceeded to "dish the Whigs" and passed the Second Reform Bill, which enfranchised all urban householders and lodgers who paid minimum annual rents of 10. In the counties, the qualification for tenants was reduced to £12. This liberalization of the franchise admitted the large majority of industrial workers, increased the electorate to about 1,200,000, but still excluded the agricultural laborers. 

The new voters endorsed the Liberals, led by Gladstone, in the elections of 1868. In his first ministry (1868-1874) Gladstone carried out many significant reforms. The injustices of the Irish land laws were mitigated by an act of 1870. By the Disestablishment Bill of 1869 the Irish Catholics were freed from paying tithes to the Anglican Church. A great advance was made towards the establishment of educational facilities for the masses, largely in response to the interest in this problem stimulated by Joseph Lancaster's Sunday Schools which had afforded a modicum of elementary instruction for the children of the working class. Schools under local boards were set up where existent facilities were inadequate. The cost was defrayed by government grants, supplemented by local taxation and fees paid by parents of children who attended. All denominational religious instruction was forbidden. By 1890, there were 20,000 of these Board Schools, attended by about 4,000,000 pupils. 

Another achievement was the passage of a Civil Service Law (1870) which authorized competitive examinations for posts in the service. An Army Reform Act (1871) abolished the practice of purchasing commissions, but its provisions were not made retroactive. A royal warrant, issued by Queen Victoria at Gladstone's behest, was necessary to overcome the obstructive tactics of the Lords. Election

by ballot was established the following year, and the creation of a Supreme Court of Judicature (1873) terminated the reforms of the first Gladstone ministry. 

The second Gladstone ministry (1880-1885) once more focused attention on reform rather than on foreign policy, which had been the chief interest of Disraeli's Conservative government (1874-1880). 

The Franchise Act of 1884, which gave the vote to the agricultural laborers, virtually established universal manhood suffrage since only servants, transients, and bachelors who lived with their parents and paid no rent were excluded. A redistribution of seats, necessitated by the extension of the ballot, was carried in 1885 which approximated the earliest Chartist demand for equal electoral districts. 

Political reform was consummated by the Parliament Bill of 1911 and the Franchise Act of 1918. By the former act, the Lords were deprived of the right to defeat money bills. With other bills the 

Lords henceforth could exercise only a suspensive veto. If the Commons passed the same measure twice more over the Lords' vetoes after a lapse of two years, the bill automatically became a law. The act of 1918 almost doubled the electorate by extending the franchise to women over thirty who owned property or whose husbands could vote. A supplementary "Flapper Bill" in 1928 gave the vote to women from twenty-one to thirty years of age on equal terms with men:

The recent history of England has also been marked by the consolidation and extension of social and economic reforms. Supplementary enactments have raised the standard of schools founded by the act of 1870: compulsory (1880) and free (1891) education was finally established, and admission to the universities has been liberalized. Trade unionism, protected, even fostered, by the government (1871, 1906), has contributed to the formation of the Labor Party, which, however, under the responsibility of government in the postwar era, has become relatively conservative. With the assistance of universal suffrage and the Labor Party great strides were made in social reform. Accident insurance (1897), sickness and unemployment insurance (1911), old age pensions (1908), and the Small Holdings Act (1907) were all designed to give greater economic security to the factory worker and, in the last-mentioned act, to the farm laborer.

England achieved its present democracy by a remarkable process of orderly reform. There was no revolution, and very little violence, despite the sharp clashes of class interests precipitated by the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

reform measures. English liberalism was the model for the world during the nineteenth century, and success of the reform movements gave hope to liberals everywhere. In one instance after another a few individuals had begun to agitate for the correction of specific abuses, and slowly, sometimes almost imperceptibly, gained against the obstructions of vested interests and public apathy. These groups grew into societies, and papers and broadsides incessantly urged the reforms until the issues attracted political notice. Mobilized public sentiment in turn exercised a pressure which eventually overcame all opposition.

FRANCE: 1814-1914 

66 In May, 1814, Louis XVIII entered Paris in a carriage drawn by white horses, to the accompaniment of tolling bells, booming cannon, and the restrained enthusiasm of the populace. The new king was a man of spirit, and, in a certain measure, a man of good sense, but prematurely old, wracked by gout, fearing all work, fleeing all contention; he regarded the throne of France as a comfortable arm chair rather than a place of honor." He had left France at the time of the flight of Louis XVI to Varennes. He had sojourned for a time in 

Russia, where his arrogance alienated the czar, and had then gone to 

England where he had received a pension. 1 

The Congress of Vienna, after deciding upon a Bourbon restoration, had stipulated that a constitution be granted to conciliate French liberals. Louis accordingly issued a charter that organized the new government as a constitutional monarchy and preserved many of the benefits of the Revolution. Equality before the law, freedom of speech and assembly, an untrammeled press, freedom from arbitrary arrests, and other civil liberties were guaranteed. 

Lands confiscated from the church and the émigrés were not to be restored, and the titles of holders of such lands were to be recognized as inviolable by the returning Bourbon régime.

The king was to enjoy an absolute veto and the sole right to initiate legislation through his appointed ministers. A bicameral legislature was established. The Chamber of Peers was made up of nobles who inherited membership or received appointment for life from the king. It had coördinate authority with the lower house except in taxation measures. The Chamber of Deputies was made up of members elected by indirect and restricted suffrage for a term of five years. Only those who paid a minimum annual tax of 300 francs were 

1 Henri Houssaye, 1814.

eligible to vote, and 1,000 francs was the amount requisite for membership in the Chamber. About 100,000 received the vote in accordance with these qualifications, while 12,000 were eligible to serve as deputies.

The new government was beset by a number of difficulties. The king's issue of laws dated in the "nineteenth year of our reign" ignored the Revolution and was interpreted as an affront. Returning émigrés demanded the restoration of their estates and threatened vengeance for the indignities they had suffered. The indiscretions of many of the repatriated nobles precipitated the "White Terror,” a wave of hysteria, during the summer of 1815. Those who had been prominently identified with Napoleon or the Revolution feared for their lives, and holders of sequestered lands placed little confidence in the assurance that restitution to the émigrés was not contemplated. 

In the demobilization of the army there was discrimination against former officers of Napoleon. The Restoration government embarked on a policy of puritanism, attempting, among other things, to enforce strict observance of the Sabbath. The funeral of a Parisian actress, who had enjoyed great popularity, caused a demonstration when church obsequies and burial in consecrated ground were forbidden. These acts of the government alone would have made the new régime unpopular, but the situation was aggravated by economic depression. There were riots against high taxes and the exportation of grain which kept domestic prices at high levels. When 

Napoleon returned from Elba in March, 1815, to inaugurate the "Hundred Days," few save the nobles mourned the expulsion of the

Bourbons. After Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo in June and his exile to Saint Helena, the allies once more installed Louis XVIII, with an army of occupation to ensure order. 

The period of 1815-1820 was characterized by liberalism, sponsored by both the Richelieu and Decazes ministries. The indemnity imposed by the allies at Vienna was paid by bond issues. Therefore the army of occupation was withdrawn in 1818 by decision of the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle. A new army law established the Napoleonic principle of " careers open to talent," but many ultra-royalists were disgruntled by the measure. A press law which required authorization before publication was replaced by a measure that required publishers to post a bond of 10,000 francs. 

Events of the year 1820 inaugurated a period of reaction. The 

Abbé Grégoire, a “regicide,” was elected to the Chamber of Deputies, but was excluded in deference to a storm of criticism from

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

conservatives. The murder of the Duke of Berry shocked public sentiment and strengthened demands for reactionary legislation. 

Rigid censorship was imposed on the press and summary procedure authorized against those charged with sedition. The Law of the 

Double Vote, designed to consolidate conservative control of the Chamber of Deputies, provided that deputies were to be chosen by colleges of electors in designated cantons, as well as in the departments. Citizens who paid a minimum tax of 1,000 francs were permitted to vote for both cantonal and departmental electors, which gave them double representation.

The swing to conservatism was accentuated during the Villèle ministry (1822-1828). Reactionary peers were appointed, clerical control of education was revived, and the political influence of the Jesuits again became strong. Emigrés were given preference in the award of military commissions; restrictions on the press were tightened; and protective tariffs were imposed to benefit landowners, with attendant high prices for the masses. 

The accession of Charles X (1824-1830) brought reactionary trends to a dangerous level. The new ruler was a leader of the fanatical group of nobles who had learned nothing since 1789. A proposal was made to reimburse the émigrés for losses sustained by them, estimated at 1,000,000,000 francs. The plan provided for the payment of 30,000,000 francs annually, representing 3 per cent interest on the estimated value of the confiscated property. The necessary funds were to be raised by lowering the interest on outstanding government bonds from 5 per cent to 4 per cent. This provision angered the bourgeoisie, who stood to lose money by the reduction of interest.

In 1827 liberals gained seats in the Chamber of Deputies, despite the electoral law of 1820. In the elections of 1830, they won the balance of power, but Charles attempted to frustrate the will of the electorate by his "July Ordinances." Claiming the right of independent legislation, “to ordain for the good of the state," the king quashed the elections and arbitrarily narrowed the franchise to large property holders to ensure conservative success in the new elections ordered. The ordinances also contained a provision authorizing the prosecution of publishers whose books or journals had a radical tendency, even if nothing specifically objectionable could be cited.

These ordinances precipitated the July Revolution of 1830. Barricades were thrown up in the streets of Paris, and the movement spread

to other parts of the country. The throne, left vacant by the flight of Charles X, was offered by the revolutionary leaders to Louis Philippe, Duke of Orleans. His choice was a compromise designed to satisfy both royalists and republicans. Louis Philippe had served in the army during the early days of the Revolution. With the establishment of the Republic, he left France to sojourn in Switzerland, England, and America until the Restoration. He was coarse, affable, and democratic. He and his green umbrella had been a familiar sight on the streets of Paris where he had seldom failed to stop to chat with workmen while on his strolls.

The moderate reforms introduced by the new régime were in keeping with the character of the revolution of 1830, which was essentially a bourgeois movement. Amendments to the constitution included a denial of the doctrine of the divine right of kings and an unequivocal renunciation of the power of independent legislation which had been claimed by Charles X. Another enactment declared that Catholicism was not the state religion. The Law of the Double 

Vote was repealed and property qualifications for suffrage were reduced to two hundred francs. Professional men were eligible to vote if their taxes were half that sum.

The Orleans monarchy, however, lasted only eighteen years, and even Louis Philippe was not permitted to end his days on the throne. 

The causes of the collapse of this régime are found in both domestic and foreign policies. There was great disappointment among the liberal monarchists and republicans over the failure to continue the policy of liberalization. The press was stifled by the "September 

Laws" of 1835, and a broadening of the suffrage was denied. As time went on, with the encouragement of his favorite minister, Guizot (1840-1848), the king tried to impose his own personal government. 

Under middle-class dominance the government made no effort to remedy the serious social evils of unemployment, low wages, long hours, and labor-union repression. On the other hand an elaborate system of corruption was developed to keep Guizot and his conservatives in power and to obtain the passage of their legislative program. 

Voters were bribed by offices and government contracts; legislators were bought by administrative appointments, promotions, raises in salaries, and railroad projects.

In the field of foreign policy the Orleans monarchy caused much dissatisfaction among nationalists and liberals alike. It refused to go to the aid of the liberation movements in Belgium and Poland in 1830 and 1831. Austria was allowed to remain dominant in Italy. Louis

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Philippe had to back down on the Egyptian question in 1840 in the face of a hostile European combination led by England. To add to the French humiliation, the English, in 1844, exacted apologies and indemnities from the French because they justifiably punished a British subject, Pritchard, for his part in a revolt on the French island of Tahiti.

In addition to the opposition of the nationalists and moderate liberals, two new unfriendly groups began to appear: the liberal 

Catholics and the socialists. The liberal Catholics, led by Lamennais, Lacordaire, and Montalembert, favored the separation of church and state, political freedom, and social reform. In spite of the pope's protests the movement regained some popularity for the clergy. Lamennais eventually left the priesthood and became a socialist. 

The socialists of the period were largely Utopian. The most influential French socialist in the field of politics was Louis Blanc who, in his book entitled The Organization of Labor, advocated government establishment of national workshops by lending money to organizations of workers who would repay the loans out of their profits. The remainder of the profits would be distributed among the workers according to their needs rather than according to ability.

In 1847 a campaign of banquets began in the provinces, fostered by the moderate middle-class reformers but promptly supported by the republicans and socialists. At these banquets the opposition deputies would denounce the government and solicit signatures to petitions. Finally, when permission was refused for a great union banquet in Paris on February 22, 1848, barricades were raised and street fighting began. Louis Philippe had to abdicate, and a provisional government of republicans and socialists proclaimed the 

Second Republic. A National Constituent Assembly of 900 salaried deputies over twenty-five years of age was elected by universal manhood suffrage. This body drew up a constitution similar to that of the United States with these three differences: (1) The government was centralized; (2) the legislature was unicameral; (3) and the president, ineligible to reëlection, had no veto power. 

The Second Republic under this constitution was short-lived. The first legislature had a monarchist majority, and the first president was Louis Napoleon Bonaparte, who represented one of the dynasties claiming the French throne. Within three years a conflict between the president and the legislature ended with a coup d'état by Louis Napoleon. After obtaining justification for this

violent seizure of power by a carefully controlled plebiscite, the president drew up a new constitution, resembling closely that of the First Empire, wherein the president had a ten-year term, the senate was appointed by the president, and the legislative body elected under the surveillance of Napoleon's supporters - became a rubber-stamp legislature. With the rigorous curbing of the freedom of the press, speech, and meeting, France returned to a ´régime of dictatorship. One year later, on December 2, 1852, the "Prince

President" was proclaimed Emperor Napoleon III. 

Although a virtual dictator of France, the new emperor had received his authority theoretically by popular will and had to depend on this will for its continuance. Through a system of secret official reports he kept himself informed about public opinion and tried to satisfy as many groups as possible. To please the clericals, he married a devout Spanish countess, Eugénie de Montijo, placed education under the clergy's control, sent an army corps to Rome to protect the pope from the Italians, and dispatched an expedition to Mexico to replace the anti-clerical Juarez with Maximilian of Hapsburg. To exalt the nationalists, he won two wars, against Russia in the Crimea (1855) and against Austria in Italy (1859), which wiped out the shame of the earlier Napoleon's defeats at Waterloo. 

To propitiate the middle class he constructed railroads, founded the French (steamship) Line, encouraged the building of the Suez Canal by de Lesseps, rebuilt Paris with beautiful boulevards and parks, subsidized new mechanized factories, negotiated free-trade treaties, created the Crédit foncier for freer credit to farmers, and held dazzling expositions. To satisfy the working classes, he legalized unions and strikes, founded free clinics and hospitals, and established foundations for pensions and accident compensation. The Second 

Empire was a period of prosperity and progress. 

And yet, in spite of these generous measures, Napoleon III became increasingly unpopular during the second decade of his reign. 

The constitutional monarchists, republicans, and socialists disliked the dictatorship which denied civil liberties and effective representation. His foreign policy became weaker and less successful. He failed to help Poland in 1863 and Denmark in 1864. He angered Catholics by withdrawing from Rome in 1866 and irritated anti-clericals by returning his troops the next year. His expedition to Mexico failed in 1867, and, miscalculating the outcome of the Austro-Prussian 

War (1866), he held aloof from hostilities, thus giving Prussia 2 free hand to unite a powerful Germany north of Austria. Likewise, •

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the emperor failed to get territorial compensations from Prussia along the Rhine.

To stem the tide of hostility at home, Napoleon began gradually to relax the dictatorship after 1860. Legislative debates were made public; the right of interpellation was conceded; freedom of speech, press, and meeting was granted; and finally, in 1870, the responsibility of the cabinet to the parliamentary majority was authorized. 

Yet these concessions did not save the Second Empire. The inevitable war with Prussia that lay just ahead spelled a doom that no mending at home could possibly forestall. 2 When France rushed into war with Prussia in 1870 over the 

Spanish succession issue and its aftermath, she had no reliable ally. 

At Metz and Sedan her armies were crushed by the Prussian juggernaut. Napoleon, captured at Sedan, was dethroned by a revolutionary junta which proclaimed the Third Republic and organized a government of national defence. Paris heroically withstood a siege until starved into submission (January, 1871). Then an assembly, elected for the purpose, concluded the Treaty of Frankfort which surrendered Alsace-Lorraine and provided for the payment of an indemnity of $1,000,000,000. A German army of occupation was to remain in northeast France until the last installment of the indemnity should be paid. The coronation of William I as Emperor of Germany, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, climaxed the humiliation of France.

There were serious obstacles to recovery. A commune was organized in Paris at the close of the war and the red flag of socialism was unfurled. Economic depression and consequent unrest gave the chief impetus to the communal movement, which had for its objective the formation of a federation of petty, self-sufficient, socialistic states in place of the centralized national government. This commune revolt was put down by June, 1871, and Thiers, the first president, turned his attention to getting rid of the German army of occupation. By floating a huge national loan he was able to "liberate the territory" by the end of 1873, but he was forced to resign on the more fundamental question of the future form of government for France. 

The monarchist majority was divided between Bourbons and

Orleanists, while the republicans insisted on the continuance of republican institutions. Thiers, wearied by the monarchist impasse, abandoned his Orleanist comrades and advocated a conservative re- 

2 See infra, p. 643.

public. Out of the conflict in the National Assembly a compromise was gradually worked out. Thiers was supplanted by a more monarchist president, MacMahon, and a series of organic laws was passed in 1875 providing for a republican government which could easily be transformed into a limited monarchy by substituting a king for the figure-head president. Nominally the executive power was vested in a president elected for a seven-year term by a joint session of both houses of the legislature. In reality, however, ministers, responsible to the legislative branch, wielded the executive power. The legislature was organized into a Senate of three hundred and a Chamber of Deputies of about six hundred. Members of the upper house were elected for a nine-year term by electoral colleges, which, in turn, were elected by universal manhood suffrage. Deputies were directly elected for four-year terms. The necessity for universal education for democratic government was recognized by the passage of laws from 1878 to 1882 that provided free schools and compulsory education for children six to thirteen years of age.

The French form of parliamentary government differs from that of England or the United States mainly in the absence of a two-party system. France has a number of parties, no one of which can secure a clear majority for any extended period. The result is that most ministries are coalition ministries; but at any time, often on trivial issues, several parties may form a new coalition, or bloc, and overthrow the ministry by withholding a vote of confidence.

The main domestic political question in France from 1875 to 1908 was the anti-clerical movement. This controversy entered into nearly every important crisis and into much important legislation. The monarchists took the side of the clericals; the republicans and socialists were usually anti-clerical. In 1877 monarchist MacMahon, with the consent of the Senate, dissolved the republican chamber over a church question, but he was repudiated at the polls by a republican victory. The education laws (1878-1882) tended to minimize clerical influence in the schools. In 1887 the Boulanger crisis seriously tested the Republic. After being dismissed as minister of war, Boulanger bid for the support of monarchists, clericals, and those eager to secure revenge against Germany. A coup d'état against the Republic was threatened, and war with Germany was imminent. By 1889, however, the movement had ended in bombast and posturing. 

Again in 1894 the treason case of a Jewish and republican captain, Alfred Dreyfus, created an acute governmental crisis. A monarchist clique in the army had caused him wrongfully to be convicted and

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

sentenced to Devil's Island for life. By 1898 all France became divided into two groups: the anti-Dreyfusard clericals and monarchists who wanted the conviction upheld and the Dreyfusard anti-clericals and republicans who wanted a retrial in the light of new evidence. 

Finally in 1899 he was pardoned by President Loubet, and later on (1906) he was completely exonerated by the Court of Cassation. 

But the whole Dreyfus affair had a profound effect on politics. To protect the Republic against what seemed to be an oblique attack by discrediting a republican officer, the various republican parties formed a defensive bloc in the Chamber. This made them strong enough to control the government and reverse the unjust decision, but it also gave them a chance to carry out their more extreme anticlerical programs. In 1901 a Law of Associations was passed compelling religious orders to be registered before they could teach in the schools, and in 1904 the Education Law prohibited any religious orders to teach after ten years had elapsed. In the same year President Loubet visited the Italian king in Rome but refrained from visiting the pope. After the pope protested, the French withdrew their embassy to the Papal See and in 1905 passed the Law of Separation which abolished the Napoleonic Concordat. Henceforth all religions - Catholic, Protestant, and Jewish - had to be self-supporting, receiving no subventions from the government. They were, however, allowed to use government-owned religious edifices by previous arrangement. The French state had become almost completely secularized. 

RUSSIA: 1815-1914 

Russia, in 1815, had a population of about 45,000,000. Natural resources were undeveloped, and, despite a multitude of onerous taxes, the annual revenue of the government averaged approximately only $55,000,000. There were poll and land taxes in addition to excises and levies on merchants and industrial gilds, yet recurrent deficits constituted a serious problem. One-third of the expenditures maintained the army, made up of conscripts who served twenty-five years under harsh discipline.

The government was as despotic as it was inefficient; the ukases of the czar were the law. There were, of course, a Council of State and a Senate, but these bodies were purely advisory. Local administration was characterized by venality and inefficiency; many officials received little or no salaries, with the consequent inducement to corruption.

Eighty per cent of the population were serfs, bound to the soil. 

Some were fiscal serfs, attached to the imperial estates; the others were subject to private landowners. Most serfs owed barschina, or labor, three or more days each week; commutation of services to quit-rents, however, was not uncommon. The serf received, in return for his labor, an allotment of approximately four acres which afforded him subsistence. These holdings were cultivated coöperatively by the serfs of each mir, or village. Volost courts, under the control of the landlords, had virtually unlimited jurisdiction over the peasantry. Forced labor also was characteristic in industry; many workshops were operated by the government. 

Alexander I (1801-1825) was at first inspired by liberal ideas instilled, it was thought, by his old Swiss tutor, La Harpe. He gave 

Poland and Finland autonomy, being, himself, king of the former and grand duke of the latter. He considered the problem of the emancipation of the serfs and education of the peasantry. Even as late as 1824 Alexander forbade the sale of lands without the peasant tenants, thus preventing evictions which often accompanied the transfer of lands.

But by 1820 the czar began to appear more reactionary. The murder of his agent, Kotzebue, in Germany, the assassination of the Duke of Berry in France, the Cato Conspiracy to kill the English king, as well as the outbreak of revolution in Spain - all of these radical developments influenced him in 1820 to abandon liberalism and pursue more repressive policies. Freedom of the press and teaching was restricted; the Polish Diet was limited in its activity. In diplomacy Alexander began to support Metternich's system of repression.

The accession of Nicholas I (1825-1855) created a crisis called the Decembrist revolt. His elder brother, Constantine, had been passed over in the succession because he had married a woman beneath royal rank, but some liberal-minded nobles began to conspire for the substitution of a constitutional monarchy under Constantine. 

This whole plot was ruthlessly suppressed. The main cause of failure was the lack of understanding by the Russian people of the principles involved. Some of the revolting troops who shouted, "Long live Constantine and the Constitution!" thought all the time that "Constitution" was the Grand Duke's wife!

This revolt and the dictatorial temperament of Nicholas I made him a devotee of Metternich's reactionary policies. A secret police, with well-nigh unlimited power, was organized to ferret out real

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

or imaginary political plots; thousands of political prisoners were consigned to the wastes of Siberia. Travel was restricted by an elaborate passport system, and a rigid censorship prevented the diffusion of liberal ideas. Universities were subjected to close governmental supervision; students or professors of liberal views were promptly dismissed and in many cases exiled. When Poland rebelled in 1830, its constitution was abrogated and it was annexed as a Russian province.
