The czar desired to isolate Russia completely from foreign influences; he was so successful that the revolutions of 1848 produced scarcely a tremor. Nicholas I died in the midst of the 

Crimean War. 

This war turned out to be a victory for Russia's enemies, and produced an active sentiment for reform among many of the nobles. 

The humiliation of the Russian army was largely attributable to blundering, bickering among high officers, thefts of supplies, and embezzlement from which not even hospital funds were immune. 

Some held that serfdom was the fundamental cause for the defeat; it was the great obstacle in the way of economic development and the attainment of a successful foreign policy. The new czar, Alexander II (1855-1881), was convinced of the necessity for reform. 

Surveillance on universities was relaxed and restriction on travel eased. Judicial reforms of greatest importance were instituted; judicial and administrative functions were differentiated, and trained judges were appointed and given adequate compensation. Trial by jury was established and appellate procedure devised. Petty cases were placed under the jurisdiction of elective magistrates. The country was divided into thirty-four districts and a district assembly, or zemstvo, established in each, made up of proprietor delegates, indirectly elected by peasants and workmen. 

Alexander II's most spectacular reforms were directed at serfdom. 

In 1861 he freed the landed serfs by ukase; two years later he liberated those held for domestic service; and finally in 1866 released the crown serfs from bondage. But this freedom had to be bought in the form of payments for the peasants' land at the rate of six per cent of the assessed valuation for forty-nine years. The mirs were held collectively responsible for the payment of taxes and redemptions. This practice often held the serf to the land, with the result that not as much labor was released for industrial development as liberals had anticipated. The reforms did not allay discontent; Marxist ideas permeated the urban proletariat, but the radicals, realizing the difficulty of converting the stolid peasantry, gradually turned to

more direct methods. The Nihilists were organized to force reforms by systematic terrorization. Alexander II, who had become reactionary after 1863, was one of their first victims; he was blown to pieces by a bomb.

This tragedy of violence helped to swing the political pendulum away from reform. The reign of Alexander III (1881-1894) was marked by reactionary measures reminiscent of the days of Nicholas I. Of far greater importance, however, was the coming of the Industrial Revolution. Railways were constructed, and industrial production was doubled. Governmental patronage for industrial development was largely due to the enlightened views of Count Sergius Witte who, as the czar's chief minister in the last years of the reign, really guided the destinies of the state. Industrialization augmented the urban proletariat, which aided the cause of liberalism. The 

Social Democratic Party was formed, with membership recruited mainly from the industrial workers. 

Under Nicholas II (1894-1917) economic development was accelerated. The czar was weak, irresolute, and unduly amenable to the suggestions of those who had secured his confidence. He was opposed to political reform, and his conservative advisers, led by Plehve, strengthened these ideas. The disasters of the Russo-Japanese 

War, which will be discussed in a later chapter, precipitated a revolution. When a crowd massed before the winter palace at St. Petersburg to present a petition, soldiers fired on the dense throng, killing hundreds. This tragic occurrence of "Red Sunday" (January 22, 1905) set in motion a series of riots, national revolts, and strikes which showed the menacing mood of the opposition. 

The czar allayed the excitement by a series of reforms. Witte was made prime minister and a Duma, or Parliament, was called in August, 1995. In October a series of decrees were issued, providing for the election of members of the Duma by manhood suffrage and the transformation of the old Council of State into an upper house. 

A supplementary edict declared that no laws could be validly issued without the sanction of the Duma. These reforms did not placate radical leaders. Miliukov and others sought the establishment of a constitutional monarchy modeled on that of England, but divisions among the leaders weakened the reform cause. By the spring of 

1906, reaction, led by the nobles and wealthy landowners and aided by the apathy of the peasantry, began to undo the reforms. A series of imperial decrees removed fundamental law from the competence of the Duma and reserved foreign affairs, as well as military and naval

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

matters, to the unlimited control of the czar. Consequently, when the Duma met in May, 1906, its failure was foredoomed and it was almost immediately prorogued. Further redemption payments for the lands of the peasants were cancelled by the czar, however, and attempts to Russianize Finland were virtually abandoned. 

Two sessions of the Duma were held in 1907 at which the electoral laws were revised to assure a conservative majority. The 

Revolution of 1905 failed to achieve major reforms for three main reasons: (1) the army remained loyal to the czar, (2) the reformers were divided and unorganized, (3) the foreign governments, even the French Republic, aided the czar by apprehending escaped reformers and by loans of money. Hope still persisted, however, for the eventual establishment of constitutional monarchy, with an adequate program of social and economic reform. The World War, however, was a strain which the Romanov dynasty could not survive. The Revolution of 1917 inaugurated a new and probably the most significant era in Russian history. 

In Italy, Germany, and the Balkans, liberalism was largely identified with nationalism, and therefore those countries will be discussed from that viewpoint in the next chapter.

CHAPTER 48 

Nationalism in Italy, Germany, and the Balkans

UNIFICATION OF ITALY 

HE failure of the diplomats at Vienna to recognize the growing spirit of nationalism in Italy and Germany was one of their major blunders. The interference of Napoleon in Italian affairs, while not undertaken in behalf of Italian unification, had tended to promote it. By reducing the states of the peninsula to three, under his general supervision, he had effected a degree of political unity; by introducing French administrative reforms, he had improved the lot of the populace. 

This condition did not endure long after the decided reversal in policy of 1815. Italy became, as a consequence, a mere "geographical expression." The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, including 

Naples and the island of Sicily, had been returned to the Bourbons, thus providing a single government for south Italy. The States of the Church, which Napoleon had seized, were returned to the pope after the French emperor's abdication and now stretched completely across central Italy, serving to prevent rather than to aid ultimate unification. The duchies of Parma, Tuscany, and Modena had been placed under Austrian princes so that they, along with the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and the Papal States, were under Austrian domination. To add further to Austrian influence in the peninsula, the rich kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia had been given to Austria, although it retained its own administrative system. 

Piedmont, Savoy, and Genoa in northwest Italy had become parts of Sardinia, which was an independent kingdom but perforce an ally of Austria. During the five years following 1815 the domestic policy of the restored King Victor Emmanuel I was marked by extreme reaction.

The conservative reaction which ensued after the Congress of Vienna was characterized in Italy by ignorance and stupidity. The

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Inquisition was revived in the Papal States. The restoration of the 

Spanish Bourbons in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies fastened governmental corruption and a harsh absolutism on its people. The economic status of the Italian masses was deplorable, while liberty of the press and individual freedom were practically non-existent. 

Worst of all in the eyes of a growing number of Italian nationalists was Austria's reactionary domination in Italy as well as in most of Europe. Under the circumstances there could be but little hope of improvement in the political status of the peninsula. The repressive measures which the powers took for the preservation of the status quo have been described in another connection.¹ In Italy, as in 

Germany, secret societies disseminated nationalistic idealism and revolutionary doctrines. The Carbonari (Charcoal Burners) was the best known of the early organizations. The secret order spread rapidly from Naples and aimed to eliminate the influence of Austria. The furtive nature of this society makes it rather difficult to assign it a definite place in the revolutionary movements of the 1820's and '30's. Perhaps its chief function was to create and to preserve an undercover spirit of Italian nationalism. 

Napoleon's work was an incentive to Italian patriots. They could hardly forget that he had removed every Italian ruler from power, and it was natural for them to believe that such things could be accomplished, anew. The lid was off with news of the successful 

Spanish revolt in 1820. Ferdinand I, King of the Two Sicilies, had been unreasonably severe in his treatment of the soldiers who had served under his predecessor, Murat, and had, as a consequence, made so many enemies that the troops rebelled. The revolt assumed such proportions that the king was forced to accede to their demand for the adoption of the Spanish Constitution of 1812. 

While the Spanish revolt had troubled Metternich, the proximity of the Neapolitan rebellion to the Austrian domain caused him to convoke the powers of the Quintuple Alliance at Troppau with a view to intervention. He reasoned that unless the revolt was checked, it would assume epidemic proportions. Of the five powers, only Russia, Austria, and Prussia agreed to the principle of intervention as interpreted by Metternich. England held that the Alliance had no business meddling with the particular form of government a people might choose. England's attitude was based on her interpretation of the purposes for which the Quintuple Alliance had been formed. Those purposes she held to be the preservation 

1 See supra, pp. 593–594.

of the boundaries of 1815, and not any particular form of government. When, at the second congress, held at Laibach, Ferdinand I declared he had made liberal concessions because of a display of military force, Austria was commissioned to restore him to absolute power. The result of Austria's invasion of Naples was a foregone conclusion. The ill-prepared Neapolitan patriots were quickly routed and absolutism was restored (1821). A second storm of unreasoned reaction fell on the unfortunate people.

As Metternich had foreseen, the revolutionary spirit was contagious. Naples had hardly been suppressed when dissatisfied Piedmontese broke out in rebellion against the reactionary policies of King Victor Emmanuel I. The revolt was motivated by both hatred of Austria and a desire for constitutional government. To insist on the adoption of the Spanish Constitution of 1812 was tantamount to a demand for war with Austria. The dilemma of the 

Sardinian king was serious. He might refuse these demands and provoke a civil war, or he might accede and face armed intervention as had been the experience of Naples. He chose to avoid the issue by abdicating in March, 1821. Charles Albert, as temporary regent, accepted the Spanish Constitution of 1812, but an already mobilized Austrian army made quick work of the unorganized 

Sardinian forces. The Austrians then placed Victor Emmanuel's brother, Charles Felix, on the throne of Sardinia with absolute power.

The ten years of Austrian domination which followed the suppression of the revolts in Naples, Piedmont, and Spain were sorry years for the peoples concerned. Insurrectionary activity of societies like the Carbonari increased apace. In 1831, Napoleon's empress, Marie Louise, who had become the Duchess of Parma in 1815, was forced to leave her state as was the Prince of Modena. 

The incompetent ecclesiastical government of the Papal States led to further revolt during which almost every major urban center except Rome declared itself independent of the pope's temporal authority. Austrian troops restored the rulers of Parma and Modena and returned the rebellious cities to the Papal States. A second insurrection broke out in the following year in the pope's domain, but now Louis Philippe of France, as well as the Austrians, sent troops. These forces remained in Italy until 1838, jockeying for a 

European balance of power. Both the revolutionary attempts of 

1820-1821 and 1831-1832 had been suppressed with Austrian arms. 

An important tendency of the movement must be noted. The first

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

revolutions had been the work of anarchists, dissatisfied military men, and others who were in a distinct minority. The second series of revolts had the support of many in the middle and lower classes who had been educated to the movement through the secret activities of organizations like the Carbonari. 

The Italian revolutionary movements had failed because they were too local in nature. The nationalistic spirit had not become widespread because the loosely knit Carbonari were unable to attain the unity within their own organization that they desired for Italy. During the decade and a half which followed the last abortive attempt in the Papal States, a number of Italian leaders began an educational campaign which emphasized the teaching of common Italian ideals and aspirations. Most influential in this group of patriots was Joseph Mazzini. Son of a Genoese physician and professor, he early attained maturity of intellect. His impressionable mind understood the sorrowful plight of a once great people, and he abandoned a promising literary career for the role of a nationalistic propagandist. Possessed of the soul of a visionary, untiring zeal, and an effective literary style, he became the prophet of Italian unity. He was arrested in 1830, under suspicion of connections with the Carbonari, and sentenced to a half-year of imprisonment. After his release he went into exile which lasted for most of his life.

In 1831 Mazzini organized the secret order known as “Young Italy." It was planned as a secret revolutionary society of Italians under forty years of age which would not only lead the revolution but lay the foundations of a United Republic of Italy. While 

Mazzini possessed genius for leadership in a great faith, he was singularly lacking in the practical requisites of a revolutionist aiming at the military humiliation of Austria. Other radicals held that his belief in the ultimate unification of Italy was fallacious. They insisted that what Italy really desired was independence, not necessarily a united Italy. They believed that this could be more effectively obtained through a federation of the Italian states for defensive and offensive purposes. Still others proposed a federation under the leadership of the papacy. The development of a sentiment of unity, or federation, could have but a single consequence -the continued growth of the nationalistic spirit. Certainly the idealistic, though revolutionary, aims of "Young Italy" could gain greater support than those of the scattered Carbonari. 

The day for which so many had hoped came in 1848. The

February Revolution in France, which resulted in the deposition of Louis Philippe, has been dealt with elsewhere. The year of revolutions would undoubtedly have come anyway, but France again was to fan the flames of a general European conflagration. The aged Metternich followed the march of events with foreboding, but found himself no longer able to thwart the forces of liberalism. 

In March the Hungarian patriot, Louis Kossuth, demanded that Austria grant Hungary governmental institutions of her own. When, a few days later, the Austrian troops refused to suppress riots in Vienna on orders from Metternich, he realized that he had come to the end of the road. The aged prince resigned and fled in disguise. During the weeks that followed, Hungary obtained autonomy under a liberal government and the success of the Magyar movement seemed assured. Hungarians gained a free press, control of their own military forces, equalization of taxes, the abolition of titles, and an expanded electorate. But Magyar refusal to grant minority rights to the Slavs brought Czech and Croatian support to conservatives in Austria and complicated the situation. Ferdinand I of 

Austria was persuaded to abdicate in favor of his eighteen-year-old nephew, Francis Joseph (who ruled until 1916), in order that the liberal concessions and promises he had made to Hungary might be legally repealed. Then, having prevailed over its own liberals, the 

Austrian government, with the aid of Czechs and Croats, moved against the Hungarian liberals. Although Kossuth proclaimed Hungarian independence, his country was defeated by the combined reactionary forces of Austria and Russia, and Hungary was relegated to the status of an Austrian province. 

When the conservative ministry in Austria fell, liberals in Germany arranged for the meeting of a German national assembly with a view to drawing up a tentative constitution for a united nation. 

The problems which the delegates to this assembly faced will be treated in another connection but it deserves mention at this point because it indicates the widespread character of the nationalistic fervor of the peoples of Europe. Let it suffice for the moment to say that the efforts of the Frankfort Parliament met with failure and the 

Germanies returned to the old and reactionary forms of government.

The rebirth of strong reactionary forces in Austria following the Hungarian revolt has been noted. Revived Austrian armies successfully crushed the unsupported Piedmontese under Charles Albert 

2 See supra, pp. 616–617.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

(1831-1849) at Custozza in late July, 1848, but harsh treatment of the vanquished Italians served to steel Charles Albert for the War of Italian Liberation. He renewed the conflict in the following year, but again failed to receive the aid of central and south Italy. Mean- · while Rome was declared a republic, with Mazzini in a leading position, and the pope was forced into Neapolitan exile. When Charles 

Albert was defeated at Novara in March, 1849, he abdicated his Sardinian throne in favor of his son Victor Emmanuel II. In the same year the Roman Republic was destroyed by a French invasion which restored Pope Pius IX to his former states. By this time the Kingdom of Sardinia, by its leadership and independent status, was becoming the nucleus for the unification of the Italian states and their ultimate liberation from the Austrian yoke - but next time a liberation with outside help rather than by the efforts of Italians alone. 

Victor Emmanuel was a competent, if not a brilliant, ruler. He was sincere, conscientious, and honest. Less than two years after his coronation he was to have as his minister one of the ablest political minds in all Europe. Count Cavour was born of noble Piedmontese stock in 1810. He was trained as an army engineer but left the service when twenty-one years of age to spend some fifteen years in the study and practice of scientific agriculture. He sponsored improved farming methods, more general use of farm machinery, and better transportation methods. He found time for travel and study of governmental problems, especially the system of England. His practical mind was an absolute opposite of that possessed by Mazzini, though both had the same end in view. Cavour envisioned an Italian nation morally united around Sardinia. When, in 1847, freedom of the press was permitted in Sardinia, he left his quiet pursuits for the role of an editor. As the outstanding proponent of the parliamentary system, he became a member of the new Sardinian parliament in 1848. He entered the cabinet two years later and became prime minister in 1852.

The successful termination of Cavour's plans for the creation of a powerful and united Italy warrants detailed observation of the actual methods employed. To take advantage of the natural supremacy which the House of Savoy had won for Sardinia in the leadership of Italy, he aimed at raising the kingdom to the economic status of a modern state. To enhance the prosperity of the little state, he increased expenditures on public works to unheard-of sums, thus expanding commerce, trade, and industry. In spite of the huge governmental debts and obligations incurred, the status of the people

was improved so materially and so rapidly that the kingdom itself achieved a degree of affluence hitherto unknown. His next steps were to increase and modernize the army, to build up a fleet, and to construct and improve the kingdom's fortifications. The support of an army of almost 100,000 men, a huge number in relation to the total population, did not become an intolerable burden because of the improved economic status of the people. Cavour's primary purpose was, of course, to rid Italy of Austrian influence; but in spite of the sound economic condition of the country, in spite of the strong and well-equipped army, Sardinia was no match for the Austrians. Full realization of this fact caused Cavour to seek aid of a strong ally. Thus it was that the Kingdom of Sardinia furnished forces to France and England in the Crimean War against Russia. 

This was an unpopular measure within the little kingdom, for it had no connection with the causes leading to the outbreak of the conflict. Cavour, however, was looking ahead in the hope that eventually an alliance would result which would give his nation the necessary strength to challenge the Austrian Empire.

A peace conference was held in Paris following the Crimean War, and Cavour gained admittance by virtue of Sardinia's contribution. 

Before these European diplomats he condemned Austrian domination of Italian affairs and heard others castigate the rulers of the Papal States and Naples. Cavour's material gains at Paris were few, but his moral victory was great and served to enhance the prestige of his kingdom. In playing for the support of some major European power against Austria, Cavour found that Napoleon III was already interested. He had taken part in Italian revolutions, he had developed the belief that a single nationality should of right be under a single government, and he was desirous of abrogating the treaties of 1815 which marked the final degradation of the first Napoleon. 

Such sentiments on the part of the French Emperor made it natural that a meeting should take place between the two interested individuals. This occurred secretly during July, 1858, at Plombières, a watering place in the Vosges mountains. There, Napoleon III verbally agreed that if Austria could be made to appear as the aggressor in any war with Sardinia, France would come to the aid of the smaller nation. No peace was to be made until Austria had been driven out of Italy. In return for this service, France was to gain 

Savoy and Nice. Cavour did his utmost to embroil Austria in war during the months which followed this secret meeting of the two highly placed conspirators. He was rewarded for his efforts even-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tually, and Austria, goaded into a declaration of war against Sardinia, found herself confronted by France as well. Austria appeared the aggressor to all Europe at the outbreak of hostilities in April, 1859. The Austrian high command erred when it failed to crush the 

Sardinians in the early weeks of the war. With the arrival of the 

French troops in June, two major battles, those of Magenta and

Solferino, were won by the French-Sardinian allies in Lombardy and it appeared that Austria would soon be forced out of Italy. At the same time the subjects of the pope with outside encouragement began to overthrow his rule, and Prussian mobilization on the Rhine was threatening France from the northeast. Principally because of these developments Napoleon halted his victorious armies and arranged the Armistice of Villafranca (July 11, 1859) without consulting the Sardinians. The cessation of hostilities came as a heartbreaking shock to the hopeful Italian patriots. Cavour resigned his office in despair, but Victor Emmanuel II saw that all was not lost and reluctantly accepted the situation. The preliminary arrangements of the Armistice were incorporated in the Peace of Zurich, November, 1859. By its terms, Sardinia gained Lombardy. France made no claims to Nice or Savoy. The other terms of the treaty were never adhered to and need no repetition at this point. 

During the course of the Austro-Sardinian War, Parma, Modena, and Tuscany, in addition to the northern portion of the Papal States, overthrew their rulers and in revolutionary assemblies voted in favor of annexation to Sardinia. England favored the scheme, and Napoleon was ready to accede in return for Savoy and Nice. Plebiscites were held in each of the states concerned during 1860 and resulted in the addition of Tuscany, Parma, Modena, and the Romagna to the Kingdom of Sardinia, and of Savoy and Nice to France. The arrangements thus consummated completely disrupted the treaties of 1815 which for so long had made Italy a "geographical expression." Sardinia now controlled all north Italy except Venetia, and to the south only Naples and the Papal States remained without the fold. 

Rebellion broke out in Sicily during the early months of 1860. The arbitrary and despotic character of the new Bourbon king, Francis II, provided the excuse for revolt. The movement afforded opportunity to one of the most romantic characters in Italian history to perform notable service in the cause of Italian unification. Joseph 

Garibaldi was born three years earlier than Cavour in the region lost to France during 1860. He spent his early life on the sea, as an ad-

herent to the cause of “Young Italy," and as a guerrilla chieftain. 

His part in the abortive Savoy insurrection of 1834 forced him into South American exile. There he added to his romantic reputation by service in the "Italian Legion.” He returned to Italy to lead volunteers against the Austrians in 1848 and appeared in Rome as defender of the Republic in 1849. Again he was harried from his native Italy. 

He returned eventually to the island of Caprera in 1854. The Austrian war in 1859 brought him out of retirement again to lead volunteers in the Italian cause. When he received news of the Sicilian revolt, he determined to lend his aid. His reputation as a leader ensured him sufficient support to carry out his plans. Cavour found that Garibaldi's determination was embarrassing to Sardinia. With characteristic diplomatic tact, Cavour secretly abetted the scheme while maintaining official aloofness. With a force numbering a little over 

1,100 (the "Red Shirts" or "The Thousand "), Garibaldi gained control of Sicily from an opposing army numbering over 20,000 men. He proclaimed himself dictator of the island under Victor 

Emmanuel II, during August, 1860.

This accomplished, Garibaldi moved across to the mainland. He faced a Bourbon force numbering close to 100,000, but the Kingdom of Naples collapsed with very little resistance and a minimum of bloodshed. The amazing rapidity and the phenomenal success of 

Garibaldi's conquest seem without parallel in recent times. He next proposed a march on Rome. Since the pope was under the protection of a French garrison, Cavour realized that this would bring the intervention of France in the rest of Italy unless properly controlled. 

Cavour therefore came to an understanding with Napoleon III under which the Sardinian troops defeated the papal forces but permitted the pope to retain Rome. Victor Emmanuel then marched his forces south into Naples, defeated the remaining Neapolitan forces, and accepted the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies from Garibaldi in Naples. 

In plebiscites held in Sicily, Naples, and the Papal States, except Rome, the vote was overwhelmingly in favor of annexation to Piedmont-Sardinia. Thus was all Italy, except Rome and Venetia, brought under a single king by 1860. Garibaldi declined all honors and returned to his island farm with but limited funds and a supply of seed-corn. The Kingdom of Sardinia was proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy on March 17, 1861. The names of Charles Albert, Mazzini, Cavour, Victor Emmanuel II, and Garibaldi must remain inseparably connected with this great achievement. 

Italy allied herself with Prussia during the Seven Weeks' War

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

(1866) against Austria. The Italian troops were defeated at Custozza, but their participation served to detain a sufficient number of Austrian troops in the south to guarantee Prussian success in the northern theater of the war. Italy's compensation was Venetia, which she received from France as intermediary for Austria. Italy had attained geographic unity with the single exception of Rome. 46

8. MEDITERRANEAN SEA 

Tunis 10 38Cavour had become interested in 1861 in obtaining Rome as the capital of the kingdom. At his instance the Italian parliament passed a declaration to the effect that Rome must eventually become the center of Italian government. At the moment any attempt to depose the pope from his temporal throne would inevitably have precipitated a war with France. There was enough work to do by way of organization and consolidation without taxing the newly formed kingdom with such a test of strength. The Italian policy was therefore

one of watchful waiting. In 1864 Italy obtained the French withdrawal from Rome in return for a promise to respect the pope's possession of the city. But when Garibaldi tried to capture Rome in 

1867 the French returned. Finally an opportunity occurred during the Franco-Prussian War (1870) when French military necessity forced the withdrawal of the garrison from Rome. This made it possible for Victor Emmanuel to march into Rome with but slight resistance from the papal forces. Thus was Italian unity achieved; 

Rome was again the Italian capital. The next year the Italian parliament passed a Law of Papal Guarantees which granted the pope political independence, full possession of the Vatican and two other designated places, a large inalienable income, and non-interference by the government in church affairs. The pope, however, rejected this settlement because it was imposed and not negotiated, and thereafter assumed the role of a prisoner in the Vatican. 

In still another way the pope endeavored to discourage coöperation with the new Italian nation. In 1868 he issued the decree Non expedit which forbade Catholics to vote or be candidates in Italian parliamentary elections. This measure resulted in the abstention from voting of about thirty-eight per cent of the voters who were in general among the more capable and reliable citizens. Italian suffrage was further limited by property and age restrictions. Only men over twenty-five years of age paying at least forty lire in taxes could vote. By these restrictions only 500,000 out of 28,000,000 were eligible. 

The political history of Italy to 1914, however, had as one of its major issues the extension of the suffrage. In 1882, during the ministry of the Left, the voting age was lowered to twenty-one and the property qualification to nineteen lire, provided the citizen was literate. Enough of the lower classes could now vote to give impetus to radical democratic and socialist movements. This situation in turn alarmed the pope to the extent that he, by the encyclical Il fermo proposito (1905), finally allowed Catholics, with the local bishop's permission, to vote when it involved the duty of defeating “subversive" candidates. Finally Giolitti in 1912 extended the suffrage to all literate males over twenty-one and even to the illiterates over thirty, thus increasing the number of qualified voters from 3,000,000 to 8,000,000 out of a total population of 40,000,000.³ 

3 For discussions of Italy's colonial and foreign affairs see pp. 694, 696, 698, 701, 702, 705.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION THE UNIFICATION OF GERMANY 

German solidarity was undoubtedly promoted by the Reformation, but the movement lost virility because of the jealousies of the duchies, principalities, and kingdoms. The most important trend towards German unity, prior to the outbreak of the French Revolutionary Wars, was the emergence of Prussia as a great power; the opportunity for leadership was to come to her time and again. The multitude of lesser German states, under nominal Austrian domination, precluded unification until Napoleon destroyed the Holy Roman Empire (1806) and partially consolidated some hundreds of south German states into the Confederation of the Rhine composed of about forty states, with Austria excluded. The Congress of 

Vienna, had it adhered strictly to the "legitimacy" rule, would have re-created these several hundred German states that had been eliminated in the consolidation process initiated by Bonaparte. Instead, the Congress retained a degree of the unification already effected. At Metternich's instance it organized the German Confederation, which varied in membership from thirty-three to thirty-nine states.

The constitution of this loose Confederation provided a diet under the permanent presidency of Austria. Representatives of the rulers in each of the thirty-odd states acted as ambassadors in this diet. 

These representatives could act only on instruction. The procedure of the diet was most complicated. It could meet in either ordinary or plenum sessions. In the first, measures were prepared and proposed by a majority vote of the large states and designated groups of the small states; in the second, the final passage was determined by a two-thirds vote of all of the states voting separately. Constitutional amendments required a unanimous vote. The larger states therefore had more votes in the diet than the smaller ones, but the distribution of voting strength was notably inequitable in relation to the population. It was possible for the less populated states decisively to outvote the populous ones. The ineptitude of the Confederation seems best illustrated by the fact that no constitutional provision was made for federal tax levies, for the maintenance of an army, or for a federal flag. The establishment of this weak machinery of federal government immeasurably retarded the German unification movement. 

The ineffective German Confederation was counterbalanced in part, however, by Prussia's establishment, in 1834, of a customs union (Zollverein) including most of the German states north of Austria.

Austrian domination in the diet and Metternich's intervention in purely German affairs served to fasten a policy of reaction on the Germanies for nearly half a century. A case in point was Metternich's insistence, following the Wartburg Festival (1817) and the assassination of the publicist Kotzebue (1819), on repressive measures which culminated in the famous Carlsbad Decrees of 1819. 

These decrees stifled academic freedom, student liberal activities, and freedom of the press, in the interest of absolutism. The Congress of Vienna had promised constitutions to the various states in the new German Confederation, and Frederick William III had promised Prussia a constitution during the "Hundred Days," but these promises were repudiated. Agitation was continued by secret societies like the Burschenschaften and athletic organizations like the Turnvereine. The French Revolution of 1830 gave Germans an opportunity to demand concessions from reactionary princes in 

Hesse, Brunswick, Saxony, Bavaria, and Hanover. Metternich reduced the value of these constitutional reforms by forcing through the diet an edict which declared void all extorted reforms. Such policies aroused German radicals and liberals as never before, but the feeling was confined within student ranks for the most part. The formation of the Zollverein served to enhance prosperity and to bind the smaller German states to Prussia.

The death of Frederick William III (1840) revived the constitution question. Many believed that Prussian leadership in Germany would be advanced by the adoption of a liberal constitution. Although the new king, Frederick William IV, brought back many exiled liberals, discontent with his general policies increased apace. 

In 1847, he called a general diet, not to draw up a constitution, but to secure funds for railroad construction. The dismissal of this diet brought the issue between king and people to a head. In the following year France established a republic, and the smaller German states revolted and obtained constitutions without much disturbance. Rioting which broke out in Berlin was promptly suppressed on orders from Frederick William IV. In retribution, a mob forced the king to bow before the corpses of those slain by his soldiers.

Meanwhile, machinery was established for calling a national parliament to prepare a constitution for all Germany. This Frankfort 

Parliament opened in May, 1848, and deliberated for more than a year. Weeks and months were wasted in argument over fundamental principles. The question of whether the whole Austrian Empire or just its German portions should be included under the new con-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

stitution was one of the most serious problems before the parliament. When Austria refused to enter the union without her non- 

German provinces, the parliament offered the constitution and the throne to Frederick William IV. The Prussian ruler spurned the proposal; the conservative element in the Frankfort Parliament accordingly withdrew. Control of the assemblage fell into the hands of the radicals, who were forcibly dispersed in 1849. No immediate benefits resulted, but the ultimate unification of the Germanies had been advanced nonetheless.

Although the Frankfort Parliament had failed to provide all Germany with a constitution, Frederick William granted one to Prussia in 1850. However, parliamentary and ministerial responsibility under it were abolished by interpretation, and aristocratic predominance was fostered by a three-class system of suffrage and representation. 

While political conditions continued deplorable, economic conditions materially improved during the period from 1850 to 1860. This was due to rapid modernization of industry and agriculture, the establishment of better banking facilities, and widespread commercial developments. Especially important was the development of the vast mineral deposits in Germany. Industry absorbed thousands of agricultural laborers. In the urban centers, speculation became the order of the day. Modern business methods, which took full advantage of scientific contributions and improved means of communication, were rapidly adopted.

Frederick William IV became mentally incapacitated and was succeeded by his brother, William I, who served first as regent, and in 1861, became king in his own right. Whereas his predecessor was most erratic, William I seems best characterized as "levelheaded."

He had seen service against Napoleon and had spent his entire career in the army. As a consequence he had a thorough knowledge of military affairs. To his practical mind, the army was essential if Prussia was to unite the Germanies. It will be recalled that universal compulsory military training became the Prussian practice as early as 1814. Although the population of Prussia had increased by fifty per cent in the interval between that date and 1859, the army remained at the old limits established in 1814. William I determined that the law must be enforced, the army increased, and the whole military establishment renovated. Provisional appropriations were granted by the Prussian Parliament for the additional regiments, but in 1862 the Chamber of Deputies absolutely refused to vote further sums to continue the king's army reforms. The constitutional question

(under the Constitution of 1850), of whether the king as commander-in-chief of the army could get funds for its operation, or whether the parliament had full control over the purse strings, thus came to a deadlock. William declined to abolish the parliament since he had sworn to support the Constitution of 1850. On the other hand he refused to give up his army reforms, and consequently decided that there was nothing left for him but abdication. 

In one last effort, he called to head the ministry an audacious monarchist, Otto von Bismarck (September, 1862). Born in 1815,

Bismarck was of the Brandenburg nobility. He had received a university training, had served in the Prussian civil service, and had acted the role of a country gentleman on the family estates. He entered politics in 1847 and opposed the adoption of a constitution. 

When it was granted, however, he supported it. He was an outspoken monarchist who insisted that Prussia was great because of her kings, not her people. He was appointed as Prussia's delegate to the reassembled Confederation diet in 1851, where he became adept in diplomacy and acquainted with representatives from all over Germany. In 1859 he was sent to Saint Petersburg. By this time he had developed into a Prussian egoist who looked on Austria as an enemy to Prussian advancement.

In the four years following 1862, conflict over the army bills continued. Finally the opposition of the lower house was disregarded by the administration, the taxes were collected, and the army reforms completed. The modernization of the army was but a first step in the plan Bismarck had evolved for the creation of a united Germany. 

He desired no unity like that achieved through Cavour's planning in Italy. There was to be no German absorption of Prussia, but Prussian absorption of the Germanies for her own advantage. The liberal plan for a modern Prussian constitution, about which the rest of the Germanies would rally, was rudely thrust aside when, in 1863, Bismarck announced his famous "blood and iron" policy. 

In conformity with the policies of the "Iron Chancellor," Prussia waged three wars between 1864 and 1870; the major result was national unity by the creation of the German Empire. The first war grew out of the complicated Schleswig-Holstein question. The king of Denmark had become the duke of these two states, and the Danes desired to annex them although the population was predominantly German. The problem was intensified when Denmark, in her new constitution (1863), incorporated into the kingdom the more Danish of the two duchies, Schleswig. The German diet proposed the dis-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

patch of an army to prevent this action, but Prussia and Austria took matters out of the hands of the Confederation and attacked Denmark. In a few weeks little Denmark was overrun and forced to sue for peace. In the Treaty of Vienna (October, 1864) Denmark ceded the duchies to Austria and Prussia. The question of their disposition provided Bismarck with the basis for a quarrel with Austria. Austria was not prepared to go to war over the question, and William I could see no good reason for fratricidal conflict, so the matter was temporarily compromised in the Convention of Gastein (August, 1865). Austria and Prussia were to own the duchies jointly, but 

Austria was to rule Holstein while Prussia assumed control of Schleswig.

The Convention of Gastein served as a one-year stopgap. During that period, Bismarck conferred with Napoleon III at Biarritz in an effort to obtain French neutrality in the event of a Prussian war with Austria. He next completed a secret alliance with Italy (April, 1866) which to become effective required the commencement of hostilities within ninety days. The steps by which Prussia and Austria were brought into this conflict were as numerous as they were devious and require no elucidation here. Bismarck entered the war, nominally for the reform of the German Confederation, actually to displace 

Austrian leadership and secure territorial gains. The conflict, known as the "Seven Weeks' War," began on June 16 and was officially over by July 26, 1866. The modernized Prussian army was prepared and led by the brilliant General von Moltke. Within two weeks, north Germany was under Prussian control. Von Moltke then dispatched three armies into Bohemia, where at Sadowa (July 3, 1866), the greatest battle since Leipzig was won by the Prussians. The south German states were also defeated in rapid order. When Bismarck feared that Napoleon might intervene, he granted Austria liberal terms in the Preliminary Peace of Nikolsburg. The definitive peace was signed at Prague (August 23, 1866). Under the terms of these treaties, Venetia went to Italy, Austria withdrew from the 

German Confederation and agreed that Prussia might form a new one, north of the river Main. Without resort to plebiscites Hanover,

Nassau, Hesse-Cassel, Frankfort, and Schleswig-Holstein were annexed to Prussia. This was done by right of conquest, not by the expressed consent of the people governed. The rest of the German states north of the Main were brought together in a North German Confederation with a constitution providing for universal manhood suffrage and the presidency of the king of Prussia. This constitution,

drawn up by Bismarck, was later to serve as the basis for that adopted by the German Empire. 

France had been caught napping while Bismarck accomplished this rapid realignment of the European balance of power. Napoleon III had misjudged the situation when he predicted that the war would be a long one and to the advantage of France. The brevity of the conflict, as well as the decisive nature of the victory of Sadowa, caused it to be considered as much a French as an Austrian defeat. At the same time Napoleon's Mexican venture was fast drawing to an inglorious end. When he opposed Prussian control of territory south of the Main, he gave Prussia excuse for a third war, one which Bismarck faced with equanimity. At this juncture Spain invited a Hohenzollern to accept her vacant throne. The youthful 

Leopold twice declined at the request of William I. Bismarck, however, prevailed on the king to permit Leopold's acceptance, since France would thus be hemmed in on two sides, or provoked into war with Prussia. The prince accepted the third invitation, but when the indignant French protested, he retracted, much to the relief of 

William I.

The elation of France at this diplomatic success knew no bounds; she now demanded that the Prussian king promise that he would never again permit a Hohenzollern candidacy for the Spanish throne. 

The king politely declined, since the matter had already been settled, and wired the substance of the French request from Ems (a watering place) to Bismarck. By condensing this Ems dispatch, Bismarck made it appear that the Prussian king had sharply rebuffed the French ambassador. He then turned the telegram over to the press and sent copies of it to the capitals of the European powers. On its publication in Paris, jingoists demanded immediate war. The government hesitated for several days, since public opinion throughout France was by no means crystallized. Finally, on July 19, 1870, war was declared.

France was totally unprepared. Her army was not in the same class with the Prussian military machine in equipment, numbers, or leadership. France had no alliances, even with friendly Austria, and she could expect no aid from either Italy or England. Russia and 

Prussia had come to terms. The first stage in the progress of the war resulted in the encirclement of one French army at Metz. A second one was defeated by the Prussians at Sedan, and Napoleon III was taken prisoner (September 1-2, 1870). On September 4,

Ferry, Favre, and Gambetta proclaimed a republic for France and

established a National Defense Government for the conduct of the war. Gambetta organized the nation for an heroic defense of the soil of France, but there could be little hope of success. With one 

French army bottled up at Metz and the other crushed at Sedan, the Prussians moved towards Paris, which surrendered after a siege of four months.

Bismarck's labors to unite the Germanies were consummated at the Palace of Versailles, when on January 18, 1871, William I was crowned emperor of Germany. Under the definitive Treaty of 

Frankfort (May, 1871), France ceded practically all of Alsace and Lorraine to Germany, and agreed to pay a billion dollar indemnity within five years. An army of occupation was to remain in France until the indemnity was paid. The results of the Franco-Prussian 

War were important to the future peace of Europe. The outstanding result was the unification of the Germanies, which meant Prussianization as well. The harsh terms which Bismarck forced on 

France left an open wound, which was one day to provoke terrible retaliation. The second Napoleonic Empire was displaced by the 

Third Republic. Alsace and Lorraine, though German in their origins, had become French through the passage of time. Therefore their annexation by Germany was to serve as the basis of an international problem about which events were to turn in 1914. 

The German Empire was erected on the constitutional pattern outlined by Bismarck for the North German Confederation. This revised document, adopted shortly after the close of the war, became effective in April, 1871. It provided for a confederation composed of some twenty-five states and one territory. A bicameral parliament was composed of a powerful Bundesrat, or upper house, made up of sixty-one representatives of the rulers of the various states, and the Reichstag, composed of nearly four hundred elected representatives. Ministerial responsibility was to the emperor, not to Parliament. The emperor's chief official was the chancellor. 

Throughout this imperial government Prussia was dominant: the emperor was the king of Prussia; the chancellor was usually the Prussian prime minister; the Prussian military system was adopted; twenty votes in the Bundesrat and 236 in the Reichstag were controlled by Prussia. This constitution, under three successive emperors, lasted until the close of the World War. No sooner had national unity been achieved than all Germany was divided by a religious controversy called the Kulturkampf. Bismarck 

4 William I, 1871-1888; Frederick III, 1888; William II, 1888-1918.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and those Germans now fired with a more fervent patriotism thought they saw in the Roman Catholics of the Empire an element of division. The Catholics were stronger in non-Prussian territory like 

Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden, Hanover, Alsace-Lorraine, and the

Polish-inhabited regions. Being hostile to Prussian dominance, they favored states' rights and therefore a weaker union. There were also religious issues. The pope had just recently denounced liberalism, modernism, and secularism in contemporary thought. To give emphasis to this a church council had also proclaimed the infallibility of the pope in all pronouncements on faith and morals. 66 These attitudes incensed the nationalists, liberals, and intellectuals in Germany who in 1872 proceeded to engage in a program of opposition denominated a struggle for civilization" (Kulturkampf). 

The Jesuits were expelled from the Empire, and the Falk (or May) Laws were passed by Prussia. These laws required German education and nationality for the priesthood, government inspection of religious seminaries, and government approval of church appointments. Violations of this legislation might lead to suspension from office, fine, imprisonment, or expulsion from the kingdom. 

Such legislation and penalties only invited resistance and martyrdom. The pope denounced Bismarck's repressive policy, and many 

Prussian bishops, declaring the legislation void, refused to obey the state. For this they were imprisoned, government subsidies were withheld from their dioceses, and Catholic worship had to be discontinued in about thirteen hundred parishes. On the political side resistance to the Kulturkampf took the form of a great increase of support to the Catholic Centrist Party, which polled 1,443,000 votes in 1874 and elected twenty-eight more representatives in the Reichstag, bringing their number up to ninety-one. 

This growing opposition together with the menacing increase in socialist strength (with which the Catholic Centrists now coöperated) led Bismarck to begin a policy of reconciliation with the new pope, Leo XIII, in 1878. By 1886 the Kulturkampf had come to an end, and Bismarck had gained the support of the Catholics in his campaigns to suppress socialism and pass protective tariffs.

Bismarck's attack on socialism was two-fold, a suppression of socialist activity on the one hand and the amelioration of working conditions by a form of state socialism on the other. The Marxian ideal was widely disseminated in Germany, but, paradoxically enough, socialism of a nationalistic nature was to have much greater import in Germany than Marxian internationalism. This was ac-

complished chiefly by the efforts of a brilliant and self-centered socialist named Ferdinand Lassalle. Lassalle, although rich and selfindulgent, became an early advocate for the laboring masses. Of his many ideas and schemes, the one most important to us at this point was his belief that only through the acquisition of political power by the proletariat could a social revolution be accomplished. He organized, therefore, a German laborers' party in 1863, but lost his life in a foolish duel the following year. In south Germany, at about this time, a Marxian disciple named William Liebknecht organized a group of Internationalists, which under the more popular leadership of August Bebel, became a second powerful labor party in 1869. By 

1875, the two groups had fused together as the Socialistic Working Men's Party of Germany. The increasing importance of this party was extremely distasteful to the aging king; to Bismarck, their rising importance called for action. The opportunity occurred when, in 

1878, two attempts were made on the life of William I by alleged socialists. Bismarck obtained the passage of a "gag " law forbidding the formation of organized groups, the holding of meetings, or the dissemination of propaganda which might be subversive to the interests of the state. The law was strictly enforced, and socialists were denied the protection of the courts. It is hardly necessary to say that such repressive measures failed to attain their full purpose. 

Bismarck went further; he determined to eliminate the basis of the socialistic organization by improving the conditions of the working classes. Social reform became for him a means of creating state patriotism and support for the monarchy which granted such benefits. His proposals were too liberal for immediate acceptance. 

Between 1883 and 1889, however, sickness, accident, and old age insurance acts were passed. Thus we find that the conservative Bismarck also fought socialism with social reform.5 

NATIONALISM IN THE BALKANS 

Just as Europe tended to represent all Western civilization in miniature, so the Balkans to some degree represented Europe on a still smaller scale. In the first place there were several racial groups in the Balkan peninsula which tended to separate into nationalities: 

Serbs, Rumanians, Bulgarians, Greeks, and Turks. In fact, however, all of the first four races were largely Slavic in origin. Then these peoples were divided in religion: there were Orthodox Catholics, Mohammedans, Roman Catholics, Armenian Christians, and Jews. 

5 For Germany's colonial and foreign affairs see pp. 694, 696–704.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

There was also an economic cleavage: Greeks, Armenians, and Jews were merchants; Turks were landowners and rulers; Bulgarians and 

Rumanians were peasant farmers; Serbs were swineherders. 

Out of these diversities there developed, as in Europe proper, several separate movements for national independence which were accompanied by deep-rooted antagonisms and bitter struggles. At the beginning of the nineteenth century the whole region belonged to the Ottoman Turks. But between 1821 and 1829 the Greeks, on the southern end, obtained their independence of Turkey. The Kingdom of Greece was formed in 1833 with a Bavarian dynasty until 

1862, and thereafter with a Danish ruling house.

The Serbs, in the northwest corner of the Balkan peninsula, were also restive under the Turkish yoke. The Montenegrin Serbs in the mountains never did completely submit to the authority of the Sultan and obtained a grudging recognition of their independence in 1799. The Serbs in the valleys farther east also tried rebellion, first unsuccessfully in 1804, but later between 1815 and 1830, under Milosh Obrenovich, they succeeded in wringing the right of selfgovernment from Turkey.

To the northeast beyond the Danube the Rumanians, partly Slavic in race and Latin in linguistic origin, inhabited the two separate principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia under the suzerainty of Turkey. In the Peace of Paris of 1856, which closed the Crimean 

War, these principalities were each granted autonomy. In 1859, however, they both elected Alexander Cuza as their hospodar, and he, in 1862, united them under one government to fulfill their dream of Rumanian national unity. The landowners, however, disliked Cuza's liberalism and replaced him by Charles of Hohenzollern in 1866. 

During the fifteen years between 1855 and 1870 the Rumanians could always count on the sympathetic support of Emperor Napo leon III of France. 

Indeed, in all the process of national resurgence in the Balkans the great powers of the rest of Europe had acted as selfish chessplayers, using the Balkan peoples as pawns. Russia, pretending to be the protector of Slavs and Orthodox Christians, tried to jostle her way toward the eastern Balkans and Constantinople. Jealous Austria tried to checkmate the Russians by obtaining influence in the western Balkans. Great Britain, likewise a rival of Russia, undertook to be a protector of Turkey. These greater rivalries sometimes caused wars, such as the Crimean War (1854-1856) and the Russo-Turkish War (1877-1878).

The latter war was caused by Russia's intervention in Turkey to prevent the Sultan's government from suppressing too harshly the Serbian and Bulgarian revolts of 1876. Russia invaded Turkey through Rumania, who found herself between two fires: the hated

Turk under whose suzerainty her people chafed and the Russian who would liberate Rumania but take away her share of Bessarabia. 

She had to accept the czar's tutelage, however, because of Russia's superior force. By 1878 the Russians had overrun Bulgaria and arrived at the very gates of Constantinople. Here they were stopped by the British fleet, which threatened to go into action against the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Russians if they went any farther. Russia and Turkey thereupon negotiated the Treaty of San Stefano which was subsequently superseded by a treaty drawn up by all the powers assembled in the Congress of Berlin (1878). The Treaty of Berlin provided for the complete independence of Rumania, Serbia, and Montenegro. Bulgaria, which would have been a large puppet state under Russian tutelage by the Treaty of San Stefano, was now reduced by England and Austria to a small autonomous principality north of the Balkan mountains under Turkish suzerainty. South of these mountains was a district of Eastern Rumelia under the Turkish administration of an approved Christian governor. Thrace, Macedonia, and Albania were to remain under complete Turkish dominance. Rumania lost southwestern Bessarabia to Russia and received the Dobruja as compensation. Austria-Hungary was given the right to occupy and administer Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to garrison the Sanjak of Novibazar. Antivari was allocated to Montenegro, and in 1881 

Greece was given Thessaly. Great Britain obtained the occupation of Cyprus, and Russia gained the Transcaucasian cities of Batum, Kars, and Ardahan.

These decisions left the Balkans more unsettled than before. Turkey was weaker and therefore the subject of ever more covetous designs of the new Balkan nations and the European powers. Serbia wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina; Rumania coveted Bessarabia and 

Transylvania; Bulgaria and Greece both hoped to obtain Macedonia. 

In 1885 Serbia and Bulgaria waged a war over the latter's annexation of Eastern Rumelia, and in 1908 the enlarged Bulgaria became an independent kingdom while Austria annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina. Russia's failure to get Constantinople explained her interest in the Balkan League of 1912 which intended to attack Turkey at the first opportune moment. The resulting Balkan Wars of 19121913, waged against Turkey and Bulgaria by other Balkan states, were an outgrowth of external and internal agitation and led indirectly to the outbreak of the World War in 1914.

CHAPTER 49 

The Culture of the Nineteenth and 

Twentieth Centuries 

POLITICAL THOUGHT: THE ADVANCE OF DEMOCRACY 

HE Age of Enlightenment brilliantly culminated in the culture of the nineteenth century. The rapid strides made by the forces of liberalism and nationalism were matched by the progress of thought, literature, and artistic efforts between 1815 and 1914.

Political thoughts and attitudes paralleled the liberal and national movements of the century. In the restoration period the trend had seemed to favor absolute monarchy. Chateaubriand in France and 

Hegel in Prussia exalted monarchy and the absolute authority of the state. The revolutionary and reform movements after 1820, however, inclined thought in the direction of democracy. 

As soon as the absolutism of the monarch was challenged, the need for some constitution (usually written) was keenly felt, in order to determine the extent and mode of limiting the king's power. By 1914 every European state had a constitution restricting royal power or defining the distribution of authority in the case of republics. Nearly every country thought of sovereignty as emanating from the nation as a whole rather than from the monarch. Certain rights were guaranteed to the individual citizen by the constitution, such as rights of habeas corpus and trial by jury as well as freedom of speech, press, meeting, petition, and religion. Indeed, Adam Smith and Herbert 

Spencer preferred very little governmental restriction of the individual beyond the limits required in preserving law and order. 

All constitutions likewise provided for some sort of representative legislature, which was usually bicameral. The members of the upper house generally differed from those of the lower house by having either titles of nobility, more than average wealth, a higher average age, or a longer term of office than those in the lower house.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Some of the upper houses were partly appointed and partly elected. 

The lower houses were always elected and usually had priority in financial legislation and in the selection of the administrative cabinet. 

Although the lower house was usually elected for terms from two to five years, it met in most cases once every year.

In Europe an invariable concomitant of parliamentary government was the control of the cabinet by the legislative majority. The chief executive, whether king or president, was in most instances a mere figurehead whose only significant function was to serve as a referee between hostile political groups. The formulation of policy and actual administration were in the charge of the cabinet which was selected and directed by a prime minister or premier, the leader, usually, of the majority party in the parliament. When a disagreement arose between cabinet and parliament, the prime minister advised the chief executive either to dissolve the lower house and call for new elections or to appoint a new prime minister and cabinet from the ranks of the opposition.

Hand in hand with the development of representative legislatures went the widening of the privilege of suffrage. By the end of the nineteenth century nearly every western European nation had adopted universal manhood suffrage. This trend was made more effective by the gradual adoption of the Australian secret ballot which abolished open and public voting with all the intimidation and bribery it entailed. The extension of the suffrage to women did not become general until after the World War, although Norway and Denmark introduced woman suffrage just before its outbreak. 

By 1920 France was the only major country of the western world without woman suffrage.

A wide use of suffrage was also introduced by the adoption of the initiative, referendum, and recall. Initiative was the practice of popular petition for the introduction of legislation, which, after being passed on by popular vote, became law. The referendum was the practice of submitting constitutional amendments, and sometimes legislation, to a vote of the people. The recall was the process of removing an elected official and the selection of a successor by popular petition and referendum. These practices existed early in the history of Switzerland. The initiative and referendum were adopted by three states of the United States before the World War and by Germany soon thereafter; the recall was also practiced in four American states prior to the World War and in the post-war period by Germany, Austria, and the Soviet Union.

Liberalism involved nationalism as well as constitutionalism. The nationalist movement was an effort on the part of peoples of the same nationality to unite into one political state or, if they were already united, to extend the influence of their national state in diplomacy and colonial expansion. Nationalism was linked with the democratic movement to the extent that it fostered self-determination for national minorities ruled by a state dominated by another nationality. At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, national aspirations were disregarded in dealing with the Italians, Belgians, Poles, Norwegians, and Germans. The partition of peoples among the dynastic states according to bargains struck by their respective absolutist monarchs was the rule of the day. However, nationalism could not be kept down any more easily than could the democratic movement. 

In most cases the two movements went together. The revolutions of 

1820, 1830, and 1848 were all nationalistic as well as democratic. 

Popular referenda (plebiscites) were often used to settle disputes arising from nationalist demands. 

Greece and Belgium gained their independence in 1829 and 1830; 

Germany and Italy became united national states between 1860 and 1871; Montenegro, Serbia, and Rumania were recognized as independent at the Congress of Berlin in 1878; and Norway and Bulgaria obtained their independence in 1906 and 1908 respectively. On the eve of the World War the most important submerged nationalities were in the empires of Russia and Austria-Hungary (Finns, Letts, Lithuanians, Poles, Czechs, Slovaks, and South Slavs).

The clash of nationalist states with conflicting diplomatic and economic interests was tempered, however, by the growing tendency to settle international disputes by arbitration. The two Englishspeaking peoples, American and British, pioneered in this field, settling thus the Maine boundary (1842), the Alabama claims (1871), the Venezuela boundary (1897), and the Alaskan boundary (1903). 

The example set by these peoples with cultural affinities led to arbitration efforts between peoples of widely differing backgrounds. 

One of the best examples was the treaty between France and Great Britain in 1903. At the Hague disarmament conference, called by 

Nicholas II of Russia in 1898, the Hague Arbitration Tribunal was founded to facilitate the solution of disagreements by peaceful means. States were not compelled to use this tribunal, however, and most disputes involving vital interests and national honor still were not usually submitted to arbitration.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION THE QUEST FOR ECONOMIC DEMOCRACY 

The rise of political democracy was seen finally to foster some forms of economic democracy. At first the Industrial Revolution, which dominated economic life in the nineteenth century, had the tendency, when left alone, to concentrate more and more wealth in fewer and fewer hands. A larger number of the working class became unemployed or reduced to poverty. The prevailing acceptance of 

Adam Smith's tenets in opposition to governmental regulation intensified this trend toward an unequal distribution of wealth. 

Eventually, however, a new school of thought began to appear which went to the other extreme in advocating government control of all important phases of social and economic life in order to reduce or prevent the concentration of wealth. Adherents of this school believed that if the welfare of society as a whole was obtained, it would automatically redound to the benefit of each individual within the society. Subordinating the individual to society, members of this group were finally called socialists. The socialists of the first half of the century were Utopian in tendency. Charles Fourier in France and 

Robert Owen in Great Britain advocated the establishment of small, self-sufficient communities where the profits would go mostly to the workers rather than to management. Two other Frenchmen, Saint- 

Simon and Louis Blanc, advocated coöperative farms and workshops. 

The former would have had the profits distributed according to ability, the latter according to need. They all believed in government aid and regulation to foster their schemes and in the abolition of inheritance.

One of the greatest contributors to socialist thought was a German scholar, Karl Marx. Instead of devising Utopian panaceas, he attempted to systematize the whole socialist concept in his principal works, The Communist Manifesto and Capital. To give the movement its place in the stream of history, he pronounced an economic interpretation of history which declared that economic forces were stronger conditioning factors in history than politics, thought, or religion. As a philosophical basis for his system Marx chose Hegel's dialectics of thesis and antithesis. Every social class, he asserted, has had its opposing class: freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, gildmaster and journeyman, noble and bourgeois, industrialist employer and factory worker. History is therefore the record of the struggle between these contending classes. Marx predicted a class struggle between the capitalist employer and the proletarian worker in which

the proletariat would be the victor because, by the concentration of wealth, the capitalists would become fewer and the exploited workers ever more numerous. By the ballot or by force the great majority would eventually succeed in overthrowing the capitalists' control of political and economic institutions. Marx's explanation of the rapid concentration of wealth under capitalism was called the surplus-value theory. If a man could produce enough wealth in six hours a day for his family to live comfortably, he could double his income in the form of luxuries or savings by the surplus value he created by working twelve hours. If, on the other hand, the employer required his employee to work twelve hours a day and paid him a wage equivalent to only a subsistence living, the employer was expropriating the surplus value to himself in the form of profits. 

Marx's suggested reforms would go far to transform government and business. He advocated social (or governmental) ownership and control of all the means of production and distribution. Individual productive enterprises would be directed by the workers in compliance with government regulations. By this means the surplus value would go to the workers; wages would be higher, hours shorter; and employment, population, consumption, and production would all become balanced. Economic insecurity would be banished, as well as the crime and violence which accompanied it. International economic rivalries and the resulting wars, Marx thought, would also gradually disappear if his proposals were adopted on a world-wide scale. Government, as we know it today, would therefore be less and less necessary as domestic crime and foreign wars disappeared. In the end governmental functions would be reduced largely to those of an economic planning commission.

Beginning with Marxism, the socialist movement since 1850 has branched out in several directions. The conservative tendencies, or movements to the "right," are represented principally by the Christian Socialists, the Revisionists, and the Fabians. The Christian Socialists, led by Maurice and Kingsley in England, wanted to socialize Christianity and christianize socialism by eliminating the capitalistic practices of competition and profit-taking which were contrary to the Christian precepts of brotherly love and the eighth commandment forbidding theft. They chose as their remedy the extension and intensification of the coöperative movement. The Revisionists, led by 

Bernstein in France, wanted to coöperate with the capitalistic parliamentary governments in bringing about the socialist state by slow and gradual reforms. The Fabians in England - who numbered

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

among their members such persons as George Bernard Shaw, H. G. 

Wells, Ramsay MacDonald, Sidney and Beatrice Webb, and Professor and Mrs. G. D. H. Cole - did not at first accept socialism as their program. Investigating, writing, and urging social reforms on 

Parliament, they kept before the minds of the British the "condition of England question" and advocated as a method the "inevitability of gradualness." After the World War, however, the Fabians in general took their place in the ranks of the moderate socialists. 

But many followers of Marx turned toward the more extreme "left" of communism, anarchism, or syndicalism. Communists, as distinguished from the more moderate socialists, favored the overthrow of capitalistic government by violent revolution rather than by the democratic ballot. Capitalistic money, they asserted, can always control the democratic ballot and legislature. Communists should therefore set up a dictatorship of the proletariat, liquidate the capitalists, and, after a period of readjustment to a classless society and a socialized government and economy, gradually reinstitute truly democratic methods. Anarchists, following the leadership of

Bakunin in Russia and Proudhon in France, opposed the use of government even for supervising economic planning. Establish cooperative production and distribution by labor ownership and control of the units of economic enterprise, they urged, and you would need no governmental compulsion. The syndicalists, like the communists, despaired of gradual democratic reforms as a road to socialism. Consequently they wanted to bring about the socialist state by a direct fight between the proletariat and the capitalists in industrial relations. By industrial unions, the general strike, the sit-down strike, breaking of machinery (sabotage), and poor workmanship, they would harass and hamper capitalistic enterprise until it would fall at the hands of organized labor rather than by political action. All of these left-wing movements were cynical about the so-called capitalistic institutions of the family, the customary moral codes, and supernatural religions. To them the family represented the smallest unit of possessive selfishness and governmental tyranny. Bourgeois morality was a pious mask behind which lurked the true face of lust and greed for power and worldly wealth. Supernatural religion, they believed, was an opiate which tried to lull the suffering masses into contentment.

In spite of the zeal and agitation of the socialists and anarchists, the actual reforms of the nineteenth-century enlightenment did not go to such extremes as those advocated by the Utopians and Marxists,

Though the bad conditions required drastic reform, public inertia and capitalist opposition made improvements both gradual and moderate. 

The favorite method for remedying the ills of industrialization was governmental legislation. Hence the laissez-faire theories of 

Adam Smith had to give way to the stark realities in factories, mines, and slums. In nearly all industrialized countries of Europe and in a few states of the United States factory acts were passed to regulate child labor, hours and wages, as well as conditions of health and safety. Social security programs were inaugurated, especially in 

Germany, France, England, and the United States, which provided for accident compensation, sickness insurance, old age pensions, and unemployment insurance. Most of these plans were based on available actuarial data and provided for contributions by employers and employees, and sometimes even by the state. In some factory towns slums were cleared, and modern, low-cost housing projects were undertaken in the interest of the health and comfort of the workers. Free medical clinics and charity hospitals were also established. For the unemployables institutions of various types existed: poorhouses for the aged, orphanages for the homeless children, asylums for the mentally deranged, and schools for the deaf and blind. 

Outdoor relief for poor families also was practiced in many industrial communities. School nurses, visiting nurses, and public health officers fought against contagious diseases.

In only rare instances did governments engage in business, as the Marxists would have desired. Telephone, telegraph, and parcel-post services were easily and logically incorporated with the existing postal service of most countries. In general the railroads of Europe were state-owned and operated because of their military and commercial value to the public. Electric power generation and water supply were government monopolies in some communities. All monopolistic public utilities and services, even if they were not owned by the government, were closely regulated by franchise contracts with the state or its subdivisions in order to guarantee to the public the maximum service at a moderate cost. Nevertheless, in contrast to the vast field of business activity, these instances of government ownership and operation were unusual exceptions to the general rule of private enterprise.

So far we have been considering only governmental attempts at economic reform. However, along with economic reform by governmental paternalism went two important movements of labor

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

self-help: trade unions and coöperatives. The combination of workers into unions in order to bargain collectively with employers on terms of equality was forbidden by law early in the nineteenth century. Adam Smith's idea of individualism and economic liberalism so pervaded the legal atmosphere that such unions were thought to be combinations in restraint of trade. Gradually, however, public opinion changed, and all industrialized countries recognized unions, collective bargaining, strikes, and picketing.
