Local unions and national specialized unions eventually combined into national federations, such as the British Trade Union Congress, the French Confédération Générale du Travail, and the American Federation of Labor. These labor organizations not only supervised labor's relations with capitalistic management but also entered politics to obtain measures favorable to labor. In England, Germany, France, Russia, and Italy distinct labor parties began to appear. Nevertheless, unions often worked under serious handicaps. General and sympathetic strikes were often outlawed; picketing was so severely restricted that strikes often could not be successfully continued; and judges were frequently sympathetic toward employers and interpreted laws to suit the latter's cause. Furthermore, the ever-increasing number of unemployed made an inexhaustible reservoir of strikebreakers. 

While on the one hand labor was using unions to get higher wages, on the other hand it fostered consumers coöperatives to make its wages go further. A group of twenty-eight weavers of 

Rochdale, in Lancashire, pooled five dollars each to found, in 1844, a coöperative retail grocery store. The plan of operation devised by these "Rochdale Equitable Pioneers," as they called themselves, was basically that used by the whole coöperative movement that followed. They would sell goods to their members and the general public for cash at the regular market price. Four times a year they would distribute the profits to members. Part would be distributed as five per cent interest on stock, part would be set aside for library or lecture funds, the remainder would be divided among the members according to the amount of their purchases. Certain other practices were usually adopted by coöperatives: single vote in meetings regardless of the amount of stock owned, purity and genuineness of the goods sold, and fair wages and hours for employees. The movement proved very successful and spread rapidly throughout England and Scotland. By 1863 there were about 454 in operation. In the following year a Wholesale Coöperative Society was organized

which bore the same relation to the retail coöperatives as the latter did to their members. Coöperation now extended to meats, drygoods, banking, transportation, shipping, and even, in some cases, to farming and manufacturing. In 1869 a Coöperative Union was formed to publicize the movement, foster favorable legislation, and furnish auditing facilities to the various units. The coöperative principle has been adopted to a limited extent on the Continent, particularly in the Scandinavian countries.

In addition to the reforms directly connected with the Industrial Revolution, the nineteenth-century enlightenment included some miscellaneous humanitarian movements. The maritime powers by 

1850 had taken measures to stop the African slave trade. Negro slavery was entirely abolished when the United States (1865) and Brazil (1888) finally outlawed it. In Russia the serfs were emancipated between 1861 and 1866. Advances in penology, begun by 

Howard and other pioneers in the eighteenth century, were continued. Increasing emphasis was placed on the moral and social rehabilitation of criminals by means of parole, vocational training, and other expedients. To ease the suffering from natural disasters as well as to care for the wounded in warfare, an international agency of the Red Cross was organized in 1863, which has since performed a noble service to mankind.

HISTORY WRITING 

In another field of the social sciences, history, the nineteenth century saw considerable progress both in its philosophical and its productive aspects. In Germany Hegel wrote The Philosophy of 

History in which he asserted that in each period a certain people predominate, and, after they have fulfilled their essential mission, decline. Hegel likewise exalted the state as the organic expression of this people and believed that the individual must be subordinated to the will of the state. In Hegel's view monarchy was the most highly developed form of government. Marx, a student of Hegel, furnished the nineteenth century with an entirely different interpretation of history. As has been noted,¹ he emphasized the influence of economic forces in the history of periods and peoples. With still another approach Carlyle in England stressed the influence of strong leaders in history in his Heroes, Hero Worship, and the Heroic in 

History and in his lives of Cromwell and Frederick the Great. Taking a somewhat more detached attitude toward history writing, the 

1 See supra, pp. 596, 654.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Italian, Croce, reminded his fellow historians that the past is generally interpreted according to the standards and influences of the present. In the Middle Ages men had a theological interpretation; during the height of industrialization, an economic and evolutionary theory; and finally, simultaneously with Einstein's relativity in science, came Croce's own idea of relativity in history writing. 

New methods in history kept pace with new interpretations. One of the leading pioneers in the field of method was Von Ranke in Prussia. He preferred the study of original sources and from them the writing of history of the past "as it really was." To facilitate this rather scientific approach, he instituted in the University of Berlin the seminar method which has been adopted since by every university school. In France Fustel de Coulanges practiced these same methods and rules of historiography. As a result of this new interest, great collections of sources have been brought together, carefully edited, and published. The Monumenta Germaniae Historica is one of these important collections dealing with German history. Archives have been established to house tons of ancient manuscripts and official documents. Two of the more famous are the British Public Record Office and the French Archives Natio nales. The recent Historical Records Survey undertaken by the 

United States, partly as a relief project, served to discover unknown sources in all states and communities of the country and to reveal to historians their value as well as their location. 

In these seminars the advanced students, using these sources, made detailed studies of some small phase or topic in history. These monographs, as they were called, served in turn as secondary sources for the more general histories. Historians became so specialized in a narrow field that it often became the practice later in the nineteenth century to make the writing of a general history a coöperative enterprise. Some of the better known examples of this form of history writing are the Cambridge Modern History, the Histoire de France, and the American Nation Series.

Although Ranke introduced a new method, he adhered rather closely to the old emphasis on political history. A broader scope of historiography began to appear, however, with his German contemporaries, Niebuhr and Mommsen, who, in their histories of Rome, stressed political institutions in their explanations of political events. Military aspects were subordinated. With the impact of the 

Industrial Revolution and Marx's economic interpretation, attention was also turned to social and economic history. Riehl and Freytag

devoted their attention to the social aspects of German history. In the realm of economic history Sombart of Germany, Sée of France, Hobson of England, and Beard of the United States all contributed notable and useful studies. This movement to include many phases of human activity in the study of history culminated in the more recent enthusiasm for cultural history, the German Kulturgeschichte, or what is often termed the New History. Cultural history was an attempt to weave together in a general narrative the political, economic, social, religious, intellectual, and artistic developments of mankind. Lamprecht and Burckhardt of Germany were pioneers in this more comprehensive endeavor, but they were later emulated by historians of other countries.

In line with the cultural emphasis in history came an adaptation of the cyclical interpretation. Oswald Spengler, a German historian, in his Decline of the West, expressed the belief that each world culture grows from primitive youth, to adult civilization, and finally to senile decadence. Demonstrating this by reference to ancient cultures, he ends by proclaiming that Western culture reached adult civilization in the nineteenth century and is now, in the urban machine age, in the process of decay.

Admiral Mahan, an American historian, not only wrote but actually made history in his epochal Influence of Sea Power on History. 

In this work he presented the theory that during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries strong sea power made possible the victory of the country possessing it. This thesis was so cogently reasoned and so well buttressed with facts that it helped influence the adoption of big-navy policies in the United States and Germany at the beginning of the twentieth century and also stimulated further naval construction in Great Britain, France, and Russia. 

GENERAL LITERATURE 

The literature of the nineteenth century followed rather closely the spirit of the various periods. In the first half of the century literary romanticism seemed to parallel the prevailing political reaction. In a revolt against the classicism and rationalism of the previous century the romanticists often preferred imaginative subjects dealing with strange places or the "far-off things of long ago." 

They were also enraptured with the beauties of nature. In all their works there was an emotional fervor which was often turned into a condemnation of the evils of the new industrial society. Among the English romanticists Wordsworth stands out as the nature poet.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

In his poems I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud and My Heart Leaps Up When I Behold he showed a sensitive love of the beauties of nature, while in his Solitary Reaper and his Tintern Abbey he carried this same inclination into the realm of human nature. In a later period Tennyson's poetry showed a romantic predilection for medieval themes as exemplified in his Idylls of the King based on the old legends of King Arthur. Coleridge, a contemporary of Wordsworth, excelled in imaginative poetry. His Ancient Mariner combined strangeness of both character and circumstance, while his Kubla Khan evoked the remote and the fanciful of the East where 

In Xanadu did Kubla Khan 

A stately pleasure-dome decree: 

Where Alph, the sacred river, ran

Through caverns measureless to man 

Down to the sunless sea. 

A later British poet, Kipling (1865-1936), bridged the gap between the romanticists and the realists by combining the theme of common, everyday objects with a setting of strange and distant places. 

The verses in Fuzzy-Wuzzy idealized "a pore benighted 'eathen ” in his "'ome in the Soudan." " In Injia's sunny clime," he declared in his poem Gunga Din, "The finest man I knew 2 

Was our regimental bhisti, Gunga Din."

We can also discern in these verses that Kipling was the poet of imperialism. "Take up the White Man's burden," he urged in the poem of that name. Britain's "dominion over palm and pine' (Recessional), according to Kipling, gave her a heavy responsibility and a great destiny.

The novel, however, rather than poetry, was to be the more typical vehicle of literary expression in the nineteenth century. Sir 

Walter Scott, in verse and prose, extolled medieval chivalry and the adventure of those far-off times. His poem, The Lay of the Last 

Minstrel, sings of the later Middle Ages when minstrelsy was already beginning to disappear. In his novels such as Quentin Durward, Count Robert of Paris, and Ivanhoe - he makes men and women of the Middle Ages live again by his clear understanding of human nature. In France, Victor Hugo was one of the leaders of the romantic movement in both prose and poetry. While his novels dealt 

2 Water-carrier.

with the past, they were realistic in portraying the sordidness and evil of that time along with its pageantry. In the novel, Notre Dame de Paris, the characters are unreal and superficial, but the mobs, the city, and particularly the cathedral itself make the past live again in the best romanticist style. His Les Misérables tended even more toward realism while retaining the imagination of the romanticists. 

This great literary masterpiece compressed within its volumes almost every conceivable human situation and circumstance, a great panorama of life itself.

Hugo's Les Misérables represented another emphasis of the romantic school, that of contemporary reform. By the novel these writers could describe the evil conditions and persuade readers to do something about them. Charles Dickens was Hugo's counterpart in England. In his Oliver Twist he revealed the bad conditions in the workhouses of England; in Pickwick Papers prison conditions were emphasized; again in Bleak House the law's delays in Chancery became his special plaint. Thackeray, while more of a realist than a romanticist, showed by his disdain for sham that he sought in vain for the heroic in the mediocrity of real life. In both his Vanity Fair and his Book of Snobs he satirized the upper and middle classes, revealing their scheming selfishness and their hypocrisy. As the procession of social novelists continued, their later representatives became more realistic. In Russia Turgenev by his Fathers and Sons denounced the abuses in Russian society and portrayed the subversive agitation they were creating. Another famous Russian author, Dostoievski, in his Crime and Punishment idealized the peasantry and revealed the good even in bad characters and sordid surroundings.

In the latter half of the nineteenth century literary efforts might be characterized as realistic. Realism was in harmony with the prevailing spirit of the time which preferred factual history, materialistic economics, positivistic philosophy, and scientific research. 

Writers in this period tried to describe life in the raw without any imaginative idealization. The psychology of the characters was carefully described, and situations were given all the photographic preciseness of environment and circumstantial frustration. Often these realists became sentimental, however, in trying to draw a moral or agitate a reform from the realistic situations they portrayed. In 

France, Flaubert was a pioneer of this literary school. In Madame 

Bovary he described the situation and psychology of an unfaithful wife of a country physician. Emile Zola was likewise a writer of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

realistic novels and short stories. He specialized in the scientific novel in which he tried to show that men were merely physical in nature and subject to the inexorable laws of environment and heredity. In Thérèse Raquin he applied this technique to individuals, while in his Rougon-Macquart series he used the same method with a whole family. Actually, however, Zola's technique was only pseudoscientific. While he insisted that the laws of nature carried out his plot, the author himself was taking liberties with science to create the plot that suited his fancy.

Two important English realists of recent times are Shaw and H. G. Wells. The former preached through the witty dialogue of his plays the lessons of socialistic reform drawn from a so-called realistic view of current practices. In Widowers' Houses Shaw attacked the evils of abused property rights; in Mrs. Warren's Profession he suggested a resemblance between ordinary business and prostitution; in Arms and the Man he ridiculed the glories of nationalistic wars. Parental moral authority, marriage, and charitable organizations received, each in turn, Shaw's sly rebuke in You Never 

Can Tell, Getting Married, and Major Barbara. Wells, in his New

Worlds for Old, offered for this chaotic world the remedy of a free and voluntary socialism. He carried his realism into the realm of the imaginative by describing in vivid detail the world of tomorrow after science will have made advances yet unattained. Psychological plays by the Norwegian playwright, Henrik Ibsen, were acclaimed by the devotees of realism. In his Doll's House he asserted the right of the individual over the claims of society, and in An Enemy of the People he showed how a health resort would conceal the contamination of its waters to preserve its business prosperity. In Russia, Count 

Leo Tolstoy's realistic novels also contained a philosophy of life. In his War and Peace he suggested that it is useless to fight against your environment and the natural course of events. A moral philosophy emerged from his Anna Karenina, wherein he contrasted the bitter sorrow of two selfish lovers with the happiness of two lovers who kept in mind the welfare of others. Anton Chekhov's plays stressed moods in men and suggested how men were deflected imperceptibly from their original attitudes and purposes by the little pin-pricks of life.

The twentieth century has likewise contributed much to the field of realistic literature. Thomas Mann in Germany has written powerful novels based upon characteristic psychological problems. His 

Buddenbrooks mirrored sympathetically the rise and fall of the

middle class in the experiences of a typical German merchant family. 

Sinclair Lewis, a Nobel prize-winning American novelist, has dealt with the middle class in more ironic vein in his novels Main Street, Babbitt, and Dodsworth. Another American, Eugene O'Neill, is known particularly for originality in his contributions to post-war drama. One of his well-known plays, Strange Interlude, introduced the innovation of elaborating the usual brief "asides " into a longer frank and revealing soliloquy interpolated in the usual insincere and deceptive conversational dialogue.

RELIGION 

Romanticism and realism both had influence on nineteenth-century religion. In the first half of the century the romantic influence was naturally more noticeable, especially in England where the 

Oxford Movement, led by Newman and Pusey, endeavored to call the English back to a more Catholic type of religion. Like the romanticists of their day, these Tractarians, as they were called, were intrigued by the medieval aspects of traditional religion, and they sought some definite spiritual authority in a world which seemed every day more unsettled. Pusey succeeded in getting an Anglo 

Catholic (High Church) movement under way in the Anglican Church, while Newman finally, in 1845, went further and embraced the Roman Catholic faith as the inevitable goal of his religious tendencies.

The later realism, however, had just the opposite effect on religion of minimizing tradition, authority, theology, and the supernatural. 

It stressed good works, evolutionary institutions and literature, and relative morality. The movement eventually had the effect of rolling up a concerted antagonism against historic Christianity and Judaism. 

Liberalism, which advocated both the political freedom of the individual and his economic freedom to follow his self-interest, did violence to the traditional Christian ideas of religious conformity, the brotherhood of man, and unselfishness. Nationalism taught an even more extreme mass selfishness and exclusiveness. Indeed nationalism became almost a competing pagan faith; religious fervor was drained off into the channel of patriotic emotion, and the nation became ever more hostile to the interference of religious institutions in politics. In the realm of economics industrialism exalted the material progress of man and made him feel that material comforts and happiness were the essential goals of human existence. Socialism was frankly based on a materialistic conception of the uni-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

verse which left little room for the recognition of spiritual or supernatural influences. Higher criticism and science likewise influenced religion. Ranke's method of historical scholarship began to be used in the study of the Bible and religious history. This higher criticism, as it was called, began to take the attitude that the books of the Bible were man-made and not directly inspired by God. It emphasized the evolutionary aspects of all religions, including Judaism and Christianity, as evidenced by their literature and practices. Strauss in Germany and Renan in France wrote biographies of Jesus revealing their conception of the founder of Christianity as a human being rather than the miraculous Son of God. The great discoveries in astronomy, geology, biology, and psychology, in their application, tended to undermine many religious concepts and institute a general trend of thought toward materialism. Laymen might conclude that both religion and science in their conflict were inclined to be unreasonable: religion denying many of the obvious facts revealed by science, science denying the existence of a spiritual side of human nature whose manifestations it could not, however, fathom or satisfactorily explain.

The effects of these realist forces on religious organizations were two-fold. On the one hand certain organizations reacted against them; in other organizations there developed new movements which tried to incorporate the new trends. The two principal manifestations of reaction were in the Catholic Church and among fundamentalist Protestants. Pope Pius IX in 1864 issued an encyclical Quanta Cura which condemned liberalism, individualism, and secularism and accompanied it with a Syllabus of Errors which denounced most of the trends discussed in this chapter, including a large part of the conclusions of science and higher criticism. The fundamentalist Protestants continued more firmly to adhere to the literal interpretation of the Bible with its assertions about creation, original sin, the vicarious atonement for sin through Christ, and the non-resistance and obedience of the lower classes.

New movements, however, were quite as prominent as a result of the impact of realism on religion. "Modernists" began to arise among Catholics, Jews, and Protestants alike, but especially among the latter. The Protestant modernists accepted many views of the higher critics and scientists, evolved therefrom new interpretations of the Bible, minimized dogma and theology, and finally stressed the practical application of religion to the problems of everyday life. 

They nevertheless adhered to a firm belief in the existence of a spirit-

ual source, called God, transcending the material universe, and in the necessity of a church. Modernism among Catholics usually took the form of anti-clericalism, a movement which, among faithful believers, showed itself by opposition both to a Catholic state church and to the activity of the clergy in politics and education. The more radical agnostic anti-clericals attacked the Catholic Church in all its aspects and showed a tendency to drop affiliations with any institutionalized religion.

PHILOSOPHY 

The philosophy of the nineteenth century was likewise touched by realism and science. The great Prussian philosopher, 'Hegel, rejected all the mystical and supernatural explanations of the universe, favored in earlier centuries, and made the individual man the axis of life. The individual had one purpose in life - himself. This metaphysics of Hegel included the conception of God not as being but as becoming. All creation` was in a constant state of change, of becoming. This, he endeavored to show by his dialectics, followed the formula of the clash of opposites. Every thesis, clashing with its antithesis, created synthesis. When black and white met, the synthesis was gray. In his political philosophy, however, Hegel subordinated the individual to the state. The superior state was one with military force and monarchical discipline. This description fitted his own Prussian state, which he greatly admired, and in the next century his political philosophy was to influence Nazi ideology. 

Another famous German philosopher, Schopenhauer, inveighed against both classical rationalism and romantic idealism. According to him the mainspring of behavior in an individual was an irrepressible will to live and dominate, not for any ideal or principle, but realistically for the satisfaction of desires, appetites, and passions. 

This same harsh and materialistic outlook on life was reflected in the philosophy of another German, Nietzsche. In his principal work, Thus Spake Zarathustra, he enunciated his superman philosophy. 

In this he ridiculed such weak and decadent characteristics as humility, gentleness, generosity, sacrifice, and goodness. These qualities, said Nietzsche, were conjured up by inferior people to defend themselves against superior men. He stigmatized Christianity as a slave religion and, like Schopenhauer, exalted the will to power.

Determined men with a will to force, by trampling down the inferior and weaker people, will rise up as supermen and will exemplify the highest form of civilization. This philosophy had a certain

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

appeal to the aristocracy, the militarists, the self-made business men, and later to the Fascists and Nazis. 

These will and force philosophers were gradually superseded by thinkers who embraced an evolutionary interpretation under the influence of Darwin. Herbert Spencer in England, while admitting the possibility of some First Cause or creator God, felt that human intelligence should concern itself only with the knowable facts of our material universe. In these facts he perceived evolutionary development of animate and inanimate objects from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous. By the "survival of the fittest" we get men and animals to evolve from common ancestry to widely differing species. The human mind and human society in the mass tend to evolve. Huxley, another Englishman, denied any spiritual aspect in life. The whole universe, he declared, was subject to material laws among which evolution was a very potent force. According to Huxley there could be no freedom of the human will because the material individual was subject to the inexorable laws of the material universe.

Auguste Comte, a French philosopher, went even further than the other evolutionist philosophers in emphasizing science as the basic explanation of the universe. He disliked abstract speculation and theoretical generalization. Let philosophers come down out of the clouds and by scientific research seek the facts of natural phenomena. Then, having the facts, they should let these facts speak for themselves rather than read into them theories and laws. This attitude formed the basis of Comte's positivist school of thought which he directed particularly to the study of society and its relationships. Comte was, therefore, one of the earliest sociologists. In his social "law of the three states " he traced his conception of the development of human thought from (1) the theological state in which phenomena were explained as divine interventions, to (2) the metaphysical state in which phenomena were explained by the abstract forces and laws of nature, to finally (3) the positivist state where causes are not sought but rather a knowledge of the phenomena themselves. Like the optimists that all these scientific philosophers were, Comte thought his own age had attained the superior state of positivism. Government, he believed, should be directed by scientific experts who knew sociological data and their meanings. 

He even went so far as to found a humanitarian religion with its positivist church. Humanity was to be worshipped at a great high altar, and great humanitarians and scientists were to be honored at

side-altars. The clergy would consist of the great scientific thinkers of the period. While John Stuart Mill did not go to such fantastic extremes as Comte, he did embrace the positivist approach and sought humanitarian reforms for the working classes, the landless, and women. Government in an age of science would, he thought, have to develop toward “state socialism." 

John Dewey, a twentieth-century American philosopher, draws his emphasis from his contemporary scientific, evolutionary, and democratic thought environment. His pragmatic instrumentalism denies any dualism in life such as means and end, cause and effect. 

Full knowledge of life must be a knowledge of the whole, both outer experience and inner reaction. Man by his contacts with his fellow man in a democratic society will come to know, through gradual experience and free reaction, the better forms of social behavior. 

This improvement in life relationships will therefore come about, according to Dewey, by realistic, gradual, but peaceful change. 

EDUCATION 

Dewey applied his philosophy particularly to the field of education, where he became the twentieth-century elaborator of the theories of Rousseau and Pestalozzi. Rousseau's ideas, as explained in his Emile, we have already considered in an earlier chapter.³ A fellow-Swiss, Pestalozzi (1746-1827), carried further the spirit of Rousseau. While Rousseau insisted that the child should receive an education suited to his natural inclinations and environment, Pestalozzi emphasized the need of a more systematic study of child psychology to find out what his natural aptitudes might be. The child, Pestalozzi thought, must not only study practical subjects but must also learn through his own activity. Absorbing the more democratic atmosphere of Switzerland, Pestalozzi also advocated education for the poor as well as the rich. 

These eighteenth-century educational philosophies laid the ground work for the present-day trend toward progressive education of which Dewey is one of the best-known leaders. Education to Dewey is not the teaching of a static culture of the past or present. Imbibing the spirit of Darwin's evolutionary theory, he asserted that education should attempt to train the ever-changing individual to make his own adjustments to an ever-changing world. Just as man is influenced by his environment, so man may also influence his environment. The student's environment should be most conducive to the 

3 See supra, pp. 525-527.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

free development of his powers of adjustment. Education should not only acquaint the child with the world about him, but it should implement the child with a knowledge of how to reshape his surroundings to suit his ideals and needs. Consequently the movement of progressive education tended to modify the methods of instruction to fit the interests of the child. The child was to meet problems and solve them as he would in life itself. An attempt should be made to show how the knowledge which is imparted is related to present and future usefulness. Wherever possible the child was to learn by performance, and instruction unrelated to activity was to be reduced to a minimum. Frequently this trend embraced the Dalton system of instruction in which the student would be given individual problems and projects whereby he would learn through independent study under the guidance of his teacher. More often, however, a modification of the Dalton system has been used by which the whole class would engage in a joint project during a part of the school day. 

In accord with these revolutionary educational methods and with the democratic political trend in many countries, the nineteenth and twentieth centuries witnessed a strong movement toward government-supported public schools. As suffrage was extended downward, the need for education for all became more apparent. At first the governments of Europe tended merely to subsidize private schools or establish elementary schools where fees were charged. In the last quarter of the nineteenth century, however, nearly every European and American country adopted free, compulsory, and nonreligious elementary education for all children. This involved in most cases the erection of state systems of education wherein the schools were owned by the state and controlled by a ministry or department of education. It was not long before every country was offering free facilities for education above the elementary grades. 

Public-supported high schools and normal schools began to appear in France, England, Germany, Japan, and the United States. These helped to prepare teachers for their duties in the elementary schools. 

As progressive education became more prominent, vocational and technical schools were added to the systems. State universities, embracing higher instruction in all the various professional and technical branches of learning, were likewise established in nearly every country. These educational facilities were eventually opened to women as well as men, although they were usually segregated in 

European countries.

SCIENCE 

We have discussed the scientific contributions of the age of the Renaissance. We have seen that the discoveries of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the scientific field, particularly the work of Galileo and Newton, were contributions of the first magnitude and went far to stimulate man's rational outlook. Nevertheless, the scientific discoveries of the period from about 1800 to our own time have been so revolutionary, so epoch-making, so fraught with possibilities of immediate application as to transcend comparison with any other period of history.

In the field of chemistry, an outstanding contribution of the nineteenth century was the formulation of the atomic theory. Dalton, who can be regarded as the most important early proposer of this theory, thought that chemical elements and compounds were ultimately composed of vast numbers of very small particles, or atoms. 

The atoms of the same element have the same atomic weight and atoms of different elements have different weights. Chemical action is the union or separation of atoms of elements. As hydrogen was'the lightest element known, he assumed that the weight of an atom of hydrogen would be one. Avogadro further developed this theory by assuming that atoms in compounds and elements were united to form molecules. It was subsequently found that metallic atoms, such as sodium, copper, barium and hydrogen, carried positive electrical charges, while radicals, such as the hydroxyl, carbonate, and sulphate, carried negative charges. Valence was then defined as the number of positive charges carried by an element, and this explained why, for example, one atom of sodium would combine with one of chlorine to form a molecule of sodium chloride, as the atom of chlorine carried one negative charge, whereas two of sodium were necessary to combine with the carbonate radical to form sodium carbonate because the carbonate radical carried two negative charges. 

Mendelyeff arranged the elements in a periodic table and showed that the properties of elements vary with their atomic weights in groups or periods of eight, with the eighth element of each group reproducing the properties of the first. There were many blank places in the periodic table, but a number of these have been filled with the discovery of new elements, the properties of which have conformed to those anticipated by the table. Since the opening of the twentieth century, however, atomic chemistry has been funda- * See supra, pp. 386, 520.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mentally altered by the quantum theory. It has been shown that the element frequently has variants, known as isotopes, while the atom has been broken down into electrons and protons by the researches of Bohr, Langmuir, and others. Indeed, it has been held that the atom is not a solid particle but is really a complex system, with its properties contingent upon the position and number of the electrons. 

Another chemical discovery of the nineteenth century of great significance was the connection between organic and inorganic chemistry. Organic substances could be made artificially from inorganic. 

This, in turn, led to the development of synthetic chemistry. As a result, today, we use hundreds of dyes, perfumes, medicines, etc. made from coal tar, while cellulose has yielded rayon, celluloid, bakelite, and innumerable other useful substances, and the possibilities of synthetic chemistry have only begun to be explored. Our presentday chemurgy is developing a large number of valuable substances from agricultural products and promises to be of major significance in the immediate future.

In physics, the most important concept introduced in the nineteenth century was that of conservation of matter, which in turn was closely linked with the experiments of Joule and others who had shown that heat was a measurable form of energy, and a given quantity of energy always produced the same corresponding quantity of heat. Helmholtz showed that energy could be neither created nor destroyed, although it could undergo a myriad of transformations. The amount of energy in the universe was a constant quantity; some of it was potential, the rest was kinetic, or energy at work, but the sum of potential and kinetic remained the same. Physicists later formulated the law which states that while the amount of energy in the universe is constant, the quantity of usable energy is being continually depleted through the loss of unusable heat or through other forms of dissipation. Recent experiments, particularly those of Millikan and Compton, in the study of cosmic rays, as well as the modern galactic astronomy as taught by Michelson, Shapley, and others, have introduced highly controversial complications in connection with these "laws," as has Einstein's view that energy is ultimate, and matter but a form of energy. 

Of greatest practical importance in the realm of physics were discoveries in electricity. Ohm devised a standard for the measurement of resistance to the passage of electrical currents, while Ampère formulated a unit, which also bears his name, for the determination of the amount of electrical current and showed that electrical cur-

rents in the same direction attracted each other, whereas those flowing in opposite directions repelled each other. This was important for later work on electrical induction as well as in the development of alternating current wherein positive and negative poles are interchanged with fixed frequency, measured in cycles, or the number of changes per second. Faraday, investigating the magnetic fields created by the passage of an electrical current, discovered the principle of induction which led directly to the invention of the dynamo and motor, particularly after the work of Gauss who formulated the principles of electrical flux, or the penetration of magnetic fields. 

Induction likewise was the basic principle on which Bell developed the telephone. The motor and dynamo were followed by Edison's invention of the incandescent light in which the illumination was produced by the white-hot glow set up by the resistance to the passage of the current of a carbon filament suspended in a partial vacuum. Edison also was largely responsible for the invention of methods for the long-range transmission of power. 

The investigation of radio-active substances and rays has been one of the most important recent spheres of scientific investigation. 

Roentgen discovered the X-ray, while Crookes and Hertz likewise made important contributions to this field. The isolation of radium from pitch-blende by the Curies was an achievement of monumental significance. Not only did the isolation of the element afford an immediately applicable boon to mankind through its use in the treatment of cancer; the work of the Curies contributed to the development of the quantum theory. It is hardly necessary to point out that the investigation of radio-activity in turn led to the invention of the vacuum tube and the spectacular application of it to the modern radio, radio telephone, and radio photographic transmission. 

A new era opened in the biological sciences with the publication, in 1859, of Darwin's Origin of Species. A number of scholars, even in ancient times, as shown in the De Rerum Natura of Lucretius, advanced the hypothesis that higher forms of life had evolved from simpler forms; indeed, Darwin's grandfather made significant suggestions in that direction. Darwin, however, was the first to state the hypothesis systematically, to bolster it with experimental evidence, and to attempt to explain the mutations of species. He held that existent species had been developed from earlier, less complex species. 

Confronted with a struggle for existence, a struggle made inevitable, as Malthus had pointed out, by the impact of organic life on the means of subsistence, only the fittest survive, that is, only those

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

species best adapted to their environment. Often survival of the species is contingent upon the emergence of new properties and attributes in individuals, brought about by the processes of natural and sexual selection. These changes, or mutations, which give greater adaptability to the environment, ensure the survival of the individuals thus distinguished and ultimately the evolution of new species. 

Many of the details of the Darwinian views have been questioned, and it is now held that struggle for existence, natural selection, and sexual selection are not the only determining factors in bringing about mutations, while recent observation of "sports," or variations from the norms of species, have opened up a new and fertile field for observation and experiment. Nevertheless, the expression, "Darwinism is dead" is completely misleading, for as a matter of fact, the basic evolutionary concept is virtually established. Darwin's work, like that of Newton before him and that of Einstein in our own day, has suffered by attempts to describe it in popular terms. 

The idea of evolution was not confined to the field of biology. 

Indeed, the concept has profoundly influenced all the natural and social sciences. Historians speak of cultural evolution; anthropologists point to the evolution of institutions from primitive forms; economists study the evolution of complex economic patterns from simpler antecedents. As summarized by Herbert Spencer in his System of Synthetic Philosophy, all things in nature as well as all human institutions have evolved from incoherent, disorganized homogeneity to a well differentiated, orderly heterogeneity. 

In astronomy, the measurement of the velocity of light, pioneered by the discovery of its wave nature by Young and Fresnel, and the invention of the spectroscope which made possible the calculation of the chemical composition of celestial bodies opened new vistas that literally stagger the imagination. It is now held that our whole solar system is merely a small part of a galactic system with at least one hundred billion stars, many of which are centers of planetary systems. In the words of Professor Shapley, " Instead of being the center of the universe, our sun is but an insignificant speck around which flits a shadow called the earth." In recent years, the work of the famous astro-physicist, Albert Einstein, has attracted world-wide attention. He holds that energy is ultimate; gravitation, which he has at least mathematically demonstrated to be the same force as magnetism, he holds to be a property of matter, which in turn is but a manifestation of energy. His famous theory of relativity holds basically that it is impossible to observe any motion in a universe from

within that universe; time and space are in reality the same, and both are considered as what he calls the fourth dimension. It can easily be seen, therefore, that modern science has apparently shattered the concept of the importance of the earth and the affairs of men in the cosmic scheme.

Discoveries in medicine in the period under discussion have proved of incalculable benefit in the prevention of disease and the amelioration of human suffering. In 1796 Jenner successfully used vaccination in the prevention of smallpox; today, this dread disease is virtually stamped out. Anesthesia, first apparently used by a Georgia dentist, was successfully applied in a major operative case by Morton in the Massachusetts General Hospital. The most fruitful discovery, however, was the demonstration of the bacterial causation of disease. 

Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, deserves the major credit for this epoch-making contribution to knowledge. In connection with his chemical investigation of the phenomenon of crystallization, he showed that living organisms could not be created; in putrefaction, fermentation, etc. the appearance of organisms could only be accounted for by the explanation that they came from outside the matter affected. Pasteur became famous when he found ways of dealing with wheat-rust that had greatly damaged the crops of France, and his development of inoculation for the prevention of anthrax that threatened to carry off most of the sheep went a long way to show him that he was on the right track in his theories as to the causation of disease. Another dramatic achievement and a major contribution to human welfare was his use of serum to prevent hydrophobia, for hitherto a person bitten by a rabid animal was virtually doomed to a slow and agonizing death. Although the scientist encountered bitter opposition from learned colleagues as well as from the ignorant, he eventually received the honor and acclaim he had so richly deserved. In the meantime, the experiments of Koch resulted in the isolation of the tuberculosis bacillus and went far to ensure the acceptance of the germ theory, of disease. Thus far, however, no specific for tuberculosis has been discovered, but careful nursing, with emphasis on nutrition and rest, has accomplished cures in a large proportion of cases.

Ever since ancient times infection had been regarded as the everpresent danger in surgical cases. A large percentage of mothers died as a result of child-bed fever, which frequently followed even apparently normal deliveries. Physicians and surgeons could not prevent these infections, and the public regarded them as afflictions sent

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

by an inscrutable Providence. Oliver Wendell Holmes notably reduced the cases of child-bed fever in his practice by meticulous cleanliness, but it was primarily the work of Semmelweiss, a Hungarian physician in the Vienna General Hospital, that showed the malady to be caused by the failure of physicians or midwives to observe sanitary precautions. Semmelweiss was at the time ridiculed by his colleagues and dismissed from his hospital post; the publication of his monograph was greeted with scorn. Lord Lister continued the work of Pasteur, Semmelweiss, and others, and antisepsis has become the indispensable adjunct of modern surgery and obstetrics. 

In recent years, the work of these pioneers has continued to bear fruit as infant mortality steadily decreases, while the life expectancy of adults increases. This latter factor, however, threatens to create acute social problems as an ever larger proportion of the population of modern countries are past fifty-five years of age. Antitoxin has been developed that has given virtually complete immunity to diphtheria, and public health agencies by urging the administration of preventive injections to children have made great strides in the eradication of this deadly disease. Then, too, pneumonia, another great scourge, has been largely checked through the preparation of serums for each of the many types of the disease. Only a few years ago, diabetes was almost invariably a death warrant until the true nature of the disease was learned and Banting's preparation of insulin resulted in the material prolongation of the lives of thousands of sufferers from the malady. The transmission of malaria by mosquitoes has been proved, with the result that vigilance in preventing breeding of the insects has tremendously reduced the prevalence of malaria. The dramatic, indeed heroic, work of Walter Reed likewise proved that the dread yellow fever was transmitted by the bite of mosquitoes, and again a remarkable victory has been scored in the never-ending quest for human welfare. Public health services, maternity clinics, free hospitalization of the poor, and recent developments in the field of socialized medicine are, or promise soon to be, factors of well-nigh immeasurable benefit to man. 

Treatment of mental diseases has kept pace with the remarkable progress made in general medicine and surgery. Adler and Freud, as well as many of their disciples, have gained marked success in the application of the methods of psychoanalysis to the treatment of mental derangements, while at the present time artificially induced fever and insulin shock have been applied with promising results.

Our age might well be termed the "Age of Science" as the lives

of all of us have been and are being profoundly affected by the fruits of research and inventiveness. Modern life, in its externals at least, is in marked contrast with that of but a century ago with the advent of the automobile, the airplane, the radio, and the countless other machines and appliances which we so casually utilize, and there is much evidence that we are much nearer to the beginning of the scientific age than to its close. 

THE FINE ARTS 

Nineteenth century contributions to the fine arts were especially distinguished in music. The period was marked by the perfecting of the symphonic form and the work of a number of great composers in this branch of musical art. The symphony can be broadly defined as abstract music, conforming to a basic pattern, as distinguished from program music wherein the composer has given definite intimations as to the ideas he wishes to convey. The symphony evolved in the latter part of the eighteenth century from the orchestral suite, the concerto grosso, and the sonata. Wolfgang Mozart (1756–1791), a 

Viennese composer whose remarkable gifts did not receive commensurate recognition during his short life, has left more than five hundred compositions, of which forty-nine are in the symphonic form, only four of which are performed with frequency. Besides his symphonies he composed a wealth of choral music, string quartets, many of which are still often heard, and twenty-two operas of which the Marriage of Figaro, the Magic Flute, and Don Giovanni have remained widely popular.

Joseph Haydn (1732-1809) was most responsible for giving the symphony its classic pattern. He composed more than one hundred symphonies, only a few of which are played today, although recent revivals of some of his well-nigh forgotten works have been well received. According to the pattern, conventionalized largely as a result of Haydn's influence, the symphony is almost invariably in four movements. The first movement, in sonata form, is the most important. It contains, according to the classic style, two themes, the first of which is tonic, that is, in the key from which the symphony is named, while the second theme, which strongly contrasts with the first, is usually in the dominant (five notes above) of this key. 

There are suitable transitional passages, variations of tempo, instrumentation, and pitch. The second movement is traditionally slow, with simple themes, hinted at in the preceding movement. In Haydn's time the third movement was the minuet, but Beethoven changed

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

this to the scherzo, lively and sparkling. The finale is usually a fast, brilliant movement that demands the utmost technical skill from the members of the orchestra. 

Haydn's pupil, Ludwig van Beethoven (1770-1827), was the greatest genius of the period if not in the entire history of music. 

His first two symphonic works showed the strong influence of his master, but his remarkable gifts and independence of spirit soon asserted themselves with the composition of his third (Eroica) symphony which he originally intended to dedicate to Napoleon. 

He has left nine symphonies, all of which are part of the standard repertory of the modern orchestra; besides the third, the greatest are the fifth, seventh, and the ninth (Choral). A piano virtuoso, he composed several concertos for that instrument as well as sonatas and one concerto for the violin, and his less pretentious works, such as the Moonlight Sonata and the Minuet in G are universally beloved. 

Another master of the first half of the nineteenth century was Franz Schubert, who died before he had reached his maturity. He composed eight symphonies; perhaps the most popular of these is the eighth, or Unfinished symphony, only two movements of which are complete. He would rank near the top of musical achievement if nothing of his work survived save his beautiful songs, of which he composed about 650. Other famous members of the German school were Felix Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Mendelssohn's best known works are his Italian and Scotch symphonies and his incidental music for Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream. 

Schumann's four symphonies retain their popularity, as do many of his compositions for the piano.

Towards the close of the century, the great figures in orchestral composition were Peter Tchaikowsky (1840-1893) and Johannes 

Brahms (1833-1897). The former's fourth, fifth, and sixth symphonies rank with the greatest masterpieces of this form of music; they are characterized by moods of melancholy and unique, sombre tonal coloration. His Nut-Cracker Suite is known to every music lover, as are his Marche Slave and the 1812 overture. In simpler vein, his songs and melodies are beautiful and frequently played, particularly the famous Andante Cantabile. Brahms has often been compared with 

Beethoven. Each of his four symphonies is a masterpiece; the first and fourth are most frequently played. They are characterized by a maturity of style and a consummate command of the resources of the orchestra. The outstanding symphonic composer of the French school was César Franck (1822-1890). While he derived many of his

harmonic ideas from Wagner, the great German operatic composer, he evinced great originality and profoundly influenced later French composers. He was the first composer to break with the tradition of the four-movement structure, and his symphony was criticized by contemporaries largely because it was written in three movements instead of four. 

Second only to the great symphonic masters in the field of instrumental music were the piano virtuosi and composers, particularly 

Franz Liszt and Frédéric Chopin. Liszt's remarkable performances as a pianist had the same effect in the development of piano technique as did Paganini in that of the violin. His best known and most mature work is probably his Les Préludes, although his Hungarian Rhapsodies, particularly the second, are in the repertories of all concert pianists and orchestras. Chopin has never been equalled for sheer melodic inventiveness; his Études for the piano, while demanding great technical mastery by the performer, contain some of the most beautiful melodic passages of all musical literature.

The nineteenth century was also marked by a wealth of operatic composition. Modern operatic programs are built around the works of Giuseppe Verdi (1813-1901) and Richard Wagner (1813-1883). 

Verdi worked on the principle that the aria, or solo passage, was allimportant. The opera was not the theatre; the story was merely a thread, and sometimes a very tenuous one, on which to hang a series of pleasing melodies, with abundant opportunity for the principal singers to exhibit their range and technique. He composed a total of twenty-six operas, but none of those composed in his youth are performed today. Of his mature works, composed after 1850, Rigoletto, Il Trovatore, La Traviata, Aida and Otello are regularly performed and promise to retain their popularity for a long time to come. The work of Wagner sharply contrasted with that of his Italian contemporary. For Wagner, opera was essentially a form of drama. The singers were primarily actors, and the music created, sustained, and advanced the dramatic themes to climaxes usually marked by arias of wonderful beauty. Naturally, there are many purely recitative passages, and the orchestra is used to provide not merely accompaniment but also a background of mood and tone color. Wagner's daring originality in harmonic structure was largely responsible for the adverse criticism that greeted many of his works, and his orchestrations likewise were greatly at variance with tradition. He composed one comic opera, Die Meistersinger; his other great works are in a tragic mood, with themes drawn from Teutonic mythology and folk legend. The

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

romantic Tannhäuser and Lohengrin, the four operas of the "Ring" (Rheingold, Walküre, Siegfried, and Götterdämmerung), Tristan und Isolde, and Parsifal are standard operatic offerings throughout the world. Many of his orchestral passages, as well as arrangements of vocal parts, are frequently performed, particularly the Good 

Friday Music from Parsifal, the Liebestod from Tristan und Isolde, and the Lohengrin and Meistersinger preludes. The overtures are especially liked; those from Tannhäuser and the Flying Dutchman as well as Rienzi are well known to all concert-goers. 

The second most important Italian operatic composer was Puccini.

His La Bohême, Tosca, and Madame Butterfly are frequently found on current programs. Mascagni's Cavalleria rusticana and Leoncavallo's I Pagliacci are two shorter works that often appear on the same program. Of the French operatic school, Massenet's Manon is a favorite, while Bizet's Carmen and Gounod's Faust likewise have become perennials.

Great controversy rages around the works of recent composers. 

Music lovers whose tastes rebel at the dissonance and apparent incoherence of the works of Stravinsky, Ravel, and many others of the modernistic school predict early oblivion for works that so sharply deviate from the classical patterns. Defenders of modernism, on the other hand, point out that composers who today are considered the great masters were in many cases ignored or even reviled by their contemporaries. It would therefore be hazardous to attempt to assign modernistic composers to places in the general history of music. 

Modernists attempt to express their moods and emotions largely, indeed in extreme instances almost exclusively, through the medium of tonal coloration. They unquestionably have a greater realization of the capacities of the orchestra in this respect than did the nineteenth century classicists. They have gone far beyond Wagner, Franck, and others, particularly of the French school, in harmonic inventiveness. No one who hears Debussy's Afternoon of a Faun or his Clair de Lune can fail to realize that the modern approach through color has wonderful potentialities. Passages of real beauty appear in many of the most recent works, but often the composer fails to realize the full possibilities of his themes; he is profligate and therefore frequently incoherent. The classics have become classics largely because of their melodic interest and the artistry of the composer in elaborating a few simple themes, as in the second movement of Beethoven's fifth symphony. It would seem therefore that by their apparent failure to express themselves in truly melodic forms

the modernists are neglecting a factor most vital for the survival and continued popularity of music. The only symphonies of a recent composer that seem clearly destined for survival are the works of Sibelius, and no recent operatic works promise to displace those of Verdi, Wagner and others who have achieved a place in the standard repertories.

ARCHITECTURE, SCULPTURE, AND PAINTING 

The period under discussion was not particularly significant or creative in architecture and sculpture. The architecture of the first half of the nineteenth century was characterized largely by the revival of classical styles, especially those of the High Renaissance and the Romanesque. Architects had to work with new building materials, to express many of their ideas in steel instead of stone. With the growing emphasis on utilitarianism, the architect began with his ground plan, rather than with the façade, and he constantly had to harmonize his architectural forms with the dominant consideration of adaptability of the building to the purpose for which it was designed. With the emergence of the skyscraper, particularly in 

America, the functional consideration threatened to exclude aesthetic elements, but in recent years architects have made remarkable progress in integrating the functional motif with the classic styles, and, indeed, abstract functionalism has evolved an intrinsic beauty of its own as evinced in a number of structures of the last decade both here and abroad.

Sculpture too began with the classicism of Canova, the Italian sculptor, and the Danish Thorvaldsen, but classicism soon yielded to the strong romantic movement which rebelled against the conventionality and rigidity of form of the classic styles. Rude executed his famous "Marseilles Group" on the Arc de Triomphe, Carpeaux carved the " Dancing Group " on the façade of the Paris Opera House in this spirit, while the English Stevens, with his statue of Wellington, and the German Reitschel were also leading exponents of this movement. From romanticism emerged the emphasis on realism as shown prominently in the works of Rodin, whose "Thinker and "Age of Bronze are internationally known, and Meunier with his statues of laborers.

Painting was characterized by greater originality. Landscape painting became a leading type. Millet painted his studies of French peasant life, of which the "Angelus " and the "Gleaners" are universally beloved. Morland, with his studies of English country life, as well as

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Constable and Turner were prominent representatives of this school. 

Cézanne, one of the greatest of the modern French painters, inaugurated a significant departure when he emphasized the integration of realism and abstraction. Drawing and line were really one with color. 

He, together with Gauguin and Van Gogh, a Dutch painter who, however, was associated with the French school, were the pioneers of what has been called the expressionistic movement wherein the artist strove to portray the intensity of his emotion by striking coloration and individualistic vagaries of form. The works of the 

American Whistler (1834-1903), particularly his so-called “symphonies" and "nocturnes," were contributions to this movement of international significance, although his portraits, such as his 

Mother," enjoy greater popularity.

Recent trends in both sculpture and painting show the powerful influence of ideas inaugurated by the expressionists. Extreme manifestations, such as the ultra-modern cubism and surrealism aim to rid art of all convention and imitation. The ultimate importance of these innovations can no more be accurately predicted than that of contemporary music. There is no doubt that the work does produce responsive reactions, and even if the latest product of the brush or chisel of the surrealist does no more than produce a feeling of irritation, it must possess virility.

CHAPTER 50 

Imperialism in the Nineteenth and

Twentieth Centuries 

HE movements of colonial expansion of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries gradually lost their momentum, and the greatest overseas empires received severe reverses between 1600 and 1820. Portugal by 1600 had lost most of her eastern possessions to the Dutch. The Dutch in turn lost important colonies to 

England in 1664 and 1815. After the Seven Years' War (1763) France was shorn of all her North American colonies, and twenty years later England lost her valuable Thirteen Colonies at the close of the American Revolution. The first colonizing power, Spain, was the last to lose her dominions. By revolutions lasting from 1815 to 1826 all the Spanish colonies on the mainland of South and Central America severed their ties with the mother country. 

This loss of overseas territory resulted in a diminished interest in colonization on the part of these commercial states during the first half of the nineteenth century. The substitution of laissez faire and free-trade ideas for the earlier mercantilism likewise fostered a neglect of colonies. A group in England, called "Little Englanders," began before 1850 to assert that colonies were burdens rather than benefits. 

Now the situation presented a reversal of that in the eighteenth century: when colonies were urged to become independent, they clung all the closer to their shunning parents. 

Interest in imperialistic projects was renewed, however, by the middle of the nineteenth century, primarily because of the Industrial Revolution. Expanded production resulting from the mechanization of industry made imperative the acquisition of new markets. When the low wages paid to factory workers deprived industry of an abundant home market, and high tariffs closed the markets of many European countries to each other, colonies became the only considerable outlet for surplus production. Moreover, the demands of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

new industry for ores, oil, cotton, wool, rubber, and other materials, became progressively greater. Exploitation of colonial regions rich in natural resources seemed the logical solution to the problem. Industrial expansion, with the attendant large profits, brought accumulations of surplus capital for which imperialistic ventures offered prospects of profitable employment. Since governments assumed the major responsibility for the protection of foreign interests, the risks involved in such investments were commensurately low. Population growth, technological displacement of workers, and recurrent periods of unemployment due to business fluctuations also offered problems aggravated by the Industrial Revolution. Colonies promised to alleviate these conditions by furnishing outlets for surplus population.

Humanitarianism and religion also played a material part in nineteenth century imperialism. Humanitarianism was a natural implication of the Deist teachings, and was powerfully stimulated by the religious revival of the eighteenth century, especially by the Methodist movement. Backward regions of the world were the charge of enlightened countries. It was the "white man's burden" to foster education, vanquish superstition, and introduce the material blessings of Western civilization. Apologists for imperialism cited the construction of roads and railways, the introduction of sanitation, and the modernization of industry as proofs of the benefits bestowed on subjugated peoples. While the profit of individuals and companies was the exclusive motive for these improvements, it was easy to palliate the exploitation of defenseless peoples by simulated altruism. 

Missionaries, both Catholic and Protestant, labored arduously, often heroically, to bring Christianity to the heathen in distant places; they often were the unwitting or unwilling allies of those whose purposes were more material.

The prevalent scientific interest also stimulated imperialism. Exploration, collection of rare flora and fauna, the quest for anthropological knowledge, frequently impelled the dispatch of expeditions into hitherto unknown regions. Desire for adventure was just as potent as in the days of the great voyages of exploration; there still were frontiers to be pushed forward, primitive dangers to be challenged.

Inventions brought the nations of the world into ever closer contact. Far-flung commercial interests necessitated the acquisition of docking and coaling facilities for vessels that plied the ship lanes. 

Navies were needed to defend holdings which often lay at great dis-

685 tances, and it was imperative that naval bases be acquired at strategic points. These factors, too, played a part in the scramble of the European nations for colonies, protectorates, and spheres of influence.

Imperialism was a natural concomitant to nationalistic fervor. 

Colonial holdings enhanced national prestige; failure to attain coveted prizes was a blow to “national honor." Statesmen fostered the delusion that imperialism promoted employment and raised the standard of living of the masses. As a matter of fact, the profits and benefits were usually for the few, while the general populace bore the burden of taxation imposed by the expense of developing and protecting colonial interests. Seldom has the confusion between selfish and national interests been more palpable. Indeed, thorough study has demonstrated the falsity of most of the premises upon which the justification of imperialism has rested. 

Imperialism of the nineteenth century introduced new forms of control quite different from the colonial type. Spheres of influence were fenced off by industrial states either by a proclamation backed by force or by a round of treaties with accommodating competitors. 

The nation claiming the sphere would endeavor to keep out all political or economic influence, or both, of other imperialistic states. 

England in the Yangtse valley of China, Russia in northern Persia, and the United States in Latin America are examples of this form of control. Protectorates offered another convenient form of imperialistic hegemony. An imperialistic nation would compel a weak or bankrupt government of a backward state to turn over the direction of police, finance, and diplomacy to its own appointed advisers, who would thereafter shelter their fellow-countrymen in an exclusive exploitation of the protectorate's natural resources and trade. Examples of protectorates might be found in England's control of Egypt after 1883, France's relations with Tunis after 1881, and the United 

States's tutelage of Cuba after 1898. 

The methods used to obtain imperialistic expansion in the nineteenth century were often much more subtle and refined than the military conquest of colonies in the earlier centuries. Loans would be made by a powerful country to a weak state in return for special privileges in controlling governmental administration, in monopolizing the construction of public works, such as railroads, roads, and waterpower dams, or in exploiting the natural resources of the region. Investments would be made in undeveloped countries, and the right of intervention would be asserted to protect those interests.
