A discussion of imperialism naturally centers in the British Empire. The War of the American Revolution proved to be not the end but the beginning of empire. In the main the causes for the accentuated British interest in imperialism were the same as those which produced the general European movement. The major dependencies of 

Britain, known as dominions, enjoy self-government with but nominal subordination to the Crown.¹ The most important of these dominions is Canada, with an area of about 3,750,000 square miles, a population of approximately 11,000,000, and a wide range of natural resources and economic interests. The Treaty of Utrecht, which closed the War of the Spanish Succession, awarded Nova Scotia and Hudson Bay to Britain. Halifax was established and the French 

Acadians expelled. The great duel between the English and French, with their respective Indian and colonial allies, the Seven Years' War, by 1763, left England in undisputed possession of the vast domain which thereupon was provisionally governed by royal proclamation. 

The initial step towards the solution of the governmental and administrative problems created by the acquisition of Canada was the passage of the Quebec Act of 1774. Boundaries of the province were declared to extend westward to the Mississippi and south to the Ohio. 

This threat to the western claims of the American Colonies was an important cause of the Revolution. French civil law was adopted in conjunction with English criminal procedure. The Roman Catholic 

Church retained all its old privileges, and the alliance of the church and the landowners with the English government was expected to ensure the success of the new regime. 

During the Revolution, various projects of union with the colonies were attempted, but Sir Guy Carleton so ably defended Canada that by the close of the conflict the danger of separation from Britain was averted. About 40,000 British sympathizers fled from the colonies to take refuge in Canada during the course of the Revolution. The influx of these United Empire Loyalists brought some adjustments in the government of Canada commensurate with the new ratio of English and French in the province. Claims of the loyalists for compensation for property they had lost were rebuffed by the United States, but were partly liquidated by England. This issue kept alive a hostility towards the United States that ensured the failure of union projects during the War of 1812. 

1 See infra, p. 721, on the British Commonwealth of Nations.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION By the Act of 1791, the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada were created. The former was English, the latter French, although there were concessions for minorities in each province. Serious revolts in 1837 indicated that profound forces of unrest were operative. A French faction, led by Joseph Papineau, attempted to create an independent republic on the St. Lawrence. Malcontents in Ontario, under the leadership of William Lyon Mackenzie, likewise rebelled. Filibustering from the American side of the Niagara caused loyal Canadians to destroy the American boat Caroline and create an acute tension in the relations between Britain and the United States. 

As a direct result of the uprisings of the preceding year Lord Durham was sent to Canada as Governor-General in 1838. The new governor was recalled when a succession of arbitrary acts provoked resentment in the provinces, but his report, published in 1839, advocated union of the two provinces and the grant of privileges of selfgovernment. The former recommendation was embodied in the 

Canada Government Act (1840), and under the administration of Baron Sydenham, progress was made towards the second major principle of the Durham Report. 

Lord Elgin's Report also advocated self-government. In 1849 the 

Canadian Parliament voted compensation for those who had sustained losses in the rebellion of 1837. Conservatives in Canada and Britain protested vehemently; serious demonstrations occurred in Montreal, but the governor insisted that the parliament was within its rights as an independent legislative body. A project for the union of New 

Brunswick and Nova Scotia led to a conference in 1864, where a broader project of union met a favorable reception, as a result of which the British North American Act was passed, effective July 1, 1867. The act created the Dominion of Canada by a union of Ontario, Quebec, and the Maritime Provinces with the exception of Newfoundland. The constitution established by the act has remained in force to the present time with little modification. In contrast to the 

American constitution, all powers not specifically assigned to the provinces are reserved to the Dominion government. Ultimately, sovereignty is vested in the British Crown, represented by a Governor-General appointed by the Crown for a five-year term. Limitations imposed on the Governor-General's authority by Parliament and Ministry correspond to those imposed on the king by the British government. Parliament is bicameral. A Senate made up of members from each province, appointed for life by the Governor-General in Council, comprises the Upper House. A House of Commons, di-

IMPERIALISM 

689 rectly elected by universal suffrage, is the fundamental governmental organ, with a responsible ministry. Quebec has 65 members; representation of the other provinces is computed at a number which has the same ratio to their respective populations. A Supreme Court was created in 1876; in 1891 the ministry was authorized to consult the court on questions of organic law. Each province has a ministry and a parliament, but only the parliaments of Nova Scotia and Quebec are bicameral. Manitoba and British Columbia were added to the Dominion in 1870-1871, and the great central provinces of Alberta and 

Saskatchewan were incorporated in 1905.

Another dominion is Australia, with an area of nearly 3,000,000 square miles. Claims of discovery of this great continent, lying entirely in the Southern Hemisphere, were made by French and Portuguese navigators as early as the sixteenth century. The Spanish expedition under De Torres and De Quirros (1606) probably sighted the mainland. Accounts of Dutch navigators of the seventeenth century did much to engender interest in exploration; Tasman claimed the island which bears his name in 1642, but the claim lapsed since the Dutch government made no attempt to settle the region. The first 

English expedition was that of William Dampier (1688), but it was not until the voyages of Captain James Cook (1769-1770) that exploration resulted in settlement. Cook's Endeavour anchored in Poverty Bay, New Zealand, and in April, 1770, landing was made on the shores of Botany Bay, on the Australian coast, where the Union Jack was hoisted and New South Wales claimed for Britain. Inland exploration began about twenty-five years later. 

A penal colony was established at Port Jackson, New South Wales, in 1788. Until the suspension of transportation (1839) and the discovery of gold in 1851, convicts furnished three-quarters of the English populace. Governors at Sydney enjoyed despotic powers; under 

General Macquarie roads, bridges, and other internal improvements did much to open the area to colonization. Sheep raising was introduced early in the nineteenth century, and within a few years it had become the major economic interest.

In 1825, Tasmania, which had been settled some years before (1803) as an auxiliary penal colony, separated from New South Wales. In the same year a military station was established on King 

George Sound which with settlements on the Swan river (18271829) furnished the nucleus of Western Australia. A settlement was made at Port Philip in 1835; by 1851 this region separated from New 

South Wales as the state of Victoria. Joint-stock ventures in the pe-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

riod 1835-1837 gave initial impetus to the settlement of South Australia.

The discovery of gold in 1851 was an event of revolutionary significance. Colonists, prospectors, and adventurers poured into the regions where strikes had been made; two thousand arrived weekly in 

Melbourne. Victoria declared its independence, and eight years later 

Queensland did likewise. Self-government was introduced, Western 

Australia being the last state to receive this privilege (1890). Abolition of penal settlement, the establishment of secular education, adult franchise, and vote by ballot were accomplished by 1900. 

Various proposals for consolidation were made in the decade 18901900, and several abortive conventions were held. Finally in 1897 a convention at Adelaide adopted a plan of union that received enthusiastic reception in Victoria, Tasmania, and South Australia. Opposition of New South Wales and the consequent refusal of Western Australia to enter the Union, as well as the refusal of Queensland to participate in the convention, prevented immediate ratification of the plan. By 1899, opposition in New South Wales had so abated that the proposal was passed by the British Parliament as the Act of 1900. 

The act organized the Commonwealth of Australia with six component states, with provision for reduction or enlargement as necessitated by consolidation or partition of any member states. Powers not especially granted to the Commonwealth government are retained by the states. Sovereignty resides in the Crown, represented by a Governor-General. A bicameral legislature includes a Senate, made up of six representatives from each state, and a House wherein representation is apportioned on the basis of population. Australia, and, to a great degree, New Zealand, have been social laboratories for the world. The Australian secret ballot has been almost universally adopted. Women received the vote in New Zealand more than twenty years before the women in Britain. Governmental operation of railways and other utilities, governmental monopoly of banking, and progressive insurance legislation have challenged the attention of the world.

Britain restored Cape Colony in South Africa to the Dutch by the Treaty of Amiens (1802) but regained in 1806 a possession which was formally recognized by the Congress of Vienna. Many Dutch settlers became dissatisfied with English rule and, as a result of the Great 

Trek (1834-1840), founded the states of Transvaal and Orange Free

State. During the Disraeli ministry, the Transvaal was annexed to

IMPERIALISM 

691 Cape Colony, but regained its independence under Gladstone. The discovery of gold in the Transvaal in 1884 brought an influx of British settlers that created tension between English and Dutch. The 

British in the meantime had acquired Natal as well as control over Egypt and the headwaters of the Nile. Cecil Rhodes, capitalist and empire builder, used friendly newspapers and other agencies to advocate a Cape to Cairo railroad. A populous mining city inhabited largely by British immigrants grew up at Johannesburg in the Transvaal, and the increasing friction between these "uitlanders" and the Boers threatened a war. A vigorous British imperialism took a more and more threatening tone toward the Dutch republics in South Africa.

In 1895 Dr. Jameson, administrator of Rhodesia, led a raid on behalf of the "uitlanders" into the Transvaal. His action, inspired by 

Cecil Rhodes and large mining interests, was not supported or countenanced by the British government, and his force was captured by the Boers. The German Emperor sent a telegram of congratulation to President Paul Kruger, the narrow and stubborn president of the

Transvaal, which accentuated the Anglo-German tension. For several years the irritation between Boers and Britons grew in intensity. 

Then, as the result of British pressure and a Boer ultimatum, war began in 1899. After courageous resistance, the Boer forces were defeated in the field by the British under Roberts, but detached bands continued guerrilla fighting until the spring of 1902. By the Peace of 

Vereeniging the Boers recognized British sovereignty, but were promised representative self-government at an early date, and given £3,000,000 for the rehabilitation of their country. Great public works were shortly undertaken under British auspices. 

As early as 1906 the Liberal ministry of Campbell-Bannerman in Great Britain gave the defeated Boers a constitution marked by many liberal features, under which General Botha soon became Prime Minister of the Transvaal. In 1909 the South Africa Act was passed by 

Parliament, providing for a great self-governing federation of states – the Transvaal, Orange Free State, Natal, and Cape Colony; and the next year the Union of South Africa became a reality. A Governor- 

General, as the representative of the Crown, was given powers more extensive than those of similar officers in Canada and Australia. A unique Senate was made up of eight members elected from each of the four states, and eight more appointed by the Governor-General. 

Members of the Assembly were elected from single-member constituencies. Noted Boer fighters, like Smuts and Botha, became strong

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

supporters of the Crown and of the new order in South Africa. The general British policy of conciliation was vindicated by the loyalty of the Union to the Empire when the World War began. 

The greatest of the crown colonies is India, the British acquisition of which has been described in a previous chapter. The administration of this great sub-continent has tried severely the genius of the English for governing other peoples. Prior to 1784, the country was ruled by the East India Company. Complaints that the natives were being exploited and that company officials were acting arbitrarily became more insistent at the very time that profits of the company were dwindling. The trial of Warren Hastings brought the problem to public attention. Hastings, a company governor, was impeached by 

Parliament on sundry charges of maladministration. He was acquitted, but the revelations made during the lengthy proceedings strengthened the demand for reform in the administration of the colony. Largely as a result of the evidence of the trial, Parliament curtailed the privileges of the company by transferring political and military authority to a board appointed by the Crown. The company retained its monopolistic privileges until 1813. 

Unrest was not allayed by these reforms, for the governors still possessed broad discretionary powers which they frequently abused. 

A great native uprising, known as the Sepoy Rebellion, which began among the Sepoys, or native troops, occurred in 1857 and was quelled with pitiless severity. An aftermath of the insurrection was the Better 

Government of India Act passed in 1858, which divested the company of its authority and privilege. Thereafter India was ruled as a crown colony. It was placed under a viceroy, responsible to a 

Secretary of State for India, who as a cabinet officer was responsible to Parliament. When Disraeli, an ardent imperialist, secured control of the Suez Canal by the purchase of the shares offered by the Khedive of Egypt, the value of Britain's eastern interests was greatly increased. In 1877, Victoria, in conformity with the Prime Minister's policy, assumed the title of "Empress of India." 

Agitation for self-government in India has become increasingly insistent, and within recent years dissatisfied elements have concentrated on demands for dominion status. The British have made a series of concessions to native sentiment. The Indian Councils Act of 1909 provided for the native election of twenty-five of the sixty-eight members of the Legislative Council. Ten years later, as a result of the 

Montague-Chelmsford report of 1918, a scheme of constitutional government was approved by Parliament, greatly increasing native

IMPERIALISM 

693 participation in both the provincial and central governments. The 

British are committed to the development of self-governing institutions in India. However, religious differences, illiteracy, and the rigid caste system have precluded the evolution of Indian nationalism on a scale sufficient to compel recognition of the full demands of Gandhi and other patriot leaders. Many Indians have gone into the civil service, and the beginnings of a parliamentary system have been established, but gains have been more apparent than real. Britain retains financial and diplomatic control without which self-government is illusory. India has been the most profitable of the British dependencies. Cotton, rice, and tea are the chief products. 

Other lucrative crown colonies are Ceylon, which produces tea, the Malay States, which afford tin and rubber, and various islands in the West Indies, which are valuable chiefly for fruit. The crown colonies in Africa, such as Nigeria, Uganda, and Kenya, produce cotton, cocoa, sugar, and foodstuffs.

IMPERIALISM AND WORLD CONFLICT 

The revival of imperialism caused frequent collisions of interests among the major European powers. An instance was furnished by events in Egypt. Ishmail Pasha, Khedive of Egypt under the nominal suzerainty of the Turkish Sultan, incurred heavy debts to European banking interests as a result of folly and extravagance. England and 

France jointly intervened, and financial control proving inadequate, they assumed political power. A serious native uprising of the 

Mahdi ensued which jeopardized the financial interests, with the result that England established sole control after France rejected an invitation to joint action. When England secured the dominant interest in the Suez Canal, possession of Egypt became vital as a link in the "life line " to the East. France soon realized she had lost a great prize. Her attempt to challenge England in the Sudan precipitated the dangerous Fashoda crisis (1898). Delcassé, the French Foreign

Minister, adopted a conciliatory attitude, and friction between the two powers abated when England gave France a free hand in Morocco (1904). 

After the middle of the nineteenth century, Africa was rapidly partitioned among the powers. World interest in the exploration of the "Dark Continent " was aroused by Stanley's rescue of Livingstone. King Leopold of Belgium was especially active in the promotion of the exploration of the Congo. A congress was convoked at 

Brussels (1876) to deal with problems incident to the opening of the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Congo to the penetration of foreign capital. A subsequent conference was held at Berlin in 1884, and the Congo Free State was created by a protocol of the following year. Belgium, in reality, enjoyed sole control and this situation was openly recognized in 1908. The barbarous treatment of the natives in the Congo constituted one of the most revolting chapters in the history of European imperialism. 

France was second only to Great Britain in the extent of her African colonial acquisitions. On the north coast she obtained a foothold in Algeria in 1830 and thence gradually expanded her control over not only the Algerian hinterland but also eastward into Tunis (1881) and westward into Morocco (1905). At the south entrance of the 

Red Sea she held the small but strategic colony of French Somaliland (1884). In 1843 the French likewise obtained a foothold on the 

Guinea and Ivory coasts of northwest Africa. Then in the decade from 1890 to 1900 French explorers and colonizers moved inland from Morocco, Tunis, the Ivory Coast, and the Congo until they obtained recognized possession of the Sahara Desert and the Wadai Sudan area. The island of Madagascar was taken in 1895. 

France's seizure of control in Tunis aroused great indignation in Italy, and was primarily responsible for the entrance of that country into the Triple Alliance (1882). Balked in north Africa, Italy turned to the east coast, where she established Eritrea (1885), Italian Somaliland (1887), and finally Tripoli on the north coast in 1911. Bismarck somewhat reluctantly brought Germany into the race with the acquisition of German Southwest and East Africa, Kamerun, and Togoland (1884-1885). The more aggressive policies of the reign of William II precipitated the Moroccan crises of 1905 and 1911, which will be discussed in connection with the origins of the World War. 

Clash of interests also marked European imperialism in the Far East. China under the Manchu emperors was an easy prey. As a result of the Opium War of 1839-1842, England acquired Hongkong and special privileges in other Chinese ports. The principle of extra-territoriality was established; that is, Europeans were declared exempt from the jurisdiction of Chinese courts in the designated ports. A second war (1856-1860) in which France also was involved resulted in the establishment of foreign legations in Peking. France, by 1885, had control of the whole eastern half of the Indo-Chinese peninsula. 

In the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) Japan obtained predominance in Korea. Soon thereafter the various imperialistic powers forced 

China to cede or lease strategic ports along her coasts: Germany obtained Kiaochow; Russia, Port Arthur; Great Britain, Wei-hai-wei;

IMPERIALISM 

695 and France, Kwang Chow Wan. This growing foreign dominance precipitated a nationalistic uprising in China known as the Boxer Rebellion (1900-1901). Foreigners were besieged in the British legation at Peking, but were rescued by an international force sent to their assistance. Heavy indemnities were imposed; the United States permitted the use of its share to defray the costs of the education of Chinese students in American universities. 

American interests in the Far East increased considerably after the acquisition of the Philippine Islands in 1898. The Open Door Policy, enunciated by John Hay, American Secretary of State, and supported by Great Britain, did much to restrain the other powers from proceeding to the outright dismemberment of China, and also provided for equal trading privileges and equal opportunities for investment. Russia and Japan came into conflict, however, owing to the extension of the former's interests into Manchuria and Korea. In the ensuing war of 1904-1905 Russia suffered several decisive defeats which, along with internal troubles, induced her to accept President Theodore Roosevelt's invitation to treat for peace. The Portsmouth Treaty awarded Japan a complete protectorate over Korea, which was annexed in 1910. Japan, reinforced by her alliance with England (1902), emerged as the dominant factor in the Far East. Her rapid assimilation of western industrialization made her a formidable competitor in the markets of the world, while her ever-increasing military strength became a threat to the principle of the "open door." These threats materialized in the conquest of Manchuria (1931-1933), and the subsequent Japanese assault upon China (1937-1939) in an undeclared but none the less bloody and devastating war. The summer of 1939 found nearly all of coastal China in Japanese hands, but a Chinese army still was valiantly resisting the invaders in the far interior.

CHAPTER 51 World War I: Its Causes and Its Course 

TORLD WAR I was, up to that time, the most appalling catastrophe in the history of Western civilization. More than 9,000,000 lives were sacrificed, while other millions of men were maimed, warped in mind, or seared in soul. The economic waste was incalculable: $223,000,000,000 is the estimate of war expenditures and property damage. The cost in terms of human anguish and the sacrifice of moral values cannot be computed. 

The fundamental causes of the conflict have become increasingly clear as several European governments have granted access to their archives. Nationalism, sedulously fostered by propaganda, imbued officials, as well as peoples, with the conviction that national interest could best be advanced by aggressive, even belligerent, policies. Nations involved in the struggle believed that they were destined to attain security, prosperity, and cultural advance at the expense of less favored countries. The Industrial Revolution, producing a demand for new markets and supplies of raw materials, had greatly stimulated imperialism, with its attendant national rivalries. 

National ambitions and rivalries resulted in the creation of alliances. 

The Triple Alliance, made up of Germany, Austria, and Italy, was counterbalanced by what was, in effect, the Triple Entente of England, France, and Russia. A succession of diplomatic crises, in the period 1878 to 1914, tightened the alliances and accentuated the divergence of interests between the two groups. Alliances greatly increased the danger, since it was difficult to localize diplomatic tension. 

So sensitive was the equilibrium that a comparatively trivial incident could precipitate a general European war. Fear and suspicion, aggravated by secret diplomacy and unstable boundaries, led to extensive military and naval preparations. When one nation increased the size of its army, or expanded its program of naval construction, other powers did likewise, creating a dangerous competition in armaments. There is no evidence that any of the nations forged these

weapons in preparation for aggression. However, with nations heavily armed, with plans for mobilization in readiness, with strategy worked out in minute detail, there was naturally greater danger of resort to force when a crisis came. The Hague Tribunal, the only available institution for the arbitration and adjudication of international issues, proved impotent to deal with a serious crisis. 

DIPLOMACY BEFORE WORLD WAR I 

The period 1870-1890 has been termed the Age of Bismarck. At the close of the Franco-Prussian War, the Iron Chancellor's policies seemed completely successful. A German Empire under Prussian domination had been founded; the attendant wave of nationalism had largely absorbed or diverted liberal elements. The powerful military machine, forged by Von Roon and Moltke, had given remarkable demonstrations of its prowess. The establishment of the 

Empire inaugurated a period of industrial expansion that was to make Germany one of the world's greatest manufacturing nations.

Annexation of Alsace and Lorraine had destroyed the possibility of a reconciliation with France. Austria resented the humiliations of 

1866 and her consequent expulsion from the Germanic confederacy; if she made an alliance with France, Bismarck's work even yet might be undone. The danger was all the more palpable in view of Germany's strained relations with Russia.

Since the enmity of France was implacable, Bismarck resolved to concentrate on a policy of friendship towards Austria and Russia. 

The fruit of this policy was the formation of the League of Three Emperors in 1873. This agreement provided for defensive coöperation. Although it gave Germany some assurance against attack, it was important principally as a prelude to a closer rapprochement with Austria. In tacit fashion, Russia agreed not to stir up unrest among the Slavs in Austria-Hungary, while Austria agreed to refrain from encouraging Polish discontent in Russia. 

The League of Three Emperors was broken down by tension in the Balkans. In 1877 Russia utilized a series of Turkish atrocities in 

Bulgaria to press her pan-Slavic policies in southeastern Europe. 

Turkey was badly defeated in the ensuing war, and was deprived of most of her European territory by the Peace of San Stefano which precipitated a general crisis. This settlement antagonized Austrian interests in the Balkans, and alarmed England and France because of the threat of ultimate Russian occupation of Constantinople. Bismarck, who professed indifference to the "Eastern Question," which

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

he said was "not worth the bones of a single Pomeranian Grenadier," offered mediation. As an "honest broker" he presided over the

Congress of Berlin (1878) which stripped Russia of many of the gains made by the San Stefano settlement. Bulgaria was deprived of 

Macedonia and Rumelia, which reverted to the Porte. Austria was assigned a protectorate over Bosnia and Herzegovina in the northwest corner of the Balkan peninsula, in contravention of the doctrine of pan-Slavism. Russian indignation centered on Germany; Gortchakov, the Russian foreign minister, partly because of his personal enmity towards Bismarck, did all he could to widen the breach. 

It was imperative for the chancellor to seek a stronger alliance with Austria; mutual danger from Russia made such an agreement feasible, indeed essential. Finally, in 1879, Bismarck was successful in negotiating the Austro-German Alliance, although he encountered some difficulty in getting Emperor William I to take this anti-Russian step. It was purely defensive. Each nation promised to aid the other in the event of a Russian attack, and they were to maintain benevolent neutrality toward each other if another power was the aggressor. 

The immediate effect was to strengthen Bismarck's hand, enabling him in 1881 to establish the Alliance of the Three Emperors with Russia and Austria-Hungary on the ruins of the old League. This new alliance guaranteed to Russia the closure of the Straits near Constantinople, to Bulgaria the eventual acquisition of Eastern Rumelia to the south, and to Austria-Hungary the future annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The Austro-German Alliance grew into the Triple Alliance of 

1882 with the adherence of Italy. The latter, ever since her capture of Rome in 1870, had feared a possible French attempt to restore that city to the pope. This francophobe attitude was heightened by the French seizure of Tunis in 1881, which effectively blocked Italian ambitions in that North African region. Italy finally overcame her anti-Austrian feeling, perpetuated by the Austrian possession of the Italian-inhabited regions of Trentino and Istria, and signed the Triple Alliance in Vienna. The agreement provided for Austrian and German assistance to Italy in the event of an attack by France. Italy, in return, promised to aid Germany if attacked by France. If any one of the allies were attacked by two or more powers, the others were bound to aid the one attacked. Italy insisted on the reservation that her commitments were not to be operative against England. When 

Austria and Russia had a disagreement in 1886, Bismarck was able to seal the breach in his defensive wall by his famous Reinsurance

Treaty with Russia in 1887 whereby Germany recognized Russia's special rights in the Balkans, and her claim to a preponderant position in Bulgaria, while the closure of the Straits was to be maintained. 

Each nation agreed to maintain neutrality if the other were attacked by a third power. When young Emperor William II " dropped the pilot" in 1890, the retired chancellor could point to a united nation, a prosperous citizenry contented by a program of state socialism, two decades of peace, and a foreign policy that afforded the maximum of security. But Bismarck's elaborate system of alliances could not be expected to last long without important changes. 

With the retirement of Bismarck, William II began to take an active part in the formulation of foreign policy. At best, his intervention was highly disturbing, and his predilection for rash statements kept his ministers nervous. Naturally the Emperor's views often were interpreted as expressions of the policies of the government, creating apprehension in the foreign offices of Europe. At William's side, as his principal adviser in foreign affairs for many years, stood the mysterious figure, Baron Friedrich von Holstein.

England and France had drawn apart as a result of the former's policies in Egypt. What had begun in 1877 as a joint Anglo-French intervention to safeguard financial interests was transformed in 1882 into sole control by Britain, largely because of England's vital interests in the Suez Canal. France accordingly moved closer toward 

Russia. Meanwhile William II made no effort to "keep the wire open to St. Petersburg," as Bismarck had counselled. Instead, he pushed

Ferdinand of Coburg, a German prince, for the throne of Bulgaria, and meddled in Turkey, sending German officers to help train the Sultan's army. A common enmity toward Germany therefore became a primary factor in the Franco-Russian rapprochement. A series of French loans to the Russian government was the prelude to diplomatic amenities that developed into military conversations. By 1894 a defensive alliance was consummated, although its terms remained secret until 1918. The agreement provided that if France was attacked by Germany, or by Italy with German support, Russia was to come to the aid of France. If Germany attacked Russia, France was to aid her ally. However, the defensive character of this alliance was somewhat compromised in 1912, when France indicated she would support her ally if a general war developed out of Balkan conflicts which Russia at that time was encouraging. From the outset, moreover, the alliance provided for joint mobilization the moment that a member of the Triple Alliance mobilized its troops.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

With the formation of the Triple Alliance and the conclusion of the Franco-Russian agreement, England began to lose faith in her policy of "splendid isolation." The British government found it difficult, however, to orient its policy towards either group of powers. In 1896, William's indiscreet telegram of congratulation to Paul 

Kruger, president of the Dutch government of Transvaal, had repercussions which unduly magnified the incident. The intervention of 

Germany in the complex Chinese situation by the seizure of Kiaochow (1898) was interpreted by Britain as a menace to her interests. 

Above all, about 1898 Germany embarked on the policy of building a big navy. A direct result was the conclusion of an Anglo-Japanese 

Alliance in 1902 which provided for mutual support in the Far East. 

Although English relations with Germany were strained by the incidents just mentioned, and kept strained by the expansion of the German fleet, friction with France also reached an acute stage when the latter seized Madagascar in 1898. The Fashoda incident of the same year brought the countries close to war. While a British army, under Kitchener, was subduing the Egyptian Sudan in 1898 by victories at Omdurman and Khartoum, Major Marchand, at the head of a French exploring expedition, had raised his country's flag at Fashoda farther up the Nile. When Kitchener arrived at Fashoda, he ordered 

Marchand to lower the French flag and evacuate his troops. Paris for a time refused to yield; each day the situation became more tense, until under the politic leadership of the foreign minister, Delcassé, France finally gave way to the English demands because she was weakened internally by the Dreyfus affair, and externally by the lack of Russian support. This crisis tended to accentuate the tension of Anglo- 

German diplomacy, because the Kaiser flirted with the French during this dispute to the discomfiture of the British. Rivalry in Samoa and covert German opposition to the British plan for a great Cape to Cairo railroad were also disturbing factors.

When Germany in 1903 secured concessions from the Sultan for the extension of a German-controlled railroad from Asia Minor to Bagdad and the Persian Gulf, a heavy obstacle was placed in the way of improved relations with the British. Plans called for the construction of a line from Konia to the Persian Gulf. England was confronted with the danger of a new route to the East that would largely replace her Suez route, and perhaps jeopardize her possession of India. She therefore impeded the project by agreements with petty native rulers, through whose territories the line was to pass. She likewise blocked the acquisition of terminal facilities on the Persian Gulf.

ST. PETER'S, ROME 

LELLOR BISMARCK

LOUIS PASTEUR RICHARD WAGNER THOMAS A. EDISON CHARLES DARWIN

Since a German alliance was virtually precluded, England drew towards France. French interests in Morocco were a powerful influence in the negotiations that culminated in the Entente of 1904, which gave France a free hand in Morocco and recognized her possession of Madagascar. France, in return, withdrew her opposition to England's control of Egypt. This Entente was not an alliance, but simply a friendly understanding, primarily upon colonial affairs. 

This agreement led to the First Morocco Crisis in 1905, when Germany brusquely demanded recognition of her interests in Morocco and offered opposition to French dominance in that region. 

President Theodore Roosevelt successfully urged the convocation of the Algeciras Conference (1906) to arbitrate the issues. A settlement was evolved which gave Germany the shadow of satisfaction, but left France with the substance of control. Moroccan sovereignty was reasserted and German interests were protected. France and her supporters, however, obtained virtual control of the bank, customs, and police in Morocco. Moreover, this conference, by presenting 

France and England with a common adversary, tended to strengthen the Entente between those two countries. 

Italy, always sensitive to the trend of British policy, began to veer from the orbit of the Triple Alliance in the direction of France. 

The Italians could never forget the Italia irredenta under Austrian control. In 1900, France and Italy signed a Mediterranean accord by which Italy recognized French dominance in Morocco and France agreed to Italian preponderance in Tripoli. The following year (1902), they made a secret neutrality agreement in which Italy promised France neutrality except when France, without provocation, attacked another power. These understandings, while nominally not in violation of the Triple Alliance, had the practical effect of destroying it, for Germany could no longer rely upon Italy's support against France.

Russo-British relations had become tense by 1905. During the 

Russo-Japanese War, the Russian fleet fired on several English fishing vessels off Dogger Bank, mistaking them for Japanese warships.

A more serious matter was the Anglo-Russian colonial dispute over 

Afghanistan, Persia, and Tibet. Conversations between the Kaiser and the Czar for a time promised to lead to an alliance. Izvolski, a strong advocate of an understanding with England, became foreign minister of Russia. Negotiations between him and the British leaders culminated in the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907). In effect, a Triple 

Entente of France, England, and Russia now balanced the alliance of

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the Central Powers, and Germany became alarmed over the threatened" encirclement."

A sharp crisis was precipitated by the Austrian annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1908). This action was in contravention of the Treaty of Berlin, although in practice the Austrian protectorate had been virtually tantamount to annexation. Russia connived at the annexation, since Izvolski hoped for concessions in the Straits by way of compensation. The hostility of England to Russian control of the 

Bosphorus foredoomed this plan. When Serbia threatened to challenge Austria, St. Petersburg, therefore, toyed with the idea of supporting her Slav protégé; but unmistakable intimations that such action would mean war with Germany caused her to desist. Meanwhile, Bulgaria had declared her independence of Turkey, and had become the theatre of a sharp Russo-German rivalry. 

Europe again came close to war as a result of the Second Moroccan Crisis of 1911. The action of France in sending troops into Morocco, on the plea that they were needed to restore order, doubtless was provocative. It was interpreted by Germany as the virtual establishment of a protectorate that would nullify the concessions procured at Algeciras. A ministerial change at Paris prevented immediate reply to German representations. The German Foreign Office, despite the 

Kaiser's opposition, then ordered a warship to Agadir and thereby greatly increased the tension. Its appearance there signified that Germany intended to demand substantial favors as the price of her consent to French policy. Through the influence of England, this dispute was settled by German recognition of France's suzerainty in Morocco in return for a large block of the French Congo. Lloyd 

George, however, in his Mansion House Speech, gave Berlin to understand that the patience of the English government was near exhaustion; another such incident would find Britain ready to accept the challenge. With the attentions of Europe focused on the Moroccan crisis, Italy seized Tripoli (1911). Her possession of it was confirmed by the Treaty of Ouchy in the following year. 

The four Balkan nations, Serbia, Greece, Montenegro, and Bulgaria, had long desired to expel Turkey from Europe and seize her possessions there; and now they were encouraged by the demonstration of Turkey's military feebleness. They formed a coalition, the Balkan League, and after Turkey had rejected a demand for Macedonian autonomy, launched an attack. In the First Balkan War (1912), the league utterly defeated Turkey. Austria insisted upon the independence of Albania. Serbia, thus deprived of one of her anticipated

rewards of the war, demanded from Bulgaria a larger share of Macedonia but was rebuffed. Bulgaria then attacked Serbia, but Greece, Rumania, and even Turkey, rallied to her defense. In this Second 

Balkan War, essentially a struggle over the division of spoils, Bulgaria was decisively defeated and forced to relinquish a considerable amount of territory by the Treaty of Bucharest (1913). Russia's hand was greatly strengthened by the Balkan Wars. The struggles sharpened the enmity between Austria and Serbia; and Serbian ambition to annex Bosnia and Herzegovina was the fuse that was to touch off the great explosion of 1914.

On June 28, 1914, the Archduke Francis Ferdinand, heir to the Austrian throne, visited Sarajevo, the Bosnian capital. The visit had been planned a year in advance. Serbian conspirators, members of a 

Black Hand organization consecrated to the liberation of their fellownationals from Austrian rule, came to Sarajevo, with the passive connivance of Serbian frontier officials, to assassinate him. Apparently aware of the plot, the Serbian government failed to stamp it out, and sent Austria only a vague general warning. While the archduke was being escorted to the city hall, one of the conspirators tossed a bomb into the tonneau of his motorcar. The archduke quickly threw the deadly missile from the car, but it exploded amid his bodyguard. The officials proceeded with the formal exercises. On the way back to his hotel, the archduke expressed a desire to visit the hospital to inquire about the condition of those injured by the bomb. His chauffeur misunderstood his instructions and turned off the main thoroughfare. 

When he realized his mistake, he reversed the car but stalled the engine. Princip, one of the conspirators, thereupon stepped down from the curb and emptied his revolver point-blank at the archduke and his wife, killing both.

The world knew that Austria would demand satisfaction from Serbia commensurate with the gravity of the incident. There seemed little reason, however, to fear a general European crisis. But when on July 23, Austria presented an indefensibly drastic ultimatum to Belgrade, tension increased to an alarming degree. Compliance with the Austrian demands would have meant a serious curtailment of Serbian sovereignty. Austria, reassured by a most unfortunate new promise of German support in whatever course she adopted, was adamant, although she realized that a declaration of war against Serbia would mean war with Russia. Serbia acceded to all points of the ultimatum except Austrian interference in her internal affairs, but four days later Austria nevertheless declared war. Germany at-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tempted to dissuade Russia from mobilization, but the Czar, unable to resist the importunities of his ministers and generals, ordered general mobilization on July 30. Germany countered by mobilization and declaration of war. In the meantime, she demanded that France clearly declare her intentions. France responded that she would have to consult her own interests and ordered mobilization. England had vainly tried to localize the struggle. When Germany, now a formidable naval power, invaded Belgium, England entered the war. 

All the major powers must share in different degree the guilt of precipitating the tragic struggle. Austria evinced a reckless desire to force a war with Serbia at all costs. The Serbian government was ready to accept practically all the terms of the ultimatum, despite the fact that she was given but forty-eight hours to reach a decision. Yet the Austrian leaders, in the face of the efforts of the powers to dissuade them, declared war in full realization that their action was almost certain to produce a general war. Germany had foolishly given 

Austria a "blank check," committing herself to support her ally before fully learning of her policy in the Serbian crisis. It is true that 

Berlin attempted to restrain Austria, but such action came too late to be effective. Then, too, it is likely that the German Foreign Office was partially cognizant of Austria's intentions towards Serbia even before the ultimatum was released. Russian mobilization destroyed the last hope of localizing the struggle, and no doubt assurances of French support hastened the Czar's order for mobilization. England, the least guilty of all the powers, is chargeable with nothing worse than inability to make her intentions clear. A firm declaration that she would stand by France might have caused Germany to hesitate, but public opinion was divided, and Sir Edward Grey, who to the last labored devotedly for peace, felt unable to give a clear assurance of Great Britain's course prior to the invasion of Belgium. The primary blame for the war, however, must rest upon certain defects in the general civilization of Europe and the world - upon greed, brutality, and stupidity; upon nationalism, imperialism, militarism, and navalism. 

The war opened with Germany's smashing drive on Paris. Using the Von Schlieffen plan, the Germans invaded France through neutral Belgium. It was hoped that France would be crushed rapidly enough to permit the withdrawal of German divisions to the eastern. front to defend East Prussia against Russian invasion. The German

General Staff had estimated that Russian mobilization would be sufficiently slow to make the plan feasible. Belgium, however, refused to permit the passage of the German forces through her territory, despite promises of subsequent compensation. The heroic resistance of the little Belgian army retarded the German advance and evoked the admiration of the world. Germany's wanton violation of the treaties guaranteeing the neutrality of Belgium turned world opinion against her and ensured Great Britain's immediate entrance into the war on the side of France. Atrocity stories, some fiction and some true, also did much to crystallize hostile sentiment toward the invaders. 

The German military machine showed startling power. Its great siege guns pulverized fortresses in a few hours, and lighter artillery unloosed devastating barrages. The fall of Paris seemed so imminent that the French government moved to Bordeaux as a precautionary measure. But the Von Schlieffen plan did not work perfectly because of blunders and the desperate Belgian resistance. In September (1914) the French and British, commanded by Joffre, were able to arrest the German advance at the decisive battle of the Marne. In the meantime, the Russians had mobililized with unexpected speed and begun an invasion of East Prussia. Their advance was stopped by Hindenburg and Ludendorf at the battle of Tannenberg, where the Russians were crushed with prodigious losses.

It was not long before several other countries entered the conflict upon one side or the other. Turkey joined the Central Powers in 1914 in order to thwart Russian designs on Constantinople. Bulgaria followed her into the same camp in 1915 to revenge herself upon Serbia for the defeat inflicted in 1913. On the other hand, Japan immediately chose the Allied side. More important still, Italy in 1915 abandoned her neutrality toward the Central Powers and joined with Great

Britain, France, and Russia on the ground that Austria was not promising her sufficient compensations in the Italian populated regions of the Trentino and the Adriatic. Rumania, too, finally came in with the Allies. 

The most striking campaign of 1915 was in Gallipoli. Here for months a British army and fleet hammered gallantly but fruitlessly at the impregnable fortifications. Allied armies on the western front remained practically idle, thus enabling the diversion of German troops to the defense of the Straits. The abortive campaign well illustrated the paramount need for promptness of movement and unity of command.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

England's enormous fleet, augmented by the warships of her allies, enjoyed a complete mastery. Germany was effectively cut off from supplies of munitions, raw materials, and foodstuffs, whereas the Allies could purchase virtually unlimited supplies from the United States and other neutral countries. The German battle fleet, whose officers often had toasted the day when England's naval supremacy would be shattered, was bottled up in the Kiel base. A German squadron was badly crippled in the battle off Dogger Bank. Later a largescale German movement resulted, half-accidentally, in an encounter off Jutland with the main British battle-fleet under the command of Beatty and Jellicoe. The Germans gained a tactical victory in this battle of Jutland (1916), the major naval encounter of the war; but fundamentally the English were victorious, since the Germans abandoned their projected attack on the English coast and fled back to their base. They never came out again. All the oceans were swept clear of German vessels, and the German colonies fell into Allied hands.

The war on the western front, fought in great trench-systems, was virtually a stalemate from 1915 to 1916. Advances of a few miles were made, only to be lost. Defensive tactics were so efficient as to prevent decisive action. Great battles raged for days, with appalling loss of life, yet left the end of the conflict as remote as ever. Introduction of new offensive weapons, such as poison gas, was tentative and experimental. Even the tank or armored car, a device brought forward by the British in September, 1916, and probably the greatest innovation of the war, was at first tried cautiously and half-heartedly; so that its effect was largely sacrificed, and defensive measures were available before the full power of the new weapon was applied. For months in 

1916, the Germans pounded at Verdun until their casualties reached the staggering figure of approximately 800,000. French losses were also fearfully high; and both nations were left temporarily almost exhausted. Before the struggle at Verdun ended, the British had launched their great offensive on the Somme river, which gained considerable ground, but only at the cost of tremendous casualty lists. On the western front the antagonists seemed unable to break their deadlock.

Allied fortunes had reached a low ebb in 1917. There was a growing disposition to seek a negotiated peace in view of the apparent impossibility of securing a decisive result. Germany's submarine warfare was beginning to exact a heavy toll on Allied shipping, and the withdrawal of Russia from the war by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk

as a consequence of the Revolution of March, 1917, was a terrific blow. At this juncture America entered the struggle. 

American public opinion had veered sharply to the Allied side for various reasons - kinship with the British peoples, the old sentimental regard for France, horror over the invasion of Belgium, dislike of the German system of government, and detestation of German" ruthlessness." Submarine warfare against merchant ships, which in 1915 had horrified the world with the sinking of the great liner Lusitania, produced intense indignation, and the protests of the American State Department to Germany were unavailing. Many American lives were lost; the situation grew intolerable. A declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare by the German admiralty in 1917, with no regard whatever for American rights, finally brought about the reluctant decision of the American government under Woodrow Wilson to enter the war. By the end of 1917, Greece, Siam, China, Japan, and most of the Latin-American nations had also joined the Allies, making the conflict a veritable World War of twenty-three nations against four. 

Germany's desperate efforts in 1918 to win the war before American troops could be brought to the front ended in failure. Not only did America send 2,000,000 men in a great expeditionary force commanded by General John J. Pershing, but she also raised the morale of the Allies and increased the effectiveness of their forces by furnishing large quantities of supplies, munitions, and credits. The last 

German drive was halted in the second battle of the Marne at Château-Thierry in July 1918; and then, under the new unified and supreme command of Marshal Foch, the Allied counter-attack proved irresistible. Drive after drive, launched with bewildering rapidity, now in France, now in Italy, now in the Balkans, again in the Holy Land, caused the exhausted lines of the Central Powers to crumble. 

Bulgaria surrendered in September, Turkey in October, and Austria- Hungary in early November. The Hindenburg Line had been broken in northeastern France, and wave on wave of French, British, and American troops began to sweep the Germans back toward the 

Rhine. Finally, on November 10, Kaiser William II fled from Germany to the Netherlands, and on the following day the new German Republic signed an armistice with Foch providing for a complete military capitulation based on adherence to Wilson's "Fourteen Points" in the final peace. A conference was to be convoked at Paris early in 1919 to draw up the definitive terms of settlement. 

The petty and selfish imperialistic aims of the Allies at the beginning of the war had begun to lose their popular attractiveness as the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

hostilities became prolonged and the casualties mounted. Early in 1918 a restatement of objectives had to be formulated along idealistic lines to stimulate the war-wearied peoples to continued effort. They were then promised by various leaders, and notably by David Lloyd George in England, that this should be "a war to end wars,” a "war to make the world safe for democracy." When the United States entered the conflict, its president emphasized these higher objectives. 

If permanent peace and a new and stable world-order based on the general acceptance of democratic ideals could be achieved, even the terrible price paid in this holocaust of mutual destruction might not be excessive. But could it? The question remained whether the peace conference could assure the fulfillment of those bright visions of international amity and progress which Woodrow Wilson was holding up before mankind.

CHAPTER 52 Europe Between Two Wars 

DIPLOMACY OF PEACE 

ORLD WAR I did not end war, and the peace settlement did not bring the war-weary peoples the permanent peace they anticipated. The responsibility for this disappointing outcome must be laid primarily at the door of the postwar statesmen of the victorious countries, but also indirectly upon the propagandainflamed peoples themselves, who impelled their leaders to seek a peace of revenge. In fact, a struggle went on at the Paris peace conference between the farsighted peace-makers and the shortsighted seekers of revenge, which ended largely in a victory for the latter. 

The former had in their favor the existence of democratic governments among both friends and foes, the acceptance of Wilson's Fourteen Points as the general basis of peace in the armistice, and Wilson's own leadership for a peace of reconciliation. The Fourteen Points outlined a settlement founded upon no idemnities, national self-determination, impartial colonial adjustments, and a league of nations. But the more shortsighted leaders in Great Britain, France, and Italy tried to carry out secret partition treaties which granted to the signatories large territorial gains at the expense of their enemies. David 

Lloyd George came to the peace conference with a recent election. mandate to take revenge on Germany. Naturally the general spirit in France, led by Premier Clemenceau and President Poincaré, was one of vengeful determination to weaken Germany so completely that she never again would endanger the security of the French Republic. The Italians under Orlando and Sonnino evinced a similar spirit.

The apostles of revenge won marked advantages from the start. 

The calling of the Peace Conference in the city of Paris was prejudicial to fair peace terms; then the defeated powers were denied participation in the negotiations; and finally a Council of Ten (two dele-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

gates each from Great Britain, France, Italy, the United States, and Japan) was appointed to make all the important decisions. Eventually meetings of the "Big Four" (Lloyd George, Clemenceau, Wilson, and Orlando) took the place of the Council of Ten when Japan limited her participation to questions involving the Far East. Whether in the Council of Ten or among the "Big Four," the selfish and shortsighted leaders had a controlling majority and proceeded to push through their program. France wanted to possess all of the Saar Basin, erect a buffer state in the Prussian Rhineland, and impose an indemnity to pay all the Allied war costs, both civil and military. Great 

Britain wanted to take all of Germany's colonies, destroy her fleet, and appropriate her merchant marine. In vain did President Wilson contend against these ambitions. He obtained only a half-victory, and even that was won in large part because of British objections to the excessive crippling of Germany. A large liberal and labor element in 

Great Britain was opposed to vengeful policies, while even the "realists" in that country comprehended the dangers of French domination of the Continent.

The Peace Treaties 

The terms imposed on Germany were embodied in the Treaty of Versailles, signed in the Hall of Mirrors in the Palace of Louis XIV on June 28, 1919. Not only did the German delegates have to accept a dictated peace, but they also had to suffer the intentional humiliation of signing in the very room where the German Empire had been exultantly proclaimed in 1871. But fate was preparing a heavy retribution for the victors as well as the vanquished. 

In territory Germany lost 25,000 square miles with a population of 6,000,000 in Europe and 1,000,000 square miles and a population of 12,000,000 in the colonies. Alsace-Lorraine went to France; Moresnet, Eupen, and Malmédy were given to Belgium by a questionable plebiscite; and the Saar Basin was put under the League of Nations for fifteen years, with the management of its coal mines confided to France. In 1935 the Saar was returned after a League plebiscite had determined that 90 per cent of its inhabitants favored Germany. In southeast Germany part of Upper Silesia was given to Poland after a plebiscite in 1921. To the north a plebiscite assigned the northern districts of Schleswig to Denmark. On the east Memel was eventually (1924) allocated to Lithuania; Danzig was set up as an internationalized port under the League of Nations; while its hinterland of the 

Polish Corridor from the Baltic southward along the Vistula river

to Warsaw, including the district of Posen, was ceded outright to Poland. 

The colonies of the defeated powers were distributed to the victors in the form of mandates under the League of Nations, which was merely an euphemistic arrangement tantamount to actual cession. 

Germany's Togoland and the Kamerun were divided between Great Britain and France. German Southwest Africa went to the British 

Union of South Africa, and German East Africa was given to Great Britain and Belgium. In the Pacific, Australia received mandates over the German portion of New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago; 

New Zealand obtained a mandate for the German islands of the Samoan group; and Japan inherited mandates over the Caroline and 

Marshall Islands as well as Germany's economic rights in Chinese Shantung and a settlement at Tsingtao. Only one of the "Big Four,” the United States, neither sought nor received a square foot of territory. "To make possible the initiation of a general limitation of armaments of all nations" (so the treaty said), Germany was allowed an army of only 100,000 long-term volunteers; a navy of only six battleships, six light cruisers, and no submarines; and no military air force. 

Her fortifications on the east were not to be changed, and on the west the Rhine was to be demilitarized for fifty miles from the east bank. Allied armies of occupation were to hold the region west of the Rhine and the bridge-heads across the river from Cologne, Coblenz, and Mainz. The cost of the occupation was to be paid by Germany and on this score the United States, which occupied the Coblenz area, demanded its share of indemnifications. An Inter-Allied 

Commission of Control was to watch over the observance of these military terms from their headquarters in Berlin. Having thus paralyzed Germany, the Allied countries promptly lost their interest in general disarmament. 

The "reparations" payments imposed on Germany were based on Article 231 of the Versailles Treaty, which affirmed "the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of 

Germany. . . ." Historians, however, have shown that, although

Germany and Austria may bear the greater guilt, some Allied countries also had a share in precipitating World War I. Yet Germany's war guilt was made the justification for her payment of all the reparations for civilian losses including pensions to the wounded, widows, and orphans. Not until two years after Germany had signed the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

treaty did the Reparations Commission finally decide on a total of $33,000,000,000. This enormous sum seemed to indicate the intention of the Allies to cripple Germany for nearly a century. 

By the Treaty of St. Germain (1919) Austria subscribed to equally drastic terms. The new state of Czechoslovakia received Bohemia and Moravia; Poland received most of Galicia; Rumania obtained 

Bukovina; Italy received the South Tyrol, Trentino, Trieste, Istria, and some ports and islands along the eastern Adriatic coast; and 

Yugoslavia (formerly Serbia and Montenegro) received Dalmatia,

Bosnia, and Herzegovina. All that remained of Austria was a small body of land extending from the North Tyrol to the Danube, including the once proud capital city of Vienna and containing only 6,500,000 population. Furthermore, Austria was positively forbidden to join the German Reich, her army was reduced to 30,000, and an undetermined burden of reparations was imposed.

Hungary, now a separate state, was compelled in 1920 to sign similar terms in the Trianon Treaty. She lost Slovakia and Ruthenia to 

Czechoslovakia, Transylvania and part of the Banat of Temesvár to Rumania, and Croatia, Slavonia, and the rest of the Banat to Yugoslavia. The port of Fiume, which was at first recognized as a free city by the Treaty of Rapallo (1920), was in 1924 acknowledged by Yugoslavia as belonging to Italy. All that remained to Hungary was 

35,000 square miles, with 8,000,000 inhabitants. She was likewise compelled to reduce her army to 35,000 men and pay an indefinite sum of reparations. 

Bulgaria's peace terms were defined in the Treaty of Neuilly (1919). Western Thrace was surrendered to Greece and a few border districts to Yugoslavia. Bulgaria's army was seriously reduced, and she was forced to promise the payment of a fixed sum of $450,000,000 as reparations.

A second treaty was necessary before peace was made with Turkey. A nationalist uprising under the leadership of Mustapha Kemel caused the rejection of the Treaty of Sèvres (1920), and drove the Greeks out of Smyrna and Asia Minor in 1922. By the Treaty of 

Lausanne (1923) the new Turkish Republic retained Constantinople and a small area around it in Europe, although the Straits and the European boundaries were demilitarized. Italy obtained the Dodecanese Islands, Greece received most of the remaining islands of the Aegean, France took a mandate over Syria and Lebanon, and Great Britain acquired a mandate over Palestine and Mesopotamia.
