provinces and Egypt, she recovered Armenia, with all of Thrace up to the Maritsa River and a small area beyond; she was allowed unrestricted possession of a great part of Asia Minor, and the abolition of foreign capitulations; and the Turkish-Iraq frontier was left to future settlement. She was also given a clear title to certain Aegean islands and the Straits. These terms were much more favorable than those of the original Sèvres Treaty.

All of the peace treaties except that of Lausanne breathed the spirit of revenge and by their severity created more problems than they solved. Boundaries were drawn with a view to strategic defense rather than to nationality. Consequently after the peace many peoples were still national minorities within a country not of their own choosing: Germans in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Italy, and Lithuania; Hungarians in Czechoslovakia and Rumania; Ukranians in

Poland, Czechoslovakia, and the Soviet Union. To ease the tensions remaining after the imposed peace, the great powers adopted certain alleviations. Among these were the mandate system and the special treaties for the protection of minorities. Under the mandate system, the colonies taken from Germany and the areas in Asia given up by Turkey passed to the League of Nations, which chose some of the victorious powers to administer them under League “mandates.”

Although the powers made annual reports to the League, and the mandates might be revoked, in reality possession of a mandate conferred nearly all the rights of ownership. The minority treaties were imposed upon Poland, Rumania, Greece, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia when they took over national minorities. They provided for equal civil and political rights by these minorities, freedom of worship, and protection in the use of their own languages and the maintenance of their own schools. The League was made the guarantor of these minority rights, and all complaints or disputes were to be submitted to the Permanent Court of International Justice. Unfortunately, these guaranties proved inadequate. It should be said here that the League of Nations, at the insistence of President Wilson, was made an integral part of the Treaty of Versailles. This institution will be discussed below at greater length,' but here it may be noted that the League acted as an instrument of enforcement for many treaty clauses, notably those affecting the Saar, plebiscites elsewhere, minorities, and mandates.

Of the victorious powers the United States alone refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles and join the League of Nations. The United 

1 See infra, pp. 714–716.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

States Senate, which has the ratifying power, was critical of the treaty for three reasons: (1) because President Wilson, one of its principal authors, was a Democrat, and the majority of the Senate was Republican; (2) because the treaty included numerous injustices, such as the right (though later relinquished) of Japanese control over Shantung which offended many Americans; (3) because Article 10 of the 

League Covenant appeared likely to involve the United States in wars in other parts of the world. The absence of the United States from the 

Council of Ambassadors and the League gave the vengeful Allies free rein to carry out the treaties and policies of the League in a callous and selfish manner.

The League of Nations 

· President Wilson was the main promoter of the League of Nations. The final Covenant was worked out from several drafts drawn up by various hands; and the authors or contributors included Colonel E. M. House and David Hunter Miller of the United States, Lord Robert Cecil of Great Britain, General Smuts of the Union of South Africa, and Léon Bourgeois of France. The articles of the 

Covenant, or constitution, of the League were made an integral part of all the peace treaties. It came into formal effect on January 10, 1920. 

The Covenant provided for a Council, an Assembly, and a Secretariat. The Council was at first made up of five permanent members (the great powers) and four non-permanent members. The membership changed from time to time until in 1939 there were only three permanent members left (Great Britain, France, and the Soviet Union) and ten non-permanent members with three-year terms expiring in rotation. The Council met three times a year, or more often if necessary. It had the executive powers of the League, while the Assembly was primarily a body for the discussion of international questions, and the focusing of world sentiment upon controversial issues.

In the Assembly every member had representation and one vote. 

In 1934 every important country (58) belonged to the League except the United States. But by 1939 Japan, Germany, Italy, and Brazil had withdrawn from membership. The Assembly held one regular session at Geneva every September, and as many more as occasion required. French and English were the official languages of the 

League, but a well organized, instantaneous translation service made it possible for a delegate to speak in his own native tongue and be

heard in French or English by earphones at the desks of the other members. The Assembly dealt with all questions lying within the terms of the League Covenant, or likely to affect the peace of the world. Its powers were largely moral. 

The Secretariat was headed by a Secretary-General and a large staff of assistants. Sir Eric Drummond was the first Secretary-General, and Joseph Avenol succeeded him. The Secretariat prepared and called meetings on instructions from Council or Assembly. It supervised arrangements, printed records and proceedings, received the copies of treaties deposited by members, and managed the finances, which involved a budget of only about $6,000,000 a year. It also collected a vast amount of accurate data on the affairs of member states, and had thus become a clearing-house for world information. 

The main purpose of the League was to preserve the peace of the world. Each member state engaged to guarantee the political independence and territorial integrity of every other member (Article 10); had the right to bring to the attention of the League any circumstance threatening the peace of the world (Article 11); it promised to settle all justiciable disputes by arbitration or judicial decision (Article 13); and finally, it agreed to bring other types of disputes before the Council for settlement (Article 15). If the Council could not settle the non-justiciable dispute by a unanimous vote of the disinterested members, then the interested parties were left free to take such action as they deemed just. If, however, a League member refused to abide by awards or decisions or, without resort to peaceful settlement, committed an overt aggression against another member of the League, that member was considered to have committed an act of war against every member of the League (Article 16). The members promised immediately to cut off all trade with the offending state; and if economic sanctions were not sufficient, the Council by unanimous vote might " recommend " a certain course of military action to the members of the League. This League procedure, however, proved so cumbersome that it appeared useful rather in encouraging a delay during which the feelings of the disputants might cool, than in actually stopping a war which had already broken out. The League settled a number of serious international quarrels, notably an Italo- Greek dispute in 1923, and a Greco-Bulgarian clash in 1925, but failed utterly to cope with disputes between the great powers after 1931.

As an aid to its work in composing international disputes a Permanent Court of International Justice, the "World Court" as it was

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

called, was organized by the League in 1920. The American jurist, Elihu Root, was one of the principal organizers of the court. It consisted of fifteen judges nominated by the League Council and elected by the League Assembly for a term of nine years. At its seat in the 

Peace Palace at The Hague this court adjudicated disputes, furnished advisory opinions on international law to the League Council, or even decided disputes according to laws and treaties if the states so agreed. Indeed, an optional clause of the protocol of the court might be accepted by a state, which obliged that state to submit all disputes involving international law or the interpretation of treaties to the court when such disputes were with other states who were willing to accept the jurisdiction of the court. Thus the jurisdiction of the court might be either voluntary or compulsory. It differed from the older Hague Court of Arbitration in that it was a tribunal of law, not of arbitration; it was permanent; and it began to build up a body of jurisprudence based upon international law and treaties. 

In spite of the fact that the use of the court was not compulsory, that Root helped form it, that one judgeship had always been assigned to an American, and that all the American presidents of the period advocated American membership, the United States Senate persistently withheld its consent to membership even with reservations. 

One branch of the League's supplementary organization which the United States did join in 1934 was the International Labor Organization. This resembled the League in its framework, having an Office, a Governing Body, and an annual Conference. Representation on the Body and in the Conference was on the basis of one-fourth each for labor and employers and one-half for the governments. John G. 

Winant, an American, was the director of the Office after 1938. 

The I. L. O. recommended certain general standards of fair labor practice to the industrial nations and drew up certain model treaties on specific reforms which it submitted to member states for ratification.

Reparations and Debts 

As early as 1923 Germany found it impossible to pay the regular installments of her $33,000,000,000 reparations charge. After a 

French punitive expedition into the rich industrial Ruhr valley had failed, the Dawes Plan (1924) and the Young Plan (1929) were adopted in succession to bring the installments within Germany's capacity to pay. But the world depression beginning in 1929 caught 

Germany as well as her creditors in its grasp, making necessary first a

moratorium (1931-1932), and finally, in the latter year, a drastic reduction of reparations to $714,000,000. Even this smaller sum was repudiated by Adolf Hitler in 1937.

Side by side with the Allied problem of getting reparations from Germany was America's task of getting repayment of war debts from her Allied debtors. When these debtor nations pleaded inability to pay and demanded at least partial cancellation as America's contribution to the common cause, the United States finally agreed to reduce the sums owed to about half the principal and interest. 

However, after the depression had arrived and Germany had repudiated her reparations, the Allies defaulted on all their debt installments. 

Finland alone continued to meet her debt obligations. While the 

Allies could cancel their reparations losses to a certain extent by defaulting on their debts, the United States, who was the creditor of last resort, suffered most of all from this policy of general repudiation. 

Limitation of Armaments 

Although Germany had been almost disarmed by the Versailles Treaty, France and her satellites, Belgium, Poland, and the Little Entente, continued to increase their armaments. The United States and England also seemed about to begin a naval race. Earnest efforts were made, however, to stem the tide of militarism. In 1922 at the 

Washington Conference the naval powers accepted a 5:5:3: 1.75: 

1.75 ratio in battleships for Great Britain, the United States, Japan, France, and Italy respectively. A Nine-Power Pact was also signed to protect Chinese sovereignty and the status quo in the Far East. 

At the London Conference (1930) Great Britain and the United States agreed on parity of tonnage for cruisers, but qualified their step by an "escalator clause" which allowed either power to step up its building in case France or Italy began a naval race. At the 

Geneva Conference (1932-1933) an effort was made to obtain land disarmament. Germany insisted on parity; France demanded security.

When no agreement seemed possible, Germany withdrew from the conference and from the League of Nations. After this futile effort to guarantee peace by diplomacy, the energies of all the great nations were turned again to the piling up of huge armaments. 

Peace Gestures 

One of the most serious deterrents to disarmament lay in the sense of insecurity among the nations. In 1923 the League Assembly tried to remedy this by strengthening the Covenant with a security treaty

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

which provided that all the signatories would come to the aid of a state which had disarmed according to a League program if that state were attacked. The League Council was to determine within four days whether an aggression had been committed. The vagueness of the term "aggression " led to the drawing up of the Geneva Protocol in 1924, which declared that all disputes must be settled by the World Court or arbitration. Any state going to war without first resorting to arbitration or some other mode of peaceful settlement of the dispute would automatically become the aggressor. This definition seemed too sweeping to Great Britain, as represented by her Conservative foreign minister, Austen Chamberlain; the Dominions feared being involved in petty European quarrels, and home sentiment seemed opposed to acceptance of the Protocol. 

Chamberlain, however, helped to promote security in the limited sphere of the Franco-German border by the Locarno Agreement of 1925. Stresemann and Briand, foreign ministers of Germany and 

France respectively, showed much good will in support of the move. 

Germany, France, and Belgium promised not to violate their mutual frontiers, and Germany promised Czechoslovakia and Poland that she would not alter her southern and eastern boundaries except by peaceful agreement. Germany also reaffirmed her promise not to remilitarize the Rhine. On the other hand, Great Britain and Italy promised to come to the aid of France, Belgium, or Germany if they were attacked on their coterminous frontiers. To further this principle of "collective security," they admitted Germany to the League in 1926 and assigned her a permanent seat in the Council. 

The following year Briand proposed an anti-war pact between 

France and the United States. Secretary of State Kellogg replied that he would like to see such a pact signed by all nations. Consequently in 1928 fifteen nations met in Paris and signed this multilateral Kellogg-Briand (or Paris) Pact. In due time all the nations adhered to the instrument. Each government declared that it outlawed war as an instrument of national policy and engaged to settle all its international disputes by peaceful means. The United States fatally qualified her obligation, however, by insisting that a war of self-defense was not included in the scope of the pact. Since every nation judges for itself what is self-defense and usually asserts that any war in which it is engaged is defensive, this reservation undermined the value of the pact. Thus between 1919 and 1932 the nations of the world seemed to be making continuous but ineffectual efforts to obtain a system of peace and security.

DOMESTIC POLICIES 

Great Britain

To mark and protect the progress which social democracy had made during the World War, Great Britain passed the Reform Bill of 1918, which gave the suffrage to all men over twenty-one regardless of property qualifications and to all women over thirty. Ten years later the " flapper "suffrage was extended to women between twentyone and thirty. When the Conservatives were defeated in 1923 upon the issue of a protective tariff, Great Britain accepted another innovation in the selection in 1924 of a Labor Party ministry with Liberal support. 

In the space of seventeen years the Laborites had increased their strength from 29 members of Parliament to 191 and from 320,000 voters to 4,350,000. Their moderately radical program for the compensated nationalization of large industries under labor management and guaranteed work at a living wage made a strong appeal to workers of both hand and brain in the troublesome years of unemployment and maladjustment right after World War I. Ramsey 

MacDonald, the Labor prime minister, was unable to carry out these policies, however, because his Liberal supporters would not tolerate sweeping changes. Indeed, they deserted him in the same year because of false rumors that he had tolerated Russian communist propaganda; and the resulting election brought the Conservatives back into power.

The Conservative ministry under Baldwin faced in 1926 the crisis of a serious strike of more than 2,000,000 workers called in sympathy with striking miners who were fighting against wage reductions. Although there was no violence, the government broke the movement in nine days by its firm resistance, taking the attitude that it could not tolerate a strike of such proportions as to endanger parliamentary government. To prevent any recurrence of the crisis, Parliament passed the Trade Unions and Trade Disputes Act of 

1927 which severely restricted union rights and activities. General and sympathetic strikes were outlawed, and picketing was practically abolished.

In 1929 the Laborites, with the aid of the Liberals, again obtained control of the government. This time they were able to pass measures providing for widows' pensions, more unemployment insurance, and coal mining reform. But the great depression of 1929–

1933 was weighing heavily on the country, and a financial crisis impelled MacDonald in 1931 to reform his government into a National cabinet of Laborites, Conservatives, and Liberals. This move split the Laborites into national and anti-coalition factions. In the elections of 1931 and 1935 the Conservatives won so many seats that ROSS

The problem of Ireland, which had troubled the British for centuries, was not completely solved by the acts of 1914 and 1920. 

The Irish nationalists insisted that the island should become an independent republic. Finally, in 1921, a compromise arrangement brought about a measure of appeasement. The Irish agreed on the maintenance of sovereignty by the Crown, but the British recognized an Irish Free State having the same dominion status as Canada. 

North Ireland refused to join the Free State and thus inspired further unionist activities to the south. By a new constitution in 1937 

Ireland substituted an elected president for the usual British governorgeneral. The problem of uniting North and South Ireland still remains a burning question.

While Ireland became a dominion, dominion status itself approached nearer to actual national independence. At the Imperial 

Conference of 1926 Great Britain recognized the dominions as sister states equal to her within a British Commonwealth of Nations ruled by one king. Thenceforth the governors-general were to be chosen on the advice of the dominion cabinets; the dominion constitutions could be amended by dominion action alone; and every dominion could carry on its own foreign relations by a separate corps of diplomatic representatives. The Statute of Westminster, passed by the British Parliament in 1931, ratified this arrangement and also provided that there should be no change in the succession without the approval of the parliaments of all the dominions. 

Within five years after the passage of this statute a question of succession arose. King George V died early in 1936 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Edward VIII. Before the year was out, however, the new bachelor king confessed his love for an American commoner twice divorced, Mrs. Wallis Warfield Simpson. Baldwin, then prime minister, expressed consternation at the prospect of a twice-divorced queen and, after consultation with the prime ministers of the dominions, reported that the opinion of the whole empire was opposed to the marriage. Without seeking the approval of any parliament, even that of his own, the prime minister gave the King the choice of his throne or Mrs. Simpson. The King offered his abdication which, under the circumstances, was rather an acquiescence in his dethronement. His next younger brother succeeded him as George VI, while he and "the woman he loved" went into exile on the Continent as the Duke and Duchess of Windsor.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION France 

From 1919 to 1924 France was governed by a National Bloc composed of the parties of the Right and Center who favored strict enforcement of the Treaty of Versailles. One of the difficult problems they had to face was the reassimilation of Alsace and Lorraine. 

France wanted Alsatians to use the French language rather than German and eliminate religious instruction from the schools. The regained provinces longed for their autonomous government and business connections with Germany. It was finally arranged that 

German could be taught in the schools and used in the public services. A certain period each week was designated for religious instruction, and autonomous government under a French commissioner-general was permitted until 1925. 

Economically the two provinces of Alsace and Lorraine had to content themselves with a gradual adjustment to life within the French national economy, and politically after 1925 they had to accept inclusion in the French centralized system as the three departments of Upper Rhine, Lower Rhine, and Moselle. Strong agitation was begun in 1926 by the Home Rule League for a return of local autonomy, and four Alsatians were convicted of conspiracy and disloyalty in 1928. During the trials another Alsatian tried to assassinate the prosecuting attorney. Although feeling subsided with the realization that there was more freedom under the French centralized system than there would be under the Nazi dictatorship in Germany, still discontent did not entirely disappear in these Rhine departments. 

Even more difficult of solution was the financial problem. While 

France was in debt to both the United States and England and was receiving very little from German reparations, she had to meet the burdensome costs of reconstruction, rearmament, and increasing government services. The franc had declined in value during the war, and it continued its depreciation in the troublesome postwar period. Finally Poincaré, as premier, stabilized the franc at 3.93 cents and instituted other drastic financial reforms which were beneficial to France until 1932, when she began to feel the effects of the world depression.

The war had had the effect of dulling the sharp dispute between clericals and anti-clericals. Both had served France loyally; the tragedies of the conflict had brought many back to the fold of the church; and Alsace and Lorraine objected to the government's anti-

clerical program inherited from the prewar period. Consequently in 1921 the French government renewed relations with the Vatican, turned over the title to church property to diocesan bodies headed by bishops, and permitted the return of some religious orders. 

The world depression, which began in 1929, did not affect France until 1932. But then her exports declined rapidly, unemployment became acute, and the tourist trade dropped off to an alarming degree. 

In the face of these conditions her statesmen found themselves in a quandary. They could not borrow easily because France was already badly in debt; they had taxed the people to the limit; the civil service officials and veterans refused to take reductions in salaries and pensions; and another depreciation of the currency would bring strong protests from the investing class, which had already suffered severely from Poincaré's earlier devaluation. A succession of mild

Radical-Socialist premiers between 1932 and 1936 failed to find a satisfactory solution.

In that difficult year of 1936 came the French parliamentary elections. Faced by the current financial difficulties, growth of French fascism, and threats from fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany, the three left parties of Radical-Socialists, Socialists, and Communists united in a Popular Front for election purposes. The Socialists alone won a plurality, and the Popular Front together had a majority. Under a Socialist premier, Léon Blum, the new government instituted a few fundamental reforms. The trade-union supporters of the Popular Front had already inaugurated sit-down strikes for better terms of employment. After the government had aided in settling the strikes on the basis of increased wages, it passed a series of measures providing for a forty-hour week, two-week vacations with pay, and legal protection for unionization and collective bargaining. From that time on, the trade unions more than doubled their membership. The new government also nationalized the French munition industries, and obtained control of the board of directors of the Bank of France.

The financial problem, however, still baffled the government. Blum depreciated the franc by 30 per cent, but had to resign when in 1937 the Senate refused to grant him dictatorial powers for the solution of other financial difficulties. His Radical-Socialist successor, Chautemps, by the use of decree took the franc off the gold standard, raised taxes, and floated new loans. But France was still financially uneasy because of the cost of increased armaments to meet the threat of fascism in Germany, Italy, and Spain. This diplomatic

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

crisis in 1938 seemed to demand a curtailment of the reform program. The need for speeding up the manufacture of munitions, it was claimed, required the relaxation of the forty-hour rule in industry. Since both the Socialists and Communists opposed any such sacrifice by labor, the new premier, Daladier, sought and found support from the right to compensate his losses on the left. This meant the break-up of the Popular Front in 1938. Events thereafter alternated rapidly from compromise with Germany (1938) to a declaration of war against her (1939), accompanied by the outlawry of the 

Communist Party. 

Soviet Russia

Autocratic Russia experienced a sudden and revolutionary change to a communistic dictatorship as early as 1917. The depravity of the czarist regime no doubt accounts for the extreme form which the revolution took. Russia was being invaded; the government under stress showed itself to be inefficient and corrupt; the imperial family was under the spell of a fanatical monk, Rasputin; and the poverty of the great mass of the people was accentuated by a slump in industry and trade induced by enemy control of outlets. In 

March, 1917, strikes broke out in Petrograd. The soldiers, sent to restore order, refused to fire on the strikers and even fraternized with them. This situation encouraged both conservative and liberal parties of the Duma to declare for a new provisional regime to supersede the czarist government. Nicholas II, faced with both military and political opposition, abdicated, went into retirement, and suffered execution in 1918 when the Bolsheviks came into power. 

Between March and November of 1917 the revolutionary govern ment passed through several stages. The provisional administration, headed by the monarchist, Prince Lvov, included also the liberal, Miliukov, and the leader of the peasant Social Revolutionary Party, Kerensky. This regime proclaimed civil liberties, general amnesty, self-government for Finns and Poles, and continuance of the war against Germany. The rising opposition to the war caused the resignation of Miliukov in May, and the reorganization of the government with a more radical emphasis under the leadership of Kerensky. 

While he continued the war, he tried to obtain an early peace without victory.

In the meantime a separate movement had been developing simultaneously among the urban workers. Their Social-Democratic Party had split into two wings; the right Menshevists, who coöperated

(C with the provisional government, and the left Bolshevists, who refused coöperation because they wanted an immediate end to hostilities. Led by two returned exiles, Lenin and Trotsky, they began to organize councils (soviets) of soldiers, workers, and peasants in all regions and cities. These soviets, having their foundations in the grass roots" back home, claimed to represent the real mass of the Russian people and encouraged desertion in the army, seizure of factories by the workers, and appropriation of lands by the peasants. When General Kornilov, in the interest of the propertied class, attempted to put down the movement, his troops were defeated by a newly organized Red Guard. Then in November, 1917, the victorious Bolsheviks proceeded to overthrow the Kerensky government, dissolve the newly elected constitutional convention, and proclaim the dictatorship of the proletariat under a “Council of People's Commissars." 

For the next two and a half years the Bolshevist regime in Russia was preoccupied with foreign affairs and wars. First Lenin, who headed the new government, made peace with Germany in the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918. In an effort to block German machinations in Russia, and also to destroy Bolshevism, the Allies invaded and held Murmansk and Archangel on the north, and Vladivostok on the east coast of Siberia. They also encouraged "White" counter-revolutionary campaigns by Kolchak in western Siberia, by Denikin and Wrangel in South Russia, by Yudenitch from the region of the Baltic, and by Poland from the west. All of these attempts failed, however, save the attack by Poland; in return for a peace treaty she obtained an extension of her boundaries at the expense of Russia. 

By the end of 1920 the new Communist regime in Russia was free to turn its attention to the internal reconstruction of the country on the basis of its radical economic principles. First a new system of government was adopted. While the suffrage was universal in principle for all over eighteen years of age, it was severely restricted by the disenfranchisement of those who received unearned incomes, who hired others for profit, who carried on capitalistic business, or who were priests, criminals, insane persons, former czarist police, or members of the royal family. Voting was done in public by the showing of hands. This gave the Communists, who ruled by a dictatorship, a chance to terrorize the voters into selecting Communistapproved representatives. The various trades and professions in the cities elected their soviets or councils. These in turn chose representatives to a city soviet, and this again sent up representatives di-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

rectly to a district soviet, a regional soviet, a provincial soviet, and its republic's congress of soviets. In the country the peasants elected a village soviet, and the villagers sent representatives only to the district soviet, in which the rural representation was proportionately lower than that of the city, for the Communist dictatorship, it must be remembered, was primarily one for the urban proletariat. This practice of indirect rural representation continued on up in pyramid fashion from districts to the soviets of regions, provinces, territories, and finally to the congress of the particular soviet republic. 

The whole territory dominated by the Communist dictatorship was divided into autonomous republics, the most important being Russia with Siberia, White Russia, Ukrainia, and Transcaucasia. The congress of each republic selected a large central executive committee which was supreme in legislative and executive functions. This body in turn chose a council of commissars to fulfill the duties of an executive cabinet. All of the republics belonged to the Union of Soviet 

Socialist Republics (U. S. S. R.) to whose Union Congress they sent representatives. This Union Congress, meeting in Moscow, likewise designated a large Union Central Executive Committee composed of two soviets: the Soviet of the Union represented the component republics in proportion to population, and the Soviet of Nationalities tried to give equal representation to each ethnic group. An inner committee (Praesidium) of this unwieldy body did a great deal of the detailed work of legislation. Its president was considered to be the titular head of the state. In addition there was a Union Council of People's Commissars which functioned as an administrative cabinet. 

Technically the Union government seemed a weak and loose confederation. It had only delegated powers, while the republics had the residuary powers and could withdraw freely. A great deal of freedom was also allowed to the republics to develop their own national languages and customs. Actually, however, the Union government, representing the dictatorship, dominated the republics with an iron hand. It controlled foreign affairs, defense, commerce, communications, industry, budgets, natural resources, legal codes, courts, and education. Whatever remained came under the jurisdiction of the autonomous republics! Needless to say, this throttle-hold prevented any voluntary secession.

Paralleling this soviet structure all the way up the line was the corresponding Communist Party organization from local cell to Union Party Congress. Since the Communist Party alone could exist, it was really here that all policy was determined. Its party leader,

while holding no office in the government, was actually the dictator of the whole vast soviet system. Considerable disagreement was allowed in the discussions of the party groups, but once a decision was made - always in harmony with the general principles of the dictator - then the party members dominating the governmental soviets promptly transformed party decisions into official action. Much later in 1936 a new constitution was adopted which allowed the secret ballot and the direct election by all citizens of representatives in the various soviets, even to those of the supreme councils of the republics and to the Council of the Union in the U. S. S. R. These changes seemed to indicate that by 1936 the goal of a happy classless society had been attained and that the opposition henceforth would be only on questions of minor policy and not on those of the fundamental economic and political systems.

Essentially, however, the Communist revolution in Russia was an economic one, and the first results of this phase were none too promising. Factories controlled by labor were inefficient and damaged by lack of skill; farms appropriated by the peasants became, in the minds of their appropriators, just so much private property to be exploited for private profit. When the state began to dictate crop levies to feed the cities, the peasants refused to raise surpluses and a serious famine ensued. In 1920 Lenin, with practical sense, instituted a compromise by his New Economic Policy. He allowed private holding of farms, which eventually enlarged a class of rich peasants called kulaks. In the cities he permitted private business men (Nepmen) to own and operate local retail establishments and small industries. Furthermore, he encouraged foreign capitalists to come in and take up temporary concessions in the heavy industries, mining, and transportation. Conditions were much improved under this N. E. P.

After Lenin's death in 1924 a struggle ensued over the leadership of the Communist Party between Stalin, party secretary, and Trotsky, commissar for war. Trotsky insisted on abolishing the non-communistic N. E. P. and on spreading the revolution rapidly to all capitalistic countries. Stalin, on the other hand, was determined to continue the N. E. P. and make communism a success in Russia before exporting it abroad. After Stalin had won the position of dictator and had exiled Trotsky, he abandoned the N. E. P. by inaugu rating the First Five-Year Plan (1928-1933). Under a State Planning 

Commission a drive was launched throughout the Soviet Union to establish state-controlled heavy industries and organize agriculture on a large-scale coöperative basis.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The world was amazed at the apparently successful strides of this program. At Dnepropetrovsk a great hydroelectric plant was completed; at Magnitogorsk an enormous steel plant with blast furnaces was opened; and the 1100-mile Turkestan-Siberian Railway was finished a full year ahead of time. Indeed, the 1933 production quotas for automobiles, tractors, agricultural machinery, sugar, coal, oil, and electrical equipment were attained in 1931. In the rural regions millions of acres were turned over to large-scale state farms, and other millions of acres were brought together by the peasants' voluntarily pooling their lands into great coöperative farms. This latter process was not accomplished, however, without considerable pressure at first. The opposition of the grasping kulaks was eliminated. by a ruthless liquidation of the whole class. Eventually by highpressure instruction and by the arrival of the new agricultural machinery coöperative farming became successful and popular. The peasantry was in the way of becoming proletariatized. 

The First Five-Year Plan was not without its disappointments, however. Iron, steel, and textiles lagged behind production quotas.

Consumers' goods generally were scarce and of poor quality. Prices were high, and wages and living standards were low. Food supplies were often inadequate. The enormous heavy-industry plants were completed, but they creaked and groaned with inefficiency and inept management, for Russia lacked skilled technicians and organiz ers. To correct these conditions the Second Five-Year Plan (19331938) was adopted to produce more and better consumers' goods, to increase skilled efficiency, and to carry out vast housing projects. 

These were all progressing ahead of schedule when the danger of war arising in the Far East and in central Europe turned much of the energies and resources of the Soviet Union back into the heavy industries for the production of munitions, airplanes, and other war materials. In 1939 the U. S. S. R., stretching from the Baltic to the 

Pacific, presented the appearance of a mighty armed fortress of conscripted men, resources, industry, and farms. Political unity was lacking, and a series of drastic "purges" shocked the world. But this colossus seemed ready to defend its new-born "Utopia" against fascist aggressors or, if the right occasion came, perchance to aid in the downfall of some shaky capitalist states. 

Fascist Italy

While the dictatorship of the proletariat persisted in Russia, a strongly nationalistic dictatorship arose in Italy. Before and after

the war Italy had been a democratic parliamentary monarchy. But the after-effects of the war had dealt heavily with the Italian economy. The government was in debt, and its budgets showed bigger deficits each year. Business and commerce stagnated, and unemployment increased at an alarming rate. Strikes broke out as the usual accompaniment of these conditions, and in some instances the workers forcibly took over the factories and tried to run them. While on the one hand the Catholics, Socialists, and Communists increased their numbers in the parliamentary opposition, the anti-clerical Liberals had such weak leadership that they were unable effectively to cope with either economic or political problems. 

In the face of such inactivity and frustration a new and vigorous Fascist Party began to appear under the leadership of Benito Mussolini. This party emphasized the national state as the highest entity in human life. All phases of national existence must be secondary to national well-being. Therefore business, labor, political parties, newspapers, education, and religion must subordinate their selfish aims to the good of the state. Instead of the state existing for the people the 

Fascists believed the people existed for the glory of the state. Thoroughly disgusted with the confusion of the time, this group, with the aid of capitalistic business and the war veterans, marched on Rome in the midst of a cabinet crisis in 1922 and prevailed upon King Victor 

Emmanuel III to appoint Mussolini as prime minister.

This appointment opened the door to the establishment of a dictatorship. Democracy and parliamentary rule through the party system were denounced by the Fascists as corrupt and disruptive because of the divisions they caused in the nation. The Parliament, cowed by the aggressive and unified attitude of the Fascists, arranged to allow a two-thirds majority in the next Chamber of Deputies to the party that had a plurality of votes. In the election of 1924 the Fascists, by their complete control of the state, won a clear majority and therefore had two-thirds of the seats. With this advantage 

Mussolini proceeded to make the state totalitarian. He abolished all parties except the Fascist, took a majority of the cabinet posts for himself, closed the Masonic lodges, suspended freedom of press, speech, and assembly, and devised a tribunal of summary justice to deal with recalcitrant political enemies. 

The kingship remained intact, but more than ever was the King a figurehead with Mussolini (Il Duce) enjoying all power and prestige. In 1934 the Fascist Grand Council under the guidance of Mussolini devised a new system of representation. The twenty-two Fas-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

cist corporations of employers and employees, organized along lines of industries and branches of production, were to choose representatives to a National Assembly of Corporations. These corporations were completely under Fascist control, and therefore the National Assembly of Corporations was designed eventually to take the place of the Chamber of Deputies as the legislature of the new corporative" state. 

One object of the totalitarian program was to make the Italian national state economically self-sufficient. The only labor organizations allowed were the Fascist-controlled corporations. Strikes and lockouts were forbidden, and compulsory arbitration of labor disputes was enjoined. Agricultural reforms were inaugurated with vigor to make Italy more independent in matters of food supply. 

Swamps were reclaimed; a reforestation program was instituted; and soil fertility was restored. The "battle of the wheat" was a veritable campaign for bigger and better wheat crops. Hydroelectric power production was greatly increased to cut down importation of coal. 

The merchant marine was enlarged to preserve to the national economy the sums formerly paid to the British and French shipping firms. 

The favorable results of these measures would have been more apparent if huge expenditures had not been made for the army, navy, and air force. All men, and even young boys, were mobilized in various military units; and great sums of money were diverted to the establishment of munition plants and the equipping and fueling of motorized units. This great military machine had to be put to some use, and the resultant military exploits (discussed in the next chapter) were to load the state with even heavier financial burdens. 

The extreme nationalism of the Fascists led them to revive interest in Italy's heritage from the Roman Empire by the discovery of new remains and the preservation of many ancient monuments and structures. This laudable effort in archaeology was paralleled by a vigorous campaign of public education. More schools were provided, and illiteracy was greatly reduced. Teachers and books had to present instruction from the Fascist viewpoint, and children and youths were placed in Fascist organizations where they would be given proper Fascist doctrines and military training.

Another significant change in education was brought about by reconciliation with the Catholic Church. Mussolini and Pope Pius XI ended the sixty-year-old feud between the Italian government and the Papacy by signing the Lateran Treaty in 1929. The Pope recognized Italy's acquisition of the former church states, and Italy rec-

ognized the complete sovereignty and independence of Vatican City under the Pope's rule. The City includes St. Peter's Cathedral, the Vatican Palace, the adjacent gardens, and the summer palace of Castle Gandolfo. Italy promised to pay the Pope $100,000,000 for the sequestrated states and signed a concordat which provided that the Pope would appoint government-approved bishops to the Italian dioceses, Italy would pay the salaries of the clergy, and religious instruction would be given in the Italian schools by teachers approved by the Church. Thus spiritual uniformity was added to the economic and political unity of the Fascist totalitarian state. 

German Democracy and Dictatorship

The collapse of the German armies in World War I brought the downfall of the imperial regime in Berlin. As early as October, 1918, Chancellor Prince Maximilian reorganized the new government on the basis of cabinet responsibility to the Reichstag and the freedom of speech, press, and assembly. These last-minute reforms satisfied neither the Allies nor the disgruntled German liberals. Mutiny broke out in the navy at Kiel, riots occurred in the large industrial cities, and unrest appeared even in the erstwhile well-disciplined army. On November 9 Kaiser William II fled to Holland and later abdicated. Chancellor Maximilian resigned, and the Social-Democratic leader, Friedrich Ebert, organized a provisional government which signed the armistice on November 11.

The new government with the support of the Catholic Centrists, the Progressives, and the left National Liberals, called for the election of a constitutional convention by universal suffrage of men and women over twenty years of age. The liberal republican coalition won 348 seats while its conservative monarchist opponents received only 63. With this overwhelming victory the convention, meeting at Weimar, made one of the most democratic constitutions then in existence. After stressing civil liberties in a bill of rights, the constitution provided for a president elected for a seven-year term and a two-house legislature. The Reichstag, or lower house, was elected for a four-year period by proportional representation. To encourage the exercise of the franchise, the constitution provided for one member for each 60,000 votes cast in a district. The Reichsrat was made up of representatives of the state governments sent with indefinite terms in rough proportion to the populations of the states. 

A National Economic Council in a sense formed a third legislative house. Made up of representatives of labor, capital, and consumers,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

it formed an advisory body to be consulted in matters of economic legislation. Its approval, however, was not necessary for the passage of a law. The cabinet was responsible to a majority in the 

Reichstag; the practices of referendum and recall were adopted; and provision was made for government appropriation of private property for public use with compensation. Although still a federal union, Germany's national government was given more jurisdiction than it had had under the imperial regime. 

In spite of the splendidly devised constitution the political developments under the German republican government were unfortunate. A large number of German people still longed for the old disciplined monarchy; a smaller communist group at the other extreme wanted a dictatorship of the proletariat. The moderate majority in between had to cope not only with these opponents but also with the harsh treatment and humiliations imposed on the republic by the democracies of the former enemy countries, who, having helped establish a German democracy, contributed thereafter greatly to its eventual downfall. To the ruinous inflation of 

1923 and 1924, caused by domestic war debts and foreign demands. for reparations, succeeded the world economic depression of 19291933. 

With a feeling of economic insecurity and nationalistic frustration, the German people began to gravitate to the parties of the extreme right and extreme left. Moderate business men, when they saw the workers moving toward communism, reacted by turning their support and their money to the aid of the extreme parties of the right. The one party on the right which benefited most from this shift was Adolf Hitler's National Socialist Party. As early as 

1922 Hitler had attacked the democratic government as a tool of Germany's former enemies and as a breeder of national disunity. 

He blamed international Jewry, Catholicism, and communism for Germany's defeat by their alleged efforts to undermine her morale in the last months of the war. He advocated a program similar to 

Mussolini's in Italy: exaltation of the state over individuals and groups, establishment of a dictatorship, economic autarchy, political uniformity, and the abolition of the Versailles Treaty. As the conditions became worse in Germany after 1929, popular attention and capitalist money turned more toward the National Socialist (Nazi) 

Party. In 1932 Hitler won 13,000,000 votes for president out of a total of 36,000,000. Later in that same year the Nazis obtained a plurality in the Reichstag. In January, 1933, Hitler was appointed as chancellor by President Hindenburg, and on the death of the latter

in 1934 Hitler became head of the state with the plain title of Der 

Führer (The Leader). 

Once in power the Nazis, instead of restoring the traditional monarchy, carried out, under the name of the Third Reich, one of the most revolutionary transformations Germany had ever experienced. The federal system was abolished by making the states mere administrative districts of the national government. All political parties were dissolved except the National Socialist, whose leader, Hitler, became the absolute dictator of all Germany. The legislature was supplanted by a ratifying Nazi Reichstag which met for a few days. each year to hail their Leader and acclaim his legislative program by unanimous and vociferous shouts. The press, radio, theatre, literature, art, and education were all censored and directed by Paul Goebbels, propaganda minister. The youth of Germany were put into organizations which would instill a uniformity of thought along 

Nazi lines.

On the economic side the Nazis strove to make Germany selfsufficient. Foreign trade on a barter basis was introduced; no imports would be made unless a corresponding amount of German exports were accepted abroad. In their attempt to make Germany economically independent the Nazis began to develop home substitutes for foreign goods. Labor unions were prohibited as well as strikes, lockouts, and collective bargaining. The workers and employers were grouped together under the Labor Front with Nazi trustees to dictate policies in industry and commerce. Materially, however, the lot of the laborer was better than that of the employer. 

Profits for capitalists were restricted by a rigid system of accounting, compulsory employment of additional workers, and large winter relief contributions. On the other hand laborers were given more employment, higher wages, and vacations. For a sum as low as six dollars the government would furnish a laborer all his travelling and living expenses for a week's vacation at some popular summer resort. Private ownership of large industries and large estates, however, was carefully preserved. Although unemployment disappeared, Germany's economic situation became worse year by year. This is partly attributable to the huge cost of the rearmament program. While 

Germany was forced to import materials for her new military machine, her exports were greatly curtailed by an ever-widening boycott of German goods by Jews, organized labor, and other supporters of democracy outside Germany in protest against the persecutions and suppressions within the Nazi state. 

Persecution of minorities was a tragically common practice in Nazi

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Germany, for the nation became almost hysterical in its racial enthusiasms and hates. Nordic superiority was erected into a sacred dogma. 

From this positive force as a source stemmed several destructive programs. On the very day that the Nazis assumed full control of the 

German state (April 1, 1933), they began to persecute the German Jews. No Jew was allowed to hold civil or military office. Later only Jews could deal with Jewish stores, doctors, dentists, or lawyers. 

Jews who offered resistance or criticism were often dispatched to concentration camps. Finally, in 1938, when a crazed Jewish exile assassinated a German attaché in Paris, the Nazis, either in a delirium of revenge or by a deliberate plan of economic liquidation, began one of the most ruthless persecutions since the days of medieval witchcraft or of the Russian pogroms. Riots were unleashed in which some 

Jews were killed, Jewish property was destroyed, and Jewish synagogues were burned. Residences of Jews were restricted to certain quarters. All employment of Jews by non-Jews was forbidden. A $400,000,000 fine was imposed on the Jewish community, and their eventual emigration - stripped of their wealth - was decreed. 

Other groups besides the Jews also suffered persecution. Active 

Communists, Social-Democrats, and Liberals were placed in unhealthful (and often brutal) concentration camps or driven from the country. Protestant and Catholic leaders who refused to minimize the Jewish heritage in their religious teachings, who continued to combat the pagan program of the extreme Nazis, or who insisted on their own youth organizations were likewise placed in concentration camps for unlimited terms of imprisonment. Even some Nazis did not escape the heavy hand of persecution. When a disaffection appeared in party ranks in 1934, Röhm and some of his followers were promptly assassinated, and a monarchist, von Schleicher, along with a few associates, was slaughtered in cold blood. While the dictatorship at home was able to suppress any reactions against persecution, it was unable to forestall a rising tide of condemnation among people of other countries. And this rising tide reached full flood at the end of a series of 

Axis aggressions which culminated in the German attack on Poland in 1939. The resulting World War II and its diplomatic antecedents will be the principal subjects of the next chapter.

CHAPTER 53 World War II and Its Diplomatic 

Antecedents

1919 peace had finally been made after the most terrible worldwide conflict humanity had up to then experienced. In the peace treaties most of the victor nations had registered their determination never to tolerate another war. They did this by joining the League of Nations and pledging themselves to observe the obligations of its Covenant. But exactly twenty years later - less than the span of a generation - these same peoples on the same six continents were again locked in an even more devastating life-and-death struggle. Inherited hate, materialistic greed, chauvinistic stubbornness, and shortsighted leadership had all combined not only to destroy the instrumentalities of peace but also to undermine the very will for peace among a warweary people. Wide is the gate and broad the way that leadeth to destruction. Here, then, is the story of that broad diplomatic highway down which humanity hurtled with ever gathering speed and of that destruction which lay at the end of the road. 

DIPLOMACY OF FORCE 

The decade from 1929 to 1939 in the field of diplomacy may be characterized by a decline in the use of peaceful means for the settlement of international disputes and a great increase in the reliance on force by the major powers of the world. Several factors account for this apparent change in procedure. The race for imperial expansion, begun about 1880, seemed to have finally given every unclaimed corner of the earth into the possession of some world power. When this saturation point was reached, there still remained a few selfstyled "have not" powers - Japan, Italy, and Germany - who either had no share or a very unsatisfactory share of overseas possessions. This feeling of land poverty and dissatisfaction was heightened by the acute distress suffered during the depression after 1929 by

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

the dense populations in these three countries. Added to these unfavorable conditions was the development of a rampant nationalism, fostered by Nazism in Germany, Fascism in Italy, and militaristic imperialism in Japan. Fascist Italy felt that her share of the colonial booty after World War I had been much too insufficient, for she had received only desert strips in western Somaliland and southern Tripoli. Germany was demanding the return of her colonies and the annexation of Austria and the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia. Japan, always desirous of expansion in China as an outlet for her excess population, manufactures, and capital, merely watched for a European crisis during which she could move with impunity toward her goal.

The Manchurian Affair 

The economic depression of 1929 seemed to give Japan just the crisis she needed for starting a great adventure in the Far East. On the pretext of protecting Japanese railway interests against Chinese bandits, the Japanese military guards seized control of Manchuria in 1931. The League of Nations appointed a commission under Lord 

Lytton which investigated and reported that Japan was in the wrong in taking Manchuria. It advised Japan to withdraw and allow Manchuria autonomy under Chinese sovereignty. Instead, Japan angrily resigned from the League and remained in Manchuria. The Chinese in retaliation began a serious boycott of Japanese goods, which drove Japan to send troops into Shanghai and the province of Jehol. China finally arranged a truce in 1932, after which Japan evacuated the Shanghai area but erected Manchuria into the dependent state of Manchukuo. The United States, in accordance with the Stimson Doctrine, and the members of the League of Nations refused to recognize the new regime in Manchukuo because it had been established by the use of force.

Hostilities reopened again in 1937 when Japan organized a buffer autonomous state around Peiping between Manchukuo and China proper. Chiang Kai-shek, leader of the Chinese nationalists, made peace with the Chinese communists and united the nation in dogged resistance. The superior Japanese military machine took over the regions of China south and west of Manchukuo, captured Shanghai and Canton, and by 1939 had driven up the Yang-tse valley, taken Nanking and Hankow, and pushed the Chinese capital back to Chungking. Peace, said the Japanese, would not be made until Chiang's regime should be overthrown and Japan's Far Eastern predominance

I 

recognized. In the meantime the resistance of the Chinese regular armies and guerrilla bands made the undeclared war a costly one for 

Japan. 

Italy and Ethiopia 

Japan's apparent success in Manchuria in 1931 and 1932 encouraged Italy to resort to similar methods of force to obtain more satisfactory colonial possessions in Ethiopia, which lay between her two colonies of Eritrea and Somaliland. Utilizing a border incident at

Ualual, Italy proceeded to invade Ethiopia from north and south in September, 1935. Since she had rejected offers of arbitration and compromise and since the League absolved both countries of blame for the border incident, this attack by Italy was judged to be in direct violation of the League Covenant and the Kellogg-Briand Pact. Great 

Britain led the way in getting the League to impose economic sanctions against Italy. This embargo, however, did not include raw materials, such as oil, which could be used in warfare. Consequently 

Italy's mechanized army rolled resistlessly over Ethiopia, which in May, 1936, was made a part of the Italian empire. Although the 

United States persisted in her nonrecognition policy in regard to the conquest of Ethiopia, Great Britain and France lifted their embargoes and in 1938 recognized Italy's acquisition of the country. Thus encouraged in her aggressive policy by the western powers, Italy early in 1939 invaded and annexed by force her Balkan neighbor, Albania. 

Spain's Civil War 

Italy had no sooner completed her campaign in Ethiopia than she became intensely interested in developments in Spain. Although 

Spain had avoided participation in World War I, her internal situation was very bad. The land was inequitably distributed, most of it belonging to the noble grandees and higher clergy, while the multitude of peasantry were landless tenants with scarcely a subsistence living. Factory conditions in the cities were so bad that the workingmen were swelling the ranks of socialists and communists and using the trade unions for general strikes. To add to the confusion, such regions as Catalonia and the Basque territory demanded autonomous government within the nation. In Spanish Morocco the Moorish tribesmen rose in revolt.

After Primo Rivera tried unsuccessfully to cope with the situation by dictatorship (1923–1930), the liberal and radical groups won the elections of 1930, forced Alfonso XIII to abdicate, and proclaimed a

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

republic. The ensuing election of a constitutional convention gave a large majority to the republican group, which included liberals, socialists, and communists. The new constitution established a democratic republic with civil and religious liberties, universal suffrage, an elected parliament and president, a cabinet responsible to parliament, and provision for autonomous local government for certain regions like Catalonia. This new republican regime began a series of drastic reforms. It separated church and state, secularized education, confiscated many estates of nobles and clergy without compensation, began distributing this land in small tracts to the landless peasants, and enacted industrial legislation regulating wages, hours, and peaceful settlement of labor disputes. 

This revolutionary program of course aroused intense opposition among the monarchists, clericals, and businessmen. When the elections of 1936 went so strongly in favor of the republicans that they had the courage to rid the army of antirepublican officers, one of these officers, Francisco Franco, raised the standard of revolt and obtained the support of monarchists, clericals, and fascists. What seemed at first a mere outbreak became in fact a fierce, prolonged civil war.

Italy's interest in the civil war was discerned from the start. Mussolini would be glad to help any movement against democracy, socialism, and trade unions. Aid to Franco would likewise embarrass 

France's new socialist government and check its possible opposition to Italian imperialistic designs in the Mediterranean. When Italy began to send troops to help Franco, a world conflict over Spain was narrowly averted by the signing of a nonintervention agreement (1936-1937). Italy, Germany, England, France, Russia, and others agreed to send no troops or war materials to either side in the Spanish civil war. Italy and Germany, however, began openly and boastfully to send large numbers of men and quantities of munitions and war planes to Franco. Soviet Russia then insisted on her right to send men and munitions to the Loyalists. France and Great Britain, fearful of setting in motion a larger world war, held to the fiction of nonintervention to such an extent that the Loyalist side was greatly handicapped. 

Franco, with an army of Spanish insurgents, Moors, Italians, and Germans, gradually obtained control of southern and western Spain (1936), Asturias and the Basque provinces (1937), Teruel (1938), and Catalonia with its large port of Barcelona (1939). Finally, in the late spring of 1939, Loyalist resistance collapsed and Franco became ruler of a prostrate and embittered Spain.

I 



Germany's Drive to the East 

The third "have not" nation, Germany, now under the supernationalistic Nazi regime, found an opportunity to expand her power and territory in the prevailing confusion. Taking advantage of the economic and political crises in France and Great Britain, the Japanese invasion of China, the Italian campaign in Ethiopia, and the Spanish civil war, Hitler proceeded to scrap the Versailles Treaty and build Germany up again to the status of a world power. In 1935 he began to rearm Germany; in 1936 he remilitarized the Rhine; in March, 1938, he suddenly marched his troops into Austria and united it with Germany. In September of that same year, by a threat of precipitating a world war, Hitler made Great Britain and France agree to Germany's acquisition of the Sudeten German areas of Czechoslovakia (the Pact of Munich). Once he saw that these two powers were inclined to capitulate before every show of force, Hitler began an unceremonious drive to the east. In March, 1939, Germany destroyed the independence of Czechoslovakia. The regions of Bohemia and 

Moravia were incorporated in the German state, Slovakia was made a German protectorate, Ruthenia was given to Hungary, and Memel was taken from Lithuania.

The Rome-Berlin Axis 

This series of aggressions, invasions, and interventions in the Far East, in the Mediterranean, and in central Europe were not isolated and spontaneous crises. Japan, Italy, and Germany continually showed sympathy toward each other in the accomplishment of their various objectives. To keep their opponents in a state of constant bewilderment, one of the three powers would begin a new crisis while another was ending one elsewhere. Finally in 1936 and 1937 this synchronized coöperation was developed into a three-cornered pact against the so-called communists. The combination thereafter was usually referred to as the Rome-Berlin Axis. Yet in August, 1939, the anticommunist alliance received a rude shock when the Berlin end of the Axis made a political agreement with Soviet Russia, the very country against which the Axis had been primarily directed. 

Such double dealing on the part of both Germany and Soviet Russia was only the culmination of a tendency everywhere to repudiate treaty obligations. All the members of the League technically violated Article 16 of the Covenant in the Ethiopian affair. Hitler purposely repudiated the Versailles Treaty. At one time or another after 

1929 the Kellogg-Briand Pact, the Locarno Agreement, the Nine

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Power Treaty, the debt-funding agreements, the Spanish nonintervention agreement, the Munich Pact, the Franco-Soviet Alliance, and the Anticomintern Pact were openly violated. Thus to the insecurity caused by the prevalence of force and violence was added a profound distrust of the good faith of nations.

I: PERIOD OF AXIS SUCCESS 

Continuing his Drang nach Osten (drive to the east), Hitler finally made demands on Poland for Danzig and the Polish Corridor. In spite of Great Britain's and France's alliances with Poland, he ordered German troops to invade Polish territory on September 1, 1939. The outbreak of this new war was facilitated by Soviet Russia's astounding about-face when she abandoned her French ally and made a nonaggression treaty with her anticommunist neighbor, Germany. This time Great Britain and France did not attempt to "appease appease" Ger- many, but instead declared war two days after the first attack on 

Poland. 

The Blitzkrieg in Poland 

While Great Britain and France were slowly gathering their forces to attack Germany from the west, Hitler determined to crush their weaker ally, Poland, by a lightning stroke of his combined ground and air forces. Two German air fleets of bombers riddled Poland's small air force on the ground and cut her railroads at their most strategic junctions, while the German mechanized infantry, supported by tanks, penetrated swiftly and deeply into Poland from East Prussia, Upper Silesia, and Slovakia. This rapid enveloping movement caught most of the Polish troops west of Warsaw; those few forces which escaped this trap were surrounded east of Warsaw by a second Nazi pincer movement and were compelled to surrender. Warsaw, under relentless air bombardment, held out until September 28, but all effective Polish resistance came to an end by October 1.

Already there were indications of a new kind of warfare. Instead of a war of position using strong and continuous land campaigns and labyrinths of trenches this was a mechanized war of movement, a Blitzkrieg or lightning war, in which motorized infantry, gasolinedriven tanks, and high-powered planes were all combined in wellsynchronized operations. Machines depended on heavy industries, and both in turn required strategic raw materials and fuel. Here then, even so early in the struggle, was the pattern of a total war which reaches back to every last farmer, miner, and factory worker.

I 

Although Soviet Russia was a neutral power associated with Germany in a nonaggression pact, she was the most alarmed of all the powers at the sight of the rapid German advance into Poland. In an effort to protect the frontiers of the U.S.S.R. and to maintain some semblance of a balance of power in eastern Europe, the Red Army, on September 17, 1939, began to invade and occupy the eastern two-fifths of Poland not yet reached by the German forces. Not wishing at that time to begin hostilities against each other, Germany and Russia signed an agreement on September 28 by which they partitioned Poland between themselves along a line running west of 

Grodno, Bialystok, and Brest-Litovsk, along the Bug River, and west of Lwow. With Poland now being completely overrun, its government fled first to Rumania and later to Great Britain. 

The Russo-Finnish War, 1939–1940 

Russia was not content with her Polish acquisitions, however. As a further defensive precaution she forced Lithuania, Latvia, and Esthonia to grant her military and naval bases (fall, 1939). Russia next turned to Finland, demanding a Finnish cession of territory north of Leningrad and the lease of the Finnish island of Hangoe. When Finland refused full compliance, Russia attacked on November 30. To the members of the League of Nations this attack appeared to be an act of unprovoked aggression by one League member against another. The U.S.S.R. was therefore promptly expelled from the 

League. This reproof, however, was of little assistance to Finland. who, after offering strong resistance against her formidable adversary, was finally forced to capitulate. On March 12, 1940, Finland signed a peace treaty by which she surrendered Viipuri and the Hangoe naval base to Russia. 

By June, 1940, following Germany's defeat of the western powers,

Russia saw the need and opportunity of making further protective acquisitions. This time she obliged Rumania to hand over Bessarabia. and Bukowina and annexed the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia, and Esthonia. These areas were later set up as four socialist republics in the U.S.S.R. 

The "Phony War" in the West

During Hitler's September Blitzkrieg in Poland, Great Britain and France were limiting themselves in the west to what was derisively called a Sitzkrieg or "phony war." Having had no intention of starting a war themselves, the two western allies were utterly unpre-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

pared when the war broke out. Instead of aiding Poland by a strong offensive in western Germany they could only strengthen the 

Maginot Line and blockade Germany by sea. However, both countries began a feverish production of armaments with a view to later operations, and, in spite of the loss of their Polish ally, firmly rejected Hitler's offer of a negotiated peace in October, 1939. In the meantime all the British dominions except Ireland came to the support of Great Britain by separate declarations of war. 

The Fall of France 

Hitler, observing Russia's encroachments from the east and Allied preparations on the west, realized that he must act quickly to retain his advantage. Consequently, early in the spring (April 9, 1940) he launched an air and sea attack against Norway and a land invasion of Denmark. This campaign was an effort to cover Germany's right flank as her troops faced the French and British and to keep open a route to Narvik, Norway, where Germany received much Swedish iron ore. Denmark was overwhelmed in a day, while Norway held out for two months. By a skillful combination of attacks by sea and air and use of parachute troops and a fifth column of saboteurs and spies, the Nazis succeeded in capturing the principal cities, ports, and airfields of southern Norway by April 15. The British rushed to the aid of Norway with a naval force and 30,000 troops, landing at Namsos on April 14. German air power, however, held off the main body of a British fleet, and German land forces by May 2 forced the British expedition to withdraw. Similar British landings near 

Narvik were driven off by June 9. The king of Norway and his government fled to Britain; and, as an initial contribution, turned over to the Allies the large Norwegian merchant fleet. In London the Norwegian exiles were greeted by a reorganized British government: Neville Chamberlain had resigned, and Winston Churchill, at the head of a new coalition cabinet, had become prime minister on the 10th of May.

On the same day Hitler's main attack against the western powers began with a lightning invasion of the Netherlands, Belgium, and 

Luxemburg. Relieved momentarily of any fear of a Russian attack, he was able to mass 240 divisions and 5,000 planes against the Allies' 130 poorly equipped divisions and France's 1,000 inferior planes. 

Holland surrendered in one week, and Queen Wilhelmina with her government had to follow the king of Norway into British exile. 

Belgium held out for ten days longer, for the French and British

I 

emerged from their Maginot Line to rush to the aid of the Belgians. 

The king of the Belgians, however, was compelled to surrender his army on May 27, and by that time the German forces, with the aid of overwhelming air power, had been able to break through the French lines at the Meuse and race their tanks to the Channel. Thus they cut off the British and French troops in Belgium from the main body of the French forces in France. But the Germans were thwarted in their attempt to annihilate the encircled British, French, and Belgian troops, which were retreating toward Dunkirk. By the superhuman efforts of the British R.A.F. and an improvised fleet of 

English small boats, 337,000 Allied soldiers were safely evacuated by 

June 2 to British shores.

The Germans now concentrated all their strength against France. 

Swinging around Paris to the east and west, they enveloped the Maginot Line from the rear, forced the French remnants to retreat into Switzerland, and after entering Paris (proclaimed an open city) overran France almost to Bordeaux and Grenoble. With France on her knees, Hitler's Axis partner, Mussolini, found sufficient courage to join the war and stab his fallen neighbor in the back. It was his hope that Italy would become the heir to France's possessions in the 

Mediterranean area. 

Thus overwhelmed, France decided, in contrast to Poland, Norway, Holland, and Belgium, to make an armistice with Germany and to choose Marshal Pétain as head of the state to carry out the policy of capitulation. On June 21, 1940, Hitler in person imposed

Germany's severe armistice terms on France at Compiègne in the same railway car where the Germans had signed the armistice of 1918. The terms provided for German occupation of the northern two-thirds of France at French expense and the disarming of the French army and navy. Pétain then set up a fascist government at 

Vichy in southern (unoccupied) France and accepted Laval as his premier. In contrast to such submissiveness, General Charles de 

Gaulle fled to England, refused to recognize the armistice, and sought to rally all like-minded Frenchmen to his standard of resistance.

The Air Battle of Britain 

The shortness of time still dogged Hitler and required him to strike swiftly at Britain before she or Russia or America could offer serious opposition to the victorious march of the Germans. Opponents with grim determination, however, faced him from across the Channel.

In the face of this stubborn challenge, Hitler launched, from August to October, 1940, four air offensives as a preliminary to invasion of the British Isles. The Luftwaffe first tried bombing and strafing the Channel ports, and, when this offensive failed, it turned successively to raids on airfields and finally to day and night raids on London. Large areas of the capital and of other British cities were laid in ruins, and nearly 100,000 civilian casualties were suffered during these attacks. But the R.A.F., outnumbered three to one by the Luftwaffe, inflicted losses on its foe at the rate of four planes for every one lost by the British.
