Hence the fighting in the skies, not mentioned in Churchill's previous challenge, had made unnecessary the battles on the beaches, fields, and hills. As Churchill said in his famous tribute to the R.A.F.: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few." 

Axis Victories in the Near East

Unable to crush the British Empire at its center, the Axis partners decided to strike next at Britain's most important lifeline, the eastern Mediterranean. Italy's entrance into the war gave them a strategic position astride the central Mediterranean; and Italy wanted to make gains at the expense of Britain, since she had been forestalled from

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

acquiring much French territory by the armistice. Against the 

200,000 poorly equipped British troops in Egypt the Italians concentrated in Tripoli and Ethiopia 500,000 men liberally supplied with tanks, trucks, and planes. About three months after the fall of France (September 13, 1940) General Graziani's army struck at the British in Egypt. But by February, 1941, the British general, Sir Archibald

Wavell, had hurled them back, penetrated Italian Libya as far as El 

Agheila, and captured 133,000 men.

The British then turned to the task of liberating Ethiopia from the Italians. With 30,000 troops they converged on Ehiopia from Eritrea, Somaliland, and Kenya, and by May, 1941, they and obtained the last surrender of Italy's 200,000 troops.

While putting down Axis-inspired revolts in Iraq and Syria in June and July, 1941, the British had to face a renewal of the war in Tripoli. 

The Germans had sent General Rommel with his Afrika Korps to retrieve the Italian situation in North Africa. Well supplied with desert equipment and 270 tanks, Rommel pushed the British back into 

Egypt in March, 1941. However, in November the British, using

American tanks, trucks, and planes, endeavored again to dislodge the Germans. After much hard fighting around Tobruk, Rommel finally withdrew into central Tripoli. But this British success did not last long. Weakened by losses of troops in the Greek campaign of 1941 and faced with German tank guns of longer range, the British were driven back by June, 1942, to El Alamein, not far from Alexandria in Egypt.

In the meantime the Germans were also trying to increase their hold on southern Europe and the northern shores of the eastern Mediterranean. Between November, 1940, and March, 1941, Hungary,

Rumania, and Bulgaria joined the Axis powers. By the Vienna Award of August, 1940, Hungary was rewarded with Transylvania, and Bulgaria with Dobruja, both at the expense of Rumania. While Italy had failed to conquer Greece in 1940, the Germans, attacking both Yugoslavia and Greece from Bulgaria the next year, overran the former and drove the British out of the latter by April. Crete and the 

Greek islands of the Aegean were occupied in May. As far as supply convoys were concerned, Britain's lifeline to Egypt by the Mediterranean was effectively cut. Britain's island bastion in the central 

Mediterranean, Malta, held out heroically against constant aerial bombardment, but Allied use of the Mediterranean was momentarily interrupted.

I 



The Invasion of Russia 

Hitler's situation, however, was becoming more desperate in 1941. 

While he could not hope to undertake the invasion of England for some time, he saw Great Britain, the United States, and Russia greatly increasing their war production and preparations. If he wished to strike his present or future adversaries separately, he had but one choice: to attack Russia before the British were ready to invade the 

Continent. In spite of the Nonaggression Pact with the U.S.S.R. he had always considered communist Russia as his principal enemy, and he coveted the rich areas under Soviet domination. Now protected on the north by his possession of Norway and on the south by his occupation of the Balkans, he launched an all-out offensive against 

Russia on June 22, 1941.

With all the advantages of surprise and prior preparation, the Germans overran the western areas of the Soviet nation, while the Russians, fighting desperately on all sections of the front, retreated slowly in the hope of trading space for time. On the north the Germans took over the Baltic states and reached the vicinity of Leningrad in two months, but, although they encircled the city and shelled it constantly, they never succeeded in capturing it.

In the center, it was the same story with Moscow. After the fall of Smolensk (August 9, 1941) the Russians withdrew, practicing the "scorched earth" policy all the way. The Germans, hard on their heels, approached the Soviet capital from north, west, and south by 

October. Here a fierce ten-weeks battle ensued, with German heavy tank formations countered by Russian massed artillery. The lines of the defenders held, and the same Russian winter weather which had thwarted Napoleon deprived Hitler of his prize. 

The German forces penetrated more deeply to the south. Kiev, Dnepropetrovsk, the Crimea, the Donetz Basin, and Rostov fell in turn before the assaults of the invaders. Along this line the stakes were high, for the route pointed toward rich oil wells and the Middle East. But Stalingrad on the Volga blocked the way. For two months (September to November, 1942) the Germans pounded the city with all they had and penetrated to its very center. But its grim defenders held on, and newly equipped Russian forces on the north and south began a pincer movement against the Nazi assailants which saved Stalingrad and completely destroyed General Paulus's army of 330,000 men (February 2, 1943). This was the turning point of battle on the eastern front.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION America Enters the War 

Since China and Japan were carrying on a separate war in the Far East, the United States was the only major power in 1941 which was still technically neutral. "Nonbelligerency " (a term adopted by 

Italy in 1939) would, however, more accurately describe America's attitude, because the government and public opinion were openly and strongly anti-Axis from the beginning of the war. With a naive belief that the conflict could be kept from America's shores Congress had passed a series of neutrality laws between 1935 and 1937 which prohibited the supplying of munitions and loans to belligerents and forbade American ships to enter combat areas. Raw materials could be sold to belligerents on a cash-and-carry basis. But with the outbreak of the war in 1939 the cash-and-carry provision was extended to all munitions; and in 1941, after the fall of France, the Lend-Lease 

Act was passed which made the United States an "Arsenal of Democracy" by furnishing the anti-Axis allies all kinds of war materials without requiring cash payments. Furthermore, in 1940 the first 

American peacetime military conscription was enacted, and in 1941 American merchant vessels were armed and ordered to resist any attacks, although the United States was still neutral. 

The American attitude toward Japan was also stiffening. While the 

Japanese abrogated the Naval Disarmament Treaty in 1934, the United States abrogated its commercial treaty with Japan in 1939. After Japan expanded her sphere of activity to French Indo-China, the American government finally took the most vigorous action short of war by freezing Japanese assets in the United States and by practically halting all exports of essential materials, such as petroleum, to Japan (1941). In desperation Japan signed a defensive alliance against the 

United States with Germany and Italy and a nonaggression pact with Soviet Russia. She would not, however, reduce or restrict her Asiatic expansion in order to satisfy peaceably the demands of the United States.

Suddenly and without warning, on December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the American Hawaiian naval base at Pearl Harbor with carrier planes. Simultaneously she struck at the Philippines, Guam, and 

Wake, as well as at British Hong Kong and Singapore. Germany and 

Italy supported these Japanese aggressions by immediate declarations of war against the United States. Thus finally, in spite of two broad protective oceans and a series of neutrality laws, the United States had been propelled into World War II. Following the Pearl Harbor

I 

attack, fifteen Latin-American countries eventually came into the war on the side of the United States. Costa Rica actually declared war a day before the American Congress took similar action; eight other Caribbean countries joined the fray on the same day that the 

United States declared war.

With the American Pacific fleet temporarily but badly crippled and the main strength of the British fleet engaged in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, the Japanese extended their control in 1942 over 

Siam, Burma, the Dutch East Indies, the northern half of New Guinea, and the Bismarck, Solomon, and Gilbert islands. At the northern end of the Pacific they occupied the islands of Attu and Kiska in the 

Aleutians. 

The Japanese advance in the Pacific, however, came to an abrupt halt within six months of its beginning. In May, 1942, a large Japanese naval force proceeded south from the Solomon Islands either to invade Australia or break her supply line to the United States. This was met by an American-Australian naval task force in the Battle of the Coral Sea, which successfully put an end to Japanese southward advance through the action of carrier-based planes. One month later a much larger Japanese naval force, aiming at Midway and the Hawaiian Islands, was smashed in the Battle of Midway by the joint defensive attacks of carrier- and land-based planes. The Japanese never succeeded in pushing farther east. One of the significant facts about these two naval battles was that they were won by air power. A new type of naval warfare was thus appearing in the Pacific to match the new type of land warfare used on the plains of Poland. 

In both, air power was the new decisive factor. 

: PERIOD OF ALLIED VICTORIES 

In the early months after the Pearl Harbor attack the United States devoted itself to mobilizing its vast industries and man power for a total war. It began to pour forth munitions and supplies for its seriously pressed allies, Britain and Russia, and the American Navy and Air Forces joined those of the British in guarding the overseas convoys carrying men and materials. 

At the same time the serious decision had to be made early in 1942 whether the main Allied effort should be directed first against Germany or Japan. Churchill joined Roosevelt in Washington for deliberations. Opinion in the United States, China, and Australia favored striking Japan first. The two Allied leaders, however, finally decided upon the priority of an anti-German campaign. The determining fac-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tors were the weakness of the American Pacific fleet after Pearl Harbor, Japan's limited resources and overextended lines, the threat of Hitler's strong position and available resources, and the fact that the three most powerful Allies could concentrate most effectively against Germany. In Washington, Churchill and Roosevelt agreed to the formation of a Combined Chiefs of Staff which would direct Anglo- American operations through combined lower commands and headquarters in every Anglo-American theater of war. This unique system was a new experiment in international organization and effort. 

Allied Victories in North Africa

In July, 1942, the Combined Chiefs of Staff decided that the Anglo- American forces were still too weak to make a direct attack against Hitler in northern France. Instead, they agreed on an invasion of 

French North Africa, to be synchronized with an Allied drive westward from Egypt against Rommel. On October 19, 1942, the British 

Eighth Army under General Montgomery, by combining artillery, infantry, tanks, and planes, smashed through Rommel's lines at El Alamein and within less than a month hurled the German forces all the way back to El Agheila in central Tripolitania. This victory, along with the heroic Russian stand at Stalingrad, was the turning point of the war in Europe. 

While Rommel was still retreating toward El Agheila, American and British forces landed in Morocco and Algeria (November 8) and within four days obtained from Darlan the surrender of the French forces in North Africa. The Clark-Darlan Agreement, as it was called, brought the North African French over to the Allied side. The Germans, however, proceeded to occupy southern France and rush their troops by air into Tunisia to protect Rommel's rear. 

The next campaign, which had to await the end of the winter rains, took place in Tunisia. By February, 1943, Rommel found himself caught in a vise between the combined British and French forces. under Montgomery and Le Clerc in Tripolitania and the British, American, and French forces under Eisenhower in Algeria. After one desperate attempt to break out at Kasserine Pass the Germans and Italians, pushed back into Cap Bon Peninsula and unable to escape from the trap, finally surrendered in May. In all, 349,000 Italians and 

Germans were killed or captured and 200,000 tons of weapons and supplies were destroyed or taken. Rommel himself managed to escape by plane.

I 



Allied Victories in Italy

With all American, British, and French land, sea, and air forces placed under General Eisenhower's command, the next Allied objective was to knock out the weakest Axis state, Italy. The island of 

Pantelleria was captured in June, 1943, and Sicily was invaded in July. In thirty-eight days all of Sicily was taken, with an Axis loss of 167,000 men as compared with an Allied loss of 31,000. More important than the mere conquest of the island was the fact that this victory brought the dismissal of Mussolini as dictator of Italy (July 25), the unconditional surrender of Italy (September 8), and finally the entrance of Italy on the side of the Allies under the Badoglio government (October). These events gave the Allies the entire Italian fleet and reopened the whole length of the Mediterranean to 

Allied shipping.

On the day following Italy's surrender, Allied troops landed at Salerno on the mainland of Italy, joined with British troops which had already cleared the toc of the peninsula of German troops, and proceeded on a slow and systematic drive to push the Germans north across the Alps. Naples and Foggia were taken in September, the latter becoming the center of a vast system of airfields from which bombers flew to northern Italy, Austria, and Germany. In 

1944, Rome, Florence, and Leghorn fell before renewed Allied drives. Finally in April, 1945, the last drive got under way, into the 

Po valley. Before the end of the month Bologna, Venice, Milan, Turin, and Genoa were all in Allied hands. With their backs to the 

Alps and their lines of communication to Germany practically cut, the Germans in Italy capitulated on May 2, leaving 160,000 captives in Allied hands. 

Allied Victories in Russia

The grim defense of Stalingrad, Moscow, and Leningrad actually turned out to be the sea wall which broke the German tidal wave. 

While the United States and Great Britain were unable to aid Russia by starting operations on a western front until 1944, the United States did pour an unending supply of Lend-Lease goods into the Soviet Union through Murmansk and Persia. In the critical year of 1943, Russia received, largely from American sources, 7,000 planes, 4,000 tanks, 247,000 trucks, 160,000 tons of munitions, and 700,000 tons of aviation gasoline. An entire oil refinery and a tire factory were transferred to Russia. By the end of the war America had furnished

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

$11,000,000,000 of Lend-Lease supplies to assist the Soviet war effort.

With this help, but more especially by their own courage and selfsacrifice, the peoples of the Soviet Union were finally able not only to drive the Axis invaders from the U.S.S.R. but also to overrun completely Rumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, eastern Germany, and eastern

Austria. During the winter of 1942-1943, Rostov, Kharkov, and 

Kursk were recaptured. The next summer the Germans were pushed back to the Dnieper River. The Ukraine and the Crimea were liberated in the winter campaign of 1943-1944, and Minsk, Brest- Litovsk, and Lwow were regained. The line then rested again on the 

Vistula. In the autumn of 1944 the Baltic states were retaken; and Finland, Rumania, and Bulgaria were forced to surrender. 

The final drives against the crippled and demoralized German remnants came in the winter and spring of 1944 and 1945, when the Russian steamroller overwhelmed Warsaw, Vienna, and Berlin and ground to a halt along the Elbe, where on April 25 they encountered at Torgau the American First Army moving east from the Rhine.

Wings Over Land and Sea 

The Russians and the entire Allied world had been waiting anxiously for the opening of a western front against the Germans. Operation 

Overlord, as it was called, was approved by the Anglo-American Combined Chiefs of Staff in December, 1943, and General Eisenhower was appointed as the Allied Supreme Commander of the new theater of operations. But two great undertakings would have to precede the main show: (1) the defeat of the German submarines along the Atlantic sea lanes to Britain; and (2) the bombardment of Germany and northern France by Allied air forces.

The use of the convoy system with strong sea and air protection brought victory in the Battle of the Atlantic. The air contribution to that victory was especially important. Long-range patrol planes equipped with radar protected the convoys for hundreds of miles out from North America and the British Isles. In the mid-Atlantic, planes from "baby flat-tops" took over the fight against the submarine wolf-packs, sinking more than 200 U-boats in 1943. From December, 1941, to June, 1944, only ten Allied ships out of seven thousand were lost in Atlantic convoys. The number of American troops collected in Great Britain in preparation for Operation Overlord rose from 

15,000 in 1943 to 1,500,000 in 1944. With them came supplies and

I 

weapons until the compact islands seemed like one vast encampment and supply depot.

The second preparatory effort necessary before invasion was the crippling of Germany's industrial and military strength by aerial bombing and strafing. Hundreds of new airfields were constructed in crowded Britain, and the number of American planes alone was increased from 2,000 to 9,500. The R.A.F. carried out pattern bombing by night; the American Eighth Air Force did precision bombing by day. During 1944 the use of radar made precision bombing possible at night and in cloudy weather also. Shuttle bombing between 

England, North Africa, Italy, and the Ukraine gave greater range. 

As a result of Allied operations, nearly every German industrial city was partly destroyed. Plane factories, ball-bearing shops, hydroelectric dams, and railroads were the principal targets. By March, 1944, Germany's fighter plane production had been cut by two-thirds. As 

D-Day approached, the raids rose to a devastating crescendo: 118,000 tons of bombs were dropped in May, 1944; 1,200 German planes were destroyed as compared with 700 Allied planes. 

From Normandy to the Elbe 

The zero hour of D-Day was 2:00 A.M. of June 6, 1944; the place was along the Normandy beaches between Le Havre and Cherbourg. 

Air bombardments, naval shelling, the dropping of three parachute divisions, the landing of six infantry divisions, the unloading of endless weapons and supplies, the shuttling back and forth across the Channel of clouds of planes and whole fleets of ships - such were the activities of the greatest amphibious assault against a continent in all history. Against defensive obstacles and increasing German resistance the Allies established a firm beachhead. Cherbourg was captured and most of the Cotentin Peninsula overrun by June 27; Caen was taken by the British on July 19. Then began the attempt to crack the German lines and fan out across France. Saint Lô fell on July 18 and 

Coutances on July 28. Through this gap American tanks began to pour west into Brittany and southeast toward the Loire River. In the latter push General Patton's tanks of the Third Army swept with amazing speed around the rear of the Germans, who were holding out against the British at Caen. A hundred thousand prisoners were taken in this Falaise Pocket by August 18. A week later Paris was recaptured, and the German armies, in confused retreat, were being pursued east of the Seine.

As the trap was being sprung at Falaise, the American and French

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

troops made new landings east of Toulon in southern France. Here, with the collaboration of the French Maquis, rapid progress was made. Toulon, Marseilles, Grenoble, the Rhone valley, and finally 

Lyons fell to the advancing Allies. By September 11, 1944, these forces of the American Seventh Army made contact with the American Third Army of the northern sector and both turned eastward toward the Rhine.

Although the Allied armies had cleared France, Luxemburg, and Belgium of the Germans, they were held up during the winter of 1944-1945 by the weather, the Siegfried Line, and Germany's reorganized forces. Indeed, for a month and a half (December 16 to January 31) the Germans made a strong counteroffensive in the Battle of the Bulge. This counteroffensive was a line plunge into the Belgian 

Ardennes with Antwerp as the goal. The Germans, however, never reached the Meuse River, to say nothing of Antwerp. The Americans and British stood firmly on the north side of the Bulge, the American 101st Airborne Division held to Bastogne in the interior of the Bulge, and elements of the Third Army drove in from the south and helped to grind off the salient entirely, causing the Germans a loss of 220,000 men.

While the Russians were moving into Germany along the Oder River in February, 1945, the western Allies began their drive to the Rhine. The American First Army crossed the famous river on an unblown bridge at Remagen on March 7, and before the month was out other Allied armies had made five more Rhine crossings. By now the German armies were thoroughly disorganized and depleted, their supplies were gone, their cities had been destroyed, their government was in flight to Denmark, and their Führer was apparently a suicide. It did not take long for the Allied forces to engulf the great industrial area of the Ruhr and sweep over Germany and Austria all the way to the Danube and even beyond the Elbe. On April 25 the 

Americans made a junction with the Russians at Torgau, and two weeks later (May 7) the German government signed an unconditional surrender of its land, air, and naval forces. After having issued the necessary surrender orders, the German government was itself dissolved. Thenceforth, all Germany and all aspects of German life came under the rule of Allied authorities. Victory in Burma The Japanese occupation of Burma was not only a threat to India but also a barrier to Allied supplies for China. Consequently, Allied forces, consisting of American, British, Indian, and Chinese troops,

late in 1943 began drives from east and west on the Japanese in North Burma in order to make possible the opening of a road north to China. At the same time Chinese troops and Merrill's American 

Marauders moved southeast down the Hukawng valley. By January, 1945, a road link to China, named the Stilwell Road in honor of the American general who had contributed so much to the success of the project, could be opened. Mandalay in central Burma and Rangoon to the south fell to the Allies in the spring. 

The Burma campaign was unique in the unbelievable miracles performed in hot and humid jungles by men of many Allied nationalities working in coöperation with the United States Air Transport Command, the United States Military Railway Service, the United States Engineer and Supply services, and British and American parachute guerrillas. As much as 46,000 tons of supplies per month were flown by air over the Himalaya Hump to China; the Stilwell Road and a parallel oil pipe line were built by the Engineers almost as rapidly as the territory was taken; and supplies and troops were flown and dropped into many parts of an otherwise impenetrable jungle country.

Allied Conquest of the Pacific 

The production of war materials and supplies in the United States so exceeded the schedule of the Allied planners that it was possible to begin powerful offensives in the Pacific long before the end of the European campaigns. Having stopped the Japanese expansion in 1942 by the victories of the Coral Sea and Midway, the Allied forces under the commands of General MacArthur and Admiral Nimitz undertook the conquest of the Japanese-held Pacific areas by three main lines of offensive penetration: (1) from New Guinea northwestward to the Philippines, (2) from Guadalcanal northwestward to the Palau Islands, and (3) from the central Pacific westward to Okinawa. 

East of New Guinea in the Solomon Islands the United States Marines landed on Guadalcanal (August, 1942). Along with severe combats on the island, there occurred between August and December, 1942, five major naval engagements as the Japanese and the Allies each tried to interrupt the other's supplies and reënforcements. These were the battles of Savo Island, the Eastern Solomons, Cape Esperance, Santa Cruz Islands, and Lunga Point. Only the first was a Japanese victory. With strong naval and air support American Marines and New Zealand troops took New Georgia and Bougainville in 1943, and in 1944 American forces occupied the Palau Islands 1,600 miles to the northwest and only 800 miles from the Philippines.

I 

In the meantime steady progress had been made in the New Guinea area by American and Australian forces. After checking the Japanese at Milnes Bay in the extreme southeast corner of New Guinea, the Allied ground, sea, and air forces joined in beating out a corridor to right and left along the eastern coast of the island. Buna, Salamaua, Lae, and Finschafen, on the New Guinea coast, and the Trobriand Islands and western New Britain Island to the east were all taken in 1943. During the next year Aitape, Hollandia, Arara, and Sansapar were all seized along the north coast of New Guinea, while off the coast the Admiralty Islands, Wakde, Biak, and Morotai (far to the west) were captured.

At this point the Americans were only 400 miles from the Philippines, which therefore were eagerly chosen as the next objective. 

Two army corps with strong naval support struck at Leyte Island in the very center of the archipelago in October, 1944. There followed immediately the famous and decisive naval battles of the Philippine Sea, in which the Japanese committed the major portion of their remaining warships, sixty in all. Within three days, by October 27,

Japanese sea power had been completely broken. About twenty Japanese ships were sunk and thirty-four were severely damaged. The 

Americans lost only six ships. After this smashing victory the Americans proceeded to take over the rest of the Philippines. Luzon was invaded at the Lingayen Gulf in January, 1945, and most of the other islands were retaken by June. During the summer of 1945 the 

Australians captured Tarakan, Brunei, and Balikpapan in Borneo.

While this successful progress was being made from New Guinea to the Philippines, other American forces further north in the central Pacific under the command of Admiral Nimitz were taking over important stepping stones to Japan itself. Starting in the Gilbert 

Islands with the capture of Tarawa and Makin in November, 1943, they proceeded in 1944 to take Kwajalein, Majuro, and Eniwetok in the Marshalls and Saipan, Tinian, and Guam in the Marianas. Early in 1945 these American forces established themselves within 350 miles of the Japanese homeland by the capture of Iwo Jima in the Volcanic Islands and Okinawa in the Ryukyus. Here the fighting was particularly bitter because of the Japanese death stands in the mountain caves and the suicide (kamikaze) plane attacks on the American ships. 

Capitulation of Japan 

With Saipan, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa in American hands, the Japanese at home began to writhe beneath the mass bombings from ever increasing air raids flown from these islands. Thirty thousand sorties

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

of B-29 Superfortresses dropped over 200,000 tons of bombs on Jarese industrial and maritime cities. Large areas of the cities were cerdotely destroyed and industry was hampered. The population is made to suffer further by the tightening Allied blockade. 

Finally, what was perhaps the greatest sensation in history occurred. 

One bomb was dropped on Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) which detroyed the entire city. This single bomb had the destructive power 

20,000 tons of T.N.T. or the loads of 2,000 Superfortresses. The orld learned that this was an atom bomb, whose explosive force was caused by the chain reaction of atomic fission. In the race for this superweapon of total war the Americans with British aid had won. 

Japan now feared the complete annihilation of every urban center. 

Three days later a second atom bomb was dropped on Nagasaki. 

At the same time Russia declared war on Japan and began to invade 

Manchuria, Korea, and southern Sakhalin. 

The Japanese now could not negotiate peace fast enough for fear of further atomic destruction. They agreed to unconditional surrender on August 14, 1945, with the promise that Emperor Hirohito, their Son of Heaven, would obey the orders of the Supreme Allied mmander, General MacArthur. The voice of the Japanese Emperor was broadcast by radio for the first time as he commanded the aying down of arms, the grounding of planes, and the silencing of naval guns. Thus the vast Japanese forces in China and their bypassed troops in the Pacific islands were subdued almost in a day by a new scientific weapon.

Total War and Its New Weapons 

Every major war usually brings with it considerable innovation in methods and weapons. In World War II such changes were vast and revolutionary. While World War I had been largely a trench war of position with the gain of a few miles being headline news, World War II was a war of rapid movement and envelopment on wheels and tank tracks and wings. An advance of fifty miles a day elicited little surprise. Infantry was motorized or even airborne; cavalry was replaced by swift heavy tanks armed with 105 mm guns or flamethrowers; heavy artillery was often self-propelled; and engineers leveled hills into airfields with powerful bulldozers. On several occasions whole nations fell within a few days beneath the wheels of mechanized war.

Planes had been used in small numbers and for limited purposes in World War I. In this latest war aircraft performed a great variety

I 

of services: bombing, strafing, fighting, pursuing, reconnoitering, submarine chasing, ship torpedoing, and transport. Army transport planes dropped whole divisions of parachute troops from the air. 

Carrier planes and the aircraft carrier ships became the most important units of navies. Some of the more significant designs of aircraft were the British Spitfire fighter, the American B-29 (Superfortress) longrange bomber, and the German jet-propelled fighter.

In previous wars land and sea fighting had been generally independent of one another. In World War II land, sea, and air power combined in tornadoes of amphibious invasions. In this amphibious warfare the LST transport ships, with a ramp lowered from the prow, became so important that whole campaigns were planned according to their availability. Along with the LST were also smaller craft: 

LCI's (landing craft infantry), LCT's (landing craft tanks), and 

DUKW's (amphibious trucks) which played essential roles in beachhead fighting and Pacific island hopping.

The three most famous inventions of the war were radar, robot bombs, and atom bombs. Radar sends out high frequency radio wave impulses and receives them back as rebounds or echoes on a radar scope. By this means radar indicates the nature and location of distant objects. The war uses of radar were numerous. It detected hostile submarines, ships, and planes; it directed the firing of antiaircraft guns; it made possible accurate hits on distant enemy ships at night before the ships were aware of their adversary's presence; it made accurate night bombing possible; it directed guided missiles to their targets; and it helped Allied planes to land in foggy weather. 

Radar was an Anglo-American invention.

The robot bomb, a German invention, was used in 1944 in an effort to terrorize the British and Americans into accepting a negotiated peace. This was actually a jet-propelled robot plane loaded with a ton of high explosive and guided to its target by a magnetic compass. Although one-fourth of the robot bombs launched found their 

London target, causing many deaths and renewed destruction, most of them were destroyed by prompt countermeasures using combined radar detection, antiaircraft fire, and aircraft pursuit. The last German hope turned out to be wasted effort. 

The atomic bomb completely eclipsed radar and the robot bomb in effectiveness and long-range significance, for it was not only infinitely more destructive but it also ushered in an entirely new era. 

Knowledge of the potential energy to be derived from the splitting of the atom antedated the war. In 1939, however, the first successful

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

experiments took place which indicated possibilities of explosive energy releases by chain reaction. Fearing that Germany might invent the atom bomb first, the British and Americans pooled their scientific knowledge and invested $2,000,000,000 in plants and equipment in the United States. Final success was not attained until after Germany's defeat, but Japan was brought to her knees by two atom bombs. The postwar world, however, stands on the threshold of an era either of great advance through the peacetime use of controlled atomic energy or of sure self-destruction if war cannot be outlawed by some new world authority.

Fifty years ago, Admiral Mahan had argued in The Influence of 

Sea Power on History that dominant sea power determined victory in world struggles.¹ While the great maritime powers of America and 

Britain did win World War II, still a new theory is beginning to emerge. Modern mechanized warfare waged with atomic weapons, tanks, planes, guns, and ships cannot be won except by a highly industrialized state possessing great scientific skill. Modern war has become total war carried on with a total weapon by and against civilians and combatants alike. Total peace or total destruction are now the only alternatives.

But the last war was waged not only against civilians; it was waged by them against the occupying Axis powers. Guerrilla bands harassed the enemy troops behind the lines, furnished channels for the transmission of military information to the Allies, aided Allied airmen and prisoners of war to escape to the Allied lines, and committed acts of sabotage where they would do the most harm to the Axis and to their puppet regimes. This activity was greatly facilitated by the use of the radio and by the parachuting of men and supplies. In the vast areas of eastern China, the jungles and hills of the Philippines, the marshes of western Russia, the forests of conquered Poland, the fiords of Norway, the cities and lowlands of Belgium and Holland, the mountains of Yugoslavia and Greece, the valleys and foothills of northern Italy, as well as over the whole expanse of France men and women of all faiths and political groups fought and died together in the grim and dangerous service of the 

Partisan underground.

The more active the underground became, the more ruthless and barbarous became the Axis methods of repression. The Partisans when caught were tortured and then executed. Whole towns and areas, which had been suspected of harboring guerrillas, were wiped 1 See page 661.

I 

out such as Lidice in Czechoslovakia, Oradour-sur-Glane in France, and the Vercors area in the French Alps. In addition to these sporadic acts of vengeance the Germans carried out a cold-blooded policy of extermination, the "genocide" of entire peoples, especially of Poles and Jews. Hundreds of thousands were herded into barren areas and left to freeze and starve. Other hundreds of thousands were crowded into concentration camps where they were worked until they died of exhaustion, or were experimented upon by medical fiends until they succumbed, or were executed en masse in gas chambers. When the Allied forces captured such horror camps as Dachau and Buchenwald, they found, nearby, piles of naked corpses of victims literally wasted to skin and bones and within the huts other skeletons of those near death, lying prone upon the tiers of bunks. Many of the perpetrators of these crimes were later apprehended, tried, and executed, either by the Allied court at Nuremberg or by the national courts in the various victim nations. But the punishment of these few can never atone for the mass suffering and death they caused nor cure the ills of mankind which underlie these reversions to savagery. 

The Cost of World War II 

One can hardly grasp the astronomical statistics which measure the cost of World War II. For the United States alone World War I cost a sum of $41,000,000,000. World War II, however, cost the United 

States $341,000,000,000. Significant of the impoverishment of America is the fact that it will require the equivalent of two full years of our total national income ($160,000,000,000) to pay for our own war expenses. The monetary cost of World War II for the entire world was $1,117,000,000,000. The cost in dead and wounded is more tragic. The killed and injured equaled the combined populations of New England, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Michigan.
