CHAPTER 54 The Postwar World 

N contrast to the end of World War I there was little exultation and optimism when peace came in August, 1945. The peoples of the world had been disillusioned by the failure of the League of Nations and they were sobered by the almost insurmountable chaos of physical exhaustion and destruction which they now faced. Western Europe, which had been the vital center and leader of a world culture, was rapidly declining. In its place was arising the leadership of two rival world powers, the democratic and capitalist United States and the totalitarian and communist Soviet Union. The nature and success of the peace settlement depended on whether these two powers chose the path of power politics or of world federation. At first these leading nations and the other countries of the world seemed to attempt to follow both paths simultaneously. 

THE UNITED NATIONS 

The hope of world federation was no longer the old League of Nations, which was abolished officially in 1946. Instead, after a preliminary period of enunciating principles and holding meetings, the anti-Axis nations established an entirely new world organization called the United Nations.

The Four Freedoms and The Atlantic Charter 

Eleven months before the United States entered the war (January, 1941), President Roosevelt proclaimed the "four freedoms," which became the ideals of the later United Nations: freedom of expression, freedom of worship, freedom from want, freedom from fear. In 

August, 1941, he and Churchill met on a warship in the Atlantic and drew up the Atlantic Charter, which proclaimed eight principles as the foundation for the postwar settlement: 

1. No territorial or other aggrandizement by the United States or 

Great Britain. 

2. Popular self-determination for territorial changes.

3. Popular self-determination for new governments. 

4. Access for all to world trade and raw materials. 

5. World collaboration for economic and social security. 

6. Security against aggression and war. 

7. Freedom of the seas. 

8. Immediate disarmament of aggresive nations and eventual disarmament of all nations.

On January 1, 1942, the anti-Axis countries took the title of the "United Nations," a name chosen by President Roosevelt, and pledged their solidarity until peace should be made. In the Declaration of Washington the United Nations subscribed to the principles of the four freedoms and the Atlantic Charter. 

Conference Stepping Stones 

A conference of the "Big Four" of the United Nations (China,

Great Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union) in Moscow in October, 1943, agreed to establish in the near future an international organization based on the sovereign equality of states and devoted to the maintenance of world peace. At a Big Four conference in 1944 at 

Dumbarton Oaks, near Washington, a draft charter for a United Nations organization was prepared. At the Yalta Conference in February, 1945, the United States, Soviet Russia, and Great Britain agreed to support the principle that in the voting procedure of the future United Nations organization each of the great powers should have the power of veto. Finally all fifty members of the United Nations met in a conference at San Francisco from April to June, 1945, and adopted after heated debate the final version of the Charter of the 

United Nations.

The United Nations Organization The purposes of the postwar United Nations Organization are: 

(1) to settle international disputes by peaceful means, (2) to take effective collective measures against aggression, (3) to assist in solving international economic, social, and cultural problems, (4) to promote respect for the fundamental human freedoms and the selfdetermination of peoples without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion. The main parts of the Organization are the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Secretariat, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, and the International Court of Justice.¹ 

1 Other subordinate or associated organizatons are the Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (U.N.È.S.C.O.), the Food and Agricultural

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The General Assembly, consisting of representatives from every member state, meets at least once a year. Each member has one vote, and a two-thirds majority is required on important matters. In matters relating to the maintenance of world peace the Assembly is limited to making recommendations (to the Security Council or to individual members), and even these recommendations must be restricted to subjects not under consideration by the Security Council. 

In addition, the Assembly approves the budget, admits new members, and elects the nonpermanent members of the Security Council and of the Trusteeship Council as well as the judges of the International Court of Justice (in this case with the concurrence of the Security Council). It also receives and approves reports from its subordinate organizations.

The Security Council, which remains in continuous session, has eleven members: five permanent members (the United States, the 

Soviet Union, Great Britain, France, and China) and six nonpermanent members, three being chosen each year for a two-year term. 

Every decision on nonprocedural matters must have a majority of seven including the favorable vote of all the permanent members the significant veto arrangement. The Security Council has the responsibility for taking "prompt and effective action . . . for the maintenance of international peace and security." This action may be in the form of economic or military sanctions. All members as well as the Military Staff Committee and the Atomic Energy Commission are obliged to carry out the Council's decisions. 

The Secretariat, headed by the Secretary-General, is the adminis trative and executive branch of the Organization. The Secretary- 

General, Trygve Lie, acts as secretary for the sessions of the main branches of the organization, supervises arrangements for meetings, directs the Secretariat staff, keeps the records, and provides for U.N. publications and correspondence. He may, on his own authority, bring to the attention of the Security Council any matter which may threaten world peace.

The Social and Economic Council consists of eighteen members, six chosen each year for a three-year term. Its decisions are by simple majority vote and may deal with recommendations or pro- 

Organization (F.A.O.), the International Labor Organization (I.L.O.), the International Trade Organization (I.T.O.), the International Civil Aviation Or ganization (I.C.A.O.), the Atomic Energy Commission, the Military Staff 

Committee, the International Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the

World Health Organization, and the International Refuge Organization (I.R.O.).

posed draft treaties on social and economic matters. It may also establish and supervise subordinate organizations to assist in these matters. 

The Trusteeship Council is composed of the permanent members of the Security Council, any other states administering trust territories, and enough other states, with three-year terms, to make the number of nontrustee members equal to the trustee members. Its decisions are by simple majority. The Trusteeship Council is designed to provide international supervision of the government and administration of territories taken from former enemies in World War I and World War II and of other territories voluntarily placed under the trust system. Strategic trust areas come under the supervision of the Security Council. 

The International Court of Justice, which replaced the old World Court, is composed of fifteen judges, five elected every three years for a nine-year term. The Court has a president, a vice-president, and a registrar and holds its sessions at The Hague. The Court is directed to render judicial decisions in all cases submitted to it by states. Member states may voluntarily accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court in all disputes involving treaties, international law, international obligations, and reparations for breaches of the first three. 

The United Nations Charter may be amended by a two-thirds vote of all the members in the General Assembly plus a favorable nonprocedural vote in the Security Council.

The United Nations Charter is in some respects an improvement on the old Covenant of the League of Nations: 

1. It is not included in the peace treaties imposed on the vanquished. 

2. All the great powers are members. 

3. Human rights are guaranteed. 

4. The Security Council remains in continuous session. 

5. The Secretary-General may submit disputes to the Security Council. 

6. War is not legally recognized. 

7. Definite national forces are to be earmarked as U.N. police forces. 

8. A Military Staff Committee will exist to direct these forces. 

9. The League unanimity rule in voting has been replaced by various systems of majority decisions. 

In other very important respects, however, the United Nations suffers from serious weaknesses. Like the League, the United Nations has no sovereign authority, and its Secretariat is a mere service organiza-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

tion and not an authoritative executive. The United Nations is an organization of sovereign states. But sovereign states, retaining their basic freedom of action by their very nature, cannot always be relied on to observe their obligations, to agree on interpretations of their obligations, or to furnish the forces or funds as required. The United Nations may not enforce its decisions upon individuals within a state, but only upon the states themselves. Yet punitive action against a powerful sovereign state is well-nigh impossible. Inconsistent with the Charter, which states that the United Nations Organization is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of states, are the clauses which provide that only 20 per cent of the United Nations membership shall have seats in the Security Council and that only five of the fifty-five members shall have the veto power. 

It is the veto clause (Article 27, Paragraph 3) which may effectively paralyze the United Nations when attempting to enforce peace, which is its main purpose. By this article all nonprocedural decisions of the Security Council must be approved by all five permanent members. But by faulty phraseology it requires a permanent member to abstain from voting when the question involves the pacific settlement of a dispute to which it is a party. Thus by removing one of the votes of permanent members when all are required, this clause presumably makes impossible the peaceful settlement in the Security Council of any dispute involving a great power. 

The greatest threat to world peace obviously comes from a possible aggression by a great power. Yet the veto clause gives each of the five great powers the right to veto military or economic sanctions aimed at itself. To expect any great power to vote for punitive action against itself is unreasonable. Punitive action even against a small state is unlikely, since most of these are closely associated with one of the great powers who can use the veto in favor of its protégé. Russia vetoed a decision against her satellite, Albania, in 1947. These features are unquestionably a retrogression from the League provisions, since the League could and did take action against both large and small nations. Well-wishers of the United Nations are therefore among the first to realize the need for fundamental changes in its Charter if it is to become an unchallenged authority in keeping the peace during future world crises. 

Early Problems of the United Nations 

The important branches of the United Nations Organization were established at London in January and February, 1946, and New York City was finally chosen as its permanent location in 1947. Al-

most immediately the Security Council and the Assembly were forced to deal with serious questions and near crises. 

Russian intervention in northern Iran was quickly brought up as a development dangerous to world peace. After many heated debates and Russian abstention from the sessions dealing with Iran, the question was solved by negotiation between Russia and Iran at the suggestion of the United Nations. The Russian forces later withdrew from Iran. In response to Russia's and France's demands for action against Franco's regime in Spain, the United Nations decided late in 1946 to have its members withdraw their ambassadors and ministers from Madrid. Some did not comply, while others continued diplomatic relations through chargés d'affaires. 

A much more serious conflict was still going on in 1947 between the United States and Russia over disarmament and the atom bomb. 

Russia insisted that disarmament of the atom bomb be taken up along with the question of disarmament as a whole, that the atom bomb be outlawed and its stockpile destroyed before arrangements should be made for future disarmament inspection and enforcement, and finally that all punitive action for the enforcement of atomic and other disarmament be decided in each instance by the Security Council, where the veto could block such punitive measures. On the other hand, the United States, which possessed the secret of the atom bomb and was supposed to have a stockpile of bombs, was determined that atomic disarmament should be dealt with before and separately from general disarmament and that the bombs should not be destroyed nor the secret revealed until secure inspection and enforcement machinery had been firmly established. The United States also insisted that enforcement should be carried out by a commission separate from the Security Council whose punitive action should be prompt and automatic after the establishment of the facts of violation and unhampered by any power of veto. Disarmament in respect to other weapons could then be handled in somewhat the same manner. The United States would also put all atomic production for peaceful uses under the control and auspices of the United Nations. 

Since this would involve outside interference in a phase of her industrial life, Soviet Russia seemed opposed at that time to any such extension of the activities of the United Nations.

An accusation by Greece that Albania, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria were aiding and abetting guerrilla revolts in northern Greece led to the dispatch of a United Nations investigating commission to the troubled area in 1947. Great Britain likewise brought before the

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

Security Council accusations against Albania, claiming that mines laid by Albania in the Corfu Channel had been responsible for damage to British ships and the loss of British lives. Although the Security 

Council voted seven to two that Albania must have had knowledge of the laying of the mines, even if she were not actually responsible for doing so, Russia vetoed the resolution put forward against Albania and effectively blocked the majority of seven (Great Britain abstaining) in the Security Council. This was the tenth time Russia had used her veto power. Up to that point the United States had used it once to counter a Russian veto of the admission of certain states to the United Nations.

OCCUPATION GOVERNMENTS AND PEACE SETTLEMENTS 

At the Casablanca Conference in January, 1943, Roosevelt and

Churchill had decided on the invasion of Sicily in the hope of knocking the weakest Axis power, Italy, out of the war. This objective raised the important question of the terms that were to be imposed on each Axis state as it sued for peace. At the same conference, therefore, the decision was made that the war would be continued until each enemy state made an unconditional surrender. This type of capitulation was thought necessary in order to enable the Allies to destroy completely the Fascist and Nazi regimes and their military power. 

Peace with Italy

Almost according to plan, Italy capitulated three weeks after the Sicily campaign, on September 8, 1943. The Long Terms of Armistice, signed on September 29, provided for unconditional surrender of all her armed forces and gave the Allies the right to establish their government over such parts of Italy as they might think necessary. 

This implied that the Allies might not rule over all of Italy, for Mussolini had already been dismissed and Marshal Badoglio's new government seemed favorable to the Allies. Indeed, in October Italy declared war on Germany and became a "cobelligerent" of the Allies. 

Thereafter the Allies became more lenient in the methods of applying the Long Terms. While the forces of Italy as a cobelligerent remained under the Supreme Allied Commander, the relationship was more one of liaison than of direct command of a surrendered army. 

Likewise, the Allies adopted a new policy on military government. 

The areas near the fighting front remained under temporary Allied government; the areas farther back came under the Italian govern-

ment, which coördinated policies with an Allied commission. As the front moved northward, more territory came under Italian jurisdiction. Political parties developed with Allied permission, and their representatives formed a provisional advisory assembly to guide a coalition cabinet. It was this regime which, in 1944, compelled the provisional retirement of Victor Emmanuel III because of his acquiescence in Mussolini's regime and the appointment of his son, Prince 

Humbert, as Lieutenant General of the Realm.

During the remainder of the war, Italy suffered heavy damages from the fighting on her soil and was further weakened by a revived Fascist government under Mussolini on the German side of the line. Yet the Italian army, navy, and guerrilla Partisans contributed a great deal to the Allied cause. In the midst of Allied victories in April, 1945, Mussolini was caught and shot by the Partisans.

In June, 1946, the first national elections, with woman suffrage, were held to choose a Constituent Assembly. This assembly was to draw up a new constitution and by referendum to determine the popular choice as between a monarchy and a republic. Before the voting 

Victor Emmanuel III, in the interest of the monarchist cause, abdicated in favor of his son, who became Humbert II. But the referendum by a two-million majority favored a republic. Thereupon 

Humbert also abdicated and followed his father into exile. The elections for the Constituent Assembly gave a plurality of seats to the Christian Democratic (Catholic) Party and more than a hundred seats each to the Socialist and Communist parties. These three groups then formed a coalition cabinet under de Gasperi and elected de 

Nicola as President of the new Republic of Italy. The Constituent 

Assembly acts as the Italian legislature until a new constitution is adopted.

In the meantime the Allies were negotiating among themselves, not with Italy, over the final peace terms to be imposed on Italy because of her earlier participation in the Axis aggressions. The main debates were over possession of Trieste and over reparations. Both Italy and 

Yugoslavia demanded Trieste. Russia, Yugoslavia, and Greece demanded heavy reparations for the suffering caused to them by Italy. 

The United States and Great Britain, on the other hand, opposed heavy reparations because they might disturb Italy's economy to such an extent that communism would gain the upper hand and because financial aid given to Italy by the United States would become indirect American reparations to Russia.

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

The final terms of the peace treaty with Italy (January, 1947) provided that: 

1. Trieste should become a Free Territory under the United Nations. 

2. Istria and a wide strip of territory on Italy's eastern border should go to Yugoslavia. 

3. Five small border rectifications in favor of France should be made on the western border of Italy. 

4. All Italian colonies should be surrendered and later distributed by the Allies. 

5. Italy's armed forces should be restricted to an army of 185,000 men, an air force of 350 planes, and a navy of two battleships, four cruisers, and four destroyers. 

6. Italy was to pay $365,000,000 as reparations. Of this, Soviet 

Russia was to receive $100,000,000, while Yugoslavia, Greece, Ethiopia, and Albania were to share the remainder. 

Peace Terms for Axis Satellites 

At the same time peace treaties were concluded for Bulgaria, Rumania, Hungary, and Finland. While Bulgaria lost and gained no territory, she had to pay $70,000,000 in reparations and have a reduced army of 55,000 men and a navy of 7,250 tons. Rumania lost 

Bessarabia to Russia, but regained Transylvania from Hungary. She was required to pay $300,000,000 in reparations and reduce her army to 120,000, her air force to 150 fighter planes, and her navy to 15,000 tons. Hungary lost Transylvania to Rumania, Ruthenia to Russia, and a small border area to Czechoslovakia. She had to pay $300,000,000 in reparations and reduce her forces to 65,000 men and 90 planes. 

Finland, to the north, relinquished Viipuri and Petsamo to Russia and granted Russia a fifty-year lease of a naval base near Helsinki. She was to pay $300,000,000 in reparations and restrict her forces to 34,400 men, 60 fighter planes, and a navy of 10,000 tons. 

Occupation of Germany

In spite of the unconditional surrender resolve of Casablanca in 1943, Germany was the only major Axis country whose surrender was absolutely unconditional.¹ Germany's capitulation was unique in the annals of the states system in that she was the only major power 1 Italy's unconditional surrender was mitigated by Allied acceptance of her status as a cobelligerent, and Japan's surrender later was accompanied by Allied agreement to the retention of her emperor.

to have had her state sovereignty and government completely obliterated by military defeat. After the Allied armies had entirely overrun her territory, they divided it into four zones of occupation. 

The Russian Zone comprised all of eastern and central Germany including the Thuringian states and Saxony. The British Zone consisted of northwestern Germany with the Ruhr and the northern

Rhineland. The American Zone in south Germany comprised Bavaria, northern Württemberg and Baden, Frankfort, Hesse, Nassau, and the 

Bremen enclave. The French received the southwestern territories of southern Württemberg, Baden, and Rhineland including Coblenz. 

The Russians turned over Silesia, Pomerania, and south and west Prussia to Polish administration with the intention of obtaining Allied acquiescence to eventual Polish annexation. Berlin itself was divided into four separate Allied zones and became the seat of the Allied Control Council for Germany, which determined uniform policies for all four zones.

The Allied Control Council and the separate Allied administrations in the four zones carried out for two years (1945-1947) the difficult tasks involved in relocation of displaced persons and return of prisoners of war; furnishing food, clothing, houses, and fuel to the civilian population; trial and punishment of war criminals; denazification of 

German administration, education, and business; demilitarization of 

German industry; the exaction of reparations, especially by the dismantling and transfer of industrial plants; the restoration of German democracy in local and state (Land) politics; and the revival of German peacetime economic life. The Allied problem of economic reconstruction was made extremely difficult because of several factors: (1) the material ruin and spiritual demoralization in Germany caused by the war; (2) Allied disagreements as to the treatment of Germany; and (3) Allied economic difficulties at home, a serious obstacle to extending vitally needed economic assistance to Germany. Even so, German economic dislocation was so great that America and Britain had to send large quantities of food and fuel to their zones in Germany. 

Finally, in 1946, with the disagreements between the four occupying powers concerning the economic reunion of all Germany still unresolved, Britain and America formed an economic unit of their two zones.

Gradually the Allies permitted democratic political activities to be resumed in Germany: first the organization of non-Nazi political parties, and later, local and state (Land) elections. As the elected regimes were established, the Allies began to shift more of the govern-

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

mental and administrative responsibilities onto the Germans, retaining only supervisory control. The principal parties which emerged from these elections were the Christian Democratic (moderate) Party with a plurality in the American Zone, the Social Democratic (socialist) Party with a plurality in the British Zone and Berlin, and the Socialist Unity (communist) Party with a plurality in the Soviet Zone. It is interesting to note that the pluralities tended to reflect the political complexions of the occupying powers. The new state constitutions in the American Zone reflected federative, democratic, and socialistic tendencies.

As the powers assembled in Moscow in March, 1947, to write the peace treaty for Germany, they had to find agreement on the solution of the following questions: the establishment of the German- 

Polish boundary, the possible cession of the Saar to France, the eventual control of the Ruhr, the dissolution of Prussia, the establishment of a federal or centralized government in Germany, a $20,000,000,000 reparation charge against Germany, demilitarization of German industry, and a possible four-power alliance to prevent the revival of 

German militarism. 

Occupation of Austria

Having opposed Hitler's forceful annexation of Austria, the victorious Allies insisted on her separation from Germany. An occupation system similar to that in Germany was established for Austria. 

The Russians occupied the east, the British the south, the Americans the north and center, and the French the west. Vienna, like Berlin, was divided into four districts, one for each ally; and uniform policies for the four zones were provided by an Allied Control Council for Austria.

After an initial delay the Allied powers recognized the provisional government of Austria under Dr. Karl Renner, who proclaimed the restoration of the republican federal constitution of 1920. In the elections of November, 1945, the Austrian Peoples (conservative) Party won a majority of the seats in the National Assembly. The Socialist 

Party formed a large minority group, while the Communists showed very little strength. Dr. Renner was elected president, and Dr. Leopold Figl became chancellor.

As the four great powers attempted to draw up the final peace terms for Austria at the Moscow Conference of 1947, they had to face the questions of Austria's southern boundary, the method of distinguishing between genuine Germany property and Austrian property con-

fiscated by the Nazis, and international control of the Danube. They had already decided to exempt Austria from reparation payments. 

Occupation of Japan

By her surrender Japan lost all her territory gained since 1895: the 

East Indies, the Marshall, Mariana, and Caroline islands, Formosa, Japanese-occupied China, Manchuria, Korea, southern Sakhalin, and the Kurile Islands. While Emperor Hirohito was allowed to retain the throne, he was required to submit to the absolute authority of the 

Supreme Allied Commander, General Douglas MacArthur. Accord ing to the Potsdam Declaration made just before Japan's surrender, Japan was to institute a genuine democratic regime. When the Allies should be satisfied with the democratic regime and when Japan should have agreed to the Allied peace terms, the military occupation might cease. Although the occupation duties were assigned to American military personnel, General MacArthur had the status of an Allied commander, and an Allied advisory commission for Japan made recommendations concerning Allied policy.

Under the Allied occupation Japan was completely disarmed and demilitarized. In the elections of 1946 three principal parties appeared. 

Strongest was the party of the right, the Liberals. The Progressives and the more radical Social Democrats were also numerous in the lower house, but the Communists gained only five seats out of the 466 of the House of Representatives. Both men and women over twenty years of age were allowed to vote. A draft constitution, approved by the Supreme Allied Commander, was revised and ratified by the newly elected Diet and promulgated by Emperor Hirohito. It went into effect in May, 1947. This constitution made war and the existence of Japanese armed forces illegal; proclaimed popular sovereignty and made the emperor a figure-head ruler; provided for equality and civil liberties; and established a supreme bicameral legislature with a House of Councillors and a House of Representatives. 

Up to the middle of 1947 no peace terms had been prepared for Japan, and the Allied occupation was still in effect. 

ALLIED COUNTRIES SINCE I The British Empire 

Many serious problems faced the British as they transformed their country from an armed camp to a land of normal peacetime activities. Two months after Germany's surrender (July, 1945) Churchill

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

called for new parliamentary elections. Although he was held in high esteem as a war leader, the people of Britain disliked the program of his Conservative Party and gave a large majority to the Labor Party (363 seats to 189). Clement Attlee became the new Labor prime minister with a program of nationalization of mines, railroads, canals, and trucking; extension of the social security measures; and continuance of the austerity program of restricted purchases in order to decrease imports in relation to exports. A great effort was made to put 

British industries into full peacetime production and to recapture the prewar world markets. Great Britain borrowed $3,750,000,000 from the United States to aid in her recovery efforts, but progress was still very slow. Coal production slumped for want of sufficient miners, and an extremely severe winter (1946-1947), which almost completely paralyzed transportation and manufacturing for over a week, caused additional serious dislocations. 

Faced with these financial and economic difficulties Great Britain had to diminish her world commitments drastically. Plans were made for withdrawal from Burma, India, and Egypt. The Palestine mandate, along with the perennial quarrel between Jews and Arabs in Palestine, was referred to the United Nations. Finally, the commitment to aid the postwar government of Greece was laid on the doorstep of the United States.

The Fourth French Republic 

After the liberation of France in 1944 a Provisional Government was established in Paris with General Charles de Gaulle as President of the Council. In October, 1945, two months after the surrender of 

Japan, the first national election occurred to choose a Constituent Assembly for the preparation of a new constitution and interim legislation. This was the first national election in which French women exercised the suffrage. The results revealed the existence of three main parties: the Communists with 148 seats, the Catholic moderate 

M.R.P. (Popular Republican Movement) with 141 seats, and the Socialists with 134 seats. Felix Gouin, a Socialist, was chosen President- Premier.

The constitution drawn up by this Constituent Assembly was rejected in May, 1946, by a majority of over a million votes in a national referendum. The following month an election of a second 

Constituent Assembly was held in which the M.R.P. received a plurality, with the Communists second and the Socialists third. This time 

Georges Bidault of the M.R.P. became President-Premier. By October

a new constitution proclaiming the Fourth French Republic was completed and accepted by popular referendum. This Constitution of 1946 provided for a two-house legislature consisting of the National Assembly and a Council of the Republic. The National Assembly is elected directly for a term of five years by the voters from geographical districts. All laws are passed by the National Assembly. 

The Council of the Republic is also elected partly by geographical districts, partly by the municipal and departmental councils. 

The Council of the Republic can only delay or suggest changes in bills submitted by the National Assembly. An Economic Council was established to give advice on matters of national economic legislation.

The executive branch is made up of the President of the Republic, a Council of Ministers, or Cabinet, and the President of the Council of Ministers, or Premier. The President of the Republic is elected by the two houses of Parliament for a term of seven years and is allowed a maximum of two terms. The Cabinet and the Premier are chosen by the President with the approval of the National Assembly. The 

Cabinet must resign if it receives a vote of censure or lack of confidence in the National Assembly. After the first eighteen months of particular National Assembly, if there have been two votes of censure or lack of confidence within any eighteen-month period, the Cabinet may decide on the dissolution of the National Assembly and the holding of new elections. This feature is an attempt to reduce the number of cabinet changes in comparison with those of the Third

Republic. 

France is joined with her overseas possessions in a French Union which has advisory governmental machinery of its own: the president of the Union, who is also the president of France, the Union High Council, and the Union Assembly. These two bodies contain representatives from France, the Associated States, and overseas territories. All colonial legislation may be considered but does not necessarily have to be approved by the Union Assembly. 

The first election of the French National Assembly (November, 

1946) resulted in a Communist victory with 186 seats to 162 for the 

M.R.P. and 108 for the Socialists. Because of the conflict between the

Communist Party and the M.R.P. the executive positions went to the intermediate Socialist Party. Vincent Auriol, Socialist, was elected president in January, 1947, and Paul Ramadier, Socialist, was chosen premier of a coalition cabinet composed of members of all three parties. The Communists, the largest party, held only four places in

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

a cabinet of twenty-six men: those of vice premier, minister of national defense, minister of labor, and minister of reconstruction. 

The problems with which the successive French regimes had to cope between 1945 and 1947 had to do in large part with the revival of industry and trade. To this end the coal mines, important nationwide industries, banks, and public utilities were nationalized. Léon 

Blum, veteran statesman of the Socialist Party, made two important contributions to French recovery. He negotiated a large loan with the United States, and he fought deflation at home by instituting a drive to reduce prices by 10 per cent. But two serious handicaps in 

1947 interfered with French efforts at recovery: insufficient shipments of coal from Germany and an uprising in Indo-China. 

The Soviet Union 

The principal postwar problems of the Soviet Union were the reconstruction of her destroyed cities and industries and the restoration of her farm lands to normal productivity. These were attacked in the typical Soviet fashion of a five-year plan beginning in February, 1946. Two other efforts in this reconstruction program were the transfer of industrial equipment from her neighboring enemy states, especially from Germany, to the Soviet Union and the use of 

890,000 German prisoners of war as reparation labor.

In order to reduce government expenses and obtain more laborers for reconstruction and production it is estimated that the Soviet armed forces were reduced from about 20,000,000 men to 6,000,000 by 1946. In line with similar changes in other large countries, the three separate Soviet fighting forces were united under the People's Commissariat of the Armed Forces in 1946. In 1947 Stalin resigned as commissar of the armed forces and limited himself to the post of premier. In June, 1946, President Kalinin died, and Nikolai M. 

Shvernik was chosen to succeed him. 

The United States of America 

While nearly all the European countries were trying to solve their postwar problems by choosing socialist or labor governments, retaining government controls over the national economy, and nationalizing key industries, the United States attempted to return to the system of capitalist free enterprise as soon as possible. Although the United 

States did not suffer from war destruction at home, she did share in the economic dislocation of the rest of the world. Two-thirds of the 

U.N.R.R.A. relief supplies of food and other necessities (amounting

to $2,700,000,000 in 1945-1946) were furnished by the United States to war-torn countries. These contributions and postwar economic dislocations created a scarcity of food, manufactured goods, and building materials and a natural tendency toward higher prices. To check this trend toward a higher cost of living the Truman administration at first tried to retain wartime price controls through the

Office of Price Administration (O.P.A.), which had successfully prevented a very appreciable rise in prices during the war. 

Two factors militated against the success of a postwar O.P.A.: a wave of strikes and a widespread desire to remove wartime controls. 

There were three general causes for the wave of postwar strikes: (1) the limited rise in prices during the war without a commensurate rise in hourly wage rates, (2) the reduction of take-home pay with the elimination of much overtime work, (3) a desire to bargain collectively when the manufacturers were eager to produce rapidly for the starved postwar market. As strikes were won and wage costs rose, business interests insisted on the lifting of price controls. Congress vacillated, removing most controls by June, 1946, and restoring them again in August. But this hesitancy tended to make producers and merchants hoard goods with the hope of an early end of the O.P.A., which only made it more difficult to keep prices in line. This trend came to a dramatic climax in 1946 when the livestock producers withheld their animals from the market while awaiting higher prices and brought on a veritable national meat famine. In the face of this crisis and under pressure from business interests, which assured the government that prices would soon decline after price restrictions were lifted, President Truman abolished the O.P.A., retaining, however, its sugar controls and rent ceilings. The immediate results were the opposite from those promised: prices rose 20 per cent above those at the time of the abolition of the O.P.A., and food and houses were almost as scarce as before because of these exorbitant prices. Another wave of strikes was threatened to match higher prices with higher wages, and thus the upward spiral of inflation was in full swing. 

In politics the American trend was away from the social reforms of the New Deal Democrats and toward the government hands-off policy of the Republicans. In November, 1946, the public, irritated by the wave of strikes and still convinced that the O.P.A. had caused rather than prevented the postwar scarcities, voted for large 

Republican majorities in both houses of Congress.

The new Congress began work under a revised organization provided by the La Follette Law of 1946, which streamlined procedures

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

and reduced the number of standing committees. It soon took up the consideration of restrictive legislation against labor unions, passed a constitutional amendment limiting the presidency to two terms,¹ and took steps to reduce taxes and government expenditures. 

President Truman's administration also tended to shift away from the New Deal toward the more conservative views of the November voters. The Cabinet changes over a year's period gradually replaced 

New Dealers with more conservative choices: Snyder in the Treasury, Krug in the Interior, Harriman in Commerce, and Schwellenbach in Labor. 

China Since the War

After the defeat of Japan, China became the great power of the Far East and one of the five great powers of the United Nations. But 

China's position in the world was weakened by the destruction and dislocation caused by the war against Japan and by the outbreak of civil war between the National government of Chiang Kai-shek and the Communist government in northern China.

Both Chinese regimes were totalitarian. The National government, which returned to its capital at Nanking, was the instrument of the Kuomintang Party and tended to preserve the economic status quo of large landholders and extortionate moneylenders. It had been the 

Kuomintang plan to set up a democratic regime after the war. Its regime, however, was honeycombed with corruption and weakened by association with the black market and scandalous administration generally.

The Communist government, with its capital at Yenan, was under the complete control of the Communist Party. Its purpose was to socialize the Chinese economy but to do this by democratic means. 

In the meantime it confiscated private wealth in its area and divided up the great landed estates for the benefit of the small farmers. There was much less corruption than among the Nationalists, but also much less with which to practice corruption. The Communists made greater progress in popular education but also showed a tendency to pervert the new literacy by distorted propaganda. 

Since both Chinese factions were patriotic and nominally devoted to essential democracy, a serious attempt was made by the United States to bring the two groups together. When Patrick Hurley returned to the United States in 1945 with charges that American State Department officials were preventing a reconciliation, President Tru- 1 This still needs the ratification of three-fourths of the states.

man sent General George C. Marshall with a specific mission to bring about an agreement between the two groups. At the same time American forces, which had been sent to China to help disarm and repatriate the surrendered Japanese troops, remained there. It was suspected that this was in order to counter possible Soviet aid to the Communist faction. In spite of American refusal to lend money to China unless a reconciliation were effected and General Marshall's impartial efforts for over a year to bring about an agreement between the two sides, all negotiations failed. General Marshall finally left in 1947, publishing a report condemning both sides for their stubbornness and mutual suspicions and commending the democratic elements of Nationalist China and the liberal elements of the Communist group. Warfare therefore continued, with the Nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek making some limited gains at the expense of the Communists, including the capture of their capital of Yenan. American Marines and other forces were gradually withdrawn in 1947. 

In the meantime the Chinese Kuomintang Party had joined with the Democratic Party in drawing up a new constitution for postwar China. The Communists had no part in this. The new document, issued in 1946 and to be put into effect in December, 1947, provided for a very modern and advanced form of democratic government. 

It is a combination of the American federal and presidential system and the European cabinet system. The president of China is elected for a term of six years by the National Assembly and may serve for only two terms. He is commander in chief of the armed forces and can conduct all phases of foreign relations subject to the review of the Legislative Yuan. He chooses the premier or head of the Executive Yuan with the consent of the president of the Legislative Yuan. 

The premier and his Executive Yuan, or cabinet, are subject to the control of the Legislative Yuan. All laws promulgated by the president must have the approval of the Legislative Yuan and the countersignature of the premier.

A National Assembly, elected every six years by all men and women twenty years of age and over, was to choose not only the president but also the vice-president and eventually to share in initiating legislation and in holding referenda. In all there are five other yuans which have more frequent sessions than the National Assembly. The appointive Executive Yuan or cabinet and the elective 

Legislative Yuan, which makes the laws and by a two-thirds vote may dismiss the Executive Yuan, have already been mentioned. The 

Control Yuan or upper house, elected by the provincial assemblies,

WESTERN CIVILIZATION 

censors, impeaches officials, and causes reconsideration of legislative and administrative acts. Finally, there are the Judicial Yuan or supreme court and the Examination Yuan or civil service commission. 

Personal liberties are affirmed by the constitution but may be suspended in emergencies, occasions which are all too vaguely defined. 

The constitution also allows a delegation of national sovereignty on a reciprocal basis for the strengthening of a world authority for the preservation of peace. The success of this constitution as well as the prosperity of China in the future depends a great deal on the solution of her innumerable postwar economic and administrative problems and her ability to bring together the two contending sides in the civil war.
